title: Accrued Expenses: Paying Later for What Has Already Been Received
snippet: The theory of accrued expenses from the accrual basis to disclosure, worked through PHE's operating accruals and set beside the industries where accruals drive the numbers
content:
In brief

  • An accrued expense is a liability for goods or services already received that the entity has not yet paid, been invoiced for, or formally agreed with the supplier. It sits between a trade payable, where the invoice fixes the amount and date, and a provision, where timing or amount is genuinely uncertain.

  • Accruals exist because of the accrual basis. An expense belongs to the period in which the entity consumed the goods or services, so at every cut-off date the entity records what it received but has not yet been billed for, and next period the invoice replaces the estimate.

  • Most accruals are mechanical: interest by the day, wages by the day worked, rig and vessel hire by the day rate, utilities by the meter. Some need estimates (bonuses, unbilled contractor work), but the uncertainty is small. When it stops being small, the item belongs to PSAK 237 as a provision.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report accrued expenses of 1,897,743 at 31 December 2024 against 2,060,218 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 6.2 percent of total assets and 30.8 percent of current liabilities (6.7 and 34.2 percent a year earlier). It is PHE's largest current liability, larger than trade payables (1,091,822) and the current portion of long-term bank loans (1,551,034).

After reading it a student should be able to say when an accrual is needed and how much to record, write the adjusting and reversing entries, tell an accrual from a payable and a provision, and read an accruals note.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What an accrued expense is

An accrued expense is a liability, so it must meet the Conceptual Framework's definition: a present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. For an accrual the past event is receiving goods or services. Once a contractor's crew has worked a day on a platform, the entity owes for that day whether or not anyone has sent a bill.

The lecture notes for this chapter (Inter 2, Ch 13, following Kieso) define current liabilities by three traits: they arise from past events, they fall due within a year, and settling them takes an outflow of cash or other resources. Accrued expenses are the clearest case of all three.

PSAK 237 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) gives the definition that separates accruals from their two neighbours (para. 11). Trade payables are liabilities for goods or services received that have been invoiced or formally agreed with the supplier. Accruals are liabilities for goods or services received that have not yet been paid, invoiced or formally agreed, including amounts due to employees such as accrued holiday pay. Estimating an accrual is sometimes necessary, "but the uncertainty is generally much less than for provisions".

Take PHE's 2024 balance sheet as the starting point for the three-way split.

The Trade payables and Decommissioning provision essays cover the outer columns.

Accrued expenses are current. PSAK 201 (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) treats trade payables and accruals for employee and other operating costs as part of the working capital used in the normal operating cycle, so they are current even if some are settled after twelve months (para. 70).

2. Why accruals exist: the accrual basis and cut-off

PSAK 201 requires financial statements, except cash flow information, to be prepared on the accrual basis (paras. 27–28). Under it an expense is recognised when the entity consumes the resource, not when cash leaves. A cash basis records the expense when paid. The two give different profits whenever service and payment fall in different periods.

The point at which one period ends and the next begins is the cut-off. Every receipt of goods or services must land on the right side of it. The accrual is the entry that pulls a December service into December when its invoice will only arrive in January.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary hires a well-intervention vessel for a routine workover, a repair that keeps an existing well producing, at a day rate of 150. The vessel works from 20 to 31 December 2024, twelve days. The owner invoices on 15 January 2025 and is paid on 14 February 2025.

Service received in 2024 = 12 days × 150 = 1,800

Cash basis

Accrual basis

Expense in 2024

0

1,800

Liability at 31 Dec 2024

none

accrued expenses 1,800

Expense in 2025

1,800

0

On the cash basis 2024 profit is overstated by 1,800 and 2025 profit understated by the same amount. The total over two years is the same; the timing is wrong in both years.

Kieso explains adjusting entries through matching. The December oil is recognised as December revenue, so the cost of keeping the well running belongs there too. Under PSAK an item must still meet the definition of a liability, but for accruals the two tests agree.

3. Recognition and measurement

When. An accrual is recognised when the goods or services are received, which means when the entity obtains control of the goods or when the supplier performs the service. Kieso's goods-in-transit rule from the inventory chapter applies to the liability side too. Goods bought FOB shipping point are owed for once they are handed to the carrier, so a purchase at sea on 31 December is both inventory and a liability, and if the invoice has not arrived it is an accrual.

How much. Most accruals need no estimate, only arithmetic. A contract fixes a rate, and records show the quantity received.

Accrued expense = contracted rate × quantity received in the period − amounts already invoiced or paid

The quantity comes from the ordinary paperwork of an operation, namely day-rate logs and daily drilling reports for rigs and vessels, timesheets for crews, meter readings for power and fuel, and goods received notes (GRN) for materials. Purchasing systems use a three-way match, in which the purchase order sets the price, the GRN proves receipt and the invoice confirms the amount. When the GRN is posted before the invoice arrives, the system books the difference to a "goods received not invoiced" account, which is an accrual by another name.

Measurement basis. Most accruals to suppliers and lenders are financial liabilities under PSAK 109 Financial Instruments (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9). They are measured at fair value on initial recognition and at amortised cost afterwards, but because they are settled within weeks, discounting changes nothing material and the undiscounted contract amount is used. PHE states this directly. Accruals are carried at "notional amounts", which approximate fair value (Note 3g(ii), Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63). Accruals to employees follow PSAK 219 Employee Benefits (formerly PSAK 24, IAS 19), which measures short-term benefits undiscounted (para. 11). Amounts owed to the government under statute, such as withheld income tax, are not contractual and so are not financial liabilities at all.

4. Typical accruals

Interest. Interest accrues by the day, but is paid on fixed dates that rarely match the reporting date. The notes illustrate this with a 12 percent note payable whose interest is accrued at each reporting date. For example (illustration), a subsidiary has a term loan of 500,000 at 6 percent a year, with interest paid semi-annually on 30 April and 31 October.

Interest accrued 1 November to 31 December = 500,000 × 6% × 2/12 = 5,000

Interest paid 30 April 2025 = 500,000 × 6% × 6/12 = 15,000, of which 5,000 belongs to 2024 and 10,000 to 2025

31 Dec 2024: Dr Interest expense 5,000 / Cr Interest payable 5,000

30 Apr 2025: Dr Interest payable 5,000, Dr Interest expense 10,000 / Cr Cash 15,000

Under the effective interest method the expense also includes amortised transaction costs; the Bank loans essay covers that. PHE's policy records accrued interest "separately from the associated borrowings within the current liabilities section" (Note 3g(ii), Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63), without saying which line holds it.

Salaries and wages. Pay periods rarely end on 31 December. For example (illustration), a field crew earns 500 a week for Monday to Friday and is paid each Friday. 31 December 2024 is a Tuesday, so two days of the week have been worked and not paid.

Accrued wages = 500 × 2/5 = 200

On payday the employer withholds amounts the employee owes to others. The notes show this with income tax, union dues and BPJS, Indonesia's social security contributions. Suppose (illustration) income tax article 21 is withheld at, say, 5 percent, and the employee's BPJS Ketenagakerjaan old-age (JHT) contribution at 2 percent of the week's gross pay.

Withholding tax = 500 × 5% = 25; BPJS = 500 × 2% = 10; net pay = 500 − 25 − 10 = 465

31 Dec 2024: Dr Salaries and wages expense 200 / Cr Salaries and wages payable 200

3 Jan 2025: Dr Salaries and wages payable 200, Dr Salaries and wages expense 300 / Cr Withholding tax payable 25, Cr BPJS payable 10, Cr Cash 465

The 25 and 10 are now owed to the tax office and BPJS. The employer's own BPJS contributions, which Kieso treats as payroll taxes, are accrued the same way, as an expense with a liability until paid. The Other taxes payable essay follows the withholding tax from there.

Paid absences and bonuses. Amounts owed to employees are accruals in the PSAK 237 sense, and PSAK 219 itself calls the short-term liability an accrued expense (para. 11(a)). Paid absences and bonuses follow their own recognition rules in PSAK 219, which the Employee benefits essay teaches. PHE carries them on a separate line, Short-term employee benefits, 409,225 of employee incentives at the end of 2024 (Note 25a, Daftar 5/119, PDF p. 136).

Utilities and operating services. The December power bill arrives in January, so the cost is accrued from the meter reading. The same logic covers most of an upstream operation, where production expenses alone were 4,647,647 in 2024, about 12,700 a day. Rigs, vessels, helicopters, catering, well services and seismic crews work through December and invoice weeks later. Section 8 shows that this kind of accrual makes up almost all of PHE's line.

5. Adjusting and reversing entries

The accrual is an adjusting entry, made at the reporting date to bring the books onto the accrual basis. When the invoice arrives next period, the liability must move off accrued expenses and the expense must not be counted twice. Kieso gives two ways of doing it.

Return to the vessel. Suppose the January invoice comes in at 1,850, not 1,800, because the contract adds a fuel surcharge based on the fuel actually burned, which the owner reports only with the invoice; the subsidiary had estimated it at nil.

Without reversing entry

With reversing entry

31 Dec 2024, adjust

Dr Production expenses 1,800 / Cr Accrued expenses 1,800

Dr Production expenses 1,800 / Cr Accrued expenses 1,800

1 Jan 2025, reverse

no entry

Dr Accrued expenses 1,800 / Cr Production expenses 1,800

15 Jan 2025, invoice

Dr Accrued expenses 1,800, Dr Production expenses 50 / Cr Trade payables 1,850

Dr Production expenses 1,850 / Cr Trade payables 1,850

14 Feb 2025, pay

Dr Trade payables 1,850 / Cr Cash 1,850

Dr Trade payables 1,850 / Cr Cash 1,850

2025 expense with reversal = −1,800 + 1,850 = 50, the same as without

The results are identical. The reversing entry lets the payables clerk post every invoice the same way without checking which ones were accrued; without it each invoice must be matched to its accrual.

An accrual begins as an estimate, becomes a trade payable when the invoice fixes the amount, and leaves when cash is paid. An entity with a long invoice lag carries more on accrued expenses and less on trade payables, with no difference in what it owes.

6. Estimates, errors and the provision boundary

Invoices after year end. The invoice arrived on 15 January, before the statements were authorised on 28 March 2025 (Note 1c, Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25). Under PSAK 210 Events after the Reporting Period (formerly PSAK 8, IAS 10) it is an adjusting event, because it gives evidence about a condition at the reporting date, the service received in December, so a material difference must be booked in 2024. Closing teams do this by truing up accruals for invoices received during the closing period; an immaterial difference such as this 50 is commonly left to fall into 2025, as in the table. Information that arrives after authorisation is a change in estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8), recognised in the period of the revision without restatement. A surcharge that was in the contract all along and simply missed would be an error, not an estimate.

Cut-off errors. A missed accrual behaves like the inventory error in the Inventories essay. Suppose (illustration) the vessel's 1,800 had not been accrued at all and the invoice was expensed in 2025.

2024: expense understated 1,800, profit overstated 1,800, liabilities understated 1,800

2025: expense overstated 1,800, profit understated 1,800, balance sheet correct

The error reverses over two years, but both years are misstated. If material and found after the 2024 statements were issued, it is corrected retrospectively under PSAK 208 by restating the comparatives. Auditors therefore search for unrecorded liabilities by tracing payments and invoices received after year end back to the period of service.

When an accrual becomes a provision. The definition draws the line at the degree of uncertainty, not at the existence of an estimate. For example (illustration), the vessel owner claims an extra 600 of standby charges for weather days in December, which the subsidiary disputes under the contract.

The Decommissioning provision essay teaches the PSAK 237 rules for the second column.

7. Accrued expenses across industries

Banks. For a bank the main accrual is interest owed to depositors. A time deposit's interest builds up daily and is paid at maturity or monthly. For example (illustration), a customer places 10,000 for three months at 5 percent a year on 1 December, with interest at maturity, using an actual/365 day count.

Interest accrued to 31 December = 10,000 × 5% × 31/365 = 42.47

Dr Interest expense 42.47 / Cr Interest payable 42.47

Indonesian banks commonly show it as "bunga yang masih harus dibayar", next to the deposits on which it accrues.

Islamic banks. A mudharabah depositor is entitled to a share of profit, not to interest, and the deposits themselves are temporary syirkah funds (dana syirkah temporer), presented outside liabilities. The liability is the share of profit allocated to depositors and not yet paid, shown as profit sharing not yet distributed, under PSAK 405 Mudharabah (formerly PSAK 105).

Construction and service contracts. When revenue is recognised over time using costs incurred as the measure of progress (an input method under PSAK 115, formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15), a missed cost accrual understates revenue as well as cost. For example (illustration), a contract priced at 10,000 has total estimated cost of 8,000. By year end the subcontractor has been invoiced for 3,000, and has done a further 1,000 of work not yet invoiced.

Without the accrual: progress = 3,000 / 8,000 = 37.5%; revenue = 10,000 × 37.5% = 3,750

With the accrual: progress = 4,000 / 8,000 = 50.0%; revenue = 10,000 × 50.0% = 5,000

Margin is 750 in the first case (3,750 − 3,000) and 1,000 in the second (5,000 − 4,000). The cut-off failure moves revenue as well as cost, so in contract businesses accruals carry far more weight than their balance suggests.

Utilities and telecom. Power distributors and telecom operators accrue purchased power or interconnection charges from meter and traffic data before the counterparty's monthly statement arrives.

Joint operations. In oil and gas, mining and infrastructure consortia, the operator incurs costs and bills the partners through a joint interest billing (JIB) statement, usually in the following month. Under PSAK 111 Joint Arrangements (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11) a joint operator recognises its share of the liabilities incurred jointly (para. 20), so a non-operator must accrue its share of costs incurred by the operator in December even before the JIB arrives. Section 9 shows how PHE divides these between lines.

Change in total = −162,475 / 2,060,218 = −7.9%; operations +5.4%; overlifting gas −95.2%

The line is almost entirely the operating accruals of section 4. The fall in the total comes from overlifting gas (section 9); underneath it the operating accruals rose 5.4 percent.

PHE's policy treats accrued expenses as financial liabilities at amortised cost, carried at notional amounts (Note 3g(ii), Daftar 5/44 and 5/46, PDF pp. 61, 63), and states that their carrying amount approximates fair value because of their short-term nature (Note 23). The full 1,897,743 appears among the financial liabilities in Note 47 (Daftar 5/222, PDF p. 239).

Overlifting is not a cost received from a supplier, so the ratios below use the operating accruals alone. Billed amounts owed to operators sit in other payables (429,695 and 300,799, Note 21), so they join trade payables on the billed side.

Operating accruals / (trade payables + operations payables) = 1,854,008 / (1,091,822 + 429,695) = 1.22 (2024); 1,759,435 / (883,688 + 300,799) = 1.49 (2023)

A ratio above 1 means more of what PHE owes for goods and services sits unbilled than billed, which fits services performed daily in the field and billed through monthly cycles.

Cash operating costs = production 4,647,647 + exploration 465,422 + general and administrative 906,779 + other operations 867,866 − dry holes 156,746 = 6,730,968 (2024); 6,061,012 − 100,703 = 5,960,309 (2023)

Days of accrued costs = 1,854,008 / 6,730,968 × 365 = 100.5 days (2024); 1,759,435 / 5,960,309 × 365 = 107.7 days (2023)

Dry holes (Note 36, Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166) are removed because they are write-offs, not cash costs. The days figure still overstates the true lag, because part of the operating accruals is likely capital spending on wells and facilities, which goes to oil and gas properties and never passes through these expense lines. PHE does not split the accruals between operating and capital spending, so the ratio shows direction only. The unbilled lag shortened by about seven days in 2024. Most of the 162,475 fall in the whole line came from overlifting, which fell by 225,828.

Note 48 on foreign-currency monetary items lists rupiah "accrued expenses and other provision" of Rp6,611,848 million, equal to 409,225 (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242), and 290,571 for 2023. Both figures equal the employee incentives in Note 25a, so the row appears to be that line under a loose label. Note 48 does not list Note 23, and the FS do not show how much of the 1,897,743 is in rupiah.

PHE's deferred tax note labels bonus balances both ways, "accrued expense for bonus" (deferred tax asset of 4,479) and "provision for bonus and incentives" (2,738 among the assets and 14,897 among the liabilities), so labels in the notes do not settle the PSAK 237 classification (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172).

9. Upstream note: overlifting and joint-operation billings

Overlifting. In a production sharing contract (PSC) each party is entitled to a share of production, but physical liftings come in cargoes and pipeline nominations that rarely match each party's entitlement at year end. PHE's policy says that lifting above the final entitlement creates a liability (overlifting) and lifting below it a receivable (underlifting). Gas volumes are valued at the price in the gas sales agreement and crude at the annual weighted average price. Because these adjustments "are not transactions with customers", they are recorded in direct cost of sales, not in revenue (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). For example (illustration), a subsidiary's final 2024 gas entitlement is 1,000 thousand MMBTU, it lifted and sold 1,030 thousand MMBTU, and the gas sales agreement price is USD 6 per MMBTU.

Overlifting = (1,030 − 1,000) thousand MMBTU × USD 6 = 180

Dr Cost of revenue, overlifting adjustment 180 / Cr Accrued expenses, overlifting gas 180

Revenue stays at the 1,030 sold, and the cost line carries the obligation to give back the excess. It is an accrual because the volume and price are fixed by records and contract, and only the timing of settlement is left open. PHE shows overlifting due to the Government in another line, Due to the Government, within a combined "Overlifting & DMO" item of 51,427 (Note 20, Daftar 5/114, PDF p. 131), and the matching underlifting receivable from SKK Migas in Due from the Government (Note 9, Daftar 5/97, PDF p. 114). Note 23 does not name the counterparty of its 11,322. Reading it as amounts owed to PSC partners or buyers is an inference. The Due from the Government essay covers the government side.

Billed and unbilled. Note 21 explains that payables from oil and gas operations are classified as other payables because they come from the proportional share of the JIB statements that operators send to PHE's non-operating subsidiaries (Daftar 5/115, PDF p. 132). If PHE's non-operated interests follow the usual sequence, a cost the operator incurs in December would sit in accrued expenses until the JIB arrives, then in other payables (429,695 at the end of 2024), and be settled against cash calls already advanced (cash call advances of 76,196, an asset; Note 15, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123) or by a top-up payment (amounts under cash calls of 28,933, Note 21). Note 23 does not confirm the first step.

10. Related lines

  • trade-payables: where an accrual goes once the invoice arrives.

  • other-payables: holds the JIB-based payables to operators.

  • short-term-employee-benefits: PHE's separate line for amounts owed to employees.

  • due-to-government-current: overlifting and DMO owed to the Government.

  • due-from-government: the underlifting receivable on the other side.

  • decommissioning-site-restoration-provision: the provision side of the boundary.

  • production-expenses: where most operating accruals are charged.

  • deferred-tax-assets: Note 43e's bonus balances.

Least-confident assertions

  • That the operating accruals of 1,854,008 are mainly costs incurred and not yet invoiced, including the non-operators' share before the JIB arrives, is read from the PSAK 237.11 definition and Note 21. Note 23 gives no further breakdown, and it may also contain capital spending and amounts that are partly estimated.

  • The counterparty of the 11,322 overlifting gas accrual is not stated. PHE also lists all of Note 23 as financial liabilities in Note 47; any overlifting settled by delivering gas rather than cash would not meet the definition of a financial liability, so that classification may be loose. Note 47 also places accrued expenses in an "other financial liabilities" column, while Note 3g(ii) describes them as measured at amortised cost.

  • Note 48's rupiah "accrued expenses and other provision" equals the employee incentives of Note 25a in both years. This page reads it as that line under a loose label, not as information about Note 23.

  • PHE labels bonus balances in Note 43e both as accruals and as provisions. The page treats this as labelling, not as evidence of how PHE classifies them on the balance sheet.

  • The JIB-to-cash-call sequence in section 9 is the usual industry practice, applied to PHE by inference from Notes 15 and 21.

  • The days-of-accrued-costs ratio uses a balance that probably includes capital accruals over an expense base without them; only the direction of change is meaningful.

  • The Islamic banking paragraph (PSAK 405 profit sharing, temporary syirkah funds) is from knowledge and was not checked against the text.

Accruals are liabilities for goods or services received that have not yet been paid, invoiced or formally agreed, including amounts due to employees such as accrued holiday pay. Estimating an accrual is sometimes necessary, "but the uncertainty is generally much less than for provisions".
Take PHE's 2024 balance sheet as the starting point for the three-way split.
not required (the obligating event can be a law or a past action)
contract rate × quantity received, sometimes estimated
best estimate of an uncertain outflow
when the invoice arrives and is paid, usually weeks
The Trade payables and Decommissioning provision essays cover the outer columns.

Accrued expenses are current. PSAK 201 (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) treats trade payables and accruals for employee and other operating costs as part of the working capital used in the normal operating cycle, so they are current even if some are settled after twelve months (para. 70).
2. Why accruals exist: the accrual basis and cut-off

PSAK 201 requires financial statements, except cash flow information, to be prepared on the accrual basis (paras. 27–28). Under it an expense is recognised when the entity consumes the resource, not when cash leaves. A
records the expense when paid. The two give different profits whenever service and payment fall in different periods.
The point at which one period ends and the next begins is the
. Every receipt of goods or services must land on the right side of it. The accrual is the entry that pulls a December service into December when its invoice will only arrive in January.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary hires a well-intervention vessel for a routine workover, a repair that keeps an existing well producing, at a day rate of 150. The vessel works from 20 to 31 December 2024, twelve days. The owner invoices on 15 January 2025 and is paid on 14 February 2025.
On the cash basis 2024 profit is overstated by 1,800 and 2025 profit understated by the same amount. The total over two years is the same; the timing is wrong in both years.

. The December oil is recognised as December revenue, so the cost of keeping the well running belongs there too. Under PSAK an item must still meet the definition of a liability, but for accruals the two tests agree.

An accrual is recognised when the goods or services are received, which means when the entity obtains control of the goods or when the supplier performs the service. Kieso's goods-in-transit rule from the inventory chapter applies to the liability side too. Goods bought FOB shipping point are owed for once they are handed to the carrier, so a purchase at sea on 31 December is both inventory and a liability, and if the invoice has not arrived it is an accrual.
Most accruals need no estimate, only arithmetic. A contract fixes a rate, and records show the quantity received.
Accrued expense = contracted rate × quantity received in the period − amounts already invoiced or paid

The quantity comes from the ordinary paperwork of an operation, namely day-rate logs and daily drilling reports for rigs and vessels, timesheets for crews, meter readings for power and fuel, and goods received notes (GRN) for materials. Purchasing systems use a

, in which the purchase order sets the price, the GRN proves receipt and the invoice confirms the amount. When the GRN is posted before the invoice arrives, the system books the difference to a "goods received not invoiced" account, which is an accrual by another name.
Most accruals to suppliers and lenders are financial liabilities under PSAK 109

(formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9). They are measured at fair value on initial recognition and at amortised cost afterwards, but because they are settled within weeks, discounting changes nothing material and the undiscounted contract amount is used. PHE states this directly. Accruals are carried at "notional amounts", which approximate fair value (Note 3g(ii), Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63). Accruals to employees follow PSAK 219

(formerly PSAK 24, IAS 19), which measures short-term benefits undiscounted (para. 11). Amounts owed to the government under statute, such as withheld income tax, are not contractual and so are not financial liabilities at all.

Interest accrues by the day, but is paid on fixed dates that rarely match the reporting date. The notes illustrate this with a 12 percent note payable whose interest is accrued at each reporting date. For example (illustration), a subsidiary has a term loan of 500,000 at 6 percent a year, with interest paid semi-annually on 30 April and 31 October.
Interest paid 30 April 2025 = 500,000 × 6% × 6/12 = 15,000, of which 5,000 belongs to 2024 and 10,000 to 2025
31 Dec 2024: Dr Interest expense 5,000 / Cr Interest payable 5,000
30 Apr 2025: Dr Interest payable 5,000, Dr Interest expense 10,000 / Cr Cash 15,000

Under the effective interest method the expense also includes amortised transaction costs; the Bank loans essay covers that. PHE's policy records accrued interest "separately from the associated borrowings within the current liabilities section" (Note 3g(ii), Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63), without saying which line holds it.

Pay periods rarely end on 31 December. For example (illustration), a field crew earns 500 a week for Monday to Friday and is paid each Friday. 31 December 2024 is a Tuesday, so two days of the week have been worked and not paid.

On payday the employer withholds amounts the employee owes to others. The notes show this with income tax, union dues and BPJS, Indonesia's social security contributions. Suppose (illustration) income tax article 21 is withheld at, say, 5 percent, and the employee's BPJS Ketenagakerjaan old-age (JHT) contribution at 2 percent of the week's gross pay.
31 Dec 2024: Dr Salaries and wages expense 200 / Cr Salaries and wages payable 200
3 Jan 2025: Dr Salaries and wages payable 200, Dr Salaries and wages expense 300 / Cr Withholding tax payable 25, Cr BPJS payable 10, Cr Cash 465

The 25 and 10 are now owed to the tax office and BPJS. The employer's own BPJS contributions, which Kieso treats as payroll taxes, are accrued the same way, as an expense with a liability until paid. The Other taxes payable essay follows the withholding tax from there.

Amounts owed to employees are accruals in the PSAK 237 sense, and PSAK 219 itself calls the short-term liability an accrued expense (para. 11(a)). Paid absences and bonuses follow their own recognition rules in PSAK 219, which the Employee benefits essay teaches. PHE carries them on a separate line, Short-term employee benefits, 409,225 of employee incentives at the end of 2024 (Note 25a, Daftar 5/119, PDF p. 136).

The December power bill arrives in January, so the cost is accrued from the meter reading. The same logic covers most of an upstream operation, where production expenses alone were 4,647,647 in 2024, about 12,700 a day. Rigs, vessels, helicopters, catering, well services and seismic crews work through December and invoice weeks later. Section 8 shows that this kind of accrual makes up almost all of PHE's line.

, made at the reporting date to bring the books onto the accrual basis. When the invoice arrives next period, the liability must move off accrued expenses and the expense must not be counted twice. Kieso gives two ways of doing it.

Return to the vessel. Suppose the January invoice comes in at 1,850, not 1,800, because the contract adds a fuel surcharge based on the fuel actually burned, which the owner reports only with the invoice; the subsidiary had estimated it at nil.
Dr Production expenses 1,800 / Cr Accrued expenses 1,800
Dr Production expenses 1,800 / Cr Accrued expenses 1,800
Dr Accrued expenses 1,800 / Cr Production expenses 1,800
Dr Accrued expenses 1,800, Dr Production expenses 50 / Cr Trade payables 1,850
Dr Production expenses 1,850 / Cr Trade payables 1,850
2025 expense with reversal = −1,800 + 1,850 = 50, the same as without

The results are identical. The reversing entry lets the payables clerk post every invoice the same way without checking which ones were accrued; without it each invoice must be matched to its accrual.

An accrual begins as an estimate, becomes a trade payable when the invoice fixes the amount, and leaves when cash is paid. An entity with a long invoice lag carries more on accrued expenses and less on trade payables, with no difference in what it owes.
6. Estimates, errors and the provision boundary
The invoice arrived on 15 January, before the statements were authorised on 28 March 2025 (Note 1c, Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25). Under PSAK 210

(formerly PSAK 8, IAS 10) it is an adjusting event, because it gives evidence about a condition at the reporting date, the service received in December, so a material difference must be booked in 2024. Closing teams do this by truing up accruals for invoices received during the closing period; an immaterial difference such as this 50 is commonly left to fall into 2025, as in the table. Information that arrives after authorisation is a change in estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8), recognised in the period of the revision without restatement. A surcharge that was in the contract all along and simply missed would be an error, not an estimate.
A missed accrual behaves like the inventory error in the Inventories essay. Suppose (illustration) the vessel's 1,800 had not been accrued at all and the invoice was expensed in 2025.
2024: expense understated 1,800, profit overstated 1,800, liabilities understated 1,800
2025: expense overstated 1,800, profit understated 1,800, balance sheet correct

The error reverses over two years, but both years are misstated. If material and found after the 2024 statements were issued, it is corrected retrospectively under PSAK 208 by restating the comparatives. Auditors therefore search for unrecorded liabilities by tracing payments and invoices received after year end back to the period of service.
When an accrual becomes a provision.

The definition draws the line at the degree of uncertainty, not at the existence of an estimate. For example (illustration), the vessel owner claims an extra 600 of standby charges for weather days in December, which the subsidiary disputes under the contract.
depends on the contract reading, perhaps on arbitration
provision if an outflow is probable and can be estimated; otherwise a contingent liability disclosed in the notes
The Decommissioning provision essay teaches the PSAK 237 rules for the second column.

For a bank the main accrual is interest owed to depositors. A time deposit's interest builds up daily and is paid at maturity or monthly. For example (illustration), a customer places 10,000 for three months at 5 percent a year on 1 December, with interest at maturity, using an actual/365 day count.
Dr Interest expense 42.47 / Cr Interest payable 42.47
Indonesian banks commonly show it as "bunga yang masih harus dibayar", next to the deposits on which it accrues.

A mudharabah depositor is entitled to a share of profit, not to interest, and the deposits themselves are temporary syirkah funds (dana syirkah temporer), presented outside liabilities. The liability is the share of profit allocated to depositors and not yet paid, shown as profit sharing not yet distributed, under PSAK 405

When revenue is recognised over time using costs incurred as the measure of progress (an input method under PSAK 115, formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15), a missed cost accrual understates revenue as well as cost. For example (illustration), a contract priced at 10,000 has total estimated cost of 8,000. By year end the subcontractor has been invoiced for 3,000, and has done a further 1,000 of work not yet invoiced.

Margin is 750 in the first case (3,750 − 3,000) and 1,000 in the second (5,000 − 4,000). The cut-off failure moves revenue as well as cost, so in contract businesses accruals carry far more weight than their balance suggests.
Power distributors and telecom operators accrue purchased power or interconnection charges from meter and traffic data before the counterparty's monthly statement arrives.
In oil and gas, mining and infrastructure consortia, the operator incurs costs and bills the partners through a joint interest billing (JIB) statement, usually in the following month. Under PSAK 111

(formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11) a joint operator recognises its share of the liabilities incurred jointly (para. 20), so a non-operator must accrue its share of costs incurred by the operator in December even before the JIB arrives. Section 9 shows how PHE divides these between lines.
Operating accruals make up 97.7 percent of the line at the end of 2024 (Note 23, Daftar 5/117, PDF p. 134).
Accrued expenses involving the subsidiaries' oil and gas operations
Change in total = −162,475 / 2,060,218 = −7.9%; operations +5.4%; overlifting gas −95.2%
The line is almost entirely the operating accruals of section 4. The fall in the total comes from overlifting gas (section 9); underneath it the operating accruals rose 5.4 percent.

PHE's policy treats accrued expenses as financial liabilities at amortised cost, carried at notional amounts (Note 3g(ii), Daftar 5/44 and 5/46, PDF pp. 61, 63), and states that their carrying amount approximates fair value because of their short-term nature (Note 23). The full 1,897,743 appears among the financial liabilities in Note 47 (Daftar 5/222, PDF p. 239).

Overlifting is not a cost received from a supplier, so the ratios below use the operating accruals alone. Billed amounts owed to operators sit in other payables (429,695 and 300,799, Note 21), so they join trade payables on the billed side.
A ratio above 1 means more of what PHE owes for goods and services sits unbilled than billed, which fits services performed daily in the field and billed through monthly cycles.

Cash operating costs = production 4,647,647 + exploration 465,422 + general and administrative 906,779 + other operations 867,866 − dry holes 156,746 = 6,730,968 (2024); 6,061,012 − 100,703 = 5,960,309 (2023)

Dry holes (Note 36, Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166) are removed because they are write-offs, not cash costs. The days figure still overstates the true lag, because part of the operating accruals is likely capital spending on wells and facilities, which goes to oil and gas properties and never passes through these expense lines. PHE does not split the accruals between operating and capital spending, so the ratio shows direction only. The unbilled lag shortened by about seven days in 2024. Most of the 162,475 fall in the whole line came from overlifting, which fell by 225,828.

Note 48 on foreign-currency monetary items lists rupiah "accrued expenses and other provision" of Rp6,611,848 million, equal to 409,225 (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242), and 290,571 for 2023. Both figures equal the employee incentives in Note 25a, so the row appears to be that line under a loose label. Note 48 does not list Note 23, and the FS do not show how much of the 1,897,743 is in rupiah.

PHE's deferred tax note labels bonus balances both ways, "accrued expense for bonus" (deferred tax asset of 4,479) and "provision for bonus and incentives" (2,738 among the assets and 14,897 among the liabilities), so labels in the notes do not settle the PSAK 237 classification (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172).
9. Upstream note: overlifting and joint-operation billings

In a production sharing contract (PSC) each party is entitled to a share of production, but physical liftings come in cargoes and pipeline nominations that rarely match each party's entitlement at year end. PHE's policy says that lifting above the final entitlement creates a liability (overlifting) and lifting below it a receivable (underlifting). Gas volumes are valued at the price in the gas sales agreement and crude at the annual weighted average price. Because these adjustments "are not transactions with customers", they are recorded in direct cost of sales, not in revenue (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). For example (illustration), a subsidiary's final 2024 gas entitlement is 1,000 thousand MMBTU, it lifted and sold 1,030 thousand MMBTU, and the gas sales agreement price is USD 6 per MMBTU.
Dr Cost of revenue, overlifting adjustment 180 / Cr Accrued expenses, overlifting gas 180

Revenue stays at the 1,030 sold, and the cost line carries the obligation to give back the excess. It is an accrual because the volume and price are fixed by records and contract, and only the timing of settlement is left open. PHE shows overlifting due to the Government in another line, Due to the Government, within a combined "Overlifting & DMO" item of 51,427 (Note 20, Daftar 5/114, PDF p. 131), and the matching underlifting receivable from SKK Migas in Due from the Government (Note 9, Daftar 5/97, PDF p. 114). Note 23 does not name the counterparty of its 11,322. Reading it as amounts owed to PSC partners or buyers is an inference. The Due from the Government essay covers the government side.

Note 21 explains that payables from oil and gas operations are classified as other payables because they come from the proportional share of the JIB statements that operators send to PHE's non-operating subsidiaries (Daftar 5/115, PDF p. 132). If PHE's non-operated interests follow the usual sequence, a cost the operator incurs in December would sit in accrued expenses until the JIB arrives, then in other payables (429,695 at the end of 2024), and be settled against cash calls already advanced (cash call advances of 76,196, an asset; Note 15, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123) or by a top-up payment (amounts under cash calls of 28,933, Note 21). Note 23 does not confirm the first step.
: where an accrual goes once the invoice arrives.
: holds the JIB-based payables to operators.
: PHE's separate line for amounts owed to employees.
: overlifting and DMO owed to the Government.
: the underlifting receivable on the other side.
: the provision side of the boundary.
: where most operating accruals are charged.

That the operating accruals of 1,854,008 are mainly costs incurred and not yet invoiced, including the non-operators' share before the JIB arrives, is read from the PSAK 237.11 definition and Note 21. Note 23 gives no further breakdown, and it may also contain capital spending and amounts that are partly estimated.

The counterparty of the 11,322 overlifting gas accrual is not stated. PHE also lists all of Note 23 as financial liabilities in Note 47; any overlifting settled by delivering gas rather than cash would not meet the definition of a financial liability, so that classification may be loose. Note 47 also places accrued expenses in an "other financial liabilities" column, while Note 3g(ii) describes them as measured at amortised cost.

Note 48's rupiah "accrued expenses and other provision" equals the employee incentives of Note 25a in both years. This page reads it as that line under a loose label, not as information about Note 23.
PHE labels bonus balances in Note 43e both as accruals and as provisions. The page treats this as labelling, not as evidence of how PHE classifies them on the balance sheet.
The JIB-to-cash-call sequence in section 9 is the usual industry practice, applied to PHE by inference from Notes 15 and 21.
The days-of-accrued-costs ratio uses a balance that probably includes capital accruals over an expense base without them; only the direction of change is meaningful.
The Islamic banking paragraph (PSAK 405 profit sharing, temporary syirkah funds) is from knowledge and was not checked against the text.

presentation.deck: The theory of accrued expenses from the accrual basis to disclosure, worked through PHE's operating accruals and set beside the industries where accruals drive the numbers
key_takeaways: An accrued expense is a liability for goods or services already received that the entity has not yet paid, been invoiced for, or formally agreed with the supplier. It sits between a trade payable, where the invoice fixes the amount and date, and a provision, where timing or amount is genuinely uncertain.

Accruals exist because of the accrual basis. An expense belongs to the period in which the entity consumed the goods or services, so at every cut-off date the entity records what it received but has not yet been billed for, and next period the invoice replaces the estimate.

Most accruals are mechanical: interest by the day, wages by the day worked, rig and vessel hire by the day rate, utilities by the meter. Some need estimates (bonuses, unbilled contractor work), but the uncertainty is small. When it stops being small, the item belongs to PSAK 237 as a provision.

title: Advances and Prepayments: Paying Before Delivery, Deferral and Classification
snippet: The theory of prepaid expenses and advances from the asset definition to impairment, worked through PHE's Notes 14 and 15 and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • A payment made before delivery buys a right to goods or services the entity controls, and that right is the asset. What the right turns into decides its path. A prepaid expense is used up into expense over time; an advance to a supplier becomes the inventory, fixed asset or oil and gas property it pays for.

  • The current and non-current split follows when the benefit is consumed. A prepayment is divided by time, the next twelve months current and the rest non-current; an advance usually takes the classification of the asset it will become.

  • Because the holder expects goods or services and no cash, advances and prepayments are non-monetary and non-financial. They keep the exchange rate of the payment date and stay outside the expected-credit-loss model, until delivery fails and the right becomes a claim for a refund. A cash call that the operator must refund in cash may be the exception. PHE's line holds 179,428 at the end of 2024, of which 99,099 is prepayments and 76,196 cash calls paid to operators.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report advances and prepayments, current portion, of 179,428 at 31 December 2024 against 177,429 a year earlier, and a non-current portion of 56 against 2,242, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The current line is 2.2 percent of current assets, and the two lines together are 0.6 percent of total assets (1.8 and 0.6 percent a year earlier). This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples. It also covers other current assets of 60,913 (210,253) and other non-current assets of 432,852 (455,380), most of which PHE calls deferred expenses (Note 14, Daftar 5/105–5/106, PDF pp. 122–123).

After reading it a student should be able to explain why a payment in advance is an asset, record and release it under both recording methods, split it between current and non-current, measure it in a foreign currency, and recognise when it has to be written down.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

No single chapter of an intermediate text covers this line. The asset definition follows the FASB and IASC frameworks and the Conceptual Framework chapter of Kieso, Weygandt and Warfield's Intermediate Accounting (IFRS edition); the deferral and adjusting entries follow Kieso's accounting-cycle chapter; the mirror image on the supplier's side follows Kieso's chapter on current liabilities. The order below runs from definition to recognition, measurement, classification, impairment and presentation.

1. Why a payment in advance is an asset

Cash has gone, and nothing has arrived yet. The question is whether that is an expense or an asset. The FASB and IASC definitions give an asset three characteristics: future economic benefit, control by the entity, and an origin in a past transaction or event. An insurance premium paid in October for a year of cover meets all three. The cover still to run is a future benefit, the entity alone can claim under the policy, and the payment is the past transaction. The 2018 Conceptual Framework (KKPK in Indonesia) words it as a present economic resource, a right with the potential to produce economic benefits, controlled by the entity as a result of past events. A prepayment is that right in its simplest form, a right to goods or services whose price is already settled.

Control matters more than ownership; the 1989 IASC Framework said that ownership is not essential to an asset. Nobody owns the unexpired part of an insurance policy in the way they own a truck, yet the payer controls the benefit and can keep others from it.

The line holds three kinds of right, distinguished by what each turns into.

  • Prepaid expenses: insurance, rent, travel and similar services consumed in operations. They become expense.

  • Advances to suppliers: payments ahead of delivery of goods, such as materials. They become inventory, then expense.

  • Advances for capital spending: payments to fabricators or contractors for equipment or wells. They become fixed assets or oil and gas properties and reach profit through depreciation or depletion.

PHE's Note 15 shows a fourth kind specific to joint operations, cash call advances, "advances made to PSC operators for oil and natural gas exploration and production activities" (Note 15, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123). Section 10 explains them.

2. Recognition: the accrual basis and the two recording methods

Under the cash basis the premium would be an expense in the month it is paid, and the months it actually protects would show nothing. The accrual basis, one of the assumptions listed in Kieso's Conceptual Framework chapter, records the effect when the benefit is consumed. A cost is first recognised as an asset and then charged as expense in the periods that use up its benefit. The part not yet used up stays on the balance sheet. That is a deferral, and the adjusting entry at period end moves the used part across.

Kieso shows two ways to book the payment, and they end in the same place. For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary pays 48,000 on 1 October 2024 for twelve months of offshore facilities insurance, part of the kind of balance behind PHE's 99,099 of prepayments.

Cost per month = 48,000 / 12 = 4,000

Expired at 31 December 2024 = 3 × 4,000 = 12,000

Unexpired at 31 December 2024 = 48,000 − 12,000 = 36,000

Asset method

Expense method

1 Oct 2024, payment

Dr Prepaid insurance 48,000 / Cr Cash 48,000

Dr Insurance expense 48,000 / Cr Cash 48,000

31 Dec 2024, adjustment

Dr Insurance expense 12,000 / Cr Prepaid insurance 12,000

Dr Prepaid insurance 36,000 / Cr Insurance expense 36,000

Result

Prepaid 36,000; expense 12,000

Prepaid 36,000; expense 12,000

The asset method suits a payment that will straddle a year end; the expense method suits a routine payment usually used up before the next close, with the adjustment made only when it is not. If the adjustment is forgotten, the asset method overstates the asset and understates expense by 12,000, and the expense method does the reverse by 36,000. Either error reverses next year, so both years are misstated.

3. Measurement after recognition: amortisation

A prepayment is measured at cost and released as the benefit is consumed. PHE's policy is that "prepayments are amortized on a straight-line basis over the estimated beneficial periods of the prepayments" (Note 3k, Daftar 5/53, PDF p. 70). Straight-line suits time-based services such as insurance and rent, where each month delivers the same cover.

Not every prepayment is consumed with time. A prepaid service that is used in events is released when each event happens. For example (illustration), 900 paid in December 2024 for crew flights in January 2025 is still a prepayment at the year end, and the whole 900 becomes expense in January when the crews fly.

31 Dec 2024: prepaid travel 900. January 2025: Dr Travel expense 900 / Cr Prepaid travel 900

Leases are the large exception. Under PSAK 116 Leases (IFRS 16), lease payments made at or before commencement are part of the cost of the right-of-use asset (para. 24(b)), so rent paid in advance on a lease longer than twelve months leaves this line at commencement. Only short-term and low-value leases, which PHE leaves outside its single lease model (Note 3n, Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74), still produce prepaid rent. PHE's right-of-use note even carries a column headed "prepaid expense reclassifications", moving 450 within its 2024 cost movements (Note 18, Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129).

4. Advances to suppliers and for capital spending

An advance is never released to expense from this line. It waits for delivery and then moves, in one entry, into whatever was delivered. The supplier sees the same transaction from the other side. Kieso's current-liabilities chapter records cash received before delivery as unearned revenue (under PSAK 115, a contract liability), which becomes revenue when the goods are handed over. The payer's advance and the supplier's contract liability are the two halves of one contract.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary orders drilling chemicals for 10,000 and pays a 30 percent advance of 3,000. The supplier delivers the next month and invoices the remaining 7,000.

Buyer (PHE subsidiary)

Supplier

Advance paid

Dr Advances to suppliers 3,000 / Cr Cash 3,000

Dr Cash 3,000 / Cr Contract liability 3,000

Delivery

Dr Inventories 10,000 / Cr Advances to suppliers 3,000 / Cr Trade payables 7,000

Dr Contract liability 3,000, Dr Trade receivables 7,000 / Cr Revenue 10,000

The chemicals then follow the inventory rules of inventories-net and become production cost when used, or part of a well if issued to drilling.

An advance for capital spending follows the same pattern with a different destination. For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays a fabricator 40 percent of a 25,000 compressor package, that is 10,000, and on delivery the package is installed on a platform under construction.

Dr Oil and gas properties, assets under construction 25,000 / Cr Advances for capital spending 10,000 / Cr Trade payables 15,000

No expense arises at any step. The 25,000 reaches profit only as the platform is depleted.

5. Classification: current or non-current

PSAK 201 Presentation of Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) classifies an asset as current when the entity expects to realise it, or intends to sell or consume it, within its normal operating cycle, holds it mainly for trading, or expects to realise it within twelve months after the reporting date (para. 66). Everything else is non-current.

Prepayments are split by time. For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays 72,000 on 1 July 2024 for a three-year policy.

Cost per month = 72,000 / 36 = 2,000

Expense 2024 = 6 × 2,000 = 12,000; unexpired at 31 December 2024 = 72,000 − 12,000 = 60,000

Current (2025) = 12 × 2,000 = 24,000; non-current (2026 to June 2027) = 60,000 − 24,000 = 36,000

Presentation entry: Dr Prepayments, non-current 36,000 / Cr Prepayments, current 36,000

Each year the next twelve months move back into current. PHE's non-current prepayments fell from 62 to nil in 2024, consistent with a long-dated prepayment running down into the current portion or being expensed (Note 15).

Advances follow their destination. An advance for inventory is current, because inventory is. For an advance towards a fixed asset or oil and gas property, PSAK 201 has no specific paragraph. Common practice presents it as non-current whatever the delivery date, because what is held is an undelivered part of a long-lived asset and its cost will be recovered over many years. Some preparers instead read "realised within twelve months" as covering conversion into the asset and present a short-dated capital advance as current. The choice moves working capital. A 10,000 capital advance presented as current would add 10,000 to current assets that will never fund suppliers or short-term debt. PHE's non-current advances fell from 2,180 to 56 in 2024 (Note 15); the note does not say what they were.

6. Foreign currency and financial-instrument status

PHE's functional currency is the US dollar (Elnusa's is the rupiah; Note 3, Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83), but many suppliers bill in rupiah. PSAK 221 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21) retranslates monetary items, rights to receive or obligations to pay a fixed or determinable number of currency units, at the closing rate. Non-monetary items carried at historical cost keep the rate of the transaction date, and the standard lists amounts prepaid for goods and services as an example (para. 16). The holder of an advance expects goods, so a weaker rupiah does not reduce what it is owed. ISAK 122 Foreign Currency Transactions and Advance Consideration (formerly ISAK 33, IFRIC 22) adds that the asset eventually received is translated at the rate of the day the advance was first recognised, with a separate date for each payment (paras. 8–9).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary orders spare parts for IDR 80 billion. It pays an advance of IDR 48 billion on 15 December 2024 at IDR 16,000 per USD. The year-end rate is IDR 16,200 per USD. The parts arrive on 15 March 2025, when the balance of IDR 32 billion is paid at IDR 16,400 per USD.

Advance = IDR 48,000,000 thousand / 16,000 = 3,000

If wrongly retranslated at year end = IDR 48,000,000 thousand / 16,200 = 2,963; loss that must not be booked = 37

Balance on delivery = IDR 32,000,000 thousand / 16,400 = 1,951

Cost of the parts = 3,000 + 1,951 = 4,951

15 Mar 2025: Dr Inventories 4,951 / Cr Advances to suppliers 3,000 / Cr Cash 1,951

The same reasoning removes the line from financial-instrument accounting. PSAK 232 Financial Instruments: Presentation (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) states that assets such as prepaid expenses, whose benefit is the receipt of goods or services, are not financial assets (para. AG11). So PSAK 109's expected-credit-loss model does not apply to them.

7. Impairment and recoverability

A prepayment is worth carrying only while its benefit is still coming. If the benefit disappears, the unexpired amount is written off at once. For example (illustration), if the shore-base yard behind a six-month prepaid rent is closed after three months with no refund, the remaining three months are expensed in the month of closure.

An advance is exposed to the supplier. While delivery is still expected, the question is whether the supplier can perform, judged by its financial condition, delivery record and any guarantee. When delivery fails and the contract is terminated, the right to goods becomes a right to a refund, which is monetary and a financial asset. The advance is derecognised and a refund claim is recognised. Because the claim is credit-impaired from the start, it is recognised at what is expected to be recovered, and later changes go through PSAK 109's impairment model. For example (illustration), the chemicals supplier of section 4 becomes insolvent before delivering, and the administrator expects unsecured creditors to recover 40 percent.

Expected recovery = 3,000 × 40% = 1,200; loss = 3,000 − 1,200 = 1,800

Dr Refund receivable 1,200, Dr Loss on supplier default 1,800 / Cr Advances to suppliers 3,000

Timing follows PSAK 210 Events after the Reporting Period (formerly PSAK 8, IAS 10). If the insolvency reveals a condition that existed at the reporting date and is known before the statements are authorised, the write-down belongs to that year; if it arises later, it belongs to the next. Suppliers that take large advances often provide an advance payment guarantee, a bank guarantee that repays the advance if they fail. It does not change the classification, but it changes the expected recovery and so the loss.

8. Advances and prepayments across industries

The deferral logic is universal, and several industries add rules of their own.

Insurers. Commissions paid to brokers before a group of insurance contracts is recognised are a prepayment of sorts. PSAK 117 Insurance Contracts (IFRS 17) recognises them as an asset for insurance acquisition cash flows, which is assessed for recoverability and derecognised into the measurement of the contracts once they are recognised, unless the insurer expenses these cash flows under the simplified premium allocation approach.

Property buyers and developers. Indonesian companies often pay large advances to buy land long before title transfers. They are non-current when the land will be a fixed asset, investment property or a land bank for future development. An advance for land a developer will build on and sell within its operating cycle follows inventory and is current. Either way it keeps the payment-date rate in a foreign-currency entity. On the other side, a developer selling apartments off plan holds the buyers' payments as contract liabilities under PSAK 115 until control of the unit passes.

Islamic finance. In a murabahah sale the customer may pay a down payment (uang muka) before the contract to show commitment. PSAK 402 Murabahah (formerly PSAK 102) calls it hamish jiddiyah, which differs from 'urbun, a deposit forfeited on cancellation. The bank holds the hamish jiddiyah as a liability and, when the sale is made, deducts it from the receivable (or from the cost of the asset sold); if the customer withdraws, the bank keeps only what covers its actual costs and returns the rest. For example (illustration), a customer pays an advance of 50 on a 1,000 murabahah. If the sale goes ahead, the receivable is 1,000 − 50 = 950; if the customer withdraws and the bank's actual cost of the cancellation is 20, the bank keeps 20 and refunds 30.

Taxes paid in advance. Prepaid income tax and input VAT look like prepayments but are claims on the government under tax law. They are presented separately. Prepaid income tax follows PSAK 212, and input VAT the VAT rules; PHE shows them on its own lines (corporate-dividend-taxes-receivable-current, other-taxes-receivable-current).

The flat total hides two large movements in opposite directions. Prepayments, described as insurance, rent, travel and other operating activities, quadrupled, while cash call advances fell by 42 percent. The note does not explain either change.

One classification point needs care. PHE's financial-instrument table for 2023 lists "advances and prepayment" of 179,671, the two portions combined, as financial assets at amortised cost, while the 2024 table omits the line (Note 47, Daftar 5/222–5/223, PDF pp. 239–240). In theory a deferred expense is the prepayment of section 2 under another name, a cost already paid and held as an asset until the periods it benefits, split by time as in section 5. PHE's description fits that only in part. In 2024 the current portion fell 149,953 and the non-current portion rose 219,926, a shift the note does not explain.

The rest of Note 14 belongs to other pages. Employee receivables are loans to employees of PT Badak NGL, financial assets normally measured at amortised cost. The restricted funds are cash that PSC operators deposit to fund site restoration in joint operations, recognised by PHE's subsidiaries in line with their participating interests. They fell 229,836, or 77.5 percent, and the note says funds not yet transferred by SKK Migas were moved, with their interest, to a joint account of SKK Migas and PHR, without linking that to the fall. 10. Upstream note: cash calls in a joint operation

In a joint operation the operator spends on behalf of all partners and bills each its share through a joint interest billing (JIB). Partners fund the operator in advance through monthly cash calls. Under PSAK 111, PHE recognises its share of the joint operation's assets and expenses (Note 3y, Daftar 5/74, PDF p. 91). A cash call paid before the spending is therefore an advance that will turn into PHE's share of whatever the operator spends.

For example (illustration), PHE holds 30 percent of a block and pays a cash call of 9,000. The operator's JIB for the month reports spending of 25,000, of which 10,000 is operating cost and 15,000 drilling of a development well.

PHE's share = 25,000 × 30% = 7,500 (operating 3,000, drilling 4,500); unspent advance = 9,000 − 7,500 = 1,500

Dr Production expenses 3,000, Dr Oil and gas properties, assets under construction 4,500 / Cr Cash call advances 7,500

If the operator had spent 35,000, PHE's share of 10,500 would exceed the 9,000 paid, and PHE would owe the operator 1,500. PHE reports such a balance, "due to operators – under cash calls" of 28,933 in other payables (Note 21, Daftar 5/115, PDF p. 132). When PHE is itself the operator, its policy recognises a receivable from or payable to the non-operators for the difference between their share of spending and the cash calls received (Note 3y, Daftar 5/75, PDF p. 92).

Whether an unspent cash call is a non-monetary advance or a monetary claim on the operator depends on the joint operating agreement. If unspent amounts are refundable in cash, the balance looks more like a receivable; if they can only be applied to future spending, it looks like an advance. PHE's 2023 table is weak evidence either way, because it also lists the prepayments, which are not financial assets.

11. Related lines

  • advances-prepayments-non-current: the non-current portion covered on this page.

  • inventories-net: the destination of advances for materials.

  • oil-gas-properties-net: the destination of capital advances and the drilling share of cash calls.

  • right-of-use-assets-net: where rent paid in advance on long leases now sits.

  • other-payables: amounts owed to operators under cash calls.

  • trade-payables: the balance due on delivery after an advance.

  • other-current-assets and other-non-current-assets: Note 14, covered in section 9.

  • decommissioning-site-restoration-provision: the obligation behind the restricted restoration funds.

  • oci-cash-flow-hedge: where the effective part of the hedge gain is deferred.

Least-confident assertions

  • Presenting a capital advance as non-current whatever the delivery date is common practice; PSAK 201 states no such requirement, and some preparers present short-dated capital advances as current.

  • The reading of cash call advances as advances that may be monetary depends on joint operating agreements that PHE does not disclose. PHE's 2023 financial-instrument table, which also lists the prepayments, is weak evidence, and its omission of the line in 2024 may be a change of view or an oversight.

  • Two readings of PHE's balances are inferences. That the non-current prepayments of 62 ran down into the current portion rests on two balances. That several of Note 14's "deferred expenses" (escrow, underlifting, the lease receivable allocation) are receivable-like rests on PHE's one-sentence description; the note gives no amounts by component.

  • The hamish jiddiyah treatment is taken from IAI's 2019 exposure draft of PSAK 102 (now PSAK 402); the final text was not opened, so its wording may differ.

  • The refund claim is recognised at the 40 percent expected to be recovered, undiscounted. Treating it as credit-impaired at recognition, with no day-one allowance, follows PSAK 109 as understood here; the paragraphs were not opened.

content.text: A payment made before delivery buys a right to goods or services the entity controls, and that right is the asset. What the right turns into decides its path. A prepaid expense is used up into expense over time; an advance to a supplier becomes the inventory, fixed asset or oil and gas property it pays for.

The current and non-current split follows when the benefit is consumed. A prepayment is divided by time, the next twelve months current and the rest non-current; an advance usually takes the classification of the asset it will become.

Because the holder expects goods or services and no cash, advances and prepayments are non-monetary and non-financial. They keep the exchange rate of the payment date and stay outside the expected-credit-loss model, until delivery fails and the right becomes a claim for a refund. A cash call that the operator must refund in cash may be the exception. PHE's line holds 179,428 at the end of 2024, of which 99,099 is prepayments and 76,196 cash calls paid to operators.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report advances and prepayments, current portion, of 179,428 at 31 December 2024 against 177,429 a year earlier, and a non-current portion of 56 against 2,242, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The current line is 2.2 percent of current assets, and the two lines together are 0.6 percent of total assets (1.8 and 0.6 percent a year earlier). This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples. It also covers other current assets of 60,913 (210,253) and other non-current assets of 432,852 (455,380), most of which PHE calls deferred expenses (Note 14, Daftar 5/105–5/106, PDF pp. 122–123).

After reading it a student should be able to explain why a payment in advance is an asset, record and release it under both recording methods, split it between current and non-current, measure it in a foreign currency, and recognise when it has to be written down.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
No single chapter of an intermediate text covers this line. The asset definition follows the FASB and IASC frameworks and the Conceptual Framework chapter of Kieso, Weygandt and Warfield's

(IFRS edition); the deferral and adjusting entries follow Kieso's accounting-cycle chapter; the mirror image on the supplier's side follows Kieso's chapter on current liabilities. The order below runs from definition to recognition, measurement, classification, impairment and presentation.
1. Why a payment in advance is an asset

Cash has gone, and nothing has arrived yet. The question is whether that is an expense or an asset. The FASB and IASC definitions give an asset three characteristics: future economic benefit, control by the entity, and an origin in a past transaction or event. An insurance premium paid in October for a year of cover meets all three. The cover still to run is a future benefit, the entity alone can claim under the policy, and the payment is the past transaction. The 2018 Conceptual Framework (KKPK in Indonesia) words it as a present economic resource, a right with the potential to produce economic benefits, controlled by the entity as a result of past events. A prepayment is that right in its simplest form, a right to goods or services whose price is already settled.

Control matters more than ownership; the 1989 IASC Framework said that ownership is not essential to an asset. Nobody owns the unexpired part of an insurance policy in the way they own a truck, yet the payer controls the benefit and can keep others from it.
The line holds three kinds of right, distinguished by what each turns into.
: insurance, rent, travel and similar services consumed in operations. They become expense.
: payments ahead of delivery of goods, such as materials. They become inventory, then expense.
: payments to fabricators or contractors for equipment or wells. They become fixed assets or oil and gas properties and reach profit through depreciation or depletion.
PHE's Note 15 shows a fourth kind specific to joint operations,
, "advances made to PSC operators for oil and natural gas exploration and production activities" (Note 15, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123). Section 10 explains them.
2. Recognition: the accrual basis and the two recording methods

Under the cash basis the premium would be an expense in the month it is paid, and the months it actually protects would show nothing. The accrual basis, one of the assumptions listed in Kieso's Conceptual Framework chapter, records the effect when the benefit is consumed. A cost is first recognised as an asset and then charged as expense in the periods that use up its benefit. The part not yet used up stays on the balance sheet. That is a
at period end moves the used part across.

Kieso shows two ways to book the payment, and they end in the same place. For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary pays 48,000 on 1 October 2024 for twelve months of offshore facilities insurance, part of the kind of balance behind PHE's 99,099 of prepayments.
Dr Insurance expense 12,000 / Cr Prepaid insurance 12,000
Dr Prepaid insurance 36,000 / Cr Insurance expense 36,000

The asset method suits a payment that will straddle a year end; the expense method suits a routine payment usually used up before the next close, with the adjustment made only when it is not. If the adjustment is forgotten, the asset method overstates the asset and understates expense by 12,000, and the expense method does the reverse by 36,000. Either error reverses next year, so both years are misstated.

A prepayment is measured at cost and released as the benefit is consumed. PHE's policy is that "prepayments are amortized on a straight-line basis over the estimated beneficial periods of the prepayments" (Note 3k, Daftar 5/53, PDF p. 70). Straight-line suits time-based services such as insurance and rent, where each month delivers the same cover.

Not every prepayment is consumed with time. A prepaid service that is used in events is released when each event happens. For example (illustration), 900 paid in December 2024 for crew flights in January 2025 is still a prepayment at the year end, and the whole 900 becomes expense in January when the crews fly.
31 Dec 2024: prepaid travel 900. January 2025: Dr Travel expense 900 / Cr Prepaid travel 900
Leases are the large exception. Under PSAK 116

(IFRS 16), lease payments made at or before commencement are part of the cost of the right-of-use asset (para. 24(b)), so rent paid in advance on a lease longer than twelve months leaves this line at commencement. Only short-term and low-value leases, which PHE leaves outside its single lease model (Note 3n, Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74), still produce prepaid rent. PHE's right-of-use note even carries a column headed "prepaid expense reclassifications", moving 450 within its 2024 cost movements (Note 18, Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129).

An advance is never released to expense from this line. It waits for delivery and then moves, in one entry, into whatever was delivered. The supplier sees the same transaction from the other side. Kieso's current-liabilities chapter records cash received before delivery as
), which becomes revenue when the goods are handed over. The payer's advance and the supplier's contract liability are the two halves of one contract.
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary orders drilling chemicals for 10,000 and pays a 30 percent advance of 3,000. The supplier delivers the next month and invoices the remaining 7,000.
Dr Advances to suppliers 3,000 / Cr Cash 3,000
Dr Inventories 10,000 / Cr Advances to suppliers 3,000 / Cr Trade payables 7,000
Dr Contract liability 3,000, Dr Trade receivables 7,000 / Cr Revenue 10,000
The chemicals then follow the inventory rules of
and become production cost when used, or part of a well if issued to drilling.

An advance for capital spending follows the same pattern with a different destination. For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays a fabricator 40 percent of a 25,000 compressor package, that is 10,000, and on delivery the package is installed on a platform under construction.
Dr Oil and gas properties, assets under construction 25,000 / Cr Advances for capital spending 10,000 / Cr Trade payables 15,000
No expense arises at any step. The 25,000 reaches profit only as the platform is depleted.
