A prepayment is worth carrying only while its benefit is still coming. If the benefit disappears, the unexpired amount is written off at once. For example (illustration), if the shore-base yard behind a six-month prepaid rent is closed after three months with no refund, the remaining three months are expensed in the month of closure.

An advance is exposed to the supplier. While delivery is still expected, the question is whether the supplier can perform, judged by its financial condition, delivery record and any guarantee. When delivery fails and the contract is terminated, the right to goods becomes a right to a refund, which is monetary and a financial asset. The advance is derecognised and a refund claim is recognised. Because the claim is credit-impaired from the start, it is recognised at what is expected to be recovered, and later changes go through PSAK 109's impairment model. For example (illustration), the chemicals supplier of section 4 becomes insolvent before delivering, and the administrator expects unsecured creditors to recover 40 percent.
Dr Refund receivable 1,200, Dr Loss on supplier default 1,800 / Cr Advances to suppliers 3,000

(formerly PSAK 8, IAS 10). If the insolvency reveals a condition that existed at the reporting date and is known before the statements are authorised, the write-down belongs to that year; if it arises later, it belongs to the next. Suppliers that take large advances often provide an
, a bank guarantee that repays the advance if they fail. It does not change the classification, but it changes the expected recovery and so the loss.
The deferral logic is universal, and several industries add rules of their own.
Commissions paid to brokers before a group of insurance contracts is recognised are a prepayment of sorts. PSAK 117
(IFRS 17) recognises them as an asset for

, which is assessed for recoverability and derecognised into the measurement of the contracts once they are recognised, unless the insurer expenses these cash flows under the simplified premium allocation approach.

Indonesian companies often pay large advances to buy land long before title transfers. They are non-current when the land will be a fixed asset, investment property or a land bank for future development. An advance for land a developer will build on and sell within its operating cycle follows inventory and is current. Either way it keeps the payment-date rate in a foreign-currency entity. On the other side, a developer selling apartments off plan holds the buyers' payments as contract liabilities under PSAK 115 until control of the unit passes.
sale the customer may pay a down payment (
) before the contract to show commitment. PSAK 402
, a deposit forfeited on cancellation. The bank holds the

as a liability and, when the sale is made, deducts it from the receivable (or from the cost of the asset sold); if the customer withdraws, the bank keeps only what covers its actual costs and returns the rest. For example (illustration), a customer pays an advance of 50 on a 1,000 murabahah. If the sale goes ahead, the receivable is 1,000 − 50 = 950; if the customer withdraws and the bank's actual cost of the cancellation is 20, the bank keeps 20 and refunds 30.

Prepaid income tax and input VAT look like prepayments but are claims on the government under tax law. They are presented separately. Prepaid income tax follows PSAK 212, and input VAT the VAT rules; PHE shows them on its own lines (
9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 15 and 14
PSAK 201 asks for material classes to be shown separately, in the statement or the notes. PHE splits the line into three classes (Note 15, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123).

The flat total hides two large movements in opposite directions. Prepayments, described as insurance, rent, travel and other operating activities, quadrupled, while cash call advances fell by 42 percent. The note does not explain either change.

One classification point needs care. PHE's financial-instrument table for 2023 lists "advances and prepayment" of 179,671, the two portions combined, as financial assets at amortised cost, while the 2024 table omits the line (Note 47, Daftar 5/222–5/223, PDF pp. 239–240). Under PSAK 232 AG11 the prepayments at least are non-financial. Cash call advances are less clear, since unspent cash can be offset or returned; section 10 comes back to them.
PHE holds a larger block of deferred costs outside this line (Note 14, Daftar 5/105–5/106, PDF pp. 122–123).
Restricted funds for site restoration in joint operations

In theory a deferred expense is the prepayment of section 2 under another name, a cost already paid and held as an asset until the periods it benefits, split by time as in section 5. PHE's description fits that only in part. Its deferred expenses relate to an escrow account for a Gabon Oil Company carry receivable, to underlifting, to a bank guarantee and to other assets of M&P; the current portion also holds receivables from underlifting for non-operators in PIEP and an allocation account for a finance lease receivable at Elnusa. Recovery "is based on the contracts in the activity's normal operating cycle". Escrow balances, underlift claims and lease receivables are claims to cash or oil, closer to receivables than to costs awaiting expense, so the label says less about their nature than the description does. In 2024 the current portion fell 149,953 and the non-current portion rose 219,926, a shift the note does not explain.

The rest of Note 14 belongs to other pages. Employee receivables are loans to employees of PT Badak NGL, financial assets normally measured at amortised cost. The restricted funds are cash that PSC operators deposit to fund site restoration in joint operations, recognised by PHE's subsidiaries in line with their participating interests. They fell 229,836, or 77.5 percent, and the note says funds not yet transferred by SKK Migas were moved, with their interest, to a joint account of SKK Migas and PHR, without linking that to the fall. How such a fund relates to the restoration provision is the subject of

. The unrealised hedge gain is the fair value of cash flow hedges of interest rates on the JTB loan, a derivative whose effective portion is deferred in OCI, with 1,395 of ineffectiveness in finance costs; hedge accounting belongs to
. The note does not describe the dead stock material.
10. Upstream note: cash calls in a joint operation
In a joint operation the operator spends on behalf of all partners and bills each its share through a
(JIB). Partners fund the operator in advance through monthly

. Under PSAK 111, PHE recognises its share of the joint operation's assets and expenses (Note 3y, Daftar 5/74, PDF p. 91). A cash call paid before the spending is therefore an advance that will turn into PHE's share of whatever the operator spends.

For example (illustration), PHE holds 30 percent of a block and pays a cash call of 9,000. The operator's JIB for the month reports spending of 25,000, of which 10,000 is operating cost and 15,000 drilling of a development well.
Dr Production expenses 3,000, Dr Oil and gas properties, assets under construction 4,500 / Cr Cash call advances 7,500

If the operator had spent 35,000, PHE's share of 10,500 would exceed the 9,000 paid, and PHE would owe the operator 1,500. PHE reports such a balance, "due to operators – under cash calls" of 28,933 in other payables (Note 21, Daftar 5/115, PDF p. 132). When PHE is itself the operator, its policy recognises a receivable from or payable to the non-operators for the difference between their share of spending and the cash calls received (Note 3y, Daftar 5/75, PDF p. 92).

Whether an unspent cash call is a non-monetary advance or a monetary claim on the operator depends on the joint operating agreement. If unspent amounts are refundable in cash, the balance looks more like a receivable; if they can only be applied to future spending, it looks like an advance. PHE's 2023 table is weak evidence either way, because it also lists the prepayments, which are not financial assets.

Presenting a capital advance as non-current whatever the delivery date is common practice; PSAK 201 states no such requirement, and some preparers present short-dated capital advances as current.

The reading of cash call advances as advances that may be monetary depends on joint operating agreements that PHE does not disclose. PHE's 2023 financial-instrument table, which also lists the prepayments, is weak evidence, and its omission of the line in 2024 may be a change of view or an oversight.

Two readings of PHE's balances are inferences. That the non-current prepayments of 62 ran down into the current portion rests on two balances. That several of Note 14's "deferred expenses" (escrow, underlifting, the lease receivable allocation) are receivable-like rests on PHE's one-sentence description; the note gives no amounts by component.
treatment is taken from IAI's 2019 exposure draft of PSAK 102 (now PSAK 402); the final text was not opened, so its wording may differ.

The refund claim is recognised at the 40 percent expected to be recovered, undiscounted. Treating it as credit-impaired at recognition, with no day-one allowance, follows PSAK 109 as understood here; the paragraphs were not opened.

presentation.deck: The theory of prepaid expenses and advances from the asset definition to impairment, worked through PHE's Notes 14 and 15 and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: A payment made before delivery buys a right to goods or services the entity controls, and that right is the asset. What the right turns into decides its path. A prepaid expense is used up into expense over time; an advance to a supplier becomes the inventory, fixed asset or oil and gas property it pays for.

The current and non-current split follows when the benefit is consumed. A prepayment is divided by time, the next twelve months current and the rest non-current; an advance usually takes the classification of the asset it will become.

Because the holder expects goods or services and no cash, advances and prepayments are non-monetary and non-financial. They keep the exchange rate of the payment date and stay outside the expected-credit-loss model, until delivery fails and the right becomes a claim for a refund. A cash call that the operator must refund in cash may be the exception. PHE's line holds 179,428 at the end of 2024, of which 99,099 is prepayments and 76,196 cash calls paid to operators.

title: Business Combinations: the Acquisition Method, Goodwill and Common Control
snippet: The theory of accounting for an acquisition from the definition of a business to pooling of interests, worked from Barito Pacific's 2025 purchases and set beside the industries where the boundary matters most
content:
In brief

  • A business combination is a transaction in which an acquirer obtains control of a business. Buying a set of assets that is not a business is an asset acquisition: the price is spread over the assets on relative fair values, and no goodwill or bargain purchase gain arises. The optional concentration test settles many cases quickly.

  • Under the acquisition method (PSAK 103) the acquirer measures the consideration and every identifiable asset and liability at acquisition-date fair value, including intangibles the seller never recorded. Goodwill is the residual. A negative residual is a bargain purchase gain in profit or loss, recognised only after the numbers have been rechecked. Provisional amounts may be corrected for up to one year.

  • When the same party controls both sides, nothing is bought from an outsider, so PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and puts the difference from the price in additional paid-in capital.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report a gain from bargain purchase of 1,868,039 for 2025, in USD thousand, against profit for the year of 1,615,634 (BRPT FS 2025, statement of profit or loss, PDF p. 17). Two purchases by its petrochemical subsidiary produced it.

After reading this page a student should be able to classify a purchase, apply the acquisition method, allocate the excess of price over book value, handle the measurement period and record a common-control combination.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Why companies combine and the legal forms

The legal form of a combination decides whose ledger the acquired assets land in, not how they are measured. The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 1) list the motives, from cost savings to tax, and classify combinations as horizontal (same line of business), vertical and conglomerate (unrelated lines). Vertical integration joins different stages of one supply chain, a refinery buying its crude supplier, rather than firms in "pasar yang berbeda" (different markets), as the notes put it.

Form

Formula

What the acquirer records in its own books

Merger

A + B = A

B's assets and liabilities directly; B is dissolved

Consolidation

A + B = C

a new company C takes over both; A and B are dissolved

Stock acquisition

A controls B

an investment in B; B keeps its own books and is consolidated

Measurement is the same for all three. In a merger the values go into A's ledger; in a stock acquisition they appear only on the consolidation worksheet (section 7). BRPT's 2025 purchases were stock acquisitions. CAPGC Pte. Ltd., a subsidiary of PT Chandra Asri Pacific Tbk (CAP), bought 100 percent of the shares of Aster Chemical and Energy Pte. Ltd. (ACE) from Shell Singapore (Note 1d, PDF p. 43).

2. What is a business: combination or asset acquisition

The acquisition method applies only when what is acquired is a business. PSAK 103 Kombinasi Bisnis (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) scopes out the acquisition of an asset or group of assets that is not a business (para. 2(b)) and combinations of entities under common control (para. 2(c)). The notes never define a business.

A business needs an input and a substantive process. A business is an integrated set of activities and assets capable of being managed to provide goods or services to customers. Outputs are not required, but it needs at least an input and a substantive process that together significantly contribute to the ability to create outputs (para. B8). An operating wind farm with turbines, a power purchase agreement (PPA) and staff is a business; a development licence with no workforce is usually not.

The concentration test is a shortcut out of the definition. Since 1 January 2021 an optional test, elected deal by deal (paras. B7A–B7B), applies. If substantially all of the fair value of the gross assets acquired is concentrated in a single identifiable asset or a group of similar assets, the set is not a business and no further analysis is needed. Cash, deferred tax assets and goodwill from deferred tax are left out of gross assets, and a tangible asset and an intangible asset are never "similar".

For example (illustration), take BRPT's acquisition of 51 percent of PT Lombok Timur Bayu Energi, a wind project company, on 3 January 2024 (Note 43, PDF pp. 231–232).

Gross assets acquired = 1 cash + 44 receivables + 2 other current + 37 fixed assets + 7,700 project development costs = 7,784

Gross assets excluding cash = 7,783

Concentration = 7,700 / 7,783 = 98.9%, substantially all in one asset

The boundary changes five things. Suppose (illustration) the buyer also paid 150 of legal fees and, had the project been a business, the development rights would have been valued independently at 6,078.

Asset acquisition

Business combination

Price allocation

Spread over assets on relative fair values

Each item at its own fair value

Goodwill or bargain purchase gain

Never

Residual, here 3,122 + 49% × 4,500 − 4,500 = 827 goodwill (before deferred tax)

Transaction costs of 150

Capitalised into the assets

Expensed (para. 53)

Deferred tax on book–tax differences

Not recognised (initial recognition exemption, PSAK 212.15(b))

Recognised, which changes goodwill

Contingent payments

No settled rule; often recognised when the obligation arises

Fair value at acquisition date (section 4)

In the business column, identifiable net assets are 6,122 − 7,700 + 6,078 = 4,500 and the non-controlling interest (NCI) at its proportionate share is 2,205. BRPT's actual entry follows the asset-acquisition column, with NCI of 49% × 6,122 = 3,000 (rounded) and no goodwill.

Dr Project development costs 7,700; Dr Cash 1; Dr Receivables 44; Dr Other current assets 2; Dr Fixed assets 37 / Cr Accrued expenses 962; Cr Taxes payable 52; Cr Trade and other payables 648; Cr NCI 3,000; Cr Cash 3,122

3. The acquisition method: acquirer and acquisition date

Control, not legal form or the signing date, fixes both the acquirer and the acquisition date, the first two of the method's four steps (para. 5).

The acquirer is the entity that obtains control under PSAK 110 Laporan Keuangan Konsolidasian (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) (para. B13). When that is unclear, the standard looks at who pays, who issues shares, whose owners and managers dominate afterwards, and relative size (paras. B14–B17). In a reverse acquisition, typical of a backdoor listing, the owners of a private company receive enough new shares of a listed shell to control it, so the private company is the accounting acquirer (para. B19).

The acquisition date is the date control passes, usually the closing date, which may differ from the signing date (paras. 8–9). It fixes the fair values, the start of consolidation and the measurement period. Shell announced its agreement to sell to CAPGC on 8 May 2024, but control passed at completion on 1 April 2025, the acquisition date in Note 43 (PDF p. 226). Aster Polymer Solutions Pte. Ltd. (APS) follows the same pattern: agreement on 6 May 2025, effective and consolidated from 1 August 2025 (PDF pp. 228–229).

4. Consideration transferred and acquisition-related costs

Consideration, the price the acquirer pays, is measured at fair value: cash paid, other assets given up, liabilities incurred to the former owners, and equity issued (para. 37). The notes' Pop Corporation example issues 100,000 shares of USD 10 par, market price USD 16, for the net assets of Son.

Consideration = 100,000 × 16 = 1,600,000; common stock = 100,000 × 10 = 1,000,000; paid-in capital = 600,000

Dr Investment in Son 1,600,000 / Cr Common stock 1,000,000; Cr Paid-in capital 600,000

Acquisition-related costs are not part of the price. Advisory, legal, accounting, valuation and internal acquisition-department costs are expensed when incurred, and the costs of issuing debt or equity follow PSAK 232 and PSAK 109 (para. 53). The notes' example reaches the same result: the 80,000 consultant fee is expensed, and SEC fees, accountants' fees and share certificates (5,000 + 10,000 + 25,000 = 40,000) reduce paid-in capital.

Dr Investment expense 80,000; Dr Paid-in capital 40,000 / Cr Cash 120,000

Deferred consideration, a fixed amount payable later, is part of the consideration at fair value and a liability from the acquisition date. ACE's provisional consideration of 671,970 was 388,745 in cash at completion plus 283,225 deferred (Note 43, PDF p. 227).

Contingent consideration depends on a future event, such as an earn-out. It enters the consideration at acquisition-date fair value (para. 39) and is classified as a liability or equity under PSAK 232 (para. 40). Later a liability is remeasured through profit or loss and an equity amount is not remeasured; neither touches goodwill after the measurement period (para. 58, restated in BRPT's policy, Note 3d, PDF p. 69). For example (illustration), an earn-out of 10,000 on two years' wind output is worth 2,800 at acquisition and 4,000 a year later.

At acquisition: included in consideration, Cr Contingent consideration liability 2,800

One year later: Dr Loss on remeasurement of contingent consideration 1,200 / Cr Contingent consideration liability 1,200

5. Recognising and measuring what was acquired

The acquirer recognises the identifiable assets and liabilities separately from goodwill (para. 10), at acquisition-date fair value (para. 18). Each must meet the definition of an asset or liability at that date, so a restructuring the buyer merely plans is not a liability (para. 11), and each must be part of the exchange, not a separate deal with the seller (para. 12).

Items the seller never recorded are still recognised. An internally built brand, a customer list or a favourable contract is invisible in the seller's books but identifiable to a buyer (para. 13; see the Intangible Assets essay). A contingent liability is recognised if it is a present obligation whose fair value can be measured, even if an outflow is not probable, which PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) would not allow outside a combination (para. 23).

Deferred tax and employee benefits follow their own standards. BRPT's policy names deferred tax under PSAK 212 (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) and employee benefits under PSAK 219 (formerly PSAK 24, IAS 19) (Note 3d, PDF p. 68).

In the notes' Pam–Sun example Sun's book net assets of 750,000 become 1,200,000 at fair value, including an unrecorded patent of 50,000 and notes payable revalued down to 135,000. Their allocation entry debits "Building – net $850.000", which is building 500,000 plus equipment 350,000. It balances, but equipment needs its own line because the two have different lives.

6. Goodwill and bargain purchase

Goodwill is what the consideration buys beyond the identifiable net assets: synergies, the assembled workforce, expected new customers. It cannot be sold on its own, so it is measured as a residual (para. 32).

Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI + fair value of any previously held interest − identifiable net assets at fair value

The notes' two Pam–Sun cases, with identifiable net assets of 1,200,000:

Case 1: goodwill

Case 2: bargain purchase

Consideration

400,000 cash + 50,000 shares × 20 = 1,400,000

40,000 shares × 20 + 200,000 bonds = 1,000,000

Residual

1,400,000 − 1,200,000 = 200,000 goodwill

1,000,000 − 1,200,000 = 200,000 gain

A bargain purchase must survive a recheck. A negative residual often signals an error. Before recognising a gain the acquirer must reassess whether it has identified every asset and liability and review how it measured the net assets, any NCI, any previously held interest and the consideration (para. 36). Whatever remains is a gain in profit or loss on the acquisition date, attributed to the acquirer (para. 34). Forced sales and sellers leaving a business are the usual causes (para. 35). The notes go straight to the gain; their Case 2 also assumes the 10 percent bonds are worth their face value of 200,000, which holds only if 10 percent is the market rate.

Take ACE as the starting point (Note 43, PDF p. 227): identifiable net assets at fair value, after deferred tax, of 2,444,134 against a provisional consideration of 671,970.

Gain = 2,444,134 − 671,970 = 1,772,164

Dr Cash 215,431; Dr Receivables 680,565; Dr Inventories 970,281; Dr Other current assets 6; Dr Right-of-use assets 307,351; Dr Fixed assets 1,604,141 / Cr Trade and other payables 563,778; Cr Other current liabilities 23,502; Cr Decommissioning and other provisions 121,519; Cr Lease liabilities 377,366; Cr Deferred tax liabilities 247,476; Cr Cash 388,745; Cr Deferred consideration 283,225; Cr Gain from bargain purchase 1,772,164

BRPT attributes the gain to a different view of ACE's strategic direction between the seller and the group. For example (illustration), had the para. 36 review found an environmental obligation with a fair value of 50,000 that the valuation missed, the gain would fall by 50,000 before deferred tax, to 1,722,164.

7. Purchase price allocation: from book value to goodwill

On a stock acquisition the parent's ledger shows only the investment, so the fair values are rebuilt on the worksheet. The notes for AKL Chapter 3 use an allocation schedule: price minus the subsidiary's book equity is the excess, which goes first to identifiable items whose fair value differs from book value, the remainder to goodwill.

Take as the starting point BRPT's acquisition of PT UPC Sidrap Bayu Energi (SBE), operator of a 75 MW wind farm with a 30-year PPA with PLN, the state electricity company, on 2 April 2024 (Note 43, PDF pp. 233–234). BRPT reports identifiable net assets of 38,459 before the PPA, a customer contract (the PPA) of 78,709, deferred tax liabilities on the step-ups of 20,941, goodwill of 12,051 and consideration of 108,278. Ownership of 99.99 percent is treated here as 100 percent. BRPT does not give SBE's book equity; assume 31,000 for illustration.

Excess of price over book equity = 108,278 − 31,000 = 77,278

Allocation of the excess

Amount

Fixed assets and other items, fair value over book (38,459 − 31,000)

7,459

Customer contract (PPA), unrecorded by SBE

78,709

Deferred tax liability on the step-ups

(20,941)

Goodwill, the remainder

12,051

Total excess

77,278

Worksheet elimination at the acquisition date:

Dr SBE share capital and retained earnings 31,000; Dr Fixed assets and other items 7,459; Dr Customer contract 78,709; Dr Goodwill 12,051 / Cr Deferred tax liability 20,941; Cr Investment in SBE 108,278

Debits and credits are both 129,219; K2 amortises the PPA afterwards.

Deferred tax can turn a gain into goodwill. Buying shares does not change the subsidiary's tax bases, so every fair value step-up is a taxable temporary difference (carrying amount above tax base, taxed as the asset is used), and PSAK 212 requires the deferred tax liability to be recognised in the acquisition accounting, which raises goodwill by the same amount (PSAK 103 para. 24 sends deferred tax to PSAK 212). For example (illustration), a step-up of 10,000 on turbines at a 22 percent tax rate:

Deferred tax liability = 22% × 10,000 = 2,200; goodwill rises by 2,200

Each year the 1,000 of extra depreciation (ten-year life) releases 22% × 1,000 = 220: Dr Deferred tax liability 220 / Cr Deferred tax expense 220

No deferred tax is recognised on goodwill itself (PSAK 212 para. 15(a)), because goodwill is the residual and a liability on it would raise goodwill again. At SBE, BREN's tax note puts 17,316 = 22% × 78,709 of the 20,941 on the contract and the rest on other step-ups (BREN FS 2025, PDF p. 121). Without the deferred tax line, identifiable net assets would be 38,459 + 78,709 = 117,168, above the price.

117,168 − 108,278 = 8,890 bargain purchase gain, instead of goodwill of 12,051

The notes' schedules leave deferred tax out.

With less than 100 percent, NCI enters the residual. In the notes' Pam–Son case (90 percent for 10,200,000; identifiable net assets at fair value 7,000,000) the price is grossed up to an "Implied fair value of sun ($10.200.000÷90%)" of 11,333,333, so NCI is 1,133,333 and goodwill 4,333,333. PSAK 103 para. 19 allows NCI at fair value, but measured on the minority shares themselves, which carry no control premium, or at the proportionate share; the NCI essay works through the choice.

Proportionate: NCI = 10% × 7,000,000 = 700,000; goodwill = 10,200,000 + 700,000 − 7,000,000 = 3,900,000

The notes' allocation entry also omits Dr Goodwill 4,333,333; as printed it debits 1,400,000 and credits 5,733,333.

8. The measurement period

Provisional amounts can be corrected against goodwill for up to one year, because valuing a refinery or a long-term contract takes months. Provisional amounts are adjusted retrospectively for new information about facts that existed at the acquisition date (para. 45). Adjustments go against goodwill or the bargain purchase gain (para. 48), and comparatives are revised as if the final figures had been booked at the acquisition date (para. 49). After the year, only errors are corrected (para. 50).

For example (illustration), BRPT paid 101,927 at completion, and a later verification required another 6,351 (Note 43, PDF p. 233). Suppose the 6,351 had been agreed eight months after closing, from completion accounts as at the acquisition date.

Initial goodwill = 101,927 − (38,459 + 78,709 − 20,941) = 101,927 − 96,227 = 5,700

Adjustment within the measurement period: Dr Goodwill 6,351 / Cr Payable to sellers 6,351; final goodwill = 12,051

BRPT's 2025 figures have two provisional elements. ACE's consideration "is provisional as the final consideration is subject to arbitration proceedings" (Note 43, PDF p. 227). APS's fair values and its gain of 95,875 are labelled provisional, and its purchase price allocation report is dated 23 March 2026 (PDF pp. 228–229).

9. Push-down accounting

Push-down accounting, which ends the notes' Chapter 3, has no PSAK counterpart. In it the subsidiary rewrites its own books to the parent's price, revaluing assets, recording goodwill and replacing retained earnings with "push-down capital". In their example Pop pays 5,000 shares at USD 55 plus 100,000 cash for Son.

Price = 5,000 × 55 + 100,000 = 375,000; Son's identifiable net assets at fair value = 590,000 − 250,000 = 340,000; goodwill = 35,000

Their balance sheet for Son prints "Goodwill $70.000" against total assets of 625,000, which fit 35,000; 70,000 is Son's land.

Under PSAK a subsidiary's own statements stay on its carrying amounts (the figures already in its books), because goodwill recorded there would be internally generated, which PSAK 238 forbids. PSAK 338's basis for conclusions uses the term differently, for carrying a parent's earlier purchase price allocation into a later common-control transfer. The 2012 text calls that conceptually right (DK19) but rules it out for common-control combinations as impracticable (DK22), and the 2025 revision moves towards it (section 10). The fair values therefore live only on the worksheet, with the same numbers:

Dr Capital stock 150,000; Dr Retained earnings 110,000; Dr Inventories 20,000; Dr Land 40,000; Dr Equipment 40,000; Dr Goodwill 35,000 / Cr Building 20,000; Cr Investment in Son 375,000

10. Business combinations under common control

When one party controls both sides before and after a transfer, no outsider has set the consideration, so fair values lose their anchor. PSAK 103 excludes these transfers (para. 2(c)), and Indonesia applies PSAK 338 Kombinasi Bisnis Entitas Sepengendali (formerly PSAK 38), set out with an acquisition-versus-pooling table in the Share Capital essay. The receiving entity pools: carrying amounts, no goodwill, the difference from the consideration in additional paid-in capital (APIC), never recycled, and comparatives restated (Note 3e, PDF pp. 70–71).

Buying out a minority holder shows where the boundary sits. PSAK 338 para. 09 reads: "Transaksi pembelian saham atau aset neto milik pemegang saham nonpengendali (yang tidak berada dalam pengendalian yang sama dengan pemegang saham pengendali) merupakan transaksi yang mencakup perubahan substansi ekonomi kepemilikan dari pemegang saham nonpengendali ke pemegang saham pengendali. Oleh karena itu, transaksi ini bukan merupakan transaksi kombinasi bisnis entitas sepengendali." Only a minority holder outside the common control is excluded.

For example (illustration, sized on BRPT's 2025 purchase in section 12), a group company pays 200,000 for 51 percent minority stakes in two companies it already controls. The stakes are carried in the consolidated statements as NCI of 161,296.

Seller outside the common control (PSAK 110 para. 23)

Seller under the same controlling shareholder (PSAK 338)

Goodwill

None

None

Difference

200,000 − 161,296 = 38,704

38,704

Entry

Dr NCI 161,296; Dr Other equity component 38,704 / Cr Cash 200,000

Dr NCI 161,296; Dr APIC 38,704 / Cr Cash 200,000

Neither route touches profit; only the equity line differs. Had the group not controlled the companies before, PSAK 103 would apply instead, with fair values and goodwill.

Carrying amounts carry old acquisitions with them. Goodwill that a transferred business recognised on an earlier third-party purchase moves across at its carrying amount (section 12 traces one case at BRPT). The 2025 revision of PSAK 338, effective 1 January 2026, switches to the transferring entity's carrying amounts rather than the transferred entity's, unless impracticable. BRPT's 2025 statements apply the 2012 text.

11. Business combinations across industries

Renewable, property and shipping companies. Single-asset companies (a permitted project, a building, a vessel) bought through their shares mostly fail the definition of a business or pass the concentration test, so no goodwill or deferred tax on the step-up arises. BRPT applied the test to PT Marina Indah Maritim (MIM) in 2024, whose fair value was "concentrated in the value of the vessel" (Note 1d, PDF p. 42).

Oil, gas and geothermal joint operations. Buying a participating interest in a joint operation that is a business is accounted for with the acquisition method's principles, including goodwill, under PSAK 111 (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11) para. 21A.

Investment entities. A qualifying fund measures controlled investees at fair value through profit or loss, outside PSAK 103 (PSAK 110 para. 31).

12. Presentation and analysis: Barito Pacific's Note 43

BRPT's 2025 profit rests on a one-off gain from bargain purchase, most of which belongs to outside shareholders. Note 43 gives the PSAK 103 para. B64 disclosures, including the combined group's results as if acquired on 1 January (B64(q)) (PDF pp. 226–229).

Without the gain the group shows a pre-tax loss, and ACE itself lost 337,222 in nine months. ACE sits under CAP, in which BRPT holds 34.63 percent directly and 3.92 percent indirectly, and under CAPGC, 80 percent owned within the CAP group (Note 1d, PDF p. 24). Common control in BRPT's notes. On 1 October 2025 the group bought the 51 percent stakes of PT Buana Primatama Niaga (BPN) in PT Chandra Shipping International (CSI) and MIM, companies CAP already controlled (Note 1d, PDF pp. 41–42), and treated it as a common-control restructuring (Notes 29 and 31, PDF pp. 212, 216). Consideration = 87,625 + 73,350 = 160,975; carrying amount acquired = 161,296; difference = 321, credited to APIC

APIC from common-control transactions: −641,745 + 321 = −641,424

Pooling also explains part of BRPT's goodwill. BRPT took Star Energy Group Holdings at carrying amounts in 2018 (Note 1d, PDF p. 52), and the Salak and Darajat goodwill from Star Energy's purchase from Chevron sits at 485,814 in both BRPT's Note 21 (PDF p. 141) and BREN's statements (272,016 + 213,798; BREN FS 2025, PDF p. 91).

Least-confident assertions

  • The CSI/MIM purchase fits PSAK 338's wording, since BPN's beneficial owner is CDI's ultimate shareholder (Note 45h), but three things stay open. The cash flow statement calls the 160,975 "additional investment in subsidiaries from non-controlling interest" (PDF p. 19). The paragraph sits in Note 31 Other equity components beside the NCI transactions. And the full 321 goes to BRPT's APIC although BRPT owns 38.55 percent of CAP, the buyer. That "ultimate shareholder of CDI" means BRPT's controlling shareholder is also read, not stated.

  • BRPT's SBE figures disagree within the FS. Note 43's table, BREN's statements (FY2024 PDF p. 82; FY2025 PDF pp. 77–78, 91) and BRPT's own SBE impairment test (Note 21, PDF p. 142: 85,020 = 78,709 − 5,740 + 12,051) use a customer contract of 78,709 and goodwill of 12,051. Note 43's text (12,333) and Note 21's cost roll-forward (customer contract 85,593 with different amortisation; goodwill addition 12,495 = 12,333 + OMI's 162) use other numbers. Section 7 uses the 78,709 and 12,051 set.

  • The book equity of 31,000 for SBE in section 7 is an assumption. BRPT does not disclose SBE's pre-acquisition carrying amounts, so the split of the excess between step-ups and goodwill is illustrative, though the fair values, goodwill and consideration are BRPT's.

  • Whether ACE's arbitration outcome will be a measurement-period adjustment depends on whether it reflects facts at 1 April 2025 and is settled by 1 April 2026; BRPT does not say. The 2026 interim statements were not checked.

  • That the Salak and Darajat goodwill entered BRPT at carrying amount under pooling is inferred from the identical 485,814 in BRPT's Note 21 and BREN's goodwill note; BRPT does not trace the goodwill through the 2018 combination.

content.text: A business combination is a transaction in which an acquirer obtains control of a

. Buying a set of assets that is not a business is an asset acquisition: the price is spread over the assets on relative fair values, and no goodwill or bargain purchase gain arises. The optional concentration test settles many cases quickly.

Under the acquisition method (PSAK 103) the acquirer measures the consideration and every identifiable asset and liability at acquisition-date fair value, including intangibles the seller never recorded. Goodwill is the residual. A negative residual is a bargain purchase gain in profit or loss, recognised only after the numbers have been rechecked. Provisional amounts may be corrected for up to one year.

When the same party controls both sides, nothing is bought from an outsider, so PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and puts the difference from the price in additional paid-in capital.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report a gain from bargain purchase of 1,868,039 for 2025, in USD thousand, against profit for the year of 1,615,634 (BRPT FS 2025, statement of profit or loss, PDF p. 17). Two purchases by its petrochemical subsidiary produced it.

After reading this page a student should be able to classify a purchase, apply the acquisition method, allocate the excess of price over book value, handle the measurement period and record a common-control combination.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. Why companies combine and the legal forms

The legal form of a combination decides whose ledger the acquired assets land in, not how they are measured. The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 1) list the motives, from cost savings to tax, and classify combinations as

(unrelated lines). Vertical integration joins different stages of one supply chain, a refinery buying its crude supplier, rather than firms in "pasar yang berbeda" (different markets), as the notes put it.
What the acquirer records in its own books
B's assets and liabilities directly; B is dissolved
a new company C takes over both; A and B are dissolved
an investment in B; B keeps its own books and is consolidated

Measurement is the same for all three. In a merger the values go into A's ledger; in a stock acquisition they appear only on the consolidation worksheet (section 7). BRPT's 2025 purchases were stock acquisitions. CAPGC Pte. Ltd., a subsidiary of PT Chandra Asri Pacific Tbk (CAP), bought 100 percent of the shares of Aster Chemical and Energy Pte. Ltd. (ACE) from Shell Singapore (Note 1d, PDF p. 43).
2. What is a business: combination or asset acquisition
The acquisition method applies only when what is acquired is a business. PSAK 103

(formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) scopes out the acquisition of an asset or group of assets that is not a business (para. 2(b)) and combinations of entities under common control (para. 2(c)). The notes never define a business.
A business needs an input and a substantive process.
A business is an integrated set of activities and assets capable of being managed to provide goods or services to customers. Outputs are not required, but it needs at least an

that together significantly contribute to the ability to create outputs (para. B8). An operating wind farm with turbines, a power purchase agreement (PPA) and staff is a business; a development licence with no workforce is usually not.
The concentration test is a shortcut out of the definition.

Since 1 January 2021 an optional test, elected deal by deal (paras. B7A–B7B), applies. If substantially all of the fair value of the gross assets acquired is concentrated in a single identifiable asset or a group of similar assets, the set is not a business and no further analysis is needed. Cash, deferred tax assets and goodwill from deferred tax are left out of gross assets, and a tangible asset and an intangible asset are never "similar".
For example (illustration), take BRPT's acquisition of 51 percent of PT Lombok Timur Bayu Energi, a wind project company, on 3 January 2024 (Note 43, PDF pp. 231–232).
Gross assets acquired = 1 cash + 44 receivables + 2 other current + 37 fixed assets + 7,700 project development costs = 7,784
Concentration = 7,700 / 7,783 = 98.9%, substantially all in one asset
Suppose (illustration) the buyer also paid 150 of legal fees and, had the project been a business, the development rights would have been valued independently at 6,078.
Spread over assets on relative fair values
Each item at its own fair value
No settled rule; often recognised when the obligation arises

In the business column, identifiable net assets are 6,122 − 7,700 + 6,078 = 4,500 and the non-controlling interest (NCI) at its proportionate share is 2,205. BRPT's actual entry follows the asset-acquisition column, with NCI of 49% × 6,122 = 3,000 (rounded) and no goodwill.

Dr Project development costs 7,700; Dr Cash 1; Dr Receivables 44; Dr Other current assets 2; Dr Fixed assets 37 / Cr Accrued expenses 962; Cr Taxes payable 52; Cr Trade and other payables 648; Cr NCI 3,000; Cr Cash 3,122
3. The acquisition method: acquirer and acquisition date
Control, not legal form or the signing date, fixes both the acquirer and the acquisition date, the first two of the method's four steps (para. 5).
is the entity that obtains control under PSAK 110

(formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) (para. B13). When that is unclear, the standard looks at who pays, who issues shares, whose owners and managers dominate afterwards, and relative size (paras. B14–B17). In a
, typical of a backdoor listing, the owners of a private company receive enough new shares of a listed shell to control it, so the private company is the accounting acquirer (para. B19).

is the date control passes, usually the closing date, which may differ from the signing date (paras. 8–9). It fixes the fair values, the start of consolidation and the measurement period. Shell announced its agreement to sell to CAPGC on 8 May 2024, but control passed at completion on 1 April 2025, the acquisition date in Note 43 (PDF p. 226). Aster Polymer Solutions Pte. Ltd. (APS) follows the same pattern: agreement on 6 May 2025, effective and consolidated from 1 August 2025 (PDF pp. 228–229).

, the price the acquirer pays, is measured at fair value: cash paid, other assets given up, liabilities incurred to the former owners, and equity issued (para. 37). The notes' Pop Corporation example issues 100,000 shares of USD 10 par, market price USD 16, for the net assets of Son.
Dr Investment in Son 1,600,000 / Cr Common stock 1,000,000; Cr Paid-in capital 600,000

are not part of the price. Advisory, legal, accounting, valuation and internal acquisition-department costs are expensed when incurred, and the costs of issuing debt or equity follow PSAK 232 and PSAK 109 (para. 53). The notes' example reaches the same result: the 80,000 consultant fee is expensed, and SEC fees, accountants' fees and share certificates (5,000 + 10,000 + 25,000 = 40,000) reduce paid-in capital.
Dr Investment expense 80,000; Dr Paid-in capital 40,000 / Cr Cash 120,000

, a fixed amount payable later, is part of the consideration at fair value and a liability from the acquisition date. ACE's provisional consideration of 671,970 was 388,745 in cash at completion plus 283,225 deferred (Note 43, PDF p. 227).

depends on a future event, such as an earn-out. It enters the consideration at acquisition-date fair value (para. 39) and is classified as a liability or equity under PSAK 232 (para. 40). Later a liability is remeasured through profit or loss and an equity amount is not remeasured; neither touches goodwill after the measurement period (para. 58, restated in BRPT's policy, Note 3d, PDF p. 69). For example (illustration), an earn-out of 10,000 on two years' wind output is worth 2,800 at acquisition and 4,000 a year later.
At acquisition: included in consideration, Cr Contingent consideration liability 2,800
One year later: Dr Loss on remeasurement of contingent consideration 1,200 / Cr Contingent consideration liability 1,200
5. Recognising and measuring what was acquired

The acquirer recognises the identifiable assets and liabilities separately from goodwill (para. 10), at acquisition-date fair value (para. 18). Each must meet the definition of an asset or liability at that date, so a restructuring the buyer merely plans is not a liability (para. 11), and each must be part of the exchange, not a separate deal with the seller (para. 12).
Items the seller never recorded are still recognised.

An internally built brand, a customer list or a favourable contract is invisible in the seller's books but identifiable to a buyer (para. 13; see the Intangible Assets essay). A contingent liability is recognised if it is a present obligation whose fair value can be measured, even if an outflow is not probable, which PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) would not allow outside a combination (para. 23).
Deferred tax and employee benefits follow their own standards.
BRPT's policy names deferred tax under PSAK 212 (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) and employee benefits under PSAK 219 (formerly PSAK 24, IAS 19) (Note 3d, PDF p. 68).

In the notes' Pam–Sun example Sun's book net assets of 750,000 become 1,200,000 at fair value, including an unrecorded patent of 50,000 and notes payable revalued down to 135,000. Their allocation entry debits "Building – net $850.000", which is building 500,000 plus equipment 350,000. It balances, but equipment needs its own line because the two have different lives.

Goodwill is what the consideration buys beyond the identifiable net assets: synergies, the assembled workforce, expected new customers. It cannot be sold on its own, so it is measured as a residual (para. 32).
Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI + fair value of any previously held interest − identifiable net assets at fair value
The notes' two Pam–Sun cases, with identifiable net assets of 1,200,000:
A bargain purchase must survive a recheck.

A negative residual often signals an error. Before recognising a gain the acquirer must reassess whether it has identified every asset and liability and review how it measured the net assets, any NCI, any previously held interest and the consideration (para. 36). Whatever remains is a gain in profit or loss on the acquisition date, attributed to the acquirer (para. 34). Forced sales and sellers leaving a business are the usual causes (para. 35). The notes go straight to the gain; their Case 2 also assumes the 10 percent bonds are worth their face value of 200,000, which holds only if 10 percent is the market rate.
Take ACE as the starting point (Note 43, PDF p. 227): identifiable net assets at fair value, after deferred tax, of 2,444,134 against a provisional consideration of 671,970.

Dr Cash 215,431; Dr Receivables 680,565; Dr Inventories 970,281; Dr Other current assets 6; Dr Right-of-use assets 307,351; Dr Fixed assets 1,604,141 / Cr Trade and other payables 563,778; Cr Other current liabilities 23,502; Cr Decommissioning and other provisions 121,519; Cr Lease liabilities 377,366; Cr Deferred tax liabilities 247,476; Cr Cash 388,745; Cr Deferred consideration 283,225; Cr Gain from bargain purchase 1,772,164

BRPT attributes the gain to a different view of ACE's strategic direction between the seller and the group. For example (illustration), had the para. 36 review found an environmental obligation with a fair value of 50,000 that the valuation missed, the gain would fall by 50,000 before deferred tax, to 1,722,164.
7. Purchase price allocation: from book value to goodwill

On a stock acquisition the parent's ledger shows only the investment, so the fair values are rebuilt on the worksheet. The notes for AKL Chapter 3 use an allocation schedule: price minus the subsidiary's book equity is the
, which goes first to identifiable items whose fair value differs from book value, the remainder to goodwill.

Take as the starting point BRPT's acquisition of PT UPC Sidrap Bayu Energi (SBE), operator of a 75 MW wind farm with a 30-year PPA with PLN, the state electricity company, on 2 April 2024 (Note 43, PDF pp. 233–234). BRPT reports identifiable net assets of 38,459 before the PPA, a customer contract (the PPA) of 78,709, deferred tax liabilities on the step-ups of 20,941, goodwill of 12,051 and consideration of 108,278. Ownership of 99.99 percent is treated here as 100 percent. BRPT does not give SBE's book equity; assume 31,000 for illustration.
Excess of price over book equity = 108,278 − 31,000 = 77,278
Fixed assets and other items, fair value over book (38,459 − 31,000)
Deferred tax liability on the step-ups
Worksheet elimination at the acquisition date:

Dr SBE share capital and retained earnings 31,000; Dr Fixed assets and other items 7,459; Dr Customer contract 78,709; Dr Goodwill 12,051 / Cr Deferred tax liability 20,941; Cr Investment in SBE 108,278
Debits and credits are both 129,219; K2 amortises the PPA afterwards.
Deferred tax can turn a gain into goodwill.

Buying shares does not change the subsidiary's tax bases, so every fair value step-up is a taxable temporary difference (carrying amount above tax base, taxed as the asset is used), and PSAK 212 requires the deferred tax liability to be recognised in the acquisition accounting, which raises goodwill by the same amount (PSAK 103 para. 24 sends deferred tax to PSAK 212). For example (illustration), a step-up of 10,000 on turbines at a 22 percent tax rate:
Deferred tax liability = 22% × 10,000 = 2,200; goodwill rises by 2,200
Each year the 1,000 of extra depreciation (ten-year life) releases 22% × 1,000 = 220: Dr Deferred tax liability 220 / Cr Deferred tax expense 220

No deferred tax is recognised on goodwill itself (PSAK 212 para. 15(a)), because goodwill is the residual and a liability on it would raise goodwill again. At SBE, BREN's tax note puts 17,316 = 22% × 78,709 of the 20,941 on the contract and the rest on other step-ups (BREN FS 2025, PDF p. 121). Without the deferred tax line, identifiable net assets would be 38,459 + 78,709 = 117,168, above the price.
117,168 − 108,278 = 8,890 bargain purchase gain, instead of goodwill of 12,051
The notes' schedules leave deferred tax out.
With less than 100 percent, NCI enters the residual.

In the notes' Pam–Son case (90 percent for 10,200,000; identifiable net assets at fair value 7,000,000) the price is grossed up to an "Implied fair value of sun ($10.200.000÷90%)" of 11,333,333, so NCI is 1,133,333 and goodwill 4,333,333. PSAK 103 para. 19 allows NCI at fair value, but measured on the minority shares themselves, which carry no control premium, or at the proportionate share; the NCI essay works through the choice.
The notes' allocation entry also omits Dr Goodwill 4,333,333; as printed it debits 1,400,000 and credits 5,733,333.

Provisional amounts can be corrected against goodwill for up to one year, because valuing a refinery or a long-term contract takes months. Provisional amounts are adjusted retrospectively for new information about facts that existed at the acquisition date (para. 45). Adjustments go against goodwill or the bargain purchase gain (para. 48), and comparatives are revised as if the final figures had been booked at the acquisition date (para. 49). After the year, only errors are corrected (para. 50).

For example (illustration), BRPT paid 101,927 at completion, and a later verification required another 6,351 (Note 43, PDF p. 233). Suppose the 6,351 had been agreed eight months after closing, from completion accounts as at the acquisition date.
Adjustment within the measurement period: Dr Goodwill 6,351 / Cr Payable to sellers 6,351; final goodwill = 12,051

BRPT's 2025 figures have two provisional elements. ACE's consideration "is provisional as the final consideration is subject to arbitration proceedings" (Note 43, PDF p. 227). APS's fair values and its gain of 95,875 are labelled provisional, and its purchase price allocation report is dated 23 March 2026 (PDF pp. 228–229).

, which ends the notes' Chapter 3, has no PSAK counterpart. In it the subsidiary rewrites its own books to the parent's price, revaluing assets, recording goodwill and replacing retained earnings with "push-down capital". In their example Pop pays 5,000 shares at USD 55 plus 100,000 cash for Son.
Price = 5,000 × 55 + 100,000 = 375,000; Son's identifiable net assets at fair value = 590,000 − 250,000 = 340,000; goodwill = 35,000
Their balance sheet for Son prints "Goodwill $70.000" against total assets of 625,000, which fit 35,000; 70,000 is Son's land.

Under PSAK a subsidiary's own statements stay on its carrying amounts (the figures already in its books), because goodwill recorded there would be internally generated, which PSAK 238 forbids. PSAK 338's basis for conclusions uses the term differently, for carrying a parent's earlier purchase price allocation into a later common-control transfer. The 2012 text calls that conceptually right (DK19) but rules it out for common-control combinations as impracticable (DK22), and the 2025 revision moves towards it (section 10). The fair values therefore live only on the worksheet, with the same numbers:
Dr Capital stock 150,000; Dr Retained earnings 110,000; Dr Inventories 20,000; Dr Land 40,000; Dr Equipment 40,000; Dr Goodwill 35,000 / Cr Building 20,000; Cr Investment in Son 375,000

When one party controls both sides before and after a transfer, no outsider has set the consideration, so fair values lose their anchor. PSAK 103 excludes these transfers (para. 2(c)), and Indonesia applies PSAK 338

(formerly PSAK 38), set out with an acquisition-versus-pooling table in the Share Capital essay. The receiving entity pools: carrying amounts, no goodwill, the difference from the consideration in additional paid-in capital (APIC), never recycled, and comparatives restated (Note 3e, PDF pp. 70–71).
Buying out a minority holder shows where the boundary sits.

PSAK 338 para. 09 reads: "Transaksi pembelian saham atau aset neto milik pemegang saham nonpengendali (yang tidak berada dalam pengendalian yang sama dengan pemegang saham pengendali) merupakan transaksi yang mencakup perubahan substansi ekonomi kepemilikan dari pemegang saham nonpengendali ke pemegang saham pengendali. Oleh karena itu, transaksi ini bukan merupakan transaksi kombinasi bisnis entitas sepengendali." Only a minority holder outside the common control is excluded.

For example (illustration, sized on BRPT's 2025 purchase in section 12), a group company pays 200,000 for 51 percent minority stakes in two companies it already controls. The stakes are carried in the consolidated statements as NCI of 161,296.
Seller outside the common control (PSAK 110 para. 23)
Seller under the same controlling shareholder (PSAK 338)
Dr NCI 161,296; Dr Other equity component 38,704 / Cr Cash 200,000
Dr NCI 161,296; Dr APIC 38,704 / Cr Cash 200,000
Neither route touches profit; only the equity line differs. Had the group not controlled the companies before, PSAK 103 would apply instead, with fair values and goodwill.
Carrying amounts carry old acquisitions with them.

Goodwill that a transferred business recognised on an earlier third-party purchase moves across at its carrying amount (section 12 traces one case at BRPT). The 2025 revision of PSAK 338, effective 1 January 2026, switches to the transferring entity's carrying amounts rather than the transferred entity's, unless impracticable. BRPT's 2025 statements apply the 2012 text.

Single-asset companies (a permitted project, a building, a vessel) bought through their shares mostly fail the definition of a business or pass the concentration test, so no goodwill or deferred tax on the step-up arises. BRPT applied the test to PT Marina Indah Maritim (MIM) in 2024, whose fair value was "concentrated in the value of the vessel" (Note 1d, PDF p. 42).
Oil, gas and geothermal joint operations.

Buying a participating interest in a joint operation that is a business is accounted for with the acquisition method's principles, including goodwill, under PSAK 111 (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11) para. 21A.
A qualifying fund measures controlled investees at fair value through profit or loss, outside PSAK 103 (PSAK 110 para. 31).
12. Presentation and analysis: Barito Pacific's Note 43

BRPT's 2025 profit rests on a one-off gain from bargain purchase, most of which belongs to outside shareholders. Note 43 gives the PSAK 103 para. B64 disclosures, including the combined group's results as if acquired on 1 January (B64(q)) (PDF pp. 226–229).
Identifiable net assets at fair value
Group revenue and profit if acquired 1 January
Profit before tax excluding the gain = 1,602,988 − 1,868,039 = (265,051)
Profit attributable to owners of the parent = 489,807 / 1,615,634 = 30.3% of profit for the year

Without the gain the group shows a pre-tax loss, and ACE itself lost 337,222 in nine months. ACE sits under CAP, in which BRPT holds 34.63 percent directly and 3.92 percent indirectly, and under CAPGC, 80 percent owned within the CAP group (Note 1d, PDF p. 24). The gain is attributed to the acquirer, CAPGC, and flows up through each layer's NCI.
BRPT's effective interest in ACE = (34.63% + 3.92% through its wholly owned Marigold) × 80% = 38.55% × 80% = 30.84%
That is roughly consistent with the 30.3 percent of group profit attributed to BRPT's owners.

On 1 October 2025 the group bought the 51 percent stakes of PT Buana Primatama Niaga (BPN) in PT Chandra Shipping International (CSI) and MIM, companies CAP already controlled (Note 1d, PDF pp. 41–42), and treated it as a common-control restructuring (Notes 29 and 31, PDF pp. 212, 216). BPN's "beneficial owner is the ultimate shareholder of CDI" (PT Chandra Daya Investasi Tbk, a CAP subsidiary; Note 45h, PDF p. 236), which fits para. 09.
Consideration = 87,625 + 73,350 = 160,975; carrying amount acquired = 161,296; difference = 321, credited to APIC

Pooling also explains part of BRPT's goodwill. BRPT took Star Energy Group Holdings at carrying amounts in 2018 (Note 1d, PDF p. 52), and the Salak and Darajat goodwill from Star Energy's purchase from Chevron sits at 485,814 in both BRPT's Note 21 (PDF p. 141) and BREN's statements (272,016 + 213,798; BREN FS 2025, PDF p. 91).
: NCI at acquisition and changes in ownership.
: PSAK 338 in full and the negative APIC it leaves.
: temporary differences on fair value step-ups.
: acquisitions in the cash flow statement and mid-year.
: the BRPT, CAP and BREN layers.

The CSI/MIM purchase fits PSAK 338's wording, since BPN's beneficial owner is CDI's ultimate shareholder (Note 45h), but three things stay open. The cash flow statement calls the 160,975 "additional investment in subsidiaries from non-controlling interest" (PDF p. 19). The paragraph sits in Note 31

beside the NCI transactions. And the full 321 goes to BRPT's APIC although BRPT owns 38.55 percent of CAP, the buyer. That "ultimate shareholder of CDI" means BRPT's controlling shareholder is also read, not stated.

BRPT's SBE figures disagree within the FS. Note 43's table, BREN's statements (FY2024 PDF p. 82; FY2025 PDF pp. 77–78, 91) and BRPT's own SBE impairment test (Note 21, PDF p. 142: 85,020 = 78,709 − 5,740 + 12,051) use a customer contract of 78,709 and goodwill of 12,051. Note 43's text (12,333) and Note 21's cost roll-forward (customer contract 85,593 with different amortisation; goodwill addition 12,495 = 12,333 + OMI's 162) use other numbers. Section 7 uses the 78,709 and 12,051 set.

The book equity of 31,000 for SBE in section 7 is an assumption. BRPT does not disclose SBE's pre-acquisition carrying amounts, so the split of the excess between step-ups and goodwill is illustrative, though the fair values, goodwill and consideration are BRPT's.

Whether ACE's arbitration outcome will be a measurement-period adjustment depends on whether it reflects facts at 1 April 2025 and is settled by 1 April 2026; BRPT does not say. The 2026 interim statements were not checked.

That the Salak and Darajat goodwill entered BRPT at carrying amount under pooling is inferred from the identical 485,814 in BRPT's Note 21 and BREN's goodwill note; BRPT does not trace the goodwill through the 2018 combination.
