presentation.deck: The theory of accounting for an acquisition from the definition of a business to pooling of interests, worked from Barito Pacific's 2025 purchases and set beside the industries where the boundary matters most
key_takeaways: A business combination is a transaction in which an acquirer obtains control of a business. Buying a set of assets that is not a business is an asset acquisition: the price is spread over the assets on relative fair values, and no goodwill or bargain purchase gain arises. The optional concentration test settles many cases quickly.

Under the acquisition method (PSAK 103) the acquirer measures the consideration and every identifiable asset and liability at acquisition-date fair value, including intangibles the seller never recorded. Goodwill is the residual. A negative residual is a bargain purchase gain in profit or loss, recognised only after the numbers have been rechecked. Provisional amounts may be corrected for up to one year.

When the same party controls both sides, nothing is bought from an outsider, so PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and puts the difference from the price in additional paid-in capital.

title: Cash and Cash Equivalents: What Counts, How It Is Controlled, and How It Moves
snippet: The theory of the cash line from definition to the cash flow statement, worked through PHE's balances and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • Cash is money the entity can spend today, meaning cash on hand and demand deposits. A cash equivalent is an investment held for short-term cash needs that converts to a known amount with insignificant risk, which in practice means a maturity of three months or less from the date it was acquired. Everything else that looks like cash, from post-dated cheques to six-month deposits, belongs on another line.

  • Cash is the asset most exposed to error and theft, so its accounting is mostly control, through an imprest petty cash fund and a bank reconciliation that separates items the bank has not yet recorded from items the books have not yet recorded. Only the second kind needs a journal.

  • The balance sheet shows where cash ended up; the cash flow statement (PSAK 207) explains how it got there, through operating, investing and financing flows plus a separate line for exchange-rate effects. Moves between cash and cash equivalents are not cash flows, and an overdraft that is part of day-to-day cash management can count as negative cash in the flow statement while staying a liability on the balance sheet.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report cash and cash equivalents of 2,614,318 at 31 December 2024 against 5,018,739 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 8.6 percent of total assets and 32.5 percent of current assets, down from 16.2 and 50.8 percent. This page uses those balances as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to say what belongs in the line, record the entries that keep it accurate, and trace a change in cash through the cash flow statement.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The order follows the chapter on cash in Kieso's Intermediate Accounting (IFRS edition) and the structure of PSAK 207.

1. What counts as cash

Cash is the one asset whose value needs no estimate, and the definition protects that. PSAK 207 Statement of Cash Flows (formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7) defines cash as cash on hand and demand deposits (para. 6). A demand deposit is a bank balance the holder can withdraw at any time without notice or penalty, such as a current account (giro) or a savings account.

The test is whether the item is money now. Kieso's textbook works through the items a cashier finds in the drawer, and they sort into three groups.

Item

Where it goes

Why

Coins, banknotes, cheques and money orders received but not yet deposited

Cash

The bank will accept them as money at once

Current accounts and savings accounts

Cash

Withdrawable on demand

Petty cash and change funds

Cash

Money on hand, kept for small payments

Post-dated cheques from customers

Trade receivables

Not payable until a later date

Cheques returned unpaid (NSF, "not sufficient funds")

Receivables

A claim on the customer, not money

Employee IOUs and travel advances

Other receivables or prepayments

Money will come back as cash or as receipts for expenses

Postage stamps, prepaid vouchers

Prepaid expenses

Already spent on a future service

Time deposits

Cash equivalents or investments

Depends on maturity at acquisition (section 2)

Overdrawn bank accounts

Liabilities

Money owed to the bank (section 4)

PHE's Note 6 has three components, cash on hand of 171, cash in banks of 2,476,825 and time deposits of 137,323 (Daftar 5/90, PDF p. 107). For a group with more than 2.6 billion dollars of cash, 171 of notes and coins is almost nothing, the pattern of a business that settles almost everything through banks.

2. Cash equivalents and the three-month rule

A cash equivalent is defined by its purpose and by the certainty of what it converts into. PSAK 207 calls cash equivalents "short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to known amounts of cash and which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value" (para. 6), held "for the purpose of meeting short-term cash commitments rather than for investment or other purposes" (para. 7). Two consequences follow.

  • Equity investments are excluded unless they are cash equivalents in substance, such as preference shares bought shortly before a fixed redemption date (para. 7). A listed share can be sold in a minute, but nobody knows for how much.

  • Maturity is measured from the date of acquisition. The standard says an investment "normally" qualifies only with a maturity of "three months or less from the date of acquisition" (para. 7). A six-month deposit therefore never becomes a cash equivalent, even when only one month is left. A two-year government bond bought with two months to run, for cash management, can qualify from the day it is bought.

PHE's policy uses the same boundary, admitting time deposits "with maturity periods of three months or less at the time of placement which are not used as collateral or are not restricted" (Note 3f, Daftar 5/38, PDF p. 55).

For example (illustration), on 1 October 2024 a PHE subsidiary has 100,000 more than it needs for the next quarter. Its treasury places 40,000 in a three-month USD deposit maturing on 1 January 2025 and 60,000 in a six-month deposit maturing on 1 April 2025, both at 5.0 percent a year.

Three-month deposit: maturity at placement = 3 months, so it is a cash equivalent

Six-month deposit: maturity at placement = 6 months, so it is a short-term investment

Interest accrued at 31 December = 40,000 × 5.0% × 3/12 = 500 (three-month); 60,000 × 5.0% × 3/12 = 750 (six-month)

Three-month deposit

Six-month deposit

1 October

Dr Cash equivalents, time deposits 40,000 / Cr Cash in banks 40,000

Dr Short-term investments, time deposits 60,000 / Cr Cash in banks 60,000

31 December

Dr Interest receivable 500 / Cr Finance income 500

Dr Interest receivable 750 / Cr Finance income 750

Cash flow statement, 2024

No flow: a move within cash and cash equivalents (para. 9)

Investing outflow of 60,000

Both deposits are measured at amortised cost, principal plus interest accrued at the deposit's own rate; here the accrued interest is shown as a receivable, though some entities add it to the deposit. They differ only in the line they sit on, and that decides whether the placement is a cash flow at all.

3. Restricted cash and compensating balances

A demand deposit stays cash even when a contract says what it may be spent on; it leaves the line only when the entity cannot withdraw it on demand. The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in April 2022 that restrictions on use agreed with a third party do not stop a deposit being cash "unless those restrictions change the nature of the deposit in a way that it would no longer meet the definition of cash". A restriction that leaves the money withdrawable is handled by disclosure.

A balance the entity cannot withdraw, because a bank blocks it as collateral or because a third party such as a regulator or a lender must consent to each withdrawal, is restricted cash. Kieso's compensating balance, a minimum deposit a lender requires as part of a loan, is the textbook case when the agreement legally blocks it. PHE shows restricted cash on two separate lines, current 154,217 and non-current 1,890,493 (Note 7, Daftar 5/93, PDF p. 110), and the companion page restricted-cash treats it in full.

4. Bank overdrafts and offsetting

An overdraft is a loan from the bank, so it is a liability. Two different rules then decide whether it may be netted against positive balances, one for the balance sheet and one for the cash flow statement.

On the balance sheet, PSAK 232 Financial Instruments: Presentation (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) allows a financial asset and a financial liability to be shown net only when the entity has a legally enforceable right to set them off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (para. 42). Accounts at different banks almost never meet the test. Accounts at the same bank meet it only if the agreement gives a set-off right and the entity intends to settle net.

In the cash flow statement, PSAK 207 makes an exception to the rule that bank borrowings are financing. Overdrafts "repayable on demand" that "form an integral part of an entity's cash management" are a negative component of cash and cash equivalents, typically where "the bank balance often fluctuates from being positive to overdrawn" (para. 8).

For example (illustration), at 31 December 2024 a PHE subsidiary has 5,000 in its account at bank X and an operating account at bank Y overdrawn by 1,200. The account at Y swings between positive and overdrawn as invoices fall due before monthly sales receipts arrive, and bank Y can call the overdraft at any time.

Balance sheet

Cash flow statement

Rule

PSAK 232.42: no right of set-off between banks X and Y

PSAK 207.8: overdraft repayable on demand and part of cash management

Cash and cash equivalents

5,000

5,000 − 1,200 = 3,800

Overdraft

1,200 within short-term bank loans

Not a financing flow; drawing and repaying it are movements within cash

The note on cash must then reconcile the 3,800 in the cash flow statement with the 5,000 on the balance sheet (para. 45). PHE's short-term bank loans of 15,775, part of which PDSI draws through a notional pooling arrangement, are shown as loans (Note 26, Daftar 5/125, PDF p. 142); its cash flow statement closes at the same 2,614,318 as the balance sheet, so no overdraft is netted into cash.

5. Controlling cash: petty cash

Small payments are made from a fund kept on hand, and the imprest system keeps it under control by fixing its size. A custodian holds a set amount. Each payment is supported by a receipt, so receipts plus remaining cash should always equal the fixed amount. When the fund runs low it is topped back up to that amount, and the expenses are recorded only then, from the receipts.

For example (illustration), a PHE field office sets up a petty cash fund of 8.0 (USD 8 thousand). By month end the custodian holds receipts for local transport 3.1, meals for a site crew 2.4 and office supplies 1.6, and counts 0.8 of cash.

Receipts + cash = 3.1 + 2.4 + 1.6 + 0.8 = 7.9, against a fund of 8.0, so 0.1 is short

Replenishment = 8.0 − 0.8 = 7.2

Establish the fund

Replenish at month end

Dr Petty cash 8.0

Dr Transport expense 3.1, Dr Meals expense 2.4, Dr Office supplies expense 1.6, Dr Cash over and short 0.1

Cr Cash in banks 8.0

Cr Cash in banks 7.2

The petty cash account moves only when the fund's fixed size is changed. Setting up and replenishing the fund move money between two cash accounts, so neither is a cash flow; the outflow is what the custodian paid out. Cash over and short is an expense when short and other income when over, and a shortage that recurs is a control finding. Kieso's other controls follow the same logic: separate handling cash from recording it, deposit receipts intact daily, and pay everything else through the bank.

6. Controlling cash: the bank reconciliation

The bank's record and the entity's record of the same account rarely agree at month end, and the bank reconciliation explains why. Each side is adjusted for what it does not yet know, until both reach the same correct balance.

Bank side: balance per bank + deposits in transit − outstanding cheques ± bank errors = correct balance

Book side: balance per books + collections and interest credited by the bank − bank charges − returned (NSF) cheques ± book errors = correct balance

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary's USD account at 31 December 2024.

  • The bank statement shows 12,480. A deposit of 1,350 made on 31 December reaches the bank in January (deposit in transit). Cheques of 2,940 issued to vendors have not been presented (outstanding cheques).

  • The books show 9,912. The bank has credited interest of 62 and a joint-venture partner's cash call of 800 paid directly into the account, and has deducted charges of 4. A cheque for 150 from a scrap buyer came back unpaid. A vendor payment of 1,250 was recorded in the books as 1,520.

Bank side = 12,480 + 1,350 − 2,940 = 10,890

Book side = 9,912 + 62 + 800 − 4 − 150 + (1,520 − 1,250) = 9,912 + 62 + 800 − 4 − 150 + 270 = 10,890

Both sides reach 10,890, which is the cash the balance sheet should show. Bank-side items need no entry, because the books are already right about them; the bank will catch up in January. Book-side items each need a journal.

Item

Journal

Interest credited

Dr Cash in banks 62 / Cr Finance income 62

Partner's cash call received

Dr Cash in banks 800 / Cr Receivable from joint operation partners 800

Bank charges

Dr Bank charges expense 4 / Cr Cash in banks 4

Returned cheque

Dr Other receivables, scrap buyer 150 / Cr Cash in banks 150

Recording error

Dr Cash in banks 270 / Cr Trade payables 270

Book balance after the five entries = 9,912 + 62 + 800 − 4 − 150 + 270 = 10,890

The recording error is credited to trade payables because the original entry debited payables with 1,520 when only 1,250 was settled.

7. Foreign currency cash and credit losses on bank balances

Cash in another currency is a monetary item, an amount fixed in units of that currency, so its value in the functional currency moves with the exchange rate. PSAK 221 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21) retranslates monetary items at the closing rate at each reporting date and takes the difference to profit or loss. PHE's functional currency is the US dollar for every entity except Elnusa, and its monetary items are translated at the closing JISDOR rate, Bank Indonesia's reference rate (Note 3r, Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83). PHE held rupiah bank accounts of 375,921 at the end of 2024 (Note 6, Daftar 5/91, PDF p. 108).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary holds IDR 154,000 million throughout 2024 to pay local vendors, while the rupiah weakens from 15,400 to 16,000 per dollar (constructed rates).

USD value at 1 January = IDR 154,000 million / 15,400 = USD 10.0 million = 10,000

USD value at 31 December = IDR 154,000 million / 16,000 = 9,625

Exchange loss = 10,000 − 9,625 = 375

Dr Foreign exchange loss 375 / Cr Cash in banks 375

No money left the account, so the 375 is not a cash flow. PSAK 207 still shows it, on a separate line after the three activities, so that opening cash plus flows plus the exchange effect equals closing cash (para. 28). If flows had occurred during the year, that line would also absorb the difference between translating them at transaction-date rates and at the closing rate (paras. 25, 28).

Bank balances are also financial assets at amortised cost, so PSAK 109 Financial Instruments (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9) requires an expected credit loss (ECL), the probability-weighted loss if the bank fails. For a bank with low credit risk the entity may assume credit risk has not increased significantly and measure only twelve-month expected losses. For example (illustration), 1,000,000 at a domestic bank with a 0.05 percent one-year probability of default and a 45 percent loss if default occurs.

ECL = 1,000,000 × 0.05% × 45% = 225

Dr Impairment loss on financial assets 225 / Cr Allowance for credit losses, cash in banks 225

The amount is usually immaterial, which is why cash notes seldom show it. PHE reports that 4,182,445 of its 4,521,534 of cash in banks and restricted cash sits with Pefindo-rated counterparties, 338,966 with Fitch, Moody's or S&P-rated ones and 123 with unrated ones (Note 49c, Daftar 5/232, PDF p. 249).

8. From the balance to the cash flow statement

The cash flow statement exists because two balances cannot explain the change between them. PSAK 207 sorts every cash flow into three activities (para. 6).

  • Operating: the principal revenue-producing activities, and anything that is not investing or financing.

  • Investing: the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and other investments not included in cash equivalents. Only spending that results in a recognised asset may be classified here (para. 16).

  • Financing: changes in equity and borrowings.

Movements between items that are all cash or cash equivalents are not flows (para. 9). Operating cash flows can be shown by the direct method, which lists gross receipts and payments, or the indirect method, which starts from profit and adjusts for non-cash items and working capital. The standard encourages the direct method (para. 19), and PHE uses it (Note 3a, Daftar 5/29, PDF p. 46).

The examples above land in the statement as follows.

Item from this page

Cash flow treatment

Three-month deposit (section 2)

No flow

Six-month deposit (section 2)

Investing outflow 60,000, and an investing inflow on maturity

Overdraft at bank Y (section 4)

Negative cash; no financing flow

Petty cash spending (section 5)

Operating outflow 7.2 (payments 7.1 and the 0.1 shortage), recorded at replenishment; setting up and topping up the fund are moves within cash

Exchange loss on rupiah (section 7)

Separate line, (375)

ECL (section 7)

Not a flow; a non-cash item in an indirect-method reconciliation

Interest and dividends are each disclosed separately and classified consistently (para. 31). Today a non-financial entity may put interest paid in operating or financing, interest and dividends received in operating or investing, and dividends paid in financing or operating (paras. 33–34). That choice ends with IFRS 18. Its amendments to IAS 7 require an entity like PHE, whose main business is not investing or lending, to classify interest and dividends paid as financing and interest and dividends received as investing, for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Indonesia's PSAK 118, ratified by DSAK IAI on 28 May 2025, takes effect on the same date.

9. Cash across industries

The definition is the same everywhere. What differs is which flows are operating, what may be netted, and whose money it is.

Banks. For a bank, deposits from customers and loans to them are the business itself, so interest paid and received are usually operating (para. 33), and deposits with fixed maturities, placements with other banks and customer loans may be reported net (para. 24). A bank's own cash and cash equivalents usually include its current account at the central bank. In Indonesia that account carries the statutory reserve requirement (giro wajib minimum, GWM), a minimum balance Bank Indonesia requires against deposits; banks commonly keep it within cash and cash equivalents even though it cannot all be spent.

Agents holding other people's money. Receipts that reflect the customer's activities more than the entity's may be shown net, for example "funds held for customers by an investment entity" and "rents collected on behalf of, and paid over to, the owners of properties" (paras. 22–23). For example (illustration), a property manager collects rent of 900 for owners, keeps a 10 percent fee and pays over the rest.

Gross presentation: receipts 900, payments to owners (810)

Net presentation: fee received 900 × 10% = 90

Whether the money held belongs in the agent's cash at all depends on whose account it is and whether the agent can draw it.

Cryptocurrency. A holding of cryptocurrency fails both tests. It is neither currency on hand nor a bank deposit, and its value is too volatile for a cash equivalent. The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in June 2019 that it is inventory if held for sale in the ordinary course of business and an intangible asset under PSAK 238 (formerly PSAK 19, IAS 38) otherwise.

Groups with subsidiaries under exchange controls. Cash held by a subsidiary in a country whose laws stop it being sent to the parent stays in the group's cash, but PSAK 207 requires disclosure of significant balances "not available for use by the group", with a commentary by management (paras. 48–49). PHE holds small balances in currencies such as the Algerian dinar (1,721 at the end of 2024, Note 6, Daftar 5/92, PDF p. 109); the FS do not say whether any of its cash is subject to such controls.

Group cash pooling. In a physical pool, balances are swept daily into one master account; in a notional pool, they stay in separate accounts and the bank pays interest on their net position. Showing the pool net needs both a set-off right and an intention to settle net (PSAK 232.42). In 2016 the IFRS Interpretations Committee looked at a notional pool that had the right but whose members kept using their own accounts before each net settlement. It concluded that the group could not claim an intention to settle the period-end balances net, so they stay gross. Other pools need their own judgement.

10. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 6

PSAK 207 asks for the policy for determining cash equivalents, the components of cash and cash equivalents, a reconciliation to the balance sheet, and significant balances not available for use (paras. 45–48). PHE gives components, banks and currencies (Note 6, Daftar 5/90–5/93, PDF pp. 107–110).

The 2024 components add to 2,614,319, one thousand above the printed total through rounding. Dollar accounts make up 2,048,144 of the 2,476,825 of cash in banks (82.7 percent), and 2,386,340 of the line (91.3 percent) sits with government-related banks (Note 44b, Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199). The cash flow statement explains the fall (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17).

A pattern of spending that left cash 589,583 higher in 2023 drew it down in 2024 because operating receipts were lower. The ratio shows the size of the buffer. Reading why it moved takes the cash flow statement, and both years of it.

11. Upstream note: cash in joint operations

Many upstream blocks are joint operations, in which each party recognises its share of the assets held jointly under PSAK 111 Joint Arrangements (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11). A non-operator usually pays the operator ahead of spending, a cash call. The payment leaves the partner's cash and becomes an advance until the operator reports how it was spent. PHE shows cash call advances of 76,196 among current advances at the end of 2024, against 132,275 a year earlier (Note 15, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123).

12. Related lines

  • restricted-cash: balances the group cannot withdraw on demand, current and non-current.

  • short-term-bank-loans: where overdrafts and pooling balances sit on the balance sheet.

  • advances-prepayments-current: cash calls paid to operators.

  • finance-income: interest on bank balances and time deposits.

  • foreign-exchange-loss-net: retranslation of non-dollar balances.

Least-confident assertions

  • That large Indonesian banks include their current account at Bank Indonesia (giro pada Bank Indonesia) in cash and cash equivalents is confirmed only through a secondary source (CNBC Indonesia on BRI, Mandiri, BCA and BNI); how much of that balance is the GWM, and whether all banks follow the same policy, was not checked in a bank's FS.

  • How a non-operator presents its share of cash still held in an operator's joint account (as cash, or within advances until the billing statement) depends on the agreement and reporting practice; PHE's FS do not say, and IFRS 11.20 was not opened.

  • The IFRS 18 amendments to IAS 7 are confirmed through secondary sources (KPMG, BDO), and PSAK 118's ratification and effective date through IAI. Whether DSAK has issued the matching amendment to PSAK 207 with the same wording was not confirmed.

  • The ECL mechanics (low-credit-risk simplification, twelve-month measure) and PSAK 232.42 are stated from knowledge of IFRS 9 and IAS 32; their paragraphs were not opened, although the 2016 cash-pooling decision restates para. 42(b).

  • Kieso's classification table and the imprest and reconciliation formats come from knowledge of the textbook; no copy was opened.

content.text: Cash is money the entity can spend today, meaning cash on hand and demand deposits. A cash equivalent is an investment held for short-term cash needs that converts to a known amount with insignificant risk, which in practice means a maturity of three months or less from the date it was acquired. Everything else that looks like cash, from post-dated cheques to six-month deposits, belongs on another line.

Cash is the asset most exposed to error and theft, so its accounting is mostly control, through an imprest petty cash fund and a bank reconciliation that separates items the bank has not yet recorded from items the books have not yet recorded. Only the second kind needs a journal.

The balance sheet shows where cash ended up; the cash flow statement (PSAK 207) explains how it got there, through operating, investing and financing flows plus a separate line for exchange-rate effects. Moves between cash and cash equivalents are not cash flows, and an overdraft that is part of day-to-day cash management can count as negative cash in the flow statement while staying a liability on the balance sheet.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report cash and cash equivalents of 2,614,318 at 31 December 2024 against 5,018,739 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 8.6 percent of total assets and 32.5 percent of current assets, down from 16.2 and 50.8 percent. This page uses those balances as the starting point for its examples.
After reading it a student should be able to say what belongs in the line, record the entries that keep it accurate, and trace a change in cash through the cash flow statement.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The order follows the chapter on cash in Kieso's
(IFRS edition) and the structure of PSAK 207.
Cash is the one asset whose value needs no estimate, and the definition protects that. PSAK 207
as cash on hand and demand deposits (para. 6). A
is a bank balance the holder can withdraw at any time without notice or penalty, such as a current account (
The test is whether the item is money now. Kieso's textbook works through the items a cashier finds in the drawer, and they sort into three groups.
Coins, banknotes, cheques and money orders received but not yet deposited
The bank will accept them as money at once
Money on hand, kept for small payments
Not payable until a later date
A claim on the customer, not money
Money will come back as cash or as receipts for expenses
Already spent on a future service

PHE's Note 6 has three components, cash on hand of 171, cash in banks of 2,476,825 and time deposits of 137,323 (Daftar 5/90, PDF p. 107). For a group with more than 2.6 billion dollars of cash, 171 of notes and coins is almost nothing, the pattern of a business that settles almost everything through banks.
2. Cash equivalents and the three-month rule

A cash equivalent is defined by its purpose and by the certainty of what it converts into. PSAK 207 calls cash equivalents "short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to known amounts of cash and which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value" (para. 6), held "for the purpose of meeting short-term cash commitments rather than for investment or other purposes" (para. 7). Two consequences follow.

unless they are cash equivalents in substance, such as preference shares bought shortly before a fixed redemption date (para. 7). A listed share can be sold in a minute, but nobody knows for how much.
Maturity is measured from the date of acquisition.

The standard says an investment "normally" qualifies only with a maturity of "three months or less from the date of acquisition" (para. 7). A six-month deposit therefore never becomes a cash equivalent, even when only one month is left. A two-year government bond bought with two months to run, for cash management, can qualify from the day it is bought.

PHE's policy uses the same boundary, admitting time deposits "with maturity periods of three months or less at the time of placement which are not used as collateral or are not restricted" (Note 3f, Daftar 5/38, PDF p. 55).

For example (illustration), on 1 October 2024 a PHE subsidiary has 100,000 more than it needs for the next quarter. Its treasury places 40,000 in a three-month USD deposit maturing on 1 January 2025 and 60,000 in a six-month deposit maturing on 1 April 2025, both at 5.0 percent a year.
Three-month deposit: maturity at placement = 3 months, so it is a cash equivalent
Six-month deposit: maturity at placement = 6 months, so it is a short-term investment
Dr Cash equivalents, time deposits 40,000 / Cr Cash in banks 40,000
Dr Short-term investments, time deposits 60,000 / Cr Cash in banks 60,000
Dr Interest receivable 500 / Cr Finance income 500
Dr Interest receivable 750 / Cr Finance income 750
No flow: a move within cash and cash equivalents (para. 9)

, principal plus interest accrued at the deposit's own rate; here the accrued interest is shown as a receivable, though some entities add it to the deposit. They differ only in the line they sit on, and that decides whether the placement is a cash flow at all.

A demand deposit stays cash even when a contract says what it may be spent on; it leaves the line only when the entity cannot withdraw it on demand. The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in April 2022 that restrictions on use agreed with a third party do not stop a deposit being cash "unless those restrictions change the nature of the deposit in a way that it would no longer meet the definition of cash". A restriction that leaves the money withdrawable is handled by disclosure.
A balance the entity cannot withdraw, because a bank blocks it as collateral or because a third party such as a regulator or a lender must consent to each withdrawal, is

, a minimum deposit a lender requires as part of a loan, is the textbook case when the agreement legally blocks it. PHE shows restricted cash on two separate lines, current 154,217 and non-current 1,890,493 (Note 7, Daftar 5/93, PDF p. 110), and the companion page

An overdraft is a loan from the bank, so it is a liability. Two different rules then decide whether it may be netted against positive balances, one for the balance sheet and one for the cash flow statement.

(formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) allows a financial asset and a financial liability to be shown net only when the entity has a legally enforceable right to set them off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (para. 42). Accounts at different banks almost never meet the test. Accounts at the same bank meet it only if the agreement gives a set-off right and the entity intends to settle net.

In the cash flow statement, PSAK 207 makes an exception to the rule that bank borrowings are financing. Overdrafts "repayable on demand" that "form an integral part of an entity's cash management" are a negative component of cash and cash equivalents, typically where "the bank balance often fluctuates from being positive to overdrawn" (para. 8).

For example (illustration), at 31 December 2024 a PHE subsidiary has 5,000 in its account at bank X and an operating account at bank Y overdrawn by 1,200. The account at Y swings between positive and overdrawn as invoices fall due before monthly sales receipts arrive, and bank Y can call the overdraft at any time.
PSAK 232.42: no right of set-off between banks X and Y
PSAK 207.8: overdraft repayable on demand and part of cash management
Not a financing flow; drawing and repaying it are movements within cash

The note on cash must then reconcile the 3,800 in the cash flow statement with the 5,000 on the balance sheet (para. 45). PHE's short-term bank loans of 15,775, part of which PDSI draws through a notional pooling arrangement, are shown as loans (Note 26, Daftar 5/125, PDF p. 142); its cash flow statement closes at the same 2,614,318 as the balance sheet, so no overdraft is netted into cash.
Small payments are made from a fund kept on hand, and the

keeps it under control by fixing its size. A custodian holds a set amount. Each payment is supported by a receipt, so receipts plus remaining cash should always equal the fixed amount. When the fund runs low it is topped back up to that amount, and the expenses are recorded only then, from the receipts.

For example (illustration), a PHE field office sets up a petty cash fund of 8.0 (USD 8 thousand). By month end the custodian holds receipts for local transport 3.1, meals for a site crew 2.4 and office supplies 1.6, and counts 0.8 of cash.
Receipts + cash = 3.1 + 2.4 + 1.6 + 0.8 = 7.9, against a fund of 8.0, so 0.1 is short
Dr Transport expense 3.1, Dr Meals expense 2.4, Dr Office supplies expense 1.6, Dr Cash over and short 0.1

The petty cash account moves only when the fund's fixed size is changed. Setting up and replenishing the fund move money between two cash accounts, so neither is a cash flow; the outflow is what the custodian paid out.

is an expense when short and other income when over, and a shortage that recurs is a control finding. Kieso's other controls follow the same logic: separate handling cash from recording it, deposit receipts intact daily, and pay everything else through the bank.
The bank's record and the entity's record of the same account rarely agree at month end, and the
explains why. Each side is adjusted for what it does not yet know, until both reach the same correct balance.
Bank side: balance per bank + deposits in transit − outstanding cheques ± bank errors = correct balance
Book side: balance per books + collections and interest credited by the bank − bank charges − returned (NSF) cheques ± book errors = correct balance
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary's USD account at 31 December 2024.

The bank statement shows 12,480. A deposit of 1,350 made on 31 December reaches the bank in January (deposit in transit). Cheques of 2,940 issued to vendors have not been presented (outstanding cheques).

The books show 9,912. The bank has credited interest of 62 and a joint-venture partner's cash call of 800 paid directly into the account, and has deducted charges of 4. A cheque for 150 from a scrap buyer came back unpaid. A vendor payment of 1,250 was recorded in the books as 1,520.

Both sides reach 10,890, which is the cash the balance sheet should show. Bank-side items need no entry, because the books are already right about them; the bank will catch up in January. Book-side items each need a journal.

Dr Cash in banks 800 / Cr Receivable from joint operation partners 800
Dr Bank charges expense 4 / Cr Cash in banks 4

Book balance after the five entries = 9,912 + 62 + 800 − 4 − 150 + 270 = 10,890
The recording error is credited to trade payables because the original entry debited payables with 1,520 when only 1,250 was settled.

Cash in another currency is a

(formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21) retranslates monetary items at the closing rate at each reporting date and takes the difference to profit or loss. PHE's functional currency is the US dollar for every entity except Elnusa, and its monetary items are translated at the closing JISDOR rate, Bank Indonesia's reference rate (Note 3r, Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83). presentation.deck: The theory of the cash line from definition to the cash flow statement, worked through PHE's balances and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: Cash is money the entity can spend today, meaning cash on hand and demand deposits. A cash equivalent is an investment held for short-term cash needs that converts to a known amount with insignificant risk, which in practice means a maturity of three months or less from the date it was acquired. Everything else that looks like cash, from post-dated cheques to six-month deposits, belongs on another line.

Cash is the asset most exposed to error and theft, so its accounting is mostly control, through an imprest petty cash fund and a bank reconciliation that separates items the bank has not yet recorded from items the books have not yet recorded. Only the second kind needs a journal.

The balance sheet shows where cash ended up; the cash flow statement (PSAK 207) explains how it got there, through operating, investing and financing flows plus a separate line for exchange-rate effects. Moves between cash and cash equivalents are not cash flows, and an overdraft that is part of day-to-day cash management can count as negative cash in the flow statement while staying a liability on the balance sheet.

title: Consolidated Cash Flows and Mid-Year Acquisitions: NCI Dividends, Cash Acquired and Preacquisition Earnings
snippet: How a group builds one cash flow statement out of many companies, where the non-controlling interests and the deals that change the group land in it, and what happens to a subsidiary's results before the day it was bought, worked through Barito Pacific's 2025 statements
content:
In brief

  • A consolidated cash flow statement reports only cash that crosses the group's boundary. Cash moving between parent and subsidiary is eliminated, so of a subsidiary's dividend only the part paid to the non-controlling interests (NCI) survives, as a financing outflow. In the indirect method the reconciliation starts from consolidated profit, NCI's share included, and deducts the profit of equity-accounted investees (associates and joint ventures carried at the investor's share of their net assets) that was not received in cash.

  • Deals that change the group are classified by what they do to control. Obtaining or losing control of a subsidiary is one investing line, net of the subsidiary's own cash acquired or given up (PSAK 207 paras. 39 and 42). Buying from or selling to the NCI while control continues is financing (para. 42A). The acquired company's balances never pass through operating cash flows.

  • A subsidiary bought during the year enters the consolidated income statement and cash flow statement from the acquisition date. The lecture notes' second approach, consolidating the full year and deducting "preacquisition earnings", is no longer allowed. Its only remnant is a note disclosure of the acquiree's revenue and profit since acquisition and on a full-year pro forma basis (PSAK 103 para. B64(q)).

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) paid dividends of 60,121 to the NCI of its subsidiaries in 2025, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, consolidated statement of cash flows, PDF p. 19). Its largest acquisition of the year, Aster Chemical and Energy Pte. Ltd. (ACE), was completed on 1 April 2025, a quarter into the year.

After reading this page a student should be able to prepare a consolidated cash flow statement by the indirect and direct methods, classify every cash flow that involves the NCI or a change in the group, and consolidate a subsidiary bought or partly sold in the middle of a year.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The order follows the lecture notes for AKL Chapter 4 (the cash flow part) and Chapter 8 (acquisitions during the period). How NCI is measured and how ownership changes are recorded in equity is in the Non-Controlling Interest essay (25-non-controlling-interest); this page takes those entries as given and follows the cash.

1. One entity, one cash pool

The group reports as if it were one company, so its only cash flows are flows with parties outside the group. The notes open the topic with the "single concept" of cash and cash equivalents, defined as in PSAK 207 Statement of Cash Flows (formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7) and covered in 08-cash-and-cash-equivalents. BRPT's policy states the consequence: all cash flows "relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).

Adding up each company's statement and removing intragroup flows gives the same answer as the notes' route, which derives the statement from the consolidated balance sheets and income statement.

The intragroup dividend shows why elimination matters. For example (illustration), parent P owns 80 percent of S, and S pays a dividend of 50.

In S's own statement: financing outflow (50)

In P's own statement: dividend received 80% × 50 = 40, operating or investing

Added together: 40 − 50 = (10)

Eliminate the 40 that stayed inside the group: consolidated financing outflow (10), dividends paid to NCI

Only the 10 paid to the NCI left the group, and only that remains in the consolidated statement.

2. The indirect method: from consolidated profit to operating cash

Under PSAK 207 the reconciliation starts from profit before attribution, so NCI's share of profit is never "added back" (paras. 18(b) and 20). The indirect method removes items that did not involve cash and adjusts for changes in working capital. The notes' example is Pop Corporation and an 80 percent-owned subsidiary, with consolidated profit of 200 for 2017, of which 150 is the controlling share and 50 is NCI's, and cash rising from 180 to 255. The notes start from the controlling share and add the NCI share back, since it increases consolidated net assets "persis seperti" the controlling share. That layout reflects older US practice, where minority interest was deducted as if it were an expense. Both reach the same figure.

Net increase = 165 + 10 − 100 = 75; cash 180 + 75 = 255

Only the cash part of an investee's profit stays in operating cash. Pop's income from its equity investee is 15, but only the 10 received as dividends was cash, so the notes deduct the "undistributed income" of 5. Dividends received may be classified as operating or investing, consistently from period to period (paras. 31 and 33). If Pop chose investing, the whole 15 comes out of the reconciliation and the 10 appears below.

Operating = 165 − 10 = 155; investing = 10 + 10 = 20; net increase still 75

The notes leave a non-cash purchase undisclosed. Their balance sheets show equipment rising from 600 to 800 after depreciation of 100, so 800 − 600 + 100 = 300 of equipment was added, and a note payable due 2019 of 300 appears where there was none. No cash line covers either, which fits equipment bought with the note, though the notes do not say so. PSAK 207 keeps such transactions out of the statement and requires them to be disclosed elsewhere (para. 43); BRPT does this in its Note 44.

NCI is reconciled, not reported. NCI moves from 80 to 110, that is 80 + 50 − 20. The 50 is non-cash attribution and the 20 is a financing outflow. Nothing about NCI belongs in operating cash flows except the profit inside the starting figure.

3. The direct method

The direct method lists gross receipts and payments, so the NCI does not appear in operating activities at all. The notes rebuild Pop's 2017 operating cash flow from the same statements.

Cash received from customers = sales 750 − increase in receivables 105 = 645

Dividends received from equity investee = 10

Cash paid to suppliers = cost of goods sold 300 + increase in inventories 45 + decrease in payables 20 = 365

Paid to employees 54, other operating expenses 47, interest 24

Net cash from operating activities = 645 + 10 − (365 + 54 + 47 + 24) = 655 − 490 = 165

PSAK 207 encourages the direct method (para. 19). BRPT uses it (Note 3b, PDF p. 67), so its operating section runs from receipts from customers of 7,939,631 to net operating cash of 309,608, and its profit attributable to NCI appears nowhere in the statement.

4. Cash flows with the non-controlling interests

Every cash flow between the group and its NCI is a transaction with owners, so it belongs in financing. That covers three kinds of flow.

Event

Consolidated classification

Basis

Subsidiary pays dividends to NCI

Financing outflow

Para. 34 permits financing or operating; the notes use financing

Subsidiary issues new shares to NCI

Financing inflow

Para. 17, contributions from owners

Parent buys shares from NCI, or sells shares to new NCI, control kept

Financing outflow or inflow

Paras. 42A–42B

A parent's purchase of more shares in a subsidiary is an investing outflow in its separate statements. In the consolidated statements it is a payment to one class of the group's own owners, since the subsidiary's assets were already fully consolidated. European enforcers required an issuer that had shown such a purchase in investing to move it to financing (ESMA, decision EECS/0119-01).

For example (illustration), P buys a further 10 percent of S from the NCI for 12,000 and keeps control.

P's separate statement: investing outflow (12,000), acquisition of investment in subsidiary

Consolidated statement: financing outflow (12,000), acquisition of non-controlling interest

Equity: NCI falls by its carrying amount for 10 percent; the difference goes to equity attributable to the parent (essay 25, section 5)

The reverse runs through the same activity. When a subsidiary issues shares to new NCI, the cash is a financing inflow even though the parent's percentage falls. Take BRPT's subsidiary PT Chandra Daya Investasi Tbk (CDI) as the starting point. It issued shares to Phoenix Power B.V. for 95,000 (Note 31, PDF p. 217) and listed on the stock exchange in July 2025, raising 77,036 + 68,428 − 3,880 of issue costs = 141,584 (Note 1, PDF p. 36). Together they cut CAP's interest in CDI from 70 to 60 percent. Both are financing inflows; BRPT shows the second as "proceeds from limited public offering of a subsidiary".

BRPT's line for subscriptions by NCI, 367,032, can be largely split from Note 1, though BRPT does not split it (inference). Glencore subscribed 146,690 for its 20 percent of CAPGC on 26 March 2025 (PDF p. 43), Phoenix paid 95,000, and the remaining 367,032 − 146,690 − 95,000 = 125,342 is close to BPN's pro-rata share of the capital injected into CSI and MIM on 1 October 2025 (section 9). The Glencore money came in at CAPGC, the company that bought ACE a week later, so NCI financing paid for part of an investing outflow.

5. Obtaining control: one investing line, net of cash acquired

When the group buys a subsidiary it acquires that company's assets and liabilities in one transaction, and PSAK 207 presents the whole transaction as a single investing line (para. 39). The amount is the cash paid less the cash and cash equivalents the subsidiary already held (para. 42), because that cash comes into the group with it. The note must disclose the total consideration, the part paid in cash, the cash in the subsidiary, and the other assets and liabilities by major category (para. 40).

BRPT's acquisition of ACE gives every element (Note 43, PDF p. 227). The consideration is provisional, meaning the price is still subject to final adjustment, here through arbitration with the seller.

Provisional consideration = 671,970

Less deferred consideration, not yet paid = 283,225

Cash paid on acquisition = 671,970 − 283,225 = 388,745

Less ACE's cash and cash equivalents acquired = 215,431

Net cash outflow = 388,745 − 215,431 = 173,314

With 6,377 for Aster Polymer Solutions Pte. Ltd. (APS), bought on 1 August (13,076 paid less 6,699 acquired, PDF p. 229), the investing line is 173,314 + 6,377 = 179,691. The 283,225 still owed is a non-cash investing transaction in Note 44 (PDF p. 235). IAS 7 does not say how its later payment is classified. Practice varies between investing, financing and a split, and IASB staff proposed in September 2026 that deferred consideration with the character of a borrowing be financing.

The acquired balances bypass operating activities. A statement built from consolidated balance sheets must strip out the balances that arrived with the subsidiary, or their arrival looks like operating activity. Take BRPT's inventories as the starting point: 398,837 at the end of 2024 and 1,273,619 at the end of 2025 (statement of financial position, PDF p. 14), with 970,281 acquired through ACE and 39,608 through APS (Note 43, PDF pp. 226 and 228).

Change on the balance sheet = 1,273,619 − 398,837 = 874,782 increase

Inventories acquired = 970,281 + 39,608 = 1,009,889

Change from operations = 874,782 − 1,009,889 = 135,107 decrease

Read naively, the balance sheet suggests 874,782 tied up in stock. With the acquisitions removed, inventories released 135,107 of cash (ignoring write-downs and translation). Likewise ACE's acquired property, plant and equipment of 1,604,141 is not capital expenditure.

Bargain purchase gains bring no cash. A bargain purchase arises when the identifiable net assets acquired are worth more than the price. ACE's were valued at 2,444,134 against consideration of 671,970, a gain of 1,772,164; APS added 95,875 (108,951 − 13,076). BRPT's income statement shows 1,868,039 of such gains (PDF p. 17). An indirect reconciliation deducts all of it, and in BRPT's direct statement it never appears. How a bargain purchase is tested belongs to K1.

6. Losing control and the full map of ownership events

Losing control mirrors obtaining it: one investing line, the proceeds received net of the cash the former subsidiary takes out of the group (paras. 39 and 42).

For example (illustration), continue essay 25's subsidiary: net assets of 425,000 including cash of 35,000 (an assumption for this page), goodwill 60,000, NCI 170,000. The parent sells 40 percent for 230,000 cash and keeps 20 percent, worth 115,000, as an associate.

Gain on loss of control = (230,000 + 115,000 + 170,000) − (425,000 + 60,000) = 30,000

Investing inflow = 230,000 − 35,000 = 195,000, disposal of subsidiary, net of cash disposed

Retained 20 percent at 115,000, and the gain of 30,000: non-cash, removed in the indirect method

Had the subsidiary held more cash than the sale raised, the line would be a net investing outflow. Cash flows from obtaining and losing control are not offset against each other (para. 41).

7. Acquisitions during the year: preacquisition earnings

A subsidiary's income before the acquisition date was earned for its former owners and was paid for in the purchase price. The notes call it preacquisition earnings, and the dividends paid out of it before that date preacquisition dividends.

The notes' example has Pop buying 90 percent of Sun for 427,500 on 1 April 2016. (The notes write Son, Sun and Pam for the same companies, and the first column of their table reads "Jan 1 – Mar 1" where the quarter ends on 31 March.)

Sun's profit: 1 January–31 March 25,000; 1 April–31 December 75,000; year 100,000

Sun's dividends: before 1 April 20,000; after 30,000

Sun's equity at 1 April = 470,000 + 25,000 − 20,000 = 475,000

Cost = 90% × 475,000 = 427,500, so there is no excess to allocate

Approach 2 overstates sales by 50,000. The notes describe two ways to exclude preacquisition earnings: leave Sun's revenue and expenses before 1 April out of the consolidated income statement, or include Sun's full year and deduct "preacquisition earnings" as a separate line. They describe the second only in words; the column below is computed here from their data.

Approach 1: from acquisition date

Approach 2: full year less preacquisition earnings (computed here)

The bottom line agrees; the top line does not. PSAK 110 Consolidated Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) includes a subsidiary's income and expenses only from the date control is gained (para. B88), and BRPT's policy says so in nearly the same words (Note 3c, PDF p. 67). Approach 1 is the only one allowed. Approach 2 was the method ARB 51 called "usually" preferable (para. 11) until FAS 160 amended it. The notes' own worksheet already follows approach 1, eliminating Sun's first-quarter sales of 50,000 and cost of sales of 25,000.

PSAK measures NCI on the acquisition date. The notes measure NCI from 1 January, 10% × 470,000 plus 10% of the first quarter's profit, 49,500, and give NCI 10 percent of the full year's dividends, 5,000, of which 2,000 was paid before Pop arrived. PSAK 103 Business Combinations (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) measures NCI at the acquisition date, here at its share of net assets because book value equals fair value.

NCI at acquisition = 10% × 475,000 = 47,500

NCI at 31 December = 47,500 + 7,500 − 10% × 30,000 = 52,000

Notes' route: 49,500 + 7,500 − 5,000 = 52,000

Check: 10% × Sun's equity at year end of 520,000 = 52,000

The closing figure agrees, but the 2,000 of dividends paid in the first quarter is not a group transaction. It reduced Sun's net assets before the acquisition and so reduced the price. Under PSAK the worksheet eliminates Sun's equity at the acquisition date.

Dr Capital stock 400,000; Dr Retained earnings at 1 April 75,000 / Cr Investment in Sun 427,500; Cr NCI 47,500

Dr Income from Sun 67,500 / Cr Dividends 27,000; Cr Investment in Sun 40,500

The second entry corrects the notes, which print "Dividend $18.000 / Investment in Son $49.500". Pop received 90% × 30,000 = 27,000 after the acquisition, and the notes' own worksheet carries 27,000 and 40,500, which is what clears Pop's investment of 427,500 + 67,500 − 27,000 = 468,000.

Sun's cash enters through the acquisition line. The consolidated cash flow statement follows the income statement: Sun's flows count from 1 April, and the purchase is one investing line. For example (illustration), if Sun held cash of 60,000 on 1 April:

Investing outflow = 427,500 − 60,000 = 367,500

Dividends to NCI in financing = 10% × 30,000 = 3,000, not the notes' 5,000

B64(q) moves preacquisition results into the notes. Leaving the first quarter out makes the year hard to compare with the next, so PSAK 103 para. B64(q) asks for the acquiree's revenue and profit since the acquisition date, and the group's revenue and profit pro forma, that is, recomputed as if the acquisition had happened at the start of the year. BRPT gives both for ACE (Note 43, PDF pp. 227–228).

ACE since 1 April: revenue 4,634,352, loss 337,222

Group pro forma for 2025: revenue 8,735,677, profit 1,589,142, against reported 7,630,662 and 1,615,634

Pro forma less reported: revenue 1,105,015 higher, profit 26,492 lower

A part-sale is recorded on the day it happens. The notes' Chapter 8 also lets a parent that sells 10 percent of a 90 percent subsidiary on 1 April record the sale as if it happened on 1 January. PSAK 110 attributes profit by the ownership actually held, so the sale is recorded on 1 April. With the subsidiary's profit of 36,000 for the year, the NCI share is 36,000 × (10% × 3/12 + 20% × 9/12) = 900 + 5,400 = 6,300, not 7,200, and the credit to the parent's equity is 40,000 − 32,900 = 7,100, not 8,000. The 40,000 received is a financing inflow either way.

8. Consolidated cash flows across industries

Investment entities do not report acquisitions net of cash. A venture capital fund or similar entity that meets PSAK 110's investment-entity definition does not consolidate its investees but measures them at fair value through profit or loss (para. 31). Buying an investee is then an investing purchase of a financial asset, and para. 42A does not apply to its stakes.

Asset acquisitions in a corporate wrapper still use the para. 39 line. Concessions, plantation land and power projects are often bought by buying the company that holds them. If the company is not a business under PSAK 103, the purchase is an asset acquisition, with no goodwill or bargain purchase, but the buyer still obtains control of a subsidiary. BRPT's wind subsidiary bought 51 percent of PT Lombok Timur Bayu Energi and PT Sukabumi Bayu Energi in January 2024 as asset acquisitions, and their cash outflows of 3,373 and 4,055 are shown as investing activities (Note 43, PDF pp. 232–233).

Joint-venture investors show large non-cash deductions. Equity-accounted ventures in property and infrastructure contribute profit without cash. BRPT's share of profit of associates and joint venture was 60,470 in 2025, and all dividends received were 5,168 (PDF pp. 17 and 19), so at least 60,470 − 5,168 = 55,302 of that profit stayed in the investees.

BRPT's group-structure flows put more cash into the group from NCI than they took out, and seven lines of its direct-method statement show them (PDF p. 19).

The dividend line ties to the NCI movement in Note 34 (PDF p. 221), where "dividend distributed and capital reduction by subsidiary to non-controlling interests" is also 60,121 (68,367 in 2024). The treasury line equals the buybacks in the statement of changes in equity, 154 by BRPT and 5,163 by subsidiaries (PDF p. 18).

Profit and cash diverge for the NCI. NCI was attributed 1,125,827 of the year's profit of 1,615,634 (PDF p. 17).

NCI share of profit = 1,125,827 / 1,615,634 = 69.7%, against 66,412 / 122,896 = 54.0% in 2024

BRPT's effective interest in ACE = (34.63% + 3.92%) × 80% = 38.55% × 80% = 30.84%

Dividends to NCI / profit attributable to NCI = 60,121 / 1,125,827 = 5.3%

BRPT holds Chandra Asri (CAP) directly and through Marigold at 38.55 percent (Note 1, PDF p. 24), and ACE sits under CAPGC, 80 percent owned within CAP. The NCI therefore took most of the non-cash bargain purchase gain of 1,868,039.

Net cash from NCI = 367,032 + 141,584 − 60,121 − 160,975 − 5,163 = 282,357

BRPT paid no dividends to its own shareholders in 2025 and spent 154 buying back its own shares.

The 160,975 sits on a classification judgement. It is the price paid on 1 October 2025 for the 51 percent of PT Chandra Shipping International (CSI) and PT Marina Indah Maritim (MIM) held by PT Buana Primatama Niaga (BPN); the shares went to CDI (Note 31, PDF p. 216; Note 1, PDF pp. 41–42). BRPT accounts for it as a business combination under common control, by the pooling method: the 321 difference between the price and the book value of net assets acquired, 161,296, goes to additional paid-in capital (Note 3e, PDF pp. 70–71; Note 29, PDF p. 212). The text supports that reading. BPN's beneficial owner is the ultimate shareholder of CDI (Note 45h, PDF p. 236), and PSAK 338 para. 09 excludes from its scope only purchases of NCI from holders not under the same common control. A business combination is a para. 39 item, hence investing.

The other reading starts from the fact that CSI and MIM were already consolidated at 49 percent through control of their boards (Note 1, PDF pp. 41–42), so control did not change, which is the case para. 42A sends to financing. BRPT's own caption, "from non-controlling interest", describes it that way. On the same day the shareholders of CSI and MIM injected new capital pro rata, BPN's 51 percent share being about 138,000 (Note 1, PDF pp. 41–42), which likely sits in the 367,032 financing inflow while the payment to BPN sits in investing. The equity result is the same under both readings; only the activity differs. Read as financing, investing would be 2,434,204 − 160,975 = 2,273,229 and financing 3,524,898 − 160,975 = 3,363,923.

10. Related essays

  • cash-and-cash-equivalents: the definition of cash, the three activities, interest and dividend classification and IFRS 18.

  • non-controlling-interest: NCI measurement, attribution and the equity entries for ownership changes.

  • long-term-investments: equity-accounted associates and joint ventures.

  • other-equity-component and additional-paid-in-capital: where differences from transactions with NCI and common-control restructurings sit.

  • K1: consideration, deferred consideration, bargain purchase, asset acquisitions and PSAK 338.

  • K2: the elimination entries this page's worksheet steps rely on.

  • K6: effective interests in multi-layer groups such as BRPT–CAP–CAPGC.

Least-confident assertions

  • The CSI/MIM classification is a judgement with support on both sides. That BPN's capital injection of about 138,000 sits in the 367,032 financing inflow is inference; BRPT does not split that line, and the US dollar amount of the CSI injection depends on the rate applied to the deed's rupiah figure.

  • The split of 367,032 into Glencore 146,690, Phoenix 95,000 and about 125,342 from BPN is inference. The BPN residual matches its pro-rata injection less the 11,623 of shares issued by converting payables (Note 44) only to within about 1,250.

  • The CDI dates conflict inside the FS. Note 31 dates the Phoenix issue 14 March 2025 and attributes the whole fall from 70 to 60 percent to it; Note 1 shows the 14 March deed raising authorised capital, the issue to Phoenix on 11 April (to 66.67 percent) and the IPO in July (to 60.0 percent). This page follows Note 1.

  • That the ACE pro forma difference reflects ACE's first quarter assumes the pro forma adds only that quarter with no other adjustments. BRPT does not explain how it was compiled.

  • The inventory calculation in section 5 ignores write-downs, translation and measurement-period changes to ACE's provisional figures, so 135,107 approximates the operating movement; BRPT does not report it.
