content.text: A consolidated cash flow statement reports only cash that crosses the group's boundary. Cash moving between parent and subsidiary is eliminated, so of a subsidiary's dividend only the part paid to the non-controlling interests (NCI) survives, as a financing outflow. In the indirect method the reconciliation starts from consolidated profit, NCI's share included, and deducts the profit of equity-accounted investees (associates and joint ventures carried at the investor's share of their net assets) that was not received in cash.

Deals that change the group are classified by what they do to control. Obtaining or losing control of a subsidiary is one investing line, net of the subsidiary's own cash acquired or given up (PSAK 207 paras. 39 and 42). Buying from or selling to the NCI while control continues is financing (para. 42A). The acquired company's balances never pass through operating cash flows.

A subsidiary bought during the year enters the consolidated income statement and cash flow statement from the acquisition date. The lecture notes' second approach, consolidating the full year and deducting "preacquisition earnings", is no longer allowed. Its only remnant is a note disclosure of the acquiree's revenue and profit since acquisition and on a full-year pro forma basis (PSAK 103 para. B64(q)).

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) paid dividends of 60,121 to the NCI of its subsidiaries in 2025, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, consolidated statement of cash flows, PDF p. 19). Its largest acquisition of the year, Aster Chemical and Energy Pte. Ltd. (ACE), was completed on 1 April 2025, a quarter into the year.

After reading this page a student should be able to prepare a consolidated cash flow statement by the indirect and direct methods, classify every cash flow that involves the NCI or a change in the group, and consolidate a subsidiary bought or partly sold in the middle of a year.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The order follows the lecture notes for AKL Chapter 4 (the cash flow part) and Chapter 8 (acquisitions during the period). How NCI is measured and how ownership changes are recorded in equity is in the Non-Controlling Interest essay (
); this page takes those entries as given and follows the cash.

The group reports as if it were one company, so its only cash flows are flows with parties outside the group. The notes open the topic with the "single concept" of cash and cash equivalents, defined as in PSAK 207
. BRPT's policy states the consequence: all cash flows "relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).
Adding up each company's statement and removing intragroup flows gives the same answer as the notes' route, which derives the statement from the consolidated balance sheets and income statement.
The intragroup dividend shows why elimination matters. For example (illustration), parent P owns 80 percent of S, and S pays a dividend of 50.
In S's own statement: financing outflow (50)
In P's own statement: dividend received 80% × 50 = 40, operating or investing
Eliminate the 40 that stayed inside the group: consolidated financing outflow (10), dividends paid to NCI
Only the 10 paid to the NCI left the group, and only that remains in the consolidated statement.
2. The indirect method: from consolidated profit to operating cash

Under PSAK 207 the reconciliation starts from profit before attribution, so NCI's share of profit is never "added back" (paras. 18(b) and 20). The indirect method removes items that did not involve cash and adjusts for changes in working capital. The notes' example is Pop Corporation and an 80 percent-owned subsidiary, with consolidated profit of 200 for 2017, of which 150 is the controlling share and 50 is NCI's, and cash rising from 180 to 255. The notes start from the controlling share and add the NCI share back, since it increases consolidated net assets "persis seperti" the controlling share. That layout reflects older US practice, where minority interest was deducted as if it were an expense. Both reach the same figure.
Investing: proceeds from sale of land 10
Financing: dividends to Pop's shareholders (80) and to NCI (20) = (100)
Only the cash part of an investee's profit stays in operating cash.

Pop's income from its equity investee is 15, but only the 10 received as dividends was cash, so the notes deduct the "undistributed income" of 5. Dividends received may be classified as operating or investing, consistently from period to period (paras. 31 and 33). If Pop chose investing, the whole 15 comes out of the reconciliation and the 10 appears below.
The notes leave a non-cash purchase undisclosed.

Their balance sheets show equipment rising from 600 to 800 after depreciation of 100, so 800 − 600 + 100 = 300 of equipment was added, and a note payable due 2019 of 300 appears where there was none. No cash line covers either, which fits equipment bought with the note, though the notes do not say so. PSAK 207 keeps such transactions out of the statement and requires them to be disclosed elsewhere (para. 43); BRPT does this in its Note 44.

NCI moves from 80 to 110, that is 80 + 50 − 20. The 50 is non-cash attribution and the 20 is a financing outflow. Nothing about NCI belongs in operating cash flows except the profit inside the starting figure.
The direct method lists gross receipts and payments, so the NCI does not appear in operating activities at all. The notes rebuild Pop's 2017 operating cash flow from the same statements.
Cash received from customers = sales 750 − increase in receivables 105 = 645
Cash paid to suppliers = cost of goods sold 300 + increase in inventories 45 + decrease in payables 20 = 365
Paid to employees 54, other operating expenses 47, interest 24

PSAK 207 encourages the direct method (para. 19). BRPT uses it (Note 3b, PDF p. 67), so its operating section runs from receipts from customers of 7,939,631 to net operating cash of 309,608, and its profit attributable to NCI appears nowhere in the statement.
4. Cash flows with the non-controlling interests
Every cash flow between the group and its NCI is a transaction with owners, so it belongs in financing. That covers three kinds of flow.
Para. 34 permits financing or operating; the notes use financing
Subsidiary issues new shares to NCI
Parent buys shares from NCI, or sells shares to new NCI, control kept

A parent's purchase of more shares in a subsidiary is an investing outflow in its separate statements. In the consolidated statements it is a payment to one class of the group's own owners, since the subsidiary's assets were already fully consolidated. European enforcers required an issuer that had shown such a purchase in investing to move it to financing (ESMA, decision EECS/0119-01).
For example (illustration), P buys a further 10 percent of S from the NCI for 12,000 and keeps control.
P's separate statement: investing outflow (12,000), acquisition of investment in subsidiary
Consolidated statement: financing outflow (12,000), acquisition of non-controlling interest
Equity: NCI falls by its carrying amount for 10 percent; the difference goes to equity attributable to the parent (essay 25, section 5)

The reverse runs through the same activity. When a subsidiary issues shares to new NCI, the cash is a financing inflow even though the parent's percentage falls. Take BRPT's subsidiary PT Chandra Daya Investasi Tbk (CDI) as the starting point. It issued shares to Phoenix Power B.V. for 95,000 (Note 31, PDF p. 217) and listed on the stock exchange in July 2025, raising 77,036 + 68,428 − 3,880 of issue costs = 141,584 (Note 1, PDF p. 36). Together they cut CAP's interest in CDI from 70 to 60 percent. Both are financing inflows; BRPT shows the second as "proceeds from limited public offering of a subsidiary".

BRPT's line for subscriptions by NCI, 367,032, can be largely split from Note 1, though BRPT does not split it (inference). Glencore subscribed 146,690 for its 20 percent of CAPGC on 26 March 2025 (PDF p. 43), Phoenix paid 95,000, and the remaining 367,032 − 146,690 − 95,000 = 125,342 is close to BPN's pro-rata share of the capital injected into CSI and MIM on 1 October 2025 (section 9). The Glencore money came in at CAPGC, the company that bought ACE a week later, so NCI financing paid for part of an investing outflow.
5. Obtaining control: one investing line, net of cash acquired

When the group buys a subsidiary it acquires that company's assets and liabilities in one transaction, and PSAK 207 presents the whole transaction as a single investing line (para. 39). The amount is the cash paid less the cash and cash equivalents the subsidiary already held (para. 42), because that cash comes into the group with it. The note must disclose the total consideration, the part paid in cash, the cash in the subsidiary, and the other assets and liabilities by major category (para. 40).
BRPT's acquisition of ACE gives every element (Note 43, PDF p. 227). The consideration is
, meaning the price is still subject to final adjustment, here through arbitration with the seller.
Less deferred consideration, not yet paid = 283,225
Less ACE's cash and cash equivalents acquired = 215,431

With 6,377 for Aster Polymer Solutions Pte. Ltd. (APS), bought on 1 August (13,076 paid less 6,699 acquired, PDF p. 229), the investing line is 173,314 + 6,377 = 179,691. The 283,225 still owed is a non-cash investing transaction in Note 44 (PDF p. 235). IAS 7 does not say how its later payment is classified. Practice varies between investing, financing and a split, and IASB staff proposed in September 2026 that deferred consideration with the character of a borrowing be financing.
The acquired balances bypass operating activities.

A statement built from consolidated balance sheets must strip out the balances that arrived with the subsidiary, or their arrival looks like operating activity. Take BRPT's inventories as the starting point: 398,837 at the end of 2024 and 1,273,619 at the end of 2025 (statement of financial position, PDF p. 14), with 970,281 acquired through ACE and 39,608 through APS (Note 43, PDF pp. 226 and 228).
Change on the balance sheet = 1,273,619 − 398,837 = 874,782 increase

Read naively, the balance sheet suggests 874,782 tied up in stock. With the acquisitions removed, inventories released 135,107 of cash (ignoring write-downs and translation). Likewise ACE's acquired property, plant and equipment of 1,604,141 is not capital expenditure.
Bargain purchase gains bring no cash.

arises when the identifiable net assets acquired are worth more than the price. ACE's were valued at 2,444,134 against consideration of 671,970, a gain of 1,772,164; APS added 95,875 (108,951 − 13,076). BRPT's income statement shows 1,868,039 of such gains (PDF p. 17). An indirect reconciliation deducts all of it, and in BRPT's direct statement it never appears. How a bargain purchase is tested belongs to K1.
6. Losing control and the full map of ownership events
Losing control mirrors obtaining it: one investing line, the proceeds received net of the cash the former subsidiary takes out of the group (paras. 39 and 42).

For example (illustration), continue essay 25's subsidiary: net assets of 425,000 including cash of 35,000 (an assumption for this page), goodwill 60,000, NCI 170,000. The parent sells 40 percent for 230,000 cash and keeps 20 percent, worth 115,000, as an associate.
Investing inflow = 230,000 − 35,000 = 195,000, disposal of subsidiary, net of cash disposed
Retained 20 percent at 115,000, and the gain of 30,000: non-cash, removed in the indirect method
Had the subsidiary held more cash than the sale raised, the line would be a net investing outflow. Cash flows from obtaining and losing control are not offset against each other (para. 41).
Only on a previously held interest or a bargain purchase
Subsidiary issues shares to new NCI
7. Acquisitions during the year: preacquisition earnings
A subsidiary's income before the acquisition date was earned for its former owners and was paid for in the purchase price. The notes call it
, and the dividends paid out of it before that date

The notes' example has Pop buying 90 percent of Sun for 427,500 on 1 April 2016. (The notes write Son, Sun and Pam for the same companies, and the first column of their table reads "Jan 1 – Mar 1" where the quarter ends on 31 March.)
Sun's profit: 1 January–31 March 25,000; 1 April–31 December 75,000; year 100,000
Cost = 90% × 475,000 = 427,500, so there is no excess to allocate

The notes describe two ways to exclude preacquisition earnings: leave Sun's revenue and expenses before 1 April out of the consolidated income statement, or include Sun's full year and deduct "preacquisition earnings" as a separate line. They describe the second only in words; the column below is computed here from their data.
Approach 2: full year less preacquisition earnings (computed here)
The bottom line agrees; the top line does not. PSAK 110

(formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) includes a subsidiary's income and expenses only from the date control is gained (para. B88), and BRPT's policy says so in nearly the same words (Note 3c, PDF p. 67). Approach 1 is the only one allowed. Approach 2 was the method ARB 51 called "usually" preferable (para. 11) until FAS 160 amended it. The notes' own worksheet already follows approach 1, eliminating Sun's first-quarter sales of 50,000 and cost of sales of 25,000.
PSAK measures NCI on the acquisition date.

The notes measure NCI from 1 January, 10% × 470,000 plus 10% of the first quarter's profit, 49,500, and give NCI 10 percent of the full year's dividends, 5,000, of which 2,000 was paid before Pop arrived. PSAK 103
(formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) measures NCI at the acquisition date, here at its share of net assets because book value equals fair value.
Check: 10% × Sun's equity at year end of 520,000 = 52,000

The closing figure agrees, but the 2,000 of dividends paid in the first quarter is not a group transaction. It reduced Sun's net assets before the acquisition and so reduced the price. Under PSAK the worksheet eliminates Sun's equity at the acquisition date.
Dr Capital stock 400,000; Dr Retained earnings at 1 April 75,000 / Cr Investment in Sun 427,500; Cr NCI 47,500
Dr Income from Sun 67,500 / Cr Dividends 27,000; Cr Investment in Sun 40,500

The second entry corrects the notes, which print "Dividend $18.000 / Investment in Son $49.500". Pop received 90% × 30,000 = 27,000 after the acquisition, and the notes' own worksheet carries 27,000 and 40,500, which is what clears Pop's investment of 427,500 + 67,500 − 27,000 = 468,000.
Sun's cash enters through the acquisition line.

The consolidated cash flow statement follows the income statement: Sun's flows count from 1 April, and the purchase is one investing line. For example (illustration), if Sun held cash of 60,000 on 1 April:
Dividends to NCI in financing = 10% × 30,000 = 3,000, not the notes' 5,000
B64(q) moves preacquisition results into the notes.

Leaving the first quarter out makes the year hard to compare with the next, so PSAK 103 para. B64(q) asks for the acquiree's revenue and profit since the acquisition date, and the group's revenue and profit
, that is, recomputed as if the acquisition had happened at the start of the year. BRPT gives both for ACE (Note 43, PDF pp. 227–228).
Group pro forma for 2025: revenue 8,735,677, profit 1,589,142, against reported 7,630,662 and 1,615,634
Pro forma less reported: revenue 1,105,015 higher, profit 26,492 lower
A part-sale is recorded on the day it happens.

The notes' Chapter 8 also lets a parent that sells 10 percent of a 90 percent subsidiary on 1 April record the sale as if it happened on 1 January. PSAK 110 attributes profit by the ownership actually held, so the sale is recorded on 1 April. With the subsidiary's profit of 36,000 for the year, the NCI share is 36,000 × (10% × 3/12 + 20% × 9/12) = 900 + 5,400 = 6,300, not 7,200, and the credit to the parent's equity is 40,000 − 32,900 = 7,100, not 8,000. The 40,000 received is a financing inflow either way.
Investment entities do not report acquisitions net of cash.

A venture capital fund or similar entity that meets PSAK 110's investment-entity definition does not consolidate its investees but measures them at fair value through profit or loss (para. 31). Buying an investee is then an investing purchase of a financial asset, and para. 42A does not apply to its stakes.
Asset acquisitions in a corporate wrapper still use the para. 39 line.

Concessions, plantation land and power projects are often bought by buying the company that holds them. If the company is not a business under PSAK 103, the purchase is an asset acquisition, with no goodwill or bargain purchase, but the buyer still obtains control of a subsidiary. BRPT's wind subsidiary bought 51 percent of PT Lombok Timur Bayu Energi and PT Sukabumi Bayu Energi in January 2024 as asset acquisitions, and their cash outflows of 3,373 and 4,055 are shown as investing activities (Note 43, PDF pp. 232–233).
Joint-venture investors show large non-cash deductions.

Equity-accounted ventures in property and infrastructure contribute profit without cash. BRPT's share of profit of associates and joint venture was 60,470 in 2025, and all dividends received were 5,168 (PDF pp. 17 and 19), so at least 60,470 − 5,168 = 55,302 of that profit stayed in the investees.
9. Presentation and analysis: Barito Pacific's cash flow statement and Notes 34, 43 and 44
BRPT's group-structure flows put more cash into the group from NCI than they took out, and seven lines of its direct-method statement show them (PDF p. 19).
Acquisition of subsidiaries, net of cash acquired
Additional investment in subsidiaries from NCI
Proceeds from NCI subscribing for shares in subsidiaries
Proceeds from limited public offering of a subsidiary (CDI's IPO)
Dividends paid by subsidiaries to NCI

The dividend line ties to the NCI movement in Note 34 (PDF p. 221), where "dividend distributed and capital reduction by subsidiary to non-controlling interests" is also 60,121 (68,367 in 2024). The treasury line equals the buybacks in the statement of changes in equity, 154 by BRPT and 5,163 by subsidiaries (PDF p. 18).
Profit and cash diverge for the NCI.
NCI was attributed 1,125,827 of the year's profit of 1,615,634 (PDF p. 17).
Dividends to NCI / profit attributable to NCI = 60,121 / 1,125,827 = 5.3%

BRPT holds Chandra Asri (CAP) directly and through Marigold at 38.55 percent (Note 1, PDF p. 24), and ACE sits under CAPGC, 80 percent owned within CAP. The NCI therefore took most of the non-cash bargain purchase gain of 1,868,039.
BRPT paid no dividends to its own shareholders in 2025 and spent 154 buying back its own shares.
The 160,975 sits on a classification judgement.

It is the price paid on 1 October 2025 for the 51 percent of PT Chandra Shipping International (CSI) and PT Marina Indah Maritim (MIM) held by PT Buana Primatama Niaga (BPN); the shares went to CDI (Note 31, PDF p. 216; Note 1, PDF pp. 41–42). BRPT accounts for it as a business combination under common control, by the pooling method: the 321 difference between the price and the book value of net assets acquired, 161,296, goes to additional paid-in capital (Note 3e, PDF pp. 70–71; Note 29, PDF p. 212). The text supports that reading. BPN's beneficial owner is the ultimate shareholder of CDI (Note 45h, PDF p. 236), and PSAK 338 para. 09 excludes from its scope only purchases of NCI from holders not under the same common control. A business combination is a para. 39 item, hence investing.

The other reading starts from the fact that CSI and MIM were already consolidated at 49 percent through control of their boards (Note 1, PDF pp. 41–42), so control did not change, which is the case para. 42A sends to financing. BRPT's own caption, "from non-controlling interest", describes it that way. On the same day the shareholders of CSI and MIM injected new capital pro rata, BPN's 51 percent share being about 138,000 (Note 1, PDF pp. 41–42), which likely sits in the 367,032 financing inflow while the payment to BPN sits in investing. The equity result is the same under both readings; only the activity differs. Read as financing, investing would be 2,434,204 − 160,975 = 2,273,229 and financing 3,524,898 − 160,975 = 3,363,923.
: the definition of cash, the three activities, interest and dividend classification and IFRS 18.
: NCI measurement, attribution and the equity entries for ownership changes.
: where differences from transactions with NCI and common-control restructurings sit.
: consideration, deferred consideration, bargain purchase, asset acquisitions and PSAK 338.
: the elimination entries this page's worksheet steps rely on.
: effective interests in multi-layer groups such as BRPT–CAP–CAPGC.

The CSI/MIM classification is a judgement with support on both sides. That BPN's capital injection of about 138,000 sits in the 367,032 financing inflow is inference; BRPT does not split that line, and the US dollar amount of the CSI injection depends on the rate applied to the deed's rupiah figure.

The split of 367,032 into Glencore 146,690, Phoenix 95,000 and about 125,342 from BPN is inference. The BPN residual matches its pro-rata injection less the 11,623 of shares issued by converting payables (Note 44) only to within about 1,250.

The CDI dates conflict inside the FS. Note 31 dates the Phoenix issue 14 March 2025 and attributes the whole fall from 70 to 60 percent to it; Note 1 shows the 14 March deed raising authorised capital, the issue to Phoenix on 11 April (to 66.67 percent) and the IPO in July (to 60.0 percent). This page follows Note 1.
That the ACE pro forma difference reflects ACE's first quarter assumes the pro forma adds only that quarter with no other adjustments. BRPT does not explain how it was compiled.

The inventory calculation in section 5 ignores write-downs, translation and measurement-period changes to ACE's provisional figures, so 135,107 approximates the operating movement; BRPT does not report it.

title: Consolidation Procedures: the Worksheet and the Elimination Entries
snippet: How a parent's books and a subsidiary's books become one set of group statements, entry by entry, worked from Barito Pacific's stake in Barito Renewables
content:
In brief

  • Consolidated statements are never recorded in anyone's ledger. They are built on a worksheet that adds the parent's and the subsidiaries' statements line by line and then removes what is internal to the group: the parent's investment against the subsidiary's equity, intragroup balances, and intragroup income, expenses and dividends (PSAK 110 B86).

  • The elimination entries run in a fixed order. Reverse the parent's income from the subsidiary and the subsidiary's dividends, record the non-controlling interest's (NCI's) share, eliminate opening equity against the investment and opening NCI, allocate and depreciate the excess paid over book value, and cancel reciprocal balances. The worksheet has three parts, profit or loss, then retained earnings, then the balance sheet, each feeding the next.

  • The method the parent uses in its own books (cost or equity method, both allowed by PSAK 227) changes the first entry and adds one conversion entry, but never the consolidated result. A worksheet that balances can still be wrong, so the ties to the parent's equity and to NCI matter more than the totals.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) list each subsidiary's "total assets before elimination" in their 2025 statements. PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk (BREN), 64.67 percent owned, has 3,867,410 at 31 December 2025, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF p. 26). What happens between such "before elimination" figures and the group's statements is the subject of this page.

After reading it a student should be able to prepare a three-part consolidation worksheet in the year of acquisition and in later years, write each elimination entry in order, adapt the worksheet to a parent that uses the cost method, and find the error when the worksheet does not balance.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's and BREN's statements are cited to their note; every other number is an illustration. Control, NCI measurement and profit attribution are taught in the Non-Controlling Interest essay and used here without re-deriving them.

1. The parent's own books decide what must be eliminated

The parent's investment in a subsidiary sits in its own books as one asset. How that asset is measured in the parent's separate financial statements (the parent's own statements, in which subsidiaries are investments) is a policy choice. PSAK 227 Separate Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 4, IAS 27) allows cost, PSAK 109 or the equity method, applied to each category of investment consistently (para. 10). The equity-method option was added in Indonesia by the amendment to PSAK 4 ratified in November 2015 and effective from 1 January 2016, following the 2014 IAS 27 amendment. Dividends from a subsidiary go to profit or loss under cost or PSAK 109, and reduce the investment under the equity method (para. 12).

The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 4) assume the parent uses the equity method "secara komplit", the complete equity method. The parent books its share of the subsidiary's profit after the depreciation of the excess it paid over book value, so its profit equals the consolidated profit attributable to its owners. Beams calls this one-line consolidation; the Long-Term Investments essay (section 5) explains the mechanism.

The running illustration. BRPT holds 64.67 percent of BREN (Note 1d). Its interest in BREN's geothermal business came through common-control transactions. BRPT acquired Star Energy Group Holdings (SEGHPL) in 2018, pooled as if combined from the start (Note 1d, PDF p. 52) at book values (policy Note 3e, PDF p. 70), and BREN acquired SEGHPL from BRPT in 2022 for new BREN shares (BREN FS 2025, Note 19b, PDF p. 115). No fair value excess arose at BRPT's level, although goodwill from Star Energy's earlier purchase of Salak and Darajat was carried across at its carrying amount; the Business Combinations essay (K1) covers both. To show every entry, suppose instead (illustration) that on 1 January 2024 BRPT had bought 65 percent of a geothermal company from outside owners. The notes call their subsidiary "Son"; this page calls it Sub. A fair value uplift is the amount by which an asset's fair value at acquisition exceeds its carrying amount in the subsidiary's books.

Goodwill = 520,000 + 248,500 − 710,000 = 58,500

The equity-method balance already contains the parent's share of Sub's retained profits and of the depreciated uplift. The cost-method balance contains neither, so the worksheet has to put them there before it can eliminate anything (section 6).

2. The worksheet has three parts, and each feeds the next

Each part of the worksheet ends in the figure the next part needs. The notes stack three parts (income statement, retained earnings statement, balance sheet), with columns for the parent, the subsidiary, the eliminations and the consolidated result.

  • Profit attributable to the owners of the parent, the last line of part one, is carried into part two.

  • Closing retained earnings, the last line of part two, is carried into part three.

  • Part three must then balance, total assets against total liabilities and equity.

PSAK 201 replaced the retained earnings statement with a statement of changes in equity, but the logic is unchanged. Every year starts again from the separate statements and repeats the entries for past events, such as the acquisition-date allocation.

PSAK 110 Consolidated Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) describes the three steps the entries perform (B86): combine like items of assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows; offset the parent's investment against its portion of the subsidiary's equity; and eliminate intragroup assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows in full. BRPT's policy repeats the third step: "All intragroup assets and liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).

3. The standard elimination sequence

The notes give six entries in a fixed order. Each removes something that would otherwise be counted twice.

Step

Problem it solves

Entry (equity-method parent)

(1) Income from subsidiary and dividends

The parent's income line repeats Sub's revenues and expenses; dividends to the parent move cash inside the group

Dr Income from Sub / Cr Dividends declared (Sub, parent's share); Cr Investment for the difference

(2) NCI share

Consolidated profit belongs partly to outside owners, and their dividends reduce their claim

Dr NCI share of profit / Cr Dividends declared (NCI's share); Cr NCI for the difference

(3) Opening equity against investment and NCI

Sub's opening equity is already represented by the investment and opening NCI

Dr Share capital and opening retained earnings (Sub), Dr Unamortised excess / Cr Investment (opening), Cr NCI (opening)

(4) Allocate the excess

The unamortised excess is a worksheet suspense account to be assigned to the assets it paid for

Dr Plant and equipment, Dr Goodwill (and inventory or cost of sales) / Cr Unamortised excess

(5) Depreciate the excess

Group depreciation follows acquisition-date fair values (PSAK 110 B88); Sub depreciates book values

Dr Depreciation / Cr Plant and equipment

(6) Reciprocal balances

Balances between group companies are neither assets nor liabilities of the group

Dr the payable / Cr the receivable; Dr intragroup income / Cr intragroup expense

Entries (1) and (2) together remove all of Sub's dividends. Entry (1) returns the investment to its opening balance, which is why entry (3) can eliminate it against opening equity. The intragroup profit eliminations of K3 and K4 can sit anywhere in the sequence without changing the result.

4. The year of acquisition

In the first year the opening equity in entry (3) is the equity at the acquisition date, and the inventory uplift reaches cost of sales because the spares were used during the year. For example (illustration), the 2024 worksheet for Sub:

(1) Dr Income from Sub 48,750 / Cr Dividends declared 26,000; Cr Investment in Sub 22,750

(2) Dr NCI share of profit 26,250 / Cr Dividends declared 14,000; Cr NCI 12,250

(3) Dr Share capital, Sub 400,000; Dr Retained earnings, Sub 200,000; Dr Unamortised excess 168,500 / Cr Investment in Sub 520,000; Cr NCI 248,500

(4) Dr Cost of sales 10,000; Dr Plant and equipment 100,000; Dr Goodwill 58,500 / Cr Unamortised excess 168,500

(5) Dr Depreciation 5,000 / Cr Plant and equipment 5,000

Entry (3) balances at 768,500 on each side. The investment, 520,000 + 48,750 − 26,000 = 542,750, is credited 22,750 + 520,000 = 542,750 and falls to zero. NCI closes at 248,500 + 12,250 = 260,750, which is 35 percent of Sub's net assets at group carrying amounts (book values plus the uplifts not yet written off).

35% × (600,000 + 90,000 − 40,000 + 100,000 − 5,000) = 35% × 745,000 = 260,750

Under the proportionate method goodwill is not part of NCI. Had control been obtained during the year, Sub's income and expenses would enter only from the acquisition date (B88), a case K5 takes up.

5. A later year: the full worksheet

From the second year on, entry (3) uses Sub's retained earnings at the start of the year and the excess still unamortised at that date. In 2025 three intragroup transactions also need entry (6).

  • On 1 July 2025 the parent lent Sub 30,000 at 6 percent a year. Half a year's interest, 30,000 × 6% × 6/12 = 900, is accrued by both and unpaid.

  • On 30 December Sub repaid 5,000 of the loan by bank transfer, which reached the parent on 2 January. Sub shows a loan payable of 25,000, while the parent still shows a receivable of 30,000. The 5,000 is cash in transit, money that has left one group company and not yet reached the other.

  • Sub's unpaid dividend of 20,000 includes 13,000 owed to the parent.

6. A parent on the cost method

A parent using the cost method reaches the same consolidated statements by changing two entries. Its investment still stands at 520,000, its opening retained earnings lack its share of Sub's retained profits, and its profit carries dividend income instead of the share of profit.

The 22,750 is the parent's share of Sub's retained profits since acquisition, 65% × (250,000 − 200,000) = 32,500, less its share of the excess already written off, 65% × 15,000 = 9,750. Entry (1) then removes only the dividend income, because the 68,250 share of profit was never in the parent's column, and the consolidated column comes out as in section 5. 7. Uniform policies and reporting dates

The worksheet adds like items only if they were measured alike and at the same date. PSAK 110 requires adjustments when a group member uses accounting policies other than the group's (B87). BRPT's policy says adjustments are made "when necessary ... to bring their accounting policies in line with the Group's accounting policies" (Note 3c, PDF p. 67). For example (illustration, separate from the section 5 worksheet), suppose Sub carries an office building it rents out at fair value under PSAK 240 (formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40), while the group uses the cost model. Sub bought the building on 1 January 2025 and booked a fair value gain of 3,000 at year end; the group's cost-model depreciation would be 400. Before the eliminations:

Dr Fair value gain 3,000; Dr Depreciation 400 / Cr Investment property 3,400

Like any adjustment to Sub's figures, its effect on profit is shared with NCI, so NCI's share of profit falls by 35% × 3,400 = 1,190.

Reporting dates should be the same. If that is impracticable, the subsidiary's most recent statements may be used, adjusted for significant transactions or events in between, provided the gap is no more than three months and the length of periods and the gap stay the same from period to period (B92–B93). The notes state the same three-month limit but only require material intervening events to be disclosed; PSAK 110 requires adjustment. For example (illustration), if Sub's year ended on 30 September and the parent lent it 10,000 on 15 November, Sub's statements would show no loan while the parent's showed a receivable. The adjustment comes first, then the elimination.

Adjust Sub: Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Loan from parent 10,000

Eliminate: Dr Loan from parent 10,000 / Cr Loan to Sub 10,000

A subsidiary with another functional currency is first translated under PSAK 221 (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21; see other-comprehensive-income).

8. Finding the error when the worksheet does not balance

Most errors show up in the balance sheet part, where totals stop agreeing; the notes advise checking each account one by one, but testing the entries first is faster.

  1. Each entry balances on its own. In the notes' own 2017 worksheet for Pam and Son, the equity elimination reads "Retained earnings $50.000; Capital stock – son $250.000; Unamortized excess $150.000 / Investment in Son $360.000; Noncontrolling interest $40.000". Debits are 450,000 and credits 400,000. Son's capital stock is 200,000; posted as written, the entry would leave the worksheet out by 50,000. The notes' worksheet itself uses 200,000.

  2. The investment and the subsidiary's equity accounts fall to zero.

  3. Each reciprocal pair cancels. Leave out entry (6a) in section 5 and the worksheet still balances. A loan to Sub of 5,000 survives in the consolidated column and cash is 5,000 short, an asset the group does not have in place of one it does.

  4. The ties hold. Consolidated profit and retained earnings attributable to owners equal the parent's under the equity method, and NCI equals its share of the subsidiary's net assets at group carrying amounts.

Check 4 catches errors that balance. The notes' Chapter 3 balance-sheet elimination one year after acquisition reads "Capital stock $60.000; Retained earnings $20.000; Goodwill $40.000 / Investment in son $108.000; Noncontrolling interest $12.000". It balances at 120,000, but Son's year-end retained earnings are 40,000 and goodwill on the notes' own figures is 20,000. Goodwill is overstated by 20,000 and 20,000 of Son's retained earnings survive into the consolidated column.

9. Consolidation procedures across industries

Groups in layers. A listed holding group can consolidate sub-group by sub-group. BREN's own statements already consolidate the Star Energy companies, so BREN's NCI can enter BRPT's worksheet as part of BREN's equity. Note 1d shows the chain, with PT Barito Wind Energy held 99.99 percent "through BREN" and PT Nefin Solar Asset 51 percent through Barito Wind Energy (PDF p. 26). K6 works through the effective interests.

Banks and structured entities. Banks consolidate securitisation vehicles and other structured entities, designed so that voting rights do not decide control, when the PSAK 110 control test is met; BRPT's policy also covers them (Note 3c, PDF p. 67).

Investment entities. An investment entity does not consolidate its investees, except subsidiaries that provide services for its investment activities, and measures them at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 110 paras. 31–32).

Mining and oil and gas. A participating interest held under a joint operating agreement is usually a joint operation under PSAK 111 (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11), and without joint control is still recognised line by line (para. 23), so there is no investment to eliminate and no NCI.

Islamic finance. A sharia subsidiary of a conventional bank is consolidated with the same entries, but it reports under PSAK 401 (formerly PSAK 101) with accounts such as murabahah receivables and temporary syirkah funds, which must be mapped to the group's chart of accounts first (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).

  • The NCI residuals in section 10 (287 in 2025, (1,100) in 2024) are unexplained. They are too large for rounding of the ownership percentage, and BREN's 2025 treasury shares (6,000,000, 0.01 percent) are already in the computation. Separately, Note 34 gives BREN's 2024 total assets as 3,798,375, liabilities as 3,062,313 and profit as 158,612, while BREN's own audited 2024 figures, unchanged as comparatives in its 2025 FS and used in BRPT's Note 1d and 2024 segment note (Note 46, PDF p. 239), are 3,787,513, 3,054,980 and 155,083. The net-asset gap equals the profit gap (3,529), and BREN's 2025 FS have no restatement note. CAP's 2024 total assets differ in the same way between Note 1d (5,663,616, PDF p. 24) and Note 34 (5,658,866, PDF p. 221), which suggests Note 34's 2024 summaries were compiled from different, perhaps preliminary, figures. That is inference.

  • The eliminations column in Note 46 (assets +139,079, depreciation +9,339) is described as behaving like an amortising consolidation adjustment. BRPT's acquisition of BREN's predecessor was accounted for under common control (Note 1d), so the adjustment probably relates to another acquisition or to something other than an excess; the FS do not say.

content.text: Consolidated statements are never recorded in anyone's ledger. They are built on a worksheet that adds the parent's and the subsidiaries' statements line by line and then removes what is internal to the group: the parent's investment against the subsidiary's equity, intragroup balances, and intragroup income, expenses and dividends (PSAK 110 B86).

The elimination entries run in a fixed order. Reverse the parent's income from the subsidiary and the subsidiary's dividends, record the non-controlling interest's (NCI's) share, eliminate opening equity against the investment and opening NCI, allocate and depreciate the excess paid over book value, and cancel reciprocal balances. The worksheet has three parts, profit or loss, then retained earnings, then the balance sheet, each feeding the next.

The method the parent uses in its own books (cost or equity method, both allowed by PSAK 227) changes the first entry and adds one conversion entry, but never the consolidated result. A worksheet that balances can still be wrong, so the ties to the parent's equity and to NCI matter more than the totals.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) list each subsidiary's "total assets before elimination" in their 2025 statements. PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk (BREN), 64.67 percent owned, has 3,867,410 at 31 December 2025, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF p. 26). What happens between such "before elimination" figures and the group's statements is the subject of this page.

After reading it a student should be able to prepare a three-part consolidation worksheet in the year of acquisition and in later years, write each elimination entry in order, adapt the worksheet to a parent that uses the cost method, and find the error when the worksheet does not balance.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's and BREN's statements are cited to their note; every other number is an illustration. Control, NCI measurement and profit attribution are taught in the
and used here without re-deriving them.
1. The parent's own books decide what must be eliminated
The parent's investment in a subsidiary sits in its own books as one asset. How that asset is measured in the parent's
(the parent's own statements, in which subsidiaries are investments) is a policy choice. PSAK 227

(formerly PSAK 4, IAS 27) allows cost, PSAK 109 or the equity method, applied to each category of investment consistently (para. 10). The equity-method option was added in Indonesia by the amendment to PSAK 4 ratified in November 2015 and effective from 1 January 2016, following the 2014 IAS 27 amendment. Dividends from a subsidiary go to profit or loss under cost or PSAK 109, and reduce the investment under the equity method (para. 12).
The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 4) assume the parent uses the equity method "secara komplit", the

. The parent books its share of the subsidiary's profit after the depreciation of the excess it paid over book value, so its profit equals the consolidated profit attributable to its owners. Beams calls this

BRPT holds 64.67 percent of BREN (Note 1d). Its interest in BREN's geothermal business came through common-control transactions. BRPT acquired Star Energy Group Holdings (SEGHPL) in 2018, pooled as if combined from the start (Note 1d, PDF p. 52) at book values (policy Note 3e, PDF p. 70), and BREN acquired SEGHPL from BRPT in 2022 for new BREN shares (BREN FS 2025, Note 19b, PDF p. 115). No fair value excess arose at BRPT's level, although goodwill from Star Energy's earlier purchase of Salak and Darajat was carried across at its carrying amount; the Business Combinations essay (K1) covers both. To show every entry, suppose instead (illustration) that on 1 January 2024 BRPT had bought 65 percent of a geothermal company from outside owners. The notes call their subsidiary "Son"; this page calls it Sub. A
is the amount by which an asset's fair value at acquisition exceeds its carrying amount in the subsidiary's books.
Sub's book equity = share capital 400,000 + retained earnings 200,000 = 600,000
Fair value uplifts: power plant +100,000 (20 years left, so 5,000 a year); spare-parts inventory +10,000 (used in 2024)
Identifiable net assets at fair value = 600,000 + 100,000 + 10,000 = 710,000

PSAK 103 lets the acquirer choose fair value or the proportionate share for NCI, deal by deal (essay 25, section 2). The proportionate share is used here. Deferred tax on the uplifts is ignored to keep the steps short; K1 adds it.
Sub earns 90,000 and pays dividends of 40,000 in 2024, then earns 110,000 and declares dividends of 50,000 in 2025, of which 20,000 is still unpaid at year end.
2024 profit as the group sees it = 90,000 − 10,000 inventory − 5,000 plant = 75,000; parent 65% = 48,750; NCI 35% = 26,250
2025 profit as the group sees it = 110,000 − 5,000 plant = 105,000; parent 65% = 68,250; NCI 35% = 36,750
Dr Investment in Sub 520,000 / Cr Cash 520,000
Dr Investment in Sub 48,750 / Cr Income from Sub 48,750
Dr Cash 26,000 / Cr Investment in Sub 26,000
Dr Investment in Sub 68,250 / Cr Income from Sub 68,250
Dr Cash 19,500, Dr Dividend receivable 13,000 / Cr Dividend income 32,500
Dr Cash 19,500, Dr Dividend receivable 13,000 / Cr Investment in Sub 32,500

The equity-method balance already contains the parent's share of Sub's retained profits and of the depreciated uplift. The cost-method balance contains neither, so the worksheet has to put them there before it can eliminate anything (section 6).
2. The worksheet has three parts, and each feeds the next

Each part of the worksheet ends in the figure the next part needs. The notes stack three parts (income statement, retained earnings statement, balance sheet), with columns for the parent, the subsidiary, the eliminations and the consolidated result.
Profit attributable to the owners of the parent, the last line of part one, is carried into part two.
Closing retained earnings, the last line of part two, is carried into part three.
Part three must then balance, total assets against total liabilities and equity.

PSAK 201 replaced the retained earnings statement with a statement of changes in equity, but the logic is unchanged. Every year starts again from the separate statements and repeats the entries for past events, such as the acquisition-date allocation.

(formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) describes the three steps the entries perform (B86): combine like items of assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows; offset the parent's investment against its portion of the subsidiary's equity; and eliminate intragroup assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows in full. BRPT's policy repeats the third step: "All intragroup assets and liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).
The notes give six entries in a fixed order. Each removes something that would otherwise be counted twice.
The parent's income line repeats Sub's revenues and expenses; dividends to the parent move cash inside the group
Dr Income from Sub / Cr Dividends declared (Sub, parent's share); Cr Investment for the difference
Consolidated profit belongs partly to outside owners, and their dividends reduce their claim
Dr NCI share of profit / Cr Dividends declared (NCI's share); Cr NCI for the difference
(3) Opening equity against investment and NCI
Sub's opening equity is already represented by the investment and opening NCI
Dr Share capital and opening retained earnings (Sub), Dr Unamortised excess / Cr Investment (opening), Cr NCI (opening)
is a worksheet suspense account to be assigned to the assets it paid for
Dr Plant and equipment, Dr Goodwill (and inventory or cost of sales) / Cr Unamortised excess
Group depreciation follows acquisition-date fair values (PSAK 110 B88); Sub depreciates book values
Dr Depreciation / Cr Plant and equipment
Balances between group companies are neither assets nor liabilities of the group
Dr the payable / Cr the receivable; Dr intragroup income / Cr intragroup expense

Entries (1) and (2) together remove all of Sub's dividends. Entry (1) returns the investment to its opening balance, which is why entry (3) can eliminate it against opening equity. The intragroup profit eliminations of K3 and K4 can sit anywhere in the sequence without changing the result.

In the first year the opening equity in entry (3) is the equity at the acquisition date, and the inventory uplift reaches cost of sales because the spares were used during the year. For example (illustration), the 2024 worksheet for Sub:
(1) Dr Income from Sub 48,750 / Cr Dividends declared 26,000; Cr Investment in Sub 22,750
(2) Dr NCI share of profit 26,250 / Cr Dividends declared 14,000; Cr NCI 12,250
(3) Dr Share capital, Sub 400,000; Dr Retained earnings, Sub 200,000; Dr Unamortised excess 168,500 / Cr Investment in Sub 520,000; Cr NCI 248,500
(4) Dr Cost of sales 10,000; Dr Plant and equipment 100,000; Dr Goodwill 58,500 / Cr Unamortised excess 168,500
(5) Dr Depreciation 5,000 / Cr Plant and equipment 5,000

Entry (3) balances at 768,500 on each side. The investment, 520,000 + 48,750 − 26,000 = 542,750, is credited 22,750 + 520,000 = 542,750 and falls to zero. NCI closes at 248,500 + 12,250 = 260,750, which is 35 percent of Sub's net assets at group carrying amounts (book values plus the uplifts not yet written off).
Under the proportionate method goodwill is not part of NCI. Had control been obtained during the year, Sub's income and expenses would enter only from the acquisition date (B88), a case K5 takes up.
5. A later year: the full worksheet
From the second year on, entry (3) uses Sub's retained earnings at the start of the year and the excess still unamortised at that date. In 2025 three intragroup transactions also need entry (6).
On 1 July 2025 the parent lent Sub 30,000 at 6 percent a year. Half a year's interest, 30,000 × 6% × 6/12 = 900, is accrued by both and unpaid.

On 30 December Sub repaid 5,000 of the loan by bank transfer, which reached the parent on 2 January. Sub shows a loan payable of 25,000, while the parent still shows a receivable of 30,000. The 5,000 is
, money that has left one group company and not yet reached the other.
Sub's unpaid dividend of 20,000 includes 13,000 owed to the parent.
For example (illustration), the opening amounts for 2025:
(1) Dr Income from Sub 68,250 / Cr Dividends declared 32,500; Cr Investment in Sub 35,750
(2) Dr NCI share of profit 36,750 / Cr Dividends declared 17,500; Cr NCI 19,250
(3) Dr Share capital, Sub 400,000; Dr Retained earnings 1 Jan, Sub 250,000; Dr Unamortised excess 153,500 / Cr Investment in Sub 542,750; Cr NCI 260,750
(4) Dr Plant and equipment 95,000; Dr Goodwill 58,500 / Cr Unamortised excess 153,500
(5) Dr Depreciation 5,000 / Cr Plant and equipment 5,000
(6a) Dr Cash in transit 5,000 / Cr Loan to Sub 5,000
(6b) Dr Loan from parent 25,000 / Cr Loan to Sub 25,000
(6c) Dr Interest payable 900 / Cr Interest receivable 900
(6d) Dr Interest income 900 / Cr Finance costs 900
(6e) Dr Dividend payable 13,000 / Cr Dividend receivable 13,000

Entry (6a) is an adjustment, not an elimination; the reciprocal balances must agree before (6b) cancels them. The notes handle a cheque in transit the same way, with "Cash $20.000 / Note receivable – Son $20.000" ahead of the eliminations.
The worksheet, Parent and Sub, year ended 31 December 2025 (illustration).
Credit balances in the income statement and equity are shown positive, expenses and dividends in parentheses; the elimination columns show the entry number.
Profit attributable to owners of the parent
Profit attributable to owners of the parent
The 1,111,800 of debits equals the 1,111,800 of credits, and total assets of 1,803,500 equal liabilities of 569,350 plus share capital 500,000, retained earnings 454,150 and NCI 280,000.
Consolidated profit attributable to owners = parent's equity-method profit = 114,150
Consolidated retained earnings = parent's equity-method retained earnings = 454,150
NCI = 35% × (Sub net assets 710,000 + plant uplift remaining 90,000) = 35% × 800,000 = 280,000
The 7,000 of dividend payable left after (6e) is owed to Sub's outside shareholders, a real group liability.
6. A parent on the cost method

A parent using the cost method reaches the same consolidated statements by changing two entries. Its investment still stands at 520,000, its opening retained earnings lack its share of Sub's retained profits, and its profit carries dividend income instead of the share of profit.
Conversion to equity basis at 1 Jan 2025 = 48,750 − 26,000 = 22,750
Parent's retained earnings, 1 Jan 2025, cost method = 400,000 − 22,750 = 377,250
Dr Investment in Sub 22,750 / Cr Retained earnings 1 Jan, parent 22,750
Dr Dividend income 32,500 / Cr Dividends declared 32,500
Dr Income from Sub 68,250 / Cr Dividends declared 32,500; Cr Investment in Sub 35,750

Entry (0) lifts the investment to 520,000 + 22,750 = 542,750, the opening balance entry (3) eliminates, and lifts the parent's opening retained earnings to the equity-method 400,000. The 22,750 is the parent's share of Sub's retained profits since acquisition, 65% × (250,000 − 200,000) = 32,500, less its share of the excess already written off, 65% × 15,000 = 9,750. Entry (1) then removes only the dividend income, because the 68,250 share of profit was never in the parent's column, and the consolidated column comes out as in section 5. The notes cover only the equity method; this section follows Beams and PSAK 227.

The worksheet adds like items only if they were measured alike and at the same date. PSAK 110 requires adjustments when a group member uses accounting policies other than the group's (B87). BRPT's policy says adjustments are made "when necessary ... to bring their accounting policies in line with the Group's accounting policies" (Note 3c, PDF p. 67). For example (illustration, separate from the section 5 worksheet), suppose Sub carries an office building it rents out at fair value under PSAK 240 (formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40), while the group uses the cost model. Sub bought the building on 1 January 2025 and booked a fair value gain of 3,000 at year end; the group's cost-model depreciation would be 400. Before the eliminations:
Dr Fair value gain 3,000; Dr Depreciation 400 / Cr Investment property 3,400
Like any adjustment to Sub's figures, its effect on profit is shared with NCI, so NCI's share of profit falls by 35% × 3,400 = 1,190.

Reporting dates should be the same. If that is impracticable, the subsidiary's most recent statements may be used, adjusted for significant transactions or events in between, provided the gap is no more than three months and the length of periods and the gap stay the same from period to period (B92–B93). The notes state the same three-month limit but only require material intervening events to be disclosed; PSAK 110 requires adjustment. For example (illustration), if Sub's year ended on 30 September and the parent lent it 10,000 on 15 November, Sub's statements would show no loan while the parent's showed a receivable. The adjustment comes first, then the elimination.
Adjust Sub: Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Loan from parent 10,000
Eliminate: Dr Loan from parent 10,000 / Cr Loan to Sub 10,000
A subsidiary with another functional currency is first translated under PSAK 221 (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21; see
8. Finding the error when the worksheet does not balance
Most errors show up in the balance sheet part, where totals stop agreeing; the notes advise checking each account one by one, but testing the entries first is faster.
Each entry balances on its own.

In the notes' own 2017 worksheet for Pam and Son, the equity elimination reads "Retained earnings $50.000; Capital stock – son $250.000; Unamortized excess $150.000 / Investment in Son $360.000; Noncontrolling interest $40.000". Debits are 450,000 and credits 400,000. Son's capital stock is 200,000; posted as written, the entry would leave the worksheet out by 50,000. The notes' worksheet itself uses 200,000.
The investment and the subsidiary's equity accounts fall to zero.

Leave out entry (6a) in section 5 and the worksheet still balances. A loan to Sub of 5,000 survives in the consolidated column and cash is 5,000 short, an asset the group does not have in place of one it does.
Consolidated profit and retained earnings attributable to owners equal the parent's under the equity method, and NCI equals its share of the subsidiary's net assets at group carrying amounts.

Check 4 catches errors that balance. The notes' Chapter 3 balance-sheet elimination one year after acquisition reads "Capital stock $60.000; Retained earnings $20.000; Goodwill $40.000 / Investment in son $108.000; Noncontrolling interest $12.000". It balances at 120,000, but Son's year-end retained earnings are 40,000 and goodwill on the notes' own figures is 20,000. Goodwill is overstated by 20,000 and 20,000 of Son's retained earnings survive into the consolidated column.

A listed holding group can consolidate sub-group by sub-group. BREN's own statements already consolidate the Star Energy companies, so BREN's NCI can enter BRPT's worksheet as part of BREN's equity. Note 1d shows the chain, with PT Barito Wind Energy held 99.99 percent "through BREN" and PT Nefin Solar Asset 51 percent through Barito Wind Energy (PDF p. 26). K6 works through the effective interests.
Banks consolidate securitisation vehicles and other
, designed so that voting rights do not decide control, when the PSAK 110 control test is met; BRPT's policy also covers them (Note 3c, PDF p. 67).

An investment entity does not consolidate its investees, except subsidiaries that provide services for its investment activities, and measures them at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 110 paras. 31–32).

A participating interest held under a joint operating agreement is usually a joint operation under PSAK 111 (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11), and without joint control is still recognised line by line (para. 23), so there is no investment to eliminate and no NCI.
A sharia subsidiary of a conventional bank is consolidated with the same entries, but it reports under PSAK 401 (formerly PSAK 101) with accounts such as murabahah receivables and temporary
funds, which must be mapped to the group's chart of accounts first (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).
10. Presentation and analysis: Barito Pacific's Notes 1d, 34 and 46

Three BRPT notes show the worksheet's outputs. Note 34 splits NCI by sub-group and gives BREN's summarised figures "before intragroup eliminations" (PDF pp. 220–222). BREN's own consolidated statements give the equity those figures come from (BREN FS 2025, statement of financial position, PDF p. 12).
BREN equity attributable to its owners (BREN FS)
Outside share of BREN's outstanding shares (net of treasury)
Expected NCI for "BREN and its subsidiaries"

With no fair value excess at BRPT's level, NCI should be the outside share of BREN's book equity plus BREN's own NCI, which is what entry (3) and the NCI roll-forward produce. The reported figure is within about 0.1 percent of that prediction in 2025 and 0.3 percent in 2024. The residuals are unexplained; BRPT does not reconcile them.

The segment note shows elimination at work on income (Note 46, PDF p. 239). Inter-segment revenue of 4,538 in 2025 (property 4,505 and others 33) is removed to reach consolidated revenue of 7,630,662, against 5,136 in 2024. The energy and resources segment's assets of 3,867,410 equal BREN's total assets, so the segment is BREN's consolidated statements. The eliminations column also adds 139,079 to assets and 9,339 to depreciation in 2025 (150,683 and 8,897 in 2024). Adjustments booked in no segment's ledger and depreciated each year behave like entries (4) and (5), but BRPT does not say what they are, and with no excess on BREN they may relate to another acquisition or to other group-level adjustments.
: control, NCI measurement, attribution, ownership changes.
: the equity method in an investor's books.
: goodwill after acquisition and its impairment.
: translation of foreign subsidiaries before consolidation.
: what consolidated retained earnings and NCI-transaction reserves contain.
: the acquisition method, the allocation of excess, deferred tax on uplifts, and common control.
: the consolidated cash flow statement (the second half of AKL Chapter 4) and mid-year acquisitions.

The NCI residuals in section 10 (287 in 2025, (1,100) in 2024) are unexplained. They are too large for rounding of the ownership percentage, and BREN's 2025 treasury shares (6,000,000, 0.01 percent) are already in the computation. Separately, Note 34 gives BREN's 2024 total assets as 3,798,375, liabilities as 3,062,313 and profit as 158,612, while BREN's own audited 2024 figures, unchanged as comparatives in its 2025 FS and used in BRPT's Note 1d and 2024 segment note (Note 46, PDF p. 239), are 3,787,513, 3,054,980 and 155,083. The net-asset gap equals the profit gap (3,529), and BREN's 2025 FS have no restatement note. CAP's 2024 total assets differ in the same way between Note 1d (5,663,616, PDF p. 24) and Note 34 (5,658,866, PDF p. 221), which suggests Note 34's 2024 summaries were compiled from different, perhaps preliminary, figures. That is inference.

The eliminations column in Note 46 (assets +139,079, depreciation +9,339) is described as behaving like an amortising consolidation adjustment. BRPT's acquisition of BREN's predecessor was accounted for under common control (Note 1d), so the adjustment probably relates to another acquisition or to something other than an excess; the FS do not say.
The Indonesian PSAK 227 text itself was not opened; paras. 10 and 12 were checked against the IAS 27 text.
The Islamic-finance mapping step in section 9 rests on knowledge of PSAK 401's presentation, not on a checked rule for consolidation.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk dan Entitas Anak, consolidated financial statements 31 December 2025 (audited, USD thousand): Note 1d (PDF pp. 24, 26, 52); Note 3c (PDF pp. 67–68); Note 3e (PDF p. 70); Note 34 (PDF pp. 220–222); Note 46 (PDF p. 239). BRPT FS. PDF pages verified against the PDF text layer.

PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk dan Entitas Anak, consolidated financial statements 31 December 2025 and 2024 (audited, USD thousand) (statement of financial position PDF p. 12; Note 19a–b, PDF pp. 114–115) and BREN FS 2024. BRPT FS (subsidiary).

Lecture notes this page follows, "AKL – Chapter 4 – Consolidation Technique and Procedurs" and "AKL – Chapter 3 – A introduction to Consolidated Financial Statements" (Rumpun Akuntansi Keuangan), summarising Beams et al.,

. NOTES. Order followed: equity-method parent, entries (1)–(6), year of acquisition, later year, locating errors, allocation of excess; reporting dates from Chapter 3. Corrections made here, checked against the PDFs: Chapter 4 gives Son's 2016 net income as "$46.000" while its worksheet shows 50,000 (46,000 is profit after the 4,000 patent amortisation, and 20% × 46,000 = 9,200 is the NCI share); the 2017 entry credits "Income from Son $20.800" where it should credit Investment in Son; the investment is "$209.000" in the text and 209,600 in the schedule; Son's 2017 income is "$600.000" for 60,000; the equipment adjustment is written "$2.0000"; the 2017 equity elimination debits "Capital stock – son $250.000" for 200,000, so it does not balance; the Pam–Son 2017 retained earnings section ends Son's balance at 130,000 where 50,000 + 60,000 − 20,000 = 90,000 (its balance sheet shows 90,000); the fair value table is headed "Inventories | Book Value" for "Fair value | Book value"; and the worksheet is headed "Pop 80% Son" in a 90 percent case. Chapter 3's year-later entry (Retained earnings 20,000; Goodwill 40,000) should be 40,000 and 20,000, as already noted in essay 25. The notes measure NCI from the implied value of the parent's price (US GAAP full goodwill); PSAK 103 uses NCI's own fair value or the proportionate share, and this page uses the proportionate share. The notes cover only the equity method, and their three-month rule only requires disclosure of intervening events; section 6 follows Beams and PSAK 227, section 7 PSAK 110 B87, B92–B93. Section 9 has no note.

title: Corporate and Dividend Taxes Receivable: Current Tax Assets, Refunds and Tax Disputes
snippet: The theory of current tax assets from the year-end tax computation to the Tax Court, worked through PHE's tax note and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • Current tax is the tax due on one year's taxable profit. When the tax already paid for a period exceeds the tax due, PSAK 212 recognises the excess as an asset, a current tax asset. In Indonesia it arises mainly from instalments and withholding, because the law allows no loss carryback.

  • The asset is measured at the amount expected to be recovered from the tax authority. Where the authority disputes the claim, ISAK 123 decides how much stays. The claim is kept in full if acceptance is probable and is otherwise measured at the most likely amount or the expected value. The contingent-asset rule of PSAK 237 does not apply to income tax.

  • The split between current and non-current follows the expected date of cash. A claim that goes through examination, objection and appeal can take years, so contested claims move into non-current assets.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report corporate and dividend taxes receivable, current portion, of 26,288 at 31 December 2024 against 12,503 a year earlier, and a non-current portion of 3,106 against 3,460, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; Note 43a, Daftar 5/151, PDF p. 168; "Daftar" is the printed page). Together they are 29,394, or 0.10 percent of total assets (0.05 percent a year earlier); the current portion is 0.33 percent of current assets. On the other side, PHE owes corporate and dividend taxes of 238,034, all current, against 582,109 a year earlier, of which 16,086 was non-current (Note 43b, Daftar 5/152, PDF p. 169). This page covers the payable lines too.

After reading this page a student should be able to explain where a current tax asset comes from, record it from instalment to refund, measure a disputed claim, and classify it between current and non-current.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Current tax: the amount due for the year

Kieso's chapter on income taxes starts with the two measures of profit. Accounting profit is measured under SAK for investors; taxable profit is measured under the tax law and determines the tax the state collects. PSAK 212 Income Taxes (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) calls the tax on taxable profit current tax (para. 5). Current tax unpaid at the reporting date is a liability; tax paid in excess of the amount due is an asset (para. 12). The companion page on deferred tax assets covers the gap between the two profits. This page stays with the current part.

The line's name comes from how upstream contractors are taxed. PHE explains that contractors under production sharing contracts (PSCs) pay tax on their share of production, less bonuses, "at a combined rate comprising corporate income tax and dividend tax" (Note 2a(ii), Daftar 5/9, PDF p. 26). The second part is a tax on profit after corporate tax, levied whether or not the profit is distributed. For a foreign company operating through an Indonesian branch it takes the form of branch profit tax under article 26 of the Income Tax Law.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary whose PSC was signed when the corporate rate was 25 percent and fixes a 20 percent dividend tax computes its 2024 taxable income as 100,000.

Corporate income tax = 100,000 × 25% = 25,000

Dividend tax = (100,000 − 25,000) × 20% = 15,000

Current tax due for 2024 = 40,000, a combined rate of 40%

31 Dec 2024: Dr Current tax expense 40,000 / Cr Corporate and dividend taxes payable 40,000

If nothing had been paid during the year, the 40,000 would be a liability due with the annual return. The general Indonesian rate is now 22 percent; a cost-recovery PSC keeps the rate of its signing date until it is extended or amended, which PHE's policy also states for deferred tax (Note 3s, Daftar 5/69, PDF p. 86).

2. How a current tax asset arises

Tax is rarely paid in one sum after the year closes. It is paid during the year, before taxable profit is known, and the year-end computation then settles the difference. PHE describes its current tax as computed on "estimated taxable income", to be adjusted when the annual return is submitted (Note 43d, Daftar 5/153, PDF p. 170).

Three routes lead to an overpayment.

  • Instalments. A general Indonesian company pays monthly instalments (PPh article 25) of roughly one-twelfth of last year's tax, so a weaker year ends overpaid. Upstream contractors pay under their own regime. PMK 81/2024 lists the taxes a contractor pays as instalments during the year, the corporate tax due at year end, and the tax on income after corporate tax, paid monthly or annually. A contractor whose provisional figures overstate the year's profit, because prices fell or recoverable costs rose late in the year, ends with an overpayment.

  • Withholding. Tax withheld by customers or collected on imports (PPh articles 22 and 23) is a credit against the year's tax. A company with many withheld receipts and low profit can be overpaid every year.

  • Assessments paid while disputed. A company that pays an assessment it is contesting holds an asset if it expects to win (section 5).

For example (illustration), the subsidiary of section 1 pays monthly instalments based on provisional figures. Side by side, a year that ends underpaid and one that ends overpaid:

Underpaid (kurang bayar)

Tax expense is 40,000 in both columns. The timing of payment never changes the expense; it decides only whether a payable or a receivable is left. PSAK 212 sets no probability threshold for the overpaid 2,000, because the cash has left. The uncertainty is about the amount due, which section 4 takes up.

3. Loss carryback and the Indonesian alternative

Kieso's chapter produces a tax receivable from a different source, the loss carryback. A company with a loss applies it against the taxable profit of the two previous years and claims a refund of the tax paid on them. PSAK 212 recognises that benefit as an asset in the year of the loss, because it is probable and measurable (paras. 13–14).

Indonesia allows no carryback. A loss can only be carried forward five years (UU PPh art. 6(2)), and that benefit is a deferred tax asset. What does happen in a loss year is that instalments paid during it become refundable. For example (illustration), a subsidiary outside PSC activities pays 9,000 of instalments in 2024 on provisional profit, and the year ends with a tax loss of 50,000.

Kieso (with carryback)

The receivable is 9,000 because nothing is due for a loss year. The 15,000 paid in earlier years stays with the state.

4. Measuring the claim: examination and assessment

A current tax asset is measured at the amount expected to be recovered from the tax authority, using the rates and law enacted at the reporting date (para. 46). For an overpayment that amount is decided by the Directorate General of Taxes (DJP) through a fixed sequence under the tax procedure law (UU KUP).

  1. Annual return. A company files within four months of year end, so by 30 April for a calendar year. A return showing an overpayment carries a refund request (restitusi).

  2. Examination. A refund request generally triggers a tax examination. DJP must issue an assessment within 12 months of the complete request, or the request is deemed granted (art. 17B). Low-risk taxpayers can receive a preliminary refund without examination (arts. 17C–17D).

  3. Assessment. An SKPLB confirms an overpayment, an SKPN finds neither overpayment nor underpayment, and an SKPKB assesses an underpayment with interest. An SKPLB is refunded after DJP offsets any other tax owed.

The examiners' corrections set the amount. For example (illustration), the subsidiary's return for 2023 showed the same 2,000 overpayment. It was filed in April 2024 and examined during 2024, and DJP disallows 3,000 of costs.

Tax effect of the corrections = 3,000 × 40% = 1,200

SKPLB = 2,000 − 1,200 = 800

Had DJP disallowed 6,000 of costs, the tax effect of 2,400 would exceed the claim, and the result would be an SKPKB for 2,400 − 2,000 = 400 plus interest. A refund claim can turn into an underpayment.

5. Uncertainty: measuring a disputed claim under ISAK 123

If the company accepts the corrections, the asset falls to 800 and 1,200 is charged to current tax expense. If it contests them, the question is how much of the claim is still "in excess of the amount due". Kieso's chapter on current liabilities lists a possible tax refund among contingent assets, recognised only when virtually certain under PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37). For income tax that rule does not apply. PSAK 237 excludes income taxes (para. 5), and in July 2014 the IFRS Interpretations Committee confirmed that IAS 12 governs recognition. An asset is recognised if the cash paid exceeds the tax expected to be due, and the reference to IAS 37 in IAS 12 para. 88 concerns disclosure only.

How much tax is "expected to be due" when the treatment is disputed is answered by ISAK 123 Uncertainty over Income Tax Treatments (formerly ISAK 34, IFRIC 23).

  1. Assume the authority examines the item with full knowledge of the facts. The chance that it goes unnoticed does not count.

  2. Ask whether the authority, including the courts, will probably accept the treatment used in the return.

  3. If acceptance is probable, measure the tax as filed (para. 10).

  4. If not, use the method that better predicts the outcome (para. 11): the most likely amount, the single most likely result, suited to an all-or-nothing dispute; or the expected value, the probability-weighted sum, suited to a range of results.

For example (illustration), the subsidiary contests all 3,000 in two items.

  • Item A, 1,750 of head-office overhead charged under an allocation method SKK Migas approved, tax effect 700. The company has won the same point in court for an earlier year and judges acceptance probable. It keeps 700 in full.

  • Item B, 1,250 of well costs DJP says served an affiliate's block, tax effect 500. Without precedent the company puts its chance at 40 percent. Acceptance is not probable, and the court will allow the costs or not.

Most likely amount for item B = 0; expected value would be 40% × 500 = 200, a result that cannot occur

Asset carried = 800 (SKPLB) + 700 (item A) = 1,500

Charge = 2,000 − 1,500 = 500

Dr Current tax expense (change in estimate for 2023 tax) 500 / Cr Corporate and dividend taxes receivable 500

The examination is new information, so the reduction is a change in estimate in the year it arises, with no restatement (PSAK 208, formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8). The company still objects to the full 1,200. If it later wins item B, the 500 reduces tax expense when acceptance becomes probable.

The same test applies when a company pays a disputed SKPKB. Since the HPP law, tax unpaid when an objection is filed is not a tax debt while the objection runs, but a lost objection or appeal carries a fine of 30 or 60 percent of the tax still unpaid (section 6). Paying first removes that base. For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays an SKPKB of 900 before objecting, on grounds it judges probable to succeed.

Dr Corporate and dividend taxes receivable (assessment in dispute) 900 / Cr Cash 900

The cash paid is certain, the tax due is not, and the excess of one over the other is the asset.

6. Interest and penalties

When a taxpayer wins an objection or appeal, DJP pays imbalan bunga, interest compensation, for the period from the assessment to the decision, up to 24 months (UU KUP art. 27B). When it loses, fines apply: 30 percent of the tax due under a rejected objection and 60 percent under a rejected appeal, computed on tax not yet paid. A refund dispute where no tax is unpaid gives little or no base for the fine.

Whether interest is income tax calls for a judgement, and the entity has no free policy choice between the two standards. The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in 2017 that an entity applies IAS 12 to interest and penalties it judges to be income taxes, and IAS 37 otherwise, and discloses the judgement under IAS 1 para. 122. Under PSAK 237, interest compensation would be a contingent asset, recognised only when virtually certain.

7. Presentation: current or non-current, gross or net

Current or non-current. An asset is current when the entity expects to realise it within twelve months of the reporting date (PSAK 201.66, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). For a tax claim the test is the expected date of cash, and the dispute timetable sets it.

One tax year now sits in both lines. A judicial review by DJP does not suspend a Tax Court decision, so a won appeal can be refunded before the Supreme Court rules. Each new contested year adds a layer, so the non-current part grows while disputes start faster than the courts close them.

The payable side. Current tax still unpaid is a liability (para. 12), measured at the amount expected to be paid (para. 46), and ISAK 123 measures an uncertain treatment the same way on either side. It is current unless, at the reporting date, the entity has a right to defer settlement for at least twelve months (PSAK 201.69(d)). A payment schedule granted by DJP, or tax that by law is not yet due while an objection runs, could give that right. For example (illustration), the underpaid column of section 2 leaves 4,000 payable with the annual return by 30 April 2025, which is current.

Gross or net. A current tax asset and a current tax liability are offset only if the entity has a legally enforceable right to set them off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (PSAK 212.71). In consolidated statements one subsidiary's receivable can be set against another's payable only if they have that right and intention together (para. 73). Indonesia has no group taxation, and each PSC usually files in its own subsidiary. So a group can show a receivable and a payable for the same kind of tax at the same date.
