Distinct from deferred tax. A current tax asset is cash already paid that the state must return, whatever the company earns next year. A deferred tax asset is a future deduction worth something only if there is future taxable profit. The first can be current or non-current; the second is always non-current (PSAK 201.56).

8. Taxes receivable across industries

The theory is the same everywhere. What differs is which taxes are income taxes, and which industries are routinely overpaid.

Final-tax industries: construction, real estate, deposits. Income taxed under a final regime is outside PSAK 212, as PHE's policy notes for its own final-taxed items (Note 3s, Daftar 5/70, PDF p. 87). A contractor whose customers withhold final tax on construction services has no income tax receivable on that revenue. The tax withheld is the final tax, an expense or a deduction from revenue, not an income tax overpayment. For example (illustration), construction revenue of 1,000 with final tax withheld at 2.65 percent.

Final tax = 1,000 × 2.65% = 26.5

Dr Final tax expense 26.5 / Cr Trade receivables 26.5

Exporters and VAT. Exporters charge 0 percent VAT on exports but pay VAT on inputs, so they hold VAT refund claims. VAT is not an income tax, so the claim is an other tax receivable outside PSAK 212 and ISAK 123. Nor is it a financial asset under PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9), because it arises from statute, not from a contract (PSAK 232 AG12, IAS 32). It is still an asset. In January 2019 the IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded that a deposit paid on a disputed tax other than income tax is an asset, not a contingent asset, accounted for by analogy under PSAK 208. PHE shows the size of this neighbour. Reimbursable VAT of 505,861 sits inside "other taxes receivable", against 29,394 of corporate and dividend taxes receivable (Note 43a). Its separate provision for impairment of tax receivable, 10,555 in both years, sits in the other-taxes line.

Manufacturers and traders with import withholding. PPh 22 collected on imports is credited against annual tax. A low-margin importer can be overpaid year after year, which is why the preliminary refund route of arts. 17C–17D exists. These companies carry a recurring, mostly current, tax receivable.

Groups with foreign branches. A foreign company's Indonesian branch, a bentuk usaha tetap (BUT), pays branch profit tax on after-tax profit, sometimes at a treaty rate. Disputes over that tax produce receivables of the kind section 9 shows at PHE.

10. Upstream note: PSC tax

Under a cost-recovery PSC the corporate and dividend tax rates are fixed by the contract, and costs disallowed for cost recovery by SKK Migas can be the same costs DJP corrects for tax, which can put one cost in dispute twice. Gross split PSCs pay tax under the prevailing law, and DJP can assess them for ten years instead of five (Note 43f, Daftar 5/156, PDF p. 173). That longer window keeps assessments, and the receivables they create, open for longer.

  • other-taxes-receivable-current: VAT and other non-income taxes, outside PSAK 212.

  • deferred-tax-assets: future deductions, as opposed to tax already paid.

Least-confident assertions

  • The monthly instalment basis for upstream contractors under PMK 81/2024 was seen only through a DDTC summary that lists the payment types without the formula. That provisional figures drive overpayments is this page's reading of PHE's Note 43d.

  • The objection, appeal, fine and interest rules of UU KUP (arts. 25–27, 27B) were checked only in secondary sources, and the judicial-review filing period in summaries that do not settle the article number. The 12-month refund rule of art. 17B was checked in DDTC and Ortax summaries.

  • That a judicial review by DJP does not suspend the Tax Court decision, so a won appeal can be refunded before the Supreme Court rules, is from a DDTC summary; when refunds are paid in practice was not checked.

  • Where the Natuna claims are carried is not stated by PHE. The page shows only that, at the end of 2023, they exceeded the whole line. Nor does PHE explain its 2023 non-current tax payable of 16,086; the deferral rights suggested for it in section 7 are possibilities under PSAK 201.69(d), not facts.

  • Treating a VAT refund claim by analogy with the 2019 agenda decision, which concerns a deposit on a disputed non-income tax, is a reading. An undisputed VAT overpayment is the same kind of statutory right, but the decision does not address it directly.

. In Indonesia it arises mainly from instalments and withholding, because the law allows no loss carryback.

The asset is measured at the amount expected to be recovered from the tax authority. Where the authority disputes the claim, ISAK 123 decides how much stays. The claim is kept in full if acceptance is probable and is otherwise measured at the most likely amount or the expected value. The contingent-asset rule of PSAK 237 does not apply to income tax.

The split between current and non-current follows the expected date of cash. A claim that goes through examination, objection and appeal can take years, so contested claims move into non-current assets.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report corporate and dividend taxes receivable, current portion, of 26,288 at 31 December 2024 against 12,503 a year earlier, and a non-current portion of 3,106 against 3,460, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; Note 43a, Daftar 5/151, PDF p. 168; "Daftar" is the printed page). This page covers the payable lines too.

After reading this page a student should be able to explain where a current tax asset comes from, record it from instalment to refund, measure a disputed claim, and classify it between current and non-current.

Had DJP disallowed 6,000 of costs, the tax effect of 2,400 would exceed the claim, and the result would be an SKPKB for 2,400 − 2,000 = 400 plus interest. A refund claim can turn into an underpayment.
5. Uncertainty: measuring a disputed claim under ISAK 123

If the company accepts the corrections, the asset falls to 800 and 1,200 is charged to current tax expense. If it contests them, the question is how much of the claim is still "in excess of the amount due". Kieso's chapter on current liabilities lists a

among contingent assets, recognised only when virtually certain under PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37). For income tax that rule does not apply. PSAK 237 excludes income taxes (para. 5), and in July 2014 the IFRS Interpretations Committee confirmed that IAS 12 governs recognition. An asset is recognised if the cash paid exceeds the tax expected to be due, and the reference to IAS 37 in IAS 12 para. 88 concerns disclosure only.
How much tax is "expected to be due" when the treatment is disputed is answered by ISAK 123
Assume the authority examines the item with full knowledge of the facts. The chance that it goes unnoticed does not count.
Ask whether the authority, including the courts, will probably accept the treatment used in the return.
If acceptance is probable, measure the tax as filed (para. 10).
If not, use the method that better predicts the outcome (para. 11): the
, the single most likely result, suited to an all-or-nothing dispute; or the
, the probability-weighted sum, suited to a range of results.
For example (illustration), the subsidiary contests all 3,000 in two items.

, 1,750 of head-office overhead charged under an allocation method SKK Migas approved, tax effect 700. The company has won the same point in court for an earlier year and judges acceptance probable. It keeps 700 in full.

, 1,250 of well costs DJP says served an affiliate's block, tax effect 500. Without precedent the company puts its chance at 40 percent. Acceptance is not probable, and the court will allow the costs or not.
Most likely amount for item B = 0; expected value would be 40% × 500 = 200, a result that cannot occur
Dr Current tax expense (change in estimate for 2023 tax) 500 / Cr Corporate and dividend taxes receivable 500

The examination is new information, so the reduction is a change in estimate in the year it arises, with no restatement (PSAK 208, formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8). The company still objects to the full 1,200. If it later wins item B, the 500 reduces tax expense when acceptance becomes probable.

The same test applies when a company pays a disputed SKPKB. Since the HPP law, tax unpaid when an objection is filed is not a tax debt while the objection runs, but a lost objection or appeal carries a fine of 30 or 60 percent of the tax still unpaid (section 6). Paying first removes that base. For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays an SKPKB of 900 before objecting, on grounds it judges probable to succeed.
Dr Corporate and dividend taxes receivable (assessment in dispute) 900 / Cr Cash 900
The cash paid is certain, the tax due is not, and the excess of one over the other is the asset.
When a taxpayer wins an objection or appeal, DJP pays

, interest compensation, for the period from the assessment to the decision, up to 24 months (UU KUP art. 27B). When it loses, fines apply: 30 percent of the tax due under a rejected objection and 60 percent under a rejected appeal, computed on tax not yet paid. A refund dispute where no tax is unpaid gives little or no base for the fine.

Whether interest is income tax calls for a judgement, and the entity has no free policy choice between the two standards. The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in 2017 that an entity applies IAS 12 to interest and penalties it judges to be income taxes, and IAS 37 otherwise, and discloses the judgement under IAS 1 para. 122. Under PSAK 237, interest compensation would be a contingent asset, recognised only when virtually certain.
7. Presentation: current or non-current, gross or net

An asset is current when the entity expects to realise it within twelve months of the reporting date (PSAK 201.66, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). For a tax claim the test is the expected date of cash, and the dispute timetable sets it.
Objection, filed within 3 months; decided within 12
Appeal to the Tax Court, filed within 3 months; decided within 12, extendable by 3
) at the Supreme Court, filed within 3 months; decided within 6
For example (illustration), at 31 December 2024 the subsidiary's 1,500 splits as follows.
SKPLB of 800 issued, refund expected in early 2025: current
Item A of 700, objection to be filed in 2025, DJP expected to reject it as it did for the earlier year, and the appeal expected to run to 2027: non-current
Dr Corporate and dividend taxes receivable, non-current 700 / Cr Corporate and dividend taxes receivable, current 700

One tax year now sits in both lines. A judicial review by DJP does not suspend a Tax Court decision, so a won appeal can be refunded before the Supreme Court rules. Each new contested year adds a layer, so the non-current part grows while disputes start faster than the courts close them.

Current tax still unpaid is a liability (para. 12), measured at the amount expected to be paid (para. 46), and ISAK 123 measures an uncertain treatment the same way on either side. It is current unless, at the reporting date, the entity has a right to defer settlement for at least twelve months (PSAK 201.69(d)). A payment schedule granted by DJP, or tax that by law is not yet due while an objection runs, could give that right. For example (illustration), the underpaid column of section 2 leaves 4,000 payable with the annual return by 30 April 2025, which is current.

A current tax asset and a current tax liability are offset only if the entity has a legally enforceable right to set them off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (PSAK 212.71). In consolidated statements one subsidiary's receivable can be set against another's payable only if they have that right and intention together (para. 73). Indonesia has no group taxation, and each PSC usually files in its own subsidiary. So a group can show a receivable and a payable for the same kind of tax at the same date. For example (illustration):

A current tax asset is cash already paid that the state must return, whatever the company earns next year. A deferred tax asset is a future deduction worth something only if there is future taxable profit. The first can be current or non-current; the second is always non-current (PSAK 201.56).
The theory is the same everywhere. What differs is which taxes are income taxes, and which industries are routinely overpaid.
Final-tax industries: construction, real estate, deposits.

Income taxed under a final regime is outside PSAK 212, as PHE's policy notes for its own final-taxed items (Note 3s, Daftar 5/70, PDF p. 87). A contractor whose customers withhold final tax on construction services has no income tax receivable on that revenue. The tax withheld is the final tax, an expense or a deduction from revenue, not an income tax overpayment. For example (illustration), construction revenue of 1,000 with final tax withheld at 2.65 percent.
Dr Final tax expense 26.5 / Cr Trade receivables 26.5
Exporters charge 0 percent VAT on exports but pay VAT on inputs, so they hold VAT refund claims. VAT is not an income tax, so the claim is an

outside PSAK 212 and ISAK 123. Nor is it a financial asset under PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9), because it arises from statute, not from a contract (PSAK 232 AG12, IAS 32). It is still an asset. In January 2019 the IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded that a deposit paid on a disputed tax other than income tax is an asset, not a contingent asset, accounted for by analogy under PSAK 208. PHE shows the size of this neighbour. Reimbursable VAT of 505,861 sits inside "other taxes receivable", against 29,394 of corporate and dividend taxes receivable (Note 43a). Its separate provision for impairment of tax receivable, 10,555 in both years, sits in the other-taxes line.
Manufacturers and traders with import withholding.

PPh 22 collected on imports is credited against annual tax. A low-margin importer can be overpaid year after year, which is why the preliminary refund route of arts. 17C–17D exists. These companies carry a recurring, mostly current, tax receivable.
A foreign company's Indonesian branch, a
(BUT), pays branch profit tax on after-tax profit, sometimes at a treaty rate. Disputes over that tax produce receivables of the kind section 9 shows at PHE.
9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 43a and 43g
Note 43a gives the composition (Daftar 5/151, PDF p. 168).
Corporate and dividend taxes receivable, current
Corporate and dividend taxes receivable, non-current
Corporate and dividend taxes payable, current (Note 43b)
Corporate and dividend taxes payable, non-current (Note 43b)
Payable to 2024 current tax = 238,034 / 1,473,547 = 16.2% (Note 43c, Daftar 5/152, PDF p. 169)

The payable fell 344,075 in 2024, and at year end it is about one-sixth of the year's current tax, which is consistent with most of it being settled during the year through the instalments of section 2. The non-current payable of 16,086 at the end of 2023 is gone by 2024. PHE does not say what it was or what right to defer it rested on.

All of the receivable belongs to subsidiaries, and the group shows it beside a payable eight times its size at the same date. That fits section 7's gross presentation if the overpaid and the underpaid amounts belong to different taxpayers or different years, which the note does not break down. PHE does not split the current portion between overpaid 2024 tax and earlier claims, so the doubling cannot be explained.

Note 43g lists the disputes. One subsidiary, which PHE calls Natuna (PSC A, Natuna Sea), shows how long a dividend-tax claim takes. For its 2018 branch profit tax it reported an overpayment of USD 7,628,906 (full amount).
September 2021: SKP Nihil, DJP finds no overpayment
1 March 2023: appeal to the Tax Court; granted in full 5 December 2023
14 March 2024: DJP applies for judicial review; Supreme Court rejects it, decision dated 30 September 2024

The English column dates the decision 31 December 2024 (Note 43g, Daftar 5/165, PDF p. 182). Either way the claim for tax year 2018 was decided in its taxpayer's favour nearly six years after the year ended. The same table lists overpayments for 2019 to 2022 still in objection, appeal or judicial review at the end of 2024 (Daftar 5/162–5/167, PDF pp. 179–184). In USD thousand, from the note's table:

At the end of 2023 the Natuna claims alone exceeded the whole line, so they cannot all have been carried in it at full value. Branch profit tax is PPh article 26, and some may sit in other taxes receivable, at a lower amount, or not at all. The note does not say which.

Under a cost-recovery PSC the corporate and dividend tax rates are fixed by the contract, and costs disallowed for cost recovery by SKK Migas can be the same costs DJP corrects for tax, which can put one cost in dispute twice. Gross split PSCs pay tax under the prevailing law, and DJP can assess them for ten years instead of five (Note 43f, Daftar 5/156, PDF p. 173). That longer window keeps assessments, and the receivables they create, open for longer.
: the contested part of the same claims, covered on this page.
: the underpaid side, shown gross and covered on this page.
: VAT and other non-income taxes, outside PSAK 212.
: future deductions, as opposed to tax already paid.
: where corrections and estimate changes are charged.

The monthly instalment basis for upstream contractors under PMK 81/2024 was seen only through a DDTC summary that lists the payment types without the formula. That provisional figures drive overpayments is this page's reading of PHE's Note 43d.

The objection, appeal, fine and interest rules of UU KUP (arts. 25–27, 27B) were checked only in secondary sources, and the judicial-review filing period in summaries that do not settle the article number. The 12-month refund rule of art. 17B was checked in DDTC and Ortax summaries.

That a judicial review by DJP does not suspend the Tax Court decision, so a won appeal can be refunded before the Supreme Court rules, is from a DDTC summary; when refunds are paid in practice was not checked.

Where the Natuna claims are carried is not stated by PHE. The page shows only that, at the end of 2023, they exceeded the whole line. Nor does PHE explain its 2023 non-current tax payable of 16,086; the deferral rights suggested for it in section 7 are possibilities under PSAK 201.69(d), not facts.

Treating a VAT refund claim by analogy with the 2019 agenda decision, which concerns a deposit on a disputed non-income tax, is a reading. An undisputed VAT overpayment is the same kind of statutory right, but the decision does not address it directly.

presentation.deck: The theory of current tax assets from the year-end tax computation to the Tax Court, worked through PHE's tax note and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: Current tax is the tax due on one year's taxable profit. When the tax already paid for a period exceeds the tax due, PSAK 212 recognises the excess as an asset, a current tax asset. In Indonesia it arises mainly from instalments and withholding, because the law allows no loss carryback.

The asset is measured at the amount expected to be recovered from the tax authority. Where the authority disputes the claim, ISAK 123 decides how much stays. The claim is kept in full if acceptance is probable and is otherwise measured at the most likely amount or the expected value. The contingent-asset rule of PSAK 237 does not apply to income tax.

The split between current and non-current follows the expected date of cash. A claim that goes through examination, objection and appeal can take years, so contested claims move into non-current assets.

title: Provision for Decommissioning and Site Restoration: Provisions, Contingencies and the Cost of Leaving a Field
snippet: The theory of provisions and contingencies from recognition to disclosure, with asset retirement obligations as the main application, worked through PHE's largest liability and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount. It is recognised when a past event has left a present obligation the entity cannot realistically avoid, an outflow is more likely than not, and the amount can be estimated. Anything weaker is a contingent liability, disclosed unless remote.

  • A provision is measured at the best estimate of what it would rationally cost to settle the obligation today. That is an expected value over a large population or the most likely outcome adjusted for skew for a single obligation, discounted at a pre-tax rate that matches the cash flows (nominal with nominal, real with real).

  • A decommissioning obligation is a provision whose cost is added to the asset that caused it. The discount unwinds as a finance cost, and changes in the estimate or the rate move the asset, not profit, until the asset is used up. PHE carries 3,826,222 of it, its largest liability.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report a provision for decommissioning and site restoration of 3,826,222 at 31 December 2024 against 3,784,917 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). It is the largest liability line, 25.0 percent of total liabilities and 12.6 percent of total assets (22.7 and 12.3 percent a year earlier). This page also covers other non-current liabilities, 281,228 (273,774 in 2023).

A student should come away able to tell a provision from a contingent liability, measure it, journal a decommissioning provision through its life, and see where other standards take over.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What a provision is

A provision is a liability whose timing or amount is uncertain (PSAK 237.10; formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37). It is still a liability, a present obligation from a past event settled by an outflow of resources. The uncertainty sets it apart from other liabilities (para. 11).

Trade payables

Accruals

Provisions

Goods or services

received

received

often none involved

Amount and date

invoiced or formally agreed

estimated, with little uncertainty

uncertain in timing or amount

PHE example, 2024

trade payables 1,091,822

accrued expenses 1,897,743

this line, 3,826,222

Allowances against assets, such as PHE's "provision for impairment of non-financial assets", are not PSAK 237 provisions (para. 7). A provision is current or non-current by expected settlement date; PHE presents this one as wholly non-current.

2. Recognition

A provision is recognised only when three conditions hold together (para. 14): a present obligation, legal or constructive, from a past event; a probable outflow of resources; and a reliable estimate.

Present obligation from a past event. The past event is the obligating event, one that leaves the entity no realistic alternative to settling (para. 17). A legal obligation comes from contract or law; a constructive obligation from the entity's own policy or practice that has created a valid expectation in others (para. 10).

The test that does most of the work is whether the obligation exists independently of the entity's future actions (para. 19). The standard's own example is upstream. Decommissioning an oil installation is provided for to the extent damage has already been done, while a cost the entity could avoid by operating differently, such as fitting new filters, is not. For example (illustration), a subsidiary that has drilled 12 wells and plans 8 more provides for plugging 12; the 8 could still go undrilled.

The same logic rules out provisions for future operating losses (para. 63); an expected loss is an impairment indicator instead (para. 65).

Probable outflow. Probable means more likely than not, a probability above 50 percent (para. 23). For many similar obligations, such as warranties, the test is applied to the class as a whole (para. 24).

Reliable estimate. The standard expects a range of outcomes to be estimable in all but extremely rare cases (para. 25). Where none can be made, the liability is disclosed as a contingent liability (para. 26).

3. Measurement

The amount recognised is the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the obligation at the reporting date (para. 36). That is the amount the entity would rationally pay to settle it, or to transfer it to a third party, today (para. 37).

Expected value for a large population. When the provision covers many items, outcomes are weighted by their probabilities (para. 39). For example (illustration), a subsidiary must plug 40 old onshore wells. Experience says 70 percent need a simple cement plug at 400 each, 25 percent need remedial cementing at 700, and 5 percent have stuck pipe that must be fished out at 1,600.

Expected cost per well = 70% × 400 + 25% × 700 + 5% × 1,600 = 280 + 175 + 80 = 535

Provision, before discounting = 40 × 535 = 21,400

Most likely outcome for a single obligation. One platform has one outcome, so the starting point is the most likely one. Other outcomes still count. If they are mostly higher, the best estimate is higher (para. 40). For example (illustration), removing one platform will most likely cost 30,000 (60 percent), but there is a 30 percent chance of 45,000 if the jacket is corroded and a 10 percent chance of 25,000 if a heavy-lift vessel is already in the area.

Most likely outcome = 30,000; probability-weighted outcome = 60% × 30,000 + 30% × 45,000 + 10% × 25,000 = 34,000

The skew is upward, so the best estimate lies above 30,000.

Risk. Uncertainty is reflected once, in the cash flows or the rate, never both (paras. 42–43 and 47).

Present value. Where timing matters, the provision is the present value of the expected outflows, at a pre-tax rate reflecting current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability (paras. 45–47). Cash flows and rate must match. Suppose the 34,000 is in today's prices, the work happens in 10 years, cost inflation is 2.5 percent and the nominal rate is 5.0 percent.

Nominal method: 34,000 × 1.025^10 = 43,523 in year-10 prices; 43,523 / 1.05^10 = 26,719

Real method: real rate = 1.05 / 1.025 − 1 = 2.439%; 34,000 / 1.02439^10 = 26,719

Mixed (today's prices at the nominal rate): 34,000 / 1.05^10 = 20,873, understated by 5,846

Future events, disposals and reimbursements. Expected technology savings count only on objective evidence, new legislation only when virtually certain (paras. 48–50), and scrap proceeds not at all (para. 51). A reimbursement, for example from an insurer, is a separate asset recognised only when virtually certain and capped at the provision (para. 53); only the expense may be shown net (para. 54).

4. Common provisions

The lecture notes list six forms. Litigation, warranties, onerous contracts and restructuring follow, environmental obligations get section 5, and consideration payable has left PSAK 237.

Litigation. A lawsuit needs a cause before the reporting date, a probable loss and an estimate; expert opinion is evidence (para. 16).

Warranties. An assurance-type warranty promises that the product works as specified, so it is a cost of the sale, provided for when the sale is made. A service-type warranty sells extra cover, a separate performance obligation under PSAK 115 (see the Deferred revenue essay). In the notes' example a seller sells 1,000 units at USD 500 each, expects warranty repairs on 100 units at USD 200 each (full amounts), pays 20 claims in the year and expects 80 next year.

Paid in the year: Dr Warranty expense 4,000 / Cr Cash, inventories 4,000

31 December: Dr Warranty expense 16,000 / Cr Warranty liability 16,000 (80 × 200)

Consideration payable to customers, such as premiums and rebates, is now part of revenue under PSAK 115. It reduces the transaction price, and an expected refund is a refund liability (see the Deferred revenue essay).

Onerous contracts. A contract is onerous when the unavoidable cost of meeting it exceeds the benefit expected from it (para. 10), and the unavoidable cost is the least net cost of exiting, the lower of the cost of fulfilling it net of what fulfilling still earns and the penalty for walking away (para. 68). Assets dedicated to the contract are tested for impairment first (para. 69). Since the 2020 amendment the cost of fulfilling includes both incremental costs and an allocation of other directly related costs. For example (illustration), a subsidiary has a drilling services contract costing 60,000 for 2025, and the programme is cancelled. Exiting costs a penalty of 25,000; re-selling the services to another operator would bring in 40,000.

Cost of fulfilling, net of benefits = 60,000 − 40,000 = 20,000; penalty = 25,000

Provision = lower of the two = 20,000

Dr Loss on onerous contract 20,000 / Cr Provision for onerous contract 20,000

Restructuring. A constructive obligation needs a detailed formal plan, started or announced to those affected (para. 72). Only direct costs not associated with continuing activities are included, so retraining staff who stay, marketing and new systems are excluded (paras. 80–81).

5. Decommissioning: the asset retirement obligation

Installing a well, platform or pipeline creates an obligation to plug, remove and restore the site at the end of field life. PHE recognises it for "oil and gas production facilities, wells, pipelines and related assets in accordance with the provisions in the PSC or in line with applicable regulations" (Note 3o, Daftar 5/60, PDF p. 77). The Oil and gas properties essay shows the asset side; this section follows the liability.

Initial recognition. The provision is recognised on installation and grows as more wells are drilled. The cost goes into the asset under PSAK 216.16(c) (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16), because removing the platform is part of what it costs to use it. The removal cost has no future benefit of its own, so it is not a separate asset (the lecture notes, following Kieso). Where the obligation arises from producing inventory during a period, as when a mine disturbs more land to extract this year's ore, the cost goes to inventory under PSAK 202 instead.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary completes an offshore platform with 20 wells on 31 December 2024. Removal and plugging are expected at the end of 2036, 12 years later. In today's prices the engineers see a 60 percent chance of 80,000, 30 percent of 100,000 and 10 percent of 140,000. Cost inflation is 2.5 percent and the pre-tax nominal discount rate 5.0 percent.

Expected cost in today's prices = 60% × 80,000 + 30% × 100,000 + 10% × 140,000 = 92,000

In 2036 prices = 92,000 × 1.025^12 = 123,730

Present value at 31 December 2024 = 123,730 / 1.05^12 = 68,897

One platform is a single obligation, so 80,000 is the most likely outcome. The other outcomes are all higher, so the best estimate lies above it, and this page uses the weighted 92,000, as section 3 allowed.

Dr Oil and gas properties 68,897 / Cr Provision for decommissioning 68,897

Unwinding of the discount. As settlement approaches, the present value rises by the discount rate. The increase is a finance cost (para. 60) that ISAK 101 (formerly ISAK 9, IFRIC 1) sends to profit or loss and forbids capitalising. PHE calls it accretion.

2025: 68,897 × 5% = 3,445; provision = 72,342

2026: 72,342 × 5% = 3,617; provision = 75,959

Dr Finance cost 3,445 / Cr Provision for decommissioning 3,445 (2026: 3,617)

Changes in estimate. The expected cash flows, their timing and the discount rate all move the provision. Under ISAK 101, for an asset carried at cost, the change is added to or deducted from the asset and depleted over its remaining life. A deduction may not exceed the asset's carrying amount, and any excess goes to profit. An addition is considered as a possible impairment indicator and, if it is one, the asset is tested. Once the asset reaches the end of its useful life, every later change goes to profit or loss. PHE's policy states the add/deduct rule, the cap and the impairment check (Note 3o).

Suppose that at the end of 2026 the market rate for this liability falls to 4.0 percent, with 10 years to go and the cash estimate unchanged.

Remeasured provision = 123,730 / 1.04^10 = 83,588; increase = 83,588 − 75,959 = 7,629

Dr Oil and gas properties 7,629 / Cr Provision for decommissioning 7,629

From 2027 the provision unwinds at 4.0 percent. Now suppose that at the end of 2033, with three years left, a cheaper plugging method cuts the 2036 estimate by 12,000, and the platform's carrying amount is down to 6,000.

Provision before the change = 123,730 / 1.04^3 = 109,996

Decrease = 12,000 / 1.04^3 = 10,668; new provision = 99,328

Dr Provision for decommissioning 10,668 / Cr Oil and gas properties 6,000 / Cr Gain on decommissioning estimate 4,668

Settlement. The provision is used only for its original purpose (para. 61). By the end of 2036 the provision has unwound to the revised nominal estimate of 123,730 − 12,000 = 111,730. If the contractor charges 115,000, the 3,270 difference is a loss of that period.

Dr Provision for decommissioning 111,730, Dr Loss on settlement 3,270 / Cr Cash 115,000

Sensitivity. A long-dated provision moves sharply with its discount rate. Take PHE's 2024 balance as the starting point, and treat it, for illustration only, as one payment 15 years away at 3.17 percent, the ratio of PHE's 2024 accretion to its opening balance (Note 29).

Implied payment in 15 years = 3,826,222 × 1.0317^15 = 6,110,428

At 4.17%: 6,110,428 / 1.0417^15 = 3,310,790, a fall of 515,432 (13.5%)

At 2.17%: 6,110,428 / 1.0217^15 = 4,428,134, a rise of 601,912 (15.7%)

The rise exceeds the fall because present value is convex in the rate. Under ISAK 101 most of either swing would land on oil and gas properties, not profit.

6. Contingent liabilities and contingent assets

A contingent liability is either a possible obligation whose existence will be confirmed only by uncertain future events outside the entity's control, or a present obligation that fails the probability or estimate test (para. 10). It is never recognised (para. 27). It is disclosed, with an estimate of its effect where practicable, unless remote (paras. 28 and 86), and becomes a provision in the period the outflow turns probable (para. 30).

Joint and several liability. The part of a joint obligation expected to be met by the others is a contingent liability, and the entity provides only for its own probable share (para. 29). For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary holds 30 percent of a block whose partners are jointly and severally liable for a 10,000 remediation order.

Provision = 30% × 10,000 = 3,000; contingent liability disclosed = 7,000, unless the partners look unable to pay

PHE discloses a real case. A 2022 ICC award orders Pertamina E&P Libya and Pertamina, jointly and severally, to pay Libya's national oil company 24,000 and 5,200 plus interest for unfulfilled exploration commitments (Note 45e(i), Daftar 5/197–5/198, PDF pp. 214–215).

PHE is also guarantor for a former Australian subsidiary's share of abandonment costs in the Basker Manta Gummy block. The operator sued in Victoria; PHE's position, on legal advice, is that it owes nothing because abandonment was not completed within five years of withdrawal (Note 45e(ii), Daftar 5/198–5/202, PDF pp. 215–219). The note discloses no amount and does not say whether a provision is held. Its place under Note 45, "commitments and contingencies", with no matching provision in Notes 28 or 29, is consistent with a contingent liability.

A contingent asset is a possible asset from past events, such as a claim being pursued in court (paras. 10 and 32). It is not recognised (paras. 31 and 33), is disclosed when an inflow is probable (para. 34), and is recognised only when virtually certain (para. 35). A liability is booked at more likely than not, an asset only at virtually certain. For example (illustration), an insurance claim of 5,000 disputed at year end is disclosed; when the insurer accepts it in writing next year, it is booked.

Dr Insurance claim receivable 5,000 / Cr Other income 5,000

7. Decommissioning funds and the other non-current liabilities

Funds set aside. Under IFRIC 5 a contributor to a decommissioning fund keeps its obligation as a liability and recognises its interest in the fund separately; without control or influence over the fund, the reimbursement right is measured at the lower of the provision and its share of the fair value of the fund's net assets. IAI's renumbering list has no ISAK for IFRIC 5, but PSAK 237.53 and the offsetting ban in PSAK 201 (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) give the same gross answer. For example (illustration), a provision of 10,000 and a fund of 6,000 appear as a liability of 10,000 and an asset of 6,000, never a net liability of 4,000.

PHE's funds sit in joint accounts with SKK Migas, usable only for restoration with its approval, and are presented as restricted cash (Note 3o, Daftar 5/61, PDF p. 78), 1,890,493 non-current at the end of 2024 (Note 7, Daftar 5/93–5/95, PDF pp. 110–112), plus its share of joint-operation funds, 66,719, in other non-current assets (Note 14b, Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122). Their fall from 296,555 is mostly a transfer into PHR's joint account (p. 123).

Other non-current liabilities. PHE's Note 28 shows why a liability with "contingent" in its name need not be a PSAK 237 item (Daftar 5/144, PDF p. 161).

PHE Masela bought a 20 percent participating interest from Shell, completed on 18 October 2023 (Note 5f, Daftar 5/88, PDF p. 105), and owes a further payment if the block's partners take a final investment decision (FID). Under PSAK 103 Business Combinations (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) contingent consideration is part of the price, recognised at fair value at the acquisition date (PHE measures it at present value under PSAK 113, Note 28) and, if it is a liability, remeasured at fair value through profit or loss (Note 3d, Daftar 5/36, PDF p. 53). PHE applies PSAK 103 to this acquired interest in a joint operation, consistent with PSAK 111's rule for interests that are businesses. PSAK 237 does not apply, both because another standard covers it (para. 5) and because a contractual obligation to pay cash is a financial liability (para. 2).

The two standards treat the same odds differently. For example (illustration), an acquirer will pay 100,000 if FID is taken in four years, judged 40 percent likely, with a discount rate of 8 percent.

Under PSAK 237 logic: outflow 40% < 50%, nothing recognised, contingent liability disclosed

Under PSAK 103: fair value = 40% × 100,000 / 1.08^4 = 29,401, recognised as part of the cost of the acquisition

A year later the odds rise to 60%: 60% × 100,000 / 1.08^3 = 47,630; Dr Loss on remeasurement 18,229 / Cr Contingent consideration liability 18,229

8. Provisions across industries

Mining. Indonesian miners provide for reclamation and post-mining closure under PP 78/2010 and also place guarantees, such as time deposits, that do not discharge the obligation, so both are shown gross. Power plants carry the same provision. Mining also tests section 5's asset-or-inventory split every year. For example (illustration), a coal pit incurs a restoration obligation of 2,000 for land disturbed to extract this year's coal and 3,000 for a haul road built to serve the mine for ten years.

Dr Inventories, coal 2,000 / Cr Provision for reclamation 2,000

Dr Mine properties 3,000 / Cr Provision for reclamation 3,000

Lessees and telecom towers. Restoring leased land puts the cost into the right-of-use asset and the obligation into a PSAK 237 provision (see the Right-of-use essay).

Levies. ISAK 121 Levies (formerly ISAK 30, IFRIC 21) makes the obligating event the activity that triggers payment under the law, not the period the levy relates to. For example (illustration), a levy of 1,200 for a year that is triggered by being in operation on 1 January is a full liability of 1,200 on 1 January, not 100 a month.

Banks and insurers. Financial guarantees and loan commitments fall under PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9), with expected credit losses, not under PSAK 237 (para. 2). Insurers' claims liabilities fall under PSAK 117 (formerly PSAK 74, IFRS 17).

9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 29

PSAK 237 asks for a reconciliation showing additions, amounts used, unused amounts reversed and the unwinding (para. 84), and for the expected timing, uncertainties, major assumptions and reimbursements (para. 85). PHE gives a three-line movement (Note 29, Daftar 5/145, PDF p. 162).

The 2024 revisions only foot as a deduction of 78,620, though they are printed without brackets. Alternatively PHE omitted a line: if 78,620 is an addition, an unprinted reduction of 157,240 is needed. The Oil and gas properties essay gives the same two readings. Three more points stand out.

  • There is no line for amounts used. Either no abandonment spending was charged in two years, or it is netted inside the revisions, though paragraph 84 asks for it separately.

  • Note 51 reports non-cash decommissioning adjustments to oil and gas properties of +12,627 in 2024 and 202,685 in 2023 (Daftar 5/235, PDF p. 252), against Note 29 revisions of 78,620 (a deduction on the footing reading) and 211,366. The gaps of 91,247 and 8,681 could be utilisation, revisions taken to profit, disposals or exchange differences; the FS do not say.

  • The discount rate, inflation assumption and timing are not disclosed. Note 29 describes ARO as the present value of costs "expected to be incurred during the terms of the PSCs" and Note 4b(ii) lists the main uncertainties (Daftar 5/80, PDF p. 97).

About half the obligation, at present value, is backed by cash usable for nothing else. The deferred tax ratio is far below PHE's tax rates, plausibly because ASR deposits are recoverable or deductible when placed (section 10), leaving much of the provision with no future deduction; the mechanics belong to the income tax essays. Note 28's 2023 lines also add to 273,785, not the 273,774 printed, a difference of 11.

10. Upstream note: abandonment and site restoration under the PSC

Indonesian upstream contractors set aside abandonment and site restoration (ASR) funds under Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Regulation 15/2018, starting in the year production becomes commercial, in a joint account with SKK Migas at a state-owned bank. Under cost recovery the amounts set aside are recoverable costs; under gross split they are deductible for income tax. PHE OSES, for example, deposited funds for both halves of 2024 on SKK Migas instruction (Note 45i, Daftar 5/208, PDF p. 225).

11. Related lines

  • oil-gas-properties-net: the asset that absorbs the initial estimate and later revisions.

  • restricted-cash-non-current: the ASR funds.

  • other-non-current-assets: funds in joint operations.

  • finance-cost: the accretion.

  • deferred-tax-liabilities: the deductible temporary difference on the provision.

  • trade-payables, accrued-expenses: the liabilities with certain or nearly certain amounts.

  • other-non-current-liabilities: covered here, section 7.

Least-confident assertions

  • That PHE treats the Basker Manta Gummy claim as a contingent liability is inferred from its place in Note 45 (commitments and contingencies) and the absence of an amount or provision. The item itself is not labelled.

  • Reading Note 29's 78,620 as a deduction rests on footing alone; PHE may instead have omitted a line of 157,240. The reasons for the gaps to Note 51 are not disclosed, and the listed causes are possibilities, not findings. That ASR deposits explain the low deferred tax ratio is this page's reading.

  • The 3.17 percent "rate" and the single 15-year payment in the sensitivity are illustrative simplifications. PHE discloses neither its discount rate nor the timing, and a portfolio of fields with different rates and dates would respond differently.

  • That Indonesia has no ISAK equivalent of IFRIC 5 rests on IAI's renumbering list, which lists only interpretations in force. Whether PHE's joint ASR accounts would fall within IFRIC 5's scope if it applied is this page's reading; PHE presents them as restricted cash.

  • The governing standards given for the Note 28 items are this page's reading of one-line descriptions. The Libya penalty may be the ICC award of Note 45e(i); the FS do not link them, and the balance shows no interest accrual. The 51.2 percent funding ratio assumes all non-current restricted cash is ASR funds, as Note 7's description implies but does not state line by line.

content.text: A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount. It is recognised when a past event has left a present obligation the entity cannot realistically avoid, an outflow is more likely than not, and the amount can be estimated. Anything weaker is a contingent liability, disclosed unless remote.

A provision is measured at the best estimate of what it would rationally cost to settle the obligation today. That is an expected value over a large population or the most likely outcome adjusted for skew for a single obligation, discounted at a pre-tax rate that matches the cash flows (nominal with nominal, real with real).

A decommissioning obligation is a provision whose cost is added to the asset that caused it. The discount unwinds as a finance cost, and changes in the estimate or the rate move the asset, not profit, until the asset is used up. PHE carries 3,826,222 of it, its largest liability.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report a provision for decommissioning and site restoration of 3,826,222 at 31 December 2024 against 3,784,917 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). It is the largest liability line, 25.0 percent of total liabilities and 12.6 percent of total assets (22.7 and 12.3 percent a year earlier). This page also covers other non-current liabilities, 281,228 (273,774 in 2023).
A student should come away able to tell a provision from a contingent liability, measure it, journal a decommissioning provision through its life, and see where other standards take over.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

A provision is a liability whose timing or amount is uncertain (PSAK 237.10; formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37). It is still a liability, a present obligation from a past event settled by an outflow of resources. The uncertainty sets it apart from other liabilities (para. 11).

Allowances against assets, such as PHE's "provision for impairment of non-financial assets", are not PSAK 237 provisions (para. 7). A provision is current or non-current by expected settlement date; PHE presents this one as wholly non-current.

A provision is recognised only when three conditions hold together (para. 14): a present obligation, legal or constructive, from a past event; a probable outflow of resources; and a reliable estimate.
Present obligation from a past event.

from the entity's own policy or practice that has created a valid expectation in others (para. 10).

The test that does most of the work is whether the obligation exists independently of the entity's future actions (para. 19). The standard's own example is upstream. Decommissioning an oil installation is provided for to the extent damage has already been done, while a cost the entity could avoid by operating differently, such as fitting new filters, is not. For example (illustration), a subsidiary that has drilled 12 wells and plans 8 more provides for plugging 12; the 8 could still go undrilled.
The same logic rules out provisions for future operating losses (para. 63); an expected loss is an impairment indicator instead (para. 65).
Probable means more likely than not, a probability above 50 percent (para. 23). For many similar obligations, such as warranties, the test is applied to the class as a whole (para. 24).
The standard expects a range of outcomes to be estimable in all but extremely rare cases (para. 25). Where none can be made, the liability is disclosed as a contingent liability (para. 26).

of the expenditure required to settle the obligation at the reporting date (para. 36). That is the amount the entity would rationally pay to settle it, or to transfer it to a third party, today (para. 37).
Expected value for a large population.

When the provision covers many items, outcomes are weighted by their probabilities (para. 39). For example (illustration), a subsidiary must plug 40 old onshore wells. Experience says 70 percent need a simple cement plug at 400 each, 25 percent need remedial cementing at 700, and 5 percent have stuck pipe that must be fished out at 1,600.
Most likely outcome for a single obligation.

One platform has one outcome, so the starting point is the most likely one. Other outcomes still count. If they are mostly higher, the best estimate is higher (para. 40). For example (illustration), removing one platform will most likely cost 30,000 (60 percent), but there is a 30 percent chance of 45,000 if the jacket is corroded and a 10 percent chance of 25,000 if a heavy-lift vessel is already in the area.
The skew is upward, so the best estimate lies above 30,000.
Uncertainty is reflected once, in the cash flows or the rate, never both (paras. 42–43 and 47).

Where timing matters, the provision is the present value of the expected outflows, at a pre-tax rate reflecting current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the liability (paras. 45–47). Cash flows and rate must match. Suppose the 34,000 is in today's prices, the work happens in 10 years, cost inflation is 2.5 percent and the nominal rate is 5.0 percent.
Mixed (today's prices at the nominal rate): 34,000 / 1.05^10 = 20,873, understated by 5,846

Expected technology savings count only on objective evidence, new legislation only when virtually certain (paras. 48–50), and scrap proceeds not at all (para. 51). A reimbursement, for example from an insurer, is a separate asset recognised only when virtually certain and capped at the provision (para. 53); only the expense may be shown net (para. 54).
The lecture notes list six forms. Litigation, warranties, onerous contracts and restructuring follow, environmental obligations get section 5, and consideration payable has left PSAK 237.
A lawsuit needs a cause before the reporting date, a probable loss and an estimate; expert opinion is evidence (para. 16).

Paid in the year: Dr Warranty expense 4,000 / Cr Cash, inventories 4,000

Since the 2020 amendment the cost of fulfilling includes both incremental costs and an allocation of other directly related costs. For example (illustration), a subsidiary has a drilling services contract costing 60,000 for 2025, and the programme is cancelled. Exiting costs a penalty of 25,000; re-selling the services to another operator would bring in 40,000.
Cost of fulfilling, net of benefits = 60,000 − 40,000 = 20,000; penalty = 25,000
Dr Loss on onerous contract 20,000 / Cr Provision for onerous contract 20,000

A constructive obligation needs a detailed formal plan, started or announced to those affected (para. 72). Only direct costs not associated with continuing activities are included, so retraining staff who stay, marketing and new systems are excluded (paras. 80–81).

Installing a well, platform or pipeline creates an obligation to plug, remove and restore the site at the end of field life. PHE recognises it for "oil and gas production facilities, wells, pipelines and related assets in accordance with the provisions in the PSC or in line with applicable regulations" (Note 3o, Daftar 5/60, PDF p. 77). The Oil and gas properties essay shows the asset side; this section follows the liability.

The provision is recognised on installation and grows as more wells are drilled. The cost goes into the asset under PSAK 216.16(c) (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16), because removing the platform is part of what it costs to use it. The removal cost has no future benefit of its own, so it is not a separate asset (the lecture notes, following Kieso). Where the obligation arises from producing inventory during a period, as when a mine disturbs more land to extract this year's ore, the cost goes to inventory under PSAK 202 instead.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary completes an offshore platform with 20 wells on 31 December 2024. Removal and plugging are expected at the end of 2036, 12 years later. In today's prices the engineers see a 60 percent chance of 80,000, 30 percent of 100,000 and 10 percent of 140,000. Cost inflation is 2.5 percent and the pre-tax nominal discount rate 5.0 percent.

One platform is a single obligation, so 80,000 is the most likely outcome. The other outcomes are all higher, so the best estimate lies above it, and this page uses the weighted 92,000, as section 3 allowed.
Dr Oil and gas properties 68,897 / Cr Provision for decommissioning 68,897
As settlement approaches, the present value rises by the discount rate. The increase is a
(para. 60) that ISAK 101 (formerly ISAK 9, IFRIC 1) sends to profit or loss and forbids capitalising. PHE calls it accretion.
Dr Finance cost 3,445 / Cr Provision for decommissioning 3,445 (2026: 3,617)

The expected cash flows, their timing and the discount rate all move the provision. Under ISAK 101, for an asset carried at cost, the change is added to or deducted from the asset and depleted over its remaining life. A deduction may not exceed the asset's carrying amount, and any excess goes to profit. An addition is considered as a possible impairment indicator and, if it is one, the asset is tested. Once the asset reaches the end of its useful life, every later change goes to profit or loss. PHE's policy states the add/deduct rule, the cap and the impairment check (Note 3o).
Suppose that at the end of 2026 the market rate for this liability falls to 4.0 percent, with 10 years to go and the cash estimate unchanged.

From 2027 the provision unwinds at 4.0 percent. Now suppose that at the end of 2033, with three years left, a cheaper plugging method cuts the 2036 estimate by 12,000, and the platform's carrying amount is down to 6,000.
Dr Provision for decommissioning 10,668 / Cr Oil and gas properties 6,000 / Cr Gain on decommissioning estimate 4,668

The provision is used only for its original purpose (para. 61). By the end of 2036 the provision has unwound to the revised nominal estimate of 123,730 − 12,000 = 111,730. If the contractor charges 115,000, the 3,270 difference is a loss of that period.

A long-dated provision moves sharply with its discount rate. Take PHE's 2024 balance as the starting point, and treat it, for illustration only, as one payment 15 years away at 3.17 percent, the ratio of PHE's 2024 accretion to its opening balance (Note 29).
The rise exceeds the fall because present value is convex in the rate. Under ISAK 101 most of either swing would land on oil and gas properties, not profit.

It is disclosed, with an estimate of its effect where practicable, unless remote (paras. 28 and 86), and becomes a provision in the period the outflow turns probable (para. 30).

The part of a joint obligation expected to be met by the others is a contingent liability, and the entity provides only for its own probable share (para. 29). PHE is also guarantor for a former Australian subsidiary's share of abandonment costs in the Basker Manta Gummy block. The operator sued in Victoria; PHE's position, on legal advice, is that it owes nothing because abandonment was not completed within five years of withdrawal (Note 45e(ii), Daftar 5/198–5/202, PDF pp. 215–219). The note discloses no amount and does not say whether a provision is held. Its place under Note 45, "commitments and contingencies", with no matching provision in Notes 28 or 29, is consistent with a contingent liability.

7. Decommissioning funds and the other non-current liabilities

Under IFRIC 5 a contributor to a decommissioning fund keeps its obligation as a liability and recognises its interest in the fund separately; without control or influence over the fund, the reimbursement right is measured at the lower of the provision and its share of the fair value of the fund's net assets. IAI's renumbering list has no ISAK for IFRIC 5, but PSAK 237.53 and the offsetting ban in PSAK 201 (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) give the same gross answer. For example (illustration), a provision of 10,000 and a fund of 6,000 appear as a liability of 10,000 and an asset of 6,000, never a net liability of 4,000.

presentation.deck: The theory of provisions and contingencies from recognition to disclosure, with asset retirement obligations as the main application, worked through PHE's largest liability and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount. It is recognised when a past event has left a present obligation the entity cannot realistically avoid, an outflow is more likely than not, and the amount can be estimated. Anything weaker is a contingent liability, disclosed unless remote.

A provision is measured at the best estimate of what it would rationally cost to settle the obligation today. That is an expected value over a large population or the most likely outcome adjusted for skew for a single obligation, discounted at a pre-tax rate that matches the cash flows (nominal with nominal, real with real).

A decommissioning obligation is a provision whose cost is added to the asset that caused it. The discount unwinds as a finance cost, and changes in the estimate or the rate move the asset, not profit, until the asset is used up. PHE carries 3,826,222 of it, its largest liability.

title: Deferred Revenue: Contract Liabilities, Take-or-Pay and Breakage
snippet: The theory of customer prepayments under PSAK 115 from the five steps to disclosure, worked through PHE's take-or-pay gas balances and set beside the industries that collect before they deliver
content:
In brief

  • Deferred revenue is a contract liability, an obligation to transfer goods or services for which the customer has already paid or for which payment is already due. It is recognised at the earlier of the two and released to revenue as each performance obligation is satisfied.

  • The amount in the liability depends on the five steps of PSAK 115. Allocation decides how much of a payment belongs to undelivered obligations, a significant financing component can make the liability grow with interest, and customer options and service warranties create obligations that must be deferred even when nothing was prepaid for them.

  • Rights that customers pay for but never use, such as unused make-up gas under a take-or-pay contract, are breakage. They become revenue in proportion to the rights customers do use or, when the seller does not expect to be entitled to breakage, only once use becomes remote.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report deferred revenue, current maturities, of 6,012 at 31 December 2024 against 4,126 a year earlier, with a non-current portion of 13,118 against 7,017, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The current line is 0.10 percent of current liabilities (0.07 percent a year earlier), and the two lines together, 19,130, are 0.12 percent of total liabilities (0.07 percent a year earlier) and 0.06 percent of total assets.

After reading, a student should be able to say when a customer payment becomes a liability, measure it through the five steps, release it with journals, and recognise the same mechanics in airlines, telecoms and property developers.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 115 Pendapatan dari Kontrak dengan Pelanggan (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15), and PHE's notes use the new number.

1. What deferred revenue is

Cash received before performance is owed back in goods or services, so it is a liability. Kieso's older vocabulary calls it unearned revenue and lists it among current liabilities. The lecture note for Ch 13 records it the classic way: 10,000 received on 2 December for goods shipped FOB destination is credited to unearned revenue, and moves to sales revenue when the goods arrive on 5 December. The same note keeps customer advances and deposits apart. A returnable deposit is owed back in cash, while unearned revenue is owed in goods or services, a line that returns in section 8.

PSAK 115 keeps the idea but rebuilds the reasoning. Its asset-liability approach recognises revenue when a contract asset rises or a contract liability falls, rather than when revenue is "earned and realised". Three balances follow.

Balance

What it is

When it arises

Receivable

An unconditional right to consideration: only the passage of time is needed before payment is due (para. 108)

Performance done, or payment due under a non-cancellable contract

Contract asset

A right to consideration conditional on something other than time, usually further performance (para. 107)

Performance done ahead of the right to bill

Contract liability

An obligation to transfer goods or services for which consideration has been received or is due (para. 106)

Payment received or due ahead of performance

The Trade receivables essay teaches the first two rows; this essay is about the third.

The contract liability is recognised "when the payment is made or the payment is due (whichever is earlier)" (para. 106). A payment that is due but unpaid creates the liability too, if the contract cannot be cancelled. For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary signs a non-cancellable contract on 1 October 2024 to drill one well and then monitor it for twelve months, for 3,000, invoiced on 1 November and payable on 1 December. On 1 December nothing has been paid and no drilling has started.

Non-cancellable, payment due: Dr Trade receivables 3,000 / Cr Contract liability 3,000

Cancellable until drilling starts: no entry, because the right to payment is not yet unconditional

Each contract is presented as one net position, a contract asset or a contract liability, never both (para. 105). PSAK 115 allows other names as long as receivables stay distinguishable (para. 109), which is why PHE and most Indonesian issuers still say pendapatan tangguhan, deferred revenue.

2. The five steps and where the liability comes from

Every contract liability is a product of the five steps that open the lecture note for Inter 2 Ch 18.

  1. Identify the contract with the customer.

  2. Identify the performance obligations, the promises to transfer a distinct good or service.

  3. Determine the transaction price, the consideration the entity expects to be entitled to.

  4. Allocate the price to the obligations in proportion to their standalone selling prices (SSP), the prices at which each would sell on its own.

  5. Recognise revenue when, or as, each obligation is satisfied by transferring control.

The contract liability is the part of consideration received or due that step 4 has assigned to obligations step 5 has not yet satisfied. In the drilling contract, drilling and monitoring are distinct, since a customer could buy either from another contractor. Suppose drilling alone would sell for 2,700 and a year of monitoring for 900 (illustration).

Total SSP = 2,700 + 900 = 3,600

Drilling = 3,000 × 2,700 / 3,600 = 2,250

Monitoring = 3,000 × 900 / 3,600 = 750

The 600 bundle discount is spread across both obligations in proportion, unless there is evidence it belongs to one of them. The customer pays the 3,000 on 5 December. Drilling runs through December on the customer's well, so the customer controls the well as it is drilled and the obligation is satisfied over time; by 31 December the well is finished.

5 December: Dr Cash 3,000 / Cr Trade receivables 3,000

31 December: Dr Contract liability 2,250 / Cr Revenue, drilling services 2,250

The liability left at the year end is 750, all current because monitoring runs through 2025. Had the price been allocated by invoice line instead of SSP, with the contract billing 2,800 for drilling and 200 for monitoring, the year-end liability would be 200 and 550 of revenue would have been pulled into 2024. Step 4 exists to stop that.

3. The transaction price: financing, refunds and rebates

The transaction price is not always the cash received, and the differences flow into the liability.

Significant financing component. When payment and performance are far apart, part of the payment is interest. If the customer pays early, the seller is borrowing from the customer, so the seller accretes interest on the contract liability and recognises more revenue than the cash received (paras. 60–65). The rate is the one a separate financing transaction between the two parties would carry, reflecting the credit of whoever receives the financing, here the seller (para. 64). For example (illustration), an industrial buyer prepays 10,000 on 1 January 2024 for gas a PHE subsidiary will deliver in full at the end of 2025, and the subsidiary could borrow for two years at 6 percent.

Year 1 interest = 10,000 × 6% = 600; liability = 10,600

Year 2 interest = 10,600 × 6% = 636; liability = 11,236

Financing component recognised

No financing adjustment (if para. 62(a) or 63 applied)

Receipt

Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Contract liability 10,000

Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Contract liability 10,000

2024

Dr Interest expense 600 / Cr Contract liability 600

no entry

2025

Dr Interest expense 636 / Cr Contract liability 636

no entry

Delivery

Dr Contract liability 11,236 / Cr Revenue 11,236

Dr Contract liability 10,000 / Cr Revenue 10,000

Revenue less finance cost is 10,000 either way, but the left column shows 11,236 of revenue and 1,236 of finance cost, which is what a buyer paying the cash price at delivery would produce plus a separate loan. In this fact pattern, with a fixed delivery date two years out, neither exception applies, but they cover many common cases. No adjustment is needed when, at inception, the gap between payment and transfer is expected to be one year or less (para. 63), and there is no significant financing component when the customer prepaid and itself decides when the goods are transferred (para. 62(a)). The second exception is the one that applies to take-or-pay make-up gas in section 5.

Refund liabilities. Consideration the seller expects to give back in cash is not transaction price at all. It is a refund liability (para. 55), a separate liability settled in cash rather than in goods. For example (illustration), a buyer pays 5,000 for gas and will receive a 2 percent volume rebate in cash, which the seller expects it to earn.

Dr Cash 5,000 / Cr Revenue 4,900 / Cr Refund liability 100

Only an obligation to deliver goods or services is a contract liability. The distinction comes back in section 8, because PHE's classification blurs it.

4. Releasing the liability: point in time or over time

The liability falls when control passes, and control passes in one of two ways. An obligation is satisfied over time if the customer receives and consumes the benefit as the entity performs, if the customer controls the asset as it is created, or if the asset has no alternative use to the seller and the seller has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date (para. 35). Otherwise it is satisfied at a point in time, judged by indicators such as a present right to payment, legal title, physical possession, transfer of risks and rewards, and the customer's acceptance (para. 38).

For over-time obligations the entity picks a measure of progress. Output methods count what has been delivered (months of service, metres drilled, BBTU of gas; one BBTU is a billion British thermal units). Input methods count effort, such as cost incurred against total expected cost, Kieso's cost-to-cost method. Monitoring is a stand-ready service delivered evenly, so time elapsed is the natural output measure.

Monthly release = 750 / 12 = 62.5

Each month of 2025: Dr Contract liability 62.5 / Cr Revenue, monitoring services 62.5

Gas delivered through a pipeline meter is released quantity by quantity. Whether that is a series of point-in-time sales or one obligation satisfied over time depends on whether the buyer consumes the gas as it arrives (IASB/FASB Transition Resource Group, July 2015). PHE's policy treats goods as generally transferred at a point in time and recognises crude and gas revenue "based on the actual lifting amount and sold to customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79). Either way a prepayment for gas is released as the gas is delivered.

5. Take-or-pay and breakage

A take-or-pay clause makes the buyer pay for a minimum quantity whether or not it takes it. Such contracts typically soften it with a make-up right: the buyer may take the gas it paid for but did not take in later years, usually only after taking that year's own minimum. PHE's policy describes this balance: deferred revenue is "amounts billed and collected involving 'take or pay' gas quantities, which will be recognized as revenue when the related gas quantity are delivered to customers or when the contract expires" (Note 3u, Daftar 5/71, PDF p. 88).

Take a contract of the kind behind PHE's line (illustration). A subsidiary sells gas at USD 6 per MMBtu, which is 6 per BBTU in USD thousand. The annual contract quantity is 2,000 BBTU and the take-or-pay level is 80 percent, so 1,600 BBTU. Make-up gas may be taken in the two years after the shortfall.

Year 1: buyer takes 1,200 BBTU; revenue = 1,200 × 6 = 7,200

Shortfall = 1,600 − 1,200 = 400 BBTU, billed and paid = 400 × 6 = 2,400

Dr Cash 2,400 / Cr Contract liability, take-or-pay 2,400

The 2,400 is not revenue in year 1. The buyer has paid for gas it can still demand, so the seller owes 400 BBTU. The buyer decides when to take it, so para. 62(a) removes any financing component. Without a make-up right the shortfall payment would be revenue in year 1, because the seller would owe nothing more for it; the make-up right is what creates the liability.

Year 2: buyer takes 1,750 BBTU; 1,600 is year 2's own minimum, paid in cash (9,600); 150 BBTU is make-up

Dr Contract liability 900 / Cr Revenue 900 (150 × 6)

Year 3: buyer takes exactly 1,600 BBTU; 250 BBTU of make-up remains unused when the right expires

The unused 250 BBTU is breakage: a right the customer paid for and never exercised. PSAK 115 gives two treatments (paras. B44–B47). If the seller expects to be entitled to breakage, it recognises the expected amount in proportion to the pattern of rights the customer exercises. If it does not, it waits until the likelihood of the customer exercising its remaining rights becomes remote. The expected amount is subject to the constraint on variable consideration, so the seller must be confident it will not reverse. Suppose the seller's history shows that 40 percent of make-up gas is never taken (illustration).

Expected make-up taken = 400 × 60% = 240 BBTU; expected breakage = 160 × 6 = 960

Year 2 share of expected use = 150 / 240 = 62.5%; breakage recognised = 960 × 62.5% = 600

Year 3 remainder at expiry = 2,400 − 900 − 600 = 900

Revenue from the 2,400

Remote approach (PHE's policy)

Proportional approach

Year 2

900

900 + 600 = 1,500

Year 3, at expiry

1,500

900

Total

2,400

2,400

Both release the same 2,400. The proportional approach brings breakage forward when the seller has evidence for it; the remote approach waits. PHE's wording, recognition "when the contract expires", fits the remote approach at its latest point and is not the proportional approach.

The current and non-current split follows the same schedule. A contract liability is current to the extent the seller expects to satisfy it within twelve months (PSAK 201.69, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1), and it is settled by delivery or expiry, not cash. At the end of year 1, under the remote approach, the seller expects 150 BBTU of make-up in year 2 (900 current) and the rest to be taken or to expire later (1,500 non-current). A seller that must hand unclaimed amounts to a government records a liability for them, not breakage revenue (para. B47).

The shortfall payment would be a refund liability, not deferred revenue, if the contract obliged the seller to return cash for gas never taken. PHE's policy says the balance becomes revenue at expiry, so it reads as an obligation to deliver gas.

6. Customer options, service warranties and upfront fees

Some contract liabilities arise without any prepayment, because part of today's price pays for something promised later.

Customer options. An option to buy more goods later is a separate performance obligation only if it gives a material right, something the customer would not get without the contract, such as a discount beyond what other customers receive (paras. B39–B40). For example (illustration), a buyer contracts for 1,000 BBTU at 6 (6,000) and receives an option to buy another 100 BBTU next year at 4.5, a discount not offered to anyone else. The seller expects 80 percent take-up.

SSP of the option = (6.0 − 4.5) × 100 × 80% = 120

Gas = 6,000 × 6,000 / 6,120 = 5,882.35; option = 6,000 × 120 / 6,120 = 117.65

On delivery: Dr Cash 6,000 / Cr Revenue 5,882.35 / Cr Contract liability 117.65

The 117.65 becomes revenue when the option is exercised or lapses.

Warranties. The lecture note for Ch 18 separates two kinds. An assurance-type warranty promises only that the product works as agreed; it is not a performance obligation and its expected cost is a provision under PSAK 237 (see the Decommissioning provision essay for provisions). A service-type warranty, sold separately or covering more than agreed specifications, is a performance obligation. For example (illustration), a compressor package sells for 1,050 with a two-year extended service plan; SSPs are 1,000 and 100.

Service plan = 1,050 × 100 / 1,100 = 95.45, held as a contract liability and released over two years

Upfront non-refundable fees. A connection fee, a joining fee or a franchise's initial fee usually pays in advance for the future goods or services, so it is deferred over the period they are supplied (paras. B48–B51). Ch 18's franchise section is the classic case.

7. Deferred revenue across industries

Subscriptions and prepaid telecom. Prepaid mobile credit is a contract liability until the subscriber uses it, and expired credit is breakage. For example (illustration), an operator sells 1,000 of prepaid credit and its history says 8 percent will expire unused, so expected use is 920.

When 460 has been used: revenue = 460 + 80 × (460 / 920) = 460 + 40 = 500; liability = 1,000 − 500 = 500

Airlines. Tickets sold for future flights sit in a liability, often called unearned transportation revenue, until the flight. Frequent-flyer miles awarded with a ticket are a material right. For example (illustration), a ticket sells for 300 and earns miles with an SSP of 15.

Ticket = 300 × 300 / 315 = 285.71, released when flown; miles = 300 × 15 / 315 = 14.29, released when redeemed or when redemption becomes remote

Real estate pre-sales. Indonesian developers collect booking fees, down payments and instalments long before handover, so contract liabilities can be large on their balance sheets. Whether revenue comes at handover or over construction depends on para. 35(c): an apartment unit has no alternative use once sold, but revenue is over time only if the developer has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date, which turns on the sale agreement and local law. The gap between payment and handover is usually long enough for a significant financing component. For example (illustration), a buyer pays 1,000 three years before handover and the developer's borrowing rate is 8 percent.

Liability at handover = 1,000 × 1.08³ = 1,259.71; revenue at handover 1,259.71; interest expense of 259.71 accreted on the liability over the three years

Construction and engineering. Billings ahead of progress give a contract liability, progress ahead of billings a contract asset, netted per contract (para. 105). The Trade receivables essay works the cost-to-cost example.

Government grants are not contract liabilities. A grant related to an asset may be presented as deferred income under PSAK 220 (formerly PSAK 61, IAS 20), but the government is not a customer receiving goods or services, so PSAK 115 does not apply.

8. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 24

PHE splits the balance into take-or-pay gas and others, each with a current and non-current portion (Note 24, Daftar 5/118, PDF p. 135).
