19,130

11,143

Growth in total = 19,130 / 11,143 − 1 = 71.7%

Take-or-pay gas = 4,718 + 10,800 = 15,518 (2024); 1,332 + 3,898 = 5,230 (2023), 2.97 times the 2023 balance

Current share = 6,012 / 19,130 = 31.4%

Total deferred revenue / revenue = 19,130 / 14,330,340 = 0.13%

The take-or-pay balance rose by 15,518 − 5,230 = 10,288; at section 5's illustrative 6 per BBTU that would be about 1,715 BBTU of unrecovered shortfall. In the mechanics of section 5 the rise is consistent with buyers taking less than their minimum quantities in 2024, while "others" fell. Two-thirds sits in non-current, consistent with make-up gas, or expiry, expected after 2025.

Note 24 gives the balances at both year-ends, which meets the first part of para. 116. It does not give the revenue recognised from the opening balance (para. 116(b)) or explain the change (para. 118). Para. 120's remaining-obligation disclosure can be skipped for sales billed per unit delivered (para. 121(b)). At 0.13 percent of revenue the omissions are immaterial under PSAK 201, but they are why a reader cannot tell how much of the 11,143 at the start of 2024 became revenue, how much was added, or how much is breakage at expiry.

PHE also presents deferred revenue as a financial liability. Its policy lists it among liabilities classified as loans and borrowings (Note 3, Daftar 5/44, PDF p. 61), a label from PSAK 55, which PSAK 109 replaced; it appears among other financial liabilities in Note 47 (Daftar 5/222, PDF p. 239); and the PSAK 107 liquidity table shows the 19,130 as a contractual outflow, 6,012 within one year and 13,118 in one to five years (Daftar 5/233, PDF p. 250). Under PSAK 232 (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32), deferred revenue is not a financial liability because it is settled by delivering goods or services, not cash (application guidance AG11). That is the lecture note's line between deposits and unearned revenue from section 1. Since PHE's own policy settles the take-or-pay balance in gas or at expiry, the classification is hard to reconcile with it, though in a line this small it is a presentation inconsistency rather than a material misstatement.

Note 43e (Daftar 5/155–5/156, PDF pp. 172–173) carries deferred tax on deferred revenue of 2,923 at the end of 2023 (2,884 in the asset schedule, 39 as a deductible item in the liability schedule) and 2,874 at the end of 2024, almost all moved from one schedule to the other (net charge 49). That is 15 percent of the 2024 balance, below any PSC tax rate, so not all of the balance appears to be a temporary difference (see the Deferred tax assets essay).

9. Upstream note

Take-or-pay protects the investment case for gas fields, whose output must flow to a contracted buyer through dedicated infrastructure. Under a PSC, a gas sales agreement covers both the contractor's and the government's share of the gas. PHE's FS state the policy and the balance but not the contract terms, the make-up period, or whether shortfall payments on the government's share sit in PHE's balance.

10. Related lines

  • deferred-revenue-non-current: the same balance, expected to be released after twelve months.

  • revenues: where the liability is released.

  • trade-receivables-net: the unconditional right that a due-date contract liability creates, and contract assets.

  • trade-payables: the boundary between obligations settled in cash and those settled in goods.

  • decommissioning-site-restoration-provision: where assurance warranties and other provisions belong.

  • deferred-tax-assets and deferred-tax-liabilities: the tax effect in Note 43e.

Least-confident assertions

  • The reading that PHE's take-or-pay balance follows the remote approach to breakage rests on the phrase "or when the contract expires" in Note 3u. PHE does not state its breakage method, and the contract terms (make-up period, refund clauses) are not disclosed.

  • Classifying deferred revenue as a financial liability conflicts with IAS 32 AG11 only if no part of the balance is refundable in cash. PHE's policy implies it is not, but the "others" component (3,612 at the end of 2024) is not described at all.

  • The reading of the 2024 increase as larger buyer shortfalls follows from the mechanics, and the 1,715 BBTU uses an illustrative price. A new contract with a larger minimum, or a reclassification, would produce the same movement, and PHE gives no roll-forward.

  • That the Note 43e tax balance on deferred revenue implies only part of the balance is a temporary difference is an inference. Different tax rates across PSCs, or balances held in entities that recognise no deferred tax, could also explain it.

  • Applying para. 62(a) to make-up gas assumes the buyer controls the timing of make-up. Contracts that fix a make-up schedule could carry a financing component.

content.text: Deferred revenue is a contract liability, an obligation to transfer goods or services for which the customer has already paid or for which payment is already due. It is recognised at the earlier of the two and released to revenue as each performance obligation is satisfied.

The amount in the liability depends on the five steps of PSAK 115. Allocation decides how much of a payment belongs to undelivered obligations, a significant financing component can make the liability grow with interest, and customer options and service warranties create obligations that must be deferred even when nothing was prepaid for them.

Rights that customers pay for but never use, such as unused make-up gas under a take-or-pay contract, are breakage. They become revenue in proportion to the rights customers do use or, when the seller does not expect to be entitled to breakage, only once use becomes remote.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report deferred revenue, current maturities, of 6,012 at 31 December 2024 against 4,126 a year earlier, with a non-current portion of 13,118 against 7,017, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The current line is 0.10 percent of current liabilities (0.07 percent a year earlier), and the two lines together, 19,130, are 0.12 percent of total liabilities (0.07 percent a year earlier) and 0.06 percent of total assets.

After reading, a student should be able to say when a customer payment becomes a liability, measure it through the five steps, release it with journals, and recognise the same mechanics in airlines, telecoms and property developers.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 115
(formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15), and PHE's notes use the new number.
Cash received before performance is owed back in goods or services, so it is a liability. Kieso's older vocabulary calls it

and lists it among current liabilities. The lecture note for Ch 13 records it the classic way: 10,000 received on 2 December for goods shipped FOB destination is credited to unearned revenue, and moves to sales revenue when the goods arrive on 5 December. The same note keeps
apart. A returnable deposit is owed back in cash, while unearned revenue is owed in goods or services, a line that returns in section 8.
PSAK 115 keeps the idea but rebuilds the reasoning. Its
recognises revenue when a contract asset rises or a contract liability falls, rather than when revenue is "earned and realised". Three balances follow.
An unconditional right to consideration: only the passage of time is needed before payment is due (para. 108)
Performance done, or payment due under a non-cancellable contract
A right to consideration conditional on something other than time, usually further performance (para. 107)
Performance done ahead of the right to bill
An obligation to transfer goods or services for which consideration has been received or is due (para. 106)
Payment received or due ahead of performance
The Trade receivables essay teaches the first two rows; this essay is about the third.

The contract liability is recognised "when the payment is made or the payment is due (whichever is earlier)" (para. 106). A payment that is due but unpaid creates the liability too, if the contract cannot be cancelled. For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary signs a non-cancellable contract on 1 October 2024 to drill one well and then monitor it for twelve months, for 3,000, invoiced on 1 November and payable on 1 December. On 1 December nothing has been paid and no drilling has started.
Non-cancellable, payment due: Dr Trade receivables 3,000 / Cr Contract liability 3,000
Cancellable until drilling starts: no entry, because the right to payment is not yet unconditional

Each contract is presented as one net position, a contract asset or a contract liability, never both (para. 105). PSAK 115 allows other names as long as receivables stay distinguishable (para. 109), which is why PHE and most Indonesian issuers still say
2. The five steps and where the liability comes from
Every contract liability is a product of the five steps that open the lecture note for Inter 2 Ch 18.
Identify the contract with the customer.
, the promises to transfer a distinct good or service.
, the consideration the entity expects to be entitled to.
Allocate the price to the obligations in proportion to their
(SSP), the prices at which each would sell on its own.
Recognise revenue when, or as, each obligation is satisfied by transferring control.

The contract liability is the part of consideration received or due that step 4 has assigned to obligations step 5 has not yet satisfied. In the drilling contract, drilling and monitoring are distinct, since a customer could buy either from another contractor. Suppose drilling alone would sell for 2,700 and a year of monitoring for 900 (illustration).

The 600 bundle discount is spread across both obligations in proportion, unless there is evidence it belongs to one of them. The customer pays the 3,000 on 5 December. Drilling runs through December on the customer's well, so the customer controls the well as it is drilled and the obligation is satisfied over time; by 31 December the well is finished.
5 December: Dr Cash 3,000 / Cr Trade receivables 3,000
31 December: Dr Contract liability 2,250 / Cr Revenue, drilling services 2,250

The liability left at the year end is 750, all current because monitoring runs through 2025. Had the price been allocated by invoice line instead of SSP, with the contract billing 2,800 for drilling and 200 for monitoring, the year-end liability would be 200 and 550 of revenue would have been pulled into 2024. Step 4 exists to stop that.
3. The transaction price: financing, refunds and rebates
The transaction price is not always the cash received, and the differences flow into the liability.

When payment and performance are far apart, part of the payment is interest. If the customer pays early, the seller is borrowing from the customer, so the seller accretes interest on the contract liability and recognises more revenue than the cash received (paras. 60–65). The rate is the one a separate financing transaction between the two parties would carry, reflecting the credit of whoever receives the financing, here the seller (para. 64). For example (illustration), an industrial buyer prepays 10,000 on 1 January 2024 for gas a PHE subsidiary will deliver in full at the end of 2025, and the subsidiary could borrow for two years at 6 percent.
No financing adjustment (if para. 62(a) or 63 applied)
Dr Interest expense 600 / Cr Contract liability 600
Dr Interest expense 636 / Cr Contract liability 636

Revenue less finance cost is 10,000 either way, but the left column shows 11,236 of revenue and 1,236 of finance cost, which is what a buyer paying the cash price at delivery would produce plus a separate loan. In this fact pattern, with a fixed delivery date two years out, neither exception applies, but they cover many common cases. No adjustment is needed when, at inception, the gap between payment and transfer is expected to be one year or less (para. 63), and there is no significant financing component when the customer prepaid and itself decides when the goods are transferred (para. 62(a)). The second exception is the one that applies to take-or-pay make-up gas in section 5.
Consideration the seller expects to give back in cash is not transaction price at all. It is a

(para. 55), a separate liability settled in cash rather than in goods. For example (illustration), a buyer pays 5,000 for gas and will receive a 2 percent volume rebate in cash, which the seller expects it to earn.
Dr Cash 5,000 / Cr Revenue 4,900 / Cr Refund liability 100
Only an obligation to deliver goods or services is a contract liability. The distinction comes back in section 8, because PHE's classification blurs it.
4. Releasing the liability: point in time or over time
The liability falls when control passes, and control passes in one of two ways. An obligation is satisfied

if the customer receives and consumes the benefit as the entity performs, if the customer controls the asset as it is created, or if the asset has no alternative use to the seller and the seller has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date (para. 35). Otherwise it is satisfied
, judged by indicators such as a present right to payment, legal title, physical possession, transfer of risks and rewards, and the customer's acceptance (para. 38).
For over-time obligations the entity picks a
count what has been delivered (months of service, metres drilled, BBTU of gas; one BBTU is a billion British thermal units).
count effort, such as cost incurred against total expected cost, Kieso's cost-to-cost method. Monitoring is a stand-ready service delivered evenly, so time elapsed is the natural output measure.
Each month of 2025: Dr Contract liability 62.5 / Cr Revenue, monitoring services 62.5

Gas delivered through a pipeline meter is released quantity by quantity. Whether that is a series of point-in-time sales or one obligation satisfied over time depends on whether the buyer consumes the gas as it arrives (IASB/FASB Transition Resource Group, July 2015). PHE's policy treats goods as generally transferred at a point in time and recognises crude and gas revenue "based on the actual lifting amount and sold to customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79). Either way a prepayment for gas is released as the gas is delivered.
A take-or-pay clause makes the buyer pay for a minimum quantity whether or not it takes it. Such contracts typically soften it with a

: the buyer may take the gas it paid for but did not take in later years, usually only after taking that year's own minimum. PHE's policy describes this balance: deferred revenue is "amounts billed and collected involving 'take or pay' gas quantities, which will be recognized as revenue when the related gas quantity are delivered to customers or when the contract expires" (Note 3u, Daftar 5/71, PDF p. 88).

Take a contract of the kind behind PHE's line (illustration). A subsidiary sells gas at USD 6 per MMBtu, which is 6 per BBTU in USD thousand. The annual contract quantity is 2,000 BBTU and the take-or-pay level is 80 percent, so 1,600 BBTU. Make-up gas may be taken in the two years after the shortfall.
Dr Cash 2,400 / Cr Contract liability, take-or-pay 2,400

The 2,400 is not revenue in year 1. The buyer has paid for gas it can still demand, so the seller owes 400 BBTU. The buyer decides when to take it, so para. 62(a) removes any financing component. Without a make-up right the shortfall payment would be revenue in year 1, because the seller would owe nothing more for it; the make-up right is what creates the liability.
Year 2: buyer takes 1,750 BBTU; 1,600 is year 2's own minimum, paid in cash (9,600); 150 BBTU is make-up
Year 3: buyer takes exactly 1,600 BBTU; 250 BBTU of make-up remains unused when the right expires

: a right the customer paid for and never exercised. PSAK 115 gives two treatments (paras. B44–B47). If the seller expects to be entitled to breakage, it recognises the expected amount in proportion to the pattern of rights the customer exercises. If it does not, it waits until the likelihood of the customer exercising its remaining rights becomes remote. The expected amount is subject to the constraint on variable consideration, so the seller must be confident it will not reverse. Suppose the seller's history shows that 40 percent of make-up gas is never taken (illustration).
Expected make-up taken = 400 × 60% = 240 BBTU; expected breakage = 160 × 6 = 960
Year 2 share of expected use = 150 / 240 = 62.5%; breakage recognised = 960 × 62.5% = 600

Both release the same 2,400. The proportional approach brings breakage forward when the seller has evidence for it; the remote approach waits. PHE's wording, recognition "when the contract expires", fits the remote approach at its latest point and is not the proportional approach.

The current and non-current split follows the same schedule. A contract liability is current to the extent the seller expects to satisfy it within twelve months (PSAK 201.69, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1), and it is settled by delivery or expiry, not cash. At the end of year 1, under the remote approach, the seller expects 150 BBTU of make-up in year 2 (900 current) and the rest to be taken or to expire later (1,500 non-current). A seller that must hand unclaimed amounts to a government records a liability for them, not breakage revenue (para. B47).

The shortfall payment would be a refund liability, not deferred revenue, if the contract obliged the seller to return cash for gas never taken. PHE's policy says the balance becomes revenue at expiry, so it reads as an obligation to deliver gas.
6. Customer options, service warranties and upfront fees
Some contract liabilities arise without any prepayment, because part of today's price pays for something promised later.
An option to buy more goods later is a separate performance obligation only if it gives a

, something the customer would not get without the contract, such as a discount beyond what other customers receive (paras. B39–B40). For example (illustration), a buyer contracts for 1,000 BBTU at 6 (6,000) and receives an option to buy another 100 BBTU next year at 4.5, a discount not offered to anyone else. The seller expects 80 percent take-up.
On delivery: Dr Cash 6,000 / Cr Revenue 5,882.35 / Cr Contract liability 117.65
The 117.65 becomes revenue when the option is exercised or lapses.
The lecture note for Ch 18 separates two kinds. An

warranty promises only that the product works as agreed; it is not a performance obligation and its expected cost is a provision under PSAK 237 (see the Decommissioning provision essay for provisions). A

warranty, sold separately or covering more than agreed specifications, is a performance obligation. For example (illustration), a compressor package sells for 1,050 with a two-year extended service plan; SSPs are 1,000 and 100.
Service plan = 1,050 × 100 / 1,100 = 95.45, held as a contract liability and released over two years

A connection fee, a joining fee or a franchise's initial fee usually pays in advance for the future goods or services, so it is deferred over the period they are supplied (paras. B48–B51). Ch 18's franchise section is the classic case.

Prepaid mobile credit is a contract liability until the subscriber uses it, and expired credit is breakage. For example (illustration), an operator sells 1,000 of prepaid credit and its history says 8 percent will expire unused, so expected use is 920.

Tickets sold for future flights sit in a liability, often called unearned transportation revenue, until the flight. Frequent-flyer miles awarded with a ticket are a material right. For example (illustration), a ticket sells for 300 and earns miles with an SSP of 15.
Ticket = 300 × 300 / 315 = 285.71, released when flown; miles = 300 × 15 / 315 = 14.29, released when redeemed or when redemption becomes remote

Indonesian developers collect booking fees, down payments and instalments long before handover, so contract liabilities can be large on their balance sheets. Whether revenue comes at handover or over construction depends on para. 35(c): an apartment unit has no alternative use once sold, but revenue is over time only if the developer has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date, which turns on the sale agreement and local law. The gap between payment and handover is usually long enough for a significant financing component. For example (illustration), a buyer pays 1,000 three years before handover and the developer's borrowing rate is 8 percent.
Liability at handover = 1,000 × 1.08³ = 1,259.71; revenue at handover 1,259.71; interest expense of 259.71 accreted on the liability over the three years
Billings ahead of progress give a contract liability, progress ahead of billings a contract asset, netted per contract (para. 105). The Trade receivables essay works the cost-to-cost example.
Government grants are not contract liabilities.
A grant related to an asset may be presented as
under PSAK 220 (formerly PSAK 61, IAS 20), but the government is not a customer receiving goods or services, so PSAK 115 does not apply.
PHE splits the balance into take-or-pay gas and others, each with a current and non-current portion (Note 24, Daftar 5/118, PDF p. 135).

title: Deferred Tax Assets: Deductible Differences, Recoverability, Rates and Losses
snippet: The theory of deferred tax assets from the two measures of profit to presentation, worked through PHE's tax note and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • A deferred tax asset exists because the income statement and the tax return recognise the same cost in different years. When a cost is expensed in the books before the tax law lets it be deducted, the future deduction is worth the tax it will save, measured at the rate expected when it is used.

  • Unlike a deferred tax liability, a deferred tax asset is recognised only to the extent that taxable profit is probable in the same taxable entity, under the same tax authority, before the deduction expires. Unused tax losses face the strictest version of that test.

  • Deferred tax assets are always non-current, are not discounted, and are offset against deferred tax liabilities of the same taxpayer where the law allows set-off. The reported line is therefore a net figure per taxpayer, and in an upstream group most deductible differences sit inside the liability line.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report deferred tax assets of 55,781 at 31 December 2024 against 95,263 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 0.18 percent of total assets at the end of 2024 (0.31 percent in 2023). This page also covers deferred tax liabilities, 2,894,578 against 2,625,374 (Note 43e), which are 9.5 percent of total assets and 51.9 times the asset line (27.6 times in 2023); section 11 explains the gap. It also covers the profit or loss line income tax expense, net, 1,771,541 against 1,766,491 (Note 43c).

After reading it a student should be able to compute deferred tax assets and liabilities from temporary differences, test whether an asset can be recognised, remeasure both for a rate change, record a tax loss, reconcile tax expense to accounting profit, and read a tax note's deferred tax table.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Every number not cited to PHE is labelled an illustration.

1. Two measures of profit

Every deferred tax balance exists because a company measures profit twice. Accounting profit (Kieso calls it pretax financial income) is profit before tax under SAK, prepared for investors and creditors. Taxable profit is profit as the tax law defines it, and it determines the tax payable to the state. PSAK 212 Income Taxes (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) calls the tax on taxable profit current tax and the total charged to profit or loss tax expense, made up of current tax plus deferred tax (paras. 5–6).

The two measures differ in two ways. A permanent difference enters one measure and never the other. A temporary difference enters both, in different years, so it reverses. Kieso explains the gap as accrual books against cash-basis tax, but Indonesian taxable profit is largely accrual-based. The differences come from specific rules: provisions deductible only when paid, tax depreciation on its own schedule, income taxed under a final regime.

2. Future taxable amounts: the deferred tax liability as the mirror

When the tax return deducts a cost earlier than the books, the company pays less tax now and more later. The later tax is a deferred tax liability.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys equipment for 90,000 with a three-year life. The books depreciate it straight line, 30,000 a year. The tax rules allow 45,000, 36,000 and 9,000. Profit before depreciation is 110,000 a year, and the combined tax rate is 40 percent (section 6 explains where a PSC rate comes from).

Taxable profit = 110,000 − 45,000 = 65,000; 110,000 − 36,000 = 74,000; 110,000 − 9,000 = 101,000

3. Future deductible amounts: the deferred tax asset

A deferred tax asset is the same mechanism run in reverse. When the books expense a cost before the tax law deducts it, the company pays more tax now and less later. The tax it will save is an asset (PSAK 212.5, 24).

PSAK 212 measures it from the balance sheet. The tax base of an asset is the amount deductible against future taxable income; the tax base of a liability is its carrying amount less whatever will be deductible when it is settled (paras. 7–8). A deductible temporary difference is a gap that will reduce future taxable profit, and the deferred tax asset is that gap times the rate.

The lecture notes this series follows illustrate it with an environmental clean-up. The largest item in PHE's deferred tax asset line is a provision of the same family, for decommissioning and site restoration, of 66,352 (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172). Unlike the clean-up, it is capitalised into the asset, so the same transaction also creates a taxable difference (section 10).

For example (illustration), in 2024 a PHE subsidiary is ordered to restore an area damaged by drilling, and an appraisal puts the cost at 5,000. The work is done and paid in 2025, and assume the tax law deducts the cost when paid. Revenue is 200,000 and other operating expenses 120,000 in both years.

4. Recoverability: when a deferred tax asset can be recognised

A deferred tax liability is recognised for almost every taxable temporary difference, because the tax will be payable whatever happens (para. 15). A deferred tax asset is different. A deduction saves tax only if there is taxable income to deduct it from. So PSAK 212 recognises the asset only to the extent that taxable profit against which the deduction can be used is probable (para. 24, 27), which practice reads as more likely than not.

Where the taxable profit can come from. The standard ranks the evidence (paras. 28–29).

  1. Taxable temporary differences in the same taxable entity, under the same tax authority, that reverse in the same periods. They are the strongest support.

  2. Forecast taxable profit in those periods, ignoring new deductible differences.

  3. Tax planning opportunities, actions the entity would take to create taxable profit in time (para. 30).

Where tax law restricts which income a deduction may be used against, only income of that type counts (para. 27A). A PSC's ring-fence is that kind of restriction, a point section 12 returns to.

Reducing the asset. The test is repeated at every reporting date. The asset is reduced to the extent that profit is no longer probable, and the reduction is reversed if profit becomes probable again (paras. 37, 56). For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary outside PSC activities, taxed at 22 percent, has deductible differences of 30,000. Its forecast shows only 20,000 of taxable profit in the reversal periods.

Full asset = 30,000 × 22% = 6,600

Recognisable = 20,000 × 22% = 4,400; not recognised = 6,600 − 4,400 = 2,200

US GAAP records the full asset with a valuation allowance; PSAK 212 recognises only the recoverable amount.

5. Temporary and permanent differences

Permanent differences change the effective tax rate and create no deferred tax, because nothing reverses. Kieso lists fines and penalties, donations and tax-exempt interest. In Indonesia the common ones are non-deductible costs, dividends that are exempt or already taxed, and income subject to final tax, which is excluded from taxable profit because a separate final tax covers it. Section 9 shows them in PHE's reconciliation.

Temporary differences reverse. Kieso describes them as timing differences between book and tax. PSAK 212 defines them through the balance sheet, which captures more, because it counts any gap between carrying amount and tax base, including revaluations and business-combination adjustments (paras. 5, 17–18).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary computes its 2024 tax.

Accounting profit before tax = 100,000

Permanent: non-deductible costs + 2,000; interest subject to final tax − 1,500

Temporary: restoration provision not yet deductible + 1,000; tax depreciation above book − 3,000

Taxable profit = 100,000 + 2,000 − 1,500 + 1,000 − 3,000 = 98,500

Current tax = 98,500 × 40% = 39,400

Deferred tax asset = 1,000 × 40% = 400; deferred tax liability = 3,000 × 40% = 1,200

Tax expense = 39,400 + 1,200 − 400 = 40,200

Dr Income tax expense 40,200, Dr Deferred tax asset 400 / Cr Deferred tax liability 1,200, Cr Income tax payable 39,400

The check is (100,000 + 2,000 − 1,500) × 40% = 40,200. The temporary differences change only the timing of tax. The permanent ones move the effective rate to 40,200 / 100,000 = 40.2 percent.

6. Tax rate considerations

Which rate. A deferred tax asset is measured at the rate expected to apply when it is used, based on rates enacted or substantively enacted (passed in all but formality) at the reporting date (para. 47). It is not discounted, however far away the reversal (para. 53). When the rate varies by year, the reversal is scheduled. For example (illustration), a deductible difference of 9,000 reverses 3,000 a year in 2025–2027 under a law that sets 22 percent for 2025 and 20 percent from 2026.

Deferred tax asset = 3,000 × 22% + 3,000 × 20% + 3,000 × 20% = 660 + 600 + 600 = 1,860

A change in the rate. When a new rate is enacted, existing balances are remeasured, and the effect goes to tax expense in the year of enactment, except where the original item went to other comprehensive income or equity (paras. 60–61A). In Indonesia, Law 2/2020 cut the corporate rate to 22 percent and scheduled 20 percent from 2022; the HPP law of October 2021 (Law 7/2021) kept 22 percent. For example (illustration), an entity outside PSC activities holds deductible differences of 10,000 reversing from 2022.

End 2020, at the enacted 20% = 2,000. End 2021, at 22% = 2,200

Dr Deferred tax asset 200 / Cr Deferred tax benefit 200

The PSC rule. A production sharing contract (PSC) fixes its own tax terms. PHE's policy states that deferred taxes from activities outside PSCs use the rate enacted at the reporting date, while those related to PSC activities use "the tax rates applied on the effective date of the PSC or the extension date or date of amendment" (Note 3s, Daftar 5/69, PDF p. 86). The rate combines corporate income tax with a tax on profit after corporate tax, which PHE calls dividend tax (Note 2a(ii), Daftar 5/9, PDF p. 26).

A PSC signed when corporate tax was 25 percent kept its 25% + 20% × (1 − 25%) = 40% through the HPP change; its rate moves only when the contract does. For example (illustration), a PSC holding deductible differences of 50,000 at 40 percent is extended on terms that apply the prevailing law.

New rate = 22% + 20% × (1 − 22%) = 37.6%

Deferred tax asset = 50,000 × 37.6% = 18,800, down from 50,000 × 40% = 20,000

A tax loss is a deduction that arrived before the income. A carryback applies it to earlier years' taxable profit and reclaims tax paid; a carryforward applies it to future years.

Without a carryback, an Indonesian loss produces at most a deferred tax asset, and only if the probable-profit test of section 4 is met. Because a loss is "strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available", an entity with recent losses needs sufficient taxable temporary differences or "convincing other evidence" (para. 35), judged against the expiry date, the causes of the loss and tax planning (para. 36).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary outside PSC activities has a 2024 tax loss of 50,000 at 22 percent, and signed sales contracts make profit before expiry probable.

8. Presentation

Classification. Deferred tax assets are never current, even the part that reverses next year (PSAK 201.56, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1).

Offset. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only if the entity has a legally enforceable right to set off current tax balances and both relate to the same authority and the same taxable entity, or to entities that intend to settle net (PSAK 212.74). Indonesia has no group taxation, so each subsidiary is its own taxable entity and the consolidated line is the sum of the subsidiaries in a net asset position. Profit or loss and OCI. Tax follows the item it relates to: to profit or loss, other comprehensive income or equity (para. 61A).

10. Deferred tax assets across industries

Final-tax industries: construction and real estate. Some Indonesian income, such as land and building transfers and construction services, is taxed under a final tax on gross receipts. PHE's policy notes that final tax is outside PSAK 212 (Note 3s, Daftar 5/70, PDF p. 87), and the revenue it covers creates no temporary difference. For example (illustration), a developer's sale of 1,000 bears final tax of 1,000 × 2.5% = 25 on the gross transfer value (PP 34/2016), an expense outside income tax with no deferred tax.

Lessees and decommissioning: airlines, telecom, retail, upstream. A lessee under PSAK 116 (IFRS 16) recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on one transaction; where tax deducts lease payments as paid, the asset creates a taxable difference and the liability a deductible one. A capitalised decommissioning obligation does the same. Since the 2021 amendment to IAS 12 (paras. 15(b), 22A), adopted into PSAK 212 (then PSAK 46) from 1 January 2023, both are recognised. For example (illustration), a lease liability and right-of-use asset of 1,000 each at 22 percent.

Deferred tax asset = 1,000 × 22% = 220; deferred tax liability = 1,000 × 22% = 220; net nil at inception

The two then unwind at different speeds, because depreciation is straight line while interest is front-loaded. PHE's table has "asset rental" rows on both sides (Note 43e).

Multinational groups and Pillar Two. The deferred tax effects of the OECD global minimum tax (15 percent) are excluded by a temporary exception (PSAK 212.4A). PHE applies it and says Indonesia's rules, PMK 136/2024, take effect for fiscal years from 1 January 2025 (Note 3s, Daftar 5/68, PDF p. 85; Note 43h, Daftar 5/180, PDF p. 197).

12. Upstream note: the ring-fence

Each PSC usually sits in its own subsidiary, which restricts which income a deduction can be used against (para. 27A) and blocks offset across PSCs (para. 74). Gross split PSCs, taxed under the prevailing law, carry losses forward ten years (PP 53/2017) and can be assessed for ten years (Note 43f, Daftar 5/156, PDF p. 173).

Least-confident assertions

  • Two readings of PHE's Note 43e are inferences. That the decommissioning deferred tax inside the liability line is netted against oil and gas property differences in the same subsidiaries is not shown by entity. Reading non-recoverable costs into "PSC adjustments" of 614,238 is a guess at one component, since PHE gives no breakdown.

  • That the restoration cost in the illustrations is deductible when paid is assumed. Under a PSC, abandonment and site restoration funding has its own cost-recovery rules, which were not researched.

  • The 2020–2021 rate history (Law 2/2020 scheduling 20 percent from 2022, then the HPP law keeping 22 percent) and the ten-year gross split carryforward (PP 53/2017) were checked only in secondary sources, not in the regulation texts.

  • Whether the IFRS edition of Kieso uses a valuation allowance account was not checked; the book is not on disk. The page attributes the allowance method to US GAAP only.

  • PHE's Note 43d reconciliation looks partly mechanical. The 2024 starting figure, 1,663,757, is almost identical to 2023's 1,663,801, which fits the stated 37 percent; at the stated 38 percent it would be 1,859,178 and the PSC adjustments 418,817 rather than 614,238. Which figure is wrong cannot be told from the note. The associates line is exactly 22 percent of the share of profit in Note 42 (162,620 × 22% = 35,776), and the dividend item (−409,211; 2023: −710,276) is copied from the parent-only reconciliation although consolidated profit contains no dividend income (Notes 40, 42). Profit before tax of 4,892,574 against 4,892,576 on the face is a rounding difference of 2. Section 9 uses the note's figures as printed.

content.text: A deferred tax asset exists because the income statement and the tax return recognise the same cost in different years. When a cost is expensed in the books before the tax law lets it be deducted, the future deduction is worth the tax it will save, measured at the rate expected when it is used.

Unlike a deferred tax liability, a deferred tax asset is recognised only to the extent that taxable profit is probable in the same taxable entity, under the same tax authority, before the deduction expires. Unused tax losses face the strictest version of that test.

Deferred tax assets are always non-current, are not discounted, and are offset against deferred tax liabilities of the same taxpayer where the law allows set-off. The reported line is therefore a net figure per taxpayer, and in an upstream group most deductible differences sit inside the liability line.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report deferred tax assets of 55,781 at 31 December 2024 against 95,263 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 0.18 percent of total assets at the end of 2024 (0.31 percent in 2023). This page also covers deferred tax liabilities, 2,894,578 against 2,625,374 (Note 43e), which are 9.5 percent of total assets and 51.9 times the asset line (27.6 times in 2023); section 11 explains the gap. It also covers the profit or loss line income tax expense, net, 1,771,541 against 1,766,491 (Note 43c).

After reading it a student should be able to compute deferred tax assets and liabilities from temporary differences, test whether an asset can be recognised, remeasure both for a rate change, record a tax loss, reconcile tax expense to accounting profit, and read a tax note's deferred tax table.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Every number not cited to PHE is labelled an illustration.
Every deferred tax balance exists because a company measures profit twice.
) is profit before tax under SAK, prepared for investors and creditors.
is profit as the tax law defines it, and it determines the tax payable to the state. PSAK 212
(formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) calls the tax on taxable profit
and the total charged to profit or loss
, made up of current tax plus deferred tax (paras. 5–6).
The two measures differ in two ways. A
enters one measure and never the other. A

enters both, in different years, so it reverses. Kieso explains the gap as accrual books against cash-basis tax, but Indonesian taxable profit is largely accrual-based. The differences come from specific rules: provisions deductible only when paid, tax depreciation on its own schedule, income taxed under a final regime.
2. Future taxable amounts: the deferred tax liability as the mirror
When the tax return deducts a cost earlier than the books, the company pays less tax now and more later. The later tax is a

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys equipment for 90,000 with a three-year life. The books depreciate it straight line, 30,000 a year. The tax rules allow 45,000, 36,000 and 9,000. Profit before depreciation is 110,000 a year, and the combined tax rate is 40 percent (section 6 explains where a PSC rate comes from).
Carrying amount at year end = 60,000; 30,000; 0. Tax base = 45,000; 9,000; 0

Tax expense is 32,000 every year, which is 40 percent of the 80,000 accounting profit, while the cash tax swings from 26,000 to 40,400. Deferred tax exists so that expense follows the profit reported while the timing of payment sits on the balance sheet.
3. Future deductible amounts: the deferred tax asset

A deferred tax asset is the same mechanism run in reverse. When the books expense a cost before the tax law deducts it, the company pays more tax now and less later. The tax it will save is an asset (PSAK 212.5, 24).
PSAK 212 measures it from the balance sheet. The
of an asset is the amount deductible against future taxable income; the tax base of a liability is its carrying amount less whatever will be deductible when it is settled (paras. 7–8). A
is a gap that will reduce future taxable profit, and the deferred tax asset is that gap times the rate.

The lecture notes this series follows illustrate it with an environmental clean-up. The largest item in PHE's deferred tax asset line is a provision of the same family, for decommissioning and site restoration, of 66,352 (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172). Unlike the clean-up, it is capitalised into the asset, so the same transaction also creates a taxable difference (section 10).

For example (illustration), in 2024 a PHE subsidiary is ordered to restore an area damaged by drilling, and an appraisal puts the cost at 5,000. The work is done and paid in 2025, and assume the tax law deducts the cost when paid. Revenue is 200,000 and other operating expenses 120,000 in both years.
End 2024: provision carrying amount 5,000, tax base 5,000 − 5,000 = 0, deductible difference 5,000
Dr Restoration expense 5,000 / Cr Restoration provision 5,000
Dr Income tax expense 30,000, Dr Deferred tax asset 2,000 / Cr Income tax payable 32,000
Dr Income tax expense 32,000 / Cr Deferred tax asset 2,000, Cr Income tax payable 30,000

Tax expense is 30,000 in 2024 (40 percent of 75,000) and 32,000 in 2025 (40 percent of 80,000). In 2024 the company paid 2,000 of tax that belongs to 2025, and the asset carries it until the deduction arrives.
4. Recoverability: when a deferred tax asset can be recognised

A deferred tax liability is recognised for almost every taxable temporary difference, because the tax will be payable whatever happens (para. 15). A deferred tax asset is different. A deduction saves tax only if there is taxable income to deduct it from. So PSAK 212 recognises the asset only to the extent that taxable profit against which the deduction can be used is
(para. 24, 27), which practice reads as more likely than not.
Where the taxable profit can come from.
in the same taxable entity, under the same tax authority, that reverse in the same periods. They are the strongest support.
in those periods, ignoring new deductible differences.
, actions the entity would take to create taxable profit in time (para. 30).
Where tax law restricts which income a deduction may be used against, only income of that type counts (para. 27A). A PSC's ring-fence is that kind of restriction, a point section 12 returns to.

The test is repeated at every reporting date. The asset is reduced to the extent that profit is no longer probable, and the reduction is reversed if profit becomes probable again (paras. 37, 56). For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary outside PSC activities, taxed at 22 percent, has deductible differences of 30,000. Its forecast shows only 20,000 of taxable profit in the reversal periods.
US GAAP records the full asset with a valuation allowance; PSAK 212 recognises only the recoverable amount.
Dr Deferred tax asset 6,600 / Cr Deferred tax benefit 6,600
Dr Deferred tax asset 4,400 / Cr Deferred tax benefit 4,400
Dr Deferred tax expense 2,200 / Cr Allowance to reduce deferred tax asset 2,200

PHE says it "provides a valuation allowance" where losses may expire unused (Note 43e, Daftar 5/156, PDF p. 173), but its table shows a negative row, "unrecognized deferred tax assets", of 15,545 at the end of 2024 against 20,052 a year earlier.
When the estimate behind the difference changes.
In a second kind of reduction the difference itself shrinks. Suppose (illustration) that in mid-2025, before work starts, the appraisal of section 3 is cut from 5,000 to 2,500.
Dr Restoration provision 2,500 / Cr Restoration expense 2,500
Dr Deferred tax expense 1,000 / Cr Deferred tax asset 1,000
Under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8) a revised estimate goes to profit or loss of the period of revision, even though the 2024 books are closed; only a prior-period
is corrected through opening retained earnings.

change the effective tax rate and create no deferred tax, because nothing reverses. Kieso lists fines and penalties, donations and tax-exempt interest. In Indonesia the common ones are non-deductible costs, dividends that are exempt or already taxed, and income subject to final tax, which is excluded from taxable profit because a separate final tax covers it. Section 9 shows them in PHE's reconciliation.

reverse. Kieso describes them as timing differences between book and tax. PSAK 212 defines them through the balance sheet, which captures more, because it counts any gap between carrying amount and tax base, including revaluations and business-combination adjustments (paras. 5, 17–18).
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary computes its 2024 tax.
Permanent: non-deductible costs + 2,000; interest subject to final tax − 1,500
Temporary: restoration provision not yet deductible + 1,000; tax depreciation above book − 3,000
Deferred tax asset = 1,000 × 40% = 400; deferred tax liability = 3,000 × 40% = 1,200
Dr Income tax expense 40,200, Dr Deferred tax asset 400 / Cr Deferred tax liability 1,200, Cr Income tax payable 39,400
The check is (100,000 + 2,000 − 1,500) × 40% = 40,200. The temporary differences change only the timing of tax. The permanent ones move the effective rate to 40,200 / 100,000 = 40.2 percent.
A deferred tax asset is measured at the rate expected to apply when it is used, based on rates

(passed in all but formality) at the reporting date (para. 47). It is not discounted, however far away the reversal (para. 53). When the rate varies by year, the reversal is scheduled. For example (illustration), a deductible difference of 9,000 reverses 3,000 a year in 2025–2027 under a law that sets 22 percent for 2025 and 20 percent from 2026.

When a new rate is enacted, existing balances are remeasured, and the effect goes to tax expense in the year of enactment, except where the original item went to other comprehensive income or equity (paras. 60–61A). In Indonesia, Law 2/2020 cut the corporate rate to 22 percent and scheduled 20 percent from 2022; the HPP law of October 2021 (Law 7/2021) kept 22 percent. For example (illustration), an entity outside PSC activities holds deductible differences of 10,000 reversing from 2022.
End 2020, at the enacted 20% = 2,000. End 2021, at 22% = 2,200
Dr Deferred tax asset 200 / Cr Deferred tax benefit 200

A production sharing contract (PSC) fixes its own tax terms. PHE's policy states that deferred taxes from activities outside PSCs use the rate enacted at the reporting date, while those related to PSC activities use "the tax rates applied on the effective date of the PSC or the extension date or date of amendment" (Note 3s, Daftar 5/69, PDF p. 86). The rate combines corporate income tax with a tax on profit after corporate tax, which PHE calls dividend tax (Note 2a(ii), Daftar 5/9, PDF p. 26).

A PSC signed when corporate tax was 25 percent kept its 25% + 20% × (1 − 25%) = 40% through the HPP change; its rate moves only when the contract does. For example (illustration), a PSC holding deductible differences of 50,000 at 40 percent is extended on terms that apply the prevailing law.
Dr Deferred tax expense 1,200 / Cr Deferred tax asset 1,200
7. Net operating losses: carryback and carryforward
A tax loss is a deduction that arrived before the income. A
applies it to earlier years' taxable profit and reclaims tax paid; a
two years; refund of past tax is a current tax asset (PSAK 212.13)
five years (UU PPh art. 6(2)); ten for gross split PSCs (PP 53/2017)
unrecovered costs carried within the contract

Without a carryback, an Indonesian loss produces at most a deferred tax asset, and only if the probable-profit test of section 4 is met. Because a loss is "strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available", an entity with recent losses needs sufficient taxable temporary differences or "convincing other evidence" (para. 35), judged against the expiry date, the causes of the loss and tax planning (para. 36).
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary outside PSC activities has a 2024 tax loss of 50,000 at 22 percent, and signed sales contracts make profit before expiry probable.
2024: Dr Deferred tax asset 11,000 / Cr Income tax benefit, loss carryforward 11,000 (50,000 × 22%)
2025: taxable profit before the loss = 30,000; loss used = 30,000; current tax = 0
Dr Deferred tax expense 6,600 / Cr Deferred tax asset 6,600 (30,000 × 22%)
Remaining asset = 20,000 × 22% = 4,400, usable until the end of 2029

Under a cost-recovery PSC, costs not yet recovered from production wait in the contractor's unrecovered-cost pool, so the five-year clock is replaced by the contract's own terms. PHE recognises deferred tax assets for both "unused tax losses and unrecovered costs (for cost recovery PSC)" under the same probable test (Note 3s, Daftar 5/69, PDF p. 86). Its 2024 table shows a tax-loss item of 67,614 inside the liability line used down to −1,313, a charge of 68,927 to profit or loss (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172).
Deferred tax assets are never current, even the part that reverses next year (PSAK 201.56, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1).

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset only if the entity has a legally enforceable right to set off current tax balances and both relate to the same authority and the same taxable entity, or to entities that intend to settle net (PSAK 212.74). Indonesia has no group taxation, so each subsidiary is its own taxable entity and the consolidated line is the sum of the subsidiaries in a net asset position. For example (illustration), two subsidiaries, each netting its own balances:
B's 8,000 of deductions appear nowhere on the face of the statement.
Tax follows the item it relates to: to profit or loss, other comprehensive income or equity (para. 61A).

Beyond the expense and its reconciliation (section 9), PSAK 212 asks for the deferred tax balances by type of difference (para. 81(g)), unrecognised deductible differences and losses with expiry dates (81(e)), and the evidence for an asset that depends on future profit after a loss (82).
9. Income tax expense and the effective tax rate

The major components of income tax expense are disclosed separately (para. 79). Para. 80 lists what they may include: current tax, adjustments to current tax of prior periods, deferred tax from temporary differences, and separately the effects of rate changes, of losses or differences not recognised before, and of write-downs of deferred tax assets. PHE shows three lines (Note 43c, Daftar 5/152, PDF p. 169); its 2023 deferred line of 14,651 also absorbs a rate change of −11,720 and a release of unrecognised assets of 26,730 (Note 43e, PDF p. 173).
Adjustments in respect of prior years
Current tax and its corrections, such as the 2023 credit of 96,013, belong to the
page. The deferred component is the profit-or-loss movement in the balances of sections 2–7, 38,095 + 259,899 = 297,994 in 2024 (section 11).
is tax expense divided by accounting profit (para. 86).

PSAK 212 asks for a reconciliation of tax expense to accounting profit times the applicable rate, or of the effective rate to the applicable rate, stating how the applicable rate is computed (para. 81(c)) and why it changed (81(d)). Temporary differences recognised at the applicable rate do not appear in it, because deferred tax charges each at its rate, as section 5's check showed. The rate moves with permanent differences, profit taxed at other rates, deductible differences left unrecognised, rate changes and corrections of earlier years.

Often the most meaningful is the domestic rate where the entity is domiciled; an entity in several jurisdictions may aggregate reconciliations at each jurisdiction's rate (para. 85). Groups whose subsidiaries carry different contract rates, as PSCs do, often start instead from a weighted average of those rates, disclosing how it is computed (para. 81(c)). For example (illustration), a PSC subsidiary taxed at 40 percent earns profit before tax of 300,000 and has 5,000 of non-deductible costs; a subsidiary outside PSC activities, taxed at 22 percent, earns 100,000.
Weighted average of the subsidiaries' rates
Profit taxed at the PSC rate
The first shows the PSC rate's excess over 22 percent as a line; the second hides it in a starting rate that moves whenever the profit mix between subsidiaries changes.

PHE prints both forms (Note 43d, Daftar 5/153–5/154, PDF pp. 170–171). The parent-only reconciliation at 22 percent runs to nil, because the parent's untaxed dividend income, 409,211 / 22% = 1,860,050, exceeds its profit of 1,619,797, and the resulting loss is not recognised ("others", 76,665). The consolidated one follows.
Dividend income − 409,211; income from associates − 35,776; income subject to final tax − 61,467; PSC adjustments + 614,238

Dividends and final-taxed income pull the rate down. The PSC adjustments, which PHE does not break down, push it up; non-recoverable contract costs are one likely component. PHE gives the weighted average rate as 38 percent for 2024, while its own figures give 1,663,757 / 4,892,574 = 34.0 percent, or the starting figure is stale (see Least-confident). PHE gives neither the basis of the 38 percent nor the reason it rose from 37.
Final-tax industries: construction and real estate.
Some Indonesian income, such as land and building transfers and construction services, is taxed under a

on gross receipts. PHE's policy notes that final tax is outside PSAK 212 (Note 3s, Daftar 5/70, PDF p. 87), and the revenue it covers creates no temporary difference. For example (illustration), a developer's sale of 1,000 bears final tax of 1,000 × 2.5% = 25 on the gross transfer value (PP 34/2016), an expense outside income tax with no deferred tax.
Lessees and decommissioning: airlines, telecom, retail, upstream.

A lessee under PSAK 116 (IFRS 16) recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on one transaction; where tax deducts lease payments as paid, the asset creates a taxable difference and the liability a deductible one. A capitalised decommissioning obligation does the same. Since the 2021 amendment to IAS 12 (paras. 15(b), 22A), adopted into PSAK 212 (then PSAK 46) from 1 January 2023, both are recognised. For example (illustration), a lease liability and right-of-use asset of 1,000 each at 22 percent.
Deferred tax asset = 1,000 × 22% = 220; deferred tax liability = 1,000 × 22% = 220; net nil at inception
The two then unwind at different speeds, because depreciation is straight line while interest is front-loaded. PHE's table has "asset rental" rows on both sides (Note 43e).

The deferred tax effects of the OECD global minimum tax (15 percent) are excluded by a temporary exception (PSAK 212.4A). PHE applies it and says Indonesia's rules, PMK 136/2024, take effect for fiscal years from 1 January 2025 (Note 3s, Daftar 5/68, PDF p. 85; Note 43h, Daftar 5/180, PDF p. 197).
PHE prints a movement table for each side (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155–5/156, PDF pp. 172–173). The totals, with the liability shown positive, are below.
Effect of change in tax rate
The asset's 2024 charge is printed without brackets; its sign follows from Note 43c (section 9).

Three things stand out. First, both lines are already net. Inside the 55,781 are oil and gas properties of −37,197, a taxable difference netted within the same subsidiaries, and the unrecognised amount of −15,545. Inside the 2,894,578, a taxable difference of 3,376,189 on oil and gas properties is reduced by deductible items, mainly the decommissioning provision (412,586) and asset rental (75,227). Second, most deductible differences therefore sit inside the liability. Of the decommissioning provision's 478,938, only 66,352 is on the asset line; PHE does not show the netting by entity. Third, profit or loss drives both movements. The asset fell 39,482 (41.4 percent) as the decommissioning difference reversed by 10,003 and the netted oil and gas difference grew by 23,927. The liability rose 269,204 (10.3 percent), 174,986 of it from oil and gas properties.
Deferred tax share of 2024 tax expense = 297,994 / 1,771,541 = 16.8%

Each PSC usually sits in its own subsidiary, which restricts which income a deduction can be used against (para. 27A) and blocks offset across PSCs (para. 74). Gross split PSCs, taxed under the prevailing law, carry losses forward ten years (PP 53/2017) and can be assessed for ten years (Note 43f, Daftar 5/156, PDF p. 173).
: the other side of the netting, covered on this page.
: current and deferred tax, and the rate reconciliation, covered on this page (section 9).
: the source of PHE's largest deductible difference.
: current tax already paid and recoverable.
: the taxable difference that absorbs the assets.

Two readings of PHE's Note 43e are inferences. That the decommissioning deferred tax inside the liability line is netted against oil and gas property differences in the same subsidiaries is not shown by entity. Reading non-recoverable costs into "PSC adjustments" of 614,238 is a guess at one component, since PHE gives no breakdown.
That the restoration cost in the illustrations is deductible when paid is assumed. Under a PSC, abandonment and site restoration funding has its own cost-recovery rules, which were not researched.

The 2020–2021 rate history (Law 2/2020 scheduling 20 percent from 2022, then the HPP law keeping 22 percent) and the ten-year gross split carryforward (PP 53/2017) were checked only in secondary sources, not in the regulation texts.
Whether the IFRS edition of Kieso uses a valuation allowance account was not checked; the book is not on disk. The page attributes the allowance method to US GAAP only.

PHE's Note 43d reconciliation looks partly mechanical. The 2024 starting figure, 1,663,757, is almost identical to 2023's 1,663,801, which fits the stated 37 percent; at the stated 38 percent it would be 1,859,178 and the PSC adjustments 418,817 rather than 614,238. Which figure is wrong cannot be told from the note. The associates line is exactly 22 percent of the share of profit in Note 42 (162,620 × 22% = 35,776), and the dividend item (−409,211; 2023: −710,276) is copied from the parent-only reconciliation although consolidated profit contains no dividend income (Notes 40, 42). Profit before tax of 4,892,574 against 4,892,576 on the face is a rounding difference of 2. Section 9 uses the note's figures as printed.

title: Due from the Government, and Other Receivables: Underlifting, the DMO fee and VAT reimbursement at a PSC contractor, and why the 'other' lines need the general credit-loss model
snippet: Underlifting, the DMO fee and VAT reimbursement at a PSC contractor, and why the 'other' lines need the general credit-loss model
content:
In brief

  • At a production sharing contractor, "due from the Government" collects three claims on the state, namely the underlift (oil the contractor was entitled to but did not lift), the DMO fee (what the state pays for crude the contractor must supply to the domestic market) and VAT the state reimburses.

  • An underlift is not revenue from contracts with customers under PSAK 115. Indonesian rules have the state pay a computed underlift in cash, which makes it a financial asset measured at the amount SKK Migas fixes, with expected credit losses; settled in barrels instead, it would be a non-financial item at cost.

  • On claims against the state the credit-loss allowance is tiny. Eligibility rulings and timing move the numbers, through write-offs and the current/non-current split. The "other receivables" lines need the general three-stage model, and in the case below one disputed item carries 85 percent of their allowance.

The reported line fell 10.4 percent, and its name hides three claims with different accounting

The balance sheet on this page reports due from the Government of 85,053 at 31 December 2024 against 94,887 a year earlier, in thousands, a fall of 9,834 or 10.4 percent. Other receivables, net, rose 2.2 percent to 28,830 (2023: 28,217), and other non-current receivables fell 10.2 percent to 3,106 (2023: 3,460). Together they are 0.39 percent of total assets at 31 December 2024 (116,989 / 30,303,898), and the face does not say what any of them contains.

This essay uses PT Hulu Energi Nusantara ("HEN"), an upstream contractor under production sharing contracts (PSCs) with SKK Migas, the government body that administers PSCs, reporting in USD under Indonesian SAK. HEN and every figure attached to it are constructed for illustration. HEN amounts are in USD thousand and volumes in thousand barrels (kbbl), except per-barrel prices in USD. "The state" below is the Government in the line's name. The case follows one block, PSC West, in which HEN holds 100 percent.

HEN's draft shows due from the Government of 34,075 at 31 December 2024, made of 24,000 for 300 kbbl of underlifted crude at USD 80 per barrel credited to revenue from contracts with customers, 675 of unpaid DMO fee and 9,400 of VAT reimbursement claims. In February 2025, before the March issue date, the auditor asks three questions. Can the underlift be revenue under PSAK 115? Do expected credit losses apply to a claim on the state? Why is a VAT claim more than a year old still current?

The governing claim of this essay is that each claim's settlement route, in barrels or in cash and within twelve months or later, decides its income line, its measurement basis, whether the credit-loss model applies and where it is presented.

This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that HEN's line falls only from 34,075 to 32,431.2, but revenue from contracts with customers falls by 24,000, and the settlement route alone is worth 10,500 of 2024 profit.

The standards are PSAK 115 (formerly 72, IFRS 15) for revenue, PSAK 109 (formerly 71, IFRS 9) and PSAK 232 (formerly 50, IAS 32) for financial assets, and PSAK 201 (formerly 1, IAS 1) for the current/non-current split.

A PSC entitlement is a waterfall, and the contractor's barrels come after the state's share and the DMO

A cost-recovery PSC divides each year's production in a fixed order, and the contractor's barrels come last. The terms below are simplified, with constructed percentages; each PSC sets its own.

  1. First tranche petroleum (FTP), here 20 percent of production, is taken before costs and split between the state and the contractor in the equity ratio.

  2. Cost recovery gives the contractor its recoverable operating and capital costs in barrels, up to what remains after FTP.

  3. The equity to be split is divided in a pre-tax ratio, 25 percent to HEN, which after the 40 percent combined PSC tax is 15 percent (25% × 60%).

  4. The domestic market obligation (DMO) requires HEN to deliver crude equal to 25 percent of production multiplied by its 25 percent pre-tax share. The state takes these barrels and pays a DMO fee priced under rules set by the Minister of Energy, here 15 percent of the Indonesian Crude Price (ICP), the monthly government reference price.

  5. Corporate and dividend tax is paid in cash on FTP share plus equity share less the net DMO, and does not reduce the barrels HEN lifts.

PSC West produced 3,600 kbbl in 2024. To isolate volumes, take one annual ICP of USD 80.

Gross production value = 3,600 kbbl × USD 80 = 288,000

FTP = 288,000 × 20% = 57,600; HEN 25% = 14,400; state 43,200

After FTP = 288,000 − 57,600 = 230,400

Cost recovery = 120,000 (2024 recoverable costs, all within the 230,400 available)

Equity to be split = 230,400 − 120,000 = 110,400; HEN 25% = 27,600; state 82,800

HEN's entitlement = 120,000 + 14,400 + 27,600 = 162,000, or 2,025 kbbl at USD 80

DMO volume = 3,600 × 25% × 25% = 225 kbbl, worth 18,000; DMO fee = 225 × USD 12 = 2,700

HEN's lifting entitlement = 2,025 − 225 = 1,800 kbbl

Taxable income = 14,400 + 27,600 − (18,000 − 2,700) = 26,700; tax at 40% = 10,680

Cost recovery follows PSC rules (capital recovered on the contract's depreciation schedule, plus prior-year costs not yet recovered), so it differs from the accounting cost used later. HEN may lift and sell 1,800 kbbl for its own account. Lifting is crude sold or split at the custody transfer point, the meter where ownership is measured and passes, and the contractor owns its oil only from that point.

Liftings follow tankers, so the contractor is overlifted or underlifted on almost every date

Entitlement accrues at about 150 kbbl a month (1,800 / 12), while liftings come in cargoes of about 300 kbbl every two months. When cumulative liftings exceed cumulative entitlement HEN is overlifted and owes the state, a liability "due to the Government". When they fall short it is underlifted and the state owes it.

Small gaps close through the next nominations (the cargo slots each party requests). The December tanker was cancelled for weather on 23 December, and the terminal had no slot left in the 2024 programme, so the year ended with an underlift of 300 kbbl, a sixth of HEN's year.

PMK 139/2024, in force from 31 December 2024, now governs the settlement. SKK Migas calculates each party's lifting entitlement for each work area (contract area) and period; it bills an overlift to the contractor and pays an underlift promptly through the Ministry of Finance from the government's USD oil and gas account (Art. 12–13), and may offset it against amounts such as an overlift or an earlier DMO-fee overpayment (Art. 16). Claims already forwarded for payment before that date continue under the revoked PMK 118/2019 and 119/2019 (Art. 37). On 30 December 2024 SKK Migas confirmed in writing that the 300 kbbl would enter its 2024 calculation as an underlift. HEN expects payment in 2025, so the claim is current.

PSAK 115 puts revenue on barrels transferred to customers, so the underlift is a claim and not a sale

HEN's draft used the entitlement method, which books revenue on entitled barrels with a receivable for an underlift or a payable for an overlift; the sales (lifting) method books revenue on barrels sold. PSAK 115 recognises revenue when control of a good passes to a customer. In March 2019 the IFRS Interpretations Committee considered a joint operator whose output received differed from its entitlement, with the shortfall settled by later deliveries, and concluded that it recognises revenue only for output transferred to its customers. The state is not a joint operator under PSAK 111 (formerly 66, IFRS 11), so the decision applies to HEN by analogy, but the logic holds, since no customer has taken the 300 kbbl.

HEN treats the DMO delivery as a sale. The PSC obliges HEN to deliver the barrels, and the state takes them for a fee, which is a contract with a customer even at 15 percent of ICP. The 2,700 fee is revenue from contracts with customers, and the unpaid 675 is a trade receivable from the state.

Revenue from contracts with customers = 1,500 kbbl × USD 80 + 2,700 = 120,000 + 2,700 = 122,700, against 146,700 in the draft

Reclassify the draft entry: Dr Revenue from contracts with customers 24,000 / Cr Other operating income, lifting imbalance 24,000

The underlift claim, payable in cash, is a contractual right to receive cash, a financial asset under PSAK 232 and PSAK 109. HEN measures it at amortised cost (the amount expected, adjusted for credit losses, with interest at the effective rate, here nil for a claim due within months), starting from the amount SKK Migas will fix, 300 kbbl at the ICP used in its calculation, 24,000. Presenting the credit as other operating income rather than as revenue is HEN's judgment; an argument exists that a state paying for barrels it took is a customer.

Settlement in barrels would change the measurement by 10,500 and remove the credit-loss allowance

Had SKK Migas carried the 300 kbbl into HEN's 2025 liftings, the IFRIC fact pattern, HEN would hold a right to future oil, a non-financial item outside PSAK 109, with no credit-loss allowance. No standard covers it, so HEN would set a policy under PSAK 208 (formerly 25, IAS 8), either at cost as a deferral of production cost or at market as a right to product. HEN bears all of PSC West's costs, 91,125 of operating costs and depletion in 2024, but receives only its 2,025 kbbl of entitlement, DMO barrels included, so the cost per barrel spreads over those.

Cost per entitled barrel = 91,125 / 2,025 = USD 45.00

Underlift at cost = 300 × 45.00 = 13,500, against 24,000 at the cash amount

Gross margin on the block, cash route = 122,700 + 24,000 − 91,125 = 55,575

Gross margin on the block, in kind at cost = 122,700 − (91,125 − 13,500) = 45,075

The 10,500 gap is margin on barrels no customer has bought; in kind it waits for the 2025 sale, while in cash the state buys out HEN's right in 2024. The regulation and SKK Migas's letter put HEN on the cash route.

VAT reimbursement fails on eligibility and timing, and the state's credit barely registers

HEN's VAT claims lose value through rejected items and slow payment, not through default. Contractors were designated VAT collectors (pemungut PPN) under PMK 73/PMK.03/2010, so HEN withholds the VAT on a vendor's invoice and deposits it to the treasury itself. PMK 139 Art. 5 ties reimbursement to VAT already deposited, and Art. 3 keeps the earlier conditions, under which a claim may be made only after the state's share is received and is capped at the state share deposited (126,000 for HEN), or at the equity share alone (82,800) where the PSC excludes FTP. Neither cap binds. A September purchase of well services of 10,000 at the 11 percent rate in force in 2024 runs as follows.

Deposit in October: Dr VAT collected payable 1,100 / Cr Cash 1,100; Dr Due from the Government, VAT reimbursement 1,100 / Cr VAT awaiting deposit 1,100

On 14 November 2024 SKK Migas rejected 1,600 of 2023 claims. 600 was VAT on costs not chargeable as operating costs, which Art. 5(2)(c) excludes, so it was never a valid claim and goes to cost.

The other 1,000 was rejected for missing original tax invoices from one vendor. HEN obtained them and resubmitted on 2 December 2024, and a 2022 claim rejected on the same ground was paid in full after resubmission, about 20 months later. The right is intact, so HEN keeps 1,000 at amortised cost; with no interest and an effective rate of nil, the delay does not change the carrying amount. A refund created only by statute is not a financial asset, because PSAK 232 requires a contract; HEN's VAT right also rests on the PSC's reimbursement clause, so HEN treats it as within PSAK 109, a judgment that varies in practice.

Current, simplified approach = 675 × 0.30% × 45% = 0.9

Non-current VAT = 1,000 × 0.30% × 45% = 1.4

Total allowance on the state = 43.8 + 1.4 = 45.2, against 600 written off and 1,000 moved to non-current

  • Presenting the cash-settled underlift as other operating income, applying the 2019 joint-operator decision by analogy, and measuring an in-kind underlift at cost are the essay's judgments; Indonesian contractors' actual policies were not reached.

HEN filed for arbitration in October 2024, its counsel expects an award in 2026, and HEN estimates recovery of 450. That one item carries 85 percent of the allowance (1,050 / 1,232).
Classification follows when the cash is expected. The 450 arrives in 2026, and 800 of the employee loans fall due after December 2025, with 8 of their 12 allowance.

A flat "other receivables" balance, like the 2.2 percent change on this page, can mean steady turnover or the same claims carried forward. Only the note's ageing, its stage table and the stage 3 share of the allowance tell them apart.
Corrected, HEN's due from the Government is 32,431.2, and the large correction sits in the income statement
HEN's line at 31 December 2024 falls by 1,643.8, from the draft's 34,075 to 32,431.2.
Resubmitted VAT moved to other non-current receivables = (1,000)

Revenue from contracts with customers falls from 146,700 to 122,700, and the 24,000 moves to other operating income; gross margin on the block stays 55,575. The auditor's three questions get three answers. The underlift is a cash claim, not revenue; credit losses apply and total 45.2; and the old VAT claim was partly invalid and partly non-current. Had SKK Migas settled the underlift in barrels, the line would have been 21,963.6 and 2024 margin 10,500 lower. The 10.4 percent fall on this page could come from any of these routes, and only the note says which.

The PSC waterfall is simplified. FTP at 20 percent shared in the equity ratio, the 25 percent pre-tax split, the DMO volume and a fee at 15 percent of ICP are constructed; real PSCs differ, and real calculations use monthly ICP, which adds price imbalances to volume ones.

Small intra-year gaps closing through nominations, and the timing of SKK Migas's period calculation and payment, are stated from general knowledge; PMK 139 Art. 12–13 says "promptly" without a deadline. Whether SKK Migas ever carries a year-end underlift into the next year in kind was not checked.

Presenting the cash-settled underlift as other operating income, applying the 2019 joint-operator decision by analogy, and measuring an in-kind underlift at cost are the essay's judgments; Indonesian contractors' actual policies were not reached.

Treating the DMO delivery as a PSAK 115 sale and PSC VAT reimbursement as a contractual financial asset are judgments that vary in practice. HEN's status as a VAT collector rests on PMK 73/PMK.03/2010, revoked on 18 October 2024 by PMK 81/2024, whose collector provisions were not read.
PSAK 115, 109, 232, 201, 208 and 111 were not opened, so they are cited by subject, not paragraph. The 30-day and 90-day presumptions are from knowledge of IFRS 9.

PMK 139/2024 on payment of claims on the government in upstream oil and gas, in force 31 December 2024: Art. 1 (definitions), Art. 3–5 (VAT reimbursement conditions, caps, exclusions including Art. 5(2)(c)), Art. 12–13 (lifting calculation; overlift billed, underlift paid), Art. 16 (offsets), Art. 37 (transition). VERIFIED (web, JDIH Kemenkeu PDF, read in the independent recheck of 2026-10-09; the document page was opened by the author).

PMK 118/PMK.02/2019 on the DMO fee, overlifting and underlifting, consolidated with PMK 51/2023 (JDIH Kemenkeu consolidated text, compiled 21 March 2024), Art. 1–5 and 8. VERIFIED (web, PDF opened). Revoked by PMK 139/2024; still relevant under Art. 37.
PMK 119/PMK.02/2019 on VAT reimbursement for upstream contractors. VERIFIED (web, DDTC News, 28 August 2019, secondary source).
PMK 73/PMK.03/2010 designating PSC contractors as VAT collectors; revoked 18 October 2024 by PMK 81/2024. VERIFIED (web, BPK and JDIH Kemenkeu database entries; text not read).

Issue 149, "Sale of output by a joint operator" (May 2019), on the March 2019 IFRS Interpretations Committee agenda decision and the cost versus fair value measurement of imbalances. VERIFIED (web, ey.com, PDF opened).
