presentation.deck: Underlifting, the DMO fee and VAT reimbursement at a PSC contractor, and why the 'other' lines need the general credit-loss model
key_takeaways: At a production sharing contractor, "due from the Government" collects three claims on the state, namely the underlift (oil the contractor was entitled to but did not lift), the DMO fee (what the state pays for crude the contractor must supply to the domestic market) and VAT the state reimburses.

An underlift is not revenue from contracts with customers under PSAK 115. Indonesian rules have the state pay a computed underlift in cash, which makes it a financial asset measured at the amount SKK Migas fixes, with expected credit losses; settled in barrels instead, it would be a non-financial item at cost.

On claims against the state the credit-loss allowance is tiny. Eligibility rulings and timing move the numbers, through write-offs and the current/non-current split. The "other receivables" lines need the general three-stage model, and in the case below one disputed item carries 85 percent of their allowance.

title: Due from the Government: Entitlement, Lifting, Underlifting and the DMO Fee
snippet: Why a production sharing contractor ends the year owed money by the state, when that claim is a receivable and when it is revenue, worked through PHE's underlifting and DMO fees and set beside other claims on governments
content:
In brief

  • Under a production sharing contract (PSC) the oil belongs to the state until it is lifted, and the contract sets how many barrels each party is entitled to. Cargoes rarely match entitlements, so at any date one party has lifted too much (overlifting) and the other too little (underlifting). A contractor's underlifting settled in cash is a claim on the state for barrels it was entitled to but did not lift.

  • Revenue under PSAK 115 needs a customer who obtains control. An underlifted barrel has gone to no customer of the contractor, so the claim is a receivable and the credit goes outside revenue from customers. The domestic market obligation (DMO) is different. The state takes crude and pays a fee, so the fee is revenue and the unpaid fee a trade-type receivable.

  • Both claims arise from a contract, so they are financial assets at amortised cost under PSAK 109 and need an expected credit loss allowance, however small a sovereign's default risk makes it. Statutory claims such as VAT refunds are not financial assets and sit elsewhere.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report due from the Government of 623,448 at 31 December 2024 against 501,429 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 2.0 percent of total assets and 7.8 percent of current assets (1.6 and 5.1 percent a year earlier), and it rose 24.3 percent in the year. This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to compute a contractor's entitlement, explain why lifting and entitlement diverge, record an underlift and a DMO delivery, decide whether each claim is revenue, a financial asset or neither, and recognise similar claims on governments in other industries.

All amounts are in USD thousand and volumes in thousand barrels (kbbl) unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Why the Government can owe a contractor

A private company cannot own Indonesian oil in the ground. The state owns it and hires a contractor through a PSC to find and produce it. The contractor bears the costs and the risk, and in return is paid in barrels. What the contractor receives is its entitlement, a share of each year's production set by the contract.

Under a cost recovery PSC, PHE's Note 2a describes the order (Daftar 5/10–5/11, PDF pp. 27–28). First tranche petroleum (FTP), 10 to 20 percent of production, is taken off the top before costs and shared between the Government and the contractor. Cost recovery then returns the contractor's recoverable costs in barrels: the current year's non-capital costs, the current year's depreciation of capital costs, and earlier costs not yet recovered. What remains, the equity to be split, is divided in the contract's ratio. Crude is valued at the Indonesian Crude Price (ICP), the government reference price, and gas at the price in each gas sales contract.

For example (illustration), a block produces 4,000 kbbl in a year at an ICP of USD 75 per barrel. FTP is 20 percent, the contractor's share of FTP and of equity is 25 percent, and recoverable costs are 120,000.

Gross production value = 4,000 × 75 = 300,000

FTP = 4,000 × 20% = 800 kbbl; contractor's share = 800 × 25% = 200 kbbl

Cost recovery = 120,000 / 75 = 1,600 kbbl

Equity to be split = 4,000 − 800 − 1,600 = 1,600 kbbl; contractor's share = 1,600 × 25% = 400 kbbl

Contractor's entitlement = 1,600 + 200 + 400 = 2,200 kbbl, worth 165,000; the state's = 1,800 kbbl

Ownership passes at lifting, the point where crude is measured and loaded at the terminal. Until then the barrels are the state's. That is why the contractor's "asset" during the year is a right to barrels, and why a gap between barrels owed and barrels taken has to be settled.

2. Entitlement versus lifting

Entitlement accrues with production, day by day. Lifting happens in cargoes. A tanker takes several hundred thousand barrels at once, and terminal slots are shared among the parties, so at any date one party has taken more than its entitlement to date and another less. The party that has lifted more is overlifted and owes the other; the one that has lifted less is underlifted and is owed.

Continue the example. Of the contractor's 2,200 kbbl, 250 kbbl go to the domestic market obligation (section 4), leaving 1,950 kbbl to lift and sell, about 162.5 kbbl a month. It lifts cargoes of 325 kbbl every two months.

The December slot went to a cargo of the state's share, so the year ends with the state overlifted by 325 kbbl and the contractor underlifted by the same amount. PHE's note describes the same position. Its underlifting receivables arise "due to SKK Migas's crude oil and natural gas lifting volumes exceeding its entitlements" (Note 9, Daftar 5/97, PDF p. 114). SKK Migas is the regulator that administers PSCs for the Government.

Two settlements are possible in principle. In kind, the contractor gets extra barrels next year. In cash, the Government pays the value of the barrels. PHE's movement in Note 9 shows settlement by payment, "payment received" of 786,361 against underlifting in 2024. Such payments, together with DMO fee claims, were governed during 2024 by PMK 118/2019 (amended by PMK 51/2023) and from 31 December 2024 by PMK 139/2024, the Minister of Finance regulation on paying claims of upstream contractors.

3. Receivable or revenue?

The question is whether the 325 kbbl is a sale. PSAK 115 (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15) recognises revenue when a performance obligation to a customer is satisfied by transferring control. A customer is a party that has contracted to obtain goods or services that are an output of the entity's ordinary activities in exchange for consideration. Kieso's five steps (identify the contract, the performance obligations, the price, allocate it, recognise when control passes) all start from such a contract.

No step fits the underlift. The contractor has transferred nothing to anyone; the state's lifter took its own share early. The IFRS Interpretations Committee reached the same conclusion in March 2019 for a joint operator whose output received differed from its entitled share. It recognises revenue only for output it has sold to its customers. The analogy has two limits. The state is not a joint operator, and the Committee's fact pattern was a shortfall made up in later deliveries, with only revenue addressed. The measurement routes below are this page's reading for a claim settled in cash.

That leaves three ways to book the imbalance, which differ in where the margin on the 325 kbbl appears. Continue the example. The five cargoes sold were 1,625 × 75 = 121,875; the full lifting entitlement is worth 1,950 × 75 = 146,250; production cost attributable to the 1,950 kbbl is USD 40 per barrel, 78,000.

Entitlement method

Underlift at price = 325 × 75 = 24,375; at cost = 325 × 40 = 13,000

Margin difference = 68,250 − 56,875 = 11,375 = 325 × (75 − 40)

The entitlement method puts non-customer barrels in revenue, which PSAK 115 does not allow. The cost route suits settlement in kind, where the asset is a right to future barrels. The price route suits settlement in cash, where the claim is a fixed sum.

PHE takes the third route. Underlifting and overlifting are valued at the "weighted average annual Crude Oil price" for crude and the gas sales contract price for gas, and because the adjustments "are not transactions with customers", they are recorded as part of direct cost of sales (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80; the Indonesian reads "dicatat sebagai bagian dari biaya langsung penjualan"). Revenue from crude and gas is recognised on "the actual lifting amount and sold to customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79).

The volume can still change after the year. PHE's policy measures imbalances against "final entitlements", which SKK Migas fixes after the period. If its calculation raises the contractor's 2024 entitlement by 13 kbbl:

Adjustment = 13 × 75 = 975; Dr Due from the Government 975 / Cr Direct cost of sales 975

The price does not move the claim after year end, because the annual average is known by then. That keeps the claim a fixed sum, which matters in section 5.

4. The domestic market obligation and its fee

A PSC also obliges the contractor to supply part of its crude to the domestic market. PHE's Note 2a(v) sets the crude rule (Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). Take the smaller of two amounts, production multiplied by national demand over national production, and 25 percent of production, then multiply by the contractor's entitlement percentage. For gas it is 25 percent of production times that percentage (Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). The DMO price for crude is the weighted average price of all crude sold by the contractor, or another price set in the PSC.

In the example, assume the 25 percent figure is the smaller.

DMO = 4,000 × 25% × 25% = 250 kbbl

DMO fee at the weighted average price = 250 × 75 = 18,750

If a PSC set the fee at 15% of ICP instead: 250 × 75 × 15% = 2,812.5, and the contractor gives up 15,937.5 of value

Here the Government is a customer. It contracts, through the PSC, to obtain crude and pays consideration for it, so the DMO delivery is a sale under PSAK 115 at the transaction price, the fee. A fee below market is still the transaction price; the value the contractor gives up is a cost of holding the contract and is never recorded as revenue.

Dr Due from the Government, DMO fees 18,750 / Cr Revenue, DMO fees 18,750

PHE's revenue note shows DMO fees on crude of 429,402 in 2024 (2023: 448,841), under revenue from related parties and the Government (Note 35, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165), and Note 9 describes the receivable as amounts due "in relation to the Subsidiaries' obligations to supply crude oil to meet the domestic market demand in accordance with the PSCs".

5. Is the claim a financial asset?

The classification decides which standard measures it. A financial asset includes a contractual right to receive cash from another entity (PSAK 232, formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32). The word that matters is contractual. Assets that are not contractual, such as income taxes created by statutory requirements imposed by governments, are not financial assets (IAS 32 AG12).

Both of PHE's claims rest on the PSC, a contract between the contractor and the state. The underlift is a right to cash for barrels the contract entitled the contractor to; the DMO fee is consideration under the same contract. Both are financial assets, held to collect fixed amounts, so they sit at amortised cost under PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9). PHE's face statement points the line to Note 3g, its financial-instruments policy, and that note lists amounts due to the Government among financial liabilities (Daftar 5/44, PDF p. 61).

Contrast a VAT refund. A contractor's right to have VAT reimbursed comes mainly from tax law and the regulations under it, so it is usually treated as a statutory claim, accounted for as a tax asset, and outside PSAK 109. Because reimbursement is also written into cost-recovery PSCs, the classification is a judgment. PHE keeps it out of this line. Reimbursable VAT of 505,861 (30,523 at the Company and 475,338 at subsidiaries) sits in other taxes receivable (Note 43a, Daftar 5/151, PDF p. 168).

6. Measurement and expected credit losses on the state

Being owed by a sovereign lowers the risk, and the model still applies. PSAK 109 requires an expected credit loss (ECL) allowance on every financial asset at amortised cost. The two claims follow different approaches because they arise differently.

  • The DMO fee receivable arises from a PSAK 115 contract with a customer and has no significant financing component, so the simplified approach is required, with lifetime ECL from recognition.

  • The underlift does not come from a contract with a customer, so the general approach applies. It starts in stage 1 with 12-month ECL and moves to lifetime ECL only if credit risk increases significantly.

For example (illustration), assume a 12-month probability of default (PD) for the state of 0.2 percent, a loss given default (LGD), the share not recovered after default, of 45 percent, and an average life of 90 days for DMO fee claims and 212 days for underlift claims (section 9). Apply them to PHE's year-end balances, scaled to each claim's expected life.

Underlift, 12-month ECL over 212 days = 534,270 × 0.2% × 45% × 212 / 365 = 279.3

DMO fees, lifetime ECL over 90 days = 89,178 × 0.2% × 45% × 90 / 365 = 19.8

Total = 299.1, or 0.0010% of PHE's total assets

For a claim expected within a year, 12-month and lifetime ECL coincide, because 12-month ECL is defined as the part of lifetime ECL from defaults possible in the next twelve months. The stage matters only if settlement stretches beyond a year. An allowance this small is immaterial, but PSAK 109 still treats it as an expectation, and an expectation is never exactly zero.

Delay without loss. A credit loss is the shortfall in cash flows discounted at the asset's original effective interest rate; PHE's policy uses "an approximation of the original EIR" (Note 3g, Daftar 5/43, PDF p. 60). A claim that bears no interest and was expected within months has an effective rate of about nil, so a payment that arrives late but in full creates almost no measurable loss. Delay changes presentation instead. A claim not expected within twelve months moves to non-current assets (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1; PHE Note 3h).

Linked claims. A government can delay paying one claim while another is unresolved. Section 9 gives a PHE example.

7. Settlement and the mirror liability

The receivable leaves the balance sheet when SKK Migas, through the Ministry of Finance, pays it, or when it is offset against something the contractor owes. Overlifting is the mirror. When the contractor has lifted more than its entitlement, it owes the Government, and the liability is valued and booked the same way.

Contractor overlifted 100 kbbl at an annual average of 75: Dr Direct cost of sales 7,500 / Cr Due to the Government 7,500

PHE shows overlifting and DMO of 51,427 under due to the Government, current portion (Note 20, Daftar 5/114, PDF p. 131), and gas overlifting of 11,322 inside accrued expenses (Note 23, Daftar 5/117, PDF p. 134). PHE presents receivables and payables to the Government gross. Netting would require a legally enforceable right to set off and an intention to settle net (PSAK 232 para. 42).

A different imbalance arises between partners in the same block. When one working-interest holder lifts less than its share, the shortfall is usually made up in later cargoes, so it is a right to barrels, a non-financial item measured at cost. PHE's other current assets include "deferred expenses related to underlifting" and "other receivables from underlifting for non-operators in PIEP whose settlement … refers to the operating cycle on the operator's side" (Note 14a, Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122), which looks like that cost route, though the note does not state the measurement basis.

8. Receivables from governments across industries

Many industries are owed money by governments. The accounting turns on the same two questions, whether there is a contract and whether the government is a customer.

Service concessions. A company that builds a toll road or a power plant for a government and is paid fixed amounts by the government, whatever the traffic, holds a financial asset under ISAK 112 Perjanjian Konsesi Jasa (formerly ISAK 16, IFRIC 12). Where payment depends on users, it holds an intangible asset instead, the right to charge them. For example (illustration), an operator is promised 10,000 a year for five years from completion, and the market rate for such a claim is 7 percent.

Receivable at completion = 10,000 × (1 − 1.07⁻⁵) / 0.07 = 41,001.97

First-year interest income = 41,001.97 × 7% = 2,870.14

The receivable follows PSAK 109 at amortised cost, with ECL on the grantor.

Government grants. A grant the government has promised for meeting a condition becomes a grant receivable once there is reasonable assurance that the entity will comply and the grant will be received (PSAK 220, formerly PSAK 61, IAS 20). The credit goes to deferred income, to the asset's cost or to profit, never to revenue from customers, because the government is not buying anything.

Compensation for regulated prices. State-owned fuel and power companies that sell below cost on government instruction may be compensated by the state. Whether such compensation is revenue, a grant or a separate receivable depends on what the government has committed to in writing and when. This page has not checked how Indonesian state-owned companies treat it.

Health providers and contractors to government. A hospital billing the national health insurer, or a builder billing a ministry, holds ordinary customer receivables (or contract assets) under PSAK 115, with the simplified ECL approach. A public counterparty changes the loss rate and leaves the model as it is.

Tax refunds of any kind are statutory claims, outside PSAK 109, as section 5 explained.

9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 9

PHE's note gives the composition and a movement for each claim (Note 9, Daftar 5/97, PDF p. 114).

Underlifting is 85.7 percent of the line. Dividing each closing balance by its year's additions gives a rough measure of how long claims wait.

Underlifting: 534,270 / 918,928 × 365 = 212 days

DMO fees: 89,178 / 362,540 × 365 = 90 days

Underlifting claims wait longer, which fits a settlement tied to SKK Migas's calculation of final entitlements after the period. Both balances are still presented as current, consistent with Note 3h's one-period test.

Note 35 lists the Government among PHE's customers. SKK Migas appears among customers with more than 10 percent of revenue, at 1,133,213 (Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165), a figure equal to the DMO fees of 429,402 plus an "Adjustment split PSC" of 703,811 that the notes do not explain. Two figures do not tie. DMO fee revenue of 429,402 exceeds the 362,540 of DMO fee additions in Note 9, and cash receipts from the Government of 1,396,379 in the cash flow statement (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17) exceed the 1,147,696 received in Note 9. PHE reconciles neither, nor the "others" lines of (21,017) and 9,264. Note 9 states that the claims are "fully collectible", the language of collectibility rather than expectation. Note 45k shows how claims link. In 2022 PHE's subsidiary PHM, proposing to pay Badak LNG tariff arrears in instalments, hoped that "PHM's DMO fee can be paid in due time", and the energy minister asked the finance minister to pay it (Daftar 5/215, PDF p. 232).

10. Upstream note: gross split contracts

PHE also holds gross split PSCs, under which production is shared by a base split adjusted by variable and progressive components and ministerial discretion, without cost recovery (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). Entitlement there is a percentage of gross production, so the waterfall in section 1 collapses to one line, but lifting in cargoes still creates imbalances. PHE's Note 2b does not describe the DMO under gross split, and this page does not assume it.

11. Related lines

  • due-to-government-current and due-to-government-non-current: overlifting, DMO and other amounts owed to the state.

  • trade-receivables-net: claims on customers for barrels lifted and sold.

  • revenues: where DMO fees are recognised.

  • production-expenses: the cost side, near where underlifting and overlifting adjustments are recorded.

  • other-taxes-receivable-current and other-taxes-receivable-non-current: reimbursable VAT.

  • other-current-assets: partner underlifting carried as deferred expenses.

Least-confident assertions

  • That PHE's underlifting is settled in cash rests on the "payment received" line in Note 9 and on PMK 139/2024. The regulation's existence, date and scope were confirmed on the web; its article-level content (SKK Migas pays an underlift, offsets allowed) comes from an earlier reading of the PDF, not re-checked here.

  • Classifying the underlift under the general ECL approach and the DMO fee under the simplified approach is this page's reading of PSAK 109; PHE recognises no allowance on either and does not say which approach it would use.

  • Reading PHE's partner underlifting in Note 14a as measured at cost is an inference from the label "deferred expenses".

  • Applying the 2019 IFRIC decision to cash-settled underlifts is an analogy twice removed (the state is not a joint operator, and the decision's shortfall was settled in kind). Treating the VAT refund as statutory is a judgment, since reimbursement is also a PSC term. How a claim whose amount moved with the oil price would be classified was not researched.

  • The sovereign PD and LGD are illustrative. Compensation receivables of Indonesian state-owned fuel and power companies were not researched, nor is it known what PHE's "Adjustment split PSC" revenue represents or where its receivable sits.

content.text: Under a production sharing contract (PSC) the oil belongs to the state until it is lifted, and the contract sets how many barrels each party is entitled to. Cargoes rarely match entitlements, so at any date one party has lifted too much (overlifting) and the other too little (underlifting). A contractor's underlifting settled in cash is a claim on the state for barrels it was entitled to but did not lift.

Revenue under PSAK 115 needs a customer who obtains control. An underlifted barrel has gone to no customer of the contractor, so the claim is a receivable and the credit goes outside revenue from customers. The domestic market obligation (DMO) is different. The state takes crude and pays a fee, so the fee is revenue and the unpaid fee a trade-type receivable.

Both claims arise from a contract, so they are financial assets at amortised cost under PSAK 109 and need an expected credit loss allowance, however small a sovereign's default risk makes it. Statutory claims such as VAT refunds are not financial assets and sit elsewhere.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report due from the Government of 623,448 at 31 December 2024 against 501,429 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 2.0 percent of total assets and 7.8 percent of current assets (1.6 and 5.1 percent a year earlier), and it rose 24.3 percent in the year. This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to compute a contractor's entitlement, explain why lifting and entitlement diverge, record an underlift and a DMO delivery, decide whether each claim is revenue, a financial asset or neither, and recognise similar claims on governments in other industries.
All amounts are in USD thousand and volumes in thousand barrels (kbbl) unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. Why the Government can owe a contractor

A private company cannot own Indonesian oil in the ground. The state owns it and hires a contractor through a PSC to find and produce it. The contractor bears the costs and the risk, and in return is paid in barrels. What the contractor receives is its
, a share of each year's production set by the contract.
Under a cost recovery PSC, PHE's Note 2a describes the order (Daftar 5/10–5/11, PDF pp. 27–28).
(FTP), 10 to 20 percent of production, is taken off the top before costs and shared between the Government and the contractor.

then returns the contractor's recoverable costs in barrels: the current year's non-capital costs, the current year's depreciation of capital costs, and earlier costs not yet recovered. What remains, the
, is divided in the contract's ratio. Crude is valued at the Indonesian Crude Price (ICP), the government reference price, and gas at the price in each gas sales contract.

For example (illustration), a block produces 4,000 kbbl in a year at an ICP of USD 75 per barrel. FTP is 20 percent, the contractor's share of FTP and of equity is 25 percent, and recoverable costs are 120,000.
Equity to be split = 4,000 − 800 − 1,600 = 1,600 kbbl; contractor's share = 1,600 × 25% = 400 kbbl
Contractor's entitlement = 1,600 + 200 + 400 = 2,200 kbbl, worth 165,000; the state's = 1,800 kbbl

, the point where crude is measured and loaded at the terminal. Until then the barrels are the state's. That is why the contractor's "asset" during the year is a right to barrels, and why a gap between barrels owed and barrels taken has to be settled.

Entitlement accrues with production, day by day. Lifting happens in cargoes. A tanker takes several hundred thousand barrels at once, and terminal slots are shared among the parties, so at any date one party has taken more than its entitlement to date and another less. The party that has lifted more is
and owes the other; the one that has lifted less is

Continue the example. Of the contractor's 2,200 kbbl, 250 kbbl go to the domestic market obligation (section 4), leaving 1,950 kbbl to lift and sell, about 162.5 kbbl a month. It lifts cargoes of 325 kbbl every two months.
December, slot taken by the state's lifter

The December slot went to a cargo of the state's share, so the year ends with the state overlifted by 325 kbbl and the contractor underlifted by the same amount. PHE's note describes the same position. Its underlifting receivables arise "due to SKK Migas's crude oil and natural gas lifting volumes exceeding its entitlements" (Note 9, Daftar 5/97, PDF p. 114). SKK Migas is the regulator that administers PSCs for the Government.
Two settlements are possible in principle.
, the contractor gets extra barrels next year.

, the Government pays the value of the barrels. PHE's movement in Note 9 shows settlement by payment, "payment received" of 786,361 against underlifting in 2024. Such payments, together with DMO fee claims, were governed during 2024 by PMK 118/2019 (amended by PMK 51/2023) and from 31 December 2024 by PMK 139/2024, the Minister of Finance regulation on paying claims of upstream contractors.
The question is whether the 325 kbbl is a sale. PSAK 115 (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15) recognises revenue when a performance obligation to a

is satisfied by transferring control. A customer is a party that has contracted to obtain goods or services that are an output of the entity's ordinary activities in exchange for consideration. Kieso's five steps (identify the contract, the performance obligations, the price, allocate it, recognise when control passes) all start from such a contract.

No step fits the underlift. The contractor has transferred nothing to anyone; the state's lifter took its own share early. The IFRS Interpretations Committee reached the same conclusion in March 2019 for a joint operator whose output received differed from its entitled share. It recognises revenue only for output it has sold to its customers. The analogy has two limits. The state is not a joint operator, and the Committee's fact pattern was a shortfall made up in later deliveries, with only revenue addressed. The measurement routes below are this page's reading for a claim settled in cash.

That leaves three ways to book the imbalance, which differ in where the margin on the 325 kbbl appears. Continue the example. The five cargoes sold were 1,625 × 75 = 121,875; the full lifting entitlement is worth 1,950 × 75 = 146,250; production cost attributable to the 1,950 kbbl is USD 40 per barrel, 78,000.
Dr Underlift asset 13,000 / Cr Production cost 13,000
Dr Due from the Government 24,375 / Cr Direct cost of sales 24,375

The entitlement method puts non-customer barrels in revenue, which PSAK 115 does not allow. The cost route suits settlement in kind, where the asset is a right to future barrels. The price route suits settlement in cash, where the claim is a fixed sum.

PHE takes the third route. Underlifting and overlifting are valued at the "weighted average annual Crude Oil price" for crude and the gas sales contract price for gas, and because the adjustments "are not transactions with customers", they are recorded as part of direct cost of sales (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80; the Indonesian reads "dicatat sebagai bagian dari biaya langsung penjualan"). Revenue from crude and gas is recognised on "the actual lifting amount and sold to customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79).

The volume can still change after the year. PHE's policy measures imbalances against "final entitlements", which SKK Migas fixes after the period. If its calculation raises the contractor's 2024 entitlement by 13 kbbl:
Adjustment = 13 × 75 = 975; Dr Due from the Government 975 / Cr Direct cost of sales 975
The price does not move the claim after year end, because the annual average is known by then. That keeps the claim a fixed sum, which matters in section 5.
4. The domestic market obligation and its fee

A PSC also obliges the contractor to supply part of its crude to the domestic market. PHE's Note 2a(v) sets the crude rule (Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). Take the smaller of two amounts, production multiplied by national demand over national production, and 25 percent of production, then multiply by the contractor's entitlement percentage. For gas it is 25 percent of production times that percentage (Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). The DMO price for crude is the weighted average price of all crude sold by the contractor, or another price set in the PSC.
In the example, assume the 25 percent figure is the smaller.
DMO fee at the weighted average price = 250 × 75 = 18,750
If a PSC set the fee at 15% of ICP instead: 250 × 75 × 15% = 2,812.5, and the contractor gives up 15,937.5 of value

Here the Government is a customer. It contracts, through the PSC, to obtain crude and pays consideration for it, so the DMO delivery is a sale under PSAK 115 at the transaction price, the fee. A fee below market is still the transaction price; the value the contractor gives up is a cost of holding the contract and is never recorded as revenue.
Dr Due from the Government, DMO fees 18,750 / Cr Revenue, DMO fees 18,750

PHE's revenue note shows DMO fees on crude of 429,402 in 2024 (2023: 448,841), under revenue from related parties and the Government (Note 35, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165), and Note 9 describes the receivable as amounts due "in relation to the Subsidiaries' obligations to supply crude oil to meet the domestic market demand in accordance with the PSCs".
5. Is the claim a financial asset?
The classification decides which standard measures it. A

includes a contractual right to receive cash from another entity (PSAK 232, formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32). The word that matters is contractual. Assets that are not contractual, such as income taxes created by statutory requirements imposed by governments, are not financial assets (IAS 32 AG12).

Both of PHE's claims rest on the PSC, a contract between the contractor and the state. The underlift is a right to cash for barrels the contract entitled the contractor to; the DMO fee is consideration under the same contract. Both are financial assets, held to collect fixed amounts, so they sit at amortised cost under PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9). PHE's face statement points the line to Note 3g, its financial-instruments policy, and that note lists amounts due to the Government among financial liabilities (Daftar 5/44, PDF p. 61).

Contrast a VAT refund. A contractor's right to have VAT reimbursed comes mainly from tax law and the regulations under it, so it is usually treated as a statutory claim, accounted for as a tax asset, and outside PSAK 109. Because reimbursement is also written into cost-recovery PSCs, the classification is a judgment. PHE keeps it out of this line. Reimbursable VAT of 505,861 (30,523 at the Company and 475,338 at subsidiaries) sits in other taxes receivable (Note 43a, Daftar 5/151, PDF p. 168).
6. Measurement and expected credit losses on the state

Being owed by a sovereign lowers the risk, and the model still applies. PSAK 109 requires an expected credit loss (ECL) allowance on every financial asset at amortised cost. The two claims follow different approaches because they arise differently.
The DMO fee receivable arises from a PSAK 115 contract with a customer and has no significant financing component, so the
is required, with lifetime ECL from recognition.
The underlift does not come from a contract with a customer, so the
applies. It starts in stage 1 with 12-month ECL and moves to lifetime ECL only if credit risk increases significantly.

For example (illustration), assume a 12-month probability of default (PD) for the state of 0.2 percent, a loss given default (LGD), the share not recovered after default, of 45 percent, and an average life of 90 days for DMO fee claims and 212 days for underlift claims (section 9). Apply them to PHE's year-end balances, scaled to each claim's expected life.
DMO fees, lifetime ECL over 90 days = 89,178 × 0.2% × 45% × 90 / 365 = 19.8
Total = 299.1, or 0.0010% of PHE's total assets

For a claim expected within a year, 12-month and lifetime ECL coincide, because 12-month ECL is defined as the part of lifetime ECL from defaults possible in the next twelve months. The stage matters only if settlement stretches beyond a year. An allowance this small is immaterial, but PSAK 109 still treats it as an expectation, and an expectation is never exactly zero.

A credit loss is the shortfall in cash flows discounted at the asset's original effective interest rate; PHE's policy uses "an approximation of the original EIR" (Note 3g, Daftar 5/43, PDF p. 60). A claim that bears no interest and was expected within months has an effective rate of about nil, so a payment that arrives late but in full creates almost no measurable loss. Delay changes presentation instead. A claim not expected within twelve months moves to non-current assets (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1; PHE Note 3h).
A government can delay paying one claim while another is unresolved. Section 9 gives a PHE example.

The receivable leaves the balance sheet when SKK Migas, through the Ministry of Finance, pays it, or when it is offset against something the contractor owes. Overlifting is the mirror. When the contractor has lifted more than its entitlement, it owes the Government, and the liability is valued and booked the same way.
Contractor overlifted 100 kbbl at an annual average of 75: Dr Direct cost of sales 7,500 / Cr Due to the Government 7,500

PHE shows overlifting and DMO of 51,427 under due to the Government, current portion (Note 20, Daftar 5/114, PDF p. 131), and gas overlifting of 11,322 inside accrued expenses (Note 23, Daftar 5/117, PDF p. 134). PHE presents receivables and payables to the Government gross. Netting would require a legally enforceable right to set off and an intention to settle net (PSAK 232 para. 42).

A different imbalance arises between partners in the same block. When one working-interest holder lifts less than its share, the shortfall is usually made up in later cargoes, so it is a right to barrels, a non-financial item measured at cost. PHE's other current assets include "deferred expenses related to underlifting" and "other receivables from underlifting for non-operators in PIEP whose settlement … refers to the operating cycle on the operator's side" (Note 14a, Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122), which looks like that cost route, though the note does not state the measurement basis.
Many industries are owed money by governments. The accounting turns on the same two questions, whether there is a contract and whether the government is a customer.
A company that builds a toll road or a power plant for a government and is paid fixed amounts by the government, whatever the traffic, holds a financial asset under ISAK 112

(formerly ISAK 16, IFRIC 12). Where payment depends on users, it holds an intangible asset instead, the right to charge them. For example (illustration), an operator is promised 10,000 a year for five years from completion, and the market rate for such a claim is 7 percent.
The receivable follows PSAK 109 at amortised cost, with ECL on the grantor.

A grant the government has promised for meeting a condition becomes a grant receivable once there is reasonable assurance that the entity will comply and the grant will be received (PSAK 220, formerly PSAK 61, IAS 20). The credit goes to deferred income, to the asset's cost or to profit, never to revenue from customers, because the government is not buying anything.

State-owned fuel and power companies that sell below cost on government instruction may be compensated by the state. Whether such compensation is revenue, a grant or a separate receivable depends on what the government has committed to in writing and when. This page has not checked how Indonesian state-owned companies treat it.
Health providers and contractors to government.

A hospital billing the national health insurer, or a builder billing a ministry, holds ordinary customer receivables (or contract assets) under PSAK 115, with the simplified ECL approach. A public counterparty changes the loss rate and leaves the model as it is.
of any kind are statutory claims, outside PSAK 109, as section 5 explained.
PHE's note gives the composition and a movement for each claim (Note 9, Daftar 5/97, PDF p. 114).
Underlifting is 85.7 percent of the line. Dividing each closing balance by its year's additions gives a rough measure of how long claims wait.

Underlifting claims wait longer, which fits a settlement tied to SKK Migas's calculation of final entitlements after the period. Both balances are still presented as current, consistent with Note 3h's one-period test.

Note 35 lists the Government among PHE's customers. SKK Migas appears among customers with more than 10 percent of revenue, at 1,133,213 (Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165), a figure equal to the DMO fees of 429,402 plus an "Adjustment split PSC" of 703,811 that the notes do not explain. Two figures do not tie. DMO fee revenue of 429,402 exceeds the 362,540 of DMO fee additions in Note 9, and cash receipts from the Government of 1,396,379 in the cash flow statement (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17) exceed the 1,147,696 received in Note 9. PHE reconciles neither, nor the "others" lines of (21,017) and 9,264. Note 9 states that the claims are "fully collectible", the language of collectibility rather than expectation. Note 45k shows how claims link. In 2022 PHE's subsidiary PHM, proposing to pay Badak LNG tariff arrears in instalments, hoped that "PHM's DMO fee can be paid in due time", and the energy minister asked the finance minister to pay it (Daftar 5/215, PDF p. 232).

PHE also holds gross split PSCs, under which production is shared by a base split adjusted by variable and progressive components and ministerial discretion, without cost recovery (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). Entitlement there is a percentage of gross production, so the waterfall in section 1 collapses to one line, but lifting in cargoes still creates imbalances. PHE's Note 2b does not describe the DMO under gross split, and this page does not assume it.
: overlifting, DMO and other amounts owed to the state.
: claims on customers for barrels lifted and sold.
: the cost side, near where underlifting and overlifting adjustments are recorded.
: partner underlifting carried as deferred expenses.

That PHE's underlifting is settled in cash rests on the "payment received" line in Note 9 and on PMK 139/2024. The regulation's existence, date and scope were confirmed on the web; its article-level content (SKK Migas pays an underlift, offsets allowed) comes from an earlier reading of the PDF, not re-checked here.

Classifying the underlift under the general ECL approach and the DMO fee under the simplified approach is this page's reading of PSAK 109; PHE recognises no allowance on either and does not say which approach it would use.
Reading PHE's partner underlifting in Note 14a as measured at cost is an inference from the label "deferred expenses".

Applying the 2019 IFRIC decision to cash-settled underlifts is an analogy twice removed (the state is not a joint operator, and the decision's shortfall was settled in kind). Treating the VAT refund as statutory is a judgment, since reimbursement is also a PSC term. How a claim whose amount moved with the oil price would be classified was not researched.

The sovereign PD and LGD are illustrative. Compensation receivables of Indonesian state-owned fuel and power companies were not researched, nor is it known what PHE's "Adjustment split PSC" revenue represents or where its receivable sits.

The notes' Ch 17 impairment material uses the outdated incurred-loss model and was not used.

presentation.deck: Why a production sharing contractor ends the year owed money by the state, when that claim is a receivable and when it is revenue, worked through PHE's underlifting and DMO fees and set beside other claims on governments

A contractor's underlifting settled in cash is a claim on the state for barrels it was entitled to but did not lift.

An underlifted barrel has gone to no customer of the contractor, so the claim is a receivable and the credit goes outside revenue from customers. The domestic market obligation (DMO) is different. title: Employee Benefits Liabilities: Short-Term Pay, Defined Benefit Plans and Indonesian Severance
snippet: The theory of employee benefit accounting under PSAK 219 from payroll accruals to the projected unit credit method, worked through PHE's pension and severance obligations and set beside the industries where these liabilities weigh most
content:
In brief

  • PSAK 219 sorts employee benefits by when they are paid. Short-term benefits are accrued undiscounted as the work is done; post-employment, other long-term and termination benefits are estimated, discounted, and recognised on their own triggers.

  • A defined contribution plan costs the employer only its contribution. A defined benefit plan leaves the employer holding the actuarial and investment risk, so it carries the present value of the promised benefit, measured by the projected unit credit method, less any plan assets.

  • Service cost and net interest on a defined benefit plan go to profit or loss, while remeasurements (actuarial gains and losses, the return on plan assets beyond interest, and changes in the asset ceiling) go to other comprehensive income and are never recycled. Indonesian statutory severance is an unfunded defined benefit plan of this kind, and since 2022 it is attributed only to the last 24 years of service before retirement age, or from hire if later.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report employee benefits liabilities, non-current portion, of 310,011 at 31 December 2024 against 318,604 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line fell 2.7 percent and is 1.0 percent of total assets in both years and 2.0 percent of total liabilities. Two neighbouring lines belong with it, short-term employee benefits of 409,225 (2023: 290,571) in current liabilities and a remeasurement of the employee benefit liability of −610 (2023: 1,430) in other comprehensive income, OCI (Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14).

A student should come away able to classify an employee benefit, measure a defined benefit obligation, split its cost between profit or loss and other comprehensive income with journals, and apply this to Indonesian severance.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 219 Imbalan Kerja (formerly PSAK 24, IAS 19 Employee Benefits).

1. Four kinds of employee benefit

PSAK 219 sorts benefits by when they fall due (para. 8), and the further away the payment, the more estimation it needs.

Category

Definition

PHE example

Measurement

Short-term

Expected to be settled wholly within 12 months after the year in which the service is rendered

salaries, incentives

undiscounted, as service is rendered

Post-employment

Payable after employment ends

pension, severance on retirement, retiree healthcare

discounted, actuarial; remeasurements to OCI

Other long-term

Everything else that is not short-term, post-employment or termination

long service awards (UTD), pre-retirement preparation period (MPPK)

discounted, actuarial; remeasurements to profit or loss

Termination

Paid because the entity ends employment early, or the employee accepts an offer to leave

voluntary early retirement packages

recognised when the offer can no longer be withdrawn

2. Short-term benefits

Payroll. Short-term benefits are recognised as the employee works, at the undiscounted amount expected to be paid, as an expense and a liability for whatever is unpaid. Amounts withheld from pay, such as income tax (PPh 21) and the employee share of BPJS contributions, are owed to the tax office and the agencies, not expenses of the employer (see the Other Taxes essay).

Compensated absences. Non-accumulating absences, such as sick leave that lapses, are expensed when taken. Accumulating absences carry forward, and the expected cost of the unused entitlement is accrued at the year end, in full if vesting (paid out if unused) and at the expected usage if non-vesting (paras. 13–16). For example (illustration), 400 employees each carry 5 unused days of leave into next year, at a daily pay of 0.25 (USD 250).

Vesting leave = 400 × 5 × 0.25 = 500

Non-vesting leave, 90% expected to be used = 400 × 5 × 0.25 × 90% = 450

Dr Employee benefits expense 450 / Cr Accrued compensated absences 450

Bonuses and profit-sharing. A bonus is recognised when the entity has a present legal or constructive obligation to pay it and can estimate it reliably (para. 19). A constructive obligation arises from established practice, so an entity that pays an incentive every year has no realistic alternative to paying it again. PHE's short-term employee benefits line consists of employee incentives, 409,225 at the end of 2024 (Note 25a, Daftar 5/119, PDF p. 136). Taking its numbers as the starting point, suppose (illustration) the 290,571 accrued for 2023 was settled in 2024 for 285,000, and the 2024 incentive is accrued at 409,225.

Settlement: Dr Short-term employee benefits 290,571 / Cr Cash 285,000 / Cr Employee benefits expense 5,571

Accrual: Dr Employee benefits expense 409,225 / Cr Short-term employee benefits 409,225

Net 2024 incentive expense = 409,225 − 5,571 = 403,654

The over-accrual, a change in estimate, reduces this year's expense. The year-end balance equals 28.2 percent of PHE's 2024 personnel costs of 1,453,337 (688,343 + 510,007 + 254,987, Notes 37–39, Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166).

3. Post-employment benefits: defined contribution and defined benefit

Who carries the risk decides the accounting. In a defined contribution (DC) plan the employer pays fixed contributions into a fund and has no obligation to pay more if the fund falls short, so the employee bears the investment risk (para. 28). In a defined benefit (DB) plan the employer promises the benefit itself, so if the fund earns less or employees live longer the employer pays the difference (para. 30).

Defined contribution

Defined benefit

Employer promises

a contribution

a benefit

Risk borne by

employee

employer

Expense

the contribution for the period

service cost + net interest

Balance sheet

unpaid contributions only

present value of obligation − plan assets

For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays 5 percent of a monthly payroll of 2,000 into a financial institution pension fund (Dana Pensiun Lembaga Keuangan, DPLK) as a DC plan, and has not yet paid December's contribution at the year end.

Dr Employee benefits expense 100 / Cr Accrued pension contributions 100

PHE's policy expenses DC contributions as incurred (Note 3q(ii), Daftar 5/64, PDF p. 81). The rest of this page is about DB plans.

4. Measuring the obligation: the projected unit credit method

PSAK 219 requires the projected unit credit method (PUCM), which measures a promise earned a little each year in three steps (para. 67).

  1. Project the benefit payable at retirement using the expected final salary.

  2. Attribute the benefit to years of service using the plan's formula (paras. 70–71), so each year of service earns one "unit".

  3. Discount the units earned to date at a rate set by reference to high-quality corporate bond yields, or government bond yields where no deep corporate bond market exists, in the currency and term of the obligation (para. 83). PHE uses government bond rates for that reason (Note 3q(iii), PDF p. 81).

The present value of units earned to date is the defined benefit obligation (DBO), of this year's unit the current service cost, and the unwinding of discount on the opening DBO the interest cost.

5. Plan assets, the net liability and the three components of cost

Plan assets are assets held by a separate fund, or qualifying insurance policies, available only to pay employee benefits and not to the employer's creditors (para. 8). They are measured at fair value and netted against the DBO.

Net defined benefit liability = DBO − fair value of plan assets (adjusted for the asset ceiling)

The cost for the period has three components, and the standard sends each to a different place (para. 120).

Net interest applies the same discount rate to the DBO and the plan assets (para. 123), so a company cannot report a high expected return on risky assets as profit; whatever the fund earns above or below that rate is a remeasurement.

The asset ceiling. When a plan is in surplus, the employer may recognise the surplus only up to the present value of the economic benefits available to it as refunds or reductions in future contributions (para. 64). For example (illustration), a plan with a surplus of 10,000 from which the employer can recover only 8,348 through lower future contributions shows an asset of 8,348, with a ceiling effect of 10,000 − 8,348 = 1,652, PHE's 2024 ceiling effect. The ceiling is applied plan by plan, so a group can show a ceiling effect inside an overall net liability.

6. Past service cost, curtailments and settlements

Plan changes hit profit or loss at once. Past service cost is the change in the DBO for service already rendered, caused by a plan amendment (introducing or changing a plan) or a curtailment (a significant reduction in the number of employees covered). It is recognised as an expense at the earlier of when the amendment or curtailment occurs and when related restructuring costs or termination benefits are recognised (para. 103). For example (illustration), a subsidiary raises a lump-sum benefit by 10 percent for a group whose DBO is 50,000.

Past service cost = 50,000 × 10% = 5,000

Dr Employee benefits expense 5,000 / Cr Net defined benefit liability 5,000

Since the 2011 revision of IAS 19 (in Indonesia from 2015) past service cost is no longer spread over the vesting period.

A settlement removes the obligation altogether, for example when the fund buys annuities from an insurer that takes over the payments. The gain or loss is the difference between the DBO settled and the price paid. For example (illustration), the fund pays an insurer 41,500 to take over pensions in payment with a DBO of 40,000.

Settlement loss = 41,500 − 40,000 = 1,500

Memo: DBO −40,000; plan assets −41,500

Dr Employee benefits expense 1,500 / Cr Net defined benefit liability 1,500

A purchased policy settles the plan only if the insurer, not the employer, becomes obliged to the pensioners.

7. Indonesian severance as a defined benefit plan

Indonesian labour law promises every permanent employee a lump sum at retirement set by a formula, so the employer carries a DB plan under PSAK 219, unfunded unless it sets assets aside. The formula sits in UU 13/2003 as amended by the Job Creation law (UU 11/2020, replaced by Perpu 2/2022 and enacted as UU 6/2023), and in its implementing regulation PP 35/2021. On retirement an employee receives (PP 35/2021, art. 56):

  • severance pay (uang pesangon) of 1.75 times the art. 40(2) scale, which rises from 1 month's wages for under one year of service to a maximum of 9 months from 8 years;

  • a long-service payment (uang penghargaan masa kerja, UPMK) of 1 times the art. 40(3) scale, from 2 months at 3 years to a maximum of 10 months from 24 years;

  • compensation for rights (uang penggantian hak), such as unused leave.

Maximum on retirement = 1.75 × 9 + 10 = 25.75 months' wages, reached at 24 years of service

Employers pay the higher of the statutory amount and their own plan or collective labour agreement, as PHE's policy says (Note 3q, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). Since Constitutional Court decision 168/PUU-XXI/2023 (31 October 2024) the statutory scale is a minimum (paling sedikit), and the court ordered a new labour law, so these multiples may change.

When the benefit is earned. For years many Indonesian actuaries attributed this benefit straight-line from the date of hire. In an agenda decision published in May 2021 the IFRS Interpretations Committee considered a plan that pays only to those employed at retirement age, capped at a number of years of consecutive service immediately before retirement, and concluded that the benefit is attributed only to the capped years before retirement age, since service before then does not reduce the service still needed. In April 2022 the DSAK IAI, the Indonesian standard setter, found that the statutory scheme has the same fact pattern. With retirement at 56 and the UPMK capped at 24 years, the obligation first arises at age 32, and the benefit is attributed to service between 32 and 56. Entities that had attributed from hire were told to assess the effect under the PSAK 25 (now PSAK 208) requirements for a change in accounting policy.

For example (illustration), an employee joined at 25, is now 40 with 15 years of service, and retires at 56 with 31. Current monthly wage is 1.5 (USD 1,500), with PHE's 7 percent salary increase and 7.1 percent discount rate, and no resignations or deaths.

Final monthly wage = 1.5 × 1.07^16 = 4.4282; benefit = 25.75 × 4.4282 = 114.027

Present value of the full benefit = 114.027 / 1.071^16 = 38.052

The later start cuts this employee's DBO by 5.728, or 31.1 percent, and raises the annual unit by 29.2 percent (31/24), so the cost moves later in the career. An employee hired at 35 would see no change, because attribution starts at hire. The younger the hiring age across a workforce, the larger the fall in the opening liability.

Funding it. PP 35/2021 art. 58 lets employer contributions to a pension programme count towards statutory severance, with the employer paying any shortfall, so a fund held for that purpose is a plan asset of the severance DB plan and does not turn it into a DC plan. PHE funds its service award (PAP, Penghargaan Atas Pengabdian) through such a DPLK programme (PPUKP) and treats its assets as plan assets (Note 25b, Daftar 5/120, PDF p. 137). All its other benefits are unfunded.

8. Other long-term and termination benefits

Other long-term benefits are measured with the same PUCM, but every element, remeasurements included, goes to profit or loss, because they are less uncertain than post-employment benefits (paras. 154–156). PHE's are long-service awards (Ulang Tahun Dinas, UTD), in cash or goods, and the pre-retirement preparation period (MPPK) (Note 3q(iv), Daftar 5/65, PDF p. 82). Its gold price and gold inflation assumptions suggest some awards are paid in gold.

For example (illustration, in Rp million), an award of 10 grams of gold at 25 years of service, earned evenly. An employee has 22 years of service. Take PHE's 2024 gold price of Rp1,462,500 per gram, gold inflation of 8 percent and the 7.1 percent discount rate.

Award value in 3 years = 10 × 1.4625 × 1.08^3 = Rp18.423 million

Obligation = 18.423 × 22 / 25 / 1.071^3 = Rp13.197 million

A 10 percent rise in the gold price adds about Rp1.320 million to the obligation, charged straight to profit or loss.

Termination benefits arise from the decision to end employment, not from service (para. 159). Only the extra paid to induce early leaving is a termination benefit. It is recognised at the earlier of when the entity can no longer withdraw the offer and when it recognises related restructuring costs under PSAK 237 (para. 165). For example (illustration), 120 employees accept a voluntary early-retirement package of 30 each, and each already carries a recognised DBO of 20.

Package = 120 × 30 = 3,600; DBO settled = 120 × 20 = 2,400; termination benefit = 3,600 − 2,400 = 1,200

Dr Net defined benefit liability 2,400, Dr Termination benefits expense 1,200 / Cr Cash 3,600

9. Employee benefits across industries

State-owned groups and banks with their own pension funds. Many run employer pension funds (Dana Pensiun Pemberi Kerja, DPPK) offering final-salary DB pensions alongside statutory severance. With large plan assets, a fall in bond yields or in asset returns can swing equity through OCI. Closing a DB plan to future accrual and moving staff to DC is a plan amendment, and any fall in the DBO, for example from removing the final-salary link, is a negative past service cost in profit or loss.

Labour-intensive industries. In plantations, textiles, footwear and manufacturing the unfunded severance obligation can be large relative to equity, and the 2022 attribution change mattered most where staff are hired young. In-kind benefits such as plantation workers' rice and housing (natura) are short-term benefits at cost.

Pension funds, insurers and share-based pay. A DPPK reports its own statements under PSAK 226 (formerly PSAK 18, IAS 26), an insurer carries annuities bought to settle a plan under PSAK 117 (formerly PSAK 74, IFRS 17), and share-based pay follows PSAK 102 (IFRS 2).

Upstream oil and gas. An operator employs a contract area's staff on behalf of all partners, who carry their shares of benefit costs through joint billings, and under a cost recovery production sharing contract (PSC) those costs are generally recoverable. PHE notes that such operators provide post-employment benefits to their own permanent staff (Note 3q, PDF p. 81).

11. Upstream note: secondees from Pertamina

Part of PHE's workforce are Pertamina employees seconded to the group. Since 2020 Pertamina's policy has required each subsidiary to recognise its share of six benefits Pertamina owes those secondees (the Pertamina pension fund DPP, PAP, retiree healthcare, repatriation, MPPK and UTD) for the period they serve there (Note 25, Daftar 5/118, PDF p. 135). Before 2020 subsidiaries were charged only an allocated expense. A DB plan that shares risk between entities under common control is not a multi-employer plan, and each entity recognises the cost charged to it under the group's agreement or policy (paras. 40–41). PHE carries the secondees' share in its DBO (46,189 post-employment at the end of 2024), and its expense table shows a separate "PT Pertamina (Persero) allocation" of 5,108 (2023: 11,658), presumably the service cost Pertamina charges under Note 3q; the FS do not say.

Least-confident assertions

  • That PHE's funded-status table and DBO movement include secondees' other long-term benefits is inferred from the 3,871 and 20,946 differences matching to the unit in both years. Direct-hire and secondee long-term balances also swapped size between years (9,407 → 38,530; 20,946 → 3,871), which may mean relabelling, so the label is less certain than the arithmetic. The English text of Note 25b dates the actuarial calculation to 2023 and the Indonesian to 2024; this page follows the Indonesian.

  • PHE's notes disagree in detail. The OCI remeasurement is −610 in the statement (labelled a gain, possibly net of the 161 of deferred tax), 13,584 in Note 25's OCI table (labelled gains although the salary assumption rose), +11,397 in the DBO movement and +9,566 in the net liability movement. Interest income on plan assets is 22,333 and 20,760; the return beyond interest appears as −535, −241 (in profit or loss, against para. 127 and PHE's policy) and 1,903; contributions are 74,643 and 74,360; benefits reduce the DBO by 30,400 and plan assets by 31,410, although only PAP is funded; the asset ceiling fell by 905 but the OCI table shows 304. The 2023 other long-term movement puts 2,269 in OCI against policy. Note 4 gives the carrying amount as US$30,271 (2023: US$125,528) in Indonesian and US$125,528 for both years in English (Daftar 5/85, PDF p. 102). MPPK is other long-term in Note 3q(iv) but listed under post-employment in Note 25b.

  • The sensitivity figures sit below the reported DBO at both rates in both years, so the 9.5-year (8.4 on the reported DBO) duration is indicative only. That the 5,108 allocation is Pertamina's service-cost charge is a reading; the FS do not say.

  • That some UTD awards are paid in gold is read from the gold assumptions; the FS do not say. The industry paragraphs (DPPK closures, plantation natura, the size of the 2022 effect on labour-intensive firms) are general practice, not researched for named companies. The treatment of PSC cost recovery of benefit costs is stated generally; PHE's FS do not describe it for employee benefits.

  • The severance example ignores resignation, death and disability, which an actuary would weight in, although the statutory formula also sets those benefits, and ignores uang penggantian hak. After decision 168/PUU-XXI/2023 a new labour law was ordered; its status at the date of this page was not checked, and it may change the multiples.

content.text: PSAK 219 sorts employee benefits by when they are paid. Short-term benefits are accrued undiscounted as the work is done; post-employment, other long-term and termination benefits are estimated, discounted, and recognised on their own triggers.

A defined contribution plan costs the employer only its contribution. A defined benefit plan leaves the employer holding the actuarial and investment risk, so it carries the present value of the promised benefit, measured by the projected unit credit method, less any plan assets.

Service cost and net interest on a defined benefit plan go to profit or loss, while remeasurements (actuarial gains and losses, the return on plan assets beyond interest, and changes in the asset ceiling) go to other comprehensive income and are never recycled. Indonesian statutory severance is an unfunded defined benefit plan of this kind, and since 2022 it is attributed only to the last 24 years of service before retirement age, or from hire if later.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report employee benefits liabilities, non-current portion, of 310,011 at 31 December 2024 against 318,604 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line fell 2.7 percent and is 1.0 percent of total assets in both years and 2.0 percent of total liabilities. Two neighbouring lines belong with it, short-term employee benefits of 409,225 (2023: 290,571) in current liabilities and a remeasurement of the employee benefit liability of −610 (2023: 1,430) in other comprehensive income, OCI (Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14).

A student should come away able to classify an employee benefit, measure a defined benefit obligation, split its cost between profit or loss and other comprehensive income with journals, and apply this to Indonesian severance.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 219

3. Post-employment benefits: defined contribution and defined benefit
Who carries the risk decides the accounting. In a
(DC) plan the employer pays fixed contributions into a fund and has no obligation to pay more if the fund falls short, so the employee bears the investment risk (para. 28). In a
(DB) plan the employer promises the benefit itself, so if the fund earns less or employees live longer the employer pays the difference (para. 30).
present value of obligation − plan assets
For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays 5 percent of a monthly payroll of 2,000 into a financial institution pension fund (
, DPLK) as a DC plan, and has not yet paid December's contribution at the year end.
Dr Employee benefits expense 100 / Cr Accrued pension contributions 100
PHE's policy expenses DC contributions as incurred (Note 3q(ii), Daftar 5/64, PDF p. 81). The rest of this page is about DB plans.
4. Measuring the obligation: the projected unit credit method
(PUCM), which measures a promise earned a little each year in three steps (para. 67).
Project the benefit payable at retirement using the expected final salary.

salary, which is what "projected" means. An actuary does the same for thousands of employees with probabilities of death, disability and resignation at each age (PHE cites Indonesian Mortality Table IV).
5. Plan assets, the net liability and the three components of cost

are assets held by a separate fund, or qualifying insurance policies, available only to pay employee benefits and not to the employer's creditors (para. 8). They are measured at fair value and netted against the DBO.
Net defined benefit liability = DBO − fair value of plan assets (adjusted for the asset ceiling)
The cost for the period has three components, and the standard sends each to a different place (para. 120).
current service cost, past service cost, settlement gains and losses

Net interest applies the same discount rate to the DBO and the plan assets (para. 123), so a company cannot report a high expected return on risky assets as profit; whatever the fund earns above or below that rate is a remeasurement.

When a plan is in surplus, the employer may recognise the surplus only up to the present value of the economic benefits available to it as refunds or reductions in future contributions (para. 64). For example (illustration), a plan with a surplus of 10,000 from which the employer can recover only 8,348 through lower future contributions shows an asset of 8,348, with a ceiling effect of 10,000 − 8,348 = 1,652, PHE's 2024 ceiling effect. The ceiling is applied plan by plan, so a group can show a ceiling effect inside an overall net liability.
6. Past service cost, curtailments and settlements
Plan changes hit profit or loss at once.

(a significant reduction in the number of employees covered). It is recognised as an expense at the earlier of when the amendment or curtailment occurs and when related restructuring costs or termination benefits are recognised (para. 103). For example (illustration), a subsidiary raises a lump-sum benefit by 10 percent for a group whose DBO is 50,000.

7. Indonesian severance as a defined benefit plan

Indonesian labour law promises every permanent employee a lump sum at retirement set by a formula, so the employer carries a DB plan under PSAK 219, unfunded unless it sets assets aside. The formula sits in UU 13/2003 as amended by the Job Creation law (UU 11/2020, replaced by Perpu 2/2022 and enacted as UU 6/2023), and in its implementing regulation PP 35/2021. On retirement an employee receives (PP 35/2021, art. 56):
) of 1.75 times the art. 40(2) scale, which rises from 1 month's wages for under one year of service to a maximum of 9 months from 8 years;
, UPMK) of 1 times the art. 40(3) scale, from 2 months at 3 years to a maximum of 10 months from 24 years;
Maximum on retirement = 1.75 × 9 + 10 = 25.75 months' wages, reached at 24 years of service

Employers pay the higher of the statutory amount and their own plan or collective labour agreement, as PHE's policy says (Note 3q, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). Since Constitutional Court decision 168/PUU-XXI/2023 (31 October 2024) the statutory scale is a minimum (
), and the court ordered a new labour law, so these multiples may change.

For years many Indonesian actuaries attributed this benefit straight-line from the date of hire. In an agenda decision published in May 2021 the IFRS Interpretations Committee considered a plan that pays only to those employed at retirement age, capped at a number of years of consecutive service immediately before retirement, and concluded that the benefit is attributed only to the capped years before retirement age, since service before then does not reduce the service still needed. In April 2022 the DSAK IAI, the Indonesian standard setter, found that the statutory scheme has the same fact pattern. With retirement at 56 and the UPMK capped at 24 years, the obligation first arises at age 32, and the benefit is attributed to service between 32 and 56. Entities that had attributed from hire were told to assess the effect under the PSAK 25 (now PSAK 208) requirements for a change in accounting policy.

For example (illustration), an employee joined at 25, is now 40 with 15 years of service, and retires at 56 with 31. Current monthly wage is 1.5 (USD 1,500), with PHE's 7 percent salary increase and 7.1 percent discount rate, and no resignations or deaths.
Present value of the full benefit = 114.027 / 1.071^16 = 38.052

The later start cuts this employee's DBO by 5.728, or 31.1 percent, and raises the annual unit by 29.2 percent (31/24), so the cost moves later in the career. PP 35/2021 art. 58 lets employer contributions to a pension programme count towards statutory severance, with the employer paying any shortfall, so a fund held for that purpose is a plan asset of the severance DB plan and does not turn it into a DC plan. PHE funds its service award (PAP,

presentation.deck: The theory of employee benefit accounting under PSAK 219 from payroll accruals to the projected unit credit method, worked through PHE's pension and severance obligations and set beside the industries where these liabilities weigh most
key_takeaways: PSAK 219 sorts employee benefits by when they are paid. Short-term benefits are accrued undiscounted as the work is done; post-employment, other long-term and termination benefits are estimated, discounted, and recognised on their own triggers.

A defined contribution plan costs the employer only its contribution. A defined benefit plan leaves the employer holding the actuarial and investment risk, so it carries the present value of the promised benefit, measured by the projected unit credit method, less any plan assets.

Service cost and net interest on a defined benefit plan go to profit or loss, while remeasurements (actuarial gains and losses, the return on plan assets beyond interest, and changes in the asset ceiling) go to other comprehensive income and are never recycled. Indonesian statutory severance is an unfunded defined benefit plan of this kind, and since 2022 it is attributed only to the last 24 years of service before retirement age, or from hire if later.

title: Finance Cost and Finance Income: Interest in Profit or Loss and Cash Flows
snippet: The theory of interest as income and expense, from accrual to coverage, worked through PHE's finance lines and set beside the industries where interest is the business itself
content:
In brief

  • Interest is the price of time on money, and the same contract produces interest expense for the borrower and interest income for the lender. Both are measured with the effective interest rate on amortised cost. A lender computes interest income on the gross carrying amount until an asset becomes credit-impaired, and from then on on the amount net of the loss allowance.

  • Finance cost is an aggregate. It collects interest on borrowings, interest on lease liabilities, the unwinding of discounted provisions and sometimes net interest on employee benefits, less whatever borrowing cost is capitalised into assets. Each piece comes from a different standard.

  • Where interest lands in profit or loss and in the cash flow statement has been a policy choice under PSAK 201 and PSAK 207. From 1 January 2027 PSAK 118 and its amendments to PSAK 207 remove most of that choice for a non-financial entity: interest on cash and investments goes to the investing category, interest on liabilities to financing, and interest paid and received follow into financing and investing cash flows.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report finance cost of 453,906 for 2024 against 459,285 for 2023, and finance income of 251,561 against 140,407, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). Finance cost is 3.2 percent of revenue in both years. Finance income is 1.8 percent of revenue in 2024, up from 1.0 percent.

After reading this page a student should be able to accrue interest on either side of a contract, compute interest income on a credit-impaired asset, take a finance cost line apart into its sources, place interest in profit or loss and in cash flows under today's rules and PSAK 118, and compute interest coverage knowing what each version leaves out.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What finance cost and finance income are

Interest compensates a lender for parting with money for a period and for the risk of not getting it back. One contract, two mirror entries. The lecture notes (in full dollars) make the point with a refinery bought for a zero-interest note: the buyer amortises the 805,103 gap between the note's face value and the refinery's fair value as interest expense, and "bagi pihak penyerah kilang minyak, $805.103 akan diakui sebagai pendapatan bunga" (Inter 2 Ch 14).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary sells surplus equipment with a fair value of 2,000 for a note of 2,805.10 due in five years, with no stated interest, when the market rate is 7 percent.

2,000 × 1.07^5 = 2,805.10, so the note carries 805.10 of interest

Year 1 interest = 2,000 × 7% = 140.00; year 2 = 2,140 × 7% = 149.80

Seller (lender)

Buyer (borrower)

Dr Notes receivable 140.00 / Cr Finance income 140.00

Dr Finance cost 140.00 / Cr Notes payable 140.00

Finance income in a non-financial entity is mostly interest on bank balances, deposits, loans granted and debt investments, plus dividends where the entity reports them there. Finance cost is broader than "interest on loans". It collects every expense that comes from the passage of time on a liability.

Piece of finance cost

Source standard

2. How interest accrues: stated rate, effective rate, day count

Interest accrues with time, whether or not cash moves. The stated (coupon) rate fixes the cash; the effective interest rate (EIR) is the rate that discounts all contractual cash flows to the initial carrying amount, and it fixes the expense or income. When a bond is priced away from par, or fees are paid, the two differ, and the gap is amortised through interest.

The lecture notes' interest-bearing note shows both sides of this. A five-year note of 1,000,000 at 8 percent annual interest, issued when the market rate is 10 percent:

PV of principal = 1,000,000 × 0.62092 = 620,920

PV of interest = 80,000 × 3.79079 = 303,263

Price = 924,183; discount = 75,817

Year 1 interest at EIR = 924,183 × 10% = 92,418.30; cash 80,000; discount amortised 12,418.30

The notes label 75,817 a "premium" and describe the factors as 8 percent and "5%, ½ annualy". The price is below face, so it is a discount, and 0.62092 and 3.79079 are the five-year annual factors at 10 percent. Their journal is right: interest expense 92,418.30 exceeds the cash because the discount is being added back to the liability.

Day count. Between coupon dates, accrued interest is principal × rate × elapsed time, and the contract decides how time is counted. For example (illustration), a deposit of 10,000 at 5 percent placed on 31 October has accrued 61 days by 31 December.

Actual/365: 10,000 × 5% × 61/365 = 83.56

Actual/360: 10,000 × 5% × 61/360 = 84.72

If the contract counts actual/360:

Dr Interest receivable 84.72 / Cr Finance income 84.72

The borrower's side of the effective interest method, with fees and floating rates, is taught on the Long-term bank loans page.

3. Finance income on financial assets

Interest income is recognised only on financial assets that the accounting model treats as earning interest. PSAK 109 sorts debt assets by the business model (hold to collect, hold to collect and sell, or other) and by whether the contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI). Assets held to collect with SPPI cash flows are at amortised cost; held to collect and sell, at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI); everything else at fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL). PHE's policy follows this test (Note 3g, Daftar 5/38–5/40, PDF pp. 55–57).
