The last row follows PSAK 201.82(a) (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1), read with the IFRS Interpretations Committee's March 2018 decision.

Premium and discount. The lecture notes' investor buys a ten-year Garuda bond of 10,000,000 with a 10 percent coupon paid semi-annually when the market rate is 9 percent.

PV of principal = 10,000,000 × 0.41464 = 4,146,400

PV of interest = 500,000 × 13.00794 = 6,503,970

Price = 10,650,370; premium = 650,370

First half-year interest income = 10,650,370 × 4.5% = 479,266.65; premium amortised = 500,000 − 479,266.65 = 20,733.35

Dr Cash 500,000 / Cr Interest income 479,266.65 / Cr Debt investment 20,733.35

The notes multiply 10,000,000 × 0.41464 as 4,146,600 and print interest income of 479,725.65, which transposes two digits of their own 479,275.65. The method is unaffected.

Credit-impaired assets. Under PSAK 109's expected credit loss (ECL) model, a loss allowance is recognised from day one: twelve-month ECL in stage 1, lifetime ECL in stage 2 after a significant increase in credit risk, and lifetime ECL in stage 3 when the asset is credit-impaired (default, severe financial difficulty, a breach such as missed payments). The allowance changes the interest base only in stage 3. Interest income is the EIR times the gross carrying amount, amortised cost before the allowance, unless the asset is credit-impaired, when it is the EIR times amortised cost, net of the allowance (para. 5.4.1).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary holds a 10,000 loan to a joint-venture partner at 8 percent, issued at par, so the EIR is 8 percent. Consider the following year under three states at the start of it.

In stage 3 the contract still runs at 800 a year. One common way to book it keeps the gross balance contractual and lets the allowance absorb the difference:

Dr Loan, gross 800 / Cr Finance income 480 / Cr Loss allowance 320

If the borrower later pays in full, the unused allowance is reversed as an impairment gain, not as interest income, which is the IFRS Interpretations Committee's 2019 view on a cured asset. The interest in the gross balance never reached profit as interest.

The lecture notes' "Alibaba" write-down of 12,680, recognised once the loss has occurred, is the old incurred-loss model.

Purchased credit-impaired assets. A debt bought already in default earns interest at a credit-adjusted EIR, the rate that discounts the cash flows the buyer expects (after losses) to the price. For example (illustration), a defaulted note bought for 5,500 that is expected to pay 6,050 in a year earns 5,500 × 10% = 550.

Other sources. Dividends are recognised when the right to receive them is established. A seller granting long deferred payment terms recognises revenue at the cash price and the financing part as interest income (PSAK 115; see the Revenues essay).

4. What goes into finance cost: the pieces owned by other pages

Every piece below is the same mechanism, a rate applied to an opening carrying amount, applied to a different liability.

Borrowings. A 100,000 three-year loan at 6 percent with a 1,500 fee is carried at 98,500 and charged at its 6.5671 percent EIR, so year-1 finance cost is 6,468.56 against 6,000 of coupon. The fee is spread over the loan's life (see the Long-term bank loans essay).

Dr Finance cost 6,468.56 / Cr Cash 6,000.00 / Cr Bank loans 468.56

Leases. A lease liability of 17,561.69 at 6 percent accrues interest of 1,053.70 in year 1. Interest is largest in the early years, so a single lease's total charge is front-loaded (see the Right-of-use assets essay).

Unwinding of provisions. A decommissioning provision of 68,897 discounted at 5 percent rises by 3,445 in the next year purely because settlement is a year nearer. ISAK 101 sends this to profit or loss as a finance cost and forbids capitalising it (see the Decommissioning provision essay). Unwinding involves no lender and no cash, yet the mathematics is that of interest.

Dr Finance cost 3,445 / Cr Provision for decommissioning 3,445

Net interest on employee benefits. A net defined benefit liability of 306,640 at a 7.1 percent discount rate gives net interest of 21,771.4. PSAK 219 does not specify where net interest is presented, so some entities show it in finance cost and others, PHE among them, in operating expenses (see the Employee benefits essay).

Capitalised borrowing costs. Interest on funds used to build a qualifying asset is part of the asset's cost under PSAK 223. In the fixed-asset illustration, 239.5 of interest goes to construction in progress instead of finance cost (see the Fixed assets essay). Income earned by temporarily investing a specific borrowing reduces the amount capitalised (PSAK 223.12), so it never reaches finance income. Finance cost is therefore interest incurred less interest capitalised. The capitalised part reaches profit later through depreciation, above operating profit.

Smaller items. Commitment fees on undrawn facilities, the ineffective part of an interest rate hedge, interest on a contract liability with a significant financing component, and exchange differences on foreign-currency borrowings to the extent they are an adjustment to interest cost (PSAK 223.6(e)) can all appear here.

5. Presentation in profit or loss: PSAK 201 now, PSAK 118 from 2027

PSAK 201 requires finance costs as a line item (para. 82(b)) and interest revenue by the EIR as another (para. 82(a)), and it forbids offsetting income and expenses unless a standard requires or permits it (para. 32). So finance income and finance cost appear gross, as PHE shows them. "Net finance cost" is an analyst's subtraction.

What PSAK 201 does not settle is where interest income sits, since it defines no operating profit. The lecture notes put interest a trading company earns "akibat dia nabung di bank" in other income inside income from operations, with "financing cost" after it (Inter 1 Ch 4).

PSAK 118 (IFRS 18), effective 1 January 2027, settles it through categories and two new subtotals, operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes (see the Production expenses essay). For an entity whose main business is neither investing nor lending to customers, interest falls as follows:

  • Investing: income from cash and cash equivalents, from associates and joint ventures accounted for by the equity method, and from investments that generate returns largely independently.

  • Financing: all income and expense on liabilities that arise only from raising finance (bank loans, bonds), plus interest expense and the effect of changes in interest rates on other liabilities: leases, provisions, defined benefit liabilities, contract liabilities.

  • Operating: everything else, by default.

For example (illustration), an entity has revenue of 10,000, operating expenses of 7,000 (including 50 of net interest on its pension liability), interest income on deposits of 200, a share of profit of an associate of 150, interest on loans of 400 and unwinding of provisions of 100.

6. Interest in the statement of cash flows

Today PSAK 207 Laporan Arus Kas (formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7) gives a non-financial entity a choice, as long as it is applied consistently (para. 31). Interest paid may be operating, because it enters profit, or financing, because it is a cost of obtaining finance. Interest received may be operating or investing (para. 33). Cash flows from interest paid and received must each be disclosed separately (para. 31), and interest paid is reported in total, whether expensed or capitalised (para. 32).

For example (illustration), an entity collects 3,000 of operating cash before any interest, pays 450 of interest and receives 190 of interest and 60 of dividends from an associate.

The same company reports operating cash flow of 2,800 or 3,000 depending on a policy choice. The amendments to PSAK 207 that come with PSAK 118 end the choice from 1 January 2027 for an entity without a specified main business of investing or lending: interest and dividends paid are financing, interest and dividends received are investing, which is option B. They also make operating profit the starting point of the indirect method.

7. Interest coverage

Coverage ratios ask how many times earnings could pay the interest bill, which is what lenders and rating agencies watch, and what loan covenants often fix. The basic form is times interest earned:

Interest coverage = earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) / interest expense

Using the figures of section 5 (illustration), with EBIT taken as profit before financing and income taxes, 3,400:

EBIT / all financing expense = 3,400 / 550 = 6.18 times

EBIT / interest on loans only = 3,400 / 400 = 8.50 times

EBIT / (550 + 30 of interest capitalised) = 3,400 / 580 = 5.86 times

(EBIT + 1,200 of depreciation and amortisation) / 550 = 4,600 / 550 = 8.36 times

Leaving unwinding and pension interest out measures the burden of debt that has to be serviced in cash. Adding capitalised interest back measures what the lenders are actually owed, since capitalisation moves interest to the balance sheet without making it cheaper. The EBITDA version, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, is closer to cash and is the usual covenant form. Net coverage, which deducts interest income first, flatters a company holding large cash balances, because the cash could be spent.

8. Finance cost across industries

Banks. For a bank, interest is revenue. Interest income on loans and interest expense on deposits are the top of the income statement, and the key measure is net interest income over average earning assets, the net interest margin (NIM). For example (illustration), interest income 9,000, interest expense 4,000, average earning assets 100,000.

Net interest income = 9,000 − 4,000 = 5,000; NIM = 5,000 / 100,000 = 5.0%

Banks usually classify interest paid and received as operating cash flows (PSAK 207.33). PSAK 118 keeps that through its exception for entities that lend to customers as a main business, which present such interest in the operating category.

Islamic finance. A sharia entity earns no interest. Under murabahah (PSAK 402, formerly PSAK 102) the bank buys an asset and sells it at cost plus an agreed margin payable in instalments, and the margin is recognised over the financing period. Under mudharabah (PSAK 405, formerly PSAK 105) funds are shared in profit by an agreed ratio (nisbah). For example (illustration), income of 500 earned on depositors' mudharabah funds with a 40 percent depositor nisbah gives them 200 of bagi hasil. The holders' share is presented as a distribution to temporary syirkah funds, not as finance cost. A non-sharia company that borrows through a sharia instrument, such as the sukuk ijarah on the Long-term bank loans page, shows the ijarah fee as an expense in its finance line.

Real estate developers. Interest on loans for projects under construction is capitalised into inventory property and reaches profit through cost of sales when units are sold. PSAK 223 lets an entity skip capitalisation for inventories produced in large quantities on a repetitive basis, but developers commonly capitalise. Reported finance cost then understates the debt burden. For example (illustration), a developer incurs 400 of interest, capitalises 300 and expenses 100, sells 60 percent of the units so 180 of capitalised interest passes through cost of sales, and reports EBIT of 2,000.

Reported coverage = 2,000 / 100 = 20.0 times

Adjusted = (2,000 + 180) / 400 = 5.45 times

10. Upstream note

Accretion is large because decommissioning provisions are large. An upstream group carries the discounted cost of plugging wells and removing platforms for decades, so its finance cost includes a slice that no lender earns. PHE's interest-rate swaps on the Jambaran-Tiung Biru loans also touch the line: the ineffective part of the hedge, 1,395 in 2024, is "included in finance costs" (Note 14, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123), presumably within other interest expenses. Whether interest is recoverable under PHE's PSCs is not disclosed in the FS.

  • That PHE's cash flow statement lacks the separate interest disclosure PSAK 207.31 requires is read from the face of the statement and Note 50; the amounts may be disclosed somewhere not found. content.text: Interest is the price of time on money, and the same contract produces interest expense for the borrower and interest income for the lender. Both are measured with the effective interest rate on amortised cost. A lender computes interest income on the gross carrying amount until an asset becomes credit-impaired, and from then on on the amount net of the loss allowance.

Finance cost is an aggregate. It collects interest on borrowings, interest on lease liabilities, the unwinding of discounted provisions and sometimes net interest on employee benefits, less whatever borrowing cost is capitalised into assets. Each piece comes from a different standard.

Where interest lands in profit or loss and in the cash flow statement has been a policy choice under PSAK 201 and PSAK 207. From 1 January 2027 PSAK 118 and its amendments to PSAK 207 remove most of that choice for a non-financial entity: interest on cash and investments goes to the investing category, interest on liabilities to financing, and interest paid and received follow into financing and investing cash flows.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report finance cost of 453,906 for 2024 against 459,285 for 2023, and finance income of 251,561 against 140,407, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). Finance cost is 3.2 percent of revenue in both years. Finance income is 1.8 percent of revenue in 2024, up from 1.0 percent.

After reading this page a student should be able to accrue interest on either side of a contract, compute interest income on a credit-impaired asset, take a finance cost line apart into its sources, place interest in profit or loss and in cash flows under today's rules and PSAK 118, and compute interest coverage knowing what each version leaves out.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. What finance cost and finance income are

Interest compensates a lender for parting with money for a period and for the risk of not getting it back. One contract, two mirror entries. The lecture notes (in full dollars) make the point with a refinery bought for a zero-interest note: the buyer amortises the 805,103 gap between the note's face value and the refinery's fair value as interest expense, and "bagi pihak penyerah kilang minyak, $805.103 akan diakui sebagai pendapatan bunga" (Inter 2 Ch 14).
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary sells surplus equipment with a fair value of 2,000 for a note of 2,805.10 due in five years, with no stated interest, when the market rate is 7 percent.
2,000 × 1.07^5 = 2,805.10, so the note carries 805.10 of interest
Dr Notes receivable 140.00 / Cr Finance income 140.00
Dr Finance cost 140.00 / Cr Notes payable 140.00
in a non-financial entity is mostly interest on bank balances, deposits, loans granted and debt investments, plus dividends where the entity reports them there.
is broader than "interest on loans". It collects every expense that comes from the passage of time on a liability.
Interest on borrowings, including amortised fees (sukuk ijarah: PSAK 410, formerly PSAK 110)
Net interest on a defined benefit liability, if presented here
Interest on contract liabilities with a significant financing component
2. How interest accrues: stated rate, effective rate, day count
Interest accrues with time, whether or not cash moves. The

(EIR) is the rate that discounts all contractual cash flows to the initial carrying amount, and it fixes the expense or income. When a bond is priced away from par, or fees are paid, the two differ, and the gap is amortised through interest.
The lecture notes' interest-bearing note shows both sides of this. A five-year note of 1,000,000 at 8 percent annual interest, issued when the market rate is 10 percent:
Year 1 interest at EIR = 924,183 × 10% = 92,418.30; cash 80,000; discount amortised 12,418.30

The notes label 75,817 a "premium" and describe the factors as 8 percent and "5%, ½ annualy". The price is below face, so it is a discount, and 0.62092 and 3.79079 are the five-year annual factors at 10 percent. Their journal is right: interest expense 92,418.30 exceeds the cash because the discount is being added back to the liability.

Between coupon dates, accrued interest is principal × rate × elapsed time, and the contract decides how time is counted. For example (illustration), a deposit of 10,000 at 5 percent placed on 31 October has accrued 61 days by 31 December.
Dr Interest receivable 84.72 / Cr Finance income 84.72
The borrower's side of the effective interest method, with fees and floating rates, is taught on the Long-term bank loans page.
Interest income is recognised only on financial assets that the accounting model treats as earning interest. PSAK 109 sorts debt assets by the
(hold to collect, hold to collect and sell, or other) and by whether the contractual cash flows are
solely payments of principal and interest

(SPPI). Assets held to collect with SPPI cash flows are at amortised cost; held to collect and sell, at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI); everything else at fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL). PHE's policy follows this test (Note 3g, Daftar 5/38–5/40, PDF pp. 55–57).
Part of the fair value change, or shown separately by policy
The last row follows PSAK 201.82(a) (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1), read with the IFRS Interpretations Committee's March 2018 decision.
The lecture notes' investor buys a ten-year Garuda bond of 10,000,000 with a 10 percent coupon paid semi-annually when the market rate is 9 percent.
First half-year interest income = 10,650,370 × 4.5% = 479,266.65; premium amortised = 500,000 − 479,266.65 = 20,733.35
Dr Cash 500,000 / Cr Interest income 479,266.65 / Cr Debt investment 20,733.35
The notes multiply 10,000,000 × 0.41464 as 4,146,600 and print interest income of 479,725.65, which transposes two digits of their own 479,275.65. The method is unaffected.

Under PSAK 109's expected credit loss (ECL) model, a loss allowance is recognised from day one: twelve-month ECL in stage 1, lifetime ECL in stage 2 after a significant increase in credit risk, and lifetime ECL in stage 3 when the asset is credit-impaired (default, severe financial difficulty, a breach such as missed payments). The allowance changes the interest base only in stage 3. Interest income is the EIR times the
, amortised cost before the allowance, unless the asset is credit-impaired, when it is the EIR times

For example (illustration), a subsidiary holds a 10,000 loan to a joint-venture partner at 8 percent, issued at par, so the EIR is 8 percent. Consider the following year under three states at the start of it.
In stage 3 the contract still runs at 800 a year. One common way to book it keeps the gross balance contractual and lets the allowance absorb the difference:
Dr Loan, gross 800 / Cr Finance income 480 / Cr Loss allowance 320

If the borrower later pays in full, the unused allowance is reversed as an impairment gain, not as interest income, which is the IFRS Interpretations Committee's 2019 view on a cured asset. The interest in the gross balance never reached profit as interest.
The lecture notes' "Alibaba" write-down of 12,680, recognised once the loss has occurred, is the old incurred-loss model.
A debt bought already in default earns interest at a

EIR, the rate that discounts the cash flows the buyer expects (after losses) to the price. For example (illustration), a defaulted note bought for 5,500 that is expected to pay 6,050 in a year earns 5,500 × 10% = 550.

Dividends are recognised when the right to receive them is established. A seller granting long deferred payment terms recognises revenue at the cash price and the financing part as interest income (PSAK 115; see the Revenues essay).
4. What goes into finance cost: the pieces owned by other pages
Every piece below is the same mechanism, a rate applied to an opening carrying amount, applied to a different liability.

A 100,000 three-year loan at 6 percent with a 1,500 fee is carried at 98,500 and charged at its 6.5671 percent EIR, so year-1 finance cost is 6,468.56 against 6,000 of coupon. The fee is spread over the loan's life (see the Long-term bank loans essay).
Dr Finance cost 6,468.56 / Cr Cash 6,000.00 / Cr Bank loans 468.56

A lease liability of 17,561.69 at 6 percent accrues interest of 1,053.70 in year 1. Interest is largest in the early years, so a single lease's total charge is front-loaded (see the Right-of-use assets essay).

A decommissioning provision of 68,897 discounted at 5 percent rises by 3,445 in the next year purely because settlement is a year nearer. ISAK 101 sends this to profit or loss as a finance cost and forbids capitalising it (see the Decommissioning provision essay). Unwinding involves no lender and no cash, yet the mathematics is that of interest.
Dr Finance cost 3,445 / Cr Provision for decommissioning 3,445

A net defined benefit liability of 306,640 at a 7.1 percent discount rate gives net interest of 21,771.4. PSAK 219 does not specify where net interest is presented, so some entities show it in finance cost and others, PHE among them, in operating expenses (see the Employee benefits essay).

Interest on funds used to build a qualifying asset is part of the asset's cost under PSAK 223. In the fixed-asset illustration, 239.5 of interest goes to construction in progress instead of finance cost (see the Fixed assets essay). Income earned by temporarily investing a specific borrowing reduces the amount capitalised (PSAK 223.12), so it never reaches finance income. Finance cost is therefore interest
. The capitalised part reaches profit later through depreciation, above operating profit.

Commitment fees on undrawn facilities, the ineffective part of an interest rate hedge, interest on a contract liability with a significant financing component, and exchange differences on foreign-currency borrowings to the extent they are an adjustment to interest cost (PSAK 223.6(e)) can all appear here.
5. Presentation in profit or loss: PSAK 201 now, PSAK 118 from 2027

PSAK 201 requires finance costs as a line item (para. 82(b)) and interest revenue by the EIR as another (para. 82(a)), and it forbids offsetting income and expenses unless a standard requires or permits it (para. 32). So finance income and finance cost appear gross, as PHE shows them. "Net finance cost" is an analyst's subtraction.
What PSAK 201 does not settle is

interest income sits, since it defines no operating profit. The lecture notes put interest a trading company earns "akibat dia nabung di bank" in other income inside income from operations, with "financing cost" after it (Inter 1 Ch 4).

PSAK 118 (IFRS 18), effective 1 January 2027, settles it through categories and two new subtotals, operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes (see the Production expenses essay). For an entity whose main business is neither investing nor lending to customers, interest falls as follows:
: income from cash and cash equivalents, from associates and joint ventures accounted for by the equity method, and from investments that generate returns largely independently.

: all income and expense on liabilities that arise only from raising finance (bank loans, bonds), plus interest expense and the effect of changes in interest rates on other liabilities: leases, provisions, defined benefit liabilities, contract liabilities.

For example (illustration), an entity has revenue of 10,000, operating expenses of 7,000 (including 50 of net interest on its pension liability), interest income on deposits of 200, a share of profit of an associate of 150, interest on loans of 400 and unwinding of provisions of 100.
Profit before financing and income taxes

Profit before tax is the same. Operating profit falls from 3,350 to 3,050 because returns on cash and on the associate leave it, and the pension interest moves out of operating expenses into financing.
6. Interest in the statement of cash flows

(formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7) gives a non-financial entity a choice, as long as it is applied consistently (para. 31). Interest paid may be operating, because it enters profit, or financing, because it is a cost of obtaining finance. Interest received may be operating or investing (para. 33). Cash flows from interest paid and received must each be disclosed separately (para. 31), and interest paid is reported in total, whether expensed or capitalised (para. 32).
For example (illustration), an entity collects 3,000 of operating cash before any interest, pays 450 of interest and receives 190 of interest and 60 of dividends from an associate.
Option B: paid in financing, received in investing

The same company reports operating cash flow of 2,800 or 3,000 depending on a policy choice. The amendments to PSAK 207 that come with PSAK 118 end the choice from 1 January 2027 for an entity without a specified main business of investing or lending: interest and dividends paid are financing, interest and dividends received are investing, which is option B. They also make operating profit the starting point of the indirect method.
Coverage ratios ask how many times earnings could pay the interest bill, which is what lenders and rating agencies watch, and what loan covenants often fix. The basic form is
Interest coverage = earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) / interest expense
Using the figures of section 5 (illustration), with EBIT taken as profit before financing and income taxes, 3,400:
EBIT / interest on loans only = 3,400 / 400 = 8.50 times

Leaving unwinding and pension interest out measures the burden of debt that has to be serviced in cash. Adding capitalised interest back measures what the lenders are actually owed, since capitalisation moves interest to the balance sheet without making it cheaper. The EBITDA version, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, is closer to cash and is the usual covenant form.
coverage, which deducts interest income first, flatters a company holding large cash balances, because the cash could be spent.
For a bank, interest is revenue. Interest income on loans and interest expense on deposits are the top of the income statement, and the key measure is
over average earning assets, the net interest margin (NIM). For example (illustration), interest income 9,000, interest expense 4,000, average earning assets 100,000.

Banks usually classify interest paid and received as operating cash flows (PSAK 207.33). PSAK 118 keeps that through its exception for entities that lend to customers as a main business, which present such interest in the operating category.
A sharia entity earns no interest. Under
(PSAK 402, formerly PSAK 102) the bank buys an asset and sells it at cost plus an agreed margin payable in instalments, and the margin is recognised over the financing period. Under
(PSAK 405, formerly PSAK 105) funds are shared in profit by an agreed ratio (
). For example (illustration), income of 500 earned on depositors' mudharabah funds with a 40 percent depositor nisbah gives them 200 of
. The holders' share is presented as a distribution to

, not as finance cost. A non-sharia company that borrows through a sharia instrument, such as the sukuk ijarah on the Long-term bank loans page, shows the ijarah fee as an expense in its finance line.

Interest on loans for projects under construction is capitalised into inventory property and reaches profit through cost of sales when units are sold. PSAK 223 lets an entity skip capitalisation for inventories produced in large quantities on a repetitive basis, but developers commonly capitalise. Reported finance cost then understates the debt burden. For example (illustration), a developer incurs 400 of interest, capitalises 300 and expenses 100, sells 60 percent of the units so 180 of capitalised interest passes through cost of sales, and reports EBIT of 2,000.
9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 40 and 41
PSAK 107 (formerly PSAK 60, IFRS 7) asks for total interest income and expense on financial instruments not at FVTPL. PHE gives both notes on one page (Note 40 and Note 41, Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167).
Interest income from cash in banks and time deposits

Both totals agree with the face of the statement. Finance cost is almost flat while its mix shifted. Loan interest fell by 14,356 as borrowings were repaid (see the Long-term bank loans essay), and accretion rose by 6,704. More than a quarter of the line is unwinding, a non-cash charge.

Several other pieces sit outside the line. Borrowing costs of 2,277 were capitalised into the Jambaran-Tiung Biru project (Note 12, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126; 11,321 in 2023), so interest incurred was at least 456,183. Net interest on employee benefits, interest cost of 46,048 less interest income on plan assets of 20,760, is 25,288, charged in cost of revenues and general and administrative expenses (Note 25b, Daftar 5/123, PDF p. 140). A share in the net profit of associates and joint ventures of 162,620 is inside other income, net (Note 42, PDF p. 167).
Implied yield = 251,561 / average cash and cash equivalents 3,816,529 = 6.6%; on cash plus restricted cash, 251,561 / 5,755,990 = 4.4% (2023: 2.96% on cash)

US dollar time deposits paid 0.75–6.92 percent in 2024 against 0.22–1.10 percent in 2023 (Note 6, Daftar 5/93, PDF p. 110), which fits the jump in interest income while cash fell from 5,018,739 to 2,614,318. How much of the restricted cash earns interest for PHE is not stated, so the true yield lies between the two figures.
(EBIT + DD&A 2,443,000 + impairment 215,666, added back as covenants usually do) / 453,906 = 8,005,148 / 453,906 = 17.64 times

The covenant on PHE's corporate facilities requires EBITDA of at least 3.00 times interest (Note 27, Daftar 5/136 and 5/140, PDF pp. 153 and 157). Its exact definitions are not disclosed, but on every version above the headroom is wide.

Recast under PSAK 118, the 251,561 of interest income and the 162,620 share of associates leave operating profit for investing, and all of Note 41 sits in financing; the Production expenses essay works the numbers.

The cash flow statement, prepared on the direct method, has no line for interest paid or received (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17). PSAK 207.31 asks for both. Interest paid may sit in "cash paid from other financing activities" (328,119), and interest received in operating receipts, but PHE does not say.

Accretion is large because decommissioning provisions are large. An upstream group carries the discounted cost of plugging wells and removing platforms for decades, so its finance cost includes a slice that no lender earns. PHE's interest-rate swaps on the Jambaran-Tiung Biru loans also touch the line: the ineffective part of the hedge, 1,395 in 2024, is "included in finance costs" (Note 14, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123), presumably within other interest expenses. Whether interest is recoverable under PHE's PSCs is not disclosed in the FS.
: lease interest, including state-owned-asset finance leases.

: holds the share of associates' profit, an investing item under PSAK 118.

That PHE's cash flow statement lacks the separate interest disclosure PSAK 207.31 requires is read from the face of the statement and Note 50; the amounts may be disclosed somewhere not found. Where interest paid sits is a guess. Similarly, showing the share of associates' profit inside other income, net looks short of PSAK 201.82(c), which asks for it on the face.

Note 41 lease interest of 17,225 exceeds the 7,354 in the Note 30 movement (Daftar 5/146, PDF p. 163) by 9,871. PHE gives no split (see the Right-of-use assets essay). Segment eliminations of intra-group interest differ between finance income (27,836) and finance cost (28,975) by 1,139, unexplained. The 4.4–6.6 percent implied yield assumes interest income relates to average cash balances, with or without restricted cash. Restricted cash is mostly site-restoration funds plus guarantee collateral and required deposits (Note 7, Daftar 5/95, PDF p. 112), and restoration funds moved by SKK Migas carry their interest with them (Note 14b, PDF p. 123), so not all of it earns interest for PHE. PHE does not say which balances earn the 251,561.

presentation.deck: The theory of interest as income and expense, from accrual to coverage, worked through PHE's finance lines and set beside the industries where interest is the business itself
key_takeaways: Interest is the price of time on money, and the same contract produces interest expense for the borrower and interest income for the lender. Both are measured with the effective interest rate on amortised cost. A lender computes interest income on the gross carrying amount until an asset becomes credit-impaired, and from then on on the amount net of the loss allowance.

Finance cost is an aggregate. It collects interest on borrowings, interest on lease liabilities, the unwinding of discounted provisions and sometimes net interest on employee benefits, less whatever borrowing cost is capitalised into assets. Each piece comes from a different standard.

Where interest lands in profit or loss and in the cash flow statement has been a policy choice under PSAK 201 and PSAK 207. From 1 January 2027 PSAK 118 and its amendments to PSAK 207 remove most of that choice for a non-financial entity: interest on cash and investments goes to the investing category, interest on liabilities to financing, and interest paid and received follow into financing and investing cash flows.

title: Fixed Assets, Net: Cost, Depreciation, Impairment and Disposal
snippet: The theory of property, plant and equipment from acquisition to derecognition, worked through PHE's fixed assets and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • Cost is everything needed to bring an asset to the place and condition in which it can work as intended, including borrowing costs on a qualifying asset, and nothing it could work without. Deferred payment, exchanges and basket purchases are all brought back to a cash-price or fair-value equivalent.

  • Depreciation allocates that cost over the asset's useful life in the pattern its benefits are used up. Whether that cost will come back is a separate question for the impairment test under PSAK 236, which, when the carrying amount is higher, writes the asset down to the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use.

  • After recognition an entity chooses, by class, between the cost model and the revaluation model. Revaluation gains go to other comprehensive income, while gains and losses on disposal go to profit or loss and never count as revenue.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report fixed assets, net, of 544,278 at 31 December 2024 against 522,121 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11). That is 1.8 percent of total assets (1.7 percent a year earlier). The wells and production installations sit on a different line, oil and gas properties, net, which holds 17,905,149, or 58.8 percent of total assets.

A student should be able to measure, depreciate, impair, revalue and derecognise an asset, with journals.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 216 Aset Tetap (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16).

1. What property, plant and equipment is

Property, plant and equipment is a tangible asset held for use in production or supply, for rental, or for administration, and expected to be used for more than one period (PSAK 216.6). Kieso's Intermediate Accounting describes it through four characteristics. It has physical form, it is used in operations, it is not held for sale, and it lasts more than one period. Without physical form an item is an intangible asset, held for speculation it is an investment (investment property under PSAK 240, formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40), and held for sale it is inventory.

An item is recognised when future economic benefits are probable and its cost can be measured reliably (para. 7). Spare parts and stand-by equipment are fixed assets when they meet the definition, and inventory otherwise (para. 8).

PHE presents wells and installations as oil and gas properties (Note 17) and leased assets as right-of-use assets (Note 18). Its fixed assets line holds land, buildings, machinery, movable assets, steel constructions and construction in progress (Note 12, Daftar 5/100, PDF p. 117).

2. Acquisition cost

Cost is the purchase price, including import duties and non-refundable taxes, less trade discounts, plus every cost directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition needed for it to operate as management intends, plus the initial estimate of dismantling and restoration (para. 16).

  • Land: price, notary and title transfer, clearing and levelling, encumbrances assumed, permanent improvements, and demolition of an old building net of salvage.

  • Buildings: materials, labour and overhead of construction, professional fees and permits.

  • Equipment: price, freight, installation, testing and insurance in transit.

Costs the asset could work without are expensed: opening a new facility, training staff, advertising, and general administration (para. 19). Capitalisation stops when the asset is ready for use, even if it is not yet used (para. 20).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys a site with an old warehouse to build a fuel depot. Note 12 lists a fuel depot under construction.

Land = 2,400 price + 60 notary and title transfer + 90 demolition − 15 salvage + 45 levelling = 2,580

Building = 3,200 construction contract + 40 permits + 110 architect's fees = 3,350

Pumps and tanks = 1,500 × (1 − 2%) trade discount + 35 freight + 50 installation + 15 testing = 1,570

Training the depot staff (20) and the opening ceremony (10) are expensed. Since 2023 in Indonesia (an IAS 16 amendment of 2020), proceeds from anything sold while testing the asset go to profit or loss with the cost of producing it, and are no longer deducted from cost.

3. Self-constructed assets

An asset built in-house raises a new question, which of the entity's own costs belong to it. Materials and direct labour are traceable. Overhead is the problem, and Kieso gives two approaches. The first assigns no fixed overhead, on the argument that the overhead would exist with or without the construction. The second, full costing, assigns a share of overhead to the asset, as it would to any product.

PSAK 216 costs a self-constructed asset like a purchased one, at what is directly attributable to bringing it to working condition (paras. 16–17, 22). Only an entity that builds similar assets for sale uses inventory costing under PSAK 202 Inventories. Internal profit and abnormal waste are excluded either way, and so is head-office administration (para. 19). Incremental workshop costs qualify. Fixed workshop overhead is a judgement. Kieso's full costing includes it, and the standard asks only whether it is directly attributable.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary's workshop builds a hydraulic workover unit (Note 12 lists one under construction). Materials 800, direct labour 300, incremental workshop costs 60, the workshop's fixed overhead allocated on labour hours 140, rework after a welding error 25.

The rest of this page uses the full-costing 1,300.

4. Borrowing costs during construction

Kieso sets out three views of interest during construction: expense it as a financing cost, capitalise interest on all funds including imputed equity, or capitalise only interest actually incurred. Kieso measures the third as avoidable interest, the interest that would have been avoided had the asset not been built. PSAK 223 Biaya Pinjaman (formerly PSAK 26, IAS 23) takes the third view and makes it mandatory. Borrowing costs directly attributable to a qualifying asset, one that necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for use or sale, are part of its cost.

Capitalisation starts when spending, borrowing and construction have all begun, pauses during long stoppages, and ends when the work is substantially complete. The amount has two parts.

  • Specific borrowings: the actual cost of a loan taken for the asset, less income from investing its unspent proceeds.

  • General borrowings: for spending financed from the general pool, the capitalisation rate, the weighted-average rate on general borrowings, applied to that spending, capped at the general interest actually incurred.

For example (illustration), the fuel depot is built during 2025. Payments are 1,200 on 1 January, 1,800 on 1 April, 1,500 on 1 September and 900 on 31 December. Weight each by the months it was tied up.

Weighted-average accumulated expenditure = 1,200 × 12/12 + 1,800 × 9/12 + 1,500 × 4/12 + 900 × 0 = 3,050

A specific loan of 2,000 at 8 percent is drawn on 1 January. 1,200 is spent that day and the other 800 sits on deposit at 4 percent until 1 April.

Specific borrowing cost = 2,000 × 8% − 800 × 4% × 3/12 = 160 − 8 = 152

Spending funded by the loan = 1,200 × 12/12 + 800 × 9/12 = 1,800

General borrowings are a bond of 10,000 at 6 percent and a bank loan of 5,000 at 9 percent.

Capitalisation rate = (600 + 450) / 15,000 = 7.0%

General borrowing cost = (3,050 − 1,800) × 7.0% = 87.5, below the 1,050 incurred

Borrowing costs capitalised = 152 + 87.5 = 239.5

Kieso's illustration deducts the whole 2,000 from weighted expenditure, (3,050 − 2,000) × 7.0% = 73.5, so 152 + 73.5 = 225.5. That treats the idle 800 as funding the depot from January while it earned deposit income. Tracing gives the loan 1,800 and the general pool 1,250. The difference of 14 (200 × 7%) vanishes when a loan is spent as it is drawn. PSAK 223 prescribes neither split, so the tracing is this page's reading.

5. Valuing acquisitions that are not plain cash purchases

An asset is recorded at its cash price equivalent or at fair value (paras. 23–24), whatever the form of payment.

Cash discounts. Kieso favours deducting a cash discount from cost whether it is taken or not, because the cash price is the real cost and a missed discount is inefficiency. The alternative records cost at the gross price when the discount is missed. PSAK 216 does not settle the choice. Its interest rule (para. 23) covers payment deferred beyond normal credit terms, and day 30 of net 30 is within them. For example (illustration), a tanker truck listed at 150 on terms 2/10, net 30.

Discount reduces cost either way

Deferred payment. When payment runs beyond normal credit terms, cost is the present value of the payments and the rest is interest over the credit period (para. 23). For example (illustration, Kieso's zero-interest-bearing note case), equipment is bought for five annual payments of 200 when the market rate is 10 percent.

Present value = 200 × 3.79079 = 758.16 (Dr Equipment / Cr Notes payable)

Year 1: interest = 10% × 758.16 = 75.82; principal repaid = 200 − 75.82 = 124.18

Year 2: interest = 10% × (758.16 − 124.18) = 63.40; principal repaid = 136.60

Basket purchases. One price for several assets is split by relative fair value. For example (illustration), land, a building and equipment bought together for 3,000 with fair values of 1,200, 1,800 and 600 (total 3,600) take 3,000 × 1,200/3,600 = 1,000, 1,500 and 500.

Exchanges. An asset received for a non-monetary asset is measured at fair value unless the exchange lacks commercial substance or neither fair value is reliable, in which case it takes the carrying amount of the asset given up (para. 24). An exchange has commercial substance when the risk, timing or amount of the cash flows changes significantly (para. 25). For example (illustration), a subsidiary trades an old workover unit (cost 1,000, accumulated depreciation 700, carrying amount 300, fair value 380) plus 600 cash for a new one.

The rule stops entities manufacturing gains by swapping similar assets.

6. Costs after acquisition

Later spending passes the same test as the original cost. It is capitalised if it adds future economic benefit and expensed if it keeps the asset working as before. Kieso sorts it into three groups.

  • Additions create something new, such as a second loading bay, and are capitalised.

  • Improvements and replacements swap a part for a better or a like one. The new part is capitalised and the carrying amount of the old part is removed, whether or not it was depreciated separately (paras. 13, 70).

  • Repairs. Ordinary repairs, minor parts, repainting and cleaning, are expensed (para. 12). A major inspection that is a condition of operating, such as an aircraft overhaul every four years, is capitalised and depreciated until the next one (para. 14).

PHE's policy states the same rules (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69). For example (illustration), the workover unit's engine, originally 200 of its 1,300 cost and 60 percent depreciated, is replaced for 260, and a routine service costs 15.

Dr Workover unit 260 / Cr Cash 260

Dr Accumulated depreciation 120, Dr Loss on replacement 80 / Cr Workover unit 200

Dr Repairs and maintenance 15 / Cr Cash 15

7. Depreciation

Cost is spent to earn revenue over several periods, so depreciation allocates the depreciable amount, cost less residual value (what the asset would fetch now if it were already at the end of its life), over the useful life, the period the entity expects to use it. Three estimates drive it.

  • Useful life reflects expected use, physical wear, technical or commercial obsolescence, and legal limits such as lease expiry (para. 56). Land is not depreciated, because its life is unlimited (para. 58).

  • Residual value, reviewed at least each year end.

  • Method, which must reflect the pattern in which the benefits are consumed (para. 60). Straight-line, diminishing balance and units of production are all allowed (para. 62). Methods based on revenue are not, because revenue reflects prices as well as use (2014 amendment).

Depreciation starts when the asset is available for use and does not stop when it sits idle, unless a usage method gives a nil charge (para. 55).

For example (illustration), the workover unit costs 1,300, has a residual value of 100 and a five-year life, and is expected to run 20,000 hours: 5,000, 4,500, 4,000, 3,500 and 3,000.

Each part with a significant cost, such as the 200 engine above, is depreciated separately as a component (para. 43). An asset bought on 1 April is depreciated for nine months in its first year, 240 × 9/12 = 180 on straight-line.

Revisions. A change in life, residual value or method is a change in estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8), applied from now on without restating the past (para. 61). For example (illustration), after two years of straight-line the carrying amount is 1,300 − 480 = 820. If the remaining life is revised to four years and the residual value to 60, depreciation becomes (820 − 60) / 4 = 190 a year.

PHE uses straight-line over 4–20 years for buildings, 2–10 for machinery, 2–5 for office and transport equipment and 10 for steel construction, reviewed each year end (Note 3i, PDF pp. 69–70). The table has no line for movable assets, the largest class.

8. Impairment

Depreciation spreads cost, and a separate test asks whether the cost will come back. PSAK 236 Penurunan Nilai Aset (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) does that. At each reporting date the entity looks for indications of impairment, external (falling prices, rising interest rates) or internal (damage, idleness, plans to dispose). If there is one, it estimates the recoverable amount, the higher of two measures.

  • Fair value less costs of disposal: what a buyer would pay, net of selling costs.

  • Value in use: the present value of the cash the asset will generate in the entity's hands.

If the carrying amount exceeds the recoverable amount, the difference is an impairment loss in profit or loss. An asset that does not generate cash on its own is tested within its cash-generating unit, the smallest group of assets with largely independent cash inflows.

For example (illustration), a fleet of fuel tanker trucks loses its main transport contract. Carrying amount 900, remaining life four years, no residual value. A dealer would pay 520 net of costs; the trucks' expected cash flows on the remaining jobs have a present value of 610.

Recoverable amount = higher of 520 and 610 = 610; impairment loss = 900 − 610 = 290

Dr Impairment loss 290 / Cr Allowance for impairment 290

New depreciation = 610 / 4 = 152.5 a year

Reversal. If the estimates later improve, the loss is reversed, but only up to the carrying amount the asset would have had with no impairment (PHE's Note 3w, Daftar 5/73, PDF p. 90). Two years on, a new contract lifts the recoverable amount to 500.

Carrying amount after two years = 610 − 2 × 152.5 = 305

Ceiling = 900 − 2 × 225 = 450, so reversal = 450 − 305 = 145 (the full 500 − 305 = 195 is capped)

Dr Allowance for impairment 145 / Cr Reversal of impairment loss 145

PHE's fixed assets carried an allowance for impairment of 5,383 at the start of 2024. It recognised 117 of new impairment and a correction of 51, ending at 5,449 (Note 12, Daftar 5/100–5/101, PDF pp. 117–118).

9. The revaluation model

After recognition an entity chooses, for each class of assets, the cost model or the revaluation model (para. 29). Under revaluation the asset is carried at fair value at the revaluation date less later depreciation and impairment, and revaluations must be frequent enough that the carrying amount stays close to fair value (para. 34). The whole class is revalued together, so that the balance sheet does not mix costs and values of different dates (paras. 36, 38).

An increase goes to other comprehensive income and accumulates in equity as revaluation surplus, except that it reverses an earlier decrease on the same asset that went to profit or loss. A decrease goes to profit or loss, except to the extent of surplus already held for that asset (paras. 39–40). At the revaluation date either the gross amount is restated consistently with the new carrying amount, for example in proportion, and accumulated depreciation becomes the difference, or accumulated depreciation is eliminated (para. 35). For example (illustration), a building with cost 1,000 and accumulated depreciation 400 is revalued to 840.

Elimination

Dr Building 400 / Cr Acc. depreciation 160, Cr Revaluation surplus 240

Both carry 840 and a surplus of 240. With twelve years left, depreciation becomes 840 / 12 = 70 a year instead of 600 / 12 = 50 on cost. The entity may transfer the 20 difference each year from revaluation surplus to retained earnings, or the whole surplus on disposal, but never through profit or loss (para. 41). Deferred tax on the surplus follows PSAK 212 (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) (para. 42).

PHE uses the cost model but discloses appraisals. Fixed assets with a carrying amount of 55,934 were appraised by independent valuers at 96,246, a Level 3 fair value (Note 12, Daftar 5/103, PDF p. 120). Had PHE revalued that group, ignoring deferred tax and assuming no single asset was worth less than its carrying amount, the line would have risen by 96,246 − 55,934 = 40,312 through other comprehensive income, and the rest of each class would have had to be revalued too.

10. Disposals

An asset is derecognised when sold or when no future benefit is expected from it. After depreciation is brought up to date, the gain or loss is net proceeds less carrying amount, in profit or loss and outside revenue (paras. 67–71).

PHE sold or disposed of fixed assets with a net book value of 65 for 43 in 2024, a loss of 22, and reports such gains and losses in other income and expense (Note 12, PDF p. 120; Note 3i, PDF p. 70). For example (illustration), suppose the 65 was one vehicle bought on 1 July 2022 for 130, with no residual value and a five-year life.

Annual depreciation = 130 / 5 = 26; to 31 December 2024 = 26 × 2.5 = 65; carrying amount = 130 − 65 = 65

Dr Depreciation expense 26 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 26 (for 2024)

Dr Cash 43, Dr Accumulated depreciation 65, Dr Loss on disposal 22 / Cr Vehicles 130

11. Fixed assets across industries

Several industries apply PSAK 216 in a particular way, or move the asset to another standard.

Oil and gas. Exploration and evaluation costs follow PSAK 106 (formerly PSAK 64, IFRS 6) until a field is commercial. PHE depletes its production assets on units of production over proved reserves (Note 3m, Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74).

Plantations. Living plants that only bear produce, such as oil palm, rubber and tea, are bearer plants. Since 1 January 2018 in Indonesia they have been fixed assets under PSAK 216, while the fruit on them stays under PSAK 241 Agriculture (formerly PSAK 69, IAS 41) until harvest. An immature plantation collects its costs like construction in progress and starts depreciating at maturity. For example (illustration), 3,000 of planting and upkeep to maturity over a 20-year productive life gives 3,000 / 20 = 150 a year.

Utilities and revaluation. PLN, the state electricity company, revalued its fixed assets in 2015, adding about Rp653.4 trillion and so raising its later depreciation (detikFinance, 2016).

Toll roads and other concessions. An operator that builds a road under a concession in which the government controls its use and takes it back at the end does not recognise the road as a fixed asset. Under ISAK 112 (formerly ISAK 16, IFRIC 12) it recognises an intangible right to charge users, or a financial asset if the grantor guarantees the cash.

Land rights in Indonesia. Indonesian land is held through rights such as hak guna bangunan that run for a term and can be extended. ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36) asks whether a right is in substance a purchase of land, a fixed asset that is not depreciated, or a right to use, which is a lease under PSAK 116. PHE's policy applies that test, and puts the initial legal costs of a right into land, undepreciated (Note 3i, PDF p. 69).

PHE does not explain the "correction" column (−17,321 of cost, +12,833 of accumulated depreciation) or why the movement table removes a net 50 on disposal while the disposal note shows 65.

13. Upstream note: who owns the equipment

Under PHE's cost recovery production sharing contracts, equipment bought for petroleum operations belongs to the Government, and the contractor may use it until SKK Migas, the upstream regulator, approves it as surplus or abandoned (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). Yet Note 12 says all fixed assets are directly owned by the group. One possible reading is that PSC equipment sits in oil and gas properties and this line holds assets of subsidiaries such as PDSI, a drilling contractor, and Elnusa, an oilfield-service company (Note 1b, Daftar 5/5–5/6, PDF pp. 22–23). The FS does not say. PHE capitalised 2,277 of borrowing costs on the JTB project financing in 2024, disclosed in the oil and gas properties note (Note 17, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126; policy 3aa, PDF p. 93).

14. Related lines

  • oil-gas-properties-net: wells, installations and development assets, depreciated on units of production.

  • right-of-use-assets-net: leased assets and land rights that are in substance leases.

  • inventories-net: the boundary for spare parts and stand-by equipment.

  • depreciation-depletion-amortization: where the 74,311 of 2024 depreciation is charged.

Least-confident assertions

  • That the fixed assets line holds group-owned assets and PSC equipment sits in oil and gas properties is this page's reading of Note 2a(vii) and Note 12 together. PHE does not say where state-owned PSC equipment is presented.

  • PHE's policy table lists lives for "transportation equipment" and other classes, but Note 12 reports a class called "movable assets" (932,365 of cost) that the table does not name. Its 2024 depreciation of 54,864 on average cost of 898,489 is 6.1 percent, which implies a life far longer than the 2–5 years for transport. This page could not match the two.

  • Including allocated fixed workshop overhead in a self-constructed asset (the full-costing 1,300) is a judgement under PSAK 216.16–17, which ask only whether a cost is directly attributable. Paragraph 22 points to inventory costing only for entities that build similar assets for sale. How Indonesian preparers treat fixed overhead was not researched.

  • Tracing the specific loan to 1,800 of expenditure, rather than deducting the whole 2,000 as Kieso does, is this page's reading of PSAK 223.12–14. The standard does not prescribe the split; the two methods differ here by 14.

  • The ISAK 112 and ISAK 336 summaries were checked against secondary sources and PHE's policy wording; neither interpretation's own text was opened.

content.text: Cost is everything needed to bring an asset to the place and condition in which it can work as intended, including borrowing costs on a qualifying asset, and nothing it could work without. Deferred payment, exchanges and basket purchases are all brought back to a cash-price or fair-value equivalent.

Depreciation allocates that cost over the asset's useful life in the pattern its benefits are used up. Whether that cost will come back is a separate question for the impairment test under PSAK 236, which, when the carrying amount is higher, writes the asset down to the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use.

After recognition an entity chooses, by class, between the cost model and the revaluation model. Revaluation gains go to other comprehensive income, while gains and losses on disposal go to profit or loss and never count as revenue.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report fixed assets, net, of 544,278 at 31 December 2024 against 522,121 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11). That is 1.8 percent of total assets (1.7 percent a year earlier). The wells and production installations sit on a different line, oil and gas properties, net, which holds 17,905,149, or 58.8 percent of total assets.
A student should be able to measure, depreciate, impair, revalue and derecognise an asset, with journals.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 216
1. What property, plant and equipment is
Property, plant and equipment is a tangible asset held for use in production or supply, for rental, or for administration, and expected to be used for more than one period (PSAK 216.6). Kieso's

describes it through four characteristics. It has physical form, it is used in operations, it is not held for sale, and it lasts more than one period. Without physical form an item is an intangible asset, held for speculation it is an investment (investment property under PSAK 240, formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40), and held for sale it is inventory.

An item is recognised when future economic benefits are probable and its cost can be measured reliably (para. 7). Spare parts and stand-by equipment are fixed assets when they meet the definition, and inventory otherwise (para. 8).

PHE presents wells and installations as oil and gas properties (Note 17) and leased assets as right-of-use assets (Note 18). Its fixed assets line holds land, buildings, machinery, movable assets, steel constructions and construction in progress (Note 12, Daftar 5/100, PDF p. 117).

Cost is the purchase price, including import duties and non-refundable taxes, less trade discounts, plus every cost directly attributable to bringing the asset to the location and condition needed for it to operate as management intends, plus the initial estimate of dismantling and restoration (para. 16).
: price, notary and title transfer, clearing and levelling, encumbrances assumed, permanent improvements, and demolition of an old building net of salvage.
: materials, labour and overhead of construction, professional fees and permits.
: price, freight, installation, testing and insurance in transit.

Costs the asset could work without are expensed: opening a new facility, training staff, advertising, and general administration (para. 19). Capitalisation stops when the asset is ready for use, even if it is not yet used (para. 20).
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys a site with an old warehouse to build a fuel depot. Note 12 lists a fuel depot under construction.
Land = 2,400 price + 60 notary and title transfer + 90 demolition − 15 salvage + 45 levelling = 2,580
Building = 3,200 construction contract + 40 permits + 110 architect's fees = 3,350
Pumps and tanks = 1,500 × (1 − 2%) trade discount + 35 freight + 50 installation + 15 testing = 1,570

Training the depot staff (20) and the opening ceremony (10) are expensed. Since 2023 in Indonesia (an IAS 16 amendment of 2020), proceeds from anything sold while testing the asset go to profit or loss with the cost of producing it, and are no longer deducted from cost.

An asset built in-house raises a new question, which of the entity's own costs belong to it. Materials and direct labour are traceable. Overhead is the problem, and Kieso gives two approaches. The first assigns no fixed overhead, on the argument that the overhead would exist with or without the construction. The second,
, assigns a share of overhead to the asset, as it would to any product.

PSAK 216 costs a self-constructed asset like a purchased one, at what is directly attributable to bringing it to working condition (paras. 16–17, 22). Only an entity that builds similar assets for sale uses inventory costing under PSAK 202

. Internal profit and abnormal waste are excluded either way, and so is head-office administration (para. 19). Incremental workshop costs qualify. Fixed workshop overhead is a judgement. Kieso's full costing includes it, and the standard asks only whether it is directly attributable.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary's workshop builds a hydraulic workover unit (Note 12 lists one under construction). Materials 800, direct labour 300, incremental workshop costs 60, the workshop's fixed overhead allocated on labour hours 140, rework after a welding error 25.
The rest of this page uses the full-costing 1,300.

Kieso sets out three views of interest during construction: expense it as a financing cost, capitalise interest on all funds including imputed equity, or capitalise only interest actually incurred. Kieso measures the third as
, the interest that would have been avoided had the asset not been built. PSAK 223
(formerly PSAK 26, IAS 23) takes the third view and makes it mandatory. Borrowing costs directly attributable to a
, one that necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for use or sale, are part of its cost.
Capitalisation starts when spending, borrowing and construction have all begun, pauses during long stoppages, and ends when the work is substantially complete. The amount has two parts.
: the actual cost of a loan taken for the asset, less income from investing its unspent proceeds.
: for spending financed from the general pool, the
, the weighted-average rate on general borrowings, applied to that spending, capped at the general interest actually incurred.

For example (illustration), the fuel depot is built during 2025. Payments are 1,200 on 1 January, 1,800 on 1 April, 1,500 on 1 September and 900 on 31 December. Weight each by the months it was tied up.
A specific loan of 2,000 at 8 percent is drawn on 1 January. 1,200 is spent that day and the other 800 sits on deposit at 4 percent until 1 April.
General borrowings are a bond of 10,000 at 6 percent and a bank loan of 5,000 at 9 percent.
General borrowing cost = (3,050 − 1,800) × 7.0% = 87.5, below the 1,050 incurred

Kieso's illustration deducts the whole 2,000 from weighted expenditure, (3,050 − 2,000) × 7.0% = 73.5, so 152 + 73.5 = 225.5. That treats the idle 800 as funding the depot from January while it earned deposit income. Tracing gives the loan 1,800 and the general pool 1,250. The difference of 14 (200 × 7%) vanishes when a loan is spent as it is drawn. PSAK 223 prescribes neither split, so the tracing is this page's reading.
5. Valuing acquisitions that are not plain cash purchases
An asset is recorded at its cash price equivalent or at fair value (paras. 23–24), whatever the form of payment.

Kieso favours deducting a cash discount from cost whether it is taken or not, because the cash price is the real cost and a missed discount is inefficiency. The alternative records cost at the gross price when the discount is missed. PSAK 216 does not settle the choice. Its interest rule (para. 23) covers payment deferred beyond normal credit terms, and day 30 of net 30 is within them. For example (illustration), a tanker truck listed at 150 on terms 2/10, net 30.
Dr Vehicles 147, Dr Discounts lost 3 / Cr Cash 150

When payment runs beyond normal credit terms, cost is the present value of the payments and the rest is interest over the credit period (para. 23). For example (illustration, Kieso's zero-interest-bearing note case), equipment is bought for five annual payments of 200 when the market rate is 10 percent.
Present value = 200 × 3.79079 = 758.16 (Dr Equipment / Cr Notes payable)

One price for several assets is split by relative fair value. For example (illustration), land, a building and equipment bought together for 3,000 with fair values of 1,200, 1,800 and 600 (total 3,600) take 3,000 × 1,200/3,600 = 1,000, 1,500 and 500.
An asset received for a non-monetary asset is measured at fair value unless the exchange lacks

or neither fair value is reliable, in which case it takes the carrying amount of the asset given up (para. 24). An exchange has commercial substance when the risk, timing or amount of the cash flows changes significantly (para. 25). For example (illustration), a subsidiary trades an old workover unit (cost 1,000, accumulated depreciation 700, carrying amount 300, fair value 380) plus 600 cash for a new one.
Dr New unit 980, Dr Acc. depreciation 700 / Cr Old unit 1,000, Cr Cash 600, Cr Gain 80
Dr New unit 900, Dr Acc. depreciation 700 / Cr Old unit 1,000, Cr Cash 600
The rule stops entities manufacturing gains by swapping similar assets.
Later spending passes the same test as the original cost. It is capitalised if it adds future economic benefit and expensed if it keeps the asset working as before. Kieso sorts it into three groups.
create something new, such as a second loading bay, and are capitalised.
swap a part for a better or a like one. The new part is capitalised and the carrying amount of the old part is removed, whether or not it was depreciated separately (paras. 13, 70).

. Ordinary repairs, minor parts, repainting and cleaning, are expensed (para. 12). A major inspection that is a condition of operating, such as an aircraft overhaul every four years, is capitalised and depreciated until the next one (para. 14).

PHE's policy states the same rules (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69). For example (illustration), the workover unit's engine, originally 200 of its 1,300 cost and 60 percent depreciated, is replaced for 260, and a routine service costs 15.

Dr Repairs and maintenance 15 / Cr Cash 15
Cost is spent to earn revenue over several periods, so depreciation allocates the
(what the asset would fetch now if it were already at the end of its life), over the

Depreciation starts when the asset is available for use and does not stop when it sits idle, unless a usage method gives a nil charge (para. 55).
For example (illustration), the workover unit costs 1,300, has a residual value of 100 and a five-year life, and is expected to run 20,000 hours: 5,000, 4,500, 4,000, 3,500 and 3,000.
Double-declining balance: 2 / 5 = 40% of opening carrying amount; year 5 takes the balance down to the residual value, 168.48 − 100 = 68.48
Every method spends the same 1,200, so the choice must follow how the asset is used.
Each part with a significant cost, such as the 200 engine above, is depreciated separately as a
(para. 43). An asset bought on 1 April is depreciated for nine months in its first year, 240 × 9/12 = 180 on straight-line.

A change in life, residual value or method is a change in estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8), applied from now on without restating the past (para. 61). For example (illustration), after two years of straight-line the carrying amount is 1,300 − 480 = 820. If the remaining life is revised to four years and the residual value to 60, depreciation becomes (820 − 60) / 4 = 190 a year.

PHE uses straight-line over 4–20 years for buildings, 2–10 for machinery, 2–5 for office and transport equipment and 10 for steel construction, reviewed each year end (Note 3i, PDF pp. 69–70). The table has no line for movable assets, the largest class.
Depreciation spreads cost, and a separate test asks whether the cost will come back. PSAK 236

(formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) does that. At each reporting date the entity looks for indications of impairment, external (falling prices, rising interest rates) or internal (damage, idleness, plans to dispose). If there is one, it estimates the
Fair value less costs of disposal

: the present value of the cash the asset will generate in the entity's hands.
If the carrying amount exceeds the recoverable amount, the difference is an impairment loss in profit or loss. An asset that does not generate cash on its own is tested within its

For example (illustration), a fleet of fuel tanker trucks loses its main transport contract. Carrying amount 900, remaining life four years, no residual value. A dealer would pay 520 net of costs; the trucks' expected cash flows on the remaining jobs have a present value of 610.
Recoverable amount = higher of 520 and 610 = 610; impairment loss = 900 − 610 = 290

An asset is derecognised when sold or when no future benefit is expected from it. After depreciation is brought up to date, the gain or loss is net proceeds less carrying amount, in profit or loss and outside revenue (paras. 67–71).

PHE sold or disposed of fixed assets with a net book value of 65 for 43 in 2024, a loss of 22, and reports such gains and losses in other income and expense (Note 12, PDF p. 120; Note 3i, PDF p. 70). For example (illustration), suppose the 65 was one vehicle bought on 1 July 2022 for 130, with no residual value and a five-year life.
Annual depreciation = 130 / 5 = 26; to 31 December 2024 = 26 × 2.5 = 65; carrying amount = 130 − 65 = 65
Dr Depreciation expense 26 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 26 (for 2024)
Dr Cash 43, Dr Accumulated depreciation 65, Dr Loss on disposal 22 / Cr Vehicles 130
Several industries apply PSAK 216 in a particular way, or move the asset to another standard.

Exploration and evaluation costs follow PSAK 106 (formerly PSAK 64, IFRS 6) until a field is commercial. PHE depletes its production assets on units of production over proved reserves (Note 3m, Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74).
Living plants that only bear produce, such as oil palm, rubber and tea, are
. Since 1 January 2018 in Indonesia they have been fixed assets under PSAK 216, while the fruit on them stays under PSAK 241

(formerly PSAK 69, IAS 41) until harvest. An immature plantation collects its costs like construction in progress and starts depreciating at maturity. For example (illustration), 3,000 of planting and upkeep to maturity over a 20-year productive life gives 3,000 / 20 = 150 a year.
PLN, the state electricity company, revalued its fixed assets in 2015, adding about Rp653.4 trillion and so raising its later depreciation (detikFinance, 2016).

An operator that builds a road under a concession in which the government controls its use and takes it back at the end does not recognise the road as a fixed asset. Under ISAK 112 (formerly ISAK 16, IFRIC 12) it recognises an intangible right to charge users, or a financial asset if the grantor guarantees the cash.
Indonesian land is held through rights such as

that run for a term and can be extended. ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36) asks whether a right is in substance a purchase of land, a fixed asset that is not depreciated, or a right to use, which is a lease under PSAK 116. PHE's policy applies that test, and puts the initial legal costs of a right into land, undepreciated (Note 3i, PDF p. 69).
PSAK 216 asks for each class's measurement basis, method, lives and a reconciliation of movements, which PHE gives (Note 12, Daftar 5/100, PDF p. 117).

Opening 522,121 + additions 101,072 − disposals (903 − 853) − net correction (17,321 − 12,833) − depreciation 74,311 − impairment 117 + impairment correction 51 = 544,278

The cash flow statement shows 101,071 paid for fixed assets (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17). Construction in progress grew from 31,354 to 48,161, led by rig equipment at 30,558 (Note 12, Daftar 5/102, PDF p. 119).

The assets are more than half used up; 115,950 of cost is fully depreciated but still in use (Note 12, PDF p. 119). PHE does not explain the "correction" column (−17,321 of cost, +12,833 of accumulated depreciation) or why the movement table removes a net 50 on disposal while the disposal note shows 65.
13. Upstream note: who owns the equipment

Under PHE's cost recovery production sharing contracts, equipment bought for petroleum operations belongs to the Government, and the contractor may use it until SKK Migas, the upstream regulator, approves it as surplus or abandoned (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). Yet Note 12 says all fixed assets are directly owned by the group. One possible reading is that PSC equipment sits in oil and gas properties and this line holds assets of subsidiaries such as PDSI, a drilling contractor, and Elnusa, an oilfield-service company (Note 1b, Daftar 5/5–5/6, PDF pp. 22–23). The FS does not say. PHE capitalised 2,277 of borrowing costs on the JTB project financing in 2024, disclosed in the oil and gas properties note (Note 17, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126; policy 3aa, PDF p. 93).
: wells, installations and development assets, depreciated on units of production.
: leased assets and land rights that are in substance leases.
: the boundary for spare parts and stand-by equipment.
: where the 74,311 of 2024 depreciation is charged.

That the fixed assets line holds group-owned assets and PSC equipment sits in oil and gas properties is this page's reading of Note 2a(vii) and Note 12 together. PHE does not say where state-owned PSC equipment is presented.

PHE's policy table lists lives for "transportation equipment" and other classes, but Note 12 reports a class called "movable assets" (932,365 of cost) that the table does not name. Its 2024 depreciation of 54,864 on average cost of 898,489 is 6.1 percent, which implies a life far longer than the 2–5 years for transport. This page could not match the two.

Including allocated fixed workshop overhead in a self-constructed asset (the full-costing 1,300) is a judgement under PSAK 216.16–17, which ask only whether a cost is directly attributable. Paragraph 22 points to inventory costing only for entities that build similar assets for sale. How Indonesian preparers treat fixed overhead was not researched.

Tracing the specific loan to 1,800 of expenditure, rather than deducting the whole 2,000 as Kieso does, is this page's reading of PSAK 223.12–14. The standard does not prescribe the split; the two methods differ here by 14.
