presentation.deck: The theory of property, plant and equipment from acquisition to derecognition, worked through PHE's fixed assets and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: Cost is everything needed to bring an asset to the place and condition in which it can work as intended, including borrowing costs on a qualifying asset, and nothing it could work without. Deferred payment, exchanges and basket purchases are all brought back to a cash-price or fair-value equivalent.

Depreciation allocates that cost over the asset's useful life in the pattern its benefits are used up. Whether that cost will come back is a separate question for the impairment test under PSAK 236, which, when the carrying amount is higher, writes the asset down to the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use.

After recognition an entity chooses, by class, between the cost model and the revaluation model. Revaluation gains go to other comprehensive income, while gains and losses on disposal go to profit or loss and never count as revenue.

title: Foreign Exchange Loss, Net: Functional Currency, Monetary Items and Where the Differences Go
snippet: The theory of foreign-currency transactions from choosing a functional currency to hyperinflation, worked through PHE's rupiah balances and set beside the industries that live with a currency mismatch
content:
In brief

  • Every entity first determines its functional currency, the currency of the economic environment that mainly sets its prices and costs, from evidence the standard ranks. Any other currency is foreign. A Jakarta company can be a dollar company, and a Paris one can be too.

  • Foreign-currency transactions are recorded at the spot rate on the transaction date. At each reporting date, monetary items (cash, receivables, payables, provisions to be paid in cash) are retranslated at the closing rate and the difference goes to profit or loss. Non-monetary items carried at cost (inventory, fixed assets, prepayments) keep their historical rate.

  • An exchange loss therefore measures the net monetary position held in a foreign currency and how the rate moved while it was held. A dollar-functional company that holds more rupiah assets than rupiah liabilities loses when the rupiah weakens. Translation of a foreign operation into a presentation currency is a different step that goes to other comprehensive income, and hyperinflation (PSAK 229) adds a restatement before any translation.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report a foreign exchange loss, net, of 4,479 for 2024 against 19,772 for 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). The loss is 0.09 percent of profit before income tax of 4,892,576 (0.44 percent of 4,492,029 in 2023). The line has no note of its own.

After reading it a student should be able to determine an entity's functional currency, record a foreign-currency transaction from invoice to settlement, sort balances into monetary and non-monetary, and explain why a dollar company reports a gain or loss when the rupiah moves.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated; rupiah amounts are in millions. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Three currencies, three questions

A group that buys in rupiah, sells in dollars and reports to a parent abroad needs a rule for which currency its books measure in. PSAK 221 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21) separates three currencies (para. 8).

Term

Definition

Question it answers

Functional currency

the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates

what the entity measures in

Foreign currency

any currency other than the functional currency

which balances can produce exchange differences

Presentation currency

the currency in which the statements are presented

what the reader sees

The standard then works in two steps (paras. 17–18). Each entity, parent or subsidiary, measures its own transactions in its functional currency, and exchange differences on its foreign-currency items go to its profit or loss. Where an entity's functional currency differs from the group's presentation currency, its statements are then translated, and that difference goes to other comprehensive income (OCI). The second step is covered in the Other Comprehensive Income essay.

PHE's functional currency is the US dollar for every entity in the group except Elnusa, whose functional currency is the rupiah, and the consolidated statements are presented in dollars (Note 3a, Daftar 5/29, PDF p. 46; Note 3r(i), Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83). For a PHE production-sharing subsidiary the rupiah is a foreign currency, even though it pays Indonesian taxes and Indonesian staff in it.

2. Determining the functional currency

The standard ranks the evidence for a functional currency, and management weighs it rather than picking a currency it prefers. The primary indicators look at operations (para. 9): the currency that mainly influences sales prices, often the currency prices are set and settled in; the currency of the country whose competitive forces and regulations mainly determine those prices; and the currency that mainly influences labour, material and other costs. Secondary indicators look at money (para. 10): the currency in which financing is raised and the currency in which operating receipts are kept. A foreign operation adds a third set (para. 11), centred on whether it is an extension of the parent or works with a significant degree of autonomy. When the indicators are mixed, management judges which currency most faithfully represents the economics, giving the primary indicators priority (para. 12).

For example (illustration), score three kinds of entity in PHE's group against the indicators. The reading of each indicator is this page's; PHE discloses no such analysis.

Indicator

Upstream PSC subsidiary

Oilfield services company (Elnusa-type)

Overseas producer (M&P-type)

Sales prices

crude and gas priced in dollars

service fees mostly in rupiah

crude priced in dollars

Costs

rigs, contractors and imported materials largely in dollars; staff and local services in rupiah

staff, fuel and local suppliers in rupiah

contractors and equipment in dollars

Financing

dollar loans and sukuk

rupiah bank loans

dollar loans

Result

US dollar

rupiah

US dollar

PHE's Note 1 lists Etablissements Maurel et Prom (M&P), domiciled in Paris and 71.09 percent owned (Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25), and Note 3r gives every entity but Elnusa the dollar as functional currency. Domicile and the currency of tax filings do not decide the matter.

A change of functional currency happens only when the underlying transactions change (paras. 13 and 36), and it is accounted for prospectively (para. 35). Every item is translated at the rate on the date of change, and the translated amounts of non-monetary items become their historical cost (para. 37). For example (illustration), a services subsidiary wins long-term dollar contracts and switches from rupiah to dollars on 1 July, when the rate is Rp16,000 per dollar. A rig it carries at Rp80,000 million is then measured at:

80,000 × 1,000 / 16,000 = 5,000, the rig's new historical cost in dollars

Nothing is restated for earlier periods, and the rig's cost is never retranslated again.

3. Initial recognition: the spot rate on the transaction date

A foreign-currency transaction is one denominated in, or requiring settlement in, a foreign currency: buying or selling at a foreign-currency price, borrowing or lending in one, or acquiring assets or incurring liabilities in one (para. 20). It is recorded in the functional currency at the spot rate on the transaction date (para. 21), the date it first qualifies for recognition. An average rate for a week or a month may be used if rates do not fluctuate significantly (para. 22). PHE's policy restates the rule (Note 3r(ii)).

For example (illustration), on 15 November 2024 a PHE subsidiary receives an invoice from a local contractor for well services of Rp16,200 million, due in 90 days, when the rate is Rp15,800 per dollar.

16,200 × 1,000 / 15,800 = 1,025.32

Dr Production expenses 1,025.32 / Cr Trade payables 1,025.32

Advance payments. When an entity pays or receives in advance, ISAK 122 Foreign Currency Transactions and Advance Consideration (formerly ISAK 33, IFRIC 22) fixes the transaction date as the date the prepayment or deferred income is first recognised. A prepayment is non-monetary (section 4), so the goods later received are measured at the rate of the advance. For example (illustration), the subsidiary prepays Rp1,580 million for chemicals when the rate is Rp15,800.

Dr Advances for purchases 100.00 / Cr Cash 100.00

On delivery, at any later rate: Dr Inventories 100.00 / Cr Advances for purchases 100.00

4. At the reporting date: monetary and non-monetary items

Monetary items follow the exchange rate after a transaction and non-monetary items carried at cost do not. The test is whether the item is a right to receive, or an obligation to deliver, a fixed or determinable number of units of currency (para. 16). Such monetary items are translated at the closing rate, the spot rate at the end of the period. Non-monetary items carried at historical cost keep the rate of the transaction date, and those carried at fair value use the rate when fair value was measured (para. 23).

Monetary: retranslate at the closing rate

Non-monetary at cost: keep the historical rate

cash and deposits

inventories

trade and other receivables

fixed assets, oil and gas properties

tax refunds receivable in cash, taxes payable

intangible assets, goodwill

trade payables, accrued expenses

right-of-use assets

bank loans, lease liabilities

prepayments and advances for goods or services

employee benefits and provisions to be paid in cash

provisions to be settled by delivering a non-monetary asset

The logic is what each item will turn into. A rupiah receivable will produce a fixed number of rupiah, so its dollar value moves with the rate. A drilling rig bought in rupiah will produce oil, not rupiah, so its dollar cost stays where it was.

Take PHE's balances as the starting point. Note 48 shows rupiah tax refund claims (presented as other taxes receivable) of Rp7,551,277 million at the end of 2023, carried at 489,104, and rupiah taxes payable of Rp2,354,077 million, carried at 152,476 (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242). Both are monetary. PHE's policy names the Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar Rate (JISDOR) as the closing rate (Note 3r(ii)); the amounts in Note 48 imply Rp15,439 per dollar at the end of 2023 and Rp16,157 at the end of 2024, which match the published JISDOR. Suppose, for illustration, both balances had stayed unchanged in rupiah through 2024.

Tax refund claims: 7,551,277 × 1,000 / 16,157 = 467,369; loss = 489,104 − 467,369 = 21,735

Taxes payable: 2,354,077 × 1,000 / 16,157 = 145,700; gain = 152,476 − 145,700 = 6,776

Net loss = 21,735 − 6,776 = 14,959

Dr Foreign exchange loss 21,735 / Cr Tax refund claims 21,735

Dr Other taxes payable 6,776 / Cr Foreign exchange gain 6,776

The rupiah lost 4.44 percent of its dollar value (1 − 15,439 / 16,157), and each rupiah asset and liability changed by the same share.

Items measured by comparing two amounts. For a non-monetary item tested against a recoverable figure, such as inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV), each side is translated at the rate on the date it was determined (para. 25). For example (illustration), spares bought for Rp3,200 million at Rp15,500 have a year-end NRV of Rp3,250 million at Rp16,157.

Cost = 3,200 × 1,000 / 15,500 = 206.45; NRV = 3,250 × 1,000 / 16,157 = 201.15

Write-down = 206.45 − 201.15 = 5.30

The spares are worth more rupiah than they cost and still need a write-down in dollars (see the Inventories essay).

5. Settlement, and where the differences go

An exchange difference arises whenever a monetary item is settled, or retranslated, at a rate different from the one last used, and it goes to profit or loss in the period it arises (para. 28). If a transaction is settled in the same period, the whole difference falls there; if it spans a year end, each period takes the part caused by that period's rate change (para. 29). The total is fixed by the rate on the transaction date and the rate on settlement. The year end only splits it.

Return to section 3's invoice of Rp16,200 million booked at 1,025.32. At 31 December 2024 the closing rate is Rp16,157, and the subsidiary pays on 13 February 2025 at, for illustration, Rp16,300.

31 December 2024: 16,200 × 1,000 / 16,157 = 1,002.66; gain = 1,025.32 − 1,002.66 = 22.66

13 February 2025: 16,200 × 1,000 / 16,300 = 993.87; gain = 1,002.66 − 993.87 = 8.80

Total gain = 1,025.32 − 993.87 = 31.45, the two steps before rounding (22.655 + 8.796)

2024

2025

Entry

Dr Trade payables 22.66 / Cr Foreign exchange gain 22.66

Dr Trade payables 1,002.66 / Cr Cash 993.87, Cr Foreign exchange gain 8.80

Kind

unrealised: the payable is retranslated

realised: rupiah are bought and paid

The standard does not separate realised from unrealised differences; both are on the same line. The well services stay at 1,025.32 in production expense, because the expense was recognised once, at the transaction-date rate (para. 21).

Three exceptions send exchange differences elsewhere.

  • Net investment in a foreign operation. A long-term loan to a foreign operation whose settlement is neither planned nor likely is in substance part of the investment (para. 15). Its exchange differences go to profit or loss in the separate statements but to OCI in the consolidated ones, recycled on disposal (para. 32).

  • Hedging. An exchange difference on a monetary item designated as a cash flow hedging instrument goes to OCI to the extent the hedge is effective (para. 27; PSAK 109). The Other Comprehensive Income essay teaches both of these routes.

  • Non-monetary items with gains in OCI. When a gain on a non-monetary item goes to OCI, such as a revaluation surplus on a foreign-currency asset, its exchange component goes with it (para. 30).

Intragroup balances do not eliminate the exchange difference. Consolidation removes intragroup balances, but a monetary item between members with different functional currencies is a commitment to convert one currency into another, so its exchange difference stays in consolidated profit or loss (para. 45). For example (illustration), a dollar-functional PHE subsidiary is owed Rp15,439 million by Elnusa, rupiah-functional, from the end of 2023.

Subsidiary: 15,439 × 1,000 / 15,439 = 1,000.00 at end 2023; 15,439 × 1,000 / 16,157 = 955.56 at end 2024; loss 44.44

Elnusa: owes Rp15,439 million in both years, no difference

The receivable and payable still cancel on consolidation, but the 44.44 loss stays in the group's profit or loss.

6. Dollar accounts, rupiah tax books

The functional currency decides the accounting books, and the tax law decides the tax books, and in Indonesia the two can differ. The tax administration law requires books in rupiah and in Indonesian unless the Minister of Finance permits a foreign language and a currency other than rupiah (UU KUP art. 28(4) and (8)). Through 2024 the permission rule was PMK 196/PMK.03/2007, last amended by PMK 123/PMK.03/2019, which lists among the taxpayers that may keep books in English and US dollars production-sharing contractors (KKKS), mining contract-of-work holders, companies listed abroad, and taxpayers whose functional currency under Indonesian accounting standards is the dollar. PMK 81/2024 partly revoked it from 1 January 2025; permission now sits in its art. 455(3), and under PER-8/PJ/2025 art. 16 oil and gas contractors only notify, while dollar-functional taxpayers apply.

A company that keeps dollar accounts but rupiah tax books has two currencies inside one tax line. PSAK 212 Income Taxes (formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) treats the effect of exchange rates on a tax base measured in another currency as a temporary difference, with the deferred tax charged to profit or loss (para. 41). For example (illustration), a dollar-functional subsidiary without dollar tax books owns a compressor bought for Rp154,390 million when the rate was Rp15,439, so its accounting cost is 10,000; ignore depreciation, and take the 22 percent Indonesian corporate rate.

Tax base at end 2024 = 154,390 × 1,000 / 16,157 = 9,555.61

Taxable temporary difference = 10,000.00 − 9,555.61 = 444.39; deferred tax liability = 444.39 × 22% = 97.77

Dr Deferred tax expense 97.77 / Cr Deferred tax liability 97.77

The rupiah's fall cut the future tax deductions measured in dollars, so tax expense rises with no change in the asset. A contractor allowed dollar tax books avoids this mismatch on its fixed assets (see the Deferred Tax essay).

7. Presentation currency and foreign operations

An entity may present its statements in any currency (para. 38). If that differs from its functional currency, it translates assets and liabilities at the closing rate, income and expenses at the rates on the transaction dates (an average rate is a common approximation, para. 40), and puts the resulting difference in OCI (para. 39). It must state the functional currency and the reason for presenting in another (para. 53). A dollar-functional company presenting in rupiah would carry a translation reserve though its business never changed.

The same procedure brings a foreign operation into consolidated statements. For PHE that means Elnusa, translated from rupiah into dollars with the difference in OCI and recycled when the operation is sold. The Other Comprehensive Income essay works it through with PHE's 2024 translation adjustments of −14,810.

8. Hyperinflation and currencies that cannot be exchanged

In a hyperinflationary economy historical amounts stop meaning anything, so translation alone would mislead. PSAK 229 Financial Reporting in Hyperinflationary Economies (formerly PSAK 63, IAS 29) gives no single threshold. Its indicators include people keeping wealth in a stable foreign currency, prices quoted in that currency, and cumulative inflation over three years approaching or exceeding 100 percent (para. 3). An entity whose functional currency is hyperinflationary restates its statements into the measuring unit current at the reporting date (para. 8). Monetary items are not restated, because they are already in current units (para. 12). Non-monetary items at cost are restated by a general price index from their acquisition date (paras. 14–15). Holding net monetary assets through inflation loses purchasing power, and the gain or loss on the net monetary position goes to profit or loss (paras. 27–28).

For example (illustration), an entity holds net monetary assets of 1,000 in local currency all year while the general price index rises from 120 to 180, and owns land bought for 2,000 when the index was 100.

Loss on net monetary position = 1,000 × (180 / 120 − 1) = 500

Land restated = 2,000 × 180 / 100 = 3,600

Only after restatement are the statements translated, all amounts at the latest closing rate (PSAK 221.42–43). An entity cannot avoid restatement by adopting its parent's currency (PSAK 221.14). PHE states that none of its subsidiaries has a hyperinflationary functional currency (Note 3r(iii), Daftar 5/67, PDF p. 84). Note 2d lists a 40 percent interest, held through the group, in Petroregional del Lago Mixed Company in Venezuela (Daftar 5/21, PDF p. 38), but the FS do not give that venture's functional currency.

Lack of exchangeability. The 2023 amendments to IAS 21 require an entity to estimate a spot rate when a currency cannot be obtained through a normal exchange mechanism, and to disclose the effects (paras. 8A–8B, 19A, 57A). PHE lists the matching amendment to PSAK 221 as effective from 1 January 2025 and says it is assessing the impact (Note 3b, Daftar 5/31, PDF p. 48).

9. Foreign exchange across industries

Coal and mineral exporters. Coal is priced in dollars, so a miner whose costs and debt are also in dollars finds the dollar functional under section 2, and it may keep dollar tax books under the same PMK list. Its exposure mirrors PHE's: rupiah VAT refunds, royalties and taxes payable, and local contractor payables. A miner with net rupiah liabilities gains when the rupiah weakens.

Plantations. Palm oil is priced against dollar and ringgit benchmarks while estate costs are in rupiah, so para. 12's judgement decides.

Airlines. Aircraft leases, fuel and maintenance are priced in dollars, and Garuda Indonesia keeps its financial statements in dollars, so for it the rupiah is the foreign currency. For a rupiah-functional airline the mismatch is built into the lease accounting, because the lease liability is monetary and the right-of-use asset is not (PSAK 116; see the Right-of-Use Assets essay). For example (illustration), a rupiah airline leases an aircraft with a liability of USD 100 million at Rp15,439 at the end of 2023; ignore payments and interest.

Liability at end 2024 = 100 × 16,157 = Rp1,615,700 million; at end 2023 = 100 × 15,439 = Rp1,543,900 million

Exchange loss = Rp71,800 million; the right-of-use asset stays at Rp1,543,900 million less depreciation

Banks. A rupiah-functional bank revalues its foreign-currency positions daily, and the differences are trading results. Bank Indonesia caps the net open position, assets less liabilities in foreign currency including off-balance-sheet positions, at 20 percent of capital (PBI 5/13/PBI/2003 as last amended by PBI 17/5/PBI/2015). For example (illustration), a bank with capital of Rp10,000,000 million is long USD 120 million.

Position at end 2023 = 120 × 15,439 = Rp1,852,680 million, 18.5% of capital

At end 2024 = 120 × 16,157 = Rp1,938,840 million, 19.4% of capital; revaluation gain Rp86,160 million

The weakening that gives the bank a gain also pushes it toward the limit without a single new trade.

10. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 48 and 49

PHE's 2024 loss is consistent with a net rupiah monetary asset held while the rupiah weakened from Rp15,439 to Rp16,157. PSAK 221 requires the amount of exchange differences recognised in profit or loss (para. 52(a)), which PHE shows on the face of the statement, and Note 48 lists the monetary items behind it (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242).

The 2024 rows sum to Rp717,211 million against the printed Rp717,207 million (rounding). Note 48's own bottom line, which adds euro and other currencies, is a net asset of 8,371 (2023: 889,478).

The implied rates match JISDOR at both dates (9,103,678 / 563,451 = Rp16,157; 7,551,277 / 489,104 = Rp15,439), and the tax refund claims equal Note 43a's total other taxes receivable. Rupiah cash ties to Note 6 (78 on hand, 375,921 in banks and 67,154 in deposits, total 443,153; Daftar 5/90–5/92, PDF pp. 107–109).

Had the opening net asset of 803,688 been held all year, the loss would have been:

12,408,133 × 1,000 / 16,157 = 767,973; loss = 803,688 − 767,973 = 35,715

The reported loss is 4,479. The position fell by 848,078 during the year (803,688 + 44,390), led by rupiah cash, which fell from 1,056,660 to 443,152 at the Note 48 rates as rupiah were spent. The rupiah's path within the year also matters, because differences are realised at settlement rates. The year-end position is a weak guide even to direction: in 2023 PHE held net rupiah assets while the rupiah strengthened to Rp15,439, and still reported a loss of 19,772. The cash flow statement's effect of exchange rate changes on cash, −19,739 (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17), is no comparator, because it also carries the translation of Elnusa's rupiah cash, which goes to OCI.

The segment note splits the loss into −6,466 from exploration and production, +29 from services and +1,958 of elimination (Note 46, Daftar 5/220, PDF p. 237). The elimination is consistent with intragroup balances between Elnusa and dollar-functional members (section 5); PHE does not explain it.

Note 49 describes PHE's exposure as minimal, because most revenue and operating spending are in dollars (Daftar 5/227, PDF p. 244), and gives a sensitivity: a 5 percent stronger rupiah would raise profit by 19,202 and a 5 percent weaker one lower it by 17,373 at the end of 2024 (Daftar 5/228, PDF p. 245). The asymmetry fits a net rupiah asset.

Implied net rupiah asset, USD thousand = 19,202 / (1 / 0.95 − 1) = 364,838; check: 17,373 / (1 − 1 / 1.05) = 364,833

That is Note 48's net rupiah position without the accrued expenses and other provisions line: (−717,207 + 6,611,848) × 1,000 / 16,157 = 364,835, and for 2023 1,094,259 against 1,094,267. Note 49's sensitivity leaves that line out; PHE does not say why.

11. Upstream note: why a PSC contractor is a dollar company

PHE's PSC subsidiaries sell crude and gas at dollar prices, recover costs in dollars, and borrow in dollars, which makes the dollar their functional currency under section 2. Their rupiah exposure comes from the Indonesian state and the local supply chain: reimbursable VAT claims, taxes payable, rupiah accruals and payables to local contractors, and employee benefits paid in rupiah. Note 25 shows foreign exchange changes of −9,019 on the obligation and −6,802 on plan assets for 2024, a net −2,217 (Daftar 5/122, PDF p. 139), although Note 48 lists no employee-benefit liability. Section 6's tax mismatch is avoided where the contract and the PMK allow dollar books, which the FS do not discuss.

12. Related lines

  • other-comprehensive-income and oci-translation-adjustments: translation of Elnusa, net investment and hedges.

  • other-taxes-receivable-current, other-taxes-receivable-non-current, other-taxes-payable: the largest rupiah monetary items.

  • cash-and-cash-equivalents: rupiah cash and the cash-flow effect of exchange rates.

  • trade-payables, accrued-expenses: rupiah liabilities that offset the assets.

  • advances-prepayments-current: non-monetary prepayments under ISAK 122.

  • deferred-tax-liabilities: temporary differences from rupiah tax bases.

Least-confident assertions

  • Note 49's sensitivity excludes Note 48's accrued expenses and other provisions (it reconciles within 9 in both years) but keeps the tax refund claims and taxes payable, which are not contractual financial instruments either. The basis for the exclusion is not disclosed.

  • Note 48 omits employee benefits; the Note 25 exchange rows may be partly Elnusa's translation. Note 3r also prints the MYR rate as USD 0.27 for 2024 against about 0.22 in the market (not verified).

  • The reconciliation of the 35,715 static loss to the reported 4,479 is a reading. PHE does not split the line into realised and unrealised parts or by currency, and the 2023 loss runs against the year-end position.

  • The indicator scoring in section 2 is an illustration of how the indicators would read. PHE does not disclose how it determined each entity's functional currency, nor the functional currency of the Venezuelan venture.

  • That PHE's PSC subsidiaries keep dollar tax books is inferred from the KKKS entry in PMK 196/2007 as amended. The FS are silent on tax bookkeeping currency.

content.text: Every entity first determines its functional currency, the currency of the economic environment that mainly sets its prices and costs, from evidence the standard ranks. Any other currency is foreign. A Jakarta company can be a dollar company, and a Paris one can be too.

Foreign-currency transactions are recorded at the spot rate on the transaction date. At each reporting date, monetary items (cash, receivables, payables, provisions to be paid in cash) are retranslated at the closing rate and the difference goes to profit or loss. Non-monetary items carried at cost (inventory, fixed assets, prepayments) keep their historical rate.

An exchange loss therefore measures the net monetary position held in a foreign currency and how the rate moved while it was held. A dollar-functional company that holds more rupiah assets than rupiah liabilities loses when the rupiah weakens. Translation of a foreign operation into a presentation currency is a different step that goes to other comprehensive income, and hyperinflation (PSAK 229) adds a restatement before any translation.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report a foreign exchange loss, net, of 4,479 for 2024 against 19,772 for 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). The loss is 0.09 percent of profit before income tax of 4,892,576 (0.44 percent of 4,492,029 in 2023). The line has no note of its own.

After reading it a student should be able to determine an entity's functional currency, record a foreign-currency transaction from invoice to settlement, sort balances into monetary and non-monetary, and explain why a dollar company reports a gain or loss when the rupiah moves.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated; rupiah amounts are in millions. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
A group that buys in rupiah, sells in dollars and reports to a parent abroad needs a rule for which currency its books measure in. PSAK 221
The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates
any currency other than the functional currency
which balances can produce exchange differences
the currency in which the statements are presented

The standard then works in two steps (paras. 17–18). Each entity, parent or subsidiary, measures its own transactions in its functional currency, and exchange differences on its foreign-currency items go to its profit or loss. Where an entity's functional currency differs from the group's presentation currency, its statements are then translated, and that difference goes to other comprehensive income (OCI). The second step is covered in the Other Comprehensive Income essay.

PHE's functional currency is the US dollar for every entity in the group except Elnusa, whose functional currency is the rupiah, and the consolidated statements are presented in dollars (Note 3a, Daftar 5/29, PDF p. 46; Note 3r(i), Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83). For a PHE production-sharing subsidiary the rupiah is a foreign currency, even though it pays Indonesian taxes and Indonesian staff in it.
The standard ranks the evidence for a functional currency, and management weighs it rather than picking a currency it prefers. The

look at operations (para. 9): the currency that mainly influences sales prices, often the currency prices are set and settled in; the currency of the country whose competitive forces and regulations mainly determine those prices; and the currency that mainly influences labour, material and other costs.

look at money (para. 10): the currency in which financing is raised and the currency in which operating receipts are kept. A foreign operation adds a third set (para. 11), centred on whether it is an extension of the parent or works with a significant degree of autonomy. When the indicators are mixed, management judges which currency most faithfully represents the economics, giving the primary indicators priority (para. 12).
For example (illustration), score three kinds of entity in PHE's group against the indicators. The reading of each indicator is this page's; PHE discloses no such analysis.
crude and gas priced in dollars
rigs, contractors and imported materials largely in dollars; staff and local services in rupiah
staff, fuel and local suppliers in rupiah

PHE's Note 1 lists Etablissements Maurel et Prom (M&P), domiciled in Paris and 71.09 percent owned (Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25), and Note 3r gives every entity but Elnusa the dollar as functional currency. Domicile and the currency of tax filings do not decide the matter.

happens only when the underlying transactions change (paras. 13 and 36), and it is accounted for prospectively (para. 35). Every item is translated at the rate on the date of change, and the translated amounts of non-monetary items become their historical cost (para. 37). For example (illustration), a services subsidiary wins long-term dollar contracts and switches from rupiah to dollars on 1 July, when the rate is Rp16,000 per dollar. A rig it carries at Rp80,000 million is then measured at:
80,000 × 1,000 / 16,000 = 5,000, the rig's new historical cost in dollars
Nothing is restated for earlier periods, and the rig's cost is never retranslated again.
3. Initial recognition: the spot rate on the transaction date

A foreign-currency transaction is one denominated in, or requiring settlement in, a foreign currency: buying or selling at a foreign-currency price, borrowing or lending in one, or acquiring assets or incurring liabilities in one (para. 20). It is recorded in the functional currency at the spot rate on the transaction date (para. 21), the date it first qualifies for recognition. An average rate for a week or a month may be used if rates do not fluctuate significantly (para. 22). PHE's policy restates the rule (Note 3r(ii)).

For example (illustration), on 15 November 2024 a PHE subsidiary receives an invoice from a local contractor for well services of Rp16,200 million, due in 90 days, when the rate is Rp15,800 per dollar.
Dr Production expenses 1,025.32 / Cr Trade payables 1,025.32
When an entity pays or receives in advance, ISAK 122
Foreign Currency Transactions and Advance Consideration

(formerly ISAK 33, IFRIC 22) fixes the transaction date as the date the prepayment or deferred income is first recognised. A prepayment is non-monetary (section 4), so the goods later received are measured at the rate of the advance. For example (illustration), the subsidiary prepays Rp1,580 million for chemicals when the rate is Rp15,800.
Dr Advances for purchases 100.00 / Cr Cash 100.00
On delivery, at any later rate: Dr Inventories 100.00 / Cr Advances for purchases 100.00
4. At the reporting date: monetary and non-monetary items

Monetary items follow the exchange rate after a transaction and non-monetary items carried at cost do not. The test is whether the item is a right to receive, or an obligation to deliver, a fixed or determinable number of units of currency (para. 16). Such
are translated at the closing rate, the spot rate at the end of the period.
carried at historical cost keep the rate of the transaction date, and those carried at fair value use the rate when fair value was measured (para. 23).
Monetary: retranslate at the closing rate
Non-monetary at cost: keep the historical rate
fixed assets, oil and gas properties
tax refunds receivable in cash, taxes payable
prepayments and advances for goods or services
employee benefits and provisions to be paid in cash
provisions to be settled by delivering a non-monetary asset

The logic is what each item will turn into. A rupiah receivable will produce a fixed number of rupiah, so its dollar value moves with the rate. A drilling rig bought in rupiah will produce oil, not rupiah, so its dollar cost stays where it was.

Take PHE's balances as the starting point. Note 48 shows rupiah tax refund claims (presented as other taxes receivable) of Rp7,551,277 million at the end of 2023, carried at 489,104, and rupiah taxes payable of Rp2,354,077 million, carried at 152,476 (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242). Both are monetary. PHE's policy names the Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar Rate (JISDOR) as the closing rate (Note 3r(ii)); the amounts in Note 48 imply Rp15,439 per dollar at the end of 2023 and Rp16,157 at the end of 2024, which match the published JISDOR. Suppose, for illustration, both balances had stayed unchanged in rupiah through 2024.
Dr Foreign exchange loss 21,735 / Cr Tax refund claims 21,735
Dr Other taxes payable 6,776 / Cr Foreign exchange gain 6,776
The rupiah lost 4.44 percent of its dollar value (1 − 15,439 / 16,157), and each rupiah asset and liability changed by the same share.
Items measured by comparing two amounts.

For a non-monetary item tested against a recoverable figure, such as inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV), each side is translated at the rate on the date it was determined (para. 25). For example (illustration), spares bought for Rp3,200 million at Rp15,500 have a year-end NRV of Rp3,250 million at Rp16,157.
The spares are worth more rupiah than they cost and still need a write-down in dollars (see the Inventories essay).
5. Settlement, and where the differences go

An exchange difference arises whenever a monetary item is settled, or retranslated, at a rate different from the one last used, and it goes to profit or loss in the period it arises (para. 28). If a transaction is settled in the same period, the whole difference falls there; if it spans a year end, each period takes the part caused by that period's rate change (para. 29). The total is fixed by the rate on the transaction date and the rate on settlement. The year end only splits it.
Return to section 3's invoice of Rp16,200 million booked at 1,025.32. At 31 December 2024 the closing rate is Rp16,157, and the subsidiary pays on 13 February 2025 at, for illustration, Rp16,300.
Total gain = 1,025.32 − 993.87 = 31.45, the two steps before rounding (22.655 + 8.796)
Dr Trade payables 22.66 / Cr Foreign exchange gain 22.66
Dr Trade payables 1,002.66 / Cr Cash 993.87, Cr Foreign exchange gain 8.80
realised: rupiah are bought and paid

The standard does not separate realised from unrealised differences; both are on the same line. The well services stay at 1,025.32 in production expense, because the expense was recognised once, at the transaction-date rate (para. 21).
Three exceptions send exchange differences elsewhere.
Net investment in a foreign operation.

A long-term loan to a foreign operation whose settlement is neither planned nor likely is in substance part of the investment (para. 15). Its exchange differences go to profit or loss in the separate statements but to OCI in the consolidated ones, recycled on disposal (para. 32).

An exchange difference on a monetary item designated as a cash flow hedging instrument goes to OCI to the extent the hedge is effective (para. 27; PSAK 109). The Other Comprehensive Income essay teaches both of these routes.
Non-monetary items with gains in OCI.
When a gain on a non-monetary item goes to OCI, such as a revaluation surplus on a foreign-currency asset, its exchange component goes with it (para. 30).
Intragroup balances do not eliminate the exchange difference.

Consolidation removes intragroup balances, but a monetary item between members with different functional currencies is a commitment to convert one currency into another, so its exchange difference stays in consolidated profit or loss (para. 45). For example (illustration), a dollar-functional PHE subsidiary is owed Rp15,439 million by Elnusa, rupiah-functional, from the end of 2023.
Elnusa: owes Rp15,439 million in both years, no difference
The receivable and payable still cancel on consolidation, but the 44.44 loss stays in the group's profit or loss.

The functional currency decides the accounting books, and the tax law decides the tax books, and in Indonesia the two can differ. The tax administration law requires books in rupiah and in Indonesian unless the Minister of Finance permits a foreign language and a currency other than rupiah (UU KUP art. 28(4) and (8)). Through 2024 the permission rule was PMK 196/PMK.03/2007, last amended by PMK 123/PMK.03/2019, which lists among the taxpayers that may keep books in English and US dollars production-sharing contractors (KKKS), mining contract-of-work holders, companies listed abroad, and taxpayers whose functional currency under Indonesian accounting standards is the dollar. PMK 81/2024 partly revoked it from 1 January 2025; permission now sits in its art. 455(3), and under PER-8/PJ/2025 art. 16 oil and gas contractors only notify, while dollar-functional taxpayers apply.
A company that keeps dollar accounts but rupiah tax books has two currencies inside one tax line. PSAK 212

(formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12) treats the effect of exchange rates on a tax base measured in another currency as a temporary difference, with the deferred tax charged to profit or loss (para. 41). For example (illustration), a dollar-functional subsidiary without dollar tax books owns a compressor bought for Rp154,390 million when the rate was Rp15,439, so its accounting cost is 10,000; ignore depreciation, and take the 22 percent Indonesian corporate rate.
Taxable temporary difference = 10,000.00 − 9,555.61 = 444.39; deferred tax liability = 444.39 × 22% = 97.77
Dr Deferred tax expense 97.77 / Cr Deferred tax liability 97.77

The rupiah's fall cut the future tax deductions measured in dollars, so tax expense rises with no change in the asset. A contractor allowed dollar tax books avoids this mismatch on its fixed assets (see the Deferred Tax essay).

An entity may present its statements in any currency (para. 38). If that differs from its functional currency, it translates assets and liabilities at the closing rate, income and expenses at the rates on the transaction dates (an average rate is a common approximation, para. 40), and puts the resulting difference in OCI (para. 39). It must state the functional currency and the reason for presenting in another (para. 53). A dollar-functional company presenting in rupiah would carry a translation reserve though its business never changed.

The same procedure brings a foreign operation into consolidated statements. For PHE that means Elnusa, translated from rupiah into dollars with the difference in OCI and recycled when the operation is sold. The Other Comprehensive Income essay works it through with PHE's 2024 translation adjustments of −14,810.
8. Hyperinflation and currencies that cannot be exchanged
In a hyperinflationary economy historical amounts stop meaning anything, so translation alone would mislead. PSAK 229

(formerly PSAK 63, IAS 29) gives no single threshold. Its indicators include people keeping wealth in a stable foreign currency, prices quoted in that currency, and cumulative inflation over three years approaching or exceeding 100 percent (para. 3). An entity whose functional currency is hyperinflationary restates its statements into the measuring unit current at the reporting date (para. 8). Monetary items are not restated, because they are already in current units (para. 12). Non-monetary items at cost are restated by a general price index from their acquisition date (paras. 14–15). Holding net monetary assets through inflation loses purchasing power, and the gain or loss on the net monetary position goes to profit or loss (paras. 27–28).

For example (illustration), an entity holds net monetary assets of 1,000 in local currency all year while the general price index rises from 120 to 180, and owns land bought for 2,000 when the index was 100.

Only after restatement are the statements translated, all amounts at the latest closing rate (PSAK 221.42–43). An entity cannot avoid restatement by adopting its parent's currency (PSAK 221.14). PHE states that none of its subsidiaries has a hyperinflationary functional currency (Note 3r(iii), Daftar 5/67, PDF p. 84). Note 2d lists a 40 percent interest, held through the group, in Petroregional del Lago Mixed Company in Venezuela (Daftar 5/21, PDF p. 38), but the FS do not give that venture's functional currency.

The 2023 amendments to IAS 21 require an entity to estimate a spot rate when a currency cannot be obtained through a normal exchange mechanism, and to disclose the effects (paras. 8A–8B, 19A, 57A). PHE lists the matching amendment to PSAK 221 as effective from 1 January 2025 and says it is assessing the impact (Note 3b, Daftar 5/31, PDF p. 48).

Coal is priced in dollars, so a miner whose costs and debt are also in dollars finds the dollar functional under section 2, and it may keep dollar tax books under the same PMK list. Its exposure mirrors PHE's: rupiah VAT refunds, royalties and taxes payable, and local contractor payables. A miner with net rupiah liabilities gains when the rupiah weakens.
Palm oil is priced against dollar and ringgit benchmarks while estate costs are in rupiah, so para. 12's judgement decides.

Aircraft leases, fuel and maintenance are priced in dollars, and Garuda Indonesia keeps its financial statements in dollars, so for it the rupiah is the foreign currency. For a rupiah-functional airline the mismatch is built into the lease accounting, because the lease liability is monetary and the right-of-use asset is not (PSAK 116; see the Right-of-Use Assets essay). For example (illustration), a rupiah airline leases an aircraft with a liability of USD 100 million at Rp15,439 at the end of 2023; ignore payments and interest.
Liability at end 2024 = 100 × 16,157 = Rp1,615,700 million; at end 2023 = 100 × 15,439 = Rp1,543,900 million
Exchange loss = Rp71,800 million; the right-of-use asset stays at Rp1,543,900 million less depreciation

A rupiah-functional bank revalues its foreign-currency positions daily, and the differences are trading results. Bank Indonesia caps the net open position, assets less liabilities in foreign currency including off-balance-sheet positions, at 20 percent of capital (PBI 5/13/PBI/2003 as last amended by PBI 17/5/PBI/2015). For example (illustration), a bank with capital of Rp10,000,000 million is long USD 120 million.
Position at end 2023 = 120 × 15,439 = Rp1,852,680 million, 18.5% of capital
At end 2024 = 120 × 16,157 = Rp1,938,840 million, 19.4% of capital; revaluation gain Rp86,160 million
The weakening that gives the bank a gain also pushes it toward the limit without a single new trade.

11. Upstream note: why a PSC contractor is a dollar company

PHE's PSC subsidiaries sell crude and gas at dollar prices, recover costs in dollars, and borrow in dollars, which makes the dollar their functional currency under section 2. Their rupiah exposure comes from the Indonesian state and the local supply chain: reimbursable VAT claims, taxes payable, rupiah accruals and payables to local contractors, and employee benefits paid in rupiah. Note 25 shows foreign exchange changes of −9,019 on the obligation and −6,802 on plan assets for 2024, a net −2,217 (Daftar 5/122, PDF p. 139), although Note 48 lists no employee-benefit liability. Section 6's tax mismatch is avoided where the contract and the PMK allow dollar books, which the FS do not discuss.
: translation of Elnusa, net investment and hedges.

Note 49's sensitivity excludes Note 48's accrued expenses and other provisions (it reconciles within 9 in both years) but keeps the tax refund claims and taxes payable, which are not contractual financial instruments either. The basis for the exclusion is not disclosed.
Note 48 omits employee benefits; the Note 25 exchange rows may be partly Elnusa's translation. Note 3r also prints the MYR rate as USD 0.27 for 2024 against about 0.22 in the market (not verified).

The reconciliation of the 35,715 static loss to the reported 4,479 is a reading. PHE does not split the line into realised and unrealised parts or by currency, and the 2023 loss runs against the year-end position.

The indicator scoring in section 2 is an illustration of how the indicators would read. PHE does not disclose how it determined each entity's functional currency, nor the functional currency of the Venezuelan venture.
That PHE's PSC subsidiaries keep dollar tax books is inferred from the KKKS entry in PMK 196/2007 as amended. The FS are silent on tax bookkeeping currency.

presentation.deck: The theory of foreign-currency transactions from choosing a functional currency to hyperinflation, worked through PHE's rupiah balances and set beside the industries that live with a currency mismatch
key_takeaways: Every entity first determines its functional currency, the currency of the economic environment that mainly sets its prices and costs, from evidence the standard ranks. Any other currency is foreign. A Jakarta company can be a dollar company, and a Paris one can be too.

Foreign-currency transactions are recorded at the spot rate on the transaction date. At each reporting date, monetary items (cash, receivables, payables, provisions to be paid in cash) are retranslated at the closing rate and the difference goes to profit or loss. Non-monetary items carried at cost (inventory, fixed assets, prepayments) keep their historical rate.

An exchange loss therefore measures the net monetary position held in a foreign currency and how the rate moved while it was held. A dollar-functional company that holds more rupiah assets than rupiah liabilities loses when the rupiah weakens. Translation of a foreign operation into a presentation currency is a different step that goes to other comprehensive income, and hyperinflation (PSAK 229) adds a restatement before any translation.

title: Impairment of Non-Financial Assets: Indicators, Recoverable Amount, Cash-Generating Units and Reversal
snippet: The theory of PSAK 236 from scope to disclosure, worked through PHE's oil and gas blocks and set beside the industries where the test bites hardest
content:
In brief

  • An asset may not be carried at more than the entity can get back from it. PSAK 236 checks this in three steps. The entity looks for indications at every reporting date, estimates the recoverable amount (the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use) when there is one, and writes the asset down to that amount if it is below the carrying amount.

  • Most long-lived assets do not earn cash on their own, so the test usually runs on a cash-generating unit (CGU). A CGU's loss goes first to its goodwill and then pro rata to its other assets, and no asset is pushed below its own recoverable amount or zero.

  • An impairment loss on any asset except goodwill is reversed when the estimates behind recoverable amount improve, but only up to the carrying amount the asset would have had with no impairment. The passage of time alone is not a reason to reverse.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report a provision for impairment of non-financial assets of 215,666 for 2024 against 707,087 for 2023, in USD thousand, on a line of its own below gross profit (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). The charge is 1.5 percent of revenue and 4.3 percent of gross profit in 2024, against 4.9 and 12.5 percent in 2023.

After reading this page a student should be able to decide when an asset must be tested, compute a recoverable amount, allocate a CGU's loss and its reversal, and record each step in journals.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What impairment is and which assets PSAK 236 covers

Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its life without asking whether that cost will come back. Impairment asks. PSAK 236 Penurunan Nilai Aset (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) requires that an asset be carried at no more than its recoverable amount, the amount to be recovered through use or sale (para. 1). An impairment loss is the excess of carrying amount over recoverable amount (para. 6).

The standard covers what other standards leave out (para. 2). Inventories follow the lower of cost and NRV in PSAK 202, financial assets the expected credit loss model of PSAK 109, and deferred tax, employee benefit and contract assets, investment property at fair value, biological assets at fair value less costs to sell and assets held for sale their own standards. What remains is the core of a balance sheet: fixed assets, oil and gas properties, right-of-use assets, intangibles, goodwill, and investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures (para. 4).

US GAAP tests in two steps. A recoverability test first compares carrying amount with the undiscounted cash flows the asset will produce; only if it fails is the asset written down to fair value. IFRS goes straight to a discounted measure. For example (illustration), a production facility carried at 500,000 is expected to produce undiscounted net cash flows of 560,000. A buyer would pay 430,000 net of costs, and the present value of its cash flows is 450,000.

US GAAP (two steps)

PSAK 236 (one step)

Test

Undiscounted cash flows 560,000 > carrying amount 500,000: passes

Recoverable amount = higher of 430,000 and 450,000 = 450,000

Loss

none

500,000 − 450,000 = 50,000

The undiscounted test ignores the time value of money, so an asset whose cash arrives slowly passes it while worth less than its carrying amount. PSAK 236 catches that asset earlier and, as section 8 shows, lets the loss come back if conditions improve; US GAAP forbids reversal for assets held and used.

2. When an asset must be tested

At the end of each reporting period the entity assesses whether there is any indication of impairment, and only if there is does it estimate recoverable amount (para. 9).

The minimum list of indications has two halves (para. 12).

  • External: a market value that has fallen more than time and use explain; adverse changes in the technological, market, economic or legal environment; higher market interest rates that raise the discount rate and lower recoverable amount materially; net assets above market capitalisation.

  • Internal: obsolescence or physical damage; an asset becoming idle, a plan to discontinue or restructure, a plan to dispose of it early; internal reports showing performance worse than expected, such as cash needs above budget or actual cash flows below it (para. 14).

Upstream, the usual triggers are price, discount rate, reserves and delays (section 11). Materiality applies. If earlier calculations showed recoverable amount well above carrying amount and nothing has happened to close the gap, no new estimate is needed (para. 15). An indication that leads to no loss may still call for a shorter useful life or a different depreciation method (para. 17).

Goodwill, intangibles with indefinite lives and intangibles not yet available for use are tested every year whether or not there is an indication (para. 10). PHE's policy follows the same split (Note 3w, Daftar 5/72, PDF p. 89).

3. Recoverable amount and fair value less costs of disposal

Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal (FVLCD) and value in use (VIU) (para. 18). A rational owner either sells the asset or keeps using it, whichever is worth more, so the asset is impaired only if both routes fall short. If either measure exceeds the carrying amount, the other need not be computed (para. 19).

Fair value is the exit price between market participants under PSAK 113 (formerly PSAK 68, IFRS 13). Costs of disposal are the incremental costs of selling, such as legal costs, transfer taxes and the cost of removing the asset; termination benefits and the cost of reorganising what remains are not (para. 28). Once an asset meets the held-for-sale criteria it leaves PSAK 236 for PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5).

For example (illustration), take as the starting point PHE's East Kalimantan and Attaka block, carried at 369,670 and written down in 2024 to an estimated recoverable amount of 305,466 (Note 17). Suppose a buyer had offered 330,000 for the participating interest, with 2,000 of legal costs and 3,000 of transfer charges.

FVLCD = 330,000 − 2,000 − 3,000 = 325,000

Recoverable amount = higher of 325,000 and 305,466 = 325,000

Impairment loss = 369,670 − 325,000 = 44,670, against 369,670 − 305,466 = 64,204 if, as PHE's figure implies, nothing above 305,466 were available

The 19,534 difference is why the standard asks which basis was used (para. 130(e)).

4. Value in use

VIU is the present value of the cash flows the entity expects from the asset (para. 6). It is entity-specific, so unlike fair value it may reflect synergies and rights only the current owner has (para. 53A). The standard builds it from five elements: expected cash flows, possible variations in their amount and timing, the time value of money, the price of bearing uncertainty, and other factors such as illiquidity (para. 30). Uncertainty may be reflected either in the cash flows or in the rate, but not in both (para. 32).

Cash flow rules. Four rules shape the projections.

  • Projections rest on reasonable and supportable assumptions, with greater weight on external evidence, and on approved budgets for at most five years unless a longer period can be justified (para. 33).

  • Cash flows are for the asset in its current condition. Inflows from a restructuring the entity is not committed to, or from spending that would enhance the asset, are left out (para. 44), while spending to maintain its current performance is included (para. 49).

  • Financing flows and income tax are left out (para. 50), because the rate already prices money and is set before tax. Cash flows of recognised liabilities, such as a decommissioning provision, are left out to avoid counting them twice (para. 43(b)); section 5 shows the exception.

  • Foreign-currency cash flows are discounted at a rate for that currency and translated at the spot rate on the test date (para. 54).

A pre-tax market rate. The discount rate is set before tax and reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks not already in the cash flows (para. 55). It is the return investors would require for cash flows of the same amount, timing and risk, often estimated from the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) of comparable listed entities (para. 56).

For example (illustration), a block's net entitlement production is 6,000 thousand barrels in 2025, declining 10 percent a year, and the contract ends after 2029. Prices follow PHE's 2024 ICP (Indonesian Crude Price) assumption of USD 73.73 to 81.56 per barrel (Note 17, Daftar 5/111, PDF p. 128). Operating and maintenance spending is USD 30 per barrel. The rate is 10.00 percent, PHE's 2024 rate. Cash flow = production × (price − 30).

A rise of 0.55 points in the rate costs 11,915 of value; a USD 5 cut in the price path costs 95,003. That is why the standard calls the price path and the rate key assumptions, those to which recoverable amount is most sensitive (para. 134(d)).

5. Cash-generating units

A well, a pipeline and a platform cannot each be valued on their own, because none of them sells oil alone. When an asset's recoverable amount cannot be estimated individually, it is estimated for its cash-generating unit, the smallest identifiable group of assets whose cash inflows are largely independent of those of other assets (paras. 6, 66).

Identifying a CGU is judgement (para. 68), and the standard gives three guides. The entity looks at how management monitors operations and decides what to keep or sell (para. 69). If an active market exists for the output of a group of assets, that group is a CGU even if the output is used internally (para. 70). And CGUs are identified consistently from period to period (para. 72). In the standard's own example, a bus company obliged by contract to run five routes has one CGU for all five, because it cannot close the loss-making route alone (para. 68). In an upstream group the usual unit is the contract area. PHE treats its participating interest in each block as one CGU (Note 17, Daftar 5/110, PDF p. 127).

Carrying amount on the same basis. The CGU's carrying amount must be built the same way as its recoverable amount (para. 75). It normally excludes recognised liabilities, but when a buyer would have to take a liability over, the liability is deducted from both sides (para. 78). Upstream, the decommissioning provision is the main case.

For example (illustration), a block is carried at 800,000, which includes capitalised decommissioning cost, and the decommissioning provision is 200,000. A buyer offers 580,000 and would take over the obligation; disposal costs are negligible. VIU before decommissioning outflows is 750,000.

FVLCD = 580,000 (already net of the obligation)

VIU = 750,000 − 200,000 = 550,000

Carrying amount of the CGU = 800,000 − 200,000 = 600,000

Impairment loss = 600,000 − higher of (580,000, 550,000) = 20,000

Comparing the 580,000 offer with the gross 800,000 would show a loss of 220,000, charging the obligation against the block while the provision stays on the balance sheet.

6. Recognising and allocating an impairment loss

For an individual asset at cost, the loss is the shortfall and goes to profit or loss immediately (paras. 59–60). Later depreciation is recomputed on the reduced carrying amount over the remaining life (para. 63), and deferred tax is recomputed against the new carrying amount (para. 64). For a revalued asset the loss is first charged against that asset's revaluation surplus in other comprehensive income (para. 61). A loss of 20 on land with a surplus of 15 is Dr Revaluation surplus (OCI) 15, Dr Impairment loss 5 / Cr Land 20.

The loss may be credited directly to the asset or to an allowance for impairment, a contra account. PHE uses the allowance ("penyisihan penurunan nilai") inside each asset's movement table (Note 17), so cost stays visible, and names the expense "provision for impairment of non-financial assets"; this page calls it impairment loss.

Allocation within a CGU. A CGU's loss must be spread over its assets in a fixed order (para. 104). It goes first to any goodwill allocated to the unit, then to the other assets pro rata to their carrying amounts. No asset may go below the highest of its FVLCD, its VIU and zero, and what cannot be absorbed is reallocated to the others (para. 105). PHE's Note 17 block tables carry a goodwill column for this first step, nil for every impaired block.

For example (illustration), a block CGU holds goodwill 20,000, wells 300,000, installations 150,000 and a field office with camp 50,000 whose FVLCD is 48,000. Recoverable amount is 400,000.

Carrying amount = 20,000 + 300,000 + 150,000 + 50,000 = 520,000; loss = 520,000 − 400,000 = 120,000

Step 1, goodwill: 20,000; remaining 100,000

Step 2, pro rata over 500,000: wells 60,000, installations 30,000, office 10,000

Step 3, floor: the office can lose only 50,000 − 48,000 = 2,000; the other 8,000 goes to wells and installations 300 : 150

Wells = 60,000 + 8,000 × 300/450 = 65,333; installations = 30,000 + 8,000 × 150/450 = 32,667

Debit

Credit

Impairment loss 120,000

Allowance for impairment, goodwill 20,000

Allowance for impairment, wells 65,333

Allowance for impairment, installations 32,667

Allowance for impairment, field office 2,000

7. Goodwill and corporate assets

Goodwill and head-office assets produce no cash flows of their own, so neither can be tested alone. Both are pushed down into CGUs.

Goodwill. From the acquisition date goodwill is allocated to the CGUs, or groups of CGUs, expected to benefit from the combination's synergies, at the lowest level at which management monitors it and never above an operating segment (para. 80). Each unit carrying goodwill is tested every year, at the same time each year, and whenever there is an indication (paras. 90, 96), after the assets and smaller units inside it (paras. 97–98). How goodwill arises and is first measured is taught in the Intangible Assets essay.

Corporate assets. A headquarters building, a data centre or a research facility contributes to several CGUs. Where a portion can be allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis, each CGU is tested with its share; otherwise the CGU is tested alone and the corporate asset is tested with the smallest group of CGUs it can be allocated to (para. 102).

For example (illustration), a regional office carried at 60,000 serves three blocks carried at 200,000 (A), 300,000 (B) and 500,000 (C), and is allocated by carrying amount. Recoverable amounts are 230,000, 290,000 and 560,000.

Shares of the office: A 12,000, B 18,000, C 30,000

A: 212,000 < 230,000, no loss; C: 530,000 < 560,000, no loss

B: 318,000 − 290,000 = 28,000 loss; to block B assets 28,000 × 300/318 = 26,415 and to the office 28,000 × 18/318 = 1,585

Without the office share, block B (300,000 against 290,000) would show a loss of only 10,000.

8. Reversing an impairment loss

Impairment losses rest on estimates, so they can come back. At each reporting date the entity asks whether a past loss on any asset other than goodwill may have decreased, using indications that mirror those of section 2: higher prices, lower market rates, favourable changes in how the asset is used (paras. 110–111). A loss is reversed only if the estimates used to measure recoverable amount have changed (para. 114). VIU rises every year because the cash flows come closer, and that unwinding of the discount is not a reason to reverse (para. 116).

The reversal has a ceiling. The new carrying amount may not exceed what the carrying amount would have been, net of depreciation, had no loss been recognised (para. 117). The reversal goes to profit or loss unless the asset is revalued (para. 119), and depreciation is recomputed afterwards (para. 121). For a CGU the reversal is spread pro rata over its assets except goodwill (para. 122). Goodwill impairment is never reversed (para. 124), because a later rise in the unit's value is likely to be internally generated goodwill, which may not be recognised (para. 125). An impairment of goodwill booked at an interim date is not reversed at year end either (ISAK 110, formerly ISAK 17, IFRIC 10).

For example (illustration), take a block with no earlier impairment, carried at 369,670 and written down to 305,466, the 2024 figures for East Kalimantan and Attaka. Suppose it depletes one fifth of its remaining carrying amount in 2025 and, at the end of 2025, a higher price forecast lifts its recoverable amount to 320,000.

Carrying amount after impairment and 2025 depletion = 305,466 × 4/5 = 244,373

Carrying amount had there been no impairment = 369,670 × 4/5 = 295,736

Reversal = 295,736 − 244,373 = 51,363 (the uncapped 320,000 − 244,373 = 75,627 is not allowed)

Dr Allowance for impairment, oil and gas properties 51,363 / Cr Reversal of impairment loss 51,363

PHE's real block was also impaired in 2023, as the PHKT block (92,607; Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129), so its ceiling would add that loss back too, net of the depletion it would have borne.

9. Exploration and evaluation assets

Exploration assets are tested under a modified regime. PSAK 106 (formerly PSAK 64, IFRS 6) replaces the indications of section 2 with its own list: an expiring exploration right, no further substantive exploration budgeted, no commercially viable discovery, or a development unlikely to recover the E&E cost in full (paras. 18–20). E&E assets may be grouped into CGUs no larger than an operating segment (para. 21), and they are tested before they are reclassified to development (para. 17). Measurement follows PSAK 236; the Oil and Gas Properties essay covers the E&E test in full.

10. Impairment across industries

Mining. A coal or nickel miner tests a mine as a CGU with the same inputs as an oil field (a commodity price path, reserves, cost per tonne and a discount rate) and treats its restoration provision as in section 5.

Plantations. Oil palms are bearer plants, fixed assets under PSAK 216, and so fall under PSAK 236; the fresh fruit bunches growing on them are biological assets at fair value less costs to sell under PSAK 241 and are outside it. The CGU question turns on para. 70. An estate that sends all its bunches to the group's own mill is still a separate CGU if bunches trade in an active market, and its VIU must use market prices for bunches, not the internal transfer price.

Telecom towers. Tenancy contracts often cover many towers at once, so a single tower's inflows are rarely independent and towers are grouped. Falling tenancy per tower is the usual indicator.

Retail stores. Each store is often a CGU, since management decides store by store whether to close. Under PSAK 116 the store's right-of-use asset sits inside the CGU, and the lease liability is excluded unless it is deducted on both sides. For example (illustration), a store with leasehold improvements of 2,000 and a right-of-use asset of 6,000 has a VIU, before lease payments, of 7,000. The loss is 8,000 − 7,000 = 1,000. Deducting the lease liability of 6,500 from both sides gives 1,500 − 500 = 1,000 as well, which is the point of paras. 78–79.

Shipping. A vessel usually is its own CGU when it trades on the spot market. For example (illustration), a tanker carried at 40,000 has a broker value of 31,000 less 500 of selling costs and a VIU of 34,000. Recoverable amount is 34,000 and the loss 6,000.

11. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 12, 16, 17 and 46

PHE's 215,666 comes from Notes 17 and 12; Notes 16 and 13 report none, and the segment note confirms the total. PSAK 236 asks for this by class, segment and material CGU (paras. 126, 129–130).

Para. 134, with the sensitivity of 134(f), applies to CGUs carrying significant goodwill. PHE's remaining goodwill (ONWJ, Note 13, Daftar 5/104, PDF p. 121) is small against the group, and PHE gives no such disclosure.

12. Upstream note: what the contract does to the test

A PSC block has a fixed term, so VIU runs to the earlier of the end of economic production and the end of the contract; an extension enters only if it is supportable, with greater weight on external evidence (para. 33(a)). The cash flows are the contractor's entitlement: cost recovery plus its share of the remaining production, less the crude it must supply to the domestic market at the DMO price (Note 2a(iii)–(v), Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). That is why the price path and the cost base enter the test together.

13. Related lines

  • oil-gas-properties-net: the allowance for impairment of 2,242,412 and the E&E test.

  • fixed-assets-net: the allowance of 5,449 and the reversal mechanics on a single asset.

  • intangible-assets-net: goodwill, its allocation to CGUs and the annual test.

  • long-term-investments: the Malaysian and Iraqi block investments and associates tested under PSAK 236.

  • depreciation-depletion-amortization: the charge that falls after an impairment and rises after a reversal.

  • decommissioning-site-restoration-provision: the liability that must be treated consistently in a CGU test.

  • right-of-use-assets-net: leased assets inside a CGU.

Least-confident assertions

  • The 215,666 reconciles only if the 5,350 in the "deductions" column of Note 17's allowance reduces the charge, as the segment note's 215,549 implies. Note 17 does not label it as a reversal, and two features weigh against one. The 5,350 sits in the deductions column with derecognised cost (304,224) and accumulated DD&A (21,382), and the block table's recovery column shows none. If it is allowance released on derecognised assets, netting it in the impairment line understates the charge by 5,350.

  • The 2023 line (707,087) equals Note 17's oil and gas impairment alone. Note 12 reports a 2023 fixed-asset impairment of 319 and Note 16 one of 2,263 on the Malaysian block investment, and neither appears in the 2023 line or in the segment note. The 2,263 probably sits in the 2023 DD&A line, which cites Note 16a and exceeds its identifiable components by 2,267 (the reconciliation in the Oil and Gas Properties essay). No home for the 319 was found.

  • Note 17 has internal slips. The English text gives the 2024 loss as US$257,554 against 220,899 in the Indonesian text and the table, both languages say the test was performed "on 31 December 2023" in the 2024 note, the 2023 block table totals 707,088 against 707,087, and policy 3m refers to impairment "Note 2w" where the policy is 3w. The "corrections" column of the allowance (+105,527) is not explained.

  • That the 2023 "PHKT block" is the 2024 "East Kalimantan and Attaka" block is read from Note 1, where PHKT holds the East Kalimantan block; Note 17 uses different names in the two years.

  • The upstream points in section 12 (contract term as the VIU horizon, entitlement cash flows) are this page's application of paras. 33 and 39 to a PSC. PHE does not describe how its cash flows are built.

  • The industry practices in section 10 (tower grouping, store-level CGUs, vessel CGUs) are common practice described from knowledge, not from a named company's statements.
