content.text: An asset may not be carried at more than the entity can get back from it. PSAK 236 checks this in three steps. The entity looks for indications at every reporting date, estimates the
(the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use) when there is one, and writes the asset down to that amount if it is below the carrying amount.
Most long-lived assets do not earn cash on their own, so the test usually runs on a
(CGU). A CGU's loss goes first to its goodwill and then pro rata to its other assets, and no asset is pushed below its own recoverable amount or zero.

An impairment loss on any asset except goodwill is reversed when the estimates behind recoverable amount improve, but only up to the carrying amount the asset would have had with no impairment. The passage of time alone is not a reason to reverse.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report a provision for impairment of non-financial assets of 215,666 for 2024 against 707,087 for 2023, in USD thousand, on a line of its own below gross profit (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). The charge is 1.5 percent of revenue and 4.3 percent of gross profit in 2024, against 4.9 and 12.5 percent in 2023.
After reading this page a student should be able to decide when an asset must be tested, compute a recoverable amount, allocate a CGU's loss and its reversal, and record each step in journals.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. What impairment is and which assets PSAK 236 covers
Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its life without asking whether that cost will come back. Impairment asks. PSAK 236
(formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) requires that an asset be carried at no more than its recoverable amount, the amount to be recovered through use or sale (para. 1). An
is the excess of carrying amount over recoverable amount (para. 6).

The standard covers what other standards leave out (para. 2). Inventories follow the lower of cost and NRV in PSAK 202, financial assets the expected credit loss model of PSAK 109, and deferred tax, employee benefit and contract assets, investment property at fair value, biological assets at fair value less costs to sell and assets held for sale their own standards. What remains is the core of a balance sheet: fixed assets, oil and gas properties, right-of-use assets, intangibles, goodwill, and investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures (para. 4).
US GAAP tests in two steps. A

first compares carrying amount with the undiscounted cash flows the asset will produce; only if it fails is the asset written down to fair value. IFRS goes straight to a discounted measure. For example (illustration), a production facility carried at 500,000 is expected to produce undiscounted net cash flows of 560,000. A buyer would pay 430,000 net of costs, and the present value of its cash flows is 450,000.
Undiscounted cash flows 560,000 > carrying amount 500,000: passes

The undiscounted test ignores the time value of money, so an asset whose cash arrives slowly passes it while worth less than its carrying amount. PSAK 236 catches that asset earlier and, as section 8 shows, lets the loss come back if conditions improve; US GAAP forbids reversal for assets held and used.
2. When an asset must be tested
At the end of each reporting period the entity assesses whether there is any
of impairment, and only if there is does it estimate recoverable amount (para. 9).
The minimum list of indications has two halves (para. 12).

: a market value that has fallen more than time and use explain; adverse changes in the technological, market, economic or legal environment; higher market interest rates that raise the discount rate and lower recoverable amount materially; net assets above market capitalisation.

: obsolescence or physical damage; an asset becoming idle, a plan to discontinue or restructure, a plan to dispose of it early; internal reports showing performance worse than expected, such as cash needs above budget or actual cash flows below it (para. 14).

Upstream, the usual triggers are price, discount rate, reserves and delays (section 11). Materiality applies. If earlier calculations showed recoverable amount well above carrying amount and nothing has happened to close the gap, no new estimate is needed (para. 15). An indication that leads to no loss may still call for a shorter useful life or a different depreciation method (para. 17).

Goodwill, intangibles with indefinite lives and intangibles not yet available for use are tested every year whether or not there is an indication (para. 10). PHE's policy follows the same split (Note 3w, Daftar 5/72, PDF p. 89).
3. Recoverable amount and fair value less costs of disposal
Recoverable amount is the higher of
fair value less costs of disposal

(VIU) (para. 18). A rational owner either sells the asset or keeps using it, whichever is worth more, so the asset is impaired only if both routes fall short. If either measure exceeds the carrying amount, the other need not be computed (para. 19).
is the exit price between market participants under PSAK 113 (formerly PSAK 68, IFRS 13).

are the incremental costs of selling, such as legal costs, transfer taxes and the cost of removing the asset; termination benefits and the cost of reorganising what remains are not (para. 28). Once an asset meets the held-for-sale criteria it leaves PSAK 236 for PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5).

For example (illustration), take as the starting point PHE's East Kalimantan and Attaka block, carried at 369,670 and written down in 2024 to an estimated recoverable amount of 305,466 (Note 17). Suppose a buyer had offered 330,000 for the participating interest, with 2,000 of legal costs and 3,000 of transfer charges.
Impairment loss = 369,670 − 325,000 = 44,670, against 369,670 − 305,466 = 64,204 if, as PHE's figure implies, nothing above 305,466 were available
The 19,534 difference is why the standard asks which basis was used (para. 130(e)).

VIU is the present value of the cash flows the entity expects from the asset (para. 6). It is entity-specific, so unlike fair value it may reflect synergies and rights only the current owner has (para. 53A). The standard builds it from five elements: expected cash flows, possible variations in their amount and timing, the time value of money, the price of bearing uncertainty, and other factors such as illiquidity (para. 30). Uncertainty may be reflected either in the cash flows or in the rate, but not in both (para. 32).

Projections rest on reasonable and supportable assumptions, with greater weight on external evidence, and on approved budgets for at most five years unless a longer period can be justified (para. 33).
Cash flows are for the asset

. Inflows from a restructuring the entity is not committed to, or from spending that would enhance the asset, are left out (para. 44), while spending to maintain its current performance is included (para. 49).

Financing flows and income tax are left out (para. 50), because the rate already prices money and is set before tax. Cash flows of recognised liabilities, such as a decommissioning provision, are left out to avoid counting them twice (para. 43(b)); section 5 shows the exception.
Foreign-currency cash flows are discounted at a rate for that currency and translated at the spot rate on the test date (para. 54).

The discount rate is set before tax and reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks not already in the cash flows (para. 55). It is the return investors would require for cash flows of the same amount, timing and risk, often estimated from the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) of comparable listed entities (para. 56).

For example (illustration), a block's net entitlement production is 6,000 thousand barrels in 2025, declining 10 percent a year, and the contract ends after 2029. Prices follow PHE's 2024 ICP (Indonesian Crude Price) assumption of USD 73.73 to 81.56 per barrel (Note 17, Daftar 5/111, PDF p. 128). Operating and maintenance spending is USD 30 per barrel. The rate is 10.00 percent, PHE's 2024 rate. Cash flow = production × (price − 30).
If the block is carried at 900,000:
At PHE's 2023 rate of 9.45%, VIU = 889,923 and the loss = 10,077
At 10.00% with every price USD 5 lower, VIU = 783,005 and the loss = 116,995
A rise of 0.55 points in the rate costs 11,915 of value; a USD 5 cut in the price path costs 95,003. That is why the standard calls the price path and the rate
, those to which recoverable amount is most sensitive (para. 134(d)).

A well, a pipeline and a platform cannot each be valued on their own, because none of them sells oil alone. When an asset's recoverable amount cannot be estimated individually, it is estimated for its
, the smallest identifiable group of assets whose cash inflows are largely independent of those of other assets (paras. 6, 66).

Identifying a CGU is judgement (para. 68), and the standard gives three guides. The entity looks at how management monitors operations and decides what to keep or sell (para. 69). If an active market exists for the output of a group of assets, that group is a CGU even if the output is used internally (para. 70). And CGUs are identified consistently from period to period (para. 72). In the standard's own example, a bus company obliged by contract to run five routes has one CGU for all five, because it cannot close the loss-making route alone (para. 68). In an upstream group the usual unit is the contract area. PHE treats its participating interest in each block as one CGU (Note 17, Daftar 5/110, PDF p. 127).
Carrying amount on the same basis.

The CGU's carrying amount must be built the same way as its recoverable amount (para. 75). It normally excludes recognised liabilities, but when a buyer would have to take a liability over, the liability is deducted from both sides (para. 78). Upstream, the decommissioning provision is the main case.

For example (illustration), a block is carried at 800,000, which includes capitalised decommissioning cost, and the decommissioning provision is 200,000. A buyer offers 580,000 and would take over the obligation; disposal costs are negligible. VIU before decommissioning outflows is 750,000.
Comparing the 580,000 offer with the gross 800,000 would show a loss of 220,000, charging the obligation against the block while the provision stays on the balance sheet.
6. Recognising and allocating an impairment loss

For an individual asset at cost, the loss is the shortfall and goes to profit or loss immediately (paras. 59–60). Later depreciation is recomputed on the reduced carrying amount over the remaining life (para. 63), and deferred tax is recomputed against the new carrying amount (para. 64). For a revalued asset the loss is first charged against that asset's revaluation surplus in other comprehensive income (para. 61). A loss of 20 on land with a surplus of 15 is Dr Revaluation surplus (OCI) 15, Dr Impairment loss 5 / Cr Land 20.
The loss may be credited directly to the asset or to an

, a contra account. PHE uses the allowance ("penyisihan penurunan nilai") inside each asset's movement table (Note 17), so cost stays visible, and names the expense "provision for impairment of non-financial assets"; this page calls it

A CGU's loss must be spread over its assets in a fixed order (para. 104). It goes first to any goodwill allocated to the unit, then to the other assets pro rata to their carrying amounts. No asset may go below the highest of its FVLCD, its VIU and zero, and what cannot be absorbed is reallocated to the others (para. 105). PHE's Note 17 block tables carry a goodwill column for this first step, nil for every impaired block.
For example (illustration), a block CGU holds goodwill 20,000, wells 300,000, installations 150,000 and a field office with camp 50,000 whose FVLCD is 48,000. Recoverable amount is 400,000.
Step 2, pro rata over 500,000: wells 60,000, installations 30,000, office 10,000
Step 3, floor: the office can lose only 50,000 − 48,000 = 2,000; the other 8,000 goes to wells and installations 300 : 150
Goodwill and head-office assets produce no cash flows of their own, so neither can be tested alone. Both are pushed down into CGUs.

From the acquisition date goodwill is allocated to the CGUs, or groups of CGUs, expected to benefit from the combination's synergies, at the lowest level at which management monitors it and never above an operating segment (para. 80). Each unit carrying goodwill is tested every year, at the same time each year, and whenever there is an indication (paras. 90, 96), after the assets and smaller units inside it (paras. 97–98). How goodwill arises and is first measured is taught in the Intangible Assets essay.

A headquarters building, a data centre or a research facility contributes to several CGUs. Where a portion can be allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis, each CGU is tested with its share; otherwise the CGU is tested alone and the corporate asset is tested with the smallest group of CGUs it can be allocated to (para. 102).

For example (illustration), a regional office carried at 60,000 serves three blocks carried at 200,000 (A), 300,000 (B) and 500,000 (C), and is allocated by carrying amount. Recoverable amounts are 230,000, 290,000 and 560,000.
Shares of the office: A 12,000, B 18,000, C 30,000
Without the office share, block B (300,000 against 290,000) would show a loss of only 10,000.

Impairment losses rest on estimates, so they can come back. At each reporting date the entity asks whether a past loss on any asset other than goodwill may have decreased, using indications that mirror those of section 2: higher prices, lower market rates, favourable changes in how the asset is used (paras. 110–111). A loss is reversed only if the estimates used to measure recoverable amount have changed (para. 114). VIU rises every year because the cash flows come closer, and that unwinding of the discount is not a reason to reverse (para. 116).

The reversal has a ceiling. The new carrying amount may not exceed what the carrying amount would have been, net of depreciation, had no loss been recognised (para. 117). The reversal goes to profit or loss unless the asset is revalued (para. 119), and depreciation is recomputed afterwards (para. 121). For a CGU the reversal is spread pro rata over its assets except goodwill (para. 122). Goodwill impairment is never reversed (para. 124), because a later rise in the unit's value is likely to be internally generated goodwill, which may not be recognised (para. 125). An impairment of goodwill booked at an interim date is not reversed at year end either (ISAK 110, formerly ISAK 17, IFRIC 10).

For example (illustration), take a block with no earlier impairment, carried at 369,670 and written down to 305,466, the 2024 figures for East Kalimantan and Attaka. Suppose it depletes one fifth of its remaining carrying amount in 2025 and, at the end of 2025, a higher price forecast lifts its recoverable amount to 320,000.
Carrying amount after impairment and 2025 depletion = 305,466 × 4/5 = 244,373
Carrying amount had there been no impairment = 369,670 × 4/5 = 295,736
Dr Allowance for impairment, oil and gas properties 51,363 / Cr Reversal of impairment loss 51,363
PHE's real block was also impaired in 2023, as the PHKT block (92,607; Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129), so its ceiling would add that loss back too, net of the depletion it would have borne.

Exploration assets are tested under a modified regime. PSAK 106 (formerly PSAK 64, IFRS 6) replaces the indications of section 2 with its own list: an expiring exploration right, no further substantive exploration budgeted, no commercially viable discovery, or a development unlikely to recover the E&E cost in full (paras. 18–20). E&E assets may be grouped into CGUs no larger than an operating segment (para. 21), and they are tested before they are reclassified to development (para. 17). Measurement follows PSAK 236; the Oil and Gas Properties essay covers the E&E test in full.

A coal or nickel miner tests a mine as a CGU with the same inputs as an oil field (a commodity price path, reserves, cost per tonne and a discount rate) and treats its restoration provision as in section 5.

, fixed assets under PSAK 216, and so fall under PSAK 236; the fresh fruit bunches growing on them are biological assets at fair value less costs to sell under PSAK 241 and are outside it. The CGU question turns on para. 70. An estate that sends all its bunches to the group's own mill is still a separate CGU if bunches trade in an active market, and its VIU must use market prices for bunches, not the internal transfer price.
Tenancy contracts often cover many towers at once, so a single tower's inflows are rarely independent and towers are grouped. Falling tenancy per tower is the usual indicator.

Each store is often a CGU, since management decides store by store whether to close. Under PSAK 116 the store's right-of-use asset sits inside the CGU, and the lease liability is excluded unless it is deducted on both sides. For example (illustration), a store with leasehold improvements of 2,000 and a right-of-use asset of 6,000 has a VIU, before lease payments, of 7,000. The loss is 8,000 − 7,000 = 1,000. Deducting the lease liability of 6,500 from both sides gives 1,500 − 500 = 1,000 as well, which is the point of paras. 78–79.

A vessel usually is its own CGU when it trades on the spot market. For example (illustration), a tanker carried at 40,000 has a broker value of 31,000 less 500 of selling costs and a VIU of 34,000. Recoverable amount is 34,000 and the loss 6,000.

PHE's 215,666 comes from Notes 17 and 12; Notes 16 and 13 report none, and the segment note confirms the total. PSAK 236 asks for this by class, segment and material CGU (paras. 126, 129–130).
Oil and gas properties, new impairment

Investments in oil and gas blocks (Malaysia, Iraq)
Total = segment note: exploration and production 215,549 + services 117
Note 17 lists the six impaired blocks (Daftar 5/111, PDF p. 128).
Mahakam and East Kalimantan and Attaka = (140,968 + 64,204) / 220,899 = 92.9% of the oil and gas charge

presentation.deck: The theory of PSAK 236 from scope to disclosure, worked through PHE's oil and gas blocks and set beside the industries where the test bites hardest
key_takeaways: An asset may not be carried at more than the entity can get back from it. PSAK 236 checks this in three steps. The entity looks for indications at every reporting date, estimates the recoverable amount (the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use) when there is one, and writes the asset down to that amount if it is below the carrying amount.

Most long-lived assets do not earn cash on their own, so the test usually runs on a cash-generating unit (CGU). A CGU's loss goes first to its goodwill and then pro rata to its other assets, and no asset is pushed below its own recoverable amount or zero.

An impairment loss on any asset except goodwill is reversed when the estimates behind recoverable amount improve, but only up to the carrying amount the asset would have had with no impairment. The passage of time alone is not a reason to reverse.

title: Intangible Assets, Net: Identifiability, Development Costs, Amortisation and Goodwill
snippet: The theory of intangible assets from definition to goodwill impairment, worked through PHE's software, land rights and goodwill and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • An intangible asset is an identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance. Identifiability, meaning separable or arising from a contract or legal right, is what divides it from goodwill.

  • Bought intangibles are recorded at cost, or at fair value when acquired in a business combination. Internally generated ones face a stricter rule. Research is always expensed, development is capitalised only from the date six criteria are all met, and brands and customer lists built in-house are never recognised.

  • A finite-life intangible is amortised over the shorter of its economic and legal life, normally straight-line with zero residual value. An indefinite-life intangible and goodwill are not amortised but tested for impairment every year, and a goodwill impairment is never reversed.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report intangible assets, net, of 71,814 at 31 December 2024 against 73,800 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 0.24 percent of total assets and 0.32 percent of non-current assets (0.24 and 0.35 percent a year earlier). It holds software and licences, land rights, and goodwill from two acquisitions (Note 13, Daftar 5/104, PDF p. 121).

A student should be able to recognise, measure, amortise and impair an intangible, and compute and test goodwill, with journals.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standards are PSAK 238 Aset Takberwujud (formerly PSAK 19, IAS 38) and, for goodwill, PSAK 103 Kombinasi Bisnis (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3).

1. What an intangible asset is

PSAK 238 defines an intangible asset as an identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance (para. 8). The lecture notes, following Kieso, reduce this to four characteristics: identifiable, no physical form, benefits over more than one period, and not held for sale. Control normally comes from legal rights (para. 13), and benefits include cost savings (para. 17).

Identifiability separates intangible assets from goodwill (para. 11). An item is identifiable if it is separable, capable of being sold, transferred or licensed on its own, or if it arises from contractual or other legal rights, transferable or not (para. 12). A software licence is both. A trained workforce is neither, so it stays in goodwill.

Kieso sorts intangibles into types, which help when an acquisition is broken down (section 7).

Type

Examples

Marketing-related

Trademarks, trade names, domain names

Customer-related

Customer lists, order backlogs, customer relationships

Artistic-related

Copyrights on books, music, pictures, video

Contract-related

Franchises, licences, permits, concessions

Technology-related

Patents, software, databases, trade secrets

Goodwill

The residual in a business combination (not identifiable)

Boundaries. Software integral to hardware, such as a machine's operating system, is part of the hardware under PSAK 216 (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16) (para. 4). PSAK 238 excludes exploration and evaluation assets, which follow PSAK 106 (formerly PSAK 64, IFRS 6), and oil, gas and mineral development and extraction (para. 2), but not software used there (para. 7).

2. Acquired intangible assets

A separately acquired intangible is measured at cost (para. 24). The recognition tests, probable benefits and reliable cost, are treated as met for a purchase, because the price reflects the buyer's expectation of benefit (paras. 25–26). Cost is the purchase price, including non-refundable taxes, less trade discounts, plus every directly attributable cost of preparing the asset for use, such as professional fees and testing (paras. 27–28). Training staff and general overhead are expensed (para. 29).

For example (illustration), within PHE's 2024 software additions of 14,038 (Note 13), suppose one item is a perpetual licence for reservoir simulation software, list price 2,000, with a 10 percent volume discount. The vendor charges 250 to install and integrate it, testing before go-live costs 120, training the engineers costs 80, and first-year support is 150, expensed over the support year.

Purchase price = 2,000 × (1 − 10%) = 1,800

Cost = 1,800 + 250 installation + 120 testing = 2,170

Kept out of cost = 80 training (expensed) + 150 support (prepaid, expensed over the year) = 230

Dr Intangible assets, software 2,170, Dr General and administrative expenses 80, Dr Prepaid expenses 150 / Cr Trade payables 2,400

An intangible received in exchange for a non-monetary asset is measured at fair value unless the exchange lacks commercial substance or neither fair value can be measured reliably (paras. 45–46), the rule the Fixed Assets essay works through. One acquired in a business combination is measured at acquisition-date fair value, separately from goodwill (paras. 33–34).

3. Internally generated intangibles: research and development

No market price confirms the value of an intangible built in-house, so PSAK 238 divides each internal project into two phases to decide when spending starts creating an asset (para. 52).

  • Research is original and planned investigation to gain new scientific or technical knowledge (para. 8), such as searching for and evaluating alternatives (para. 56). No asset is recognised from it, and the spending is expensed when incurred (para. 54).

  • Development is applying research findings to a plan or design for new or substantially improved products, processes or systems before commercial use (para. 8), such as designing and testing prototypes (para. 59). It is capitalised only when the entity can show all six criteria (para. 57):

    1. technical feasibility of completing the asset;

    2. the intention to complete it and use or sell it;

    3. the ability to use or sell it;

    4. how it will generate probable future benefits, through a market or, if used internally, its usefulness;

    5. adequate technical, financial and other resources to finish it;

    6. the ability to measure its cost reliably.

If research cannot be told apart from development, the whole project is treated as research (para. 53). Cost starts from the date the criteria are first met, and earlier spending stays in expense and cannot be reinstated (paras. 65, 71). Only directly attributable costs qualify; overhead and training do not (paras. 66–67). The lecture notes, following Kieso, expense personnel and contract-service costs as incurred and record purchased R&D items at fair value. Under PSAK 238 both follow the phase, capitalised in development once the criteria are met, and separately purchased items are measured at cost (para. 24). Materials and equipment with alternative future uses become inventory or fixed assets, as the notes say.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary builds production-surveillance software in 2024. From January to March it studies feasibility and evaluates vendor products (300) and codes a rough prototype (150). On 1 April the budget is approved and the design is shown to work, so all six criteria are met. From April to December it spends 700 on programmers, 260 on contract coders and 140 on testing, and is charged 90 of head-office overhead and 60 for training field operators.

Before 1 April (criteria not met)

From 1 April (criteria met)

Expensed

research 300 + development before criteria 150 = 450

90 overhead + 60 training = 150

Capitalised

none

700 + 260 + 140 = 1,100

Dr Research and development expense 450 / Cr Cash and accrued expenses 450

Dr Intangible assets, software under development 1,100, Dr General and administrative expenses 150 / Cr Cash and accrued expenses 1,250

Of 1,700 spent, 1,100 becomes an asset. The 150 prototype is development work (para. 59), but it came before the criteria were met, so it stays in expense although it fed the final product (para. 71).

What is never capitalised. Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists are not recognised, because their cost cannot be told apart from developing the business as a whole (paras. 63–64). The notes let a self-developed trademark carry its attorney, registration, design, consulting and successful defence costs. PSAK 238.63 does not recognise an internally generated brand at all, so these costs are expensed.

Cloud software. The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in 2019 that a software-as-a-service (SaaS) contract is usually a service, and in 2021 that configuring or customising the supplier's software is expensed as the service is received unless it creates an asset the customer controls. For example (illustration), a three-year SaaS contract for a production-accounting system costs 150 a year, and the supplier charges 90 up front for configuration that is not distinct from the subscription. The 150 is expensed each year, and the 90 is a prepayment expensed at 90 / 3 = 30 a year.

The upstream parallel. The notes give geologists' work as an example of research, and PHE likewise expenses geological and geophysical costs under PSAK 106 (Note 3m(i), Daftar 5/56, PDF p. 73; see the Oil and Gas Properties essay).

4. Amortisation

How an intangible is amortised depends on whether its useful life is finite or indefinite (paras. 88–89). An intangible with a finite life is amortised. One with an indefinite life, with no foreseeable limit to the period over which it will bring in net cash, is not (para. 107).

Useful life reflects expected use, obsolescence, competitors' actions, maintenance needed and legal limits (para. 90). A right arising from a contract or law is amortised over no more than its term (para. 94). Renewal periods count only if renewal is evidenced, its conditions will be met and its cost is small relative to its benefits (para. 96).

Residual value is assumed to be zero unless a third party has committed to buy the asset or an active market will exist at the end of its life (para. 100).

Method. Amortisation starts when the asset is available for use and follows the pattern in which benefits are consumed, with straight-line when that pattern cannot be determined reliably (paras. 97–98). A revenue-based method is presumed inappropriate, because revenue reflects prices and volumes as well as use (para. 98A), unless the right itself is defined by a revenue limit (paras. 98B–98C). Period and method are reviewed each year end, and a change is a change in estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8) (para. 104).

For example (illustration), the surveillance software goes live on 1 January 2025 with a five-year life. The simulation licence is perpetual, but the subsidiary expects to replace it after seven years as the technology dates.

Surveillance software = 1,100 / 5 = 220 a year; simulation licence = 2,170 / 7 = 310 a year

Dr Amortisation expense 530 / Cr Accumulated amortisation, software 530

At the end of 2026 the surveillance software carries 1,100 − 2 × 220 = 660. If its remaining life is revised to two years, amortisation becomes 660 / 2 = 330 a year from 2027, with no restatement.

Land rights. Indonesian land rights such as hak guna bangunan (HGB, a right to build) run for a term and can be extended. PHE's policy puts the initial legal costs of a land right into land, undepreciated, and treats rights that are leases in substance under PSAK 116 (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69; the Right-of-Use Assets essay explains the ISAK 336 test). Extension and renewal costs have a term of their own, so they are commonly carried as an intangible and amortised over the extended term. For example (illustration), fees of 60 to extend an HGB for 20 years are amortised at 60 / 20 = 3 a year.

Indefinite life. For example (illustration), a subsidiary buys a trade name for 5,000, renewable every ten years at a small fee, with no plan to stop using it. It is not amortised but tested for impairment each year (para. 108), and the life assessment is reviewed each period (para. 109). If in 2027 management decides to retire the name in four years, it is tested for impairment and then amortised at 5,000 / 4 = 1,250 a year.

5. Subsequent costs, revaluation and derecognition

Later spending is only rarely capitalised, because most of it maintains benefits already expected (para. 20). The notes capitalise the cost of successfully defending a patent; under PSAK 238 a defence keeps existing benefits and is normally expensed.

An entity may choose the revaluation model for a class of intangibles only where fair value can be measured in an active market (paras. 72, 75). Patents, brands and software are unique, so the model is rare. PHE uses cost.

An intangible is derecognised on disposal or when no further benefit is expected, with the gain or loss in profit or loss. For example (illustration), take PHE's 2024 software deductions (Note 13), cost 5,580 and accumulated amortisation 2,768, as systems retired with no proceeds.

Carrying amount = 5,580 − 2,768 = 2,812

Dr Accumulated amortisation, software 2,768, Dr Loss on derecognition 2,812 / Cr Intangible assets, software 5,580

6. Impairment

An intangible is written down when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, under PSAK 236 Penurunan Nilai Aset (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36). The mechanism is taught in the Fixed Assets and Oil and Gas Properties essays; intangibles differ in when the test is required.

Asset

When tested

Reversal

Finite-life intangible

When there is an indication of impairment

Allowed, up to the carrying amount with no impairment

Indefinite-life intangible

Every year, and on an indication

Allowed, same cap

Not yet available for use

Every year

Allowed, same cap

Goodwill

Every year, within a cash-generating unit

Never (PSAK 236.124)

The notes define the test against recoverable amount, but their patent example uses an appraised fair value. Fair value less costs of disposal is only one leg; value in use may be higher when the asset is worth more in the entity's own use. PHE's policy lists the same annual tests (Note 3w, Daftar 5/72, PDF p. 89).

For example (illustration), suppose instead that the surveillance software served one field, and in late 2025 the subsidiary's contract for that field is not extended. The software cannot be sold, so fair value less costs of disposal is nil, and value in use for the remaining months is 250.

Carrying amount at 31 December 2025 = 1,100 − 220 = 880

Impairment loss = 880 − higher of (0, 250) = 630

Dr Impairment loss on non-financial assets 630 / Cr Allowance for impairment, software 630

7. Goodwill

Goodwill is what a buyer pays beyond the fair value of the identifiable assets and liabilities it gets, such as the assembled workforce and expected synergies. It is not identifiable, so it falls outside PSAK 238 (para. 3(f)) and is measured under PSAK 103. Internally generated goodwill is never recognised.

Measurement. Under the acquisition method the acquirer measures identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value at the acquisition date, including intangibles the acquiree never recorded. Goodwill is the residual. Acquisition costs are expensed; PHE puts them in general and administrative expenses (Note 3d, Daftar 5/35, PDF p. 52).

Goodwill = consideration transferred + non-controlling interest (NCI) − fair value of identifiable net assets

For example (illustration, in the structure of the lecture notes' example), a PHE subsidiary buys 100 percent of an oilfield-services company for 120,000 cash.

Book value

Fair value

Inventories

10,500

7,500

Customer contracts (order backlog)

none

6,000

(16,500)

(16,500)

Goodwill = 120,000 − 84,000 = 36,000

Dr Fixed assets 61,500, Dr Inventories 12,000, Dr Receivables 10,500, Dr Cash 7,500, Dr Intangible assets, customer contracts 6,000, Dr Intangible assets, software 3,000, Dr Goodwill 36,000 / Cr Liabilities 16,500, Cr Cash 120,000

Of the 58,000 paid above book value, 22,000 is fair value step-ups, including 6,000 of customer contracts the seller never recorded, and 36,000 is goodwill. Deferred tax on the step-ups is ignored here; PHE carries a deferred tax liability of 7,760 labelled "excess fair value over NBV" (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172).

Non-controlling interest. When less than 100 percent is bought, PSAK 103 lets the acquirer measure NCI, acquisition by acquisition, at fair value or at its proportionate share of identifiable net assets, a choice PHE's policy states (Note 3d). Suppose the subsidiary buys 80 percent for 96,000, and the other 20 percent has a fair value of 23,000.

NCI at proportionate share

NCI at fair value

NCI

20% × 84,000 = 16,800

23,000

Goodwill

96,000 + 16,800 − 84,000 = 28,800

96,000 + 23,000 − 84,000 = 35,000

Whose goodwill

The parent's only

The parent's and the NCI's

Bargain purchase. A price below the fair value of net assets is first rechecked, and any excess left is a gain in profit or loss. Bought for 80,000, the company above gives a gain of 84,000 − 80,000 = 4,000.

No amortisation. PSAK 22 (1994) amortised goodwill over five to twenty years; the revision that adopted IFRS 3 replaced amortisation with an annual impairment test. PHE's Note 13 still shows the old amortisation (section 9).

Impairment of goodwill. Goodwill brings in no cash on its own, so from the acquisition date it is allocated to the cash-generating units (CGUs) expected to benefit from the combination (PHE Note 3d, Daftar 5/37, PDF p. 54), and each is tested every year (Note 3w, Daftar 5/73, PDF p. 90). A unit's impairment loss goes first to goodwill and then to its other assets pro rata to carrying amount (PSAK 236.104), with no asset taken below the highest of its fair value less costs of disposal, value in use and zero (para. 105). For example (illustration), a one-block CGU carries oil and gas properties of 400,000, goodwill of 50,000 and current assets of 30,000, and lower price forecasts cut its recoverable amount to 420,000. The current assets (receivables and inventories) are measured under their own standards and sit outside PSAK 236 (para. 2), so they take no share of the loss.

Impairment loss = (400,000 + 50,000 + 30,000) − 420,000 = 60,000

To goodwill = 50,000; to oil and gas properties = 60,000 − 50,000 = 10,000

Dr Impairment loss on non-financial assets 60,000 / Cr Goodwill (accumulated impairment) 50,000, Cr Allowance for impairment, oil and gas properties 10,000

If prices recover, the 10,000 may be reversed up to its ceiling, but the 50,000 never is (PSAK 236.124), because a later rise in the unit's value may be internally generated goodwill.

8. Intangible assets across industries

Telecommunications. A mobile operator's up-front spectrum licence fee is amortised over the licence term, and annual frequency usage fees are expensed as they fall due. For example (illustration), an up-front fee of 1,000 for a ten-year licence is amortised at 1,000 / 10 = 100 a year.

Pharmaceuticals. Feasibility and benefits are hard to show before a regulator approves a drug, so drug makers commonly expense development until approval. A compound bought in mid-development is capitalised at cost, because a purchase always meets the recognition test (para. 25).

Toll roads and power concessions. Under ISAK 112 (formerly ISAK 16, IFRIC 12), an operator that builds infrastructure for a government that controls its use, its prices and the asset at the end does not recognise the road as a fixed asset. It recognises an intangible right to charge users when it bears traffic risk, or a financial asset when the grantor guarantees the cash. For example (illustration), a toll road built for 5,000 under a 40-year concession (intangible measured at the fair value of the construction service, here assumed equal to cost) is amortised at 5,000 / 40 = 125 a year straight-line, or at 5,000 × 2% = 100 under a traffic-based method in a first year carrying 2 percent of expected total traffic. A toll-revenue method is presumed inappropriate (para. 98A). A power producer selling to PLN, the state electricity company, may fall under ISAK 112 or the lease rules, depending on who controls the plant.

Plantations. Plantation land is held through hak guna usaha (HGU), a cultivation right of limited term. The right is tested under ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36; see the Fixed Assets essay), and extension costs have commonly been carried as amortised intangibles. For tax, the Income Tax Law lists the costs of extending HGB and HGU, and goodwill, among expenditure amortised in four-, eight-, sixteen- or twenty-year groups, or, since UU HPP (2021), over the actual useful life where it exceeds twenty years (UU PPh art. 11A(2), (2a); PMK 72/2023).

9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 13

PHE gives the movement table PSAK 238.118 asks for (Note 13, Daftar 5/104, PDF p. 121).

Opening 73,800 + additions 14,038 − carrying amount derecognised (5,580 − 2,768) − net correction (2,257 − 2,195) − amortisation 13,150 = 71,814

Goodwill dominates the line. PHE does not split the allowance of 33,379 by class. If all of it is the fully impaired Nunukan goodwill, the remaining ONWJ goodwill is 113,470 − 26,755 − 33,379 = 53,336, or 74.3 percent of the line, and software and land rights make up the other 18,478.

Goodwill and land rights in Note 13. Goodwill arose from the 2009 acquisition of ONWJ Ltd. and the 2013 acquisition of PHE Nunukan Company, whose goodwill was fully impaired in 2021; when the Nunukan block was impaired by a further 53,303 in 2023, the Note 17 table's goodwill column showed none for it (Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129). On the 53,336 reading ONWJ's gross goodwill is 80,091, and the 26,755 of accumulated amortisation, unchanged in both years, is 33.4 percent of it, which fits amortisation charged before the revised PSAK 22 took effect in 2011. If, as secondary sources say, the revision required that amortisation to be eliminated against cost, PHE's gross presentation does not follow it, though net goodwill is unchanged. Land rights are HGB with terms ending between 2024 and 2045, amortised although management expects renewal, at a 2024 charge of 26 on average cost of 576.5, about 22 years. Since policy 3i sends initial legal costs to land, the amortised intangible is most likely extension costs, the treatment of the former ISAK 25.

Software amortisation rate = 13,124 / ((87,693 + 93,921) / 2) = 14.5% (2024); 6,505 / ((82,412 + 87,693) / 2) = 7.6% (2023)

Accumulated amortisation / cost, software = 75,691 / 93,921 = 80.6% (77.0% in 2023)

On straight-line, 14.5 percent implies an average life of about seven years and 7.6 percent about thirteen, measured on gross cost that still includes fully amortised software, so the life of assets still being amortised is shorter. Amortisation doubled from 6,532 to 13,150 while software cost rose 7.1 percent in 2024, and four-fifths of the software's cost is already consumed.

The FS do not show useful lives, the amortisation method or the line item carrying amortisation for software and land rights (para. 118(a), (b), (d)), so the doubling cannot be explained. The policies cover only goodwill (Note 3d), and the DD&A line in profit or loss cites Notes 12, 16a and 17 but not 13 (Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14). The "correction" columns (−2,230 of software cost, +2,181 of accumulated amortisation) are unexplained. In 2023 software deductions removed 865 of cost but 875 of accumulated amortisation, a negative carrying amount of 10. The critical estimates note calls "goodwill or intangible assets not ready to use" examples of indefinite useful life (Daftar 5/82, PDF p. 99, both language columns), but an asset not yet ready for use is tested annually because amortisation has not started, not because its life is indefinite.

10. Upstream note

Under PHE's cost recovery production sharing contracts (PSCs), materials and equipment bought for petroleum operations belong to the Government (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). The FS do not say whether software falls under that clause. The goodwill here arose because PHE bought companies holding PSC interests (ONWJ Ltd. and PHE Nunukan Company).

11. Related lines

  • oil-gas-properties-net: exploration and evaluation assets, PSC interests, and the CGUs that carry goodwill.

  • fixed-assets-net: software integral to hardware, and initial legal costs of land rights.

  • right-of-use-assets-net: land rights that are leases in substance.

  • depreciation-depletion-amortization and impairment-non-financial-assets: where amortisation and impairment are presumably charged.

  • long-term-investments: goodwill inside associates.

  • deferred-tax-liabilities: deferred tax on fair value step-ups.

Least-confident assertions

  • That the allowance of 33,379 belongs wholly to Nunukan goodwill, so that ONWJ goodwill is 53,336 net, is an inference. Note 13 does not split the allowance, and the FS do not give each acquisition's original goodwill.

  • That the 26,755 of accumulated amortisation predates the revised PSAK 22 is inferred from the 2009 acquisition date and the 33.4 percent ratio. PSAK 22 (2010), effective 1 January 2011, is reported in secondary sources to have required eliminating accumulated amortisation against goodwill cost on transition, as IFRS 3 (2004) did; PHE still presents the 26,755 gross. The transition paragraph itself was not opened.

  • The reading that PHE's intangible land rights are extension costs, as the former ISAK 25 is understood to have required, reconciles Note 13 with policy 3i, but PHE does not say so. No text of ISAK 25 or of ISAK 336's paragraph on renewal costs (DK09) could be found.

  • The industry paragraphs describe common practice under the standards, not checked against any named company's statements.

  • Expensing patent defence costs and trademark registration fees under PSAK 238, against Kieso's capitalisation, is this page's reading of paragraphs 20 and 63; neither paragraph names those costs.

content.text: An intangible asset is an identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance. Identifiability, meaning separable or arising from a contract or legal right, is what divides it from goodwill.

Bought intangibles are recorded at cost, or at fair value when acquired in a business combination. Internally generated ones face a stricter rule. Research is always expensed, development is capitalised only from the date six criteria are all met, and brands and customer lists built in-house are never recognised.

A finite-life intangible is amortised over the shorter of its economic and legal life, normally straight-line with zero residual value. An indefinite-life intangible and goodwill are not amortised but tested for impairment every year, and a goodwill impairment is never reversed.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report intangible assets, net, of 71,814 at 31 December 2024 against 73,800 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 0.24 percent of total assets and 0.32 percent of non-current assets (0.24 and 0.35 percent a year earlier). It holds software and licences, land rights, and goodwill from two acquisitions (Note 13, Daftar 5/104, PDF p. 121).
A student should be able to recognise, measure, amortise and impair an intangible, and compute and test goodwill, with journals.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standards are PSAK 238
(formerly PSAK 19, IAS 38) and, for goodwill, PSAK 103

PSAK 238 defines an intangible asset as an identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance (para. 8). The lecture notes, following Kieso, reduce this to four characteristics: identifiable, no physical form, benefits over more than one period, and not held for sale. Control normally comes from legal rights (para. 13), and benefits include cost savings (para. 17).
separates intangible assets from goodwill (para. 11). An item is identifiable if it is

, capable of being sold, transferred or licensed on its own, or if it arises from contractual or other legal rights, transferable or not (para. 12). A software licence is both. A trained workforce is neither, so it stays in goodwill.
Kieso sorts intangibles into types, which help when an acquisition is broken down (section 7).
Customer lists, order backlogs, customer relationships
Copyrights on books, music, pictures, video
The residual in a business combination (not identifiable)

Software integral to hardware, such as a machine's operating system, is part of the hardware under PSAK 216 (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16) (para. 4). PSAK 238 excludes exploration and evaluation assets, which follow PSAK 106 (formerly PSAK 64, IFRS 6), and oil, gas and mineral development and extraction (para. 2), but not software used there (para. 7).

A separately acquired intangible is measured at cost (para. 24). The recognition tests, probable benefits and reliable cost, are treated as met for a purchase, because the price reflects the buyer's expectation of benefit (paras. 25–26). Cost is the purchase price, including non-refundable taxes, less trade discounts, plus every directly attributable cost of preparing the asset for use, such as professional fees and testing (paras. 27–28). Training staff and general overhead are expensed (para. 29).

For example (illustration), within PHE's 2024 software additions of 14,038 (Note 13), suppose one item is a perpetual licence for reservoir simulation software, list price 2,000, with a 10 percent volume discount. The vendor charges 250 to install and integrate it, testing before go-live costs 120, training the engineers costs 80, and first-year support is 150, expensed over the support year.
Kept out of cost = 80 training (expensed) + 150 support (prepaid, expensed over the year) = 230
Dr Intangible assets, software 2,170, Dr General and administrative expenses 80, Dr Prepaid expenses 150 / Cr Trade payables 2,400

An intangible received in exchange for a non-monetary asset is measured at fair value unless the exchange lacks commercial substance or neither fair value can be measured reliably (paras. 45–46), the rule the Fixed Assets essay works through. One acquired in a business combination is measured at acquisition-date fair value, separately from goodwill (paras. 33–34).
3. Internally generated intangibles: research and development
No market price confirms the value of an intangible built in-house, so PSAK 238 divides each internal project into two phases to decide when spending starts creating an asset (para. 52).

is original and planned investigation to gain new scientific or technical knowledge (para. 8), such as searching for and evaluating alternatives (para. 56). No asset is recognised from it, and the spending is expensed when incurred (para. 54).

is applying research findings to a plan or design for new or substantially improved products, processes or systems before commercial use (para. 8), such as designing and testing prototypes (para. 59). It is capitalised only when the entity can show all six criteria (para. 57):
technical feasibility of completing the asset;
the intention to complete it and use or sell it;
the ability to use or sell it;
how it will generate probable future benefits, through a market or, if used internally, its usefulness;
adequate technical, financial and other resources to finish it;
the ability to measure its cost reliably.

If research cannot be told apart from development, the whole project is treated as research (para. 53). Cost starts from the date the criteria are first met, and earlier spending stays in expense and cannot be reinstated (paras. 65, 71). Only directly attributable costs qualify; overhead and training do not (paras. 66–67). The lecture notes, following Kieso, expense personnel and contract-service costs as incurred and record purchased R&D items at fair value. Under PSAK 238 both follow the phase, capitalised in development once the criteria are met, and separately purchased items are measured at cost (para. 24). Materials and equipment with alternative future uses become inventory or fixed assets, as the notes say.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary builds production-surveillance software in 2024. From January to March it studies feasibility and evaluates vendor products (300) and codes a rough prototype (150). On 1 April the budget is approved and the design is shown to work, so all six criteria are met. From April to December it spends 700 on programmers, 260 on contract coders and 140 on testing, and is charged 90 of head-office overhead and 60 for training field operators.
Dr Research and development expense 450 / Cr Cash and accrued expenses 450
Dr Intangible assets, software under development 1,100, Dr General and administrative expenses 150 / Cr Cash and accrued expenses 1,250

Of 1,700 spent, 1,100 becomes an asset. The 150 prototype is development work (para. 59), but it came before the criteria were met, so it stays in expense although it fed the final product (para. 71).

Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists are not recognised, because their cost cannot be told apart from developing the business as a whole (paras. 63–64). The notes let a self-developed trademark carry its attorney, registration, design, consulting and successful defence costs. PSAK 238.63 does not recognise an internally generated brand at all, so these costs are expensed.

The IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded in 2019 that a software-as-a-service (SaaS) contract is usually a service, and in 2021 that configuring or customising the supplier's software is expensed as the service is received unless it creates an asset the customer controls. For example (illustration), a three-year SaaS contract for a production-accounting system costs 150 a year, and the supplier charges 90 up front for configuration that is not distinct from the subscription. The 150 is expensed each year, and the 90 is a prepayment expensed at 90 / 3 = 30 a year.

The notes give geologists' work as an example of research, and PHE likewise expenses geological and geophysical costs under PSAK 106 (Note 3m(i), Daftar 5/56, PDF p. 73; see the Oil and Gas Properties essay).

How an intangible is amortised depends on whether its useful life is finite or indefinite (paras. 88–89). An intangible with a finite life is amortised. One with an indefinite life, with no foreseeable limit to the period over which it will bring in net cash, is not (para. 107).

reflects expected use, obsolescence, competitors' actions, maintenance needed and legal limits (para. 90). A right arising from a contract or law is amortised over no more than its term (para. 94). Renewal periods count only if renewal is evidenced, its conditions will be met and its cost is small relative to its benefits (para. 96).
is assumed to be zero unless a third party has committed to buy the asset or an active market will exist at the end of its life (para. 100).

Amortisation starts when the asset is available for use and follows the pattern in which benefits are consumed, with straight-line when that pattern cannot be determined reliably (paras. 97–98). A revenue-based method is presumed inappropriate, because revenue reflects prices and volumes as well as use (para. 98A), unless the right itself is defined by a revenue limit (paras. 98B–98C). Period and method are reviewed each year end, and a change is a change in estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8) (para. 104).

For example (illustration), the surveillance software goes live on 1 January 2025 with a five-year life. The simulation licence is perpetual, but the subsidiary expects to replace it after seven years as the technology dates.
Surveillance software = 1,100 / 5 = 220 a year; simulation licence = 2,170 / 7 = 310 a year
Dr Amortisation expense 530 / Cr Accumulated amortisation, software 530
At the end of 2026 the surveillance software carries 1,100 − 2 × 220 = 660. If its remaining life is revised to two years, amortisation becomes 660 / 2 = 330 a year from 2027, with no restatement.

(HGB, a right to build) run for a term and can be extended. PHE's policy puts the initial legal costs of a land right into land, undepreciated, and treats rights that are leases in substance under PSAK 116 (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69; the Right-of-Use Assets essay explains the ISAK 336 test). Extension and renewal costs have a term of their own, so they are commonly carried as an intangible and amortised over the extended term. For example (illustration), fees of 60 to extend an HGB for 20 years are amortised at 60 / 20 = 3 a year.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary buys a trade name for 5,000, renewable every ten years at a small fee, with no plan to stop using it. It is not amortised but tested for impairment each year (para. 108), and the life assessment is reviewed each period (para. 109). If in 2027 management decides to retire the name in four years, it is tested for impairment and then amortised at 5,000 / 4 = 1,250 a year.

Later spending is only rarely capitalised, because most of it maintains benefits already expected (para. 20). The notes capitalise the cost of successfully defending a patent; under PSAK 238 a defence keeps existing benefits and is normally expensed.
An entity may choose the revaluation model for a class of intangibles only where fair value can be measured in an
(paras. 72, 75). Patents, brands and software are unique, so the model is rare. PHE uses cost.

An intangible is derecognised on disposal or when no further benefit is expected, with the gain or loss in profit or loss. For example (illustration), take PHE's 2024 software deductions (Note 13), cost 5,580 and accumulated amortisation 2,768, as systems retired with no proceeds.
Dr Accumulated amortisation, software 2,768, Dr Loss on derecognition 2,812 / Cr Intangible assets, software 5,580
An intangible is written down when its carrying amount exceeds its
, the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, under PSAK 236
(formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36). The mechanism is taught in the Fixed Assets and Oil and Gas Properties essays; intangibles differ in when the test is required.
When there is an indication of impairment
Allowed, up to the carrying amount with no impairment
Every year, and on an indication
Every year, within a cash-generating unit

The notes define the test against recoverable amount, but their patent example uses an appraised fair value. Fair value less costs of disposal is only one leg; value in use may be higher when the asset is worth more in the entity's own use. PHE's policy lists the same annual tests (Note 3w, Daftar 5/72, PDF p. 89).

For example (illustration), suppose instead that the surveillance software served one field, and in late 2025 the subsidiary's contract for that field is not extended. The software cannot be sold, so fair value less costs of disposal is nil, and value in use for the remaining months is 250.
Dr Impairment loss on non-financial assets 630 / Cr Allowance for impairment, software 630

Goodwill is what a buyer pays beyond the fair value of the identifiable assets and liabilities it gets, such as the assembled workforce and expected synergies. It is not identifiable, so it falls outside PSAK 238 (para. 3(f)) and is measured under PSAK 103. Internally generated goodwill is never recognised.

Under the acquisition method the acquirer measures identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value at the acquisition date, including intangibles the acquiree never recorded. Goodwill is the residual. Acquisition costs are expensed; PHE puts them in general and administrative expenses (Note 3d, Daftar 5/35, PDF p. 52).
Goodwill = consideration transferred + non-controlling interest (NCI) − fair value of identifiable net assets
For example (illustration, in the structure of the lecture notes' example), a PHE subsidiary buys 100 percent of an oilfield-services company for 120,000 cash.

Dr Fixed assets 61,500, Dr Inventories 12,000, Dr Receivables 10,500, Dr Cash 7,500, Dr Intangible assets, customer contracts 6,000, Dr Intangible assets, software 3,000, Dr Goodwill 36,000 / Cr Liabilities 16,500, Cr Cash 120,000

Of the 58,000 paid above book value, 22,000 is fair value step-ups, including 6,000 of customer contracts the seller never recorded, and 36,000 is goodwill. Deferred tax on the step-ups is ignored here; PHE carries a deferred tax liability of 7,760 labelled "excess fair value over NBV" (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172).

When less than 100 percent is bought, PSAK 103 lets the acquirer measure NCI, acquisition by acquisition, at fair value or at its proportionate share of identifiable net assets, a choice PHE's policy states (Note 3d). Suppose the subsidiary buys 80 percent for 96,000, and the other 20 percent has a fair value of 23,000.
A price below the fair value of net assets is first rechecked, and any excess left is a gain in profit or loss. Bought for 80,000, the company above gives a gain of 84,000 − 80,000 = 4,000.

PSAK 22 (1994) amortised goodwill over five to twenty years; the revision that adopted IFRS 3 replaced amortisation with an annual impairment test. PHE's Note 13 still shows the old amortisation (section 9).

Goodwill brings in no cash on its own, so from the acquisition date it is allocated to the cash-generating units (CGUs) expected to benefit from the combination (PHE Note 3d, Daftar 5/37, PDF p. 54), and each is tested every year (Note 3w, Daftar 5/73, PDF p. 90). A unit's impairment loss goes first to goodwill and then to its other assets pro rata to carrying amount (PSAK 236.104), with no asset taken below the highest of its fair value less costs of disposal, value in use and zero (para. 105). For example (illustration), a one-block CGU carries oil and gas properties of 400,000, goodwill of 50,000 and current assets of 30,000, and lower price forecasts cut its recoverable amount to 420,000. The current assets (receivables and inventories) are measured under their own standards and sit outside PSAK 236 (para. 2), so they take no share of the loss.
To goodwill = 50,000; to oil and gas properties = 60,000 − 50,000 = 10,000
Dr Impairment loss on non-financial assets 60,000 / Cr Goodwill (accumulated impairment) 50,000, Cr Allowance for impairment, oil and gas properties 10,000
If prices recover, the 10,000 may be reversed up to its ceiling, but the 50,000 never is (PSAK 236.124), because a later rise in the unit's value may be internally generated goodwill.

A mobile operator's up-front spectrum licence fee is amortised over the licence term, and annual frequency usage fees are expensed as they fall due. For example (illustration), an up-front fee of 1,000 for a ten-year licence is amortised at 1,000 / 10 = 100 a year.

Feasibility and benefits are hard to show before a regulator approves a drug, so drug makers commonly expense development until approval. A compound bought in mid-development is capitalised at cost, because a purchase always meets the recognition test (para. 25).

Under ISAK 112 (formerly ISAK 16, IFRIC 12), an operator that builds infrastructure for a government that controls its use, its prices and the asset at the end does not recognise the road as a fixed asset. It recognises an intangible right to charge users when it bears traffic risk, or a financial asset when the grantor guarantees the cash. For example (illustration), a toll road built for 5,000 under a 40-year concession (intangible measured at the fair value of the construction service, here assumed equal to cost) is amortised at 5,000 / 40 = 125 a year straight-line, or at 5,000 × 2% = 100 under a traffic-based method in a first year carrying 2 percent of expected total traffic. A toll-revenue method is presumed inappropriate (para. 98A). A power producer selling to PLN, the state electricity company, may fall under ISAK 112 or the lease rules, depending on who controls the plant.

(HGU), a cultivation right of limited term. The right is tested under ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36; see the Fixed Assets essay), and extension costs have commonly been carried as amortised intangibles. For tax, the Income Tax Law lists the costs of extending HGB and HGU, and goodwill, among expenditure amortised in four-, eight-, sixteen- or twenty-year groups, or, since UU HPP (2021), over the actual useful life where it exceeds twenty years (UU PPh art. 11A(2), (2a); PMK 72/2023).
PHE gives the movement table PSAK 238.118 asks for (Note 13, Daftar 5/104, PDF p. 121).
Opening 73,800 + additions 14,038 − carrying amount derecognised (5,580 − 2,768) − net correction (2,257 − 2,195) − amortisation 13,150 = 71,814

Goodwill dominates the line. PHE does not split the allowance of 33,379 by class. If all of it is the fully impaired Nunukan goodwill, the remaining ONWJ goodwill is 113,470 − 26,755 − 33,379 = 53,336, or 74.3 percent of the line, and software and land rights make up the other 18,478.
Goodwill and land rights in Note 13.

Goodwill arose from the 2009 acquisition of ONWJ Ltd. and the 2013 acquisition of PHE Nunukan Company, whose goodwill was fully impaired in 2021; when the Nunukan block was impaired by a further 53,303 in 2023, the Note 17 table's goodwill column showed none for it (Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129). On the 53,336 reading ONWJ's gross goodwill is 80,091, and the 26,755 of accumulated amortisation, unchanged in both years, is 33.4 percent of it, which fits amortisation charged before the revised PSAK 22 took effect in 2011. If, as secondary sources say, the revision required that amortisation to be eliminated against cost, PHE's gross presentation does not follow it, though net goodwill is unchanged. Land rights are HGB with terms ending between 2024 and 2045, amortised although management expects renewal, at a 2024 charge of 26 on average cost of 576.5, about 22 years. Since policy 3i sends initial legal costs to land, the amortised intangible is most likely extension costs, the treatment of the former ISAK 25.

On straight-line, 14.5 percent implies an average life of about seven years and 7.6 percent about thirteen, measured on gross cost that still includes fully amortised software, so the life of assets still being amortised is shorter. Amortisation doubled from 6,532 to 13,150 while software cost rose 7.1 percent in 2024, and four-fifths of the software's cost is already consumed.

The FS do not show useful lives, the amortisation method or the line item carrying amortisation for software and land rights (para. 118(a), (b), (d)), so the doubling cannot be explained. The policies cover only goodwill (Note 3d), and the DD&A line in profit or loss cites Notes 12, 16a and 17 but not 13 (Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14). The "correction" columns (−2,230 of software cost, +2,181 of accumulated amortisation) are unexplained. In 2023 software deductions removed 865 of cost but 875 of accumulated amortisation, a negative carrying amount of 10. The critical estimates note calls "goodwill or intangible assets not ready to use" examples of indefinite useful life (Daftar 5/82, PDF p. 99, both language columns), but an asset not yet ready for use is tested annually because amortisation has not started, not because its life is indefinite.

Under PHE's cost recovery production sharing contracts (PSCs), materials and equipment bought for petroleum operations belong to the Government (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). The FS do not say whether software falls under that clause. The goodwill here arose because PHE bought companies holding PSC interests (ONWJ Ltd. and PHE Nunukan Company).
: exploration and evaluation assets, PSC interests, and the CGUs that carry goodwill.
: software integral to hardware, and initial legal costs of land rights.
: land rights that are leases in substance.
: where amortisation and impairment are presumably charged.
: deferred tax on fair value step-ups.

That the allowance of 33,379 belongs wholly to Nunukan goodwill, so that ONWJ goodwill is 53,336 net, is an inference. Note 13 does not split the allowance, and the FS do not give each acquisition's original goodwill.

That the 26,755 of accumulated amortisation predates the revised PSAK 22 is inferred from the 2009 acquisition date and the 33.4 percent ratio. PSAK 22 (2010), effective 1 January 2011, is reported in secondary sources to have required eliminating accumulated amortisation against goodwill cost on transition, as IFRS 3 (2004) did; PHE still presents the 26,755 gross. The transition paragraph itself was not opened.

The reading that PHE's intangible land rights are extension costs, as the former ISAK 25 is understood to have required, reconciles Note 13 with policy 3i, but PHE does not say so. No text of ISAK 25 or of ISAK 336's paragraph on renewal costs (DK09) could be found.
The industry paragraphs describe common practice under the standards, not checked against any named company's statements.
Expensing patent defence costs and trademark registration fees under PSAK 238, against Kieso's capitalisation, is this page's reading of paragraphs 20 and 63; neither paragraph names those costs.
