content.text: When one group company sells a plant asset to another above its carrying amount, the seller books a gain the group has not earned, because the asset has not left the group. Consolidation removes the gain in full and puts the asset back at the seller's carrying amount, the

For land the gain stays eliminated until the land is sold outside the group. For a depreciable asset the buyer depreciates the transfer price, so each year's excess depreciation is corrected, and the gain comes back piece by piece over the remaining life.

Direction decides who bears the gain. A downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) falls wholly on the parent's owners; an upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) is shared with the non-controlling interest (NCI). Intercompany leases and bonds bought back within the group follow the same logic.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report property, plant and equipment, net, of 5,660,112 at 31 December 2025 against 3,489,851 a year earlier, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, statement of financial position, PDF p. 14). Inside that group, PT Krakatau Chandra Energi (KCE) completed a land sale and purchase with PT Chandra Asri Alkali (CAA) and PT Chandra Cilegon Port (CCP) during 2025 for 26,223 (Note 45h, PDF p. 237). All three are subsidiaries of PT Chandra Asri Pacific Tbk (CAP), which BRPT consolidates (Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–25), and BRPT's policy is that intragroup transactions "are eliminated in full on consolidation" (Note 3c, PDF p. 68).

After reading this page a student should be able to eliminate an intercompany gain on land and depreciable assets in the year of transfer, in later years and on sale outside, split it between the parent and NCI, and treat intercompany leases and bond holdings the same way.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. Why an intercompany transfer creates a gain the group has not earned
A group earns a gain on an asset only when the asset leaves the group. PSAK 110

(formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) requires profits and losses on intragroup transactions recognised in assets such as inventory and fixed assets to be eliminated in full (para. B86(c)), because for the economic unit nothing has changed.
The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 6) start from the same point. A transfer above book value creates an
, recorded by the seller but not earned by the group, which must be removed from the consolidated statements and, where the parent uses the
(the investment at cost plus its share of the subsidiary's profit, less dividends), from the parent's own
. The notes call the equity method a "one-line consolidation" (AKL Chapter 2): it must give the parent the same profit as full consolidation, condensed into one line.

NCI, the worksheet and depreciation itself come from earlier essays (section 11). Inventory (K3) works the same way; the difference is time. An inventory gain usually comes back within a year, a gain on equipment over its remaining life, and a gain on land only if the land is sold outside.
2. Land: the gain is eliminated until the land is sold outside

, formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16, para. 58), so nothing in the buyer's books ever corrects the gain. The consolidation entry has to remove it in the year of sale and put it back on the worksheet every year until the land leaves the group.

The notes add "paten yang memiliki masa manfaat yang tidak terbatas" to this class, but a patent has a finite legal life. The class is land and intangibles with an indefinite useful life, which PSAK 238 (formerly PSAK 19, IAS 38) does not amortise.
For example (illustration), take BRPT's 26,223 as the transfer price. Parent P owns 70 percent of subsidiary S, the same percentage CDI holds in KCE (Note 1d). The seller carried the land at 16,223.
Group cost of the land = 16,223, whoever holds it
The worksheet entry is the same in both directions; what differs is whose profit carried the gain.
Dr Gain on sale of land 10,000 / Cr Land 10,000
Dr Income from subsidiary 10,000 / Cr Investment in S 10,000
Dr Income from subsidiary 7,000 / Cr Investment in S 7,000 (70% × 10,000)

The holder still carries the land at 26,223 and the seller's retained earnings still contain the gain, so each year's worksheet repeats the elimination against opening equity, which under P's equity method sits in the investment account.
Dr Investment in S 10,000 / Cr Land 10,000
Dr Investment in S 7,000, Dr NCI 3,000 / Cr Land 10,000

The notes print the upstream entry "Investment in Sun $18.000 / Noncontrolling interest share $2.000 / Land $20.000" among the 2016 entries, introduced only by "Apabila Pop memutuskan untuk menggunakan tanah tersebut". It is the later-years entry: in the year of sale the gain is still in the income statement, and the notes' own 2016 worksheet debits "Gain on sale". The debit is also to the opening NCI balance, not to
Suppose the holder sells the land to an outside buyer for 30,000.
Dr Investment in S 10,000 / Cr Gain on sale of land 10,000
Dr Investment in S 7,000, Dr NCI 3,000 / Cr Gain on sale of land 10,000
P's books mirror it (Dr Investment in S / Cr Income from subsidiary, 10,000 or 7,000), and in the upstream case 3,000 of the 13,777 group gain goes to NCI.
3. Depreciable assets: the gain comes back through depreciation

A depreciable asset corrects itself slowly. The buyer depreciates the transfer price, the group should depreciate the group cost, and correcting the difference each year releases a slice of the gain into consolidated profit, the

For example (illustration), on 1 January 2025 one company sells equipment to the other. BRPT depreciates machinery and heavy equipment straight-line over 4–37 years (Note 3n, PDF p. 90); take five years remaining, no residual value.
Seller's cost 50,000, accumulated depreciation 20,000, carrying amount 30,000
At the end of 2025 the buyer carries 40,000 − 8,000 = 32,000 and the group 30,000 − 6,000 = 24,000; the 8,000 gap is the gain not yet realised.
(a) Dr Gain on sale of equipment 10,000 / Cr Equipment 10,000
(b) Dr Accumulated depreciation 2,000 / Cr Depreciation expense 2,000
A partial worksheet, with the parent as buyer:
Consolidated equipment, net, is 30,000 − 6,000 = 24,000. Entry (a) is the notes'

form restores the seller's cost and accumulated depreciation (Dr Gain 10,000, Dr Equipment 10,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 20,000), showing 50,000 less 26,000 at year end, also 24,000, and closer to what the group would disclose had the transfer never happened. The notes describe it in words but name no account for the 10,000 debit, which is Equipment.
A sale on 31 December needs only entry (a) that year; correction (b) starts the next.
4. Downstream and upstream: who bears the gain

The elimination entries are the same in both directions; the split between the parent's owners and NCI is not. A downstream gain is the parent's own, so NCI share is computed on the subsidiary's reported profit. An upstream gain is part of the subsidiary's profit, so the parent bears its percentage and NCI the rest.

The notes put this as "unrealized profit yang harus dieleminasi juga sebesar kepemilikan parent". That holds for the parent's equity-method income. On consolidation the whole gain is eliminated in both directions (PSAK 110 para. B86(c)), and only its allocation is proportional.

For example (illustration), continue the equipment case with P owning 70 percent of S. In 2025 S reports profit of 60,000 and P's own profit, before income from S, is 100,000; the 10,000 gain sits with the seller.
S's realised profit for the group

Consolidated profit is the same; only its attribution moves. In the downstream case the 2,000 correction goes wholly to P, because the excess depreciation in S's books comes from P's gain. The notes' upstream truck example gives 80% × 50,000 + 80% × 1,000 − 80% × 3,000 = 38,400 by the same formula. It lists the truck's remaining life as "5 years" but depreciates "÷ 3 years", and the investment reaches 80 percent of S's equity three years after the sale, so three years is the consistent figure.
Suppose S's equity was 200,000 at the start of 2025, P bought its 70 percent at book value, and no dividends were paid, so S's equity is 260,000 at year end.

The investment account always equals the parent's share of the subsidiary's book equity less the unrealised gain it bears, which is how the notes reconcile the investment in their combined example: 540,000 less 5,000 and 14,400 gives 520,600.
5. Later years and the sale outside the group

From the second year the gain has left the income statement and sits in opening retained earnings, so the worksheet removes it from opening equity and continues the depreciation correction. With the parent on the equity method, the opening debit goes to the investment account (downstream) or to the investment account and NCI (upstream).

For example (illustration), the worksheet at 31 December 2026 for the equipment case. The unrealised gain at the start of the year is 8,000, and accumulated depreciation has to be cut by two years of correction, 4,000.
Each side totals 12,000. In P's books, Dr Investment in S / Cr Income from subsidiary, 2,000 downstream or 1,400 upstream, repeats each year to 2029.
If the parent keeps the investment at cost in its separate statements, as PSAK 227
(formerly PSAK 4, IAS 27) allows, the opening debits go to its opening retained earnings instead (K2).
Suppose the buyer sells the equipment to an outsider on 31 December 2027 for 25,000.
Unrealised at the start of 2027 = 10,000 − 2 × 2,000 = 6,000: 2,000 through depreciation, 4,000 as extra gain
Dr Investment in S 6,000 / Cr Depreciation expense 2,000, Cr Gain on sale 4,000
Dr Investment in S 4,200, Dr NCI 1,800 / Cr Depreciation expense 2,000, Cr Gain on sale 4,000
The asset has left both ledgers, so no asset account is touched, and nothing remains to eliminate.

The notes' combined Pam–Sun example (three transfers at once) recomputes cleanly: income from Sun 90% × 80,000 + 5,000 + 90% × 4,000 − 32,000 + 4,000 = 52,600, NCI share 10% × 84,000 = 8,400. Its NCI entry is reversed. The notes write "Noncontrolling interest $8.400 / Dividends $3.000 / Noncontrolling interest share $5.400"; it should be Dr NCI share 8,400 / Cr Dividends 3,000; Cr NCI 5,400.
6. Sideways sales, losses and deferred tax

(lateral) sale is treated like an upstream sale from the seller's side: the gain is eliminated in full and borne by the seller's owners, the parent's effective share and the seller's NCI. BRPT's KCE–CAA/CCP land sale is of this kind. Note 45h names KCE first and Note 16 (PDF p. 137) shows KCE holding investment-property land, so KCE is the likely seller, though the note does not say so. BRPT owns 34.63 percent of CAP directly and 3.92 percent through Marigold, 38.55 percent in all, which it treats as control because CAP's board composition gives it power over CAP's relevant activities (Note 4, PDF p. 112; see

on control with less than a majority). CAP holds CDI at 60 percent; CDI holds KCE at 70 percent and CSP at 99.99 percent; CSP holds CCP at 100 percent; CAP holds CAA through CAP2 at 99.99 percent (Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–25).

For example (illustration), if KCE were the seller and the gain were 10,000, BRPT's owners would bear 16.19% × 10,000 = 1,619 of the elimination and the NCI at the three levels the other 8,381. Had CAA or CCP sold, BRPT's owners would bear about 3,855 or 2,313. The Mutual Holdings essay (K6) works the layered allocation.

A loss on an intercompany sale is eliminated the same way with the signs reversed, unless the price shows the asset has lost value. PSAK 110 para. B86 adds that intragroup losses may indicate an impairment that must be recognised in the consolidated statements. For example (illustration), equipment carried at 30,000 is sold within the group for 22,000. If its

under PSAK 236 (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36), the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, is also 22,000, the 8,000 loss is an impairment the group would have booked anyway, and it stays; otherwise it is eliminated.
The notes do not mention tax. The buyer's
, the amount the tax authority lets it deduct, is the transfer price, while the consolidated carrying amount is the group cost. The gap is a
, one that lowers future taxable profit, under PSAK 212
(formerly PSAK 46, IAS 12). For example (illustration), with a 22 percent rate, the equipment case at the end of 2025:
Temporary difference = 32,000 tax base (tax depreciation of 8,000 assumed equal to book) − 24,000 group carrying amount = 8,000
Deferred tax asset = 22% × 8,000 = 1,760; Dr Deferred tax asset 1,760 / Cr Income tax expense 1,760

The asset unwinds by 22% × 2,000 = 440 a year as the gain is realised. PSAK 212 measures it at the buyer's rate, and PSAK 110 para. B86(c) sends these differences to PSAK 212. Indonesian land transfers bear a 2.5 percent final tax on the gross price (PP 34/2016), outside PSAK 212's mechanics. That tax is paid to the state, so it is a real group expense and is not eliminated (about 656 on 26,223 if fully taxable); the land elimination itself usually carries no deferred tax.
An intragroup lease is not a lease for the group, which owns and uses the asset. Under PSAK 116
(formerly PSAK 73, IFRS 16) the lessee books a

and a lease liability at the present value of the payments, then depreciation and interest, while the lessor of an operating lease keeps the asset and books rental income. Consolidation removes the lessee's side and the rental income, leaving the asset and its depreciation in the lessor's books.

BRPT's property segment (building and hotel management) earned 4,505 of inter-segment revenue in 2025, eliminated with 33 from "others" (Note 46, PDF p. 239); the note does not say whether it is rent.
For example (illustration), take 4,505 as an annual rent, paid in arrears for five years, discounted at 8 percent.
Lessee's year 1: depreciation = 17,987.2 / 5 = 3,597.4; interest = 8% × 17,987.2 = 1,439.0; total expense 5,036.4
Lessee's year-end balances: lease liability = 17,987.2 × 1.08 − 4,505 = 14,921.1; ROU asset = 17,987.2 − 3,597.4 = 14,389.7
Dr Rental income 4,505.0, Dr Lease liability 14,921.1 / Cr ROU asset 14,389.7, Cr Depreciation expense 3,597.4, Cr Interest expense 1,439.0

Both sides total 19,426.1. Consolidated profit in year 1 is 5,036.4 − 4,505.0 = 531.4 above the two companies' combined profit, because the lessee's front-loaded expense goes with the lessor's flat income; over five years the differences net to zero. An intragroup sale and leaseback is eliminated the same way: no gain, no ROU asset, and the asset stays at group cost.

When one group company buys another's bonds from outside holders, the group has retired its own debt, and consolidation books a gain or loss the issuer never recorded. The owner's notes have no AKL Chapter 7 (in Beams,
), so this section follows Beams and PSAK 109

(formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9). PSAK 109 says a debt repurchased by its issuer is extinguished (para. B3.3.2) and the difference between its carrying amount and the price paid goes to profit or loss (para. 3.3.3). The consolidated statements therefore show a
gain or loss on retirement, one that exists only in the group's view, in the year of purchase.

For example (illustration), BRPT issued Rp 400 billion of Series A shelf-registration bonds in July 2025, equivalent to 24,487 (Note 1c, PDF p. 24). Take a simplified USD version: P has bonds with face value 20,000 outstanding, an 8 percent coupon paid each 31 December, and an unamortised discount of 400 with four years left. On 1 January S, 70 percent owned, buys half of them in the market for 10,300.
Carrying amount of the half in P's books = 10,000 − 200 = 9,800
The interest lines then no longer cancel. Following Beams, discount and premium are amortised straight-line.
P's interest expense on the half = 800 + 200 / 4 = 850
Dr Bonds payable 10,000, Dr Interest income 725, Dr Loss on constructive retirement 500 / Cr Unamortised discount 150, Cr Interest expense 850, Cr Investment in bonds 10,225
Consolidated profit is 500 − 125 = 375 below the combined profit.
, the unrealised loss is 500 − 125 = 375 at the start:

Dr Bonds payable 10,000, Dr Interest income 725, Dr Investment in S 375 (where P's equity-method entries carried the loss) / Cr Unamortised discount 100, Cr Interest expense 850, Cr Investment in bonds 10,150

Beams assigns the whole constructive gain or loss to the issuer, here P, so NCI is unaffected; if S were the issuer, its NCI would share it. PSAK 109 does not settle that allocation. And PSAK 109 requires the effective interest method, not straight-line; the total of 500 is the same, only its timing across the four years differs.

An in-house contractor's margin on a plant built for a group power producer is an intercompany profit on a depreciable asset, released over the plant's life, which BRPT sets at 20–30 years (Note 3n). The deferred margin, and any deferred tax asset on it, stays in the consolidated balance sheet for decades.

When a developer sells land from its inventory to a group hotel or rental subsidiary, the group eliminates the revenue and margin and reclassifies the land to fixed assets or investment property (PSAK 240, formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40) at the developer's cost.
Heavy equipment sold to a group mine and depreciated on units of production releases the gain with output rather than with time.
Investasi pada Entitas Asosiasi dan Ventura Bersama

(formerly PSAK 15, IAS 28) para. 28, the investor recognises gains on upstream and downstream transactions only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests, so it eliminates only its own share. The IASB has proposed full recognition instead (ED/2024/7); redeliberations began in October 2025.
10. Presentation and analysis: Barito Pacific's Notes 3c, 14, 45 and 46
A correct elimination makes the transaction disappear, so BRPT's FS show four traces only.
Intragroup assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows "eliminated in full on consolidation"
KCE with CAA and CCP, completed in 2025, 26,223
"Elimination of gain on sale of land between CAP and SRI", (11,440) in 2025 and 2024; carrying amount of the interest nil
Inter-segment revenue 4,538 eliminated (2024: 5,136); elimination column adds 9,339 to depreciation (2024: 8,897)

KCE, CAA and CCP are all consolidated, so the 26,223 should leave the group's land at its original cost, and it leaves no visible trace. The place to look is KCE's investment-property land (Note 16, PDF p. 137), which moved only by translation, from 16,622 to 16,507 (Note 16b, PDF p. 135). The note names neither the seller nor any gain.

PT Synthetic Rubber Indonesia (SRI) is 45 percent owned through CAP. The group's share of SRI's net assets is 7,044 (45% × 15,652, rounded), against an 11,440 land-gain elimination and a carrying amount of nil, which the note explains. SRI's 2025 profit share, 45% × 16,965 = 7,634, is disclosed as unrecognised, because the elimination exceeds the group's share of net assets, so the interest stays at zero until cumulative profits cover the 11,440 (policy, Note 3, PDF p. 86). On that reading the balancing "excess" row should be 11,440 − 7,044 = 4,396 (2024: 11,440 + 592 = 12,032), not the 11,440 printed, a presentation slip. If 11,440 is the 45 percent share under PSAK 228 para. 28, the whole gain was 11,440 / 45% = 25,422, a reading of the arithmetic.

The four segments add to 203,474 + 93,449 + 1,623 + 980 = 299,526, and the elimination column takes consolidated depreciation up to 308,865. Correcting depreciation on intercompany gains lowers group depreciation (on losses it raises it), as section 3 showed, so a positive 9,339 must be dominated by something else, most likely depreciation of fair value uplifts from acquisitions recorded only at group level. The note does not show how much intercompany asset profit, if any, the column contains.
: depreciation methods, useful lives and impairment, which this page corrects rather than re-teaches.
: NCI measurement and attribution, used in sections 2–5.
: the lessee's side of PSAK 116, eliminated in section 7.
: the temporary difference on eliminated gains.
: associates and the PSAK 228 partial elimination.
K1 (business combinations), K2 (the worksheet and elimination order), K3 (intercompany inventory), K5 (consolidated cash flows), K6 (mutual holdings and layered allocation).

The seller in the KCE–CAA/CCP land sale is probably KCE (Note 16) but not stated, and the seller's gain is not disclosed. The effective interests (16.19, 38.55 and 23.13 percent) use year-end Note 1d percentages; CAP's stake in CDI fell from 70 to 60 percent in 2025, and at 70 percent the effective interest in KCE would be 18.89 percent.

The "excess of share of losses" row in Note 14 repeats 11,440 where 4,396 (2024: 12,032) would balance. The treatment is clear from the unrecognised-profit disclosure, so the row is read as a presentation error. In 2013–14 the IFRS Interpretations Committee favoured eliminating the full share and presenting any excess as a deferred gain; the IASB's narrow-scope amendment was never finalised, and BRPT floors the interest at nil instead.

Reading the positive 9,339 depreciation elimination in Note 46 as acquisition fair value depreciation is inference. BRPT does not explain the column, and the 4,505 of property inter-segment revenue may not be rent.
That the land elimination carries no deferred tax rests on reading final tax (PP 34/2016) as outside PSAK 212's scope. The 22 percent rate ignores the reduced rate some listed companies qualify for.
Allocating a constructive bond gain or loss wholly to the issuer follows Beams. PSAK 109 is silent on the allocation to NCI, and other textbooks split it between issuer and holder.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk dan Entitas Anak, consolidated financial statements 31 December 2025 and 2024 (audited, USD thousand): statement of financial position (PDF p. 14); Note 1c and 1d (PDF pp. 24–25); Note 3c (PDF p. 68); Note 3 equity-method policy (PDF p. 86); Note 3n (PDF p. 90); Note 4, control over CAP (PDF p. 112); Note 14, including the unrecognised share of profit (PDF p. 125); Note 16 (PDF pp. 135, 137); Note 45 (PDF pp. 235–237); Note 46 (PDF p. 239). : land downstream and upstream, sale to outsiders, depreciable assets, piecemeal recognition, the truck example and the combined Pam–Sun example. NOTES. Corrections made here: patents removed from the non-depreciable class (finite legal life); the elimination "sebesar kepemilikan parent" clarified as applying to the parent's income only; in the upstream land case the separate incomes are swapped ($180,000 for Son and $140,000 for Pop, where 90% × $140,000 = $126,000 is the figure used), "$108.000 ($126.000 − $108.000)" should read $126,000 − $18,000, the entry "Investment 18,000 / Noncontrolling interest share 2,000 / Land 20,000" belongs to later years and debits NCI, not NCI share, and the worksheet's NCI rows are swapped (1 January 60,000 plus share 12,000 = 72,000); the gross-form debit of $10,000 has no account named (Equipment); the truck's remaining life reads "5 years" where three is used; the combined example's NCI entry is reversed (Dr NCI share 8,400 / Cr Dividends 3,000, Cr NCI 5,400); the worksheet headers read "80%" in 90 percent cases; the combined worksheet's NCI rows are misplaced as in the upstream land worksheet. The remaining figures in the notes' examples recompute. Sections 6 (deferred tax, losses), 7 and 9 have no note.
No owner's note exists for intercompany bonds (Beams Chapter 7 is missing from the set). Section 8 follows Beams,

, ch. 7 (constructive retirement, allocation to the issuer, straight-line amortisation), not on disk, NOT VERIFIED; and PSAK 109 (IFRS 9) paras. 3.3.3 and B3.3.2, VERIFIED (web, secondary: IFRIC 19 text on ifrs.org; ifrscommunity.com, "Derecognition of financial liabilities").

presentation.deck: How a group removes the gain one of its companies books when it sells land, equipment or buildings to another, and how that gain comes back as depreciation, as an outside sale, or through leases and bonds, with Barito Pacific's 2025 statements as the starting numbers
key_takeaways: When one group company sells a plant asset to another above its carrying amount, the seller books a gain the group has not earned, because the asset has not left the group. Consolidation removes the gain in full and puts the asset back at the seller's carrying amount, the group cost.

For land the gain stays eliminated until the land is sold outside the group. For a depreciable asset the buyer depreciates the transfer price, so each year's excess depreciation is corrected, and the gain comes back piece by piece over the remaining life.

Direction decides who bears the gain. A downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) falls wholly on the parent's owners; an upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) is shared with the non-controlling interest (NCI). Intercompany leases and bonds bought back within the group follow the same logic.

title: Inventories, Net: Cost, Cost Flow and the Lower of Cost and NRV
snippet: The theory of inventory accounting from definition to disclosure, worked through PHE's materials and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • Inventory accounting answers three questions in order: which goods belong to the entity, what they cost, and whether that cost will come back. Control settles the first, the cost elements and a cost formula the second, and the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV) the third.

  • A cost formula only divides one pool of cost between the balance sheet and profit or loss. When prices rise, FIFO leaves the most on the balance sheet and weighted average less. LIFO, which leaves the least, is no longer allowed.

  • Not every industry follows the cost model. Agricultural produce enters inventory at fair value less costs to sell at harvest (PSAK 241), commodity broker-traders may carry stock at fair value less costs to sell, and producers of minerals and crops may carry it at NRV. PHE's materials follow the plain cost model, with an allowance of 45,911 against 852,308 of cost at the end of 2024.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report inventories, net, of 806,397 at 31 December 2024 against 658,712 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 2.6 percent of total assets and 10.0 percent of current assets (2.1 and 6.7 percent a year earlier).

After reading it a student should be able to explain each step of inventory accounting, record it in journals, and see where other industries depart from the cost model.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What inventory is

PSAK 202 Inventories (formerly PSAK 14, IAS 2) defines it in three parts: assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, assets in the process of production for such sale, and materials or supplies to be consumed in production or in rendering services (para. 6).

The three parts follow three business models. A trader holds merchandise; a manufacturer holds raw materials, work in process and finished goods; a service or extractive business holds the materials and supplies it consumes.

PHE is the third kind. Its policy names "spare parts, chemicals and others" (Note 3j, Daftar 5/53, PDF p. 70), and Note 11 shows one category, general materials, held by the subsidiaries (Daftar 5/99–5/100, PDF pp. 116–117). There is no crude oil in the line. The revenue policy explains why little would be expected: PHE recognises crude revenue "based on the actual lifting amount and sold to customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79), so production cost goes to expense with the barrels sold instead of collecting as a stock of product.

Inventory is current even if part of it will be used after twelve months, because it is consumed in the normal operating cycle (PSAK 201.66(a) and 68, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). Spare parts and stand-by equipment used over more than one period are fixed assets under PSAK 216 (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16, para. 8). A drill bit used up in one well is inventory; a spare compressor that will run for ten years is not.

2. Perpetual and periodic systems

In a perpetual system the inventory account moves with every receipt and issue, so the balance is known at any moment. In a periodic system purchases go to a purchases account and inventory is updated only after a year-end count, so usage is a residual.

Usage = opening inventory + purchases − closing inventory (counted)

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary opens a new shore base with no stock, buys 3,000 of drilling chemicals, and issues 2,400 to operations according to its issue slips. The year-end count finds 560.

Perpetual

Periodic

Purchase

Dr Inventories 3,000 / Cr Trade payables 3,000

Dr Purchases 3,000 / Cr Trade payables 3,000

Issues

Dr Production expenses 2,400 / Cr Inventories 2,400

no entry

Year end

Book 600, count 560: Dr Inventory shortage 40 / Cr Inventories 40

Usage = 0 + 3,000 − 560 = 2,440: Dr Inventories 560, Dr Production expenses 2,440 / Cr Purchases 3,000

Both end with 560 on the balance sheet. Only the perpetual system shows that 40 went missing and puts it on a line someone has to explain; the periodic system buries it in usage. That is why Kieso stresses that a perpetual system still needs counts. The ledger says what should be there, and only the count says what is.

3. Which goods are included

The rule is control, not location. Kieso gives the standard cases.

  • Goods in transit follow the shipping terms. Under FOB (free on board) shipping point, title, freight and risk pass to the buyer when the seller hands the goods to the carrier, so goods at sea are the buyer's. Under FOB destination they stay the seller's until they arrive.

  • Consigned goods stay with the consignor. The consignee holds them but does not control them.

  • Special agreements need a closer look. A sale with a buy-back obligation may leave the goods with the seller, and under a sale with a right of return the seller removes the goods but records a refund liability and an asset for the right to recover them (PSAK 115).

So a PHE subsidiary counts casing on a ship bought FOB shipping point although nobody has seen it, and leaves out a supplier's consigned chemicals although they sit in its warehouse.

PHE's contracts show the principle working against legal title. Under its production sharing contracts (PSCs), "materials, supplies and equipment acquired by the PSC Contractors … belongs to the Government", while the contractor has "the right to utilise" them until SKK Migas, the upstream regulator, approves them as surplus or abandoned (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). PHE still carries them as inventory, consistent with control: the contractor decides where each joint of pipe goes and consumes it.

4. Which costs are included

Cost is everything it took to bring an item to its present location and condition (PSAK 202.10). Kieso splits costs into two families. Product costs attach to the goods: purchase price, import duties and taxes that are not recoverable (para. 11), transport and other directly attributable costs, less trade discounts (para. 11), plus conversion costs for a manufacturer (section 8). Period costs are expensed as incurred: selling, administrative and general costs, and storage after arrival unless production needs it (para. 16).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 600 joints of casing from an overseas mill, FOB shipping point, list price USD 2.50 thousand per joint, with a 4 percent trade discount.

Invoice = 600 × 2.50 × (1 − 4%) = 1,440

Cost at 31 December, at sea = 1,440 + 72 ocean freight and insurance = 1,512

Cost on arrival = 1,512 + 18 non-recoverable import charges + 30 port handling and trucking = 1,560

Cash discounts for prompt payment follow one of two methods. The gross method records the invoice amount and deducts the discount only when earned. The net method records the discounted price from the start, on the view that it is the real price, so a missed discount is a finance cost under other income and expense. Suppose terms of 2/10, net 30, so paying within ten days saves 1,440 × 2% = 28.8.

Gross method

Net method

Purchase

Dr Inventories 1,440 / Cr Trade payables 1,440

Dr Inventories 1,411.2 / Cr Trade payables 1,411.2

Paid within 10 days

Dr Trade payables 1,440 / Cr Inventories 28.8 / Cr Cash 1,411.2

Dr Trade payables 1,411.2 / Cr Cash 1,411.2

Paid late

Dr Trade payables 1,440 / Cr Cash 1,440

Dr Trade payables 1,411.2, Dr Purchase discounts lost 28.8 / Cr Cash 1,440

Paid on time, both reach a shelf cost of 1,560 − 28.8 = 1,531.2, or USD 2.552 thousand per joint. Paid late, the gross method leaves 28.8 inside the casing, while the net method shows it as the cost of financing the purchase. Kieso prefers the net method. PSAK 202 does not settle the choice: its interest rule (para. 18) covers settlement beyond normal credit terms, and day 30 of net 30 is within them. IFRS practice deducts discounts taken and generally leaves a missed discount in cost, the gross-method result.

5. Cost formulas

When identical items are bought at different prices, which price leaves with an issue? A cost formula answers that. It does not change the total; it only splits one pool of cost between what is used up and what stays on the shelf. PSAK 202 allows three answers (paras. 23–25).

  • Specific identification tracks each item's actual cost. It is required for items that are not interchangeable or are set aside for one project, such as a wellhead built for one well.

  • First-in, first-out (FIFO) assumes the oldest items go first, so closing stock carries the latest prices.

  • Weighted average gives every unit the pool's average cost, once for the period (periodic) or after every purchase (moving average, in a perpetual system).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary's tubing ledger for one year, in USD thousand per joint:

1 January: on hand 200 joints at 1.20 = 240.00

10 March: buy 300 joints at 1.30 = 390.00

15 May: issue 350 joints to a routine workover (a repair of an existing well)

5 September: buy 250 joints at 1.45 = 362.50

20 November: issue 150 joints to a new development well

Cost available = 992.50 for 750 joints; closing stock 250 joints

FIFO: issues = 200 × 1.20 + 150 × 1.30 + 150 × 1.30 = 630.00; closing = 250 × 1.45 = 362.50

Periodic average: 992.50 / 750 = 1.32333; issues = 500 × 1.32333 = 661.67; closing = 250 × 1.32333 = 330.83

Moving average: after March (240.00 + 390.00) / 500 = 1.26, so May issue = 441.00 and 189.00 remains; after September (189.00 + 362.50) / 400 = 1.37875, so November issue = 206.81 and closing = 344.69

All three split the same 992.50. With prices rising, FIFO leaves the most on the shelf and the least in expense; the averages sit in between. LIFO would leave the oldest prices on the shelf (200 × 1.20 + 50 × 1.30 = 305.00, periodic), which is why IAS 2 removed it in 2003, because in a long inflation the balance sheet would carry prices from decades ago. Indonesian income tax law is narrower still and accepts only average and FIFO (UU PPh art. 10(6)).

The same formula must be used for inventories of similar nature and use across a group (paras. 25–26). An issue lands according to what the material does: the routine workover keeps a well producing, so its cost is a production expense, while the development well is a new asset, so its cost is capitalised into oil and gas properties and reaches profit later through depletion on a unit-of-production basis (para. 35). PHE uses the weighted average (Note 3j).

6. Lower of cost and net realisable value

Cost says what was spent to get an item onto the shelf, but not whether that spending will come back. The lower of cost and NRV rule closes that gap. An asset should not be carried at more than the entity expects to recover from it (para. 9), and a loss that has already happened belongs in this period.

NRV = estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business − estimated costs to complete − estimated costs to sell

There are only two possibilities. If NRV is above cost, nothing happens. The rule only writes down, and an expected gain waits for the sale. If NRV is below cost, the item is written down to NRV and the difference is expensed.

Unit of comparison. The comparison is made item by item. Similar items may be grouped only when they cannot practicably be judged one by one, and writing down a whole class such as "all spares" is not allowed (para. 29). For example (illustration), suppose 51,000 of PHE's 852,308 of materials at cost (Note 11) is surplus that SKK Migas has approved for sale, so each item has a selling price.

Comparing totals would let 1,800 of headroom on grade S pipe hide 1,700 of losses on the other two items.

Materials held for use. Most of PHE's stock is never sold, so there is no selling price to use. PSAK 202 looks at what the material turns into. Materials held for use in production are not written down below cost while the product they go into is expected to sell at or above cost (para. 32), because the material's value is recovered through the product. For an upstream group the "product" is the oil and gas the field produces, or the well the material builds. That is a reading by analogy, since that output never sits in inventory. Only when the product no longer covers its cost is the material written down, and replacement cost may then be the best available measure of its NRV. For example (illustration), drilling chemicals bought for 1,000 whose replacement price has fallen to 850.

Field still economic: no write-down, carried at 1,000

Field no longer covers its cost: write-down = 1,000 − 850 = 150

At an upstream group the test therefore bites mainly on stock that will not be used at all: obsolete grades, parts for retired equipment, materials that have sat too long (para. 28). PHE describes its allowance in those terms, for "obsolete, unuseable and slow-moving materials" (Note 3j).

Recording the write-down. Kieso gives two methods that differ only in where the expense sits. The COGS method folds it into cost of goods sold, for PHE production expenses; the loss method shows it on its own line. Either way most entities credit an allowance, a contra account, so the item ledger stays at cost and the balance sheet shows the net figure. That is where the line gets the "net" in its name. Take PHE's 2024 numbers as the starting point (Note 11): cost 852,308, allowance needed at year end 45,911, opening allowance 37,639. Assume, for illustration, that the whole movement is new write-downs with no scrapping or reversals.

Net charge for 2024 = 45,911 − 37,639 = 8,272; inventories, net = 852,308 − 45,911 = 806,397

COGS method

Loss method

Dr Loss due to decline in inventory value 8,272

Cr Allowance for decline in value 8,272

Cr Allowance for decline in value 8,272

Profit and the net 806,397 are the same under both. PHE does not say which line carries the charge.

Recovery and scrapping. When the reason for a write-down goes away, it is reversed, but only up to the original write-down, so an item never returns above cost (para. 33), and the reversal reduces the period's inventory expense (para. 34). For example (illustration), in 2025, slow-moving pipe carrying an allowance of 4,000 is taken up for a new well campaign.

Dr Allowance for decline in value 4,000 / Cr Recovery of inventory loss 4,000

If the pipe were scrapped at the value already provided for, cost and allowance would leave together (Dr Allowance and Dr Cash for any scrap proceeds / Cr Inventories) and profit would not move.

7. Other valuation bases and estimation methods

Purchase commitments. A loss can arise before the goods arrive. Kieso recognises it when the market price falls below a non-cancellable contract price. PSAK reaches it through PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37): a contract is onerous when the unavoidable cost of meeting it exceeds the benefit expected from it (para. 10). For example (illustration), a subsidiary has a non-cancellable order for casing at 10,000 for 2025 delivery, and by the end of 2024 the market price is 7,000. If the casing is still going into economic wells, section 6 says it would not be written down on delivery, so nothing is booked. If the drilling programme has been cancelled, a provision of 3,000 is recognised.

Dr Loss on onerous purchase commitment 3,000 / Cr Provision 3,000

On delivery: Dr Inventories 7,000, Dr Provision 3,000 / Cr Cash 10,000

Basket purchases. Items bought for one price share it by their relative standalone sales value. For example (illustration), a lot of used rig spares bought for 900, with standalone values of 600 for pumps and 300 each for valves and fittings (1,200 in total).

Pumps = 900 × 600 / 1,200 = 450; valves = fittings = 900 × 300 / 1,200 = 225

Dr Inventories, pumps 450, Dr Inventories, valves 225, Dr Inventories, fittings 225 / Cr Cash 900

The gross profit method. When stock cannot be counted, after a fire or for an interim report, it is estimated from the normal margin. For example (illustration), opening stock 800, purchases 3,600, sales 5,000, normal gross margin 25 percent.

Cost of goods sold = 5,000 × 75% = 3,750; closing inventory = 800 + 3,600 − 3,750 = 650

It rests on a past margin that may no longer hold, so Kieso treats it as an estimate or a check, not a basis for annual statements.

The retail method. Retailers apply the same logic through a ratio of cost to retail price, accepted where many fast-moving items share similar margins (para. 22). Markups raise retail prices above the original and markdowns cut them below it. For example (illustration), a retail subsidiary has opening stock of 50 at cost and 100 at retail, purchases of 2,000 at cost and 3,500 at retail, net markups of 200, net markdowns of 50 and sales of 2,500.

Goods available: cost 2,050; retail 3,600 + 200 markups = 3,800

Ratio A (markups only) = 2,050 / 3,800 = 53.95%

Retail after markdowns = 3,800 − 50 = 3,750; ratio B = 2,050 / 3,750 = 54.67%

Closing stock at retail = 3,750 − 2,500 = 1,250

At cost: A = 1,250 × 53.95% = 674.3; B = 1,250 × 54.67% = 683.3

Ratio A leaves markdowns out of the denominator, so it gives the lower closing stock, the conventional version that approximates the lower of cost and market.

Errors. Closing inventory is subtracted to get the expense, so overstating it by 1,000 makes this year's profit 1,000 too high and, as next year's opening stock, next year's 1,000 too low. The error reverses over two years, but both years are misstated. A material error found later is corrected retrospectively under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8).

8. Inventory across industries

Manufacturing. Cost includes conversion costs: direct labour and a systematic share of production overhead (para. 12). Fixed overhead is spread on normal capacity, not actual output, so a quiet year does not make each unit look dearer (para. 13). In an abnormally busy year the rate is reduced instead, so units are not carried above cost, and variable overhead follows actual use. For example (illustration), fixed overhead 1,200, normal capacity 1,000 units, actual output 800.

Rate = 1,200 / 1,000 = 1.2 per unit; into inventory = 800 × 1.2 = 960; expensed as idle capacity = 1,200 − 960 = 240

Standard costs may be used if they approximate actual cost and are reviewed regularly (para. 21).

Agriculture. Living animals and plants are biological assets under PSAK 241 Agriculture (formerly PSAK 69, IAS 41), not inventory. They are measured at fair value less costs to sell (not NRV), with each period's change in profit or loss, because growth itself is how value is created. At harvest the produce becomes inventory, and its fair value less costs to sell at that moment becomes its cost under PSAK 202 (para. 20). Plants that only bear produce, such as oil palms, rubber or tea, are bearer plants and are fixed assets under PSAK 216; the produce growing on them stays in PSAK 241 until harvest. For example (illustration), a plantation harvests 10,000 tonnes of fresh fruit bunches when their fair value is 0.19 per tonne (USD 190) and costs to sell are 0.01 per tonne. The produce on the trees was carried at 1,500 at the last reporting date.

Fair value less costs to sell at harvest = 10,000 × (0.19 − 0.01) = 1,800

Remeasure to harvest: Dr Biological assets 300 / Cr Gain on change in fair value less costs to sell 300

Harvest: Dr Inventories, fresh fruit bunches 1,800 / Cr Biological assets 1,800

The 300 gain at harvest (IAS 41.28) recognises growth as it happens. From there the bunches are ordinary inventory, so milling into crude palm oil adds conversion costs to the 1,800, and the lower of cost and NRV applies.

Producers of minerals and crops, and commodity traders. PSAK 202 exempts two groups from its measurement rules (para. 3). Producers of agricultural and forest products, of produce after harvest, and of minerals and mineral products may measure at NRV where that is established industry practice, for example when sale is assured by a forward contract or a government guarantee, or an active market exists (para. 4). Commodity broker-traders, who buy to profit from short-term price moves, may measure at fair value less costs to sell (para. 5), in both cases with changes in profit or loss.

Mining. Ore stockpiles and concentrate are inventory at the lower of cost and NRV. In an open-pit mine the cost of removing waste rock during production is split between inventory, for ore extracted now, and a stripping activity asset, for access to ore later (ISAK 120, formerly ISAK 29, IFRIC 20). In Indonesia this replaced PSAK 33, which was revoked from 2014.

Real estate. Land and buildings a developer holds for sale are inventory (para. 8). The same building would be investment property under PSAK 240 (formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40) if held for rent or capital appreciation, and a fixed asset under PSAK 216 if used by the entity. Intention decides the classification.

Financial instruments are never inventory under PSAK 202 (para. 2(b)), even for a securities dealer; they follow PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9).

9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 11

PSAK 202 asks for the policy, the carrying amount by classification, the amount expensed, write-downs and reversals, and stock pledged (para. 36). PHE gives gross cost, the allowance and its movement (Note 11, Daftar 5/99, PDF p. 116).

852,308

(45,911)

Allowance coverage = 37,639 / 696,351 = 5.41% (2023); 45,911 / 852,308 = 5.39% (2024)

The allowance grew in step with cost, so the 22.4 percent rise in the net line came from more materials at a steady coverage ratio. PHE prints one combined movement a year (−3,084 in 2023, +8,272 in 2024), and one net figure can hide several events. For example (illustration), the 2023 deduction of 3,084 could be all reversals (profit up 3,084), all scrapping of fully provided stock (profit unchanged), or new write-downs of 2,000 with 4,000 scrapped and 1,084 reversed (profit down 916).

Inventory turnover = inventory expensed / average inventory; days in inventory = 365 / turnover

For example (illustration), if PHE's subsidiaries had used 1,600,000 of materials in 2024, turnover would be 1,600,000 / ((806,397 + 658,712) / 2) = 2.18 times, about 167 days. PHE does not disclose the total amount of inventories expensed. Note 39 gives material usage of 163,694 for its other operations only (Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166), and the cash flow statement uses the direct method (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17), so the real ratio cannot be computed. PHE also keeps 6,809 of "dead stock material" outside the line, in other non-current assets (Note 14b, Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122).

10. Upstream note: cost recovery

Under a cost recovery PSC, material costs are recovered from production (Note 2a(iii), Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). A deferred tax liability on "non-capital inventory" of 17,193 (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172) suggests such materials are deducted for PSC purposes before issue. Gross split contracts have no cost recovery (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). The inventory accounting is the same under both.

11. Related lines

  • oil-gas-properties-net: where materials issued to development wells are capitalised.

  • fixed-assets-net: the boundary for major spares and stand-by equipment.

  • production-expenses: issued consumables and, under the COGS method, write-downs.

  • trade-payables: the other side of purchases.

  • other-non-current-assets: holds the dead stock material.

  • deferred-tax-liabilities: the temporary difference on non-capital inventory.

Least-confident assertions

  • The control argument for carrying government-owned materials is this page's reading. PHE does not explain why it recognises them. That non-capital materials are recovered before they are issued is read from Note 43e, not stated in the FS, and a deferred tax liability can have other causes.

  • How PSAK 202 treats a missed settlement discount is not stated in the standard. The reading follows the 2004 IFRIC discussion and firm guidance.

  • Applying the PSAK 202 materials rule (para. 32) to an upstream group, where the product never sits in inventory, is a reading by analogy, as is using it to decide that the casing commitment is not onerous.

  • That little crude would be held at year end is inferred from the revenue policy. The FS state no policy for crude inventory.

content.text: Inventory accounting answers three questions in order: which goods belong to the entity, what they cost, and whether that cost will come back. Control settles the first, the cost elements and a cost formula the second, and the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV) the third.

A cost formula only divides one pool of cost between the balance sheet and profit or loss. When prices rise, FIFO leaves the most on the balance sheet and weighted average less. LIFO, which leaves the least, is no longer allowed.

Not every industry follows the cost model. Agricultural produce enters inventory at fair value less costs to sell at harvest (PSAK 241), commodity broker-traders may carry stock at fair value less costs to sell, and producers of minerals and crops may carry it at NRV. PHE's materials follow the plain cost model, with an allowance of 45,911 against 852,308 of cost at the end of 2024.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report inventories, net, of 806,397 at 31 December 2024 against 658,712 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 2.6 percent of total assets and 10.0 percent of current assets (2.1 and 6.7 percent a year earlier).
After reading it a student should be able to explain each step of inventory accounting, record it in journals, and see where other industries depart from the cost model.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

That is why Kieso stresses that a perpetual system still needs counts. The ledger says what should be there, and only the count says what is.
The rule is control, not location. Kieso gives the standard cases.

follow the shipping terms. Under FOB (free on board) shipping point, title, freight and risk pass to the buyer when the seller hands the goods to the carrier, so goods at sea are the buyer's. Under FOB destination they stay the seller's until they arrive.
stay with the consignor. The consignee holds them but does not control them.

need a closer look. A sale with a buy-back obligation may leave the goods with the seller, and under a sale with a right of return the seller removes the goods but records a refund liability and an asset for the right to recover them (PSAK 115).
So a PHE subsidiary counts casing on a ship bought FOB shipping point although nobody has seen it, and leaves out a supplier's consigned chemicals although they sit in its warehouse.

PHE's contracts show the principle working against legal title. Under its production sharing contracts (PSCs), "materials, supplies and equipment acquired by the PSC Contractors … belongs to the Government", while the contractor has "the right to utilise" them until SKK Migas, the upstream regulator, approves them as surplus or abandoned (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). PHE still carries them as inventory, consistent with control: the contractor decides where each joint of pipe goes and consumes it.
Cost is everything it took to bring an item to its present location and condition (PSAK 202.10). Kieso splits costs into two families.

attach to the goods: purchase price, import duties and taxes that are not recoverable (para. 11), transport and other directly attributable costs, less trade discounts (para. 11), plus conversion costs for a manufacturer (section 8).
are expensed as incurred: selling, administrative and general costs, and storage after arrival unless production needs it (para. 16).
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 600 joints of casing from an overseas mill, FOB shipping point, list price USD 2.50 thousand per joint, with a 4 percent trade discount.
Cost at 31 December, at sea = 1,440 + 72 ocean freight and insurance = 1,512
Cost on arrival = 1,512 + 18 non-recoverable import charges + 30 port handling and trucking = 1,560
Cash discounts for prompt payment follow one of two methods. The
records the invoice amount and deducts the discount only when earned. The

records the discounted price from the start, on the view that it is the real price, so a missed discount is a finance cost under other income and expense. Suppose terms of 2/10, net 30, so paying within ten days saves 1,440 × 2% = 28.8.
Dr Trade payables 1,440 / Cr Inventories 28.8 / Cr Cash 1,411.2
Dr Trade payables 1,411.2, Dr Purchase discounts lost 28.8 / Cr Cash 1,440

Paid on time, both reach a shelf cost of 1,560 − 28.8 = 1,531.2, or USD 2.552 thousand per joint. Paid late, the gross method leaves 28.8 inside the casing, while the net method shows it as the cost of financing the purchase. Kieso prefers the net method. PSAK 202 does not settle the choice: its interest rule (para. 18) covers settlement beyond normal credit terms, and day 30 of net 30 is within them. IFRS practice deducts discounts taken and generally leaves a missed discount in cost, the gross-method result.

When identical items are bought at different prices, which price leaves with an issue? A cost formula answers that. It does not change the total; it only splits one pool of cost between what is used up and what stays on the shelf. PSAK 202 allows three answers (paras. 23–25).
tracks each item's actual cost. It is required for items that are not interchangeable or are set aside for one project, such as a wellhead built for one well.
assumes the oldest items go first, so closing stock carries the latest prices.
gives every unit the pool's average cost, once for the period (periodic) or after every purchase (moving average, in a perpetual system).
For example (illustration), a subsidiary's tubing ledger for one year, in USD thousand per joint:
15 May: issue 350 joints to a routine workover (a repair of an existing well)
20 November: issue 150 joints to a new development well
Cost available = 992.50 for 750 joints; closing stock 250 joints

Moving average: after March (240.00 + 390.00) / 500 = 1.26, so May issue = 441.00 and 189.00 remains; after September (189.00 + 362.50) / 400 = 1.37875, so November issue = 206.81 and closing = 344.69

All three split the same 992.50. With prices rising, FIFO leaves the most on the shelf and the least in expense; the averages sit in between. LIFO would leave the oldest prices on the shelf (200 × 1.20 + 50 × 1.30 = 305.00, periodic), which is why IAS 2 removed it in 2003, because in a long inflation the balance sheet would carry prices from decades ago. Indonesian income tax law is narrower still and accepts only average and FIFO (UU PPh art. 10(6)).

The same formula must be used for inventories of similar nature and use across a group (paras. 25–26). An issue lands according to what the material does: the routine workover keeps a well producing, so its cost is a production expense, while the development well is a new asset, so its cost is capitalised into oil and gas properties and reaches profit later through depletion on a unit-of-production basis (para. 35). PHE uses the weighted average (Note 3j).
6. Lower of cost and net realisable value

Cost says what was spent to get an item onto the shelf, but not whether that spending will come back. The lower of cost and NRV rule closes that gap. An asset should not be carried at more than the entity expects to recover from it (para. 9), and a loss that has already happened belongs in this period.
NRV = estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business − estimated costs to complete − estimated costs to sell

There are only two possibilities. If NRV is above cost, nothing happens. The rule only writes down, and an expected gain waits for the sale. If NRV is below cost, the item is written down to NRV and the difference is expensed.

The comparison is made item by item. Similar items may be grouped only when they cannot practicably be judged one by one, and writing down a whole class such as "all spares" is not allowed (para. 29). For example (illustration), suppose 51,000 of PHE's 852,308 of materials at cost (Note 11) is surplus that SKK Migas has approved for sale, so each item has a selling price.
Item by item: write-down = 51,000 − 49,300 = 1,700. As a whole: NRV 51,100 > cost 51,000, no write-down
Comparing totals would let 1,800 of headroom on grade S pipe hide 1,700 of losses on the other two items.

Most of PHE's stock is never sold, so there is no selling price to use. PSAK 202 looks at what the material turns into. Materials held for use in production are not written down below cost while the product they go into is expected to sell at or above cost (para. 32), because the material's value is recovered through the product. For an upstream group the "product" is the oil and gas the field produces, or the well the material builds. That is a reading by analogy, since that output never sits in inventory. Only when the product no longer covers its cost is the material written down, and replacement cost may then be the best available measure of its NRV. For example (illustration), drilling chemicals bought for 1,000 whose replacement price has fallen to 850.
Field still economic: no write-down, carried at 1,000
Field no longer covers its cost: write-down = 1,000 − 850 = 150

At an upstream group the test therefore bites mainly on stock that will not be used at all: obsolete grades, parts for retired equipment, materials that have sat too long (para. 28). PHE describes its allowance in those terms, for "obsolete, unuseable and slow-moving materials" (Note 3j).
Kieso gives two methods that differ only in where the expense sits. The
folds it into cost of goods sold, for PHE production expenses; the

shows it on its own line. Either way most entities credit an allowance, a contra account, so the item ledger stays at cost and the balance sheet shows the net figure. That is where the line gets the "net" in its name. Take PHE's 2024 numbers as the starting point (Note 11): cost 852,308, allowance needed at year end 45,911, opening allowance 37,639. Assume, for illustration, that the whole movement is new write-downs with no scrapping or reversals.
Dr Loss due to decline in inventory value 8,272
Cr Allowance for decline in value 8,272
Cr Allowance for decline in value 8,272
Profit and the net 806,397 are the same under both. PHE does not say which line carries the charge.

When the reason for a write-down goes away, it is reversed, but only up to the original write-down, so an item never returns above cost (para. 33), and the reversal reduces the period's inventory expense (para. 34). For example (illustration), in 2025, slow-moving pipe carrying an allowance of 4,000 is taken up for a new well campaign.
Dr Allowance for decline in value 4,000 / Cr Recovery of inventory loss 4,000
If the pipe were scrapped at the value already provided for, cost and allowance would leave together (Dr Allowance and Dr Cash for any scrap proceeds / Cr Inventories) and profit would not move.
7. Other valuation bases and estimation methods

A loss can arise before the goods arrive. Kieso recognises it when the market price falls below a non-cancellable contract price. PSAK reaches it through PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37): a contract is

when the unavoidable cost of meeting it exceeds the benefit expected from it (para. 10). For example (illustration), a subsidiary has a non-cancellable order for casing at 10,000 for 2025 delivery, and by the end of 2024 the market price is 7,000. If the casing is still going into economic wells, section 6 says it would not be written down on delivery, so nothing is booked. If the drilling programme has been cancelled, a provision of 3,000 is recognised.
Dr Loss on onerous purchase commitment 3,000 / Cr Provision 3,000
On delivery: Dr Inventories 7,000, Dr Provision 3,000 / Cr Cash 10,000
Items bought for one price share it by their
. For example (illustration), a lot of used rig spares bought for 900, with standalone values of 600 for pumps and 300 each for valves and fittings (1,200 in total).
Dr Inventories, pumps 450, Dr Inventories, valves 225, Dr Inventories, fittings 225 / Cr Cash 900

When stock cannot be counted, after a fire or for an interim report, it is estimated from the normal margin. For example (illustration), opening stock 800, purchases 3,600, sales 5,000, normal gross margin 25 percent.
Cost of goods sold = 5,000 × 75% = 3,750; closing inventory = 800 + 3,600 − 3,750 = 650
It rests on a past margin that may no longer hold, so Kieso treats it as an estimate or a check, not a basis for annual statements.
Retailers apply the same logic through a ratio of cost to retail price, accepted where many fast-moving items share similar margins (para. 22).
raise retail prices above the original and

cut them below it. For example (illustration), a retail subsidiary has opening stock of 50 at cost and 100 at retail, purchases of 2,000 at cost and 3,500 at retail, net markups of 200, net markdowns of 50 and sales of 2,500.
Ratio A leaves markdowns out of the denominator, so it gives the lower closing stock, the conventional version that approximates the lower of cost and market.

Closing inventory is subtracted to get the expense, so overstating it by 1,000 makes this year's profit 1,000 too high and, as next year's opening stock, next year's 1,000 too low. The error reverses over two years, but both years are misstated. A material error found later is corrected retrospectively under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8).
: direct labour and a systematic share of production overhead (para. 12). Fixed overhead is spread on

, not actual output, so a quiet year does not make each unit look dearer (para. 13). In an abnormally busy year the rate is reduced instead, so units are not carried above cost, and variable overhead follows actual use. For example (illustration), fixed overhead 1,200, normal capacity 1,000 units, actual output 800.
Rate = 1,200 / 1,000 = 1.2 per unit; into inventory = 800 × 1.2 = 960; expensed as idle capacity = 1,200 − 960 = 240
Standard costs may be used if they approximate actual cost and are reviewed regularly (para. 21).

(formerly PSAK 69, IAS 41), not inventory. They are measured at fair value less costs to sell (not NRV), with each period's change in profit or loss, because growth itself is how value is created. At harvest the produce becomes inventory, and its fair value less costs to sell at that moment becomes its cost under PSAK 202 (para. 20). Plants that only bear produce, such as oil palms, rubber or tea, are

and are fixed assets under PSAK 216; the produce growing on them stays in PSAK 241 until harvest. For example (illustration), a plantation harvests 10,000 tonnes of fresh fruit bunches when their fair value is 0.19 per tonne (USD 190) and costs to sell are 0.01 per tonne. The produce on the trees was carried at 1,500 at the last reporting date.
Fair value less costs to sell at harvest = 10,000 × (0.19 − 0.01) = 1,800
Remeasure to harvest: Dr Biological assets 300 / Cr Gain on change in fair value less costs to sell 300
Harvest: Dr Inventories, fresh fruit bunches 1,800 / Cr Biological assets 1,800

The 300 gain at harvest (IAS 41.28) recognises growth as it happens. From there the bunches are ordinary inventory, so milling into crude palm oil adds conversion costs to the 1,800, and the lower of cost and NRV applies.
Producers of minerals and crops, and commodity traders.

PSAK 202 exempts two groups from its measurement rules (para. 3). Producers of agricultural and forest products, of produce after harvest, and of minerals and mineral products may measure at NRV where that is established industry practice, for example when sale is assured by a forward contract or a government guarantee, or an active market exists (para. 4). Commodity broker-traders, who buy to profit from short-term price moves, may measure at fair value less costs to sell (para. 5), in both cases with changes in profit or loss.

Ore stockpiles and concentrate are inventory at the lower of cost and NRV. In an open-pit mine the cost of removing waste rock during production is split between inventory, for ore extracted now, and a
, for access to ore later (ISAK 120, formerly ISAK 29, IFRIC 20). In Indonesia this replaced PSAK 33, which was revoked from 2014.

Land and buildings a developer holds for sale are inventory (para. 8). The same building would be investment property under PSAK 240 (formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40) if held for rent or capital appreciation, and a fixed asset under PSAK 216 if used by the entity. Intention decides the classification.
are never inventory under PSAK 202 (para. 2(b)), even for a securities dealer; they follow PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9).

PSAK 202 asks for the policy, the carrying amount by classification, the amount expensed, write-downs and reversals, and stock pledged (para. 36). PHE gives gross cost, the allowance and its movement (Note 11, Daftar 5/99, PDF p. 116).
Less allowance for decline in value

The allowance grew in step with cost, so the 22.4 percent rise in the net line came from more materials at a steady coverage ratio. PHE prints one combined movement a year (−3,084 in 2023, +8,272 in 2024), and one net figure can hide several events. For example (illustration), the 2023 deduction of 3,084 could be all reversals (profit up 3,084), all scrapping of fully provided stock (profit unchanged), or new write-downs of 2,000 with 4,000 scrapped and 1,084 reversed (profit down 916).
Inventory turnover = inventory expensed / average inventory; days in inventory = 365 / turnover

For example (illustration), if PHE's subsidiaries had used 1,600,000 of materials in 2024, turnover would be 1,600,000 / ((806,397 + 658,712) / 2) = 2.18 times, about 167 days. PHE does not disclose the total amount of inventories expensed. Note 39 gives material usage of 163,694 for its other operations only (Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166), and the cash flow statement uses the direct method (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17), so the real ratio cannot be computed. PHE also keeps 6,809 of "dead stock material" outside the line, in other non-current assets (Note 14b, Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122).

Under a cost recovery PSC, material costs are recovered from production (Note 2a(iii), Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). A deferred tax liability on "non-capital inventory" of 17,193 (Note 43e, Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172) suggests such materials are deducted for PSC purposes before issue. Gross split contracts have no cost recovery (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). The inventory accounting is the same under both.
: where materials issued to development wells are capitalised.
: the boundary for major spares and stand-by equipment.
: issued consumables and, under the COGS method, write-downs.
: the temporary difference on non-capital inventory.

The control argument for carrying government-owned materials is this page's reading. PHE does not explain why it recognises them. That non-capital materials are recovered before they are issued is read from Note 43e, not stated in the FS, and a deferred tax liability can have other causes.
How PSAK 202 treats a missed settlement discount is not stated in the standard. The reading follows the 2004 IFRIC discussion and firm guidance.

Applying the PSAK 202 materials rule (para. 32) to an upstream group, where the product never sits in inventory, is a reading by analogy, as is using it to decide that the casing commitment is not onerous.
That little crude would be held at year end is inferred from the revenue policy. The FS state no policy for crude inventory.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi dan Entitas Anak, consolidated financial statements 31 December 2024 (audited, USD thousand): statement of financial position (Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11); cash flow statement (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17); Note 2a(iii) and 2a(vii) (Daftar 5/10–5/11, PDF pp. 27–28); Note 2b (Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34); Note 3j (Daftar 5/53, PDF p. 70); Note 3p (Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79); Note 11 (Daftar 5/99–5/100, PDF pp. 116–117); Note 14b (Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122); Note 39 (Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166); Note 43e (Daftar 5/155, PDF p. 172). NOTES. The notes do not cover cost formulas or inventory errors; section 5 and the errors paragraph follow Kieso (ref. 8) and IAS 2.23–27.

Lecture notes, "Inter 1 – Chapter 9 – Inventories: Additional Valuation Issues" (Rumpun Akuntansi Keuangan): lower of cost and NRV, COGS and loss methods, allowance, recovery, agricultural inventory, purchase commitments, relative standalone sales value, gross profit and retail methods. NOTES. Of section 8, only agriculture has a note; the rest follows IAS 2.2–5, 2.8, 2.12–13 and the standards named.

), paras. 2–6, 8–13, 16, 18, 20–29, 32–36. VERIFIED (web, IAS 2 text reproduced at prg.kz; Grant Thornton IAS 2 factsheet). The 2003 removal of LIFO is from knowledge, NOT VERIFIED.

) and the 2014 bearer plants amendments to IAS 16 and IAS 41. Scope VERIFIED (web, IFRS Foundation, "Agriculture: Bearer Plants", June 2014); IAS 41.12–13 and 28 VERIFIED (web, IAS Plus; PKF; ACCA DipIFR). The FFB price is an illustration, not a market figure.
(IAS 1), paras. 66(a), 68. VERIFIED (web, Ind AS 16 mirror; ifrscommunity.com).
