presentation.deck: The theory of inventory accounting from definition to disclosure, worked through PHE's materials and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: Inventory accounting answers three questions in order: which goods belong to the entity, what they cost, and whether that cost will come back. Control settles the first, the cost elements and a cost formula the second, and the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV) the third.

A cost formula only divides one pool of cost between the balance sheet and profit or loss. When prices rise, FIFO leaves the most on the balance sheet and weighted average less. LIFO, which leaves the least, is no longer allowed.

Not every industry follows the cost model. Agricultural produce enters inventory at fair value less costs to sell at harvest (PSAK 241), commodity broker-traders may carry stock at fair value less costs to sell, and producers of minerals and crops may carry it at NRV. PHE's materials follow the plain cost model, with an allowance of 45,911 against 852,308 of cost at the end of 2024.

title: Inventories, Net, at an Upstream Contractor: Ownership, cost, cost formulas, and why the allowance for stock that will never be used sets the number
snippet: Ownership, cost, cost formulas, and why the allowance for stock that will never be used sets the number
content:
In brief

  • At an upstream production sharing contractor, inventory is mostly pipe, spare parts and chemicals waiting to be used in wells and facilities. Crude is a small part, because the contractor owns its oil only from the lifting and usually sells it soon after.

  • A spare part has no selling price, so the lower-of-cost-and-net-realisable-value test turns into a question about use. Stock that nothing will consume is written down to scrap value through an allowance, which is the "net" in the line's name.

  • Two judgments move the figure more than the cost formula does, the size of that allowance and whether a large spare is inventory or property, plant and equipment. In the case below they remove 7,150 of an 8,250 rise; with two cut-off corrections, a 22.8 percent rise becomes 4.7 percent.

The reported line rose 22.9 percent, and the face of the balance sheet cannot say how much of that is usable stock

The balance sheet on this page reports inventories, net, of 809,397 at 31 December 2024 against 658,712 a year earlier, in thousands. That is a rise of 150,685, or 22.9 percent, in a year when total assets fell 2.9 percent. The line is 2.7 percent of total assets at 31 December 2024 (809,397 / 30,303,898), against 2.1 percent a year earlier. The face shows one net figure, without the gross cost, the allowance deducted from it or the composition of the stock.

To see what sits behind such a line, this essay uses PT Hulu Energi Nusantara ("HEN"), an upstream oil and gas contractor operating under production sharing contracts (PSCs) with SKK Migas, reporting in USD under Indonesian SAK with a 31 December year end. HEN and every figure attached to it are constructed for illustration. HEN amounts are in USD thousand, except per-barrel prices in USD.

HEN's draft balance sheet at 31 December 2025 shows a gross ledger of 45,800 less an allowance of 1,400, so inventories, net, of 44,400, against 36,150 at the end of 2024, a rise of 22.8 percent. The external auditor has sent the CFO four questions. Why does the count include 900 of chemicals the supplier says it still owns? Why is a casing shipment that left the mill on 28 December missing? Why does a 4,200 spare compressor bundle sit in inventory? And why is the allowance for obsolete stock still last year's 1,400 when a drilling campaign was cancelled in 2025?

The governing claim of this essay is that at an upstream contractor the inventory line is a store of materials held for use, so its reported value depends less on how cost is measured than on two judgments, how much of the stock will never be used and which items are property, plant and equipment. "Net" means net of the first judgment, and the second decides what reaches the line at all.

This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that a change in inventories, net, at a PSC contractor cannot be read without the allowance movement and the spare-parts policy, because in HEN's case those two items explain 87 percent of the draft's growth (7,150 of 8,250).

The governing standard is PSAK 202 Inventories (formerly PSAK 14, IAS 2). The boundary with property, plant and equipment is PSAK 216 (formerly 16, IAS 16), and presentation is PSAK 201 (formerly 1, IAS 1).

Inventory starts where control passes, which is not always where the goods sit

An item belongs in HEN's inventory when HEN controls it, wherever it sits. Under FOB shipping point, the buyer takes on the goods, the freight and the risk when the seller hands them to the carrier. Under FOB destination, all three stay with the seller until the goods arrive. Goods on consignment stay in the consignor's inventory, because the party holding them has not acquired them.

Both rules bite at HEN's year-end count. A chemicals supplier keeps a vendor-managed stock (stock the supplier owns and replenishes on the customer's site) of corrosion inhibitor at HEN's shore base. HEN pays only for drums it draws. At the count, 900 of undrawn drums were counted as HEN's and entered the ledger through a count adjustment that reduced production costs. HEN has no right to them until it draws them, so the adjustment is reversed.

Dr Production costs 900
Cr Inventories 900

The casing runs the other way. HEN bought 600 joints from an overseas mill FOB shipping point, loaded on 28 December. At sea on 31 December, they were already HEN's, at the cost incurred by then (built in the next section).

Dr Inventories 1,512
Cr Trade payables (mill invoice) 1,440
Cr Accrued freight and insurance 72

Under Indonesian PSCs, equipment and materials the contractor imports generally become state property on import, while the contractor keeps the right to use them and recovers their cost through the contract. The casing at sea is therefore still HEN's in law as well as in substance. Once landed, HEN keeps recognising it, because an asset under the conceptual framework is a resource the entity controls, and HEN decides, within its approved work programme, where each joint goes.

Cost is what it took to bring the item to its shelf, and nothing spent to store or sell it

The cost of an inventory item is its purchase price plus every cost needed to bring it to its present location and condition, less trade discounts. The owner's notes list purchase price, import duties and taxes the buyer cannot recover, transport, and other directly attributable costs. Storage after arrival, administration and selling costs are expenses of the period, and recoverable VAT is a receivable. The casing builds up its cost as it moves.

List price = 600 joints × USD 2.50 thousand = 1,500

Trade discount = 1,500 × 4% = 60

Invoice = 1,500 − 60 = 1,440

Cost at 31 December 2025, at sea = 1,440 + 72 ocean freight and insurance = 1,512

Cost on arrival in January = 1,512 + 18 non-recoverable import charges + 30 port handling and trucking = 1,560

The mill's terms are 2/10, net 30, so HEN may deduct 2 percent if it pays by 7 January 2026. The owner's notes give two methods. The gross method records the full 1,440 and reduces cost only when the discount is taken. The net method records 1,440 × 98% = 1,411.2 from the start and treats a missed discount as a finance cost. At the year end the casing is 1,512 under the gross method and 1,483.2 under the net method, a gap of 28.8. HEN uses the gross method and pays on 5 January, so it credits inventories with 28.8 in January.

Cost on the shelf after the discount = 1,560 − 28.8 = 1,531.2, or USD 2.552 thousand per joint, under either method

Had HEN paid late, the gross method would leave 28.8 in the casing and the net method would expense it, which this essay prefers, because a charge for paying late is the price of credit.

FIFO and weighted average differ only in which purchase price stays on the shelf, and PSAK 202 no longer allows LIFO

A cost formula decides which purchase prices leave with each issue and which stay in the closing balance. PSAK 202 allows first-in, first-out (FIFO) or weighted average for interchangeable items, one formula for inventories of similar nature and use, and specific cost for items that are not interchangeable, such as a purpose-built wellhead ordered for one well. LIFO was removed from IAS 2 in its 2003 revision and is not available.

Where an issued cost goes depends on what the material does. Material used to keep an existing well producing, such as a workover (a repair of an existing well), is operating cost. Material that creates a new well or facility becomes part of oil and gas properties. HEN's tubing line in 2025, at USD thousand per joint, shows both.

1 January: on hand 200 joints at 1.20 = 240.00

10 March: purchase 300 joints at 1.30 = 390.00

15 May: issue 350 joints to a workover (production cost)

5 September: purchase 250 joints at 1.45 = 362.50

20 November: issue 150 joints to a development well (oil and gas properties)

Cost available = 240.00 + 390.00 + 362.50 = 992.50; on hand at year end = 250 joints

FIFO issues the oldest prices first.

May issue = 200 × 1.20 + 150 × 1.30 = 435.00

November issue = 150 × 1.30 = 195.00

Closing = 250 × 1.45 = 362.50

A perpetual system (one that updates the ledger at every receipt and issue) usually keeps a moving weighted average, recalculated after each purchase.

Average after March = (240.00 + 390.00) / 500 = 1.26

May issue = 350 × 1.26 = 441.00; remaining 150 × 1.26 = 189.00

Average after September = (189.00 + 362.50) / 400 = 1.37875

November issue = 150 × 1.37875 = 206.81

Closing = 250 × 1.37875 = 344.69

Both formulas allocate the same 992.50. FIFO leaves 17.81 more on the shelf, and the weighted average sends 6.00 more to production cost and 11.81 more into the well. On a stock that turns over about twice a year (500 joints issued against an average 225 on hand), with prices up 21 percent (1.20 to 1.45), the formula changed the closing balance by 4.9 percent of the FIFO figure. The next two sections move HEN's line by thousands.

Lower of cost and net realisable value becomes a test of use when an item has no selling price

PSAK 202 carries inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV), the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less the estimated costs of completion and of sale. The owner's notes write it as NRV = selling price − costs to complete − costs to sell.

Crude shows the formula working. Under an Indonesian PSC the contractor takes title to its share of oil at the lifting, the loading of a tanker at which each party takes its share, so crude still in shared tanks is not HEN's inventory. On 29 December HEN lifted 40,000 barrels at a production cost of USD 65.00 per barrel, 2,600, and sold them on delivered terms, with title passing at the discharge port in January. With a constructed realised price of USD 68.00 and freight of USD 1.50 per barrel, NRV is USD 66.50, above cost, so no write-down is made. At a price of USD 62.00 the formula would give one.

NRV = 62.00 − 1.50 = USD 60.50 per barrel

Write-down = (65.00 − 60.50) × 40,000 / 1,000 = 180

The other 39,612 of the ledger (45,800 − 900 + 1,512 − 4,200 − 2,600 crude) is materials HEN never sells. PSAK 202 has a rule for materials held for producing inventory. They are not written down below cost if the product they go into will sell at or above cost, and replacement cost may be the best evidence of their NRV. Consumables issued to operations flow into the cost of the crude, so the rule applies to them by direct analogy. Casing that will be capitalised into a well does not go into inventory at all, so the question becomes whether the well it joins is recoverable, a PSAK 236 view. Both readings reach the same answer, which is the essay's reading rather than a quoted rule. If steel prices fall 10 percent while HEN's fields are economic, the casing stays at cost. The same casing with no well to go into is written down to scrap value.

The test therefore bites on stock that will not be used, estimated in two layers. Known unusable items are written down individually; the rest is provided for by time since last movement. A cancelled campaign left HEN 3,000 of tubulars in a grade none of its fields uses, and a scrap dealer quotes 300.

Specific write-down = 3,000 − 300 = 2,700

The remaining 36,612 is aged at rates set in HEN's policy (constructed).

Allowance required = 2,700 + 1,650 = 4,350, held in a separate account deducted from inventories

The allowance moves both ways, and its reversal is capped at what was written down

The allowance is re-estimated at every reporting date, and PSAK 202 requires a write-down to be reversed when its cause no longer exists, up to the original write-down, as a reduction of the inventory expense. The owner's notes book it as a debit to the allowance and a credit to a recovery account.

HEN's allowance moved three ways in 2025. Items fully provided in 2024, at a cost of 400, were scrapped, removing cost and allowance together with no effect on profit. A lot of casing costing 1,200 had been written down by 600 in 2024, at the 50 percent rate, because it had not moved for more than three years. In 2025 HEN approved a 2026 development well that will use it, so the 600 is reversed and the casing returns to its cost of 1,200, no higher. The new charge brings the balance to 4,350.

Opening allowance, 1 January 2025 = 1,800

Used on scrapped items = (400)

Reversal for casing reserved for the approved well = (600)

New write-downs = 3,550

Closing allowance = 1,800 − 400 − 600 + 3,550 = 4,350

Net charge to 2025 profit = 3,550 − 600 = 2,950

Dr Allowance for inventory obsolescence 400 / Cr Inventories 400

Dr Allowance for inventory obsolescence 600 / Cr Reversal of inventory write-down 600

Dr Inventory write-down expense 3,550 / Cr Allowance for inventory obsolescence 3,550

The draft carried the allowance at 1,400 (1,800 less the 400 used), so through the allowance alone it overstated profit by 2,950. At HEN's constructed issue rate of 3,000 a month, that is one month of warehouse issues, while the stock covers 13 months (39,612 / 3,000), which is where slow-moving stock builds up.

A spare part used over more than one period is plant, and the call moves the number in both directions

PSAK 216 treats spare parts, stand-by equipment and servicing equipment as property, plant and equipment when they are held for use in production and expected to be used during more than one period. Otherwise they are inventory. Filters, seals and bits are consumed when used and stay in inventory however many are bought. A rotating spare, a major component swapped into a machine and then run for years, belongs in property, plant and equipment.

HEN's 4,200 compressor bundle is such a spare. It was bought in 2025 to serve either of the two gas compressors on HEN's platform, so a failure does not halt gas sales while a replacement is shipped, and once installed it will run for years. It moves to oil and gas properties, from current to non-current assets.

Dr Oil and gas properties, production facilities 4,200
Cr Inventories 4,200

The current/non-current boundary on this line runs mostly through that call. PSAK 201 keeps inventory consumed in the normal operating cycle current even when it will not be used within twelve months, so slow-moving operating materials stay current. Materials held for capital work, or as long-term reserve stock, may be classified non-current, and contractors differ; HEN's policy keeps all warehouse materials current. Once in property, plant and equipment, the bundle is depreciated from when it is available for use and tested for impairment under PSAK 236 (formerly 48, IAS 36) with its cash-generating unit, the smallest group of assets that generates independent cash inflows.

The call cuts both ways. Moving a usable spare out lowers the line with no effect on profit. Moving an unusable item would often avoid an NRV write-down, since it is tested with the cash-generating unit unless idle or held for disposal. The cancelled-campaign tubulars cannot qualify, because PSAK 216 asks whether an item is expected to be used, and an auditor checks that obsolete stock is not among the capitalised spares.

Corrected, HEN's inventory rose 4.7 percent, and most of the draft's growth was a compressor and a stale allowance

HEN's inventories, net, at 31 December 2025 are 37,862, up 4.7 percent on 36,150, against the draft's 44,400.

Draft inventories, net = 45,800 − 1,400 = 44,400

Remove consignment chemicals = (900)

Add casing in transit, FOB shipping point = +1,512

Move compressor bundle to oil and gas properties = (4,200)

Raise the allowance from 1,400 to 4,350 = (2,950)

Reported inventories, net = 44,400 − 900 + 1,512 − 4,200 − 2,950 = 37,862

In gross terms, materials of 39,612 plus crude of 2,600 give 42,212, less the allowance of 4,350. The two judgments alone take the draft to 37,250, a rise of 3.0 percent; the two cut-off corrections add a net 612. Profit before tax falls by 3,850, of which 2,950 is the allowance and 900 the consignment reversal. The bundle adds 4,200 to oil and gas properties and reaches profit through depreciation over its life. The cost formula accounts for none of the change.

The reported line on this page rose 22.9 percent in 2024. HEN's case shows that this percentage alone cannot tell more usable stock from stale allowances or capital spares held as inventory. The notes to the financial statements can, if they disclose gross cost, the allowance movement and the policy for capital spares.

  • PSC terms are stated from general knowledge and were not checked against a contract or SKK Migas rules: imported materials becoming state property on import, and the contractor taking title to its oil at the lifting. If title to crude passed earlier, crude in shared storage would also be inventory.

  • Applying the PSAK 202 materials rule to consumables by analogy, and judging capital materials by whether the well they join is recoverable (PSAK 236), is the essay's reading. The standard's rule is written for materials that go into inventory.

  • Classification of capital-project materials varies in practice. HEN's policy of keeping all warehouse materials current is a constructed choice.

  • Ageing rates, the scrap quote and the two-layer allowance are constructed; real contractors set rates by item class and experience.

  • PSAK 202, 216, 201 and 236 were not opened, so they are cited by subject, not paragraph. When a stand-by spare starts depreciating is a policy choice in practice, and how write-downs interact with cost recovery is outside this essay.

The governing claim of this essay is that at an upstream contractor the inventory line is a store of materials held for use, so its reported value depends less on how cost is measured than on two judgments, how much of the stock will never be used and which items are property, plant and equipment. "Net" means net of the first judgment, and the second decides what reaches the line at all.

This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that a change in inventories, net, at a PSC contractor cannot be read without the allowance movement and the spare-parts policy, because in HEN's case those two items explain 87 percent of the draft's growth (7,150 of 8,250).
(formerly PSAK 14, IAS 2). The boundary with property, plant and equipment is PSAK 216 (formerly 16, IAS 16), and presentation is PSAK 201 (formerly 1, IAS 1).

Both rules bite at HEN's year-end count. A chemicals supplier keeps a vendor-managed stock (stock the supplier owns and replenishes on the customer's site) of corrosion inhibitor at HEN's shore base. The casing runs the other way. HEN bought 600 joints from an overseas mill FOB shipping point, loaded on 28 December. At sea on 31 December, they were already HEN's, at the cost incurred by then (built in the next section).

Under Indonesian PSCs, equipment and materials the contractor imports generally become state property on import, while the contractor keeps the right to use them and recovers their cost through the contract. Cost is what it took to bring the item to its shelf, and nothing spent to store or sell it

The cost of an inventory item is its purchase price plus every cost needed to bring it to its present location and condition, less trade discounts. Cost available = 240.00 + 390.00 + 362.50 = 992.50; on hand at year end = 250 joints

title: Investment Properties: Definition, Cost and Fair Value Models, Transfers
snippet: The theory of investment property from the definition to disclosure under PSAK 240, worked from PHE's small balance and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • Investment property is land or a building held to earn rentals, for capital appreciation, or both. Use decides the line, so the same building is a fixed asset while the entity occupies it, inventory while a developer holds it for sale, and investment property once it is leased out to others under an operating lease.

  • After initial recognition at cost an entity chooses one model for all its investment property. The cost model depreciates the property as PSAK 216 does and discloses fair value. The fair value model stops depreciation and puts every change in fair value through profit or loss.

  • A property changes line only when its use changes, with evidence. Under the cost model a transfer moves the carrying amount unchanged. Under the fair value model the gain built up while the entity occupied the property goes to other comprehensive income (apart from any reversal of an earlier impairment) and never reaches profit later, while a gain on inventory goes straight to profit.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report investment properties of 3,149 at 31 December 2024 against 3,301 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 0.01 percent of total assets, and the face of the statement gives it no note reference. This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to classify a property, measure it under both models, record transfers and disposals in journals, and see where other industries depart from the general rules.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The standard is PSAK 240 Investment Property (formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40), and the sections follow its order.

1. What investment property is

Investment property is property (land or a building, or part of a building, or both) held by the owner, or by a lessee as a right-of-use asset, to earn rentals or for capital appreciation or both, instead of for use in producing goods or services or for administration, or for sale in the ordinary course of business (PSAK 240.5). Property held for use is owner-occupied property and falls under PSAK 216 Fixed Assets (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16); property held for sale in the ordinary course is inventory under PSAK 202.

The definition exists because such property produces cash differently. A rented building generates cash flows largely independently of the entity's other assets, while a building used in operations earns cash only together with the plant, people and contracts around it (para. 7). A separate line lets a reader see the part of the asset base whose value can be judged on its own.

The standard's examples mark the boundary (paras. 8–9).

Investment property

Not investment property

Land held for long-term capital appreciation

Property held for sale or being developed for sale (inventory)

Land held for a currently undetermined future use

Property held for future use as owner-occupied property

A building leased out under operating leases

Property occupied by employees, even at market rent

A vacant building held to be leased out

Owner-occupied property awaiting disposal

Property being built for future use as investment property

Property leased out under a finance lease

Land held with no decided use counts as held for capital appreciation, so indecision lands it on this line. Staff housing stays owner-occupied whatever rent the staff pay, because the entity houses its people to run its business.

The standard also excludes biological assets (PSAK 241) and mineral rights and reserves such as oil and natural gas (para. 4). An upstream company's reserves are never investment property, however they are held.

2. Hard cases: mixed use, services and groups

Partly owner-occupied property. If the rented portion and the owner-occupied portion could be sold separately, or leased out separately under a finance lease (one that transfers substantially all the risks and rewards and so works like a sale), each portion is classified by its own use. If they could not, the whole property is investment property only if the owner-occupied portion is insignificant (para. 10).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary owns a 20-floor office tower in Jakarta and leases out all but its own floors.

Strata titles exist for each floor: the leased floors are investment property, the subsidiary's floors fixed assets

One title, subsidiary uses 1 floor: own use = 1 / 20 = 5%, so the whole tower is likely investment property

One title, subsidiary uses 6 floors: own use = 6 / 20 = 30%, so the whole tower stays in fixed assets

The standard gives no percentage for "insignificant". The entity develops criteria, applies them consistently, and discloses them when classification is difficult (paras. 14, 75(c)).

Ancillary services. A property stays investment property if the services provided to occupants are insignificant to the arrangement, such as security and maintenance for office tenants (para. 11). An owner-managed hotel is owner-occupied, because the services to guests are significant (para. 12). Cases between the two need judgement. A hotel owner who hands day-to-day running to a manager but keeps significant exposure to the hotel's operating cash flows is closer to running a business than to holding an investment (para. 13).

Property let within a group. A building one subsidiary leases to another is investment property in the lessor's own financial statements but owner-occupied in the consolidated statements, because the group uses it (para. 15). For example (illustration), with strata titles, the PHE subsidiary in the tower leases 4 floors to a fellow PHE subsidiary for 120 a year. In its own books the 120 is rental income on investment property. On consolidation the income and the matching rent expense are eliminated and the 4 floors are presented as fixed assets.

3. Recognition and initial measurement

Investment property is recognised when future economic benefits are probable and cost can be measured reliably (para. 16), and measured initially at cost, including transaction costs (para. 20). Cost is the purchase price and directly attributable expenditure such as legal fees and property transfer taxes (para. 21). It excludes start-up costs, operating losses before the planned occupancy is reached, and abnormal waste (para. 23).

For example (illustration), the PHE subsidiary buys a warehouse to lease to a logistics company for 4,000, pays a transfer tax of 5 percent and notary and legal fees of 40, spends 15 on an opening ceremony, and runs at a loss of 60 while the first tenant fits out.

Cost = 4,000 + 4,000 × 5% + 40 = 4,240

Expensed: opening ceremony 15; operating loss 60

Dr Investment property 4,240 / Cr Cash 4,240

If payment is deferred, cost is the cash price equivalent and the rest is interest over the credit period (para. 24). Suppose instead the seller accepts 2,000 now and 2,100 in a year, and the subsidiary's borrowing rate is 5 percent.

Cash price equivalent = 2,000 + 2,100 / 1.05 = 4,000; interest = total payments 4,100 − 4,000 = 100

A property acquired in exchange for another asset is measured at fair value unless the exchange lacks commercial substance or neither fair value can be measured reliably (para. 27).

After acquisition, day-to-day servicing (labour, consumables, minor parts) is expensed as repairs and maintenance (para. 18). Replacing a part, such as interior walls, is capitalised if the recognition criteria are met, and the replaced part is derecognised (para. 19).

4. The cost model and the fair value model

PSAK 240 makes the entity choose one model and apply it to all its investment property (para. 30). It also requires every entity to measure fair value, either for measurement or for disclosure (para. 32), and encourages, but does not require, a valuation by an independent qualified valuer.

  • Under the cost model the property is carried as a fixed asset is under PSAK 216, at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment losses (para. 56).

  • Under the fair value model the property is remeasured at fair value at each reporting date and not depreciated. A gain or loss from a change in fair value is recognised in profit or loss in the period it arises (paras. 33, 35). Fair value reflects rental income from current leases (para. 40), and equipment such as lifts that is part of the building is not counted again as a separate asset (para. 50).

A change from the fair value model to the cost model is "highly unlikely" to give a more relevant presentation (para. 31), so in practice the choice is one-way.

For example (illustration), take PHE's 2024 balance of 3,149 as the cost at 1 January 2025 of one rented building, land 1,049 and building 2,100, with 15 years of life left. Fair value is 3,600 at 31 December 2024, 3,750 a year later and 3,520 at the end of 2026. Rent is 300 a year and the landlord's costs 40.

Measurement theory offers one way to read the choice. Historical cost reports a holding gain, the rise in an asset's value while it is held, only when the asset is sold. Edwards and Bell's current-cost income separates operating profit from holding gains so the decision to hold can be judged on its own (Godfrey et al., Accounting Theory). Capital appreciation is one of the two purposes in the definition, so on this reading the holding gain on investment property is part of performance, which is where the fair value model puts it. The cost of that relevance is reliability. Rarely traded property is valued from unobservable inputs (Level 3 under PSAK 113 Fair Value Measurement, formerly PSAK 68, IFRS 13), and the valuer's assumptions then drive profit. The IASB's own reasons in the Basis for Conclusions were not checked.

When fair value cannot be measured. The entity is presumed able to measure fair value reliably. Only in exceptional cases, when comparable transactions are rare and no reliable alternative such as a discounted cash flow exists, does a fair-value-model entity carry that one property at cost under PSAK 216, with residual value assumed to be zero, until disposal (para. 53). The evidence must be clear when the property is first acquired or first becomes investment property. Property under construction may be held at cost until its fair value becomes measurable or construction ends (paras. 53–53A). A property already at fair value stays there even if the market thins (para. 55).

Impairment. Under the cost model the property is tested under PSAK 236 like any fixed asset. Under the fair value model a fall in value is already in profit, so no separate test is needed.

5. Transfers

A property moves into or out of investment property when, and only when, its use changes, meaning it starts or stops meeting the definition and there is evidence of the change (para. 57). A change in management's intentions alone is not evidence. The standard gives four examples of evidence.

  • start of owner-occupation, or of development for owner-occupation (out to fixed assets);

  • start of development with a view to sale (out to inventory);

  • end of owner-occupation (in from fixed assets);

  • inception of an operating lease to another party (in from inventory).

The list became examples in a 2016 amendment, effective 2018, which also added the sentence on intentions. Before it, the list read as complete and left out property under construction. A decision to sell an investment property without developing it leaves it in investment property until derecognition, and redevelopment for continued renting does not move it to fixed assets (para. 58).

Under the cost model a transfer moves the carrying amount unchanged (para. 59). For example (illustration), a staff mess building owned by a PHE subsidiary outside the PSCs, with cost 3,300 and accumulated depreciation 400, is leased to a drilling contractor when crews leave.

Dr Investment property 3,300, Dr Accumulated depreciation, fixed assets 400 / Cr Fixed assets 3,300, Cr Accumulated depreciation, investment property 400

Under the fair value model the entry depends on where the property comes from.

The asymmetry follows the property's history. Up to the date of change the owner-occupied building was under PSAK 216, so its gain is treated as a PSAK 216 revaluation, and revaluation gains on fixed assets go to equity. The PSAK 216 treatment has two refinements (para. 62). A decrease goes to profit unless it uses up an existing surplus on the same property. An increase goes to profit to the extent it reverses an earlier impairment loss on that property. On later disposal the surplus may move to retained earnings within equity, never through profit. Going the other way, if crews move back into a fair-value property worth 3,750 with 25 years of life left, 3,750 becomes its cost under PSAK 216 and depreciation is 3,750 / 25 = 150 a year.

6. Disposals

Investment property is derecognised on disposal, by sale or by entering into a finance lease as lessor, or when it is permanently withdrawn from use with no future benefit expected (paras. 66–67). The date of a sale is the date the buyer obtains control under PSAK 115 Revenue from Contracts with Customers (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15). The gain or loss is the net disposal proceeds less the carrying amount, in profit or loss (para. 69).

For example (illustration), the building in section 4 is sold at the end of 2026 for 3,520, with selling costs of 70.

Net proceeds = 3,520 − 70 = 3,450

Cost model: gain = 3,450 − 2,869 = 581; profit over 2025–2026 = 240 + 581 = 821

Fair value model: loss = 3,450 − 3,520 = (70); profit over 2025–2026 = 440 − 70 = 370

Cost model: Dr Cash 3,450, Dr Accumulated depreciation 280 / Cr Investment property 3,149, Cr Gain on disposal 581

Fair value model: Dr Cash 3,450, Dr Loss on disposal 70 / Cr Investment property 3,520

The difference of 821 − 370 = 451 equals the gap at the start, 3,600 − 3,149. Under the fair value model that gain belongs to the years before 2025; under the cost model it waits for the sale. Before the sale, a property highly likely to be sold within a year is presented as held for sale under PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5), which measures it only under the cost model (para. 56(a)). Compensation from insurers or others for property damaged or lost is income when it becomes receivable, separate from the loss itself (paras. 72–73).

7. Disclosure

Both models disclose which model is used, the classification criteria when classification is difficult, the extent of independent valuation, rental income and direct operating expenses, restrictions on realisability, and contractual obligations to buy, build or repair (para. 75). A fair-value-model entity adds a reconciliation of the carrying amount showing additions, disposals, net fair value gains or losses and transfers (para. 76). A cost-model entity adds depreciation methods and lives, gross amounts and accumulated depreciation, the same kind of reconciliation, and the fair value of the property (para. 79). A reader of a cost-model entity can therefore rebuild the fair value carrying amount, but not the split between profit and OCI that the fair value model would have produced.

8. Investment property across industries

Industries meet the definition's edges in different places, and two of them have their own interpretations in Indonesia.

Real estate developers. One building can be inventory, investment property or a fixed asset depending on intention, so a developer's balance sheet often carries all three. A mall the developer keeps and leases is investment property, the apartments it builds to sell are inventory under PSAK 202, and its own office is a fixed asset. When unsold units are leased out instead, the inventory-to-investment-property transfer in section 5 sends the fair value gain to profit.

Hotels and serviced property. Serviced apartments and malls with heavy management sit on the hotel judgement line of section 2 (paras. 12–13).

Telecommunication towers. ISAK 331 (formerly ISAK 31) limits "building" in PSAK 240 to a structure with the physical features usually associated with a building, namely walls, a floor and a roof attached to the asset. The question that prompted it was whether leased towers qualify, and the IFRS Interpretations Committee had doubted that a tower is a building. A tower leased to operators therefore stays a fixed asset leased out under PSAK 116 Leases, at cost or under the PSAK 216 revaluation model, whose gains go to OCI. OJK had issued SEOJK 27/SEOJK.04/2015 on leased tower assets and revoked it after ISAK 31, requiring issuers to follow current SAK in filings from 2018 (SEOJK 36/SEOJK.04/2016). For example (illustration), a tower costing 200 with a 20-year life is depreciated 200 / 20 = 10 a year; had it been investment property at a fair value risen to 230, profit would have carried a gain of 30 instead.

Plantations and land rights. Plants and produce are outside PSAK 240 (para. 4(a)). Land in Indonesia is held under rights such as HGU and HGB, and ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36) decides whether a right is in substance a purchase of land (PSAK 216, or PSAK 240 if held for rent) or a lease (PSAK 116). PHE's own policy applies that test to its land rights (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69).

Insurers and funds. An entity may choose separate models for investment property backing liabilities whose returns are linked to that property, such as unit-linked funds, and for all other investment property (para. 32A).

Banks. Property taken over from defaulting borrowers is usually held for sale; it becomes investment property only when the bank starts leasing it out, because a decision alone is not evidence of a change in use (para. 57; NOT VERIFIED for Indonesian bank practice).

Islamic finance. An asset leased out under ijarah is accounted for by the lessor as an ijarah asset under PSAK 407 Akuntansi Ijarah (formerly PSAK 107) instead of PSAK 240 (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).

Oil, gas and mining. Mineral rights and reserves are excluded (para. 4(b)). Only land and buildings held outside operations can reach this line.

9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's balance

PHE reports the line on the face of the statement of financial position with no note reference, and its summary of material accounting policies contains no investment property policy (Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; Note 3, PDF pp. 46–93). The term appears nowhere else in the FS. The model used, the fair value, rental income and the roll-forward are therefore not disclosed.

Change = 3,149 − 3,301 = (152), or (4.6%)

PSAK 201 lists investment property among the line items the face must show, which explains why a line of 0.01 percent of total assets exists at all. PSAK 201 also lets an entity omit a disclosure that is not material, which may explain the missing note; the FS does not say so. The fall of 152 fits more than one story. Under the cost model it could be a year's depreciation; for example (illustration), if all of the 3,301 were a building with no additions, 152 would imply 3,301 / 152 = 21.7 years of life remaining. Under the fair value model it could be a fall in value with no depreciation at all. A disposal, a transfer or a translation difference would also fit. The reconciliation required by para. 76 or 79(d) is what would tell them apart.

10. Upstream note: property the PSCs own

Under PHE's cost recovery production sharing contracts (PSCs), materials, supplies and equipment acquired for oil and gas operations belong to the Government, and the contractor has the right to use them (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). Under gross split PSCs the old PSC's assets, owned by the Directorate General of State Assets (DJKN), are used under a lease scheme with rent set on appraised fair value (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). PHE's related parties include the Ministry of Finance as a provider of asset rental services (Note 44, Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199). Property used in PSC operations is therefore state property that PHE uses or leases, so it cannot be PHE's investment property. The 3,149 is likely to be property held outside the PSCs, but the FS does not say what it is.

11. Related lines

  • fixed-assets-net: owner-occupied property, and the source or destination of most transfers.

  • right-of-use-assets-net: property held under leases, which is investment property only if subleased under operating leases.

  • inventories-net: property held for sale in the ordinary course of business.

  • other-income-expense-net: where rental income and fair value changes would be presented.

  • other-comprehensive-income: the revaluation surplus on transfers from fixed assets under the fair value model.

Least-confident assertions

  • That the 3,149 is property held outside the PSCs is an inference from Note 2; the FS does not describe the property, its model or its fair value.

  • The materiality explanation for the missing note is this page's reading, and the PSAK 201 paragraphs behind it (IAS 1.54(b) and 31) were not checked against the text.

  • Reading the fair value model through Edwards and Bell's holding gains is this page's interpretation; the IASB's Basis for Conclusions was not opened.

  • The Kieso IFRS edition was not checked for where it covers investment property; this page follows the order of PSAK 240 instead of a textbook chapter.

  • PSAK 240 paragraph numbers are taken from IAS 40, assuming the Indonesian adoption keeps IFRS numbering; the PSAK text itself was not opened.

content.text: Investment property is land or a building held to earn rentals, for capital appreciation, or both. Use decides the line, so the same building is a fixed asset while the entity occupies it, inventory while a developer holds it for sale, and investment property once it is leased out to others under an operating lease.

After initial recognition at cost an entity chooses one model for all its investment property. The cost model depreciates the property as PSAK 216 does and discloses fair value. The fair value model stops depreciation and puts every change in fair value through profit or loss.

A property changes line only when its use changes, with evidence. Under the cost model a transfer moves the carrying amount unchanged. Under the fair value model the gain built up while the entity occupied the property goes to other comprehensive income (apart from any reversal of an earlier impairment) and never reaches profit later, while a gain on inventory goes straight to profit.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report investment properties of 3,149 at 31 December 2024 against 3,301 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 0.01 percent of total assets, and the face of the statement gives it no note reference. This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to classify a property, measure it under both models, record transfers and disposals in journals, and see where other industries depart from the general rules.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The standard is PSAK 240
(formerly PSAK 13, IAS 40), and the sections follow its order.

Investment property is property (land or a building, or part of a building, or both) held by the owner, or by a lessee as a right-of-use asset, to earn rentals or for capital appreciation or both, instead of for use in producing goods or services or for administration, or for sale in the ordinary course of business (PSAK 240.5). Property held for use is
(formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16); property held for sale in the ordinary course is inventory under PSAK 202.

The definition exists because such property produces cash differently. A rented building generates cash flows largely independently of the entity's other assets, while a building used in operations earns cash only together with the plant, people and contracts around it (para. 7). A separate line lets a reader see the part of the asset base whose value can be judged on its own.
The standard's examples mark the boundary (paras. 8–9).

Property held for sale or being developed for sale (inventory)
Land held for a currently undetermined future use
Property held for future use as owner-occupied property
A building leased out under operating leases
Property occupied by employees, even at market rent
A vacant building held to be leased out
Property being built for future use as investment property
Property leased out under a finance lease

Land held with no decided use counts as held for capital appreciation, so indecision lands it on this line. Staff housing stays owner-occupied whatever rent the staff pay, because the entity houses its people to run its business.

The standard also excludes biological assets (PSAK 241) and mineral rights and reserves such as oil and natural gas (para. 4). An upstream company's reserves are never investment property, however they are held.

Strata titles exist for each floor: the leased floors are investment property, the subsidiary's floors fixed assets

Up to the date of change the owner-occupied building was under PSAK 216, so its gain is treated as a PSAK 216 revaluation, and revaluation gains on fixed assets go to equity. A developer's unsold units were inventory, and making them investment property at fair value is treated like a sale of inventory, so the gain goes to profit (para. 64).
Dr Investment property 3,400, Dr Accumulated depreciation 400 / Cr Fixed assets 3,300, Cr OCI, revaluation surplus 500
Dr Investment property 2,100 / Cr Inventories 1,800, Cr Gain on transfer from inventory 300

The PSAK 216 treatment has two refinements (para. 62). A decrease goes to profit unless it uses up an existing surplus on the same property. An increase goes to profit to the extent it reverses an earlier impairment loss on that property. For example (illustration), if the mess building had been impaired by 100 two years earlier, so that its carrying amount without the impairment would have been 3,000:
Increase to 3,400: first 3,000 − 2,900 = 100 to profit; remaining 3,400 − 3,000 = 400 to OCI

On later disposal the surplus may move to retained earnings within equity, never through profit. Going the other way, if crews move back into a fair-value property worth 3,750 with 25 years of life left, 3,750 becomes its cost under PSAK 216 and depreciation is 3,750 / 25 = 150 a year.

Investment property is derecognised on disposal, by sale or by entering into a finance lease as lessor, or when it is permanently withdrawn from use with no future benefit expected (paras. 66–67). The date of a sale is the date the buyer obtains control under PSAK 115
(formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15). The gain or loss is the net disposal proceeds less the carrying amount, in profit or loss (para. 69).
For example (illustration), the building in section 4 is sold at the end of 2026 for 3,520, with selling costs of 70.
Fair value model: loss = 3,450 − 3,520 = (70); profit over 2025–2026 = 440 − 70 = 370
Cost model: Dr Cash 3,450, Dr Accumulated depreciation 280 / Cr Investment property 3,149, Cr Gain on disposal 581
Fair value model: Dr Cash 3,450, Dr Loss on disposal 70 / Cr Investment property 3,520

The difference of 821 − 370 = 451 equals the gap at the start, 3,600 − 3,149. Under the fair value model that gain belongs to the years before 2025; under the cost model it waits for the sale. Before the sale, a property highly likely to be sold within a year is presented as held for sale under PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5), which measures it only under the cost model (para. 56(a)). Compensation from insurers or others for property damaged or lost is income when it becomes receivable, separate from the loss itself (paras. 72–73).

Both models disclose which model is used, the classification criteria when classification is difficult, the extent of independent valuation, rental income and direct operating expenses, restrictions on realisability, and contractual obligations to buy, build or repair (para. 75). A fair-value-model entity adds a reconciliation of the carrying amount showing additions, disposals, net fair value gains or losses and transfers (para. 76). A cost-model entity adds depreciation methods and lives, gross amounts and accumulated depreciation, the same kind of reconciliation, and the fair value of the property (para. 79). A reader of a cost-model entity can therefore rebuild the fair value carrying amount, but not the split between profit and OCI that the fair value model would have produced.
Industries meet the definition's edges in different places, and two of them have their own interpretations in Indonesia.

One building can be inventory, investment property or a fixed asset depending on intention, so a developer's balance sheet often carries all three. A mall the developer keeps and leases is investment property, the apartments it builds to sell are inventory under PSAK 202, and its own office is a fixed asset. When unsold units are leased out instead, the inventory-to-investment-property transfer in section 5 sends the fair value gain to profit.
Serviced apartments and malls with heavy management sit on the hotel judgement line of section 2 (paras. 12–13).

ISAK 331 (formerly ISAK 31) limits "building" in PSAK 240 to a structure with the physical features usually associated with a building, namely walls, a floor and a roof attached to the asset. The question that prompted it was whether leased towers qualify, and the IFRS Interpretations Committee had doubted that a tower is a building. A tower leased to operators therefore stays a fixed asset leased out under PSAK 116

, at cost or under the PSAK 216 revaluation model, whose gains go to OCI. OJK had issued SEOJK 27/SEOJK.04/2015 on leased tower assets and revoked it after ISAK 31, requiring issuers to follow current SAK in filings from 2018 (SEOJK 36/SEOJK.04/2016). For example (illustration), a tower costing 200 with a 20-year life is depreciated 200 / 20 = 10 a year; had it been investment property at a fair value risen to 230, profit would have carried a gain of 30 instead.

Plants and produce are outside PSAK 240 (para. 4(a)). Land in Indonesia is held under rights such as HGU and HGB, and ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36) decides whether a right is in substance a purchase of land (PSAK 216, or PSAK 240 if held for rent) or a lease (PSAK 116). PHE's own policy applies that test to its land rights (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69).

An entity may choose separate models for investment property backing liabilities whose returns are linked to that property, such as unit-linked funds, and for all other investment property (para. 32A).

Property taken over from defaulting borrowers is usually held for sale; it becomes investment property only when the bank starts leasing it out, because a decision alone is not evidence of a change in use (para. 57; NOT VERIFIED for Indonesian bank practice).
An asset leased out under ijarah is accounted for by the lessor as an ijarah asset under PSAK 407
(formerly PSAK 107) instead of PSAK 240 (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).
Mineral rights and reserves are excluded (para. 4(b)). Only land and buildings held outside operations can reach this line.

PHE reports the line on the face of the statement of financial position with no note reference, and its summary of material accounting policies contains no investment property policy (Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; Note 3, PDF pp. 46–93). The term appears nowhere else in the FS. The model used, the fair value, rental income and the roll-forward are therefore not disclosed.

PSAK 201 lists investment property among the line items the face must show, which explains why a line of 0.01 percent of total assets exists at all. PSAK 201 also lets an entity omit a disclosure that is not material, which may explain the missing note; the FS does not say so. The fall of 152 fits more than one story. Under the cost model it could be a year's depreciation; for example (illustration), if all of the 3,301 were a building with no additions, 152 would imply 3,301 / 152 = 21.7 years of life remaining. Under the fair value model it could be a fall in value with no depreciation at all. A disposal, a transfer or a translation difference would also fit. The reconciliation required by para. 76 or 79(d) is what would tell them apart.
10. Upstream note: property the PSCs own

Under PHE's cost recovery production sharing contracts (PSCs), materials, supplies and equipment acquired for oil and gas operations belong to the Government, and the contractor has the right to use them (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). Under gross split PSCs the old PSC's assets, owned by the Directorate General of State Assets (DJKN), are used under a lease scheme with rent set on appraised fair value (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). PHE's related parties include the Ministry of Finance as a provider of asset rental services (Note 44, Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199). Property used in PSC operations is therefore state property that PHE uses or leases, so it cannot be PHE's investment property. The 3,149 is likely to be property held outside the PSCs, but the FS does not say what it is.
: owner-occupied property, and the source or destination of most transfers.
: property held under leases, which is investment property only if subleased under operating leases.
: property held for sale in the ordinary course of business.
: where rental income and fair value changes would be presented.
: the revaluation surplus on transfers from fixed assets under the fair value model.
That the 3,149 is property held outside the PSCs is an inference from Note 2; the FS does not describe the property, its model or its fair value.
The materiality explanation for the missing note is this page's reading, and the PSAK 201 paragraphs behind it (IAS 1.54(b) and 31) were not checked against the text.
Reading the fair value model through Edwards and Bell's holding gains is this page's interpretation; the IASB's Basis for Conclusions was not opened.
The Kieso IFRS edition was not checked for where it covers investment property; this page follows the order of PSAK 240 instead of a textbook chapter.
PSAK 240 paragraph numbers are taken from IAS 40, assuming the Indonesian adoption keeps IFRS numbering; the PSAK text itself was not opened.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi dan Entitas Anak, consolidated financial statements 31 December 2024 (audited, USD thousand): statement of financial position (Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11); Note 2a(vii) (Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28); Note 2b (Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34); Note 3 policies (PDF pp. 46–93, no investment property policy found); Note 3i (Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69); Note 44 related parties (Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199). VERIFIED (PHE FS 2024, on disk).

None of the lecture notes this series follows covers investment property. Sections follow the structure of IAS 40 itself (definitions, classification, recognition, measurement at recognition, measurement after recognition, transfers, disposals, disclosure). Kieso, Weygandt and Warfield,
, IFRS edition, was not opened for this topic; NOT VERIFIED.
Lecture notes, "TA – Chapter 6 – Accounting Measurement Systems" (Rumpun Akuntansi Keuangan; Godfrey, Hodgson, Tarca, Hamilton and Holmes,

), paras. 4–5, 7–16, 18–21, 23–24, 27, 30–33, 35, 40, 50, 53–53A, 55–67, 69, 72–73, 75–76, 79. VERIFIED (web, IFRS Foundation text of IAS 40 including the 2016 amendments, hosted by ISEG Lisboa; re-read in full for the independent recheck). The 2016 amendment
and its 2018 effective date: VERIFIED (web, same text; EFRAG endorsement documents).

ISAK 331 (formerly ISAK 31) building characteristics and the tower question behind it: VERIFIED (web, IAI, ED ISAK 31, 8 Sept 2015, paras. 06 and 10 and basis; Binus Accounting, "Penerbitan ISAK 31", 2016, for the final text and effective date). PSAK 216, 202, 105, 113, 115, 116, 201, 236, 241, 407, ISAK 336: numbers and titles VERIFIED (web, IAI,
Perubahan Penomoran PSAK dan ISAK dalam SAK Indonesia
); content STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED, including PSAK 201's line-item and materiality paragraphs (IAS 1.54(b), 31) and PSAK 105's measurement scope (IFRS 5.5(d)).

presentation.deck: The theory of investment property from the definition to disclosure under PSAK 240, worked from PHE's small balance and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: Investment property is land or a building held to earn rentals, for capital appreciation, or both. Use decides the line, so the same building is a fixed asset while the entity occupies it, inventory while a developer holds it for sale, and investment property once it is leased out to others under an operating lease.

After initial recognition at cost an entity chooses one model for all its investment property. The cost model depreciates the property as PSAK 216 does and discloses fair value. The fair value model stops depreciation and puts every change in fair value through profit or loss.

A property changes line only when its use changes, with evidence. Under the cost model a transfer moves the carrying amount unchanged. Under the fair value model the gain built up while the entity occupied the property goes to other comprehensive income (apart from any reversal of an earlier impairment) and never reaches profit later, while a gain on inventory goes straight to profit.

title: Long-Term Bank Loans: Amortised Cost, Classification and Sukuk
snippet: The theory of long-term borrowings from pricing to derecognition, worked through PHE's syndicated loans and a subsidiary's sukuk ijarah, and set beside the industries that borrow differently
content:
In brief

  • A loan is recognised at the cash actually received, net of the costs of arranging it, and then carried at amortised cost. The effective interest rate spreads coupons, fees, discounts and premiums over the loan's life as one interest expense, so the carrying amount climbs or falls to the amount repayable.

  • The current/non-current split turns on one question, asked at the reporting date: does the borrower have a right to defer settlement for at least twelve months? Since the 2024 amendments to PSAK 201, only covenants tested on or before that date can take the right away; later covenants are disclosed.

  • A loan leaves the balance sheet when it is repaid, extinguished or modified so much that it is in substance a new loan (the 10 percent test). Sukuk follow their own standard, PSAK 410: a sukuk ijarah is a liability with costs amortised straight-line, and a sukuk mudharabah is temporary syirkah funds, outside liabilities.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report long-term bank loans, non-current portion, of 1,675,895 at 31 December 2024 against 3,467,995 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 5.5 percent of total assets (11.2 percent a year earlier). With the current maturities of 1,551,034, PHE owes its banks 3,226,929 on long-term facilities. Alongside sit short-term bank loans (15,775), a shareholder loan from PT Pertamina (Persero) (74,873) and sukuk (43,289).

After reading this page a student should be able to price and record a borrowing, run it at amortised cost, classify it, account for its modification or early repayment, and tell a sukuk from a bond.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Borrowings are financial liabilities under PSAK 109 Instrumen Keuangan (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9).

1. What long-term borrowings are

A borrowing is non-current when it is not due within twelve months of the reporting date and the entity has a right to defer settlement beyond that.

  • Bonds payable are debt sold to many investors under one trust deed (indenture): secured or unsecured, term or serial (maturing in pieces), callable, convertible, or deep discount (zero-coupon).

  • Notes payable are written promises to one lender. A bank term loan is a note in all but name.

  • Syndicated loans are one loan agreement funded by many banks through a facility agent. Most of PHE's line is this kind (Note 27, Daftar 5/130, PDF p. 147).

A bullet loan repays all principal at maturity; an amortising loan repays in instalments. A floating-rate loan resets its coupon to a benchmark, such as the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), plus a fixed margin. PHE's two corporate facilities are unsecured, priced at Term SOFR plus a margin, and mix semi-annual instalments with bullets (Note 27, PDF pp. 152–157).

2. Pricing a borrowing: par, discount and premium

A lender pays the present value of what it will receive, discounted at the market rate for that risk. If the stated (coupon) rate equals the market rate, the price equals face value, at par. If the coupon is below the market rate, investors pay less, at a discount; if above, more, at a premium.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary issues a five-year bond with face value 100,000 and a 6 percent annual coupon when the market rate is 7 percent.

PV of principal = 100,000 × 0.71299 = 71,298.62

PV of interest = 6,000 × 4.10020 = 24,601.18

Price = 95,899.80; discount = 100,000 − 95,899.80 = 4,100.20

0.71299 is 1 / 1.07^5 and 4.10020 is the five-year annuity factor at 7 percent. The lecture notes run the same calculation semi-annually for a Pertamina depot bond (face 2,500,000, 8 percent coupon, 10 percent market) and arrive at a discount of 311,154; with the correct annuity factor (12.46221, not 12.46621) it is 311,554.

Dr Cash 95,899.80 / Cr Bonds payable 95,899.80

3. Initial measurement and the effective interest method

PSAK 109 recognises a financial liability at fair value, net of transaction costs directly attributable to it, when it is not carried at fair value through profit or loss (para. 5.1.1). Arrangement and legal fees are transaction costs. PHE's policy says the same (Note 3g, Daftar 5/44, PDF p. 61).

Afterwards the liability is carried at amortised cost: the initial amount, plus interest at the effective interest rate (EIR), less cash paid. The EIR is the rate that discounts the contractual cash flows exactly to the initial carrying amount. It folds the coupon, fees and any discount or premium into one rate, so the cost of borrowing is charged at a constant rate on the carrying amount over the loan's life instead of landing in the year the fee was paid.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary draws a three-year bullet term loan of 100,000, a slice on the scale of PHE's 940,000 bullet, at a fixed 6 percent paid annually and pays a 1,500 arrangement fee.

Initial carrying amount = 100,000 − 1,500 = 98,500

EIR solves 98,500 = 6,000 / (1 + r) + 6,000 / (1 + r)^2 + 106,000 / (1 + r)^3, so r = 6.5671%

Interest owed but unpaid at year end is shown separately as accrued interest in current liabilities, not added to the loan (PHE policy, Note 3g, Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63).

Floating-rate loans. When the coupon resets to a benchmark, the cash flows are re-estimated each period and the EIR moves with them (para. B5.4.5). The fee is still spread over the expected life. PHE deducts unamortised arrangement fees of 1,080 and 4,636 from gross principal of 3,232,645 (Note 27), only 0.18 percent of it.

Accruing between dates. If a coupon date falls after the year end, the elapsed part is accrued. The lecture notes accrue three months of the depot bond (3/6 of the coupon and of the discount amortisation) but credit Cash; no cash moves at an accrual, so the credit is Interest payable.

4. Borrowings not at face value

When a note carries no interest, or interest below market, its face value overstates what was borrowed. The liability is the present value at a market rate, and the gap becomes interest over the term.

Zero-interest notes. For example (illustration), a subsidiary buys a compressor by signing a note to pay 50,000 in three years, interest-free, when it could borrow at 8 percent. The compressor's cash price is not known, so the entity uses that estimated market rate, the imputed rate.

Note = 50,000 × 0.79383 = 39,691.61, recorded as Dr Equipment 39,691.61 / Cr Notes payable 39,691.61

Interest: year 1 = 3,175.33, year 2 = 3,429.36, year 3 = 3,703.70; closing balance 50,000.00

If the asset's fair value is known, it fixes the liability instead, and the implicit rate is backed out from it. Recording the compressor at 50,000 would overstate the asset and hide 10,308.39 of interest inside depreciation.

Below-market loans. A shareholder that lends cheaply is partly lending and partly contributing capital. For example (illustration), a parent lends 20,000 for three years at 2 percent when the market rate is 8 percent.

Fair value = 400 × 2.57710 + 20,000 × 0.79383 = 1,030.84 + 15,876.64 = 16,907.48

Dr Cash 20,000 / Cr Loan from parent 16,907.48 / Cr Equity, capital contribution 3,092.52

The parent gave the 3,092.52 as owner. A below-market loan from the government is a government grant under PSAK 220 (formerly PSAK 61, IAS 20, para. 10A), with the benefit deferred and released to profit. PHE's shareholder loan from Pertamina is interest-bearing: 7,259 of interest on an average balance of 75,581 is 9.6 percent (Note 44h–i, Daftar 5/187, PDF p. 204).

5. Current portion and current/non-current classification

A liability is current if the entity expects to settle it within its operating cycle, holds it for trading, must settle it within twelve months of the reporting date, or has no right at the reporting date to defer settlement for at least twelve months (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1, para. 69). The test is a right that exists at the reporting date. Management's intention to repay early, or to refinance, does not change it.

The current portion. An amortising loan is split: instalments due within twelve months are current, the rest non-current. The Company's 2023 facility A2, a 24-month bullet (Note 27, Daftar 5/139, PDF p. 156) drawn for 940,000 in May and October 2023 (PDF p. 157), sat in non-current at 31 December 2023 because it fell due more than twelve months later. A year on, it was due within twelve months. Reconstructed from the facility terms (PHE gives only the totals):

Company syndicated loans, current: 2023 = 400,000 (B1) + 300,000 (accordion) + 122,320 (A1) = 822,320; 2024 = 940,000 (A2) + 122,320 (A1) = 1,062,320

Company non-current: 2023 = 940,000 + 305,360 = 1,245,360; 2024 = 305,360 − 122,320 = 183,040

That one reclassification explains more than half of the fall in this line, from 3,467,995 to 1,675,895, without a dollar being repaid.

Refinancing. A loan due within twelve months stays current even if a refinancing is signed after the reporting date but before the statements are issued (para. 72). It is non-current only if, at the reporting date, the entity already has the right under an existing facility to roll it over for at least twelve months (para. 73).

Covenants and breach. A covenant is a condition in the loan agreement, such as a maximum leverage ratio. PHE's two corporate facilities require consolidated EBITDA of at least 3.00 times interest, net debt of at most 2.00 times tangible net worth, and net worth of at least USD 8 billion (Note 27, PDF pp. 153 and 157). If a breach makes the loan repayable on demand at the reporting date, the loan is current, even if the lenders agree after year end not to call it (para. 74). It stays non-current only if the lenders agreed by the reporting date to a grace period ending at least twelve months later (para. 75).

The 2024 amendments, Non-current Liabilities with Covenants, added which covenants count. Only covenants the entity must meet on or before the reporting date affect classification; covenants tested later do not, but the entity must disclose them and any sign it may struggle to meet them (paras. 72B, 76ZA). PHE adopted the amendment with no significant effect (Note 3b, Daftar 5/30, PDF p. 47). For example (illustration), a 500,000 loan with a leverage covenant of 2.00:

Situation at 31 December 2024

Classification

Covenant tested at 31 December, ratio 1.60

Non-current

Ratio 2.30 at 31 December; waiver with 15 months' grace signed 15 December

Non-current

Ratio 2.30 at 31 December; same waiver signed 20 February 2025

Current; waiver disclosed as a non-adjusting event

Covenant first tested 30 June 2025

Non-current, with the covenant disclosed

6. Modification and extinguishment

A financial liability is removed when it is extinguished: paid, cancelled or expired (PSAK 109 para. 3.3.1). The difference between its carrying amount and what is paid goes to profit or loss (para. 3.3.3).

Early repayment. For example (illustration), the loan of section 3 is repaid at the end of year 2, at par plus a 1 percent prepayment fee.

Loss = 100,000 + 1,000 − 99,467.88 = 1,532.12

Dr Bank loans 99,467.88, Dr Loss on extinguishment 1,532.12 / Cr Cash 101,000

The unamortised fee of 532.12 is written off at once. PHE's Note 27 implies an event of this kind: PEP's facility A2 balance is nil at the end of 2024 although it had 84 months to run from 2022, while 21,646 of interest was charged on it during the year (PDF pp. 152 and 155). Long-term repayments in Note 50 (1,643,239) exceed the 1,366,241 due in 2024 by 276,998, close to the 276,800 of PEP's A2 that was non-current at the end of 2023, so that balance appears to have been prepaid. PHE does not describe the repayment.

Settlement with assets or shares. When a creditor accepts an asset, the asset is first remeasured to fair value and the rest is a gain on extinguishment. When it accepts shares, ISAK 119 (IFRIC 19) measures the shares at fair value. For example (illustration), a 20,000 loan settled with shares worth 16,000:

Dr Bank loans 20,000 / Cr Share capital and share premium 16,000 / Cr Gain on extinguishment 4,000

Modification. If the lender changes the terms, PSAK 109 asks whether they are substantially different: whether the present value of the new cash flows, including fees, discounted at the original EIR, differs by at least 10 percent from the present value of the remaining original cash flows, which at the original EIR is the carrying amount (para. B3.3.6). For example (illustration), a 100,000 loan at 6 percent with three years left is renegotiated in two ways.

A: five years at 5%, fee 500

B: principal cut to 85,000, five years at 4%

PV of new flows at 6%

96,287.64

77,838.98

Change

3.71%

22.16%

Result

Modification

Extinguishment

Accounting

Remeasure at 6%: 95,787.64; gain 4,212.36; fee 500 reduces the carrying amount

Derecognise; new loan at fair value at the market rate of 8%: 71,424.79

Journal

Dr Bank loans 4,212.36 / Cr Gain on modification 4,212.36; Dr Bank loans 500 / Cr Cash 500

Dr Bank loans (old) 100,000 / Cr Bank loans (new) 71,424.79 / Cr Gain on extinguishment 28,575.21

The 10 percent test is a floor, not the whole test. A change that alters the instrument's nature, such as a new currency or an added equity conversion feature, is usually treated as substantially different even below 10 percent (practice, STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED). The lecture notes' restructuring example takes route B. Morgan National Bank cuts a 10,500,000 note to 9,000,000 at 8 percent for five years, and the new note at the 15 percent market rate is worth 6,837,779, a gain of 3,662,221. PHE's policy follows PSAK 109 (Note 3g, Daftar 5/47, PDF p. 64).

Benchmark reform. When LIBOR ended in 2023, loans moved to SOFR plus a credit adjustment spread (CAS). PSAK 109 lets a change required by the reform, on an economically equivalent basis, be treated as a reset of a floating rate: the EIR is updated and no gain or loss arises (paras. 5.4.7–5.4.9). PHE's project loan for Jambaran-Tiung Biru moved from LIBOR + 2.95 percent to SOFR + CAS + 2.95 percent on Tranche A, and from LIBOR + 2.15 percent to SOFR + CAS + 2.15 percent on Tranche B, after September 2023 (Note 27, Daftar 5/132, PDF p. 149).

7. The fair value option and off-balance-sheet financing

A borrower may designate a liability at fair value through profit or loss to remove an accounting mismatch (para. 4.2.2). The change in fair value due to the borrower's own credit risk then goes to other comprehensive income (OCI), not profit (para. 5.7.7). Own-credit amounts in OCI are never recycled to profit. For example (illustration, the split is this page's), a note of 500 falls to 480, 15 of it from the issuer's weaker credit and 5 from higher market rates.

Dr Notes payable 20 / Cr OCI 15 / Cr Gain in profit or loss 5

The lecture notes' Edmond example blames the whole fall on credit risk yet credits income; under PSAK 109 all 20 would go to OCI. PHE carries all its borrowings at amortised cost (Note 3g, PDF p. 61).

Off-balance-sheet financing keeps debt out of the borrower's statements, through unconsolidated project companies or special purpose entities. The notes say a parent need not consolidate a subsidiary owned below 50 percent. Under PSAK 110 (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) control decides, whatever the shareholding. A financial guarantee the parent gives a lender is recognised at fair value and then carried at the higher of the expected credit loss and the unamortised initial amount (PSAK 109 para. 4.2.1(c)); a comfort letter that is not a guarantee is not recognised. PIEP gave one in 2017 for its subsidiary M&P's syndicated loan and states it "shall not be construed as acting as a guarantor" (Note 27, Daftar 5/134, PDF p. 151). Because M&P is consolidated, its loan is already in PHE's borrowings; the letter matters only in PIEP's own accounts.

8. Sukuk: the issuer's side

A sukuk is a sharia security representing an undivided share in assets, in the benefit of assets, or in an investment activity. The holder earns a share of rent or profit rather than interest. Indonesia's issuer accounting sits in PSAK 410 Akuntansi Sukuk (formerly PSAK 110; the new PSAK 110 is consolidation, a renumbering trap) and covers two forms.

Sukuk ijarah

Sukuk mudharabah

What the holder owns

Benefit of a leased asset; return is rent (ijarah fee)

Share of a business venture; return is a profit share (nisbah)

Initial measurement

Fair value (nominal adjusted for premium or discount), less transaction costs

Nominal; transaction costs a separate deferred charge

Afterwards

Costs and premium or discount amortised straight-line as sukuk issuance expense; ijarah fee expensed when due

Costs amortised straight-line; the holders' share is a distribution of revenue, not an expense

Presentation

Liability, net of unamortised costs

Temporary syirkah funds, between liabilities and equity (last among liabilities if the entity has no such section)

Both forms spread costs straight-line, where PSAK 109 would use the effective interest rate. PHE's own policy lists the sukuk payable among loans and borrowings at amortised cost under the EIR method (Note 3g, PDF pp. 61 and 63), and never cites PSAK 410.

PHE's sukuk payable is a sukuk ijarah issued by its subsidiary Elnusa on 11 August 2020: Rp700,000 million, five years, an ijarah fee of Rp63,000 million a year (9 percent) paid quarterly, maturing 11 August 2025 (Note 22, Daftar 5/116–5/117, PDF pp. 133–134). For example (illustration), translate it at one constant rate, so nominal 43,325 and issuance costs 224 as in Note 22.

On issue: Dr Cash 43,101 / Cr Sukuk ijarah payable 43,101

Each quarter: Dr Ijarah expense 974.81 / Cr Cash 974.81, where 974.81 = 43,325 × 9% / 4

Each year: Dr Sukuk issuance expense 44.80 / Cr Sukuk ijarah payable 44.80, where 44.80 = 224 / 5

Note 22 shows the net: 43,325 − 224 + 188 = 43,289. Islamic tranches also appear inside PHE's bank loans: a wakala (agency-based) tranche of the Jambaran-Tiung Biru financing and a Bank Syariah Indonesia facility to an Elnusa subsidiary. PHE reports both as bank loans; the wakala tranche is priced off SOFR like the conventional tranches (Note 27, PDF pp. 148 and 160).

9. Borrowings across industries

Banks. Borrowings, subordinated debt and deposits are all financial liabilities at amortised cost, but banks present the balance sheet in order of liquidity without a current/non-current split, which PSAK 201 allows when it is more relevant (para. 60). Maturity analysis then moves to the notes.

Power, toll roads and other project finance. A project company borrows non-recourse: lenders are repaid only from the project's cash flows. Covenants centre on the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), cash flow available for debt service divided by principal and interest due. For example (illustration), cash available 13,000 against debt service of 10,000 gives 1.30 against a covenant of 1.20. Lenders often require a debt service reserve account, which the borrower shows as restricted cash (see the Restricted cash essay). Interest during construction is capitalised under PSAK 223 (see the Fixed assets essay).

Mining and plantations. Many Indonesian commodity exporters borrow in USD because they sell in USD, a natural hedge. Many also have the US dollar as functional currency (PSAK 221, IAS 21), as PHE does, so the loan creates no exchange differences. A company whose functional currency is the rupiah carries the gains and losses through profit unless it designates a hedge.

State-owned enterprises. Funds on-lent by the government through subsidiary loan agreements are borrowings. Any below-market element is a grant under PSAK 220 when the government acts as lender or regulator; when it lends as the SOE's shareholder, the logic of a parent's loan (section 4) points to a capital contribution. Which applies is a judgement on the facts.
