11. Upstream note: project finance at Jambaran-Tiung Biru

PEPC financed the Jambaran-Tiung Biru gas development through a trustee borrowing structure: facilities of 1,679,940 after a 166,460 cancellation. The 122,859 remaining in the trustee accounts is carried as restricted cash (Note 27, PDF pp. 148–150). Half of each tranche's notional is swapped from the floating benchmark to fixed base rates of 1.79–1.99 percent (315,000 of 630,000; 479,970 of 959,940), so half the notional was hedged at the effective date; the swaps' amortisation profile is not disclosed. Tranches amortise semi-annually to 2029 and 2034, the longest-dated part of the line.

12. Related lines

  • long-term-bank-loans-current, short-term-bank-loans, other-loans-current, sukuk-payables: the rest of PHE's borrowings, covered on this page.

  • cash-and-cash-equivalents and restricted-cash: the other side of net debt and the trustee account.

  • finance-cost: interest at the effective rate.

  • fixed-assets-net: capitalised borrowing costs.

  • lease-liabilities-current: the other interest-bearing debt (see the Right-of-use assets essay).

Least-confident assertions

  • That PEP prepaid about 277,000 of its facility A2 in 2024 is inferred from Note 27 and Note 50; PHE does not describe it, and the 8,527 fall in unamortised fees is consistent with but does not prove a write-off.

  • PHE appears to measure the sukuk ijarah under PSAK 109 rather than PSAK 410. Its policy puts the sukuk among loans at amortised cost by the EIR method, and the amortised costs (83.9 and 61.7 percent of the total at the end of 2024 and 2023) fit an effective-interest pattern (about 82–88 and 60–65 percent) rather than straight line (87.8 and 67.7 percent). With costs of 224 on 43,325 the difference is immaterial. The sukuk is also shown as non-current although it matures in August 2025.

  • The PSAK 410 treatment in section 8 is from an IAI teaching deck that disclaims being IAI's official view. The standard's text was not opened.

  • The covenant proxy of 0.05 uses total equity and reported cash. The agreements' definitions are not disclosed.

  • Other PHE slips not used in the body: Note 27's facility A1 total reads 943,480,000 for 943,840,000 (PDF p. 155); facility interest (299,827 with the shareholder loan) exceeds Note 41's 297,328 by 2,499, mostly the 2,277 capitalised (Note 12), with 222 and the location of the sukuk fee and M&P's interest undisclosed. The industry notes in section 9 are general practice, not checked against named companies.

content.text: A loan is recognised at the cash actually received, net of the costs of arranging it, and then carried at amortised cost. The effective interest rate spreads coupons, fees, discounts and premiums over the loan's life as one interest expense, so the carrying amount climbs or falls to the amount repayable.

The current/non-current split turns on one question, asked at the reporting date: does the borrower have a right to defer settlement for at least twelve months? Since the 2024 amendments to PSAK 201, only covenants tested on or before that date can take the right away; later covenants are disclosed.

A loan leaves the balance sheet when it is repaid, extinguished or modified so much that it is in substance a new loan (the 10 percent test). Sukuk follow their own standard, PSAK 410: a sukuk ijarah is a liability with costs amortised straight-line, and a sukuk mudharabah is temporary syirkah funds, outside liabilities.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report long-term bank loans, non-current portion, of 1,675,895 at 31 December 2024 against 3,467,995 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 5.5 percent of total assets (11.2 percent a year earlier). With the current maturities of 1,551,034, PHE owes its banks 3,226,929 on long-term facilities. Alongside sit short-term bank loans (15,775), a shareholder loan from PT Pertamina (Persero) (74,873) and sukuk (43,289).
After reading this page a student should be able to price and record a borrowing, run it at amortised cost, classify it, account for its modification or early repayment, and tell a sukuk from a bond.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Borrowings are financial liabilities under PSAK 109
A borrowing is non-current when it is not due within twelve months of the reporting date and the entity has a right to defer settlement beyond that.

are written promises to one lender. A bank term loan is a note in all but name.
are one loan agreement funded by many banks through a facility agent. Most of PHE's line is this kind (Note 27, Daftar 5/130, PDF p. 147).
loan repays all principal at maturity; an

loan resets its coupon to a benchmark, such as the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR), plus a fixed margin. PHE's two corporate facilities are unsecured, priced at Term SOFR plus a margin, and mix semi-annual instalments with bullets (Note 27, PDF pp. 152–157).
2. Pricing a borrowing: par, discount and premium
A lender pays the present value of what it will receive, discounted at the market rate for that risk. If the stated (coupon) rate equals the market rate, the price equals face value,
. If the coupon is below the market rate, investors pay less,
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary issues a five-year bond with face value 100,000 and a 6 percent annual coupon when the market rate is 7 percent.

is the five-year annuity factor at 7 percent. The lecture notes run the same calculation semi-annually for a Pertamina depot bond (face 2,500,000, 8 percent coupon, 10 percent market) and arrive at a discount of 311,154; with the correct annuity factor (12.46221, not 12.46621) it is 311,554.
3. Initial measurement and the effective interest method
PSAK 109 recognises a financial liability at fair value,

directly attributable to it, when it is not carried at fair value through profit or loss (para. 5.1.1). Arrangement and legal fees are transaction costs. PHE's policy says the same (Note 3g, Daftar 5/44, PDF p. 61).
Afterwards the liability is carried at
: the initial amount, plus interest at the

(EIR), less cash paid. The EIR is the rate that discounts the contractual cash flows exactly to the initial carrying amount. It folds the coupon, fees and any discount or premium into one rate, so the cost of borrowing is charged at a constant rate on the carrying amount over the loan's life instead of landing in the year the fee was paid.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary draws a three-year bullet term loan of 100,000, a slice on the scale of PHE's 940,000 bullet, at a fixed 6 percent paid annually and pays a 1,500 arrangement fee.
Dr Interest expense 6,468.56 / Cr Cash 6,000.00 / Cr Bank loans 468.56
Interest owed but unpaid at year end is shown separately as accrued interest in current liabilities, not added to the loan (PHE policy, Note 3g, Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63).

When the coupon resets to a benchmark, the cash flows are re-estimated each period and the EIR moves with them (para. B5.4.5). The fee is still spread over the expected life. PHE deducts unamortised arrangement fees of 1,080 and 4,636 from gross principal of 3,232,645 (Note 27), only 0.18 percent of it.

If a coupon date falls after the year end, the elapsed part is accrued. The lecture notes accrue three months of the depot bond (3/6 of the coupon and of the discount amortisation) but credit Cash; no cash moves at an accrual, so the credit is Interest payable.

When a note carries no interest, or interest below market, its face value overstates what was borrowed. The liability is the present value at a market rate, and the gap becomes interest over the term.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary buys a compressor by signing a note to pay 50,000 in three years, interest-free, when it could borrow at 8 percent. The compressor's cash price is not known, so the entity uses that estimated market rate, the
Note = 50,000 × 0.79383 = 39,691.61, recorded as Dr Equipment 39,691.61 / Cr Notes payable 39,691.61
Interest: year 1 = 3,175.33, year 2 = 3,429.36, year 3 = 3,703.70; closing balance 50,000.00

If the asset's fair value is known, it fixes the liability instead, and the implicit rate is backed out from it. Recording the compressor at 50,000 would overstate the asset and hide 10,308.39 of interest inside depreciation.
A shareholder that lends cheaply is partly lending and partly contributing capital. For example (illustration), a parent lends 20,000 for three years at 2 percent when the market rate is 8 percent.
Dr Cash 20,000 / Cr Loan from parent 16,907.48 / Cr Equity, capital contribution 3,092.52

The parent gave the 3,092.52 as owner. A below-market loan from the government is a government grant under PSAK 220 (formerly PSAK 61, IAS 20, para. 10A), with the benefit deferred and released to profit. PHE's shareholder loan from Pertamina is interest-bearing: 7,259 of interest on an average balance of 75,581 is 9.6 percent (Note 44h–i, Daftar 5/187, PDF p. 204).

A liability is current if the entity expects to settle it within its operating cycle, holds it for trading, must settle it within twelve months of the reporting date, or has no right at the reporting date to defer settlement for at least twelve months (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1, para. 69). The test is a right that exists at the reporting date. Management's intention to repay early, or to refinance, does not change it.

An amortising loan is split: instalments due within twelve months are current, the rest non-current. The Company's 2023 facility A2, a 24-month bullet (Note 27, Daftar 5/139, PDF p. 156) drawn for 940,000 in May and October 2023 (PDF p. 157), sat in non-current at 31 December 2023 because it fell due more than twelve months later. A year on, it was due within twelve months. Reconstructed from the facility terms (PHE gives only the totals):
That one reclassification explains more than half of the fall in this line, from 3,467,995 to 1,675,895, without a dollar being repaid.

A loan due within twelve months stays current even if a refinancing is signed after the reporting date but before the statements are issued (para. 72). It is non-current only if, at the reporting date, the entity already has the right under an existing facility to roll it over for at least twelve months (para. 73).

is a condition in the loan agreement, such as a maximum leverage ratio. PHE's two corporate facilities require consolidated EBITDA of at least 3.00 times interest, net debt of at most 2.00 times tangible net worth, and net worth of at least USD 8 billion (Note 27, PDF pp. 153 and 157). If a breach makes the loan repayable on demand at the reporting date, the loan is current, even if the lenders agree after year end not to call it (para. 74). It stays non-current only if the lenders agreed
the reporting date to a grace period ending at least twelve months later (para. 75).

, added which covenants count. Only covenants the entity must meet on or before the reporting date affect classification; covenants tested later do not, but the entity must disclose them and any sign it may struggle to meet them (paras. 72B, 76ZA). PHE adopted the amendment with no significant effect (Note 3b, Daftar 5/30, PDF p. 47). For example (illustration), a 500,000 loan with a leverage covenant of 2.00:
Ratio 2.30 at 31 December; waiver with 15 months' grace signed 15 December
Ratio 2.30 at 31 December; same waiver signed 20 February 2025
Current; waiver disclosed as a non-adjusting event
A financial liability is removed when it is
: paid, cancelled or expired (PSAK 109 para. 3.3.1). The difference between its carrying amount and what is paid goes to profit or loss (para. 3.3.3).
For example (illustration), the loan of section 3 is repaid at the end of year 2, at par plus a 1 percent prepayment fee.
Dr Bank loans 99,467.88, Dr Loss on extinguishment 1,532.12 / Cr Cash 101,000

The unamortised fee of 532.12 is written off at once. PHE's Note 27 implies an event of this kind: PEP's facility A2 balance is nil at the end of 2024 although it had 84 months to run from 2022, while 21,646 of interest was charged on it during the year (PDF pp. 152 and 155). Long-term repayments in Note 50 (1,643,239) exceed the 1,366,241 due in 2024 by 276,998, close to the 276,800 of PEP's A2 that was non-current at the end of 2023, so that balance appears to have been prepaid. PHE does not describe the repayment.

When a creditor accepts an asset, the asset is first remeasured to fair value and the rest is a gain on extinguishment. When it accepts shares, ISAK 119 (IFRIC 19) measures the shares at fair value. For example (illustration), a 20,000 loan settled with shares worth 16,000:
Dr Bank loans 20,000 / Cr Share capital and share premium 16,000 / Cr Gain on extinguishment 4,000
If the lender changes the terms, PSAK 109 asks whether they are
: whether the present value of the new cash flows, including fees, discounted at the

EIR, differs by at least 10 percent from the present value of the remaining original cash flows, which at the original EIR is the carrying amount (para. B3.3.6). For example (illustration), a 100,000 loan at 6 percent with three years left is renegotiated in two ways.
B: principal cut to 85,000, five years at 4%
Remeasure at 6%: 95,787.64; gain 4,212.36; fee 500 reduces the carrying amount
Derecognise; new loan at fair value at the market rate of 8%: 71,424.79
Dr Bank loans 4,212.36 / Cr Gain on modification 4,212.36; Dr Bank loans 500 / Cr Cash 500
Dr Bank loans (old) 100,000 / Cr Bank loans (new) 71,424.79 / Cr Gain on extinguishment 28,575.21

The 10 percent test is a floor, not the whole test. A change that alters the instrument's nature, such as a new currency or an added equity conversion feature, is usually treated as substantially different even below 10 percent (practice, STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED). The lecture notes' restructuring example takes route B. Morgan National Bank cuts a 10,500,000 note to 9,000,000 at 8 percent for five years, and the new note at the 15 percent market rate is worth 6,837,779, a gain of 3,662,221. PHE's policy follows PSAK 109 (Note 3g, Daftar 5/47, PDF p. 64).
When LIBOR ended in 2023, loans moved to SOFR plus a

(CAS). PSAK 109 lets a change required by the reform, on an economically equivalent basis, be treated as a reset of a floating rate: the EIR is updated and no gain or loss arises (paras. 5.4.7–5.4.9). PHE's project loan for Jambaran-Tiung Biru moved from LIBOR + 2.95 percent to SOFR + CAS + 2.95 percent on Tranche A, and from LIBOR + 2.15 percent to SOFR + CAS + 2.15 percent on Tranche B, after September 2023 (Note 27, Daftar 5/132, PDF p. 149).
7. The fair value option and off-balance-sheet financing

A borrower may designate a liability at fair value through profit or loss to remove an accounting mismatch (para. 4.2.2). The change in fair value due to the borrower's own credit risk then goes to other comprehensive income (OCI), not profit (para. 5.7.7). Own-credit amounts in OCI are never recycled to profit. For example (illustration, the split is this page's), a note of 500 falls to 480, 15 of it from the issuer's weaker credit and 5 from higher market rates.
Dr Notes payable 20 / Cr OCI 15 / Cr Gain in profit or loss 5

The lecture notes' Edmond example blames the whole fall on credit risk yet credits income; under PSAK 109 all 20 would go to OCI. PHE carries all its borrowings at amortised cost (Note 3g, PDF p. 61).

presentation.deck: The theory of long-term borrowings from pricing to derecognition, worked through PHE's syndicated loans and a subsidiary's sukuk ijarah, and set beside the industries that borrow differently
key_takeaways: A loan is recognised at the cash actually received, net of the costs of arranging it, and then carried at amortised cost. The effective interest rate spreads coupons, fees, discounts and premiums over the loan's life as one interest expense, so the carrying amount climbs or falls to the amount repayable.

The current/non-current split turns on one question, asked at the reporting date: does the borrower have a right to defer settlement for at least twelve months? Since the 2024 amendments to PSAK 201, only covenants tested on or before that date can take the right away; later covenants are disclosed.

A loan leaves the balance sheet when it is repaid, extinguished or modified so much that it is in substance a new loan (the 10 percent test). Sukuk follow their own standard, PSAK 410: a sukuk ijarah is a liability with costs amortised straight-line, and a sukuk mudharabah is temporary syirkah funds, outside liabilities.

title: Long-Term Investments: Classification, the Equity Method and Joint Arrangements
snippet: The theory of investments in other entities from debt securities to associates, worked through PHE's stakes in Donggi Senoro LNG and Seplat and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • An investment's accounting follows the investor's power over the investee. Debt securities and small equity stakes are financial assets under PSAK 109, sorted by business model and cash-flow terms into amortised cost, fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) or fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL). Significant influence or joint control of net assets brings the equity method, and control brings consolidation.

  • The equity method books the investor's share of the investee's profit as income when it is earned and treats a dividend as cash leaving the investment. Any price paid above the investor's share of book value is allocated to the investee's assets and goodwill, and the allocation is unwound through the share of profit.

  • Loss recognition stops when the investment reaches zero, impairment tests the whole investment as one asset, and losing significant influence remeasures what is left at fair value. A participating interest in an oil and gas block is normally a joint operation, recognised line by line in oil and gas properties instead of on this line.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report long term investments of 1,103,172 at 31 December 2024 against 1,602,821 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line fell 499,649, or 31.2 percent, and its share of total assets fell from 5.2 to 3.6 percent. Note 16 splits it into investments in oil and gas blocks (591,684), investments in associates and joint venture (511,425) and other investment (63) (Daftar 5/107, PDF p. 124). This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to classify an investment, record it under each measurement basis, run the equity method from acquisition to disposal, and say where other industries depart from these rules.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What the line holds and why classification comes first

Kieso's Intermediate Accounting (IFRS edition) opens its investments chapter with two motives for investing in another entity's securities: to earn a return on spare cash, and to secure an operating or financial relationship with the investee. The motive matters because the accounting follows what the investor can do with the investee, and that runs on a scale.

Investor's position

Typical holding

Standard

Measurement

Creditor (debt securities)

Bonds, notes

PSAK 109 Financial Instruments (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9)

Amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL

Control (subsidiary)

The percentages are rebuttable presumptions. Holding 20 percent or more of the votes is presumed to give significant influence unless it can be clearly shown not to, and holding less is presumed not to (PSAK 228.5). Influence usually shows in board representation, a part in policy and dividend decisions, material transactions, interchange of managers, or essential technical information (para. 6).

Kieso lists an investment in a subsidiary as a long-term investment. That holds only in the parent's separate statements (section 9); in consolidated statements such as PHE's the subsidiary's assets and liabilities replace it.

An equity-method investment stays non-current unless it is held for sale under PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5) (PSAK 228.15); a bond moves to current assets when it falls due within twelve months.

PHE keeps its financial-asset investments on other lines. Its policy puts quoted FVOCI debt instruments in other non-current financial assets, elects FVOCI for unlisted equity and leaves listed equity at FVTPL (Note 3g, Daftar 5/40–41, PDF pp. 57–58). Sections 2 to 4 teach rules PHE applies there.

2. Debt investments: business model and contractual cash flows

PSAK 109 classifies a debt investment by two tests. The business model test asks whether the entity holds the asset to collect contractual cash flows, to collect and sell, or for neither (trading). The cash-flow characteristics test asks whether those cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest, as a plain bond's are. Together they give three categories.

  • Held to collect and passing the cash-flow test: amortised cost.

  • Held to collect and sell and passing the cash-flow test: FVOCI, meaning fair value on the balance sheet with changes parked in other comprehensive income (OCI), the part of comprehensive income kept out of profit.

  • Everything else, including trading: FVTPL, with every fair value change in profit or loss.

Amortised cost is the amount at initial recognition, less principal repaid, plus or minus the cumulative amortisation of any premium or discount by the effective interest method, less any loss allowance.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary invests surplus dollars on 1 January in a five-year USD bond with face value 10,000 and a 4 percent annual coupon, when the market yield is 5 percent.

Price = 400 × annuity factor (5%, 5 years) + 10,000 × discount factor (5%, 5 years) = 9,567.05

Year 1 interest revenue = 9,567.05 × 5% = 478.35; coupon received = 400.00; discount amortised = 78.35

Amortised cost at year end = 9,567.05 + 78.35 = 9,645.40

At year end yields have fallen and the bond's fair value is 9,800.

Amortised cost

FVOCI

FVTPL

Purchase

Interest revenue is the same 478.35 under all three, because FVOCI keeps the effective interest in profit and only parks the fair value change. Under FVTPL the split is a presentation choice; only the 632.95 in profit is fixed. If the FVOCI bond is sold on 2 January for 9,800, the 154.60 leaves OCI and enters profit as a realised gain. This reclassification adjustment (the notes' "recycling", their chapter's last topic) stops the gain being counted twice in comprehensive income.

Dr Cash 9,800.00 / Cr Debt investment 9,645.40, Cr Fair value adjustment 154.60

Dr OCI, unrealised holding gain 154.60 / Cr Gain on sale of debt investment 154.60

3. Impairment of debt investments: expected credit losses

PSAK 109 replaced the incurred-loss model that older editions of Kieso teach, which waits for a loss event and discounts the lost cash flows, with expected credit losses (ECL) from the day of purchase. Stage 1 carries twelve months of expected loss. Stage 2 carries lifetime loss once credit risk has risen significantly. Stage 3, when the borrower is credit-impaired (in default or severe distress), keeps lifetime loss and computes interest on the carrying amount net of the allowance.

ECL = probability of default × loss given default × exposure at default

For example (illustration), on the bond above:

Stage 1: 0.5% × 45% × 10,000 = 22.50

Stage 2, lifetime default probability 6%: 6% × 45% × 10,000 = 270.00

Dr Impairment loss 22.50 / Cr Loss allowance 22.50

For an FVOCI bond the loss still goes to profit, with the credit to OCI, because the asset is already at fair value.

4. Equity securities below significant influence

Below significant influence PSAK 109 starts from FVTPL. Any shares not held for trading (and not contingent consideration in a business combination) may be designated at initial recognition, share by share and irrevocably, to FVOCI. Strategic stakes, such as one held to secure supply, are the usual case.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 1,000,000 shares of a listed drilling contractor at USD 0.50 a share to secure rig access, paying broker fees of 5. At year end the price is USD 0.46, a dividend of 20 has been received, and next year the shares are sold at USD 0.55.

FVTPL

FVOCI (elected)

Purchase

Dr Equity investment 500, Dr Transaction cost expense 5 / Cr Cash 505

Dr Equity investment 505 / Cr Cash 505

Dividend

Dr Cash 20 / Cr Dividend income 20

Dr Cash 20 / Cr Dividend income 20

Year end, value 460

Dr Unrealised holding loss, profit or loss 40 / Cr Fair value adjustment 40

Dr OCI 45 / Cr Fair value adjustment 45

Sale at 550

Dr Cash 550, Dr Fair value adjustment 40 / Cr Equity investment 500, Cr Gain on sale 90

Dr Fair value adjustment 90 / Cr OCI 90; Dr Cash 550 / Cr Equity investment 505, Cr Fair value adjustment 45; cumulative OCI 45 may move to retained earnings

Kieso's example records broker fees as an expense, which is right only under FVTPL; under every other basis they are part of cost. A dividend is income in both columns, because the investor has never booked a share of the investee's profit; the one exception is a dividend that clearly repays part of the cost (IFRS 9 B5.7.1). The FVOCI gain never reaches profit, even on sale, because FVOCI equity, unlike FVOCI debt, is never recycled and has no impairment test. PHE's own policy states the same three rules (Note 3g).

5. Significant influence and the equity method

Once the investor can influence dividend policy, dividend income stops measuring what it earns, because the investor could time its income by voting for or against a payout. Beams' Advanced Accounting gives this as the reason fair value is forbidden at this level. PSAK 228 also rules it out, except for the fund exemption in section 9, and instead extends the investor's statements to include its share of the investee's profit or loss (para. 11).

The mechanism has three moves (para. 10).

Initial carrying amount = cost

+ investor's share of the investee's profit after acquisition (to profit or loss), and of its OCI (to OCI)

− distributions received

Cost includes directly attributable costs such as professional fees.

Take PHE's 2024 numbers for its 29 percent associate PT Donggi Senoro LNG (DSLNG) as the starting point: opening carrying amount 299,171, share of profit 53,860, dividends 49,300 (Note 16b, Daftar 5/108, PDF p. 125). The comparison follows Beams' layout. The left column shows only the dividend, because under PSAK 109 the stake would also be remeasured to fair value.

Below significant influence (PSAK 109, dividend line only)

Equity method

Investee earns 185,700

no entry

Dr Investment in associate 53,860 / Cr Share of profit of associates 53,860 (29% × 185,700 = 53,853; PHE books 53,860)

Investee pays dividends, 29% = 49,300

Dr Cash 49,300 / Cr Dividend income 49,300

Dr Cash 49,300 / Cr Investment in associate 49,300

Income for the year

299,171 + 53,860 − 49,300 = 303,731

Booking the dividend as income under the equity method would count DSLNG's profit twice, when earned and when paid out.

Beams calls this one-line consolidation. Profit and equity come out as if DSLNG had been consolidated, but on one line in each statement. The test is whether the carrying amount equals the investor's share of the investee's net assets plus any unamortised excess paid. With DSLNG's net assets of 1,334,590 − 417,540 = 917,050 at the end of 2024, PHE's share is 29% × 917,050 = 265,944.5, against a carrying amount of 265,952. The near-match suggests that little excess over book value remains inside PHE's investment.

6. Paying above book value and transactions with the investee

When the price differs from the investor's share of book value, the difference is explained asset by asset. Beams allocates it in order to the investee's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, with the remainder as goodwill (PSAK 228.32). Goodwill stays inside the investment and is not amortised; amounts allocated to inventory or plant are unwound as the investee sells the inventory or depreciates the plant.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 29 percent of an LNG company for 300,000 on 1 January. Book net assets are 900,000; the plant's fair value exceeds its book value by 100,000 over a remaining life of 25 years; LNG inventory exceeds book by 5,000. Deferred tax on the uplifts is ignored to keep the steps short.

Share of book value = 29% × 900,000 = 261,000

Allocated to plant = 29% × 100,000 = 29,000; to inventory = 29% × 5,000 = 1,450

Goodwill = 300,000 − 261,000 − 29,000 − 1,450 = 8,550

In year 1 the investee earns 180,000, sells the inventory, and pays dividends of 140,000.

Share of profit = 29% × 180,000 − 1,450 inventory − 29,000 / 25 plant = 52,200 − 1,450 − 1,160 = 49,590

Dividends received = 29% × 140,000 = 40,600

Closing carrying amount = 300,000 + 49,590 − 40,600 = 308,990

Dr Investment in associate 49,590 / Cr Share of profit of associates 49,590

Dr Cash 40,600 / Cr Investment in associate 40,600

If the price had been 285,000, the excess over book value (24,000) would fall short of the fair value uplift (30,450). That 6,450 is a bargain purchase, included as income in the share of profit in the year of acquisition (para. 32(b)). Beams also describes an older US treatment that used it to reduce non-current assets instead.

Profit on sales between investor and investee is eliminated to the extent of the investor's interest (para. 28). For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary sells gas to a 29 percent associate at a profit of 2,000, and the associate still holds the LNG at year end; the 580 below is recognised when that LNG is sold to an outside buyer.

Unrealised profit eliminated = 29% × 2,000 = 580: Dr Share of profit of associates 580 / Cr Investment in associate 580

7. Losses, impairment and the end of the equity method

Losses beyond zero. The investor stops recognising its share of losses once its interest reaches zero (para. 38). The interest includes long-term interests that are in substance part of the net investment, such as a loan with no planned repayment, but not trade receivables or secured loans. Beyond that a liability arises only for legal or constructive obligations or payments made on the investee's behalf (para. 39). For example (illustration), a 25 percent exploration associate carried at 6,000 drills a dry well and loses 40,000.

Share of loss = 25% × 40,000 = 10,000; recognised = 6,000; unrecognised, tracked outside the accounts = 4,000

Dr Share of loss of associates 6,000 / Cr Investment in associate 6,000

If it earns 20,000 next year, the share of 5,000 first covers the 4,000 unrecognised loss, and only 1,000 is booked.

PSAK 228 is silent on the mirror case, a dividend above a carrying amount already at zero. With no obligation to repay, practice takes the excess to profit, as PHE did in 2023 (section 10).

Impairment. Objective evidence of impairment includes financial difficulty, default, and adverse changes in the investee's market; for equity, a significant or prolonged fall in fair value below cost is itself evidence (paras. 41A–41C). The whole carrying amount is then tested under PSAK 236 (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) as a single asset against its recoverable amount, the higher of value in use and fair value less costs of disposal (para. 42). Because no part of the loss is allocated to the goodwill inside, the whole loss can later be reversed. For example (illustration), take Seplat's 2024 carrying amount of 214,773 (Note 16b) and suppose the market value of the stake fell to 180,000, costs of disposal were 2,000, and value in use were 195,000.

Recoverable amount = higher of 195,000 and 180,000 − 2,000 = 195,000

Impairment loss = 214,773 − 195,000 = 19,773: Dr Impairment loss 19,773 / Cr Investment in associate 19,773

Discontinuing. When significant influence ends, the retained interest becomes a financial asset at fair value, and the difference between that fair value plus any proceeds and the carrying amount goes to profit (para. 22(b)). Amounts in OCI are recycled as if the investee had disposed of the related assets (para. 22(c)). For example (illustration), PHE sells 19 of its 29 percent of DSLNG for 190,000 and the remaining 10 percent is worth 100,000.

Gain = 190,000 + 100,000 − 265,952 = 24,048

Dr Cash 190,000, Dr Equity investment (FVOCI or FVTPL) 100,000 / Cr Investment in associate 265,952, Cr Gain on loss of significant influence 24,048

Beams, following US GAAP of its time, carries the retained stake at its old book value with no gain, and restates retained earnings retroactively when a stake grows from 10 to 20 percent. PSAK 228 does neither, and PHE's policy remeasures any retained investment at fair value (Note 3l, Daftar 5/55, PDF p. 72).

8. Joint arrangements: joint ventures and joint operations

A joint arrangement exists when two or more parties share control and relevant decisions need unanimous consent. PSAK 111 then asks what the parties hold. Parties to a joint venture have rights only to the net assets and use the equity method. Parties to a joint operation have rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities, and each recognises its own share of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses. PHE's policy uses this split and adds that the structure, the legal form of any separate vehicle and the contractual terms decide it (Note 3y, Daftar 5/73–74, PDF pp. 90–91).

For example (illustration), PHE holds a 10 percent participating interest in a block, and the operator spends 50,000 on a development well.

Joint operation (direct interest)

Joint venture (interest held through a company)

Dr Oil and gas properties 5,000 / Cr Cash call payable 5,000

No entry until the company reports profit; then Dr Investment / Cr Share of profit

A participating interest held directly under a joint operating agreement is the usual upstream case. Where a majority of partners decide, no joint control exists and the arrangement falls outside PSAK 111, but each partner still recognises its own share. PHE nonetheless carries its Malaysian block interests on this line at cost, which its policy note does not explain (section 10).

9. Long-term investments across industries

Industries with their own rules move the boundaries of section 1's scale, mostly toward fair value.

Banks. A bank's securities book is classified portfolio by portfolio by business model, so the same government bond can be at amortised cost in the treasury's hold-to-collect book and at FVTPL on the trading desk. A reclassification is allowed only when the business model itself changes, and then prospectively from the first day of the next reporting period, with no restatement; FVOCI equity is never reclassified (PSAK 109; ref. 6).

Insurers, venture capital and funds. An associate or joint venture held by a venture capital organisation, mutual fund, unit trust or investment-linked insurance fund may be measured at FVTPL instead of the equity method, investee by investee at initial recognition (PSAK 228.18). For example (illustration), a fund holds 25 percent of a start-up bought for 1,000; the start-up earns 400 and the stake's fair value rises to 1,250.

Equity method income = 25% × 400 = 100; FVTPL income = 1,250 − 1,000 = 250

Investment entities. An investment entity carries even its subsidiaries at FVTPL instead of consolidating them. A subsidiary that is not itself an investment entity and provides services for the parent's investment activities is still consolidated (PSAK 110.31–32; ref. 7).

Islamic finance. Sharia investments follow the PSAK 4xx series. A sukuk holder classifies the investment under PSAK 410 Akuntansi Sukuk (formerly PSAK 110), which since its 2015 revision mirrors PSAK 109: amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL by business model and contractual terms (ref. 7). A musyarakah partner under PSAK 406 Akuntansi Musyarakah (formerly PSAK 106) records its capital contribution as an investment in the partnership (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).

Separate financial statements. A parent's own statements may carry subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures at cost, under PSAK 109, or by the equity method (PSAK 227). This is the case Kieso's presentation describes.

  • The table's total exceeds Note 16's 511,425 by 63, the amount of "other investment".

Associates turned just over half their 2024 profit into cash.

Cash conversion = dividends / share of profit = 68,082 / 124,942 = 54.5%

Return on equity-method investments = 124,942 / ((514,238 + 511,488) / 2) = 24.4%

"Others" (39,905 of profit on an opening 3,113) inflates the second ratio. DSLNG and Seplat alone earn 85,037 / ((511,125 + 480,725) / 2) = 17.1% and pay out 68,082 / 85,037 = 80.1%.

Other income, net, carries the share of associates as 162,620 = 124,942 − 11,236 + 48,914 of "dividend receivables actualisation" (Note 42, Daftar 5/150–151, PDF pp. 167–168). The 11,236 reverses a 2023 gain that Note 16b explains as a dividend from PRDL, a Venezuelan associate, above the investment's carrying amount (section 7). Note 42's footnote calls the reversal a restatement of Seplat's minority interests, and the FS does not reconcile the two.

The larger component, investments in oil and gas blocks (591,684, or 53.6 percent of the line), fits none of the textbook categories. Note 16a describes it as investments of the subsidiary PIEP in Malaysian Blocks K, SK-309, SK-311 and SK-314A, measured at cost (Daftar 5/107, PDF p. 124). Note 2d lists the same blocks among the Group's foreign participating interests (Block K 24 percent, SK 309 and SK 311 25.5 percent each, the last two under joint operating contracts; Daftar 5/20, PDF p. 37). The schedule treats them like a cost-model asset, with amortisation of 81,381 and impairment of 2,263 in 2023, and an impairment test with no loss in 2024. The Malaysian balance moved 609,421 + 45,966 − 63,703 = 591,684. The Iraqi balance of 479,099 left the line in full, labelled "termination of recognition", although Note 2f still lists the 20 percent West Qurna-1 interest. That deduction accounts for most of the line's 499,649 fall. The FS gives no policy for the category and does not say where the 479,099 went.

11. Upstream note: blocks, service contracts and partners abroad

The Iraqi interest is a 20 percent share of the West Qurna-1 technical service contract, under which contractors earn remuneration and cost recovery fees instead of a share of production (Note 2f, Daftar 5/23–24, PDF pp. 40–41). Seplat and PRDL are held through Maurel & Prom, a 71.09 percent subsidiary domiciled in Paris (Note 1, Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25; Note 42). The 20.46 percent is M&P's holding, consolidated in full, so PHE's look-through interest in Seplat is 71.09% × 20.46% = 14.5% and 28.91 percent of M&P's result belongs to non-controlling interests. The line mixes an Indonesian LNG plant, oil producers in Nigeria and Venezuela, and Malaysian contract interests.

12. Related lines

  • oil-gas-properties-net: where directly held participating interests (joint operations) are normally recognised.

  • other-non-current-assets: where PHE keeps its quoted FVOCI debt instruments and other financial-asset investments.

  • other-income-expense-net: where PHE presents its share of profit of associates.

  • other-receivables-net: dividends declared but not yet received.

  • cash-and-cash-equivalents: short-dated debt instruments classified as cash equivalents instead of investments.

  • other-comprehensive-income: the OCI side of FVOCI investments and of associates' OCI.

Least-confident assertions

  • Why PHE presents its Malaysian participating interests on this line at cost, and where the Iraqi 479,099 went, are not disclosed. Reading the category as a contract interest measured like a cost-model asset rests on the movement schedule alone.

  • Non-controlling interests inside Seplat are the cause the FS itself points to (Note 3l; Note 42 footnote) for the gap between 376,997 and 214,773, but the split is not given, and acquisition-date fair value adjustments from PHE's purchase of M&P may also play a part. The completion of Seplat's Mobil Producing Nigeria acquisition on 12 December 2024 was checked on the web; its effect on the gap was not.

  • Taking a dividend above a zero carrying amount to profit follows common practice, which PSAK 228 does not state. The Note 16b and Note 42 descriptions of the 11,236 (PRDL dividend; Seplat minority restatement) were not reconciled.

  • The musyarakah treatment under PSAK 406 and the separate-statement options under PSAK 227 are stated from knowledge; their texts were not opened.

  • IFRS 9 paragraph numbers are not given for the classification tests because the official text was not opened; the tests themselves were checked against secondary sources.

content.text: An investment's accounting follows the investor's power over the investee. Debt securities and small equity stakes are financial assets under PSAK 109, sorted by business model and cash-flow terms into amortised cost, fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) or fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL). Significant influence or joint control of net assets brings the equity method, and control brings consolidation.

The equity method books the investor's share of the investee's profit as income when it is earned and treats a dividend as cash leaving the investment. Any price paid above the investor's share of book value is allocated to the investee's assets and goodwill, and the allocation is unwound through the share of profit.

Loss recognition stops when the investment reaches zero, impairment tests the whole investment as one asset, and losing significant influence remeasures what is left at fair value. A participating interest in an oil and gas block is normally a joint operation, recognised line by line in oil and gas properties instead of on this line.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report long term investments of 1,103,172 at 31 December 2024 against 1,602,821 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line fell 499,649, or 31.2 percent, and its share of total assets fell from 5.2 to 3.6 percent. Note 16 splits it into investments in oil and gas blocks (591,684), investments in associates and joint venture (511,425) and other investment (63) (Daftar 5/107, PDF p. 124). This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to classify an investment, record it under each measurement basis, run the equity method from acquisition to disposal, and say where other industries depart from these rules.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. What the line holds and why classification comes first

(IFRS edition) opens its investments chapter with two motives for investing in another entity's securities: to earn a return on spare cash, and to secure an operating or financial relationship with the investee. The motive matters because the accounting follows what the investor can do with the investee, and that runs on a scale.
Investments in Associates and Joint Ventures
Joint control of net assets (joint venture)

The percentages are rebuttable presumptions. Holding 20 percent or more of the votes is presumed to give significant influence unless it can be clearly shown not to, and holding less is presumed not to (PSAK 228.5). Influence usually shows in board representation, a part in policy and dividend decisions, material transactions, interchange of managers, or essential technical information (para. 6).
Kieso lists an investment in a subsidiary as a long-term investment. That holds only in the parent's
statements (section 9); in consolidated statements such as PHE's the subsidiary's assets and liabilities replace it.

An equity-method investment stays non-current unless it is held for sale under PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5) (PSAK 228.15); a bond moves to current assets when it falls due within twelve months.

PHE keeps its financial-asset investments on other lines. Its policy puts quoted FVOCI debt instruments in other non-current financial assets, elects FVOCI for unlisted equity and leaves listed equity at FVTPL (Note 3g, Daftar 5/40–41, PDF pp. 57–58). Sections 2 to 4 teach rules PHE applies there.
2. Debt investments: business model and contractual cash flows
PSAK 109 classifies a debt investment by two tests. The
test asks whether the entity holds the asset to collect contractual cash flows, to collect and sell, or for neither (trading). The
test asks whether those cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest, as a plain bond's are. Together they give three categories.
and passing the cash-flow test: amortised cost.
and passing the cash-flow test: FVOCI, meaning fair value on the balance sheet with changes parked in other comprehensive income (OCI), the part of comprehensive income kept out of profit.
Everything else, including trading: FVTPL, with every fair value change in profit or loss.
is the amount at initial recognition, less principal repaid, plus or minus the cumulative amortisation of any premium or discount by the effective interest method, less any loss allowance.
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary invests surplus dollars on 1 January in a five-year USD bond with face value 10,000 and a 4 percent annual coupon, when the market yield is 5 percent.
Price = 400 × annuity factor (5%, 5 years) + 10,000 × discount factor (5%, 5 years) = 9,567.05
Year 1 interest revenue = 9,567.05 × 5% = 478.35; coupon received = 400.00; discount amortised = 78.35
At year end yields have fallen and the bond's fair value is 9,800.
Dr Cash 400.00, Dr Debt investment 78.35 / Cr Interest revenue 478.35
Dr Fair value adjustment 154.60 / Cr OCI, unrealised holding gain 154.60
Dr Fair value adjustment 154.60 / Cr Unrealised holding gain, profit or loss 154.60

Interest revenue is the same 478.35 under all three, because FVOCI keeps the effective interest in profit and only parks the fair value change. Under FVTPL the split is a presentation choice; only the 632.95 in profit is fixed. If the FVOCI bond is sold on 2 January for 9,800, the 154.60 leaves OCI and enters profit as a realised gain. This
(the notes' "recycling", their chapter's last topic) stops the gain being counted twice in comprehensive income.
Dr Cash 9,800.00 / Cr Debt investment 9,645.40, Cr Fair value adjustment 154.60
Dr OCI, unrealised holding gain 154.60 / Cr Gain on sale of debt investment 154.60
3. Impairment of debt investments: expected credit losses
PSAK 109 replaced the incurred-loss model that older editions of Kieso teach, which waits for a loss event and discounts the lost cash flows, with

(ECL) from the day of purchase. Stage 1 carries twelve months of expected loss. Stage 2 carries lifetime loss once credit risk has risen significantly. Stage 3, when the borrower is credit-impaired (in default or severe distress), keeps lifetime loss and computes interest on the carrying amount net of the allowance.
ECL = probability of default × loss given default × exposure at default
For example (illustration), on the bond above:
Dr Impairment loss 22.50 / Cr Loss allowance 22.50
For an FVOCI bond the loss still goes to profit, with the credit to OCI, because the asset is already at fair value.

Below significant influence PSAK 109 starts from FVTPL. Any shares not held for trading (and not contingent consideration in a business combination) may be designated at initial recognition, share by share and irrevocably, to FVOCI. Strategic stakes, such as one held to secure supply, are the usual case.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 1,000,000 shares of a listed drilling contractor at USD 0.50 a share to secure rig access, paying broker fees of 5. At year end the price is USD 0.46, a dividend of 20 has been received, and next year the shares are sold at USD 0.55.
Dr Equity investment 500, Dr Transaction cost expense 5 / Cr Cash 505
Dr Unrealised holding loss, profit or loss 40 / Cr Fair value adjustment 40
Dr OCI 45 / Cr Fair value adjustment 45
Dr Cash 550, Dr Fair value adjustment 40 / Cr Equity investment 500, Cr Gain on sale 90
Dr Fair value adjustment 90 / Cr OCI 90; Dr Cash 550 / Cr Equity investment 505, Cr Fair value adjustment 45; cumulative OCI 45 may move to retained earnings

Kieso's example records broker fees as an expense, which is right only under FVTPL; under every other basis they are part of cost. A dividend is income in both columns, because the investor has never booked a share of the investee's profit; the one exception is a dividend that clearly repays part of the cost (IFRS 9 B5.7.1). The FVOCI gain never reaches profit, even on sale, because FVOCI equity, unlike FVOCI debt, is never recycled and has no impairment test. PHE's own policy states the same three rules (Note 3g).
5. Significant influence and the equity method
Once the investor can influence dividend policy, dividend income stops measuring what it earns, because the investor could time its income by voting for or against a payout. Beams'

gives this as the reason fair value is forbidden at this level. PSAK 228 also rules it out, except for the fund exemption in section 9, and instead extends the investor's statements to include its share of the investee's profit or loss (para. 11).
+ investor's share of the investee's profit after acquisition (to profit or loss), and of its OCI (to OCI)
Cost includes directly attributable costs such as professional fees.

Take PHE's 2024 numbers for its 29 percent associate PT Donggi Senoro LNG (DSLNG) as the starting point: opening carrying amount 299,171, share of profit 53,860, dividends 49,300 (Note 16b, Daftar 5/108, PDF p. 125). The comparison follows Beams' layout. The left column shows only the dividend, because under PSAK 109 the stake would also be remeasured to fair value.
Below significant influence (PSAK 109, dividend line only)
Dr Investment in associate 53,860 / Cr Share of profit of associates 53,860 (29% × 185,700 = 53,853; PHE books 53,860)
Dr Cash 49,300 / Cr Investment in associate 49,300
Booking the dividend as income under the equity method would count DSLNG's profit twice, when earned and when paid out.

. Profit and equity come out as if DSLNG had been consolidated, but on one line in each statement. The test is whether the carrying amount equals the investor's share of the investee's net assets plus any unamortised excess paid. With DSLNG's net assets of 1,334,590 − 417,540 = 917,050 at the end of 2024, PHE's share is 29% × 917,050 = 265,944.5, against a carrying amount of 265,952. The near-match suggests that little excess over book value remains inside PHE's investment.
6. Paying above book value and transactions with the investee

When the price differs from the investor's share of book value, the difference is explained asset by asset. Beams allocates it in order to the investee's identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, with the remainder as goodwill (PSAK 228.32). Goodwill stays inside the investment and is not amortised; amounts allocated to inventory or plant are unwound as the investee sells the inventory or depreciates the plant.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 29 percent of an LNG company for 300,000 on 1 January. Book net assets are 900,000; the plant's fair value exceeds its book value by 100,000 over a remaining life of 25 years; LNG inventory exceeds book by 5,000. Deferred tax on the uplifts is ignored to keep the steps short.
In year 1 the investee earns 180,000, sells the inventory, and pays dividends of 140,000.
Dr Investment in associate 49,590 / Cr Share of profit of associates 49,590
Dr Cash 40,600 / Cr Investment in associate 40,600
If the price had been 285,000, the excess over book value (24,000) would fall short of the fair value uplift (30,450). That 6,450 is a
, included as income in the share of profit in the year of acquisition (para. 32(b)). Beams also describes an older US treatment that used it to reduce non-current assets instead.

Profit on sales between investor and investee is eliminated to the extent of the investor's interest (para. 28). For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary sells gas to a 29 percent associate at a profit of 2,000, and the associate still holds the LNG at year end; the 580 below is recognised when that LNG is sold to an outside buyer.
Unrealised profit eliminated = 29% × 2,000 = 580: Dr Share of profit of associates 580 / Cr Investment in associate 580
7. Losses, impairment and the end of the equity method

The investor stops recognising its share of losses once its interest reaches zero (para. 38). The interest includes long-term interests that are in substance part of the net investment, such as a loan with no planned repayment, but not trade receivables or secured loans. Beyond that a liability arises only for legal or constructive obligations or payments made on the investee's behalf (para. 39). For example (illustration), a 25 percent exploration associate carried at 6,000 drills a dry well and loses 40,000.
Share of loss = 25% × 40,000 = 10,000; recognised = 6,000; unrecognised, tracked outside the accounts = 4,000
Dr Share of loss of associates 6,000 / Cr Investment in associate 6,000
If it earns 20,000 next year, the share of 5,000 first covers the 4,000 unrecognised loss, and only 1,000 is booked.
PSAK 228 is silent on the mirror case, a dividend above a carrying amount already at zero. With no obligation to repay, practice takes the excess to profit, as PHE did in 2023 (section 10).

Objective evidence of impairment includes financial difficulty, default, and adverse changes in the investee's market; for equity, a significant or prolonged fall in fair value below cost is itself evidence (paras. 41A–41C). The whole carrying amount is then tested under PSAK 236 (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) as a single asset against its recoverable amount, the higher of value in use and fair value less costs of disposal (para. 42). Because no part of the loss is allocated to the goodwill inside, the whole loss can later be reversed. For example (illustration), take Seplat's 2024 carrying amount of 214,773 (Note 16b) and suppose the market value of the stake fell to 180,000, costs of disposal were 2,000, and value in use were 195,000.
Impairment loss = 214,773 − 195,000 = 19,773: Dr Impairment loss 19,773 / Cr Investment in associate 19,773

When significant influence ends, the retained interest becomes a financial asset at fair value, and the difference between that fair value plus any proceeds and the carrying amount goes to profit (para. 22(b)). Amounts in OCI are recycled as if the investee had disposed of the related assets (para. 22(c)). For example (illustration), PHE sells 19 of its 29 percent of DSLNG for 190,000 and the remaining 10 percent is worth 100,000.
Dr Cash 190,000, Dr Equity investment (FVOCI or FVTPL) 100,000 / Cr Investment in associate 265,952, Cr Gain on loss of significant influence 24,048

Beams, following US GAAP of its time, carries the retained stake at its old book value with no gain, and restates retained earnings retroactively when a stake grows from 10 to 20 percent. PSAK 228 does neither, and PHE's policy remeasures any retained investment at fair value (Note 3l, Daftar 5/55, PDF p. 72).
8. Joint arrangements: joint ventures and joint operations
exists when two or more parties share control and relevant decisions need unanimous consent. PSAK 111 then asks what the parties hold. Parties to a
have rights only to the net assets and use the equity method. Parties to a

have rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities, and each recognises its own share of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses. PHE's policy uses this split and adds that the structure, the legal form of any separate vehicle and the contractual terms decide it (Note 3y, Daftar 5/73–74, PDF pp. 90–91).
For example (illustration), PHE holds a 10 percent participating interest in a block, and the operator spends 50,000 on a development well.
Joint venture (interest held through a company)
Dr Oil and gas properties 5,000 / Cr Cash call payable 5,000
No entry until the company reports profit; then Dr Investment / Cr Share of profit

A participating interest held directly under a joint operating agreement is the usual upstream case. Where a majority of partners decide, no joint control exists and the arrangement falls outside PSAK 111, but each partner still recognises its own share. PHE nonetheless carries its Malaysian block interests on this line at cost, which its policy note does not explain (section 10).
Industries with their own rules move the boundaries of section 1's scale, mostly toward fair value.

A bank's securities book is classified portfolio by portfolio by business model, so the same government bond can be at amortised cost in the treasury's hold-to-collect book and at FVTPL on the trading desk. A reclassification is allowed only when the business model itself changes, and then prospectively from the first day of the next reporting period, with no restatement; FVOCI equity is never reclassified (PSAK 109; ref. 6).

An associate or joint venture held by a venture capital organisation, mutual fund, unit trust or investment-linked insurance fund may be measured at FVTPL instead of the equity method, investee by investee at initial recognition (PSAK 228.18). For example (illustration), a fund holds 25 percent of a start-up bought for 1,000; the start-up earns 400 and the stake's fair value rises to 1,250.

An investment entity carries even its subsidiaries at FVTPL instead of consolidating them. A subsidiary that is not itself an investment entity and provides services for the parent's investment activities is still consolidated (PSAK 110.31–32; ref. 7).
Sharia investments follow the PSAK 4xx series. A sukuk holder classifies the investment under PSAK 410
(formerly PSAK 110), which since its 2015 revision mirrors PSAK 109: amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL by business model and contractual terms (ref. 7). A musyarakah partner under PSAK 406
(formerly PSAK 106) records its capital contribution as an investment in the partnership (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).
A parent's own statements may carry subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures at cost, under PSAK 109, or by the equity method (PSAK 227). This is the case Kieso's presentation describes.
Disclosure of Interests in Other Entities

presentation.deck: The theory of investments in other entities from debt securities to associates, worked through PHE's stakes in Donggi Senoro LNG and Seplat and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: An investment's accounting follows the investor's power over the investee. Debt securities and small equity stakes are financial assets under PSAK 109, sorted by business model and cash-flow terms into amortised cost, fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) or fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL). Significant influence or joint control of net assets brings the equity method, and control brings consolidation.

The equity method books the investor's share of the investee's profit as income when it is earned and treats a dividend as cash leaving the investment. Any price paid above the investor's share of book value is allocated to the investee's assets and goodwill, and the allocation is unwound through the share of profit.

Loss recognition stops when the investment reaches zero, impairment tests the whole investment as one asset, and losing significant influence remeasures what is left at fair value. A participating interest in an oil and gas block is normally a joint operation, recognised line by line in oil and gas properties instead of on this line.

title: Long-Term Investments: Splitting a 31 Percent Fall: How the equity method, impairment and FVOCI each move the line, and how a reader separates cash received from value lost
snippet: How the equity method, impairment and FVOCI each move the line, and how a reader separates cash received from value lost
content:
In brief

  • The line mixes holdings under different rules. Associates (significant influence) and joint ventures (joint control of net assets) use the equity method, small equity stakes sit at fair value, and some debt sits at amortised cost. Subsidiaries never appear on the consolidated line.

  • An equity-method investment falls with every dividend received, because the profit behind the dividend was booked when the investee earned it. A profitable associate that pays out generously shrinks the line.

  • A fall has five possible sources (shares of losses, dividends, impairment, disposal or reclassification, and fair-value or currency changes), and only some are losses. In the constructed 2025 case, USD 29.0 million of a USD 49.0 million fall is cash received or a move to current assets.

The line fell 30.8 percent, and the page alone cannot say how much of that was a loss

On the page, long-term investments fell from 1,602,821 at 31 December 2023 to 1,109,172 at 31 December 2024, in thousands, a fall of 493,649 or 30.8 percent. The line's share of total assets dropped from 5.1 percent to 3.7 percent, and the page gives no notes reference for it.

PT Hulu Energi Nusantara ("HEN") is an upstream contractor operating production sharing contracts (PSCs) with SKK Migas, the government body that supervises upstream oil and gas. HEN is fictional and every HEN figure is constructed. It reports in US dollars under Indonesian SAK, and all HEN amounts are in USD million. At the audit committee meeting on the 2025 accounts, a member reads that long-term investments fell from USD 160.0 million at 31 December 2024 to USD 111.0 million at 31 December 2025, a fall of 30.6 percent, and asks two questions. Did HEN lose USD 49.0 million on its stakes? And should the committee accept management's USD 17.0 million write-down of HEN's LNG joint venture?

The governing claim of this essay is that a fall in long-term investments says nothing about value until it is split by mechanism. Dividends from equity-method investees and reclassifications to current assets reduce the line without any loss, while shares of profit and loss, impairments and fair-value changes record changes in value, and each follows its own rule. This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that USD 29.0 million of HEN's fall is cash received or a change of line, and USD 20.0 million is a net value change (USD 32.0 million of losses against USD 12.0 million of share of profit). The figure the committee must challenge is the USD 17.0 million impairment, because it rests on management's own forecast.

PSAK numbers follow the 2024 scheme (old numbers: 228 was 15, 109 was 71, 236 was 48, 111 was 66, 110 was 65, 201 was 1, 221 was 10); IFRS equivalents are in the references.

The line holds whatever the investor influences without controlling, and subsidiaries never sit on it

Which rule measures a holding depends on the investor's power over the investee, and the ownership percentage only guides that judgment. HEN's line held five items:

Holding

Below 20 percent an equity investor is presumed to lack significant influence, and PSAK 109 measures the shares at fair value through profit or loss (FVTPL), unless the investor elects at initial recognition, irrevocably and for shares not held for trading, to send fair-value changes to other comprehensive income (FVOCI). From 20 to 50 percent the investor is presumed to have significant influence, the power to take part in the investee's financial and operating decisions without controlling them, and PSAK 228 requires the equity method. Both presumptions can be rebutted. A joint venture, where the parties share control by unanimous consent and have rights to the net assets, also uses the equity method. Control under PSAK 110, usually but not always gained through a majority of the votes, replaces the investment with the subsidiary's assets and liabilities line by line. The study notes show a subsidiary as a long-term investment, which holds only in the parent's separate statements.

Debt is sorted by two tests in PSAK 109, the business model (hold to collect, collect and sell, or neither) and whether the contractual cash flows are only principal and interest on the principal. HEN holds its 5 percent bond, bought at par, to maturity, so it sits at amortised cost. A bond held to collect and sell would sit at FVOCI and recycle on sale, meaning the gains parked in OCI are moved into profit when the bond is sold.

The notes impair amortised-cost debt only after a loss event; PSAK 109 replaced that incurred-loss approach with expected credit losses (ECL), booked from the day of purchase. Stage 1 carries twelve months of expected loss. Stage 2 carries lifetime loss once credit risk has risen significantly. Stage 3, once the borrower has actually defaulted or is in severe distress (credit-impaired), keeps lifetime loss but computes interest income on the carrying amount net of the allowance. HEN's bond is in stage 1, where the allowance multiplies the chance of default within a year, the share lost on default, and the amount at risk:

12-month ECL = probability of default × loss given default × exposure

= 0.3% × 40% × USD 14.0 million = USD 0.0168 million

The allowance rounds to zero at one decimal, so the bond is carried at USD 14.0 million. It also marks the line's current boundary. At 31 December 2025 it falls due within twelve months, so PSAK 201 moves USD 14.0 million to current assets with no change in value. An equity-method investment stays non-current unless it is held for sale under PSAK 105 (was 58).

Under the equity method a dividend is cash leaving the investment, because the profit behind it was booked when the investee earned it

The equity method treats the stake as a claim on the investee's net assets, booking income when they grow and cash, but no income, when they are paid out. HEN bought 30 percent of PT Pipa Gas Selat on 1 January 2023 for USD 56.0 million, exactly 30 percent of its fair net assets, so no goodwill sits inside the investment:

The pipeline's USD 40.0 million profit raised HEN's claim by USD 12.0 million, recognised as income. Its USD 50.0 million dividend cut the claim by USD 15.0 million and raised HEN's cash by the same amount. Booking the 15.0 as income too would report 27.0 of income on 12.0 of earnings and leave 74.0 on the line while 15.0 sat in the bank. The pipeline used cash released by refinancing its own debt to pay out 125 percent of its 2025 profit, so HEN's most profitable associate shrank the line by USD 3.0 million in its best year.

An equity-method investment is tested for impairment as one asset, so the whole write-down can later be reversed

PT Kilang LNG Timur's commissioning, the testing and start-up of the plant, slipped by a year in 2025, and its buyers reopened the offtake price, the contracted price for the LNG they take. The joint venture lost USD 8.0 million in the year, of which HEN's half is USD 4.0 million:

Dr Share of loss of joint ventures 4.0 / Cr Investment in joint venture 4.0

Evidence such as a significant adverse change in the investee's market (IAS 28 paragraphs 41A–41C) triggers a test of the whole carrying amount under PSAK 236. The carrying amount is compared with the recoverable amount, the higher of value in use (the present value of the cash flows the investment is expected to produce) and fair value less costs of disposal. Management's discounted model of HEN's share of the joint venture's cash flows gives a value in use of USD 27.0 million (constructed input). A buyer has offered USD 25.0 million, non-binding, and selling would cost USD 0.5 million.

Carrying amount before the test = 48.0 − 4.0 = 44.0

Fair value less costs of disposal = 25.0 − 0.5 = 24.5

Recoverable amount = higher of 27.0 and 24.5 = 27.0

Impairment loss = 44.0 − 27.0 = 17.0

Dr Impairment loss on investment in joint venture 17.0 / Cr Investment in joint venture 17.0

The loss is larger than HEN's whole 12.0 share of the pipeline's profit in its best year.

PSAK 236 never reverses a goodwill impairment, so it matters that an equity-method investment is tested as one asset and no part of its loss is allocated to goodwill inside it (IAS 28 paragraph 42). HEN paid no premium for Kilang either. If the estimates behind the recoverable amount improve, for example once the plant starts up, all USD 17.0 million can be reversed, up to the carrying amount the investment would have had without the impairment.

Every USD 1.0 million added to value in use removes USD 1.0 million of loss until value in use reaches USD 44.0 million; on the downside the fair-value floor of USD 24.5 million caps the loss at USD 19.5 million.

When the share of losses exceeds the investment, the investor stops at zero and tracks the rest off the books

PT Cakra Eksplorasi drilled a dry exploration well in 2025, wrote off its exploration and evaluation assets under PSAK 106 (was 64), and reported a net loss after tax of USD 40.0 million (constructed). HEN's 25 percent share is larger than its investment:

Share of loss = 25% × 40.0 = 10.0

Loss recognised, limited to the carrying amount = 6.0

Loss not recognised, tracked outside the accounts = 10.0 − 6.0 = 4.0

Dr Share of loss of associates 6.0 / Cr Investment in associate 6.0

PSAK 228 stops loss recognition when the investor's interest reaches zero (IAS 28 paragraphs 38–39). The interest includes long-term interests that form part of the net investment, such as a shareholder loan with no planned repayment. Beyond them a liability arises only from a legal obligation, a constructive obligation (one created by the investor's own conduct or promises), or payments made on the associate's behalf. HEN has none of these. If Cakra earns USD 20.0 million in 2026, HEN's share is USD 5.0 million, the first USD 4.0 million offsets the unrecognised loss, and HEN books USD 1.0 million.

A commitment to meet an associate's cash calls (the operator's requests for each partner's share of spending) may be the obligation that turns an unrecognised loss into a provision.

Below 20 percent at FVOCI, the dividend is income and the value change never reaches profit

HEN holds 200 million shares of PT Jasa Sumur Tbk, 4 percent of the company, to secure drilling services, and elected FVOCI when it bought them. The shares trade in rupiah. Under PSAK 221 their fair value is translated at the rate on the measurement date, and because an FVOCI share's whole fair-value change goes to OCI, the currency part goes there too.

31 Dec 2024: 200 million × IDR 2,400 = IDR 480 billion; at IDR 16,000 per USD = USD 30.0 million

31 Dec 2025: 200 million × IDR 2,080 = IDR 416 billion; at IDR 16,640 per USD = USD 25.0 million

Price effect, at the opening rate = 200 million × (IDR 2,080 − IDR 2,400) / 16,000 = −USD 4.0 million

Currency effect = IDR 416 billion / 16,640 − IDR 416 billion / 16,000 = 25.0 − 26.0 = −USD 1.0 million

Dr Other comprehensive income, fair value reserve 5.0 / Cr Investment in equity instruments 5.0

Both effects land in the same reserve; the reader's split shows that one fifth of the fall comes from the dollar strengthening 4 percent against the rupiah, from IDR 16,000 to IDR 16,640.

Jasa Sumur also paid a dividend of IDR 80 a share, IDR 16 billion in total, received when the rate was IDR 16,000:

Dr Cash 1.0 / Cr Dividend income 1.0

Here the dividend is income, because HEN never booked a share of Jasa Sumur's profit; the exception is a dividend that clearly recovers part of the cost. The fair-value loss never reaches profit. FVOCI equity has no impairment test under PSAK 109, and on sale the cumulative reserve may move to retained earnings within equity but is never recycled (IFRS 9 paragraphs 5.7.5 and B5.7.1). The USD 5.0 million fall reduces HEN's total comprehensive income and leaves its profit untouched in every year.

A participating interest in a PSC is usually a joint operation, so most of an upstream group's partnerships never reach this line

An upstream group's most common partnership, a participating interest in a PSC shared under a joint operating agreement, usually stays off this line. Under PSAK 111, parties to a joint operation have rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities and recognise their own shares of each, while parties to a joint venture have rights only to the net assets and use the equity method. A contractor party to the PSC takes its share of production and bears its share of costs, the profile of a joint operation. Many operating agreements let a majority of partners decide, so no joint control exists and the arrangement falls outside PSAK 111, but each partner still recognises its own share. Either way, a participating interest held directly by HEN would appear inside oil and gas properties, receivables, payables, revenue and costs.

The boundary moves with the legal vehicle. Indonesian practice ring-fences PSCs, keeping each contract's costs and taxes separate and often holding each contract in its own company, so a partner may own shares in that company instead of the participating interest. HEN's 25 percent of PT Cakra Eksplorasi is that case, an associate measured in one line although its economics resemble a 25 percent participating interest. A separate company points toward a joint venture without settling it, because the agreements decide: if they give the parties the output and make them fund the liabilities, PSAK 111 still finds a joint operation.

HEN's USD 49.0 million fall is USD 29.0 million of cash and reclassification and a USD 20.0 million net value change

Only one row of HEN's 2025 roll-forward rests on HEN management's own forecast. The rest come from the investees' audited results, a quoted price, an exchange rate or a maturity date.

Profit for 2025 carries 12.0 − 4.0 − 6.0 − 17.0 = −15.0 of the net value change and OCI −5.0. Pairing the pipeline's profit with value and its dividend with cash is a choice of presentation; netting the two instead would show only 3.0 of dividends in excess of earnings.

HEN did not lose USD 49.0 million. It recognised USD 32.0 million of losses against USD 12.0 million of share of profit, and USD 17.0 million of those losses rests on a forecast. The committee should not accept the impairment until management has tested the three inputs that drive value in use (the commissioning date, the renegotiated offtake price and the discount rate), and should require disclosure under PSAK 112 of the USD 4.0 million unrecognised loss in Cakra with any funding commitment behind it.

A reader of the reported page can triangulate from the share of results and impairment lines in the income statement, dividends received in the cash flow statement, and fair-value movements in OCI. No current line that could hold a reclassified investment grew materially (other current assets rose 1,997 thousand), and the page has no short-term investment or held-for-sale line, so it shows no sign of a large reclassification.

Least-confident assertions

  • The joint operation reading of a PSC participating interest is the usual pattern, not a verified rule. Whether joint control exists depends on the operating agreement's voting terms, and where a PSC is held through a ring-fenced company the classification under PSAK 111 turns on that company's agreements. No actual PSC or joint operating agreement was opened.

  • Paragraph references (IAS 28 paragraphs 38–39, 41A–41C and 42; IFRS 9 paragraphs 5.7.5 and B5.7.1) come from knowledge of the IFRS texts and were not opened. The PSAK equivalents are assumed to follow the same paragraph numbering, and the former numbers for PSAK 111, 110, 105 and 221 were not checked.

  • The page inference assumes a reclassified investment would appear in a current line that grew. A reclassification could be offset by an unrelated fall in the same line.
