PT Kilang LNG Timur's commissioning, the testing and start-up of the plant, slipped by a year in 2025, and its buyers reopened the offtake price, the contracted price for the LNG they take. The joint venture lost USD 8.0 million in the year, of which HEN's half is USD 4.0 million:
Dr Share of loss of joint ventures 4.0 / Cr Investment in joint venture 4.0

Evidence such as a significant adverse change in the investee's market (IAS 28 paragraphs 41A–41C) triggers a test of the whole carrying amount under PSAK 236. The carrying amount is compared with the recoverable amount, the higher of value in use (the present value of the cash flows the investment is expected to produce) and fair value less costs of disposal. Management's discounted model of HEN's share of the joint venture's cash flows gives a value in use of USD 27.0 million (constructed input). A buyer has offered USD 25.0 million, non-binding, and selling would cost USD 0.5 million.
Fair value less costs of disposal = 25.0 − 0.5 = 24.5
Dr Impairment loss on investment in joint venture 17.0 / Cr Investment in joint venture 17.0
The loss is larger than HEN's whole 12.0 share of the pipeline's profit in its best year.

PSAK 236 never reverses a goodwill impairment, so it matters that an equity-method investment is tested as one asset and no part of its loss is allocated to goodwill inside it (IAS 28 paragraph 42). HEN paid no premium for Kilang either. If the estimates behind the recoverable amount improve, for example once the plant starts up, all USD 17.0 million can be reversed, up to the carrying amount the investment would have had without the impairment.

Every USD 1.0 million added to value in use removes USD 1.0 million of loss until value in use reaches USD 44.0 million; on the downside the fair-value floor of USD 24.5 million caps the loss at USD 19.5 million.
When the share of losses exceeds the investment, the investor stops at zero and tracks the rest off the books

PT Cakra Eksplorasi drilled a dry exploration well in 2025, wrote off its exploration and evaluation assets under PSAK 106 (was 64), and reported a net loss after tax of USD 40.0 million (constructed). HEN's 25 percent share is larger than its investment:
Loss recognised, limited to the carrying amount = 6.0
Loss not recognised, tracked outside the accounts = 10.0 − 6.0 = 4.0
Dr Share of loss of associates 6.0 / Cr Investment in associate 6.0

PSAK 228 stops loss recognition when the investor's interest reaches zero (IAS 28 paragraphs 38–39). The interest includes long-term interests that form part of the net investment, such as a shareholder loan with no planned repayment. Beyond them a liability arises only from a legal obligation, a constructive obligation (one created by the investor's own conduct or promises), or payments made on the associate's behalf. HEN has none of these. If Cakra earns USD 20.0 million in 2026, HEN's share is USD 5.0 million, the first USD 4.0 million offsets the unrecognised loss, and HEN books USD 1.0 million.
A commitment to meet an associate's cash calls (the operator's requests for each partner's share of spending) may be the obligation that turns an unrecognised loss into a provision.
Below 20 percent at FVOCI, the dividend is income and the value change never reaches profit

HEN holds 200 million shares of PT Jasa Sumur Tbk, 4 percent of the company, to secure drilling services, and elected FVOCI when it bought them. The shares trade in rupiah. Under PSAK 221 their fair value is translated at the rate on the measurement date, and because an FVOCI share's whole fair-value change goes to OCI, the currency part goes there too.
31 Dec 2024: 200 million × IDR 2,400 = IDR 480 billion; at IDR 16,000 per USD = USD 30.0 million
31 Dec 2025: 200 million × IDR 2,080 = IDR 416 billion; at IDR 16,640 per USD = USD 25.0 million
Price effect, at the opening rate = 200 million × (IDR 2,080 − IDR 2,400) / 16,000 = −USD 4.0 million
Currency effect = IDR 416 billion / 16,640 − IDR 416 billion / 16,000 = 25.0 − 26.0 = −USD 1.0 million
Dr Other comprehensive income, fair value reserve 5.0 / Cr Investment in equity instruments 5.0
Both effects land in the same reserve; the reader's split shows that one fifth of the fall comes from the dollar strengthening 4 percent against the rupiah, from IDR 16,000 to IDR 16,640.
Jasa Sumur also paid a dividend of IDR 80 a share, IDR 16 billion in total, received when the rate was IDR 16,000:

Here the dividend is income, because HEN never booked a share of Jasa Sumur's profit; the exception is a dividend that clearly recovers part of the cost. The fair-value loss never reaches profit. FVOCI equity has no impairment test under PSAK 109, and on sale the cumulative reserve may move to retained earnings within equity but is never recycled (IFRS 9 paragraphs 5.7.5 and B5.7.1). The USD 5.0 million fall reduces HEN's total comprehensive income and leaves its profit untouched in every year.
A participating interest in a PSC is usually a joint operation, so most of an upstream group's partnerships never reach this line

An upstream group's most common partnership, a participating interest in a PSC shared under a joint operating agreement, usually stays off this line. Under PSAK 111, parties to a joint operation have rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities and recognise their own shares of each, while parties to a joint venture have rights only to the net assets and use the equity method. A contractor party to the PSC takes its share of production and bears its share of costs, the profile of a joint operation. Many operating agreements let a majority of partners decide, so no joint control exists and the arrangement falls outside PSAK 111, but each partner still recognises its own share. Either way, a participating interest held directly by HEN would appear inside oil and gas properties, receivables, payables, revenue and costs.

The boundary moves with the legal vehicle. Indonesian practice ring-fences PSCs, keeping each contract's costs and taxes separate and often holding each contract in its own company, so a partner may own shares in that company instead of the participating interest. HEN's 25 percent of PT Cakra Eksplorasi is that case, an associate measured in one line although its economics resemble a 25 percent participating interest. A separate company points toward a joint venture without settling it, because the agreements decide: if they give the parties the output and make them fund the liabilities, PSAK 111 still finds a joint operation.
HEN's USD 49.0 million fall is USD 29.0 million of cash and reclassification and a USD 20.0 million net value change
Only one row of HEN's 2025 roll-forward rests on HEN management's own forecast. The rest come from the investees' audited results, a quoted price, an exchange rate or a maturity date.
Share of loss, limited to carrying amount
Cash received and change of line = 15.0 + 14.0 = 29.0
Net value change recognised in profit and OCI = 32.0 − 12.0 = 20.0

Profit for 2025 carries 12.0 − 4.0 − 6.0 − 17.0 = −15.0 of the net value change and OCI −5.0. Pairing the pipeline's profit with value and its dividend with cash is a choice of presentation; netting the two instead would show only 3.0 of dividends in excess of earnings.

HEN did not lose USD 49.0 million. It recognised USD 32.0 million of losses against USD 12.0 million of share of profit, and USD 17.0 million of those losses rests on a forecast. The committee should not accept the impairment until management has tested the three inputs that drive value in use (the commissioning date, the renegotiated offtake price and the discount rate), and should require disclosure under PSAK 112 of the USD 4.0 million unrecognised loss in Cakra with any funding commitment behind it.

A reader of the reported page can triangulate from the share of results and impairment lines in the income statement, dividends received in the cash flow statement, and fair-value movements in OCI. No current line that could hold a reclassified investment grew materially (other current assets rose 1,997 thousand), and the page has no short-term investment or held-for-sale line, so it shows no sign of a large reclassification.

The joint operation reading of a PSC participating interest is the usual pattern, not a verified rule. Whether joint control exists depends on the operating agreement's voting terms, and where a PSC is held through a ring-fenced company the classification under PSAK 111 turns on that company's agreements. No actual PSC or joint operating agreement was opened.

Paragraph references (IAS 28 paragraphs 38–39, 41A–41C and 42; IFRS 9 paragraphs 5.7.5 and B5.7.1) come from knowledge of the IFRS texts and were not opened. The PSAK equivalents are assumed to follow the same paragraph numbering, and the former numbers for PSAK 111, 110, 105 and 221 were not checked.
The page inference assumes a reclassified investment would appear in a current line that grew. A reclassification could be offset by an unrelated fall in the same line.
). NOTES. Incurred-loss impairment corrected to ECL.

presentation.deck: How the equity method, impairment and FVOCI each move the line, and how a reader separates cash received from value lost
key_takeaways: The line mixes holdings under different rules. Associates (significant influence) and joint ventures (joint control of net assets) use the equity method, small equity stakes sit at fair value, and some debt sits at amortised cost. Subsidiaries never appear on the consolidated line.

An equity-method investment falls with every dividend received, because the profit behind the dividend was booked when the investee earned it. A profitable associate that pays out generously shrinks the line.

A fall has five possible sources (shares of losses, dividends, impairment, disposal or reclassification, and fair-value or currency changes), and only some are losses. In the constructed 2025 case, USD 29.0 million of a USD 49.0 million fall is cash received or a move to current assets.

title: Mutual Holdings and Complex Group Structures
snippet: How a group attributes profit when its companies own each other, from connecting affiliates to subsidiaries holding parent shares, worked through Barito Pacific's layered geothermal and petrochemical chains
content:
In brief

  • In a complex structure, control decides which companies are consolidated, and the effective interest decides how their profit and net assets are split. The effective interest is found by multiplying percentages down each ownership path and adding the paths together. A company can be a subsidiary while the parent's effective interest in it is below 50 percent.

  • When companies own each other, each one's profit depends on the other's, so the split needs simultaneous equations. The equations add mutual profit twice. Only the shares held by outsiders, multiplied by each equation's result, add back to the group's total profit.

  • When a subsidiary holds shares of its parent, Beams offers two treatments, the treasury stock approach and the conventional approach. PSAK 232 treats parent shares held by any group member as treasury shares, deducted from equity at cost, so the treasury stock approach is the one that fits Indonesian standards. Holdings between subsidiaries are eliminated, and there is no treasury alternative for them.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report non-controlling interests (NCI) of 3,802,216 at 31 December 2025, against total equity of 6,045,632, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, statement of financial position, PDF p. 16). Outside shareholders own 62.9 percent of the group's equity and took 1,125,827 of the year's profit of 1,615,634, or 69.7 percent (PDF p. 17), because BRPT reaches its geothermal plants through six or seven layers of companies, some partly owned, some owning the same company from two directions. It controls Chandra Asri with an effective interest of 38.55 percent.

After reading this page a student should be able to compute effective interests in any chain, allocate profit through connecting affiliates with unrealised profits, solve the equations for mutual holdings, choose between the treasury stock and conventional approaches, and read a group's ownership table.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note and PDF page. Every other number is an illustration, or comes from the lecture notes' examples, labelled as such.

1. Direct and indirect holdings: recap and effective interest

An indirect holding works by the same consolidation procedure as a direct one, once each company's profit is restated on an equity basis from the bottom up. The father–son–grandson chain of AKL Chapter 9, section A, is covered in the Non-Controlling Interest essay (FSLI 25, section 7). Pop owns 80 percent of Son and Son owns 70 percent of Toy. Toy's profit is allocated to Son first, then Son's enlarged profit to Pop.

Pop's profit on an equity basis = 100,000 + 80% × 50,000 + 80% × 70% × 40,000 = 162,400

The effective interest is the share of a company's profit and net assets that finally reaches a given owner. It follows two rules.

Along one path: multiply the percentages

Across several paths into the same company: add the products

BRPT owns 64.67 percent of PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk (BREN), which owns all of Star Energy Group Holdings Pte. Ltd. (SEGHPL). SEGHPL reaches Star Energy Geothermal Salak, Ltd. (SEG-SL) through a chain in which BREN reports its own effective interest as 80.91 percent (BREN FS 2025, Note 1, PDF p. 18; BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–27).

BRPT's effective interest in SEG-SL = 64.67% × 80.91% = 52.32%

The other 47.68 percent belongs to two groups of outsiders: those inside BREN's group (100% − 80.91% = 19.09%) and BREN's own outside shareholders (35.33% × 80.91% = 28.59%). The three shares add to 100 percent.

Control is a separate test, and it travels down the chain whole. PSAK 110 Laporan Keuangan Konsolidasian (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) asks whether the investor has power, exposure to variable returns and the link between them. BRPT controls BREN, BREN controls SEGHPL, and so on down. Each subsidiary of a subsidiary is a subsidiary of BRPT, at whatever effective interest the multiplication gives. Consolidation brings in 100 percent of SEG-SL's assets, and the effective interest only decides how its profit is split between BRPT's owners and the NCI.

2. Connecting affiliates

In a connecting-affiliate structure the allocation has to start from the bottom company, because profit reaches the parent by two routes at once. The term means that the parent and one of its subsidiaries both hold shares in the same company. The notes' example (section B) has Pet owning 70 percent of Sal and 60 percent of Tai, and Sal owning 20 percent of Tai. The problem is order. Tai's profit must reach Sal before Sal's profit can reach Pet, so the schedule starts with the company nobody else in the group sits below.

BRPT's own structure contains one. Star Energy Geothermal Holdings (Salak-Darajat) B.V. (Holdings BV) is owned 51 percent by Star Energy Geothermal Pte. Ltd. (SEGPL) and 49 percent by Star Energy Geothermal Netherlands B.V. (SEG-NBV). SEGHPL owns 90 percent of SEGPL and 100 percent of SEG-NBV (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 26–27).

SEGHPL's effective interest in Holdings BV = 90% × 51% + 100% × 49% = 45.9% + 49.0% = 94.9%

BREN's table shows 94.90 percent for Holdings BV (PDF p. 18), so the rule reproduces the company's own figure.

The allocation schedule with unrealised profits. Intercompany profits are removed before anything is allocated, and they are charged to the company that recorded them. Profit sitting in a buyer's inventory or land has not yet been earned from outsiders (K3, K4). For example (illustration), use the SEGHPL structure with these separate profits for one year, each before any income from the companies below it:

The downstream gain falls wholly on the parent, because the parent recorded it. The upstream profit was recorded by SEGPL, so its 10 percent outside owners bear 10% × 2,000 = 200 of it through the lower NCI. The NCI in Holdings BV is zero, yet its outside owners still exist. They sit one level up, as SEGPL's 10 percent, and take 10% × 51% × 40,000 = 2,040 of Holdings BV's profit.

Effective-interest check: SEGHPL takes 94.9% × 40,000 = 37,960 of Holdings BV's profit; 37,960 + 2,040 = 40,000

The worksheet removes both unrealised profits first:

Dr Gain on sale of land 3,000 / Cr Land 3,000

Dr Cost of sales 2,000 / Cr Inventories 2,000

On the parent's books. Under the equity method the parent's profit equals the controlling share, 85,160. In the notes, Pet's income from Sal is 70% × 39,000 − 70% × 5,000 upstream − 10,000 downstream = 13,800.

3. Parent shares held by a subsidiary

Parent shares held by a subsidiary are, for the group, shares it has bought back from itself. A mutual holding exists when two affiliated companies each hold shares in the other. The first case in the notes (section C) is a subsidiary owning shares of its parent. From the group's view those shares are not outstanding. The group has bought back part of itself, and the question is how to show that and how to split profit.

In the notes' example Pam buys 90 percent of Son on 1 January 2016 for 540,000, when Son's equity is 600,000 (capital 400,000, retained earnings 200,000), so there is no goodwill. Son buys 10 percent of Pam on 5 January 2016 for 140,000, when Pam's equity is 1,400,000 (capital 1,000,000 in shares of 10 par, retained earnings 400,000). Separate profits for 2016 are 100,000 for Pam and 60,000 for Son, with no dividends.

The treasury stock approach treats Pam's shares held by Son as if Pam had bought them back. Son's investment in Pam is reclassified to treasury shares at cost and deducted from consolidated equity, and the mutual holding is otherwise ignored in profit. Son has no income from Pam in 2016.

Pam's income from Son = 90% × 60,000 = 54,000; Pam's profit = 100,000 + 54,000 = 154,000

NCI share = 10% × 60,000 = 6,000; NCI at year end = 10% × (600,000 + 60,000) = 66,000

Consolidated equity = 1,000,000 + 554,000 − 140,000 + 66,000 = 1,480,000 = other assets of 960,000 + 520,000

The conventional approach treats Pam's shares held by Son as constructively retired, and lets Son's outside owners share in Pam's profit through Son's 10 percent stake. Then neither company's profit on an equity basis can be found first, because each includes a share of the other. The notes solve it with two equations.

P = Pam's profit on a consolidated basis, including mutual profit; S = the same for Son

P = 100,000 + 0.9S

S = 60,000 + 0.1P

Substituting:

P = 100,000 + 0.9 × (60,000 + 0.1P) = 154,000 + 0.09P

0.91P = 154,000; P = 169,230.77

S = 60,000 + 0.1 × 169,230.77 = 76,923.08

P + S = 246,153.85, far above the combined separate profit of 160,000, because each figure includes the other's share. Each result is then multiplied by the share held outside the pair:

Profit attributable to Pam's own shareholders = 90% × 169,230.77 = 152,307.69

NCI = 10% × 76,923.08 = 7,692.31

Check: 152,307.69 + 7,692.31 = 160,000

Pam's equity-method income from Son is 90 percent of S less 10 percent of P, the part of Pam's own profit that belongs to Son: 69,230.77 − 16,923.08 = 52,307.69. On Pam's own books the conventional approach also debits capital stock 100,000 and retained earnings 40,000 and credits the investment in Son 140,000, so Pam's equity method shows 900,000 of capital and the investment falls to 400,000 before income.

The second year. In 2017 Pam earns 120,000 separately and pays dividends of 60,000, 6,000 of them to Son. Son earns 80,000 and pays 40,000.

Both columns hold the same consolidated net assets of 1,480,000 at the end of 2016. Only the split between the parent's owners and the NCI differs. The conventional approach gives NCI more, because Son's outside owners are treated as owning 10% × 10% = 1 percent of Pam.

Converting retained earnings. The notes reuse the same equations to put two years of undistributed earnings onto an equity basis. The separate increases in net assets from 2016 to 2017 are 196,000 for Pam (100,000 + 120,000 − 60,000 + 36,000 received) and 106,000 for Son (60,000 + 80,000 − 40,000 + 6,000 received).

P = 196,000 + 0.9S; S = 106,000 + 0.1P, so P = 320,219.78 and S = 138,021.98

To Pam's retained earnings: 90% × 320,219.78 = 288,197.80; to NCI: 10% × 138,021.98 = 13,802.20

288,197.80 + 13,802.20 = 302,000

Which approach PSAK permits. PSAK 232 Instrumen Keuangan: Penyajian (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) para. 33 deducts the cost of an entity's own equity instruments that it reacquires from equity, records no gain or loss on their purchase, sale, issue or cancellation, and states that such shares may be acquired and held by the entity "or by other members of the consolidated group". PSAK 110 para. B86 eliminates intragroup equity in full. Together they make the parent's shares held by a subsidiary treasury shares of the group, shown at cost as a deduction. That is the treasury stock approach's presentation, and it rules out the conventional approach's balance sheet, with capital cut to 900,000 and retained earnings to 360,000 as if the shares were cancelled. Para. 33 does not say whether Son's NCI shares in Pam's profit through those shares, so the conventional profit split is a question PSAK leaves open. Earnings per share follow the presentation. Under PSAK 233 (formerly PSAK 56, IAS 33) the 10,000 shares held by Son are not outstanding, so 2016 earnings per share are 154,000 / 90,000 = 1.711, ignoring the four days before Son's purchase, against 152,307.69 / 90,000 = 1.692 under the conventional split.

A second attribution point is open as well. Beams gives NCI 10 percent of Son's whole 2017 profit of 86,000, including the 6,000 dividend received from Pam. On a strict group view that dividend is not income, so NCI's share of profit would be 10% × 80,000 = 8,000, and the 600 by which the dividend enlarges NCI's claim would be a transfer within equity from the parent's owners. NCI ends at 70,600 either way. PSAK gives no explicit guidance on this split.

In Indonesia the case is rare. UU 40/2007 on limited companies art. 36(1) forbids a company to issue shares to be owned by itself or by another company whose shares it owns directly or indirectly. Shares obtained by operation of law, gift or bequest are exempt (art. 36(2)) but must be transferred within one year (art. 36(3)). BRPT's FS show no subsidiary holding BRPT shares. PT Barito Pacific Lumber, which holds 0.58 percent, belongs to Prajogo Pangestu, not to the group (Note 28, PDF p. 211; Note 45, PDF p. 235). BRPT's treasury shares of 1,600 consist of shares the Company bought back itself (Note 30, PDF pp. 212–213).

4. Subsidiaries that hold each other

When two subsidiaries own each other, the treasury stock approach has nothing to work on, because neither holding is in the parent. The notes' case (section D): Pam owns 80 percent of Set, Set owns 70 percent of Ton, and Ton owns 10 percent of Set. Set's outside owners hold the remaining 10 percent and Ton's hold 30 percent. Separate profits for 2018, excluding income from affiliates, are 112,000 for Pam, 51,000 for Set and 40,000 for Ton. Three companies give three equations.

P = 112,000 + 0.8S

S = 51,000 + 0.7T

T = 40,000 + 0.1S

Solving the pair that loops first:

S = 51,000 + 0.7 × (40,000 + 0.1S) = 79,000 + 0.07S

0.93S = 79,000; S = 84,946.24

T = 40,000 + 0.1 × 84,946.24 = 48,494.62

P = 112,000 + 0.8 × 84,946.24 = 179,956.99

Pam's shares are held only by its own shareholders, so P is the controlling share. NCI is each subsidiary's outside percentage times its equation result:

NCI in Set = 10% × 84,946.24 = 8,494.62

NCI in Ton = 30% × 48,494.62 = 14,548.39

Check: 179,956.99 + 8,494.62 + 14,548.39 = 203,000 = 112,000 + 51,000 + 40,000

Pam's equity-method income from Set is 80% × 84,946.24 = 67,956.99, and Set's from Ton is 70% × 48,494.62 = 33,946.24. Ton carries its 10 percent of Set at cost and records only its 3,000 dividend, which the worksheet eliminates.

The same answer as effective interests. The equations can be turned around to say what share of each company's own profit reaches each owner. Write the holdings as a matrix W, invert (I − W) with Python, and multiply each column of the inverse by that company's outside share:

B86), so Set's NCI is the outside 10 percent only. The equations remain the arithmetic for attributing profit.

The notes' goodwill is grossed up from the parent's price. The notes give goodwill of 25,000 on Pam's 260,000 for 80 percent of Set's 300,000 equity, and 10,000 on Set's 112,000 for 70 percent of Ton's 150,000. Both gross up the price: 260,000 / 80% − 300,000 = 25,000. PSAK 103 Kombinasi Bisnis (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) para. 19 measures NCI at its own fair value, which also gives full goodwill but not by grossing up a price that includes a control premium, or at its share of net assets. Under the second option goodwill would be 260,000 − 80% × 300,000 = 20,000 and 112,000 − 70% × 150,000 = 7,000.

5. Effective interests in a real multi-layer group

In a real group the same rules apply, but disclosure tables mix direct and effective percentages. BRPT's Note 1d shows, for each subsidiary, the holding by the company directly above it. BREN's Note 1 shows BREN's effective interest. Combining the two (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–28; BREN FS 2025, Note 1, PDF p. 18):

Three things follow. First, BRPT consolidates CAP, ACE and Krakatau Chandra Energi with effective interests of 38.55, 30.84 and 16.19 percent. BRPT explains its control of CAP by the composition of CAP's board, which gives it power over CAP's relevant activities (Note 4, PDF p. 112). Each step below CAP is a majority holding, so control passes down.

Second, BREN's 80.91 percent for SEGSDBV is more than the main path gives. Holdings BV owns 80.20 percent of SEGSDBV (BREN FS 2025, Note 1, PDF p. 26), and 94.90% × 80.20% = 76.11%. The difference matches SEGHPL's 24.24 percent purchase of ACEHI Netherlands B.V., which BRPT says raised SEGHPL's indirect ownership of SEGSDBV to 80.91 percent (BRPT FS 2025, Note 31, PDF p. 218): 24.24% × 19.80% = 4.80%, and 76.11% + 4.80% = 80.91%.

Third, the 5 percent "direct ownership" of SEGSS, Darajat Geothermal Indonesia (DGI), Star Energy Geothermal Indonesia (SEGI) and Halmahera (SEGH) is held outside BREN's group. BREN's own notes name Barito Pacific as the 5 percent holder of SEGI and SEGH (BREN FS 2025, Note 1, PDF pp. 25–26). BREN's effective figures (76.86 percent and 85.50 percent) equal 95 percent of the path above, so in BREN's own statements that 5 percent is NCI, and in BRPT's statements it is the parent's own. The same shares are NCI at one level of reporting and controlling interest at the next. A structure like this keeps two shareholders in each Indonesian limited company, which UU 40/2007 art. 7(1) and 7(5)–(6) require.

A treasury share at the subsidiary moves the effective interest. BREN bought back 6,000,000 of its own shares in 2025 (Note 31, PDF p. 217). BRPT holds 86,514,146,666 of BREN's 133,786,220,000 issued shares (BREN FS 2025, Note 19a, PDF p. 114).

On issued shares: 86,514,146,666 / 133,786,220,000 = 64.6660%

On outstanding shares: 86,514,146,666 / (133,786,220,000 − 6,000,000) = 64.6689%

Profit is attributed on outstanding shares, because treasury shares carry no claim, and here the two bases differ by 0.003 percentage points. BRPT records the buybacks by BREN and CAP as transactions with NCI: of the 5,163 paid (1,930 by BREN and 3,233 by CAP), 2,495 reduces other equity components and 2,668 reduces NCI (statement of changes in equity, PDF p. 18).

6. Complex structures across industries

Banks and structured entities. A bank may consolidate a securitisation vehicle or a fund in which it owns no shares at all, because PSAK 110 tests control through power and variable returns, not equity. Its effective equity interest may be zero, and the vehicle's equity is then NCI or, if redeemable, a liability (FSLI 25 section 9).

Investment entities. A parent that qualifies as an investment entity does not consolidate its subsidiaries; it measures them at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 110 para. 31), except subsidiaries that provide investment-related services (para. 32). A venture fund's layered portfolio companies therefore never enter a chain calculation. A non-investment parent above it still consolidates everything, including what the fund holds (para. 33).

Conglomerate pyramids and the two-shareholder rule. Indonesian groups stack listed companies, as BRPT does with BREN, CAP and Chandra Daya Investasi, and many subsidiaries carry a small stake held by a sister company to keep two shareholders. Each listed layer adds outsiders, and each small stake is NCI in a sub-group's statements but not in the group's.

BRPT discloses NCI by sub-group, its movement, and summarised financial information for the two subsidiaries with material NCI (Note 34, PDF pp. 220–221), as PSAK 112 (formerly PSAK 67, IFRS 12) para. 12 asks.

The BREN line is two layers of outsiders. BREN's own NCI is 246,651, mostly ACEHI (176,028) and DGA SEG B.V. (50,971) inside the Star Energy chain (BREN FS 2025, Note 20, PDF p. 116). Above that sit BREN's own outside shareholders. BREN's equity attributable to its owners, 636,868 (PDF p. 12), is already net of its treasury shares, so their share is measured on outstanding shares, 1 − 64.66886% = 35.33114% (section 5).

35.33114% × 636,868 = 225,013

225,013 + 246,651 = 471,664, against BRPT's 471,951; difference 287

The difference of 287 is 0.06 percent of the line, and likely reflects consolidation adjustments made at BRPT's level that BREN's statements do not carry. BRPT does not reconcile the two. The same layering explains profit: of BREN's profit of 165,137, BRPT's owners take 64.6689% × 132,198 = 85,491, and NCI at BRPT's level is 32,939 + 46,707 = 79,646.

Attributable profit follows effective interests, not the top holding. BRPT's owners took 30.3 percent of 2025 profit (489,807 of 1,615,634). CAP produced most of the group's profit (1,447,986 before intragroup elimination, Note 34), and BRPT's effective interest in CAP is 38.55 percent (34.63 direct plus 3.92 through Marigold). A rough bridge, 38.55% × 1,447,986 + 85,491 = 643,690, leaves 153,883 above the owners' actual 489,807. Part of the gap comes from outsiders below CAP, such as the 20 percent of CAPGC above Aster and the 40 percent of CDI; the rest is parent-level costs and consolidation adjustments that the FS do not split. Anyone valuing BRPT from consolidated profit would overstate what its shareholders earn by a factor of 1,615,634 / 489,807 = 3.3.

8. Related essays

  • FSLI 25 non-controlling-interest: the control test, NCI measurement, attribution, ownership changes, and the father–son–grandson chain this page builds on.

  • FSLI 22 share-capital (also covers other-equity-component): treasury shares under PSAK 232 and where differences from transactions with NCI sit.

  • FSLI 04 long-term-investments: the equity method used bottom up in each chain.

  • K1 Business Combinations: goodwill and the NCI measurement choice.

  • K2 Consolidation Worksheet: the elimination sequence.

  • K3 and K4: the unrealised profits inside the allocation schedule.

  • K5: cash flows from transactions with NCI.

Least-confident assertions

  • Reading BRPT's Note 1d is partly inference. The table gives direct holdings for Holdings BV (51 and 49 percent) but apparently effective ones elsewhere (90 percent for SEG-WW, which BREN reports as its effective interest). The ACEHI row shows "indirect ownership through ACEHI 19.80" while BREN shows ACEHI as an NCI holder. Linking the 4.80 percent to SEGHPL's 24.24 percent of ACEHI rests on the arithmetic matching BRPT's 80.91 percent statement. BRPT's table also gives 80.19 percent for Holdings BV's stake in SEGSDBV and no 2024 figure for the ACEHI row, although the ACEHI shares were registered in December 2023; the page uses BREN's 80.20 percent, the only figure that reproduces 80.91.

  • That BRPT holds the 5 percent "direct ownership" of SEGSS and DGI is read from BRPT's table wording and from BREN's matching effective percentages. BREN names Barito Pacific as the holder only for SEGI and SEGH.

  • How to attribute a parent's dividend paid to a subsidiary with NCI (Beams' 8,600 in profit, against 8,000 in profit plus a 600 equity transfer) is not settled by PSAK. PSAK 232 para. 33 settles presentation (treasury shares) but not whether Son's NCI shares in the parent's profit, so the conventional profit split, and this dividend point, remain policy choices.

  • UU 40/2007 art. 36 bans issuing shares to a cross-holder. Whether a subsidiary may buy existing parent shares on the market is not settled by its text, and secondary sources read it differently.

  • The 287 difference between BRPT's NCI in BREN and BREN's two layers has no disclosed explanation, and the split of the 153,883 bridge in section 7 between outsiders below CAP and parent-level items is not disclosed.

content.text: In a complex structure, control decides which companies are consolidated, and the

decides how their profit and net assets are split. The effective interest is found by multiplying percentages down each ownership path and adding the paths together. A company can be a subsidiary while the parent's effective interest in it is below 50 percent.

When companies own each other, each one's profit depends on the other's, so the split needs simultaneous equations. The equations add mutual profit twice. Only the shares held by outsiders, multiplied by each equation's result, add back to the group's total profit.

When a subsidiary holds shares of its parent, Beams offers two treatments, the treasury stock approach and the conventional approach. PSAK 232 treats parent shares held by any group member as treasury shares, deducted from equity at cost, so the treasury stock approach is the one that fits Indonesian standards. Holdings between subsidiaries are eliminated, and there is no treasury alternative for them.

PT Barito Pacific Tbk and subsidiaries (BRPT) report non-controlling interests (NCI) of 3,802,216 at 31 December 2025, against total equity of 6,045,632, in USD thousand (BRPT FS 2025, statement of financial position, PDF p. 16). Outside shareholders own 62.9 percent of the group's equity and took 1,125,827 of the year's profit of 1,615,634, or 69.7 percent (PDF p. 17), because BRPT reaches its geothermal plants through six or seven layers of companies, some partly owned, some owning the same company from two directions. It controls Chandra Asri with an effective interest of 38.55 percent.

After reading this page a student should be able to compute effective interests in any chain, allocate profit through connecting affiliates with unrealised profits, solve the equations for mutual holdings, choose between the treasury stock and conventional approaches, and read a group's ownership table.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from BRPT's statements are cited to their note and PDF page. Every other number is an illustration, or comes from the lecture notes' examples, labelled as such.
1. Direct and indirect holdings: recap and effective interest

An indirect holding works by the same consolidation procedure as a direct one, once each company's profit is restated on an equity basis from the bottom up. The father–son–grandson chain of AKL Chapter 9, section A, is covered in the Non-Controlling Interest essay (FSLI 25, section 7). Pop owns 80 percent of Son and Son owns 70 percent of Toy. Toy's profit is allocated to Son first, then Son's enlarged profit to Pop.
is the share of a company's profit and net assets that finally reaches a given owner. It follows two rules.
Along one path: multiply the percentages
Across several paths into the same company: add the products

BRPT owns 64.67 percent of PT Barito Renewables Energy Tbk (BREN), which owns all of Star Energy Group Holdings Pte. Ltd. (SEGHPL). SEGHPL reaches Star Energy Geothermal Salak, Ltd. (SEG-SL) through a chain in which BREN reports its own effective interest as 80.91 percent (BREN FS 2025, Note 1, PDF p. 18; BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–27).

The other 47.68 percent belongs to two groups of outsiders: those inside BREN's group (100% − 80.91% = 19.09%) and BREN's own outside shareholders (35.33% × 80.91% = 28.59%). The three shares add to 100 percent.
Control is a separate test, and it travels down the chain whole. PSAK 110

(formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) asks whether the investor has power, exposure to variable returns and the link between them. BRPT controls BREN, BREN controls SEGHPL, and so on down. Each subsidiary of a subsidiary is a subsidiary of BRPT, at whatever effective interest the multiplication gives. Consolidation brings in 100 percent of SEG-SL's assets, and the effective interest only decides how its profit is split between BRPT's owners and the NCI.

In a connecting-affiliate structure the allocation has to start from the bottom company, because profit reaches the parent by two routes at once. The term means that the parent and one of its subsidiaries both hold shares in the same company. The notes' example (section B) has Pet owning 70 percent of Sal and 60 percent of Tai, and Sal owning 20 percent of Tai. The problem is order. Tai's profit must reach Sal before Sal's profit can reach Pet, so the schedule starts with the company nobody else in the group sits below.

BRPT's own structure contains one. Star Energy Geothermal Holdings (Salak-Darajat) B.V. (Holdings BV) is owned 51 percent by Star Energy Geothermal Pte. Ltd. (SEGPL) and 49 percent by Star Energy Geothermal Netherlands B.V. (SEG-NBV). SEGHPL owns 90 percent of SEGPL and 100 percent of SEG-NBV (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 26–27).
SEGHPL's effective interest in Holdings BV = 90% × 51% + 100% × 49% = 45.9% + 49.0% = 94.9%
BREN's table shows 94.90 percent for Holdings BV (PDF p. 18), so the rule reproduces the company's own figure.
The allocation schedule with unrealised profits.

Intercompany profits are removed before anything is allocated, and they are charged to the company that recorded them. Profit sitting in a buyer's inventory or land has not yet been earned from outsiders (K3, K4). For example (illustration), use the SEGHPL structure with these separate profits for one year, each before any income from the companies below it:
SEGHPL (parent) 20,000, which includes a 3,000 gain on land sold to Holdings BV and still held there (downstream)
SEGPL 30,000, which includes 2,000 of profit on drilling materials sold to SEGHPL and still in its inventory (upstream)
Allocate Holdings BV: 51% to SEGPL, 49% to SEG-NBV

The downstream gain falls wholly on the parent, because the parent recorded it. The upstream profit was recorded by SEGPL, so its 10 percent outside owners bear 10% × 2,000 = 200 of it through the lower NCI. The NCI in Holdings BV is zero, yet its outside owners still exist. They sit one level up, as SEGPL's 10 percent, and take 10% × 51% × 40,000 = 2,040 of Holdings BV's profit.
Effective-interest check: SEGHPL takes 94.9% × 40,000 = 37,960 of Holdings BV's profit; 37,960 + 2,040 = 40,000
The worksheet removes both unrealised profits first:
Dr Gain on sale of land 3,000 / Cr Land 3,000
Dr Cost of sales 2,000 / Cr Inventories 2,000
Under the equity method the parent's profit equals the controlling share, 85,160. In the notes, Pet's income from Sal is 70% × 39,000 − 70% × 5,000 upstream − 10,000 downstream = 13,800.
3. Parent shares held by a subsidiary
Parent shares held by a subsidiary are, for the group, shares it has bought back from itself. A

exists when two affiliated companies each hold shares in the other. The first case in the notes (section C) is a subsidiary owning shares of its parent. From the group's view those shares are not outstanding. The group has bought back part of itself, and the question is how to show that and how to split profit.

In the notes' example Pam buys 90 percent of Son on 1 January 2016 for 540,000, when Son's equity is 600,000 (capital 400,000, retained earnings 200,000), so there is no goodwill. Son buys 10 percent of Pam on 5 January 2016 for 140,000, when Pam's equity is 1,400,000 (capital 1,000,000 in shares of 10 par, retained earnings 400,000). Separate profits for 2016 are 100,000 for Pam and 60,000 for Son, with no dividends.

treats Pam's shares held by Son as if Pam had bought them back. Son's investment in Pam is reclassified to treasury shares at cost and deducted from consolidated equity, and the mutual holding is otherwise ignored in profit. Son has no income from Pam in 2016.
Income from Son / Investment in Son
Capital stock and retained earnings, Son / Investment in Son; NCI

treats Pam's shares held by Son as constructively retired, and lets Son's outside owners share in Pam's profit through Son's 10 percent stake. Then neither company's profit on an equity basis can be found first, because each includes a share of the other. The notes solve it with two equations.
P = Pam's profit on a consolidated basis, including mutual profit; S = the same for Son
P + S = 246,153.85, far above the combined separate profit of 160,000, because each figure includes the other's share. Each result is then multiplied by the share held outside the pair:
Profit attributable to Pam's own shareholders = 90% × 169,230.77 = 152,307.69

Pam's equity-method income from Son is 90 percent of S less 10 percent of P, the part of Pam's own profit that belongs to Son: 69,230.77 − 16,923.08 = 52,307.69. On Pam's own books the conventional approach also debits capital stock 100,000 and retained earnings 40,000 and credits the investment in Son 140,000, so Pam's equity method shows 900,000 of capital and the investment falls to 400,000 before income.
In 2017 Pam earns 120,000 separately and pays dividends of 60,000, 6,000 of them to Son. Son earns 80,000 and pays 40,000.
Parent shares held by Son are bought back; Son's stake earns nothing for the group
Parent shares are retired; Son's outside owners share in Pam's profit through Son

Both columns hold the same consolidated net assets of 1,480,000 at the end of 2016. Only the split between the parent's owners and the NCI differs. The conventional approach gives NCI more, because Son's outside owners are treated as owning 10% × 10% = 1 percent of Pam.

The notes reuse the same equations to put two years of undistributed earnings onto an equity basis. The separate increases in net assets from 2016 to 2017 are 196,000 for Pam (100,000 + 120,000 − 60,000 + 36,000 received) and 106,000 for Son (60,000 + 80,000 − 40,000 + 6,000 received).

(formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) para. 33 deducts the cost of an entity's own equity instruments that it reacquires from equity, records no gain or loss on their purchase, sale, issue or cancellation, and states that such shares may be acquired and held by the entity "or by other members of the consolidated group". PSAK 110 para. B86 eliminates intragroup equity in full. Together they make the parent's shares held by a subsidiary treasury shares of the group, shown at cost as a deduction. That is the treasury stock approach's presentation, and it rules out the conventional approach's balance sheet, with capital cut to 900,000 and retained earnings to 360,000 as if the shares were cancelled. Para. 33 does not say whether Son's NCI shares in Pam's profit through those shares, so the conventional profit split is a question PSAK leaves open. Earnings per share follow the presentation. Under PSAK 233 (formerly PSAK 56, IAS 33) the 10,000 shares held by Son are not outstanding, so 2016 earnings per share are 154,000 / 90,000 = 1.711, ignoring the four days before Son's purchase, against 152,307.69 / 90,000 = 1.692 under the conventional split.

A second attribution point is open as well. Beams gives NCI 10 percent of Son's whole 2017 profit of 86,000, including the 6,000 dividend received from Pam. On a strict group view that dividend is not income, so NCI's share of profit would be 10% × 80,000 = 8,000, and the 600 by which the dividend enlarges NCI's claim would be a transfer within equity from the parent's owners. NCI ends at 70,600 either way. PSAK gives no explicit guidance on this split.
In Indonesia the case is rare.

UU 40/2007 on limited companies art. 36(1) forbids a company to issue shares to be owned by itself or by another company whose shares it owns directly or indirectly. Shares obtained by operation of law, gift or bequest are exempt (art. 36(2)) but must be transferred within one year (art. 36(3)). BRPT's FS show no subsidiary holding BRPT shares. PT Barito Pacific Lumber, which holds 0.58 percent, belongs to Prajogo Pangestu, not to the group (Note 28, PDF p. 211; Note 45, PDF p. 235). BRPT's treasury shares of 1,600 consist of shares the Company bought back itself (Note 30, PDF pp. 212–213).

When two subsidiaries own each other, the treasury stock approach has nothing to work on, because neither holding is in the parent. The notes' case (section D): Pam owns 80 percent of Set, Set owns 70 percent of Ton, and Ton owns 10 percent of Set. Set's outside owners hold the remaining 10 percent and Ton's hold 30 percent. Separate profits for 2018, excluding income from affiliates, are 112,000 for Pam, 51,000 for Set and 40,000 for Ton. Three companies give three equations.
Solving the pair that loops first:
Pam's shares are held only by its own shareholders, so P is the controlling share. NCI is each subsidiary's outside percentage times its equation result:

Pam's equity-method income from Set is 80% × 84,946.24 = 67,956.99, and Set's from Ton is 70% × 48,494.62 = 33,946.24. Ton carries its 10 percent of Set at cost and records only its 3,000 dividend, which the worksheet eliminates.
The same answer as effective interests.

The equations can be turned around to say what share of each company's own profit reaches each owner. Write the holdings as a matrix W, invert (I − W) with Python, and multiply each column of the inverse by that company's outside share:
Share of each company's own profit going to

The divisor 0.93 = 1 − 0.7 × 0.1 is the loop: of each dollar Set earns, 7 cents comes back to Set through Ton. PSAK 110 treats Ton's 10 percent of Set as intragroup equity to be eliminated (para. B86), so Set's NCI is the outside 10 percent only. The equations remain the arithmetic for attributing profit.
The notes' goodwill is grossed up from the parent's price.

The notes give goodwill of 25,000 on Pam's 260,000 for 80 percent of Set's 300,000 equity, and 10,000 on Set's 112,000 for 70 percent of Ton's 150,000. Both gross up the price: 260,000 / 80% − 300,000 = 25,000. PSAK 103

(formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3) para. 19 measures NCI at its own fair value, which also gives full goodwill but not by grossing up a price that includes a control premium, or at its share of net assets. Under the second option goodwill would be 260,000 − 80% × 300,000 = 20,000 and 112,000 − 70% × 150,000 = 7,000.
5. Effective interests in a real multi-layer group

In a real group the same rules apply, but disclosure tables mix direct and effective percentages. BRPT's Note 1d shows, for each subsidiary, the holding by the company directly above it. BREN's Note 1 shows BREN's effective interest. Combining the two (BRPT FS 2025, Note 1d, PDF pp. 24–28; BREN FS 2025, Note 1, PDF p. 18):

Profit is attributed on outstanding shares, because treasury shares carry no claim, and here the two bases differ by 0.003 percentage points. BRPT records the buybacks by BREN and CAP as transactions with NCI: of the 5,163 paid (1,930 by BREN and 3,233 by CAP), 2,495 reduces other equity components and 2,668 reduces NCI (statement of changes in equity, PDF p. 18).

A bank may consolidate a securitisation vehicle or a fund in which it owns no shares at all, because PSAK 110 tests control through power and variable returns, not equity. Its effective equity interest may be zero, and the vehicle's equity is then NCI or, if redeemable, a liability (FSLI 25 section 9).

A parent that qualifies as an investment entity does not consolidate its subsidiaries; it measures them at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 110 para. 31), except subsidiaries that provide investment-related services (para. 32). A venture fund's layered portfolio companies therefore never enter a chain calculation. A non-investment parent above it still consolidates everything, including what the fund holds (para. 33).
Conglomerate pyramids and the two-shareholder rule.

Indonesian groups stack listed companies, as BRPT does with BREN, CAP and Chandra Daya Investasi, and many subsidiaries carry a small stake held by a sister company to keep two shareholders. Each listed layer adds outsiders, and each small stake is NCI in a sub-group's statements but not in the group's.
7. Presentation and analysis: Barito Pacific's Note 34

BRPT discloses NCI by sub-group, its movement, and summarised financial information for the two subsidiaries with material NCI (Note 34, PDF pp. 220–221), as PSAK 112 (formerly PSAK 67, IFRS 12) para. 12 asks.
The BREN line is two layers of outsiders.

BREN's own NCI is 246,651, mostly ACEHI (176,028) and DGA SEG B.V. (50,971) inside the Star Energy chain (BREN FS 2025, Note 20, PDF p. 116). Above that sit BREN's own outside shareholders. BREN's equity attributable to its owners, 636,868 (PDF p. 12), is already net of its treasury shares, so their share is measured on outstanding shares, 1 − 64.66886% = 35.33114% (section 5).

The difference of 287 is 0.06 percent of the line, and likely reflects consolidation adjustments made at BRPT's level that BREN's statements do not carry. BRPT does not reconcile the two. The same layering explains profit: of BREN's profit of 165,137, BRPT's owners take 64.6689% × 132,198 = 85,491, and NCI at BRPT's level is 32,939 + 46,707 = 79,646.
Attributable profit follows effective interests, not the top holding.

BRPT's owners took 30.3 percent of 2025 profit (489,807 of 1,615,634). CAP produced most of the group's profit (1,447,986 before intragroup elimination, Note 34), and BRPT's effective interest in CAP is 38.55 percent (34.63 direct plus 3.92 through Marigold). A rough bridge, 38.55% × 1,447,986 + 85,491 = 643,690, leaves 153,883 above the owners' actual 489,807. Part of the gap comes from outsiders below CAP, such as the 20 percent of CAPGC above Aster and the 40 percent of CDI; the rest is parent-level costs and consolidation adjustments that the FS do not split. Anyone valuing BRPT from consolidated profit would overstate what its shareholders earn by a factor of 1,615,634 / 489,807 = 3.3.

Reading BRPT's Note 1d is partly inference. The table gives direct holdings for Holdings BV (51 and 49 percent) but apparently effective ones elsewhere (90 percent for SEG-WW, which BREN reports as its effective interest). The ACEHI row shows "indirect ownership through ACEHI 19.80" while BREN shows ACEHI as an NCI holder. Linking the 4.80 percent to SEGHPL's 24.24 percent of ACEHI rests on the arithmetic matching BRPT's 80.91 percent statement. BRPT's table also gives 80.19 percent for Holdings BV's stake in SEGSDBV and no 2024 figure for the ACEHI row, although the ACEHI shares were registered in December 2023; the page uses BREN's 80.20 percent, the only figure that reproduces 80.91.

That BRPT holds the 5 percent "direct ownership" of SEGSS and DGI is read from BRPT's table wording and from BREN's matching effective percentages. BREN names Barito Pacific as the holder only for SEGI and SEGH.

How to attribute a parent's dividend paid to a subsidiary with NCI (Beams' 8,600 in profit, against 8,000 in profit plus a 600 equity transfer) is not settled by PSAK. PSAK 232 para. 33 settles presentation (treasury shares) but not whether Son's NCI shares in the parent's profit, so the conventional profit split, and this dividend point, remain policy choices.
UU 40/2007 art. 36 bans issuing shares to a cross-holder. Whether a subsidiary may buy existing parent shares on the market is not settled by its text, and secondary sources read it differently.

The 287 difference between BRPT's NCI in BREN and BREN's two layers has no disclosed explanation, and the split of the 153,883 bridge in section 7 between outsiders below CAP and parent-level items is not disclosed.

presentation.deck: How a group attributes profit when its companies own each other, from connecting affiliates to subsidiaries holding parent shares, worked through Barito Pacific's layered geothermal and petrochemical chains
key_takeaways: In a complex structure, control decides which companies are consolidated, and the effective interest decides how their profit and net assets are split. The effective interest is found by multiplying percentages down each ownership path and adding the paths together. A company can be a subsidiary while the parent's effective interest in it is below 50 percent.

When companies own each other, each one's profit depends on the other's, so the split needs simultaneous equations. The equations add mutual profit twice. Only the shares held by outsiders, multiplied by each equation's result, add back to the group's total profit.

When a subsidiary holds shares of its parent, Beams offers two treatments, the treasury stock approach and the conventional approach. PSAK 232 treats parent shares held by any group member as treasury shares, deducted from equity at cost, so the treasury stock approach is the one that fits Indonesian standards. Holdings between subsidiaries are eliminated, and there is no treasury alternative for them.

title: Non-Controlling Interest: Control, Attribution and Changes in Ownership
snippet: The theory of non-controlling interests from the control test to loss of control, worked through PHE's partly owned subsidiaries and set beside the industries where outside owners take other forms
content:
In brief

  • Consolidation adds 100 percent of a controlled subsidiary's assets, liabilities, income and expenses, even when the parent owns less than all of it. The non-controlling interest (NCI) is the outside owners' share of that subsidiary's equity. It is equity of the group, presented separately from the parent's owners' equity, and it absorbs its share of profit, other comprehensive income (OCI) and losses, even into a deficit.

  • At acquisition the acquirer chooses, deal by deal, to measure NCI at fair value or at its proportionate share of the identifiable net assets (PSAK 103). At the acquisition date the choice changes goodwill and NCI by the same amount and nothing else.

  • While control lasts, buying from or selling to the NCI is a transaction between owners. No gain or loss is recognised, no new goodwill arises, and the difference goes to the parent's equity. Only gaining or losing control is remeasured through profit or loss.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report non-controlling interest of 674,235 at 31 December 2024 against 644,429 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 4.5 percent of total equity (4.5 percent a year earlier) and 2.2 percent of total assets (2.1 percent). Of the year's profit of 3,121,035, 119,560 is attributed to NCI (Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15).

After reading this page a student should be able to measure NCI at acquisition, roll it forward through profit, OCI and dividends, record a change in ownership with and without loss of control, compute NCI in a chain of holdings, and read a group's NCI disclosures.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What a non-controlling interest is

NCI exists because consolidation is all-or-nothing on the asset side and proportionate on the ownership side. PSAK 110 Laporan Keuangan Konsolidasian (formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) defines it as equity in a subsidiary not attributable, directly or indirectly, to a parent.

The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 3) explain why the group is reported as one entity. Separate legal companies under one management are one economic unit, so their statements are combined line by line and the parent's investment account is replaced by the subsidiary's assets and liabilities. At 90 percent ownership all of the subsidiary's cash is still consolidated, and the outsiders' 10 percent is shown as a claim inside equity.

Control decides who consolidates. The notes date from the old PSAK 4 era and say control is usually obtained through "hak mayoritas (lebih dari 50%)", with exceptions for indirect holdings. PSAK 110 replaced that with three elements, all of which must be present: power over the investee's relevant activities, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns. PHE's policy repeats them (Note 3c, Daftar 5/33, PDF p. 50) and adds that, with less than a majority of votes, it considers contractual arrangements, other contractual rights and potential voting rights (Daftar 5/34, PDF p. 51). Majority ownership is the usual route to control, but the test is the three elements. A 45 percent holder whose remaining shares are spread among thousands of small holders may control; a 60 percent holder whose shareholder agreement gives the 40 percent holder a veto over the budget may not.

The notes' PSAK 4 exclusions, temporary control and restrictions on transferring funds, no longer exist; a subsidiary held for sale is consolidated under PSAK 105 (IFRS 5).

NCI is equity. The notes first place NCI "pada bagian sesi liabilities ... dibawah heading non current liabilities" and then cite GAAP: NCI "harus ditampilkan dalam balancesheet sebagai bagian yang terpisah dari komponen equity", which can be misread as outside equity. The current rule puts it within equity, separately from the parent's owners' equity (PSAK 110 para. 22). The outside shareholders own residual interests that nobody owes them, so they are not a liability. The same logic places NCI's share of profit below profit for the year as an attribution, not as an expense.

Profit for the year = profit attributable to owners of the parent + profit attributable to NCI

PHE 2024: 3,121,035 = 3,001,475 + 119,560

2. Measuring NCI at acquisition

When a parent buys less than 100 percent of a business, the subsidiary's identifiable assets and liabilities still enter the group at full fair value under PSAK 103 Kombinasi Bisnis (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3). The question is what figure to put on the NCI. PSAK 103 para. 19 gives a choice, made separately for each business combination, for NCI that are present ownership interests entitling holders to a proportionate share of net assets on liquidation:

  • fair value, usually the market price of the shares the parent did not buy, or

  • proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets.

Goodwill is the residual in both cases.

Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI + fair value of previously held interest − identifiable net assets at fair value

PHE's policy states that it makes this choice for each combination (Note 3d, Daftar 5/35, PDF p. 52).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 60 percent of a listed oilfield-services company for 300,000 cash. The target's book net assets are 350,000. Its equipment is worth 50,000 more than book, with ten years of life left, so identifiable net assets at fair value are 400,000. The 40 percent left in public hands trades at a total market value of 180,000.

Fair value method

Proportionate share method

NCI

180,000

40% × 400,000 = 160,000

Goodwill

300,000 + 180,000 − 400,000 = 80,000

300,000 + 160,000 − 400,000 = 60,000

Goodwill recognised for

parent and NCI ("full goodwill")

parent only

The 20,000 gap is the NCI's share of goodwill. The fair value method books it, and the proportionate method leaves it out. Nothing else differs. The elimination entry on the consolidation worksheet under the proportionate method:

Dr Share capital and retained earnings, subsidiary 350,000; Dr Equipment 50,000; Dr Goodwill 60,000 / Cr Investment in subsidiary 300,000; Cr NCI 160,000

The lecture notes measure NCI by grossing up the price, as Beams does: "Implied fair value of sun ($10.200.000÷90%)", so NCI is 10 percent of that implied value. PSAK 103 asks for the NCI's own fair value instead, because the parent's price per share usually includes a control premium that the outside shares do not carry. Grossing up the illustration gives 300,000 / 60% = 500,000, NCI of 200,000 and goodwill of 100,000, which overstates both by 20,000 against the market price of the minority shares.

Acquisition costs are expensed under either method (Note 3d). Goodwill itself and its impairment are covered in the Intangible Assets essay.

3. Profit, OCI and dividends after acquisition

After acquisition NCI moves with three things: its share of the subsidiary's profit after consolidation adjustments, its share of OCI, and dividends paid to the outside owners.

NCI at end = NCI at start + NCI share of profit + NCI share of OCI − dividends to NCI ± changes in ownership

The share of profit is computed on the subsidiary's profit as the group sees it. Extra depreciation on fair value uplifts reduces it. So do unrealised profits on upstream sales (a subsidiary selling to its parent), which the notes for AKL Chapter 5 allocate between parent and NCI, while downstream profits fall wholly on the parent.

For example (illustration), continue the section 2 subsidiary under the proportionate method. In its first year it reports profit of 70,000, pays dividends of 30,000, and records a translation loss in OCI of 10,000. The equipment uplift of 50,000 depreciates over ten years.

Group-basis profit = 70,000 − 50,000 / 10 = 65,000

NCI share of profit = 40% × 65,000 = 26,000; parent share = 60% × 65,000 = 39,000

NCI share of OCI = 40% × (10,000) = (4,000)

Dividends to NCI = 40% × 30,000 = 12,000

NCI at end = 160,000 + 26,000 − 4,000 − 12,000 = 170,000

The check is that NCI equals 40 percent of the subsidiary's net assets at group carrying amounts, 400,000 + 65,000 − 10,000 − 30,000 = 425,000, and 40% × 425,000 = 170,000. Under the fair value method NCI would be 190,000, the same 20,000 of goodwill above it.

The worksheet entries follow the order in the notes for AKL Chapter 4, with the parent using the equity method in its own books:

Step

Entry

1. Remove the parent's equity-method income, OCI share and dividends

Dr Income from subsidiary 39,000 / Cr Dividends 18,000; Cr Investment in subsidiary 21,000; and Dr Investment in subsidiary 6,000 / Cr Translation reserve 6,000 to reverse the parent's own OCI entry

2. Record NCI's share

Dr NCI share of profit 26,000 / Cr Dividends 12,000; Cr NCI 14,000

3. Eliminate opening equity, recognise uplift, goodwill and opening NCI

the section 2 entry

4. Depreciate the uplift

Dr Depreciation expense 5,000 / Cr Equipment 5,000

5. Attribute OCI

Dr NCI 4,000 / Cr Translation reserve 4,000

The parent's investment closes at 300,000 + 39,000 − 18,000 − 6,000 = 315,000, and steps 1 and 3 remove 300,000 + 21,000 − 6,000 = 315,000 of it. Step 5 then puts the translation loss into the group once, 6,000 to the parent and 4,000 to NCI.

PHE's numbers. PHE attributes 119,560 of profit and 111,073 of total comprehensive income to NCI (Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15), so NCI's share of OCI was 111,073 − 119,560 = (8,487). The group's whole OCI was 3,083,675 − 3,121,035 = (37,360).

NCI share of profit = 119,560 / 3,121,035 = 3.8%; NCI share of OCI = 8,487 / 37,360 = 22.7%

NCI took a far larger share of the OCI loss than of profit. Elnusa, 51.10 percent owned (Note 1b, Daftar 5/6, PDF p. 23), is the only group entity with the rupiah as functional currency (Note 3a, Daftar 5/29, PDF p. 46), so the translation loss of 14,810 is its loss.

NCI share of translation loss = 48.90% × 14,810 = 7,242, about 85% of NCI's OCI loss of 8,487

The hedge loss of 21,940 arises in near-wholly-owned companies, so NCI takes little of it. PHE does not attribute OCI by subsidiary.

4. Losses that exceed the NCI

Losses are attributed to NCI even when this drives NCI into deficit (PSAK 110 para. B94). PHE's policy says so in the same words (Note 3c, Daftar 5/34, PDF p. 51). The older rule in PSAK 4 and pre-2008 IAS 27 charged the excess to the parent unless the minority had a binding obligation to fund it, and later profits went to the parent until the losses it had absorbed were recovered.

For example (illustration), a 70 percent-owned subsidiary has net assets of 20,000, so NCI is 30% × 20,000 = 6,000. It then loses 50,000.

Current rule (PSAK 110)

Old rule (PSAK 4, pre-2008 IAS 27)

Loss attributed to NCI

30% × 50,000 = 15,000

6,000, capped at the NCI balance

Loss attributed to parent

70% × 50,000 = 35,000

50,000 − 6,000 = 44,000

NCI after the loss

6,000 − 15,000 = (9,000)

0

A deficit NCI is the outside owners' share of a subsidiary whose liabilities exceed its assets. It does not mean they owe the group anything.

5. Changes in ownership without loss of control

PSAK 110 para. 23 treats any change in the parent's ownership that leaves control intact as a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners. Once the group view is taken, the group has not sold or bought any asset. Shares in the group have changed hands between two classes of its owners. So:

  • no gain or loss is recognised and goodwill is not remeasured;

  • NCI is adjusted to reflect the new relative interests;

  • the difference between the consideration and the NCI adjustment goes directly to equity attributable to the parent (para. B96).

The notes for AKL Chapter 8 state the same rule: if control is kept, the sale "akan diperlukan sebagai equity transaction. Tidak ada gain or losses yang diakui." They record the difference in additional paid-in capital, a US practice. PSAK names no equity account; Indonesian groups commonly use an "other equity component" or a reserve for transactions with NCI, and PHE's statement of changes in equity has a column for "equity adjustments (other equity component)" (Daftar 3, PDF p. 16).

For example (illustration), take the section 3 subsidiary at the start of its second year: net assets at group carrying amounts 425,000, parent 60 percent, NCI 170,000.

(a) Parent sells 5% for 25,000

(b) Parent buys 20% from NCI for 80,000

Ownership after

55% parent, 45% NCI

80% parent, 20% NCI

NCI adjustment

+5% × 425,000 = +21,250

−20% × 425,000 = −85,000

Difference to parent's equity

25,000 − 21,250 = 3,750 credit

85,000 − 80,000 = 5,000 credit

Entry

Dr Cash 25,000 / Cr NCI 21,250; Cr Other equity 3,750

Dr NCI 85,000 / Cr Cash 80,000; Cr Other equity 5,000

Under the proportionate method the NCI adjustment above uses net assets only. Whether a share of goodwill should also move to or from NCI is a policy question that PSAK 110 does not settle, and practice differs.

In the parent's separate statements, with the investment at cost under PSAK 227 (IAS 27), sale (a) shows no gain, because the 5 percent cost 300,000 × 5/60 = 25,000. At any other price the gain or loss there would be moved into equity on consolidation.

The subsidiary issues shares to outsiders. The parent's percentage falls without the parent selling anything. The notes use a subsidiary with 10,000 shares and equity of 200,000, 80 percent held by the parent, issuing 2,000 new shares to outside investors at 35 each.

Equity after = 200,000 + 2,000 × 35 = 270,000; parent's share = 8,000 / 12,000 = 66.67%

Parent's interest = 66.67% × 270,000 = 180,000, against 80% × 200,000 = 160,000 before

NCI = 33.33% × 270,000 = 90,000, against 40,000 before

Consolidated entry: Dr Cash 70,000 / Cr NCI 50,000; Cr Other equity 20,000

Issuing below book value moves equity the other way. At 15 per share the notes find a decrease of 6,667. A subsidiary buying back its own shares from outside holders works in reverse. The parent's percentage rises, NCI falls by the share bought back, and any difference again stays in equity.

Accumulated OCI, such as a translation reserve, is reallocated to the new percentages (PSAK 221 para. 48C; see the OCI essay).

6. Gaining and losing control

Control obtained in stages. When a parent that already owns part of an investee gains control, the earlier holding is remeasured to fair value at the acquisition date and the gain or loss goes to profit or loss (PSAK 103 para. 42). PHE's policy says this (Note 3d, Daftar 5/35, PDF p. 52). The notes for AKL Chapter 8 give an example: 5 percent bought for 7,000 and another 5 percent for 8,000, then 80 percent for 210,000.

Implied value of 100% = 210,000 / 80% = 262,500

Fair value of the earlier 10% = 10% × 262,500 = 26,250; carrying amount = 7,000 + 8,000 = 15,000

Gain on remeasurement = 26,250 − 15,000 = 11,250

The notes write the calculation as "($262.500 -$7.000 - $8.000)", which does not give 11,250. The steps follow the notes in carrying the earlier 10 percent at cost and valuing it from the parent's price. Under PSAK 109 the stake would already be at fair value, so the para. 42 gain is only the movement since the last reporting date, and it stays in OCI if the FVOCI election was made. Valuing it at 10% of 262,500 also assumes no control premium, the simplification section 2 criticised.

Control lost. When the parent loses control it derecognises the subsidiary's assets (including goodwill) and liabilities and the NCI, recognises the consideration and any retained interest at fair value, and takes the difference to profit or loss (PSAK 110 paras. 25 and B98–B99). Amounts in OCI are reclassified as if the parent had disposed of the assets directly, so the translation reserve is recycled.

Gain or loss = (fair value of consideration + fair value of retained interest + carrying amount of NCI) − (carrying amount of net assets + goodwill)

The notes give this formula under the heading "Sale of an interest resulting in consolidation"; the event is a deconsolidation.

For example (illustration), back in the section 3 subsidiary with the parent at 60 percent: net assets 425,000, goodwill 60,000, NCI 170,000, and the parent's share of the translation reserve 60% × (10,000) = (6,000). The parent sells 40 percent for 230,000 and keeps 20 percent, now an associate, with a fair value of 115,000.

Gain = (230,000 + 115,000 + 170,000) − (425,000 + 60,000) = 515,000 − 485,000 = 30,000

Translation reserve recycled = (6,000); net gain in profit or loss = 24,000

Dr Cash 230,000; Dr Investment in associate 115,000; Dr NCI 170,000 / Cr Net assets of subsidiary 425,000; Cr Goodwill 60,000; Cr Gain on loss of control 30,000

Dr Loss on reclassification of translation reserve 6,000 / Cr Translation reserve 6,000

The 115,000 becomes the cost of the associate under the equity method. The Long-Term Investments essay covers that method.

7. Indirect holdings

In a chain of ownership the NCI in a grandchild has two layers, its own outside owners and the outside owners of the intermediate company. The notes for AKL Chapter 9 recommend an allocation schedule worked from the bottom up: each company first takes its share of the company below it, then passes its own profit up.

PHE has two such chains in Note 1. Elnusa, 51.10 percent owned, owns subsidiaries such as PT Elnusa Petrofin at 99.99 percent. Etablissements Maurel et Prom (M&P), listed in Paris, is 71.09 percent owned by PT Pertamina Internasional Eksplorasi dan Produksi (PIEP), which PHE owns at 99.999998 percent (Note 1b, Daftar 5/4, 5/6 and 5/8, PDF pp. 21, 23, 25).

PHE's effective interest in Elnusa Petrofin = 51.10% × 99.99% = 51.09%

PHE's effective interest in M&P = 99.999998% × 71.09% = 71.09%

For example (illustration), suppose Elnusa earns 20,000 from its own operations and Petrofin earns 10,000.

Elnusa level: attributable to Elnusa's owners = 20,000 + 99.99% × 10,000 = 29,999; NCI in Petrofin = 0.01% × 10,000 = 1

PHE level: attributable to PHE = 51.10% × 29,999 = 15,329.49

Total NCI = 1 + 48.90% × 29,999 = 1 + 14,669.51 = 14,670.51

Check: 15,329.49 + 14,670.51 = 30,000

8. Presentation and disclosure

  • Statement of financial position: a separate line within equity (PSAK 110 para. 22; PSAK 201 para. 54(q), formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1).

  • Statement of profit or loss and OCI: profit and total comprehensive income each split between owners of the parent and NCI (PSAK 201 para. 81B).

  • Statement of changes in equity: a column reconciling opening and closing NCI.

  • Statement of cash flows: dividends paid to NCI are financing cash flows, as the notes for AKL Chapter 4 say. Cash paid or received in changes of ownership without loss of control is also financing (PSAK 207 para. 42A, formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7). Only obtaining or losing control is investing (para. 39).

PSAK 112 Pengungkapan Kepentingan dalam Entitas Lain (formerly PSAK 67, IFRS 12) paras. 12 and B10–B11 ask, for each subsidiary with NCI material to the group, for its name and principal place of business, the NCI's ownership and voting share, the profit allocated to NCI, accumulated NCI, dividends paid to NCI and summarised financial information.

9. Non-controlling interest across industries

Listed holding groups. Indonesian conglomerates often hold majority stakes in subsidiaries that are themselves listed, so the outside shareholders of each listed child sit in the parent's NCI. Consolidated profit and profit attributable to the parent can then diverge widely, and analysts work from the attributable figures.

Banks and sharia units. A conventional bank's sharia business unit (unit usaha syariah, UUS) is a division, so it has no NCI. A spin-off into a separate sharia bank (bank umum syariah) creates a subsidiary, and NCI appears if outside investors subscribe. UU 4/2023 on financial-sector development (P2SK) left the spin-off conditions to OJK (art. 68), and POJK 12/2023 requires a spin-off within two years once the unit's assets reach 50 percent of the parent bank's assets and/or IDR 50 trillion. Inside a sharia subsidiary, temporary syirkah funds (profit-sharing deposits) sit between liabilities and equity under the sharia presentation standard and are not NCI.

Consolidated funds. An insurer or asset manager that controls a mutual fund consolidates it. The outside unitholders can redeem their units for cash, so their interest is a financial liability in the consolidated statements, even if the fund itself presents the units as equity (PSAK 232, IAS 32, para. AG29A). For example (illustration), an insurer holds 70 percent of a fund with net asset value of 100,000.

Liability to outside unitholders = 30% × 100,000 = 30,000

Fund earns 8,000: Dr Change in third-party unitholders' interest (expense) 2,400 / Cr Liability to unitholders 2,400

The 2,400 reduces consolidated profit, unlike an NCI share, which is only an attribution.

Put options written over NCI. A parent that promises to buy the outside owners' shares on demand records a liability for the present value of the redemption amount (PSAK 232 para. 23), because it has a contract to deliver cash.

Note 1 shows where the outside owners sit (Daftar 5/4–5/8, PDF pp. 21–25): 48.90 percent of Elnusa (IDX: ELSA); 28.91 percent of M&P through PIEP; 45 percent of PT Badak NGL (55 percent owned); and stakes of 0.000002 to 1 percent in dozens of companies held at 99 percent or more, including Elnusa's own subsidiaries. M&P's own NCI in its subsidiaries also enters PHE's NCI. PHE gives no split of the 674,235 by subsidiary.

NCI return = 119,560 / ((644,429 + 674,235) / 2) = 119,560 / 659,332 = 18.1%
