PHE's single shareholder group takes 80 percent of profit as dividends (Note 34, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165), while the subsidiaries with outside owners, mostly listed companies, distribute far less of theirs.

The 2024 "equity adjustment in subsidiaries" is the one ownership event in the line. NCI fell by 53,470, the parent's equity rose by 6,138 (6,140 in other equity component, less 2 in retained earnings), and total equity fell by 47,332. That is arithmetically what section 5(b) produces: buying out outside owners carried at 53,470 for 47,332 would credit the parent with 6,138. No such transaction or cash flow is disclosed. Note 42 reports a gain on sale of subsidiaries of 34,242 (Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167) and the cash flow statement a net investing receipt of 64,578 from sales and additions of investments in subsidiaries (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17). Those more likely relate to TPDC's exercise in January 2024 of its call option over M&P's Mnazi Bay interest in Tanzania, which cut M&P's share from 80 to 60 percent (Note 5g, Daftar 5/88, PDF p. 105); a sale to an outsider would not reduce NCI.

11. Upstream note: partners are not NCI

Most of PHE's blocks are shared with other contractors. Those partners hold participating interests in a production sharing contract, which is a joint arrangement, so each party records its own share of assets, liabilities, revenue and costs. Their shares never enter PHE's NCI. The many companies held at 99 percent fit Indonesian company law, which requires a limited company to be founded by at least two persons and to restore two shareholders within six months if it falls to one (UU 40/2007 art. 7(1) and 7(5)–(6)).

12. Related lines

  • share-capital and additional-paid-in-capital: the parent's contributed equity, and common-control restructurings.

  • other-equity-component: where differences from transactions with NCI may sit.

  • retained-earnings: dividends to the parent's owners and the profit attributable to them.

  • other-comprehensive-income: translation and hedge reserves, their attribution and recycling.

  • long-term-investments: associates and joint ventures, including a retained interest after loss of control.

  • intangible-assets-net: goodwill on business combinations.

Least-confident assertions

  • The 2024 equity adjustment (NCI −53,470, parent +6,138) has no disclosed transaction or cash flow. Reading it as a purchase or redemption of NCI shares rests on the numbers alone, and any cash paid would sit in an undisclosed financing line. Linking the investing receipt and the Note 42 gain to TPDC's call option (Note 5g) is also inference; PHE does not connect them.

  • Elnusa's translation explains about 7,242 of NCI's OCI loss of 8,487. The other 1,245 is unexplained (hedge losses in subsidiaries with small outside stakes, or associates' OCI, are candidates); PHE does not attribute OCI by subsidiary.

  • No PSAK 112 para. 12 table of subsidiaries with material NCI was found in PHE's FS (searched for NCI, KNP and the subsidiaries' names). With 674,235 of NCI spread over Elnusa, M&P and Badak NGL, at least one is likely material, so the disclosure is either elsewhere or missing.

  • Who holds the 1 percent stakes in PHE's 99 percent subsidiaries is not disclosed. If they are held by other PHE companies they are not NCI at all. PT Pertamina Pedeve Indonesia holds 0.0032 percent of PHE itself (Note 32, Daftar 5/147, PDF p. 164), which makes it the likely nominee; if so, the stakes are NCI in PHE's statements though inside Pertamina's group. The ownership percentages of M&P (71.09 percent) and Elnusa (about 51 percent) were checked only against secondary and older sources.

  • The banking rules in section 9 (P2SK art. 68, POJK 12/2023 thresholds and two-year window) were seen only in news reports, and a revision of P2SK was under discussion in 2026. The presentation of temporary syirkah funds on consolidation follow general practice, not a checked rule.

content.text: Consolidation adds 100 percent of a controlled subsidiary's assets, liabilities, income and expenses, even when the parent owns less than all of it. The non-controlling interest (NCI) is the outside owners' share of that subsidiary's equity. It is equity of the group, presented separately from the parent's owners' equity, and it absorbs its share of profit, other comprehensive income (OCI) and losses, even into a deficit.

At acquisition the acquirer chooses, deal by deal, to measure NCI at fair value or at its proportionate share of the identifiable net assets (PSAK 103). At the acquisition date the choice changes goodwill and NCI by the same amount and nothing else.

While control lasts, buying from or selling to the NCI is a transaction between owners. No gain or loss is recognised, no new goodwill arises, and the difference goes to the parent's equity. Only gaining or losing control is remeasured through profit or loss.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report non-controlling interest of 674,235 at 31 December 2024 against 644,429 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 4.5 percent of total equity (4.5 percent a year earlier) and 2.2 percent of total assets (2.1 percent). Of the year's profit of 3,121,035, 119,560 is attributed to NCI (Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15).

After reading this page a student should be able to measure NCI at acquisition, roll it forward through profit, OCI and dividends, record a change in ownership with and without loss of control, compute NCI in a chain of holdings, and read a group's NCI disclosures.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
NCI exists because consolidation is all-or-nothing on the asset side and proportionate on the ownership side. PSAK 110
(formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10) defines it as equity in a subsidiary not attributable, directly or indirectly, to a parent.

The lecture notes (AKL Chapter 3) explain why the group is reported as one entity. Separate legal companies under one management are one economic unit, so their statements are combined line by line and the parent's investment account is replaced by the subsidiary's assets and liabilities. At 90 percent ownership all of the subsidiary's cash is still consolidated, and the outsiders' 10 percent is shown as a claim inside equity.

The notes date from the old PSAK 4 era and say control is usually obtained through "hak mayoritas (lebih dari 50%)", with exceptions for indirect holdings. PSAK 110 replaced that with three elements, all of which must be present: power over the investee's relevant activities, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns. PHE's policy repeats them (Note 3c, Daftar 5/33, PDF p. 50) and adds that, with less than a majority of votes, it considers contractual arrangements, other contractual rights and potential voting rights (Daftar 5/34, PDF p. 51). Majority ownership is the usual route to control, but the test is the three elements. A 45 percent holder whose remaining shares are spread among thousands of small holders may control; a 60 percent holder whose shareholder agreement gives the 40 percent holder a veto over the budget may not.
The notes' PSAK 4 exclusions, temporary control and restrictions on transferring funds, no longer exist; a subsidiary held for sale is consolidated under PSAK 105 (IFRS 5).

The notes first place NCI "pada bagian sesi liabilities ... dibawah heading non current liabilities" and then cite GAAP: NCI "harus ditampilkan dalam balancesheet sebagai bagian yang terpisah dari komponen equity", which can be misread as outside equity. The current rule puts it within equity, separately from the parent's owners' equity (PSAK 110 para. 22). The outside shareholders own residual interests that nobody owes them, so they are not a liability. The same logic places NCI's share of profit below profit for the year as an attribution, not as an expense.
Profit for the year = profit attributable to owners of the parent + profit attributable to NCI
When a parent buys less than 100 percent of a business, the subsidiary's identifiable assets and liabilities still enter the group at full fair value under PSAK 103

(formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3). The question is what figure to put on the NCI. PSAK 103 para. 19 gives a choice, made separately for each business combination, for NCI that are present ownership interests entitling holders to a proportionate share of net assets on liquidation:
, usually the market price of the shares the parent did not buy, or
of the acquiree's identifiable net assets.
Goodwill is the residual in both cases.
Goodwill = consideration transferred + NCI + fair value of previously held interest − identifiable net assets at fair value
PHE's policy states that it makes this choice for each combination (Note 3d, Daftar 5/35, PDF p. 52).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys 60 percent of a listed oilfield-services company for 300,000 cash. The target's book net assets are 350,000. Its equipment is worth 50,000 more than book, with ten years of life left, so identifiable net assets at fair value are 400,000. The 40 percent left in public hands trades at a total market value of 180,000.

The 20,000 gap is the NCI's share of goodwill. The fair value method books it, and the proportionate method leaves it out. Nothing else differs. The elimination entry on the consolidation worksheet under the proportionate method:
Dr Share capital and retained earnings, subsidiary 350,000; Dr Equipment 50,000; Dr Goodwill 60,000 / Cr Investment in subsidiary 300,000; Cr NCI 160,000

The lecture notes measure NCI by grossing up the price, as Beams does: "Implied fair value of sun ($10.200.000÷90%)", so NCI is 10 percent of that implied value. PSAK 103 asks for the NCI's own fair value instead, because the parent's price per share usually includes a control premium that the outside shares do not carry. Grossing up the illustration gives 300,000 / 60% = 500,000, NCI of 200,000 and goodwill of 100,000, which overstates both by 20,000 against the market price of the minority shares.
Acquisition costs are expensed under either method (Note 3d). Goodwill itself and its impairment are covered in the Intangible Assets essay.
3. Profit, OCI and dividends after acquisition
After acquisition NCI moves with three things: its share of the subsidiary's profit after consolidation adjustments, its share of OCI, and dividends paid to the outside owners.
NCI at end = NCI at start + NCI share of profit + NCI share of OCI − dividends to NCI ± changes in ownership
The share of profit is computed on the subsidiary's profit

. Extra depreciation on fair value uplifts reduces it. So do unrealised profits on upstream sales (a subsidiary selling to its parent), which the notes for AKL Chapter 5 allocate between parent and NCI, while downstream profits fall wholly on the parent.

For example (illustration), continue the section 2 subsidiary under the proportionate method. In its first year it reports profit of 70,000, pays dividends of 30,000, and records a translation loss in OCI of 10,000. The equipment uplift of 50,000 depreciates over ten years.
NCI share of profit = 40% × 65,000 = 26,000; parent share = 60% × 65,000 = 39,000

The check is that NCI equals 40 percent of the subsidiary's net assets at group carrying amounts, 400,000 + 65,000 − 10,000 − 30,000 = 425,000, and 40% × 425,000 = 170,000. Under the fair value method NCI would be 190,000, the same 20,000 of goodwill above it.
The worksheet entries follow the order in the notes for AKL Chapter 4, with the parent using the equity method in its own books:
1. Remove the parent's equity-method income, OCI share and dividends
Dr Income from subsidiary 39,000 / Cr Dividends 18,000; Cr Investment in subsidiary 21,000; and Dr Investment in subsidiary 6,000 / Cr Translation reserve 6,000 to reverse the parent's own OCI entry
Dr NCI share of profit 26,000 / Cr Dividends 12,000; Cr NCI 14,000
3. Eliminate opening equity, recognise uplift, goodwill and opening NCI

The parent's investment closes at 300,000 + 39,000 − 18,000 − 6,000 = 315,000, and steps 1 and 3 remove 300,000 + 21,000 − 6,000 = 315,000 of it. Step 5 then puts the translation loss into the group once, 6,000 to the parent and 4,000 to NCI.

PHE attributes 119,560 of profit and 111,073 of total comprehensive income to NCI (Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15), so NCI's share of OCI was 111,073 − 119,560 = (8,487). The group's whole OCI was 3,083,675 − 3,121,035 = (37,360).
NCI share of profit = 119,560 / 3,121,035 = 3.8%; NCI share of OCI = 8,487 / 37,360 = 22.7%

NCI took a far larger share of the OCI loss than of profit. Elnusa, 51.10 percent owned (Note 1b, Daftar 5/6, PDF p. 23), is the only group entity with the rupiah as functional currency (Note 3a, Daftar 5/29, PDF p. 46), so the translation loss of 14,810 is its loss.
NCI share of translation loss = 48.90% × 14,810 = 7,242, about 85% of NCI's OCI loss of 8,487
The hedge loss of 21,940 arises in near-wholly-owned companies, so NCI takes little of it. PHE does not attribute OCI by subsidiary.

Losses are attributed to NCI even when this drives NCI into deficit (PSAK 110 para. B94). PHE's policy says so in the same words (Note 3c, Daftar 5/34, PDF p. 51). The older rule in PSAK 4 and pre-2008 IAS 27 charged the excess to the parent unless the minority had a binding obligation to fund it, and later profits went to the parent until the losses it had absorbed were recovered.
For example (illustration), a 70 percent-owned subsidiary has net assets of 20,000, so NCI is 30% × 20,000 = 6,000. It then loses 50,000.
A deficit NCI is the outside owners' share of a subsidiary whose liabilities exceed its assets. It does not mean they owe the group anything.
5. Changes in ownership without loss of control

PSAK 110 para. 23 treats any change in the parent's ownership that leaves control intact as a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners. Once the group view is taken, the group has not sold or bought any asset. Shares in the group have changed hands between two classes of its owners. So:
no gain or loss is recognised and goodwill is not remeasured;
NCI is adjusted to reflect the new relative interests;
the difference between the consideration and the NCI adjustment goes directly to equity attributable to the parent (para. B96).

The notes for AKL Chapter 8 state the same rule: if control is kept, the sale "akan diperlukan sebagai equity transaction. Tidak ada gain or losses yang diakui." They record the difference in additional paid-in capital, a US practice. PSAK names no equity account; Indonesian groups commonly use an "other equity component" or a reserve for transactions with NCI, and PHE's statement of changes in equity has a column for "equity adjustments (other equity component)" (Daftar 3, PDF p. 16).
For example (illustration), take the section 3 subsidiary at the start of its second year: net assets at group carrying amounts 425,000, parent 60 percent, NCI 170,000.
Dr Cash 25,000 / Cr NCI 21,250; Cr Other equity 3,750
Dr NCI 85,000 / Cr Cash 80,000; Cr Other equity 5,000

Under the proportionate method the NCI adjustment above uses net assets only. Whether a share of goodwill should also move to or from NCI is a policy question that PSAK 110 does not settle, and practice differs.

In the parent's separate statements, with the investment at cost under PSAK 227 (IAS 27), sale (a) shows no gain, because the 5 percent cost 300,000 × 5/60 = 25,000. At any other price the gain or loss there would be moved into equity on consolidation.
The subsidiary issues shares to outsiders.

The parent's percentage falls without the parent selling anything. The notes use a subsidiary with 10,000 shares and equity of 200,000, 80 percent held by the parent, issuing 2,000 new shares to outside investors at 35 each.
Consolidated entry: Dr Cash 70,000 / Cr NCI 50,000; Cr Other equity 20,000

Issuing below book value moves equity the other way. At 15 per share the notes find a decrease of 6,667. A subsidiary buying back its own shares from outside holders works in reverse. The parent's percentage rises, NCI falls by the share bought back, and any difference again stays in equity.
Accumulated OCI, such as a translation reserve, is reallocated to the new percentages (PSAK 221 para. 48C; see the OCI essay).

When a parent that already owns part of an investee gains control, the earlier holding is remeasured to fair value at the acquisition date and the gain or loss goes to profit or loss (PSAK 103 para. 42). PHE's policy says this (Note 3d, Daftar 5/35, PDF p. 52). The notes for AKL Chapter 8 give an example: 5 percent bought for 7,000 and another 5 percent for 8,000, then 80 percent for 210,000.
Fair value of the earlier 10% = 10% × 262,500 = 26,250; carrying amount = 7,000 + 8,000 = 15,000

The notes write the calculation as "($262.500 -$7.000 - $8.000)", which does not give 11,250. The steps follow the notes in carrying the earlier 10 percent at cost and valuing it from the parent's price. Under PSAK 109 the stake would already be at fair value, so the para. 42 gain is only the movement since the last reporting date, and it stays in OCI if the FVOCI election was made. Valuing it at 10% of 262,500 also assumes no control premium, the simplification section 2 criticised.

When the parent loses control it derecognises the subsidiary's assets (including goodwill) and liabilities and the NCI, recognises the consideration and any retained interest at fair value, and takes the difference to profit or loss (PSAK 110 paras. 25 and B98–B99). Amounts in OCI are reclassified as if the parent had disposed of the assets directly, so the translation reserve is recycled.
Gain or loss = (fair value of consideration + fair value of retained interest + carrying amount of NCI) − (carrying amount of net assets + goodwill)
The notes give this formula under the heading "Sale of an interest resulting in consolidation"; the event is a

For example (illustration), back in the section 3 subsidiary with the parent at 60 percent: net assets 425,000, goodwill 60,000, NCI 170,000, and the parent's share of the translation reserve 60% × (10,000) = (6,000). The parent sells 40 percent for 230,000 and keeps 20 percent, now an associate, with a fair value of 115,000.
Translation reserve recycled = (6,000); net gain in profit or loss = 24,000
Dr Cash 230,000; Dr Investment in associate 115,000; Dr NCI 170,000 / Cr Net assets of subsidiary 425,000; Cr Goodwill 60,000; Cr Gain on loss of control 30,000
Dr Loss on reclassification of translation reserve 6,000 / Cr Translation reserve 6,000
The 115,000 becomes the cost of the associate under the equity method. The Long-Term Investments essay covers that method.

In a chain of ownership the NCI in a grandchild has two layers, its own outside owners and the outside owners of the intermediate company. The notes for AKL Chapter 9 recommend an allocation schedule worked from the bottom up: each company first takes its share of the company below it, then passes its own profit up.

PHE has two such chains in Note 1. Elnusa, 51.10 percent owned, owns subsidiaries such as PT Elnusa Petrofin at 99.99 percent. Etablissements Maurel et Prom (M&P), listed in Paris, is 71.09 percent owned by PT Pertamina Internasional Eksplorasi dan Produksi (PIEP), which PHE owns at 99.999998 percent (Note 1b, Daftar 5/4, 5/6 and 5/8, PDF pp. 21, 23, 25).
PHE's effective interest in Elnusa Petrofin = 51.10% × 99.99% = 51.09%
For example (illustration), suppose Elnusa earns 20,000 from its own operations and Petrofin earns 10,000.
Elnusa level: attributable to Elnusa's owners = 20,000 + 99.99% × 10,000 = 29,999; NCI in Petrofin = 0.01% × 10,000 = 1

An insurer or asset manager that controls a mutual fund consolidates it. The outside unitholders can redeem their units for cash, so their interest is a financial liability in the consolidated statements, even if the fund itself presents the units as equity (PSAK 232, IAS 32, para. AG29A). For example (illustration), an insurer holds 70 percent of a fund with net asset value of 100,000.
Fund earns 8,000: Dr Change in third-party unitholders' interest (expense) 2,400 / Cr Liability to unitholders 2,400
The 2,400 reduces consolidated profit, unlike an NCI share, which is only an attribution.
A parent that promises to buy the outside owners' shares on demand records a liability for the present value of the redemption amount (PSAK 232 para. 23), because it has a contract to deliver cash.
PHE has no note for NCI. The movement comes from the statement of changes in equity (Daftar 3, PDF p. 16).

Note 1 shows where the outside owners sit (Daftar 5/4–5/8, PDF pp. 21–25): 48.90 percent of Elnusa (IDX: ELSA); 28.91 percent of M&P through PIEP; 45 percent of PT Badak NGL (55 percent owned); and stakes of 0.000002 to 1 percent in dozens of companies held at 99 percent or more, including Elnusa's own subsidiaries. M&P's own NCI in its subsidiaries also enters PHE's NCI. PHE gives no split of the 674,235 by subsidiary.
Dividends declared in 2024 against 2023 profit: NCI 27,797 / 125,852 = 22.1%; parent 2,079,749 / 2,599,686 = 80.0%

PHE's single shareholder group takes 80 percent of profit as dividends (Note 34, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165), while the subsidiaries with outside owners, mostly listed companies, distribute far less of theirs.

The 2024 "equity adjustment in subsidiaries" is the one ownership event in the line. NCI fell by 53,470, the parent's equity rose by 6,138 (6,140 in other equity component, less 2 in retained earnings), and total equity fell by 47,332. That is arithmetically what section 5(b) produces: buying out outside owners carried at 53,470 for 47,332 would credit the parent with 6,138. No such transaction or cash flow is disclosed. Note 42 reports a gain on sale of subsidiaries of 34,242 (Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167) and the cash flow statement a net investing receipt of 64,578 from sales and additions of investments in subsidiaries (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17). Those more likely relate to TPDC's exercise in January 2024 of its call option over M&P's Mnazi Bay interest in Tanzania, which cut M&P's share from 80 to 60 percent (Note 5g, Daftar 5/88, PDF p. 105); a sale to an outsider would not reduce NCI.
11. Upstream note: partners are not NCI

Most of PHE's blocks are shared with other contractors. Those partners hold participating interests in a production sharing contract, which is a joint arrangement, so each party records its own share of assets, liabilities, revenue and costs. Their shares never enter PHE's NCI. The many companies held at 99 percent fit Indonesian company law, which requires a limited company to be founded by at least two persons and to restore two shareholders within six months if it falls to one (UU 40/2007 art. 7(1) and 7(5)–(6)).
: the parent's contributed equity, and common-control restructurings.
: where differences from transactions with NCI may sit.
: dividends to the parent's owners and the profit attributable to them.
: translation and hedge reserves, their attribution and recycling.
: associates and joint ventures, including a retained interest after loss of control.

The 2024 equity adjustment (NCI −53,470, parent +6,138) has no disclosed transaction or cash flow. Reading it as a purchase or redemption of NCI shares rests on the numbers alone, and any cash paid would sit in an undisclosed financing line. Linking the investing receipt and the Note 42 gain to TPDC's call option (Note 5g) is also inference; PHE does not connect them.

Elnusa's translation explains about 7,242 of NCI's OCI loss of 8,487. The other 1,245 is unexplained (hedge losses in subsidiaries with small outside stakes, or associates' OCI, are candidates); PHE does not attribute OCI by subsidiary.

No PSAK 112 para. 12 table of subsidiaries with material NCI was found in PHE's FS (searched for NCI, KNP and the subsidiaries' names). With 674,235 of NCI spread over Elnusa, M&P and Badak NGL, at least one is likely material, so the disclosure is either elsewhere or missing.

Who holds the 1 percent stakes in PHE's 99 percent subsidiaries is not disclosed. If they are held by other PHE companies they are not NCI at all. PT Pertamina Pedeve Indonesia holds 0.0032 percent of PHE itself (Note 32, Daftar 5/147, PDF p. 164), which makes it the likely nominee; if so, the stakes are NCI in PHE's statements though inside Pertamina's group. The ownership percentages of M&P (71.09 percent) and Elnusa (about 51 percent) were checked only against secondary and older sources.

The banking rules in section 9 (P2SK art. 68, POJK 12/2023 thresholds and two-year window) were seen only in news reports, and a revision of P2SK was under discussion in 2026. The presentation of temporary syirkah funds on consolidation follow general practice, not a checked rule.

presentation.deck: The theory of non-controlling interests from the control test to loss of control, worked through PHE's partly owned subsidiaries and set beside the industries where outside owners take other forms
key_takeaways: Consolidation adds 100 percent of a controlled subsidiary's assets, liabilities, income and expenses, even when the parent owns less than all of it. The non-controlling interest (NCI) is the outside owners' share of that subsidiary's equity. It is equity of the group, presented separately from the parent's owners' equity, and it absorbs its share of profit, other comprehensive income (OCI) and losses, even into a deficit.

At acquisition the acquirer chooses, deal by deal, to measure NCI at fair value or at its proportionate share of the identifiable net assets (PSAK 103). At the acquisition date the choice changes goodwill and NCI by the same amount and nothing else.

While control lasts, buying from or selling to the NCI is a transaction between owners. No gain or loss is recognised, no new goodwill arises, and the difference goes to the parent's equity. Only gaining or losing control is remeasured through profit or loss.

title: Oil and Gas Properties, Net: Finding Costs, Development, Depletion, Decommissioning and Impairment
snippet: The theory of upstream asset accounting from the first seismic line to the last plugged well, worked through PHE's numbers and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • Upstream asset accounting answers four questions in order: which finding costs become an asset, what a field costs to develop, how that cost is released as barrels are produced, and whether the cost left will come back. The cost policy settles the first, PSAK 216 the second, units-of-production depletion the third, and the impairment test of PSAK 236 the fourth.

  • Successful efforts and full cost split the same exploration spending differently. Successful efforts expenses a dry hole at once, while full cost keeps it on the balance sheet and releases it with the successful barrels. Under PSAK 106 full cost survives only inside exploration and evaluation.

  • The cost of a field includes the present value of the cost to remove it. Decommissioning enters the asset on day one, grows each year as a finance cost, and a change in its estimate adjusts the asset's cost, in most cases leaving profit untouched. PHE carries 17,905,149 of oil and gas properties, net, with 2,242,412 of accumulated impairment against them.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report oil and gas properties, net, of 17,905,149 at 31 December 2024 against 16,130,290 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 58.8 percent of total assets and 79.9 percent of non-current assets (52.2 and 76.8 percent a year earlier). This page also covers two profit or loss lines the asset feeds: exploration expenses, 465,422 against 266,573 (Note 36), and depreciation, depletion and amortisation (DD&A), 2,443,000 against 2,856,853 (Notes 12, 16a, 17) (Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14).

After reading it a student should be able to follow upstream spending from exploration to production, record it in journals, compute depletion and a decommissioning provision, build the exploration and DD&A lines from the notes, and see where other industries differ.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Reserves are in million barrels of oil equivalent (MMBOE, gas converted to oil barrels by energy content), so USD thousand per MMBOE equals USD per barrel. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

Intermediate texts barely touch exploration accounting or depletion by reserves, so the order is that of an extractive-industries text, with Kieso's chapters on property, intangibles and provisions where they apply.

1. What oil and gas properties are

Oil and gas properties are the capitalised cost of finding, developing and later removing the wells and facilities that produce hydrocarbons. The line exists because upstream spending buys barrels that come out over decades. Expensing it when paid would show a loss in the years of drilling and pure profit in the years of production, so accrual accounting holds the cost as an asset and releases it as the barrels are sold (Kieso's expense-recognition principle).

The life of a field has four phases, and each has its own rule.

  • Acquisition: buying the right to explore. Under Indonesian production sharing contracts (PSCs) this includes the signature bonus paid to the government on signing.

  • Exploration and evaluation (E&E): seismic surveys, exploration wells and appraisal wells drilled to measure a discovery. PSAK 106 Exploration for and Evaluation of Mineral Resources (formerly PSAK 64, IFRS 6) governs this phase.

  • Development: production wells, platforms, pipelines and processing plant. These are property, plant and equipment under PSAK 216 (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16).

  • Production: the cost is depleted, and at the end the field is decommissioned under PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37).

PHE's Note 17 mirrors these phases (Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126). At the end of 2024 its cost of 41,972,216 sat in wells (26,793,570), installations (10,917,429), signature and production bonuses (1,034,863), and two assets-under-construction accounts, exploration and evaluation wells (946,010) and development wells (2,280,344).

The line is non-current in full (PSAK 201.66, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). Use sets the boundary with fixed assets (fixed-assets-net); a shore base serves the company generally, a well serves one field.

2. Exploration and evaluation: successful efforts and full cost

Exploration is a lottery with expensive tickets, and the accounting question is what to do with the losing ones. A company may drill five exploration wells to find one field. Are the four dry holes a cost of the one field, or a loss?

Two answers. Successful efforts says a cost is an asset only if it found something. Exploration wells are capitalised while their result is pending; a well that finds proved reserves stays as an asset, and a dry hole is expensed. Full cost says the dry holes were the price of the discovery. Every finding cost in a large pool, often a whole country, is capitalised and depleted against all production from that pool.

Kieso's research and development rule follows the same logic. Research is expensed because no specific asset can yet be shown, and development is capitalised once feasibility is demonstrated. Geological and geophysical work sits on the research side. Successful efforts applies that test well by well; full cost treats the whole programme as one development.

What PSAK 106 allows. IFRS 6 lets each entity choose which expenditures it recognises as E&E assets and apply that policy consistently, from rights to explore and studies to exploratory drilling (para. 9). Development expenditure may not be held as E&E (para. 10). An E&E asset stops being classified as such once technical feasibility and commercial viability are demonstrable, and it must be tested for impairment before it is reclassified (para. 17). So a full-cost-style policy is possible, but only inside E&E. Once a field is developed its cost falls under PSAK 216 and PSAK 236, which work asset by asset or cash-generating unit by unit, and a country-wide pool is no longer allowed.

PHE uses successful efforts. Geological and geophysical costs, including seismic, are expensed; exploration well costs are capitalised as "assets under construction – exploration and evaluation wells" until it is known whether they found proved reserves; a successful well is tested for impairment and transferred to development wells, and a dry hole is charged to profit (Note 3m(i), Daftar 5/56, PDF p. 73).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary spends 10,000 on seismic over a new block in 2024 and drills two exploration wells. Well A, 40,000, finds proved reserves. Well B, 25,000, finds water.

Successful efforts

Full cost (US pool)

Seismic

Dr Exploration expense 10,000 / Cr Cash 10,000

Dr Oil and gas properties, cost pool 10,000 / Cr Cash 10,000

Drilling both wells

Dr AUC – E&E wells 65,000 / Cr Cash 65,000

Dr Oil and gas properties, cost pool 65,000 / Cr Cash 65,000

Well B dry

Dr Exploration expense, dry hole 25,000 / Cr AUC – E&E wells 25,000

no entry

Well A commercial, after impairment test

Dr AUC – development wells 40,000 / Cr AUC – E&E wells 40,000

no entry

Successful efforts: 2024 expense = 10,000 + 25,000 = 35,000; asset = 40,000

Full cost: 2024 expense = 0; asset = 75,000

Over the field's life both methods expense the full 75,000, and US full cost moves 35,000 of expense from 2024 into the production years. Under PSAK 106 a full-cost-style policy could hold the 35,000 only while the area is still in E&E. At reclassification the costs face the para. 17 test, and the standard does not say a dry hole may be carried into a field's development cost. Section 8 shows what PHE's exploration expense contains.

When E&E is impaired. PSAK 106 replaces the usual impairment indicators with its own list (paras. 19–20): the right to explore has expired or soon will and is not expected to be renewed, no further substantive exploration in the area is budgeted or planned, exploration has not found commercially viable quantities and the entity has decided to stop, or a development is likely but the E&E cost will not be recovered in full. E&E assets may be grouped for the test, but no group may be larger than an operating segment (para. 21).

3. Development costs

Once a field is declared commercial, its cost is built up the way Kieso builds the cost of any fixed asset, from everything spent to bring the asset to the condition and location needed for use. That means the purchase price of casing, wellheads and equipment, less discounts, plus transport, installation and testing, plus the rig time and services to drill the wells.

Dry development wells. A development well that disappoints is still capitalised. PHE's policy capitalises "unsuccessful development wells" into development wells (Note 3m(ii), Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74). The field's reserves are already proved, so a poor development well is treated as part of the cost of draining a known reservoir; a dry exploration well is a search that found nothing.

Borrowing costs. Interest paid while a platform is built is part of the price of having it ready, so PSAK 223 (formerly PSAK 26, IAS 23) capitalises the borrowing costs of a qualifying asset; the weighted-average accumulated expenditures method is worked through on the fixed-assets-net page. PHE capitalised 2,277 of borrowing costs on the Jambaran-Tiung Biru (JTB) gas development financing in 2024, against 11,321 in 2023 (Note 17, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126).

Later spending. Kieso sorts spending after acquisition into additions, improvements and replacements, which are capitalised because they add future benefit, and ordinary repairs, which are expensed. In a field the same test separates a workover that restores a well's flow, which is repair and maintenance, from a sidetrack or recompletion that reaches new reservoir and adds reserves, which is an improvement.

4. Depletion by units of production

A field's cost should be released in proportion to the barrels it gives up. Straight-line depreciation would charge the same amount in a year when the field is shut for maintenance as in a year at peak output. The units-of-production (UOP) method charges each barrel the same share of cost.

Depletion for the year = cost to deplete × production in the year / (reserves at year end + production in the year)

Cost to deplete is the carrying amount before the year's depletion. The denominator is the reserves at the start of the year, rebuilt from the year-end estimate so that revisions made during the year count.

Which reserves. The reserve base must fit the cost being divided. Proved developed reserves can be produced through wells and facilities already in place, so they match cost already spent. Proved undeveloped reserves need further wells; if they are in the base, the future development costs (FDC) to reach them must be added to the cost. PHE depletes production assets "on the basis of proved reserves, from the date of commercial production of the respective field" (Note 3m(iii), Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74), and defines proved reserves as developed plus undeveloped (Note 4b(i), Daftar 5/78, PDF p. 95). The policy does not say whether FDC is added.

For example (illustration), one PHE field enters 2024 with a cost to deplete of 600,000. It produces 5 MMBOE. At year end its proved developed reserves are 45 MMBOE and its total proved reserves 70 MMBOE, with FDC of 150,000 to drill the undeveloped part.

Proved developed base

Proved base with FDC

Rate

600,000 / (45 + 5) = 12.00 per BOE

(600,000 + 150,000) / (70 + 5) = 10.00 per BOE

2024 depletion

12.00 × 5 = 60,000

10.00 × 5 = 50,000

Without the FDC, the proved base would give 600,000 / 75 = 8.00 per BOE, spreading today's cost over barrels that still need money to reach. If maintenance had halved output to 2.5 MMBOE, UOP on the developed base would charge 30,000, while straight-line over a ten-year remaining life would still charge 600,000 / 10 = 60,000.

Dr Depreciation, depletion and amortisation 60,000 / Cr Accumulated depletion 60,000

PHE's 2024 depletion of oil and gas properties was 2,187,085 (Note 17; section 8).

Reserve revisions. A new reservoir study is new information, so a revision is a change in accounting estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8), applied from the period of the change onward, with no restatement of past depletion. For example (illustration), the field enters 2025 at 600,000 − 60,000 = 540,000 and again produces 5 MMBOE. Its developed reserves would have been 40 MMBOE at the end of 2025, but a study cuts them to 30.

Without the revision: 540,000 / (40 + 5) × 5 = 60,000

With the revision: 540,000 / (30 + 5) = 15.43 per BOE; × 5 = 77,143

Extra 2025 depletion = 77,143 − 60,000 = 17,143

5. Decommissioning

Installing a well or platform creates an obligation to plug, remove and restore at the end of field life. Kieso records it as an environmental provision with a matching asset. The removal cost has no future benefit of its own, so it becomes part of the asset's cost. PSAK 237 recognises a provision when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable and the amount can be estimated reliably, at the best estimate discounted where the effect is material. PSAK 216.16(c) adds the same amount to the asset.

Two things happen afterwards. First, the discount unwinds. Each year the provision grows by the discount rate as settlement approaches, and the increase is charged as a finance cost. Second, estimates change. Under ISAK 101 (formerly ISAK 9, IFRIC 1), for an asset carried at cost, a change in the expected cost, its timing or the discount rate is added to or deducted from the asset's cost in the period of the change; a deduction may not exceed the asset's carrying amount, and any excess goes to profit. An addition is a sign the asset may not be recoverable, so the asset is considered for impairment. PHE's policy states all of this (Note 3o, Daftar 5/60, PDF p. 77).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary installs a wellhead platform on 1 January 2024, expected to be removed at the end of 2038 for 50,000, discounted at 4 percent over 15 years. At the end of 2025 the removal estimate rises to 60,000 after rig rates climb, with 13 years left.

Initial provision = 50,000 / 1.04^15 = 27,763

2024 unwinding = 27,763 × 4% = 1,111; provision = 28,874

2025 unwinding = 28,874 × 4% = 1,155; provision before revision = 30,029

Revised provision = 60,000 / 1.04^13 = 36,034; increase = 36,034 − 30,029 = 6,005

Event

Debit

Credit

1 Jan 2024, installation

Oil and gas properties 27,763

Provision for decommissioning 27,763

31 Dec 2024 and 2025, unwinding

Finance cost 1,111 and 1,155

Provision for decommissioning 1,111 and 1,155

31 Dec 2025, revised estimate

Oil and gas properties 6,005

Provision for decommissioning 6,005

The 6,005 does not touch 2025 profit. It is depleted over the platform's remaining barrels, and the impairment test of section 6 decides whether the higher cost is still recoverable. When the work is done, any difference between the provision and the amount paid is a gain or loss.

PHE's provision stood at 3,826,222 at the end of 2024 (Note 29, Daftar 5/145, PDF p. 162). Its 2024 accretion of 119,925 on an opening balance of 3,784,917 is 3.17 percent, which suggests the average discount rate across its fields is of that order.

6. Impairment

Depletion allocates cost without asking whether it will come back, and the impairment test of PSAK 236 (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) asks. When there is an indication of impairment, the carrying amount of a cash-generating unit (CGU), the smallest group of assets with largely independent cash inflows, is compared with its recoverable amount, the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. Oil and gas assets rarely generate cash on their own, and PHE treats its participating interest in each block as one CGU (Note 17, Daftar 5/110, PDF p. 127). Its 2024 indicators included a lower crude price assumption, a higher discount rate, a reserve downgrade and a proposed divestment, and it discounted at 10 percent.

The largest 2024 loss was on the Mahakam block, written down by 140,968 from 1,256,237 to a recoverable amount of 1,115,269 (Note 17, Daftar 5/111, PDF p. 128). A loss can later be reversed, up to the carrying amount the asset would have had without it, which US full cost does not allow (section 7). For the full PSAK 236 test, see the Impairment of non-financial assets essay.

7. Oil and gas properties across industries

Mining. PSAK 106 covers all mineral resources, so a coal or nickel miner makes the same E&E policy choice and depletes mine development cost by units of production over ore reserves. Open-pit mining must also strip waste rock to reach ore. Under ISAK 120 (formerly ISAK 29, IFRIC 20) production-phase stripping that yields ore now is inventory cost, and stripping that improves access to ore later is a stripping activity asset, allocated by a production measure. For example (illustration), a miner spends 10,000 to remove 5,000,000 tonnes of waste while mining 1,000,000 tonnes of ore, where the expected ratio for this part of the pit is 3 tonnes of waste per tonne of ore.

Expected waste = 1,000,000 × 3 = 3,000,000 tonnes; excess = 2,000,000 tonnes

Stripping activity asset = 10,000 × 2,000,000 / 5,000,000 = 4,000; inventory = 6,000

United States full cost and the ceiling test. US GAAP still allows full cost beyond exploration, with country pools capped at a ceiling, broadly proved reserves' future net cash flows discounted at 10 percent plus unproved property costs, after tax. For example (illustration), a pool with 900,000 of capitalised cost, a discounted proved-reserve value of 800,000 and unproved costs of 50,000 is written down by 900,000 − (800,000 + 50,000) = 50,000, before tax. A ceiling write-down cannot be reversed when prices recover. PSAK 236 allows reversal and tests far smaller units than a country.

Joint operations. Most upstream assets are held with partners. Under PSAK 111 Joint Arrangements (formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11) a party to a joint operation recognises its share of the assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses line by line. PHE applies that rule (Note 3y, Daftar 5/74, PDF p. 91). For example (illustration), if the operator of a block in which PHE holds 30 percent spends 200,000 on development wells, PHE's oil and gas properties rise by 200,000 × 30% = 60,000, funded through cash calls.

9. Upstream note: who owns the wells

Under a cost-recovery PSC, "materials, supplies and equipment acquired by the PSC Contractors … belongs to the Government", while the contractor may use them until SKK Migas, the upstream regulator, approves them as surplus or abandoned (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). PHE still carries the wells and facilities. An asset under the Conceptual Framework is a resource the entity controls, control is the present ability to direct its use and obtain its benefits, and the 1989 Framework already said that ownership is not essential. A plausible reading is that the contractor directs the use of the wells and recovers their cost, though PHE does not explain why it recognises them.

Annual cost recovery under the PSC comprises the year's non-capital costs, depreciation of capital costs, and earlier unrecovered costs (Note 2a(iii), Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). Book depletion and PSC depreciation follow different schedules, and the gap between them is a temporary difference for deferred tax. Under gross split contracts there is no cost recovery, and the old PSC assets, now owned by the Directorate General of State Assets (DJKN), are used under a lease scheme (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34).

  • inventories-net: materials issued to development wells.

  • PHE's policy says depletion uses "proved reserves" and defines them as developed plus undeveloped; whether PHE adds future development costs to the base is not disclosed, so the FDC treatment shown is the textbook rule and may differ from PHE's practice.

  • The 3.17 percent "average discount rate" is accretion over the opening provision, so only a rough figure. The reading that Note 29's 78,620 is a reduction rests on footing alone; PHE may have omitted a line rather than a bracket.

content.text: Upstream asset accounting answers four questions in order: which finding costs become an asset, what a field costs to develop, how that cost is released as barrels are produced, and whether the cost left will come back. The cost policy settles the first, PSAK 216 the second, units-of-production depletion the third, and the impairment test of PSAK 236 the fourth.

Successful efforts and full cost split the same exploration spending differently. Successful efforts expenses a dry hole at once, while full cost keeps it on the balance sheet and releases it with the successful barrels. Under PSAK 106 full cost survives only inside exploration and evaluation.

The cost of a field includes the present value of the cost to remove it. Decommissioning enters the asset on day one, grows each year as a finance cost, and a change in its estimate adjusts the asset's cost, in most cases leaving profit untouched. PHE carries 17,905,149 of oil and gas properties, net, with 2,242,412 of accumulated impairment against them.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report oil and gas properties, net, of 17,905,149 at 31 December 2024 against 16,130,290 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 58.8 percent of total assets and 79.9 percent of non-current assets (52.2 and 76.8 percent a year earlier). This page also covers two profit or loss lines the asset feeds: exploration expenses, 465,422 against 266,573 (Note 36), and depreciation, depletion and amortisation (DD&A), 2,443,000 against 2,856,853 (Notes 12, 16a, 17) (Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14).

After reading it a student should be able to follow upstream spending from exploration to production, record it in journals, compute depletion and a decommissioning provision, build the exploration and DD&A lines from the notes, and see where other industries differ.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Reserves are in million barrels of oil equivalent (MMBOE, gas converted to oil barrels by energy content), so USD thousand per MMBOE equals USD per barrel. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

Intermediate texts barely touch exploration accounting or depletion by reserves, so the order is that of an extractive-industries text, with Kieso's chapters on property, intangibles and provisions where they apply.
1. What oil and gas properties are

Oil and gas properties are the capitalised cost of finding, developing and later removing the wells and facilities that produce hydrocarbons. The line exists because upstream spending buys barrels that come out over decades. Expensing it when paid would show a loss in the years of drilling and pure profit in the years of production, so accrual accounting holds the cost as an asset and releases it as the barrels are sold (Kieso's expense-recognition principle).
The life of a field has four phases, and each has its own rule.
: buying the right to explore. Under Indonesian production sharing contracts (PSCs) this includes the signature bonus paid to the government on signing.
: seismic surveys, exploration wells and appraisal wells drilled to measure a discovery. PSAK 106
Exploration for and Evaluation of Mineral Resources
: production wells, platforms, pipelines and processing plant. These are property, plant and equipment under PSAK 216 (formerly PSAK 16, IAS 16).
: the cost is depleted, and at the end the field is decommissioned under PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37).

PHE's Note 17 mirrors these phases (Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126). At the end of 2024 its cost of 41,972,216 sat in wells (26,793,570), installations (10,917,429), signature and production bonuses (1,034,863), and two assets-under-construction accounts, exploration and evaluation wells (946,010) and development wells (2,280,344).
The line is non-current in full (PSAK 201.66, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). Use sets the boundary with fixed assets (
); a shore base serves the company generally, a well serves one field.
2. Exploration and evaluation: successful efforts and full cost

Exploration is a lottery with expensive tickets, and the accounting question is what to do with the losing ones. A company may drill five exploration wells to find one field. Are the four dry holes a cost of the one field, or a loss?
says a cost is an asset only if it found something. Exploration wells are capitalised while their result is pending; a well that finds proved reserves stays as an asset, and a dry hole is expensed.
says the dry holes were the price of the discovery. Every finding cost in a large pool, often a whole country, is capitalised and depleted against all production from that pool.

Kieso's research and development rule follows the same logic. Research is expensed because no specific asset can yet be shown, and development is capitalised once feasibility is demonstrated. Geological and geophysical work sits on the research side. Successful efforts applies that test well by well; full cost treats the whole programme as one development.

IFRS 6 lets each entity choose which expenditures it recognises as E&E assets and apply that policy consistently, from rights to explore and studies to exploratory drilling (para. 9). Development expenditure may not be held as E&E (para. 10). An E&E asset stops being classified as such once technical feasibility and commercial viability are demonstrable, and it must be tested for impairment before it is reclassified (para. 17). So a full-cost-style policy is possible, but only inside E&E. Once a field is developed its cost falls under PSAK 216 and PSAK 236, which work asset by asset or cash-generating unit by unit, and a country-wide pool is no longer allowed.

PHE uses successful efforts. Geological and geophysical costs, including seismic, are expensed; exploration well costs are capitalised as "assets under construction – exploration and evaluation wells" until it is known whether they found proved reserves; a successful well is tested for impairment and transferred to development wells, and a dry hole is charged to profit (Note 3m(i), Daftar 5/56, PDF p. 73).
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary spends 10,000 on seismic over a new block in 2024 and drills two exploration wells. Well A, 40,000, finds proved reserves. Well B, 25,000, finds water.
Dr Oil and gas properties, cost pool 10,000 / Cr Cash 10,000
Dr AUC – E&E wells 65,000 / Cr Cash 65,000
Dr Oil and gas properties, cost pool 65,000 / Cr Cash 65,000
Dr Exploration expense, dry hole 25,000 / Cr AUC – E&E wells 25,000
Well A commercial, after impairment test
Dr AUC – development wells 40,000 / Cr AUC – E&E wells 40,000

Over the field's life both methods expense the full 75,000, and US full cost moves 35,000 of expense from 2024 into the production years. Under PSAK 106 a full-cost-style policy could hold the 35,000 only while the area is still in E&E. At reclassification the costs face the para. 17 test, and the standard does not say a dry hole may be carried into a field's development cost. Section 8 shows what PHE's exploration expense contains.

PSAK 106 replaces the usual impairment indicators with its own list (paras. 19–20): the right to explore has expired or soon will and is not expected to be renewed, no further substantive exploration in the area is budgeted or planned, exploration has not found commercially viable quantities and the entity has decided to stop, or a development is likely but the E&E cost will not be recovered in full. E&E assets may be grouped for the test, but no group may be larger than an operating segment (para. 21).

Once a field is declared commercial, its cost is built up the way Kieso builds the cost of any fixed asset, from everything spent to bring the asset to the condition and location needed for use. That means the purchase price of casing, wellheads and equipment, less discounts, plus transport, installation and testing, plus the rig time and services to drill the wells.

A development well that disappoints is still capitalised. PHE's policy capitalises "unsuccessful development wells" into development wells (Note 3m(ii), Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74). The field's reserves are already proved, so a poor development well is treated as part of the cost of draining a known reservoir; a dry exploration well is a search that found nothing.
Interest paid while a platform is built is part of the price of having it ready, so PSAK 223 (formerly PSAK 26, IAS 23) capitalises the borrowing costs of a
; the weighted-average accumulated expenditures method is worked through on the
page. PHE capitalised 2,277 of borrowing costs on the Jambaran-Tiung Biru (JTB) gas development financing in 2024, against 11,321 in 2023 (Note 17, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126).

Kieso sorts spending after acquisition into additions, improvements and replacements, which are capitalised because they add future benefit, and ordinary repairs, which are expensed. In a field the same test separates a
that restores a well's flow, which is repair and maintenance, from a
that reaches new reservoir and adds reserves, which is an improvement.

A field's cost should be released in proportion to the barrels it gives up. Straight-line depreciation would charge the same amount in a year when the field is shut for maintenance as in a year at peak output. The
(UOP) method charges each barrel the same share of cost.
Depletion for the year = cost to deplete × production in the year / (reserves at year end + production in the year)
is the carrying amount before the year's depletion. The denominator is the reserves at the start of the year, rebuilt from the year-end estimate so that revisions made during the year count.
The reserve base must fit the cost being divided.
reserves can be produced through wells and facilities already in place, so they match cost already spent.
reserves need further wells; if they are in the base, the

(FDC) to reach them must be added to the cost. PHE depletes production assets "on the basis of proved reserves, from the date of commercial production of the respective field" (Note 3m(iii), Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74), and defines proved reserves as developed plus undeveloped (Note 4b(i), Daftar 5/78, PDF p. 95). The policy does not say whether FDC is added.

For example (illustration), one PHE field enters 2024 with a cost to deplete of 600,000. It produces 5 MMBOE. At year end its proved developed reserves are 45 MMBOE and its total proved reserves 70 MMBOE, with FDC of 150,000 to drill the undeveloped part.

Without the FDC, the proved base would give 600,000 / 75 = 8.00 per BOE, spreading today's cost over barrels that still need money to reach. If maintenance had halved output to 2.5 MMBOE, UOP on the developed base would charge 30,000, while straight-line over a ten-year remaining life would still charge 600,000 / 10 = 60,000.
Dr Depreciation, depletion and amortisation 60,000 / Cr Accumulated depletion 60,000
PHE's 2024 depletion of oil and gas properties was 2,187,085 (Note 17; section 8).

A new reservoir study is new information, so a revision is a change in accounting estimate under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8), applied from the period of the change onward, with no restatement of past depletion. For example (illustration), the field enters 2025 at 600,000 − 60,000 = 540,000 and again produces 5 MMBOE. Its developed reserves would have been 40 MMBOE at the end of 2025, but a study cuts them to 30.

Installing a well or platform creates an obligation to plug, remove and restore at the end of field life. Kieso records it as an environmental provision with a matching asset. The removal cost has no future benefit of its own, so it becomes part of the asset's cost. PSAK 237 recognises a provision when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow is probable and the amount can be estimated reliably, at the best estimate discounted where the effect is material. PSAK 216.16(c) adds the same amount to the asset.
Two things happen afterwards. First, the discount

. Each year the provision grows by the discount rate as settlement approaches, and the increase is charged as a finance cost. Second, estimates change. Under ISAK 101 (formerly ISAK 9, IFRIC 1), for an asset carried at cost, a change in the expected cost, its timing or the discount rate is added to or deducted from the asset's cost in the period of the change; a deduction may not exceed the asset's carrying amount, and any excess goes to profit. An addition is a sign the asset may not be recoverable, so the asset is considered for impairment. PHE's policy states all of this (Note 3o, Daftar 5/60, PDF p. 77).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary installs a wellhead platform on 1 January 2024, expected to be removed at the end of 2038 for 50,000, discounted at 4 percent over 15 years. At the end of 2025 the removal estimate rises to 60,000 after rig rates climb, with 13 years left.

The 6,005 does not touch 2025 profit. It is depleted over the platform's remaining barrels, and the impairment test of section 6 decides whether the higher cost is still recoverable. When the work is done, any difference between the provision and the amount paid is a gain or loss.

PHE's provision stood at 3,826,222 at the end of 2024 (Note 29, Daftar 5/145, PDF p. 162). Its 2024 accretion of 119,925 on an opening balance of 3,784,917 is 3.17 percent, which suggests the average discount rate across its fields is of that order.

Depletion allocates cost without asking whether it will come back, and the impairment test of PSAK 236 (formerly PSAK 48, IAS 36) asks. When there is an indication of impairment, the carrying amount of a
(CGU), the smallest group of assets with largely independent cash inflows, is compared with its

, the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. Oil and gas assets rarely generate cash on their own, and PHE treats its participating interest in each block as one CGU (Note 17, Daftar 5/110, PDF p. 127). Its 2024 indicators included a lower crude price assumption, a higher discount rate, a reserve downgrade and a proposed divestment, and it discounted at 10 percent.

The largest 2024 loss was on the Mahakam block, written down by 140,968 from 1,256,237 to a recoverable amount of 1,115,269 (Note 17, Daftar 5/111, PDF p. 128). A loss can later be reversed, up to the carrying amount the asset would have had without it, which US full cost does not allow (section 7). For the full PSAK 236 test, see the Impairment of non-financial assets essay.
7. Oil and gas properties across industries

PSAK 106 covers all mineral resources, so a coal or nickel miner makes the same E&E policy choice and depletes mine development cost by units of production over ore reserves. Open-pit mining must also strip waste rock to reach ore. Under ISAK 120 (formerly ISAK 29, IFRIC 20) production-phase stripping that yields ore now is inventory cost, and stripping that improves access to ore later is a

, allocated by a production measure. For example (illustration), a miner spends 10,000 to remove 5,000,000 tonnes of waste while mining 1,000,000 tonnes of ore, where the expected ratio for this part of the pit is 3 tonnes of waste per tonne of ore.
United States full cost and the ceiling test.
US GAAP still allows full cost beyond exploration, with country pools capped at a

, broadly proved reserves' future net cash flows discounted at 10 percent plus unproved property costs, after tax. For example (illustration), a pool with 900,000 of capitalised cost, a discounted proved-reserve value of 800,000 and unproved costs of 50,000 is written down by 900,000 − (800,000 + 50,000) = 50,000, before tax. A ceiling write-down cannot be reversed when prices recover. PSAK 236 allows reversal and tests far smaller units than a country.
Most upstream assets are held with partners. Under PSAK 111
(formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11) a party to a

recognises its share of the assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses line by line. PHE applies that rule (Note 3y, Daftar 5/74, PDF p. 91). For example (illustration), if the operator of a block in which PHE holds 30 percent spends 200,000 on development wells, PHE's oil and gas properties rise by 200,000 × 30% = 60,000, funded through cash calls.
PHE gives the movement table PSAK 216 asks for (Note 17, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126).

presentation.deck: The theory of upstream asset accounting from the first seismic line to the last plugged well, worked through PHE's numbers and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: Upstream asset accounting answers four questions in order: which finding costs become an asset, what a field costs to develop, how that cost is released as barrels are produced, and whether the cost left will come back. The cost policy settles the first, PSAK 216 the second, units-of-production depletion the third, and the impairment test of PSAK 236 the fourth.

Successful efforts and full cost split the same exploration spending differently. Successful efforts expenses a dry hole at once, while full cost keeps it on the balance sheet and releases it with the successful barrels. Under PSAK 106 full cost survives only inside exploration and evaluation.

The cost of a field includes the present value of the cost to remove it. Decommissioning enters the asset on day one, grows each year as a finance cost, and a change in its estimate adjusts the asset's cost, in most cases leaving profit untouched. PHE carries 17,905,149 of oil and gas properties, net, with 2,242,412 of accumulated impairment against them.

title: Other Comprehensive Income: Why It Exists, What It Holds and When It Comes Back
snippet: The theory of other comprehensive income from its purpose to recycling, worked through PHE's translation and hedge reserves and set beside the industries where OCI moves equity most
content:
In brief

  • Other comprehensive income (OCI) holds gains and losses on remeasuring assets and liabilities that the standards keep out of profit or loss, because putting them there would make profit a worse guide to performance. Profit plus OCI is comprehensive income, every change in equity in the period except transactions with owners and retrospective adjustments.

  • Each OCI item is either recycled or not. Translation differences on foreign operations, cash flow hedge results and fair value changes on debt investments at FVOCI later leave OCI, mostly by reclassification to profit or loss. Revaluation surpluses, remeasurements of defined benefit plans and fair value changes on equity investments at FVOCI never are, though they may be moved within equity to retained earnings.

  • When an item is recycled, the reclassification adjustment takes it out of OCI in the same period it enters profit or loss, so comprehensive income counts it once. The tax on each item follows it into OCI.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report accumulated other comprehensive income of 103,851 at 31 December 2024 against 132,724 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; "Daftar" is the printed page). The balance is 0.69 percent of total equity of 15,107,352 (0.94 percent a year earlier). The flow behind it is in the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income: translation adjustments of −14,810 (2023: 2,595), cash flow hedges, net of tax, of −21,940 (2023: −2,649), and a remeasurement of the employee benefit liability of −610 (2023: 1,430), a total of −37,360 (Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14).

After reading it a student should be able to say why an item goes to OCI, record translation, hedge, FVOCI and revaluation entries, and follow an amount into accumulated OCI and, where required, back to profit or loss.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. Why other comprehensive income exists

OCI exists because some changes in the value of assets and liabilities say little about how the period went. The lecture notes on Kieso's chapter 4 open with the income statement's purpose, to evaluate past performance and predict future performance. A gain that comes only from the rupiah weakening, or from rates moving a ten-year swap, makes that prediction harder, yet leaving such changes off the balance sheet would carry assets and liabilities at stale amounts.

The standards resolve this with a second section of the performance statement. The 2018 Conceptual Framework (in Indonesia the KKPK, Kerangka Konseptual Pelaporan Keuangan) makes profit or loss the primary source of information about performance and lets the IASB, standard by standard and only in exceptional circumstances, send a change in the current value of an asset or liability to OCI where that makes profit more relevant or more faithful (paras. 7.15–7.17). It presumes that OCI is recycled later when that improves profit for that period (para. 7.19). No general principle selects the items.

The two sections add up to comprehensive income, the change in equity from everything except transactions with owners in their capacity as owners (PSAK 201.7, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). If every non-owner change in equity passes through one statement, nothing reaches equity unreported, apart from retrospective corrections of opening balances (PSAK 208) and transfers between components. PHE's 2024 figures show the identity.

Profit for the year 3,121,035 + OCI (−14,810 − 21,940 − 610) = 3,121,035 − 37,360 = 3,083,675 total comprehensive income

2. Presenting OCI: the two groups and reclassification adjustments

An entity presents profit or loss and OCI either in one statement with two sections or in two statements, the second starting from profit (PSAK 201.10A), as the lecture notes on chapter 17 set out. PHE uses one statement (Daftar 2/1–2/2, PDF pp. 14–15). Within the OCI section the items are grouped by what will happen to them later (PSAK 201.82A):

Will not be reclassified to profit or loss

May be reclassified to profit or loss

Revaluation surplus on fixed assets and intangibles (PSAK 216, PSAK 238)

Translation differences on foreign operations (PSAK 221)

Remeasurements of defined benefit plans (PSAK 219)

Effective portion of cash flow hedges and net investment hedges, and the cost of hedging (PSAK 109)

Fair value changes on equity investments designated at FVOCI (PSAK 109)

Fair value changes on debt investments at FVOCI (PSAK 109)

Own-credit changes on liabilities designated at fair value (PSAK 109)

Insurance finance income or expense, where the OCI option is taken (PSAK 117)

Share of associates' and joint ventures' OCI that will not be reclassified

Share of associates' and joint ventures' OCI that may be reclassified

A loss in the right-hand column is one that profit will see later; one on the left never reaches profit. OCI is also attributed between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests (para. 81B), because a subsidiary's OCI belongs partly to its outside shareholders. From 1 January 2027 PSAK 118 (IFRS 18) replaces PSAK 201; it keeps the OCI section and its two groups and changes mainly the profit-or-loss section above it.

Reclassification adjustments. When a recycled item is realised, its gain or loss enters profit, but it was already counted in comprehensive income when it went to OCI, so it must leave OCI in the same period. That deduction is a reclassification adjustment (paras. 7, 92–93). The lecture notes on Kieso's chapter 17 introduce it with debt investments held to collect and sell, measured at fair value through OCI (FVOCI). Interest at the effective rate, expected credit losses and exchange differences go to profit, the remaining fair value change to OCI, and on derecognition the cumulative OCI goes to profit (PSAK 109.4.1.2A, 5.7.10–5.7.11).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary buys US dollar bonds at par for 10,000 on 1 January 2024, coupon 5 percent paid annually, held to collect and sell. At the end of 2024 their fair value is 10,400. On 31 December 2025, after the second coupon, it sells them for 10,250.

Over two years comprehensive income is 1,250, the coupons of 1,000 plus 250 of gain over cost. Without the reclassification adjustment the total would be 1,500, with the 250 counted in 2024's OCI and again in 2025's profit.

The lecture notes need three corrections here. Their recycling example for "perusahaan Ali" reads "Fair value of portofilio : $34.000 / Less cost of portofolio : $34.000 / Unrealized gain : $4.000"; the cost must be 30,000. Their Saratoga sale states a price of "$95.000.000" but debits cash of $98,500,000, and its entry ("Cash $98.500.000 / Debt Investment $98.185.648,32 / Gain on sale of debt investment $314.351,68") removes only the amortised cost, leaving both the fair value adjustment and the unrealised holding gain on the books. Under PSAK 109 the asset leaves at fair value and the gain is reclassified at the sale, as in the last journal above. And their FVOCI impairment example follows an incurred-loss model; under PSAK 109 the expected credit loss on FVOCI debt is charged to profit with the other side in OCI, so the asset stays at fair value (para. 5.5.2).

3. Accumulated OCI in equity

What passes through OCI collects in equity as accumulated other comprehensive income, one of the components of equity in the lecture notes on Kieso's chapter 15. As those notes put it, the statement of changes in equity reconciles each component from opening to closing, with OCI analysed by item there or in the notes (PSAK 201.106–106A). Groups often keep one reserve per kind (translation, cash flow hedge, fair value, revaluation surplus), because the components leave equity by different routes: reclassification to profit or loss, transfer within equity to retained earnings for items never recycled, or, for hedges of non-financial items, removal into the asset's carrying amount.

PHE keeps one column for all of it. Its statement of changes in equity moves accumulated OCI from 132,724 to 103,851 by the owners' share of the year's OCI and nothing else (Daftar 3, PDF p. 16).

Owners' share of OCI = total comprehensive income to owners 2,972,602 − profit to owners 3,001,475 = −28,873

132,724 − 28,873 = 103,851

4. Translation of foreign operations

Translation differences arise because a group reports in one currency and some of its members keep their books in another. PSAK 221 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21) separates the functional currency, that of the primary economic environment that mainly drives an entity's prices and costs, from the presentation currency the statements are presented in. Foreign-currency monetary items are retranslated into the functional currency through profit or loss (see the Foreign Exchange Loss essay; PHE's foreign exchange loss, net, of 4,479 in 2024 is of this kind). Translation into another presentation currency is a separate step.

PHE's functional currency is the US dollar for every entity except Elnusa, whose functional currency is the rupiah, and the consolidated statements are presented in dollars (Note 3a and 3r, Daftar 5/29 and 5/66, PDF pp. 46 and 83). Elnusa's statements are translated as PSAK 221.39 requires, and PHE's policy restates it (Note 3r(iii), Daftar 5/67, PDF p. 84): assets and liabilities at the closing JISDOR rate, income and expenses at average rates, and "all of the resulting exchange differences are recognized in other comprehensive income".

Why the difference goes to OCI. It arises from translating opening net assets at a new closing rate and profit at average rates (para. 41). Neither changes Elnusa's rupiah cash flows, and nothing is realised until the parent sells, so the difference stays out of profit until disposal.

For example (illustration), take Elnusa's net assets in rupiah as Rp5,000,000 million at the start of 2024, about half its total assets before elimination of 621,898 (Note 1b), and its profit as Rp500,000 million, with no dividends. The closing rates implied by PHE's Note 48 are Rp15,439 per dollar for 2023 (6,377,542 / 413.080, trade payables) and Rp16,157 for 2024 (8,369,504 / 518.011) (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242). Assume an average rate for 2024 of Rp15,850.

Opening net assets = 5,000,000 / 15,439 = 323,855

Profit = 500,000 / 15,850 = 31,546

Closing net assets = 5,500,000 / 16,157 = 340,410

Translation difference = 340,410 − 323,855 − 31,546 = −14,991

From opening net assets: 5,000,000 × (1 / 16,157 − 1 / 15,439) = −14,392; from profit: 500,000 × (1 / 16,157 − 1 / 15,850) = −599

The rupiah lost 4.44 percent against the dollar (1 − 15,439 / 16,157), so the subsidiary is worth fewer dollars. PHE owns 51.10 percent of Elnusa (Note 1b, Daftar 5/6, PDF p. 23), so 48.90 percent of the difference belongs to non-controlling interests (para. 41).

NCI = 14,991 × 48.90% = 7,331; owners = 14,991 × 51.10% = 7,660

Dr OCI, translation adjustments 14,991 / Cr Net assets of Elnusa (translated) 14,991, attributed as 7,660 to the owners' translation reserve and 7,331 to NCI

Recycling on disposal. When the foreign operation is disposed of, the owners' cumulative translation difference is reclassified to profit or loss as part of the gain or loss on disposal (para. 48). Losing control counts as a disposal even if an interest is kept (para. 48A). The NCI's share is derecognised with the NCI and never recycled (para. 48B). If PHE sold all of Elnusa and the owners' reserve for it held −7,660, that loss would leave equity with the sale.

Dr Loss on disposal of subsidiary 7,660 / Cr Translation reserve 7,660

A partial sale that keeps control is a transaction with owners. The proportionate share of the reserve is re-attributed to NCI, not recycled (para. 48C; see the Non-controlling Interest essay).

5. Cash flow hedges

Hedge accounting exists to fix a timing mismatch. A derivative is measured at fair value through profit or loss (PSAK 109.4.1.4), while the hedged risk may be a cash flow that does not exist yet, such as next year's floating-rate interest, so the swap's value would swing through profit years before the interest it fixes. PSAK 109 offers three relationships (para. 6.5.2), all restated in PHE's policy (Note 3g(iv), Daftar 5/47–5/51, PDF pp. 64–68): a fair value hedge, where both sides go to profit; a cash flow hedge of variable cash flows from a recognised item or a highly probable forecast transaction; and a hedge of a net investment in a foreign operation, accounted for like a cash flow hedge.

Qualifying. The relationship must be designated and documented at inception and meet three effectiveness requirements: an economic relationship between hedged item and hedging instrument, credit risk not dominating the value changes, and a hedge ratio equal to the one actually used (para. 6.4.1).

The mechanism. For a cash flow hedge the cash flow hedge reserve is set at the lower, in absolute amounts, of the cumulative gain or loss on the instrument and the cumulative change in value of the hedged cash flows since inception. The part of the instrument's result that fits inside that limit is the effective portion and goes to OCI; the rest is ineffectiveness and goes to profit or loss (para. 6.5.11(a)–(c)). The hedged item's change is usually measured with a hypothetical derivative, a perfect swap on the hedged cash flows.

PHE's subsidiary PT Pertamina EP Cepu (PEPC, 99 percent owned) borrowed for the Jambaran–Tiung Biru (JTB) gas project at SOFR plus a credit adjustment spread and margin, with 1,208,418 outstanding at the end of 2024 (Note 27, Daftar 5/132, PDF p. 149). It has swapped the loan to fixed rates of 1.7910 to 1.9866 percent on notionals of 839,970 at the effective dates, the largest being Conventional Tranche B, 479,970 at 1.7910 percent to March 2029 (Note 27, Daftar 5/133, PDF p. 150), and accounts for the swaps as cash flow hedges (Note 14b, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123). With SOFR far above those rates the swaps are an asset, the unrealised hedge gain of 50,769 (2023: 66,533) in other non-current assets. When markets expect rate cuts, the fixed rate is worth less and the asset falls. For example (illustration), measure from a designation at the start of 2024, so that the year's change is the cumulative change.

Getting out of the reserve. If the hedged transaction produces a non-financial asset or liability, such as equipment bought in euros under a forward, the reserve goes into the asset's initial cost as a basis adjustment. Otherwise, as for PEPC's interest, it is reclassified to profit or loss when the hedged cash flows affect profit (para. 6.5.11(d)). Suppose (illustration) SOFR averages 5.10 percent over a year and the swap settles net on Tranche B's original notional (the amortisation profile is not disclosed).

Net settlement received = 479,970 × (5.10% − 1.7910%) = 15,882
