presentation.deck: The theory of indirect and withheld taxes from the VAT invoice to the Tax Court, worked through PHE's reimbursable VAT and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: Taxes other than income tax fall outside PSAK 212. For each one, the accounting depends on who bears the tax. Tax the entity collects or withholds for the state is a liability. Tax it pays and can recover is a receivable. Tax it pays and cannot recover is part of the cost of what it bought.

Value added tax (VAT) is collected at every stage of a supply chain, and each business pays the state only output VAT less input VAT. When input exceeds output, the business is owed money. It carries the excess forward or claims a refund, and exporters and suppliers to VAT collectors are owed money most months.

An upstream oil and gas contractor sells crude and piped gas whose supply is exempt from VAT, so it cannot credit its input VAT. Under its production sharing contract (PSC) the government reimburses that VAT out of the state's share of production. At PHE, reimbursable VAT is 505,861 of the 563,451 other taxes receivable at the end of 2024, 475,338 of it in the subsidiaries that hold the PSCs.

title: Production Expenses and the Statement of Profit or Loss: Function, Nature, Subtotals and PSAK 118
snippet: How the statement of profit or loss is built, from what it must show to the new PSAK 118 categories, worked through PHE's production, administration and other operating costs and set beside banks, insurers, retailers and airlines
content:
In brief

  • An expense line is a classification choice. Under PSAK 201 an entity analyses its expenses either by nature (what was consumed: staff, materials, depreciation) or by function (what the cost was for: production, administration), whichever is more reliable and relevant. An entity that uses function must also disclose depreciation, amortisation and employee benefits by nature.

  • PSAK 201 fixes a list of line items, including impairment of financial assets and the share of associates, but no operating subtotal, so "gross profit" and "operating profit" mean what each entity decides. Other income and expense is a residual for items outside the main business, and no item may be called extraordinary.

  • PSAK 118 (IFRS 18), effective in Indonesia from 1 January 2027, sorts every income and expense into operating, investing and financing categories, requires operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes as subtotals, and brings management-defined performance measures into an audited note.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report production expenses of 4,647,647 for 2024 against 4,233,242 for 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). That is 32.4 percent of revenues of 14,330,340 (29.1 percent in 2023) and 49.8 percent of the 9,330,714 PHE calls "total costs of revenue". The same statement shows general and administration expenses of 906,779 (2023: 826,447), expense from other operations of 867,866 (2023: 734,750) and other income, net, of 315,440 (2023: expense of 112,753).

After reading it a student should be able to say what the statement of profit or loss must show, classify an expense by nature and by function, build single-step and multiple-step statements, and recast a statement into the PSAK 118 categories.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What the statement of profit or loss is for

The statement of profit or loss reports performance over a period, and the period is what makes evaluation possible. The lecture notes on Kieso's chapter 4 give it three uses (evaluating past performance, predicting future performance, assessing risk) and three limits (unmeasurable items such as a good manager, method choice, estimates).

The statement records income and expenses as the Conceptual Framework (KKPK in Indonesia) defines them, increases and decreases in assets or liabilities that change equity other than through owners. Expenses enter by three routes, as the theory notes on expenses set out: direct association with revenue (matching), systematic allocation over the periods that benefit (depreciation, depletion), and immediate recognition when no future benefit exists. PHE's policy is shorter: "Expenses are recognized when incurred on an accrual basis" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80).

Quality of earnings. Because profit is used to predict, the notes stress quality of earnings, whether this year's profit is a guide to next year's; they treat smoothing as management's aim and warn that excessive earnings management lowers quality. One-off items lower it too.

Gross profit change = 4,999,626 − 5,650,519 = −650,893

Profit before income tax change = 4,892,576 − 4,492,029 = +400,547

Lower impairment = 707,087 − 215,666 = 491,421; other income swing = 315,440 − (−112,753) = 428,193

Gross profit fell while pre-tax profit rose 8.9 percent on 2023, mainly through a lower impairment charge and an other-income line that turned from expense to income, part of which belongs to earlier years (section 9).

2. What the statement must show

PSAK 201 Presentation of Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) lists the line items that must appear: revenue, with interest revenue under the effective interest method shown separately; gains and losses on derecognising financial assets at amortised cost; finance costs; impairment losses and reversals on financial assets under PSAK 109 (para. 82(ba)); share of profit or loss of associates and joint ventures under the equity method; tax expense; a single amount for discontinued operations; and profit or loss (paras. 81A–82; insurers add the PSAK 117 lines). The OCI section and the allocation of profit and comprehensive income between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests follow (paras. 81B–82A). Further line items, headings and subtotals are added when they help a reader understand performance (para. 85). An added subtotal must be made of recognised amounts, labelled clearly, presented consistently, and not given more prominence than the required totals (para. 85A).

The OCI section is taught in the Other Comprehensive Income essay, and the split of profit (3,001,475 to owners and 119,560 to non-controlling interests in 2024, Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15) in the Non-controlling Interest essay. Earnings per share under PSAK 233 (formerly PSAK 56, IAS 33) is required only of entities whose ordinary shares are traded publicly or are being listed, so PHE, a non-listed subsidiary of PT Pertamina (Persero), shows none. The notes give the formula as net income less preference dividends "dibagi total outstanding share"; the denominator is the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding in the period, not the year-end count.

3. Classifying expenses by nature or by function

Every expense can be described two ways. By nature it is what was consumed: employee benefits, materials, outside services, depreciation. By function it is what the cost was for: cost of sales, distribution, administration. PSAK 201 requires an analysis by one or the other, whichever gives information that is reliable and more relevant (para. 99), and the choice depends on history, industry and the nature of the entity (para. 105).

The nature method needs no allocation, so it is simpler and harder to manipulate. The function method shows the business model, gross margin above all, but rests on judgmental allocations, which is why PSAK 201 makes an entity that classifies by function disclose additional information on the nature of expenses, including depreciation and amortisation and employee benefits expense (para. 104).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary records 6,000 of costs in a year by nature: employee benefits 1,000, contractor and outside services 2,400, materials used 600, depreciation and depletion 1,800, office rent and utilities 200. Production staff take 600 of the employee cost and administration 400; field contractors take 2,000 of the services and consultants 400; 550 of materials go to the field and 50 to offices.

Profit is the same under both. The function column needs a note disclosing employee benefits of 1,000 and depreciation and depletion of 1,800, and it is mixed, because depreciation keeps its nature label. PSAK 201 does not expressly provide for that mixture; PSAK 118 does (section 7). Charging the costs out to functions is one entry.

Dr Production expenses 3,150, Dr General and administration expenses 1,050 / Cr Employee benefits expense 1,000, Cr Outside services 2,400, Cr Materials used 600, Cr Rent and utilities 200

What production expense holds at an upstream company. For an oil and gas producer the function "production" means the cost of lifting hydrocarbons from wells that already exist: operating and maintaining wells and facilities, field support, the field workforce, and the materials issued to routine work (see the Inventories essay). Finding costs are a separate function, exploration, and the cost of the wells themselves reaches profit through depreciation, depletion and amortisation (DD&A); both are taught in the Oil and Gas Properties essay. Analysts divide production expense by volume to get lifting cost per barrel of oil equivalent (boe). For example (illustration), if PHE's group had produced 380 million boe in 2024:

Lifting cost = USD 4,647,647 thousand / 380,000 thousand boe = USD 12.23 per boe

PHE's financial statements give no volumes, so the real figure cannot be computed from them.

4. Single-step and multiple-step formats

The same expenses can be laid out in three formats, which the lecture notes describe. A single-step statement adds all revenues and income, adds all expenses, and subtracts once. A multiple-step statement separates the main business from the rest and shows subtotals along the way. A condensed statement itemises revenue but shows expenses in a few totals, with the detail in schedules.

For example, take PHE's 2024 figures. In single-step form other income enters as one net figure, because PHE gives no gross amount.

Revenues and income = 14,330,340 + 251,561 finance income + 315,440 other income, net = 14,897,341

Expenses = 9,330,714 costs of revenue + 215,666 impairment + 453,906 finance cost + 4,479 foreign exchange loss = 10,004,765

Profit before income tax = 14,897,341 − 10,004,765 = 4,892,576

The multiple-step form in the lecture notes runs: sales revenue, less cost of goods sold, equals gross profit; less selling and administrative expenses, plus or minus other income and expense, equals income from operations; less financing costs equals income before tax; less tax equals income from continuing operations. PHE uses a multiple-step form but draws the first line differently. Its "costs of revenue" (this page keeps that term for PHE's line and "cost of sales" for the generic concept) include exploration and general and administration. DD&A of producing wells belongs there under any function layout, as factory depreciation does in a manufacturer's cost of sales (see the Inventories essay). Recast with administration below gross profit, as in the notes, gross profit changes.

The bottom line is the same, but the gross margin moves 6.3 points, so gross margins compare only between companies that draw the line in the same place. PHE does not say why it draws it there. One reading (see Least-confident) is that under a production sharing contract (PSC) administration and exploration are operating costs recovered from production (section 10), so the entity treats them as part of the cost of earning its entitlement revenue.

5. Gross profit, operating profit and other income and expense

Gross profit is net revenue less cost of sales, and the notes call it useful for evaluating performance and predicting future profit. Operating profit is not defined by PSAK 201. An entity may present it, but leaving out clearly operating items such as inventory write-downs or restructuring costs because they are irregular would mislead (IAS 1.BC56).

The lecture notes put other income and expense inside income from operations and say the IASB requires it ("IASB menyaratkan"). PSAK 201 contains no such requirement, since it defines no operating subtotal, and under PSAK 118 not all of it stays there. The notes' example of other income is "interest revenue akibat dia nabung di bank" for a trading company; under PSAK 118 that interest goes to the investing category, below operating profit.

What other income and expense holds. It collects income and expenses outside the main revenue-producing activity: gains and losses on disposals, penalties received from vendors, donations, contributions. The Conceptual Framework's income includes both revenue, from ordinary activities, and gains, which may or may not be ordinary; the theory notes on expenses make the same point, that the framework "tidak memisahkan biaya dengan rugi".

Netting. Income and expenses are not offset unless a standard requires or permits it (para. 32), but gains and losses on disposals of non-current assets are presented net of the carrying amount and selling costs (para. 34(a)). For example (illustration), a subsidiary sells a compressor that cost 500, with accumulated depreciation of 420, for 110.

Carrying amount = 500 − 420 = 80; gain = 110 − 80 = 30

Dr Cash 110, Dr Accumulated depreciation 420 / Cr Fixed assets 500, Cr Gain on disposal of fixed assets 30

Only the 30 reaches other income, instead of 110 of income against 80 of expense.

6. Unusual items, discontinued operations and intraperiod tax allocation

No extraordinary items. PSAK 201 forbids presenting any item as extraordinary, on the face of the statement or in the notes (para. 87). Material items are instead disclosed by nature and amount (para. 97). Typical cases are write-downs of inventories or fixed assets and their reversals, restructuring costs, disposals of fixed assets and investments, discontinued operations, litigation settlements and other reversals of provisions (para. 98). The lecture notes place restructuring severance in other expense; under the function method it can equally go to the staff's function, with its amount disclosed.

Discontinued operations. A discontinued operation under PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5) is a component that has been disposed of or is held for sale and is a separate major line of business or geographical area, part of a single plan to dispose of one, or a subsidiary acquired only to resell, the three cases the lecture notes list. Its result is presented as a single amount after tax, so that the lines above show the business that continues. For example (illustration), take the services segment's 2024 profit before tax of 89,566 (Note 46, Daftar 5/220, PDF p. 237) and suppose the group had decided to sell the whole segment and that it qualified. Assume a tax rate of 22 percent, the general rate under UU HPP (Elnusa, a listed company, may qualify for 19 percent under PP 30/2020 if it meets the float and shareholder conditions; that is ignored here), and a loss of 10,000 on remeasuring the segment to fair value less costs to sell.

Profit after tax = 89,566 × (1 − 22%) = 69,861

Remeasurement loss after tax = 10,000 × (1 − 22%) = 7,800

Profit from discontinued operations = 69,861 − 7,800 = 62,061

Intraperiod tax allocation. Each section of the statement carries its own tax, so the 62,061 is presented net, and tax expense on continuing operations excludes the tax on the discontinued segment. The notes call this "interperiod tax allocation"; the term for allocation within one period is intraperiod. Interperiod allocation is deferred tax, taught in the Deferred Tax essay.

7. PSAK 118: categories, subtotals and management-defined performance measures

PSAK 118 exists because PSAK 201 left the middle of the statement to each entity, so two companies' "operating profit" could hold different things. The IASB issued IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements in April 2024, effective 1 January 2027. DSAK IAI ratified PSAK 118 on 28 May 2025 with the same effective date, and it replaces PSAK 201. PHE's 2024 statements were authorised on 28 March 2025 (Note 1c, Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25), before the ratification, so their list of standards not yet effective does not include it. Early application is permitted, and sharia entities stay under PSAK 401.

Five categories, three new. Every item of income and expense goes into one of five categories: operating, investing, financing, income taxes and discontinued operations.

  • Investing holds the returns on assets that earn largely independently of the entity's other resources: income from associates and joint ventures accounted for by the equity method (always here), and income from cash and cash equivalents and other investments.

  • Financing holds income and expenses on liabilities that only raise finance, such as bank loans and sukuk, plus interest and the unwinding of discounts on other liabilities: leases, decommissioning provisions, defined benefit liabilities.

  • Operating is the residual, everything not in another category.

Foreign exchange differences follow the category of the item that produced them. An entity whose main business is lending, such as a bank, classifies its interest income and expense in operating.

Required subtotals. Operating profit, profit before financing and income taxes, and profit. Gross profit is optional.

For example (illustration), recast PHE's 2024 statement. Assume that the foreign exchange loss arises on operating balances such as tax receivables and payables, that the gain on sale of subsidiaries stays in operating, and that the net interest on the defined benefit liability, which PHE now charges to costs of revenue and administration (Note 25b, Daftar 5/123, PDF p. 140), moves to financing.

Net interest on the defined benefit liability = interest cost 46,048 − interest income 20,760 = 25,288

Other income in operating = 315,440 − 162,620 share of associates = 152,820

Profit before tax does not move. Within it, 414,181 of investment returns leave operating profit and 25,288 of interest leaves production and administration. Every part of Note 41 is financing for a company whose main business is not lending (see the Finance Cost essay).

Function, nature or both. PSAK 118 allows a mixed presentation, the column from section 3, if it gives the most useful structured summary. A cost-of-sales line must include all inventory expense. An entity presenting any line by function must disclose in one note, for each function, the amounts of depreciation, amortisation, employee benefits, impairment losses and reversals, and inventory write-downs and reversals (para. 83). For the section 3 subsidiary it would show employee benefits of 600 in production and 400 in administration.

Management-defined performance measures (MPMs). An MPM is a subtotal of income and expenses that an entity uses in public communications outside the financial statements to express management's view of an aspect of overall performance, other than the subtotals PSAK 118 lists or another standard requires. Each MPM is disclosed in one note with an explanation, a reconciliation to the most comparable listed subtotal, and the tax and non-controlling-interest effect of each reconciling item. The listed subtotals include gross profit and "operating profit before depreciation, amortisation and impairments" within the scope of PSAK 236 (para. 118), so an EBITDA computed that way is not an MPM. For example (illustration), from the recast above:

Operating profit before DD&A and impairment = 4,957,589 + 2,443,000 + 215,666 = 7,616,255

If PHE published an "adjusted EBITDA" that also added back the BUMD contribution of 52,791, that figure, 7,669,046, would be an MPM. Its note would reconcile it to 7,616,255 and show the tax effect of the add-back, at an illustrative 40 percent rate 52,791 × 40% = 21,116.

8. The statement of profit or loss across industries

Banks have no cost of sales. Their main income is the margin between interest earned and interest paid, so the statement opens with net interest income, and under PSAK 118 that interest is operating. Islamic banks report murabahah margins and bagi hasil (profit-sharing) under the PSAK 4xx series instead. For example (illustration), interest income 1,000, interest expense 450, fee income 120, operating expenses 300, expected credit losses 80.

Net interest income = 1,000 − 450 = 550; operating income = 550 + 120 = 670; profit before tax = 670 − 300 − 80 = 290

Insurers follow PSAK 117 Insurance Contracts (formerly PSAK 74, IFRS 17), effective from 1 January 2025 (PHE Note 3b, Daftar 5/32, PDF p. 49). Premiums received are no longer revenue. The statement shows insurance revenue as service is provided, insurance service expenses, the net result of reinsurance, and a separate insurance finance income or expense beside investment income. For example (illustration), insurance revenue 1,000, insurance service expenses 820, net reinsurance expense 30, investment income 90, insurance finance expense 60.

Insurance service result = 1,000 − 820 − 30 = 150; net financial result = 90 − 60 = 30; total = 180

Retailers classify by function. Cost of sales is mostly inventory expense under PSAK 202, so gross margin measures pricing and shrinkage (see the Inventories essay), and store and head-office costs fall below it.

Airlines usually classify by nature (fuel, staff, maintenance, airport charges, depreciation), since a flight's cost has no useful split into cost of sales and administration.

9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 37, 38, 39 and 42

PHE classifies by function above gross profit and by nature in the notes (Notes 37–39, Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166).

Personnel share of production expense = 688,343 / 4,647,647 = 14.8% (2023: 12.3%), up 31.8% in a year

Note 38 splits administration into salaries and benefits of 510,007, office and rental of 202,308, consultants of 143,632 and others of 50,382, for a total of 906,779. Expense from other operations is "the direct costs associated with goods and services provided by Elnusa and PDSI", the service subsidiaries, led by outside services of 340,911 (up 54.7 percent on 2023), so it is the services segment's cost of sales after intra-group eliminations (Note 39).

Note 46 gives a second view (Daftar 5/220, PDF p. 237). It splits the same 9,330,714 into cost of revenues 5,980,936 (exploration, production and other operations, 5,980,935 by the face lines), DD&A 2,443,000, and salaries 473,026 and others 433,752, which together are the G&A line (906,778 against 906,779; in 2023 they tie exactly). It also shows an "operating profit" of 5,099,400, which is gross profit less impairment plus other income, net, a subtotal that does not appear on the face of the statement.

PHE discloses depreciation by function only for fixed assets (74,311, Note 12, Daftar 5/101, PDF p. 118) and oil and gas properties (2,187,085, Note 17, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126). Personnel cost appears in three notes (together 1,453,337), but exploration administration of 123,932 (Note 36) is not split, so the total employee benefits expense PSAK 201.104 asks for cannot be read.

Note 42 (Daftar 5/150–5/151, PDF pp. 167–168) shows what other income collects: a contribution to regional government-owned enterprises (BUMD) of 52,791, vendor penalties of 72,502, a gain on the sale of subsidiaries of 34,242, a net credit of 57,813 for impairment and correction of receivables, and the share of associates and a joint venture of 162,620 (51.6 percent of the line). PSAK 201.82(c) and (ba) list the last two as face line items. Of the 428,193 swing, 254,946 came from the smaller BUMD contribution and 90,552 from 2023 items that did not recur (a profit-sharing correction and incident costs). The share of associates fell 87,658, and PHE states that its 2024 figure includes 234,223 of PRDL income for 2019–2023 recorded in the year.

10. Upstream note: cost recovery and lifting imbalances

Under a cost recovery PSC the contractor recovers current-year non-capital costs, current-year amortisation of capital costs and earlier unrecovered costs from production (Note 2a(iii), Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). Production, administration and exploration costs all feed that recovery, which fits PHE placing them together above gross profit. PHE also books adjustments for overlifting and underlifting, lifting more or less than its final entitlement, "as part of direct sales costs" because they are "not transactions with customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). Gross split contracts have no cost recovery; the balances are taught in the Due from the Government essay.

11. Related lines

  • general-administrative-expenses, expense-from-other-operations: the other function lines, sections 3, 4 and 9.

  • other-income-expense-net: the residual line, sections 5 and 9.

  • exploration-expenses, depreciation-depletion-amortization: the rest of costs of revenue, taught in the Oil and Gas Properties essay.

  • revenues: the top line and entitlement revenue.

  • impairment-non-financial-assets: the line below gross profit.

  • finance-income, finance-cost: the investing and financing categories under PSAK 118.

  • inventories-net: materials issued to production.

Least-confident assertions

  • That PHE puts administration and exploration in costs of revenue because PSC cost recovery treats them as operating costs is this page's reading. PHE does not explain its layout.

  • The PSAK 118 recast rests on stated assumptions: the foreign exchange loss is treated as operating, the gain on sale of subsidiaries stays in operating, the residual, because the investing category covers associates, joint ventures and unconsolidated subsidiaries (secondary sources; none addresses a consolidated subsidiary directly), and the defined benefit net interest is taken as 46,048 − 20,760 from Note 25b, leaving aside a 241 "return on plan assets" that Note 25b also shows in profit or loss.

  • Note 38's 2024 rows (510,007 + 202,308 + 143,632 + 50,382) add to 906,329, not the 906,779 printed and carried to the face of the statement, a gap of 450, checked on the PDF page; it equals a transposition of 50,832 to 50,382 in "others". Note 37 prints "2..631.022". Note 46 calls a 2024 loss of 4,479 "foreign exchange gain, net" and prints 2023 DD&A as 2,856,854 against 2,856,853 on the face.

  • Note 46 splits G&A into salaries of 473,026 and others of 433,752; Note 38 puts 510,007 in salaries and benefits. The 36,981 difference in the salary row is not explained. The segment "operating profit" of 5,099,400 includes the share of associates, which PSAK 118 would place in investing.

  • PHE presents its 162,620 share of associates and its 57,813 receivable credit inside other income, net, though PSAK 201.82(c) and (ba) list both as face line items; PHE may judge them immaterial (para. 31), at 3.3 and 1.2 percent of profit before tax.

  • PHE booked 234,223 of PRDL associate income for 2019–2023 in 2024 profit (Daftar 5/151, PDF p. 168), more than the 124,942 "income of associates" row it sits in. If it corrects an error, PSAK 208 would require restating comparatives; PHE does not say why it did not.

content.text: An expense line is a classification choice. Under PSAK 201 an entity analyses its expenses either by nature (what was consumed: staff, materials, depreciation) or by function (what the cost was for: production, administration), whichever is more reliable and relevant. An entity that uses function must also disclose depreciation, amortisation and employee benefits by nature.

PSAK 201 fixes a list of line items, including impairment of financial assets and the share of associates, but no operating subtotal, so "gross profit" and "operating profit" mean what each entity decides. Other income and expense is a residual for items outside the main business, and no item may be called extraordinary.

PSAK 118 (IFRS 18), effective in Indonesia from 1 January 2027, sorts every income and expense into operating, investing and financing categories, requires operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes as subtotals, and brings management-defined performance measures into an audited note.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report production expenses of 4,647,647 for 2024 against 4,233,242 for 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). That is 32.4 percent of revenues of 14,330,340 (29.1 percent in 2023) and 49.8 percent of the 9,330,714 PHE calls "total costs of revenue". The same statement shows general and administration expenses of 906,779 (2023: 826,447), expense from other operations of 867,866 (2023: 734,750) and other income, net, of 315,440 (2023: expense of 112,753).

After reading it a student should be able to say what the statement of profit or loss must show, classify an expense by nature and by function, build single-step and multiple-step statements, and recast a statement into the PSAK 118 categories.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. What the statement of profit or loss is for

The statement of profit or loss reports performance over a period, and the period is what makes evaluation possible. The lecture notes on Kieso's chapter 4 give it three uses (evaluating past performance, predicting future performance, assessing risk) and three limits (unmeasurable items such as a good manager, method choice, estimates).

as the Conceptual Framework (KKPK in Indonesia) defines them, increases and decreases in assets or liabilities that change equity other than through owners. Expenses enter by three routes, as the theory notes on expenses set out: direct association with revenue (matching), systematic allocation over the periods that benefit (depreciation, depletion), and immediate recognition when no future benefit exists. PHE's policy is shorter: "Expenses are recognized when incurred on an accrual basis" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80).
Because profit is used to predict, the notes stress
, whether this year's profit is a guide to next year's; they treat smoothing as management's aim and warn that excessive earnings management lowers quality. One-off items lower it too.

Gross profit fell while pre-tax profit rose 8.9 percent on 2023, mainly through a lower impairment charge and an other-income line that turned from expense to income, part of which belongs to earlier years (section 9).

(formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) lists the line items that must appear: revenue, with interest revenue under the effective interest method shown separately; gains and losses on derecognising financial assets at amortised cost; finance costs; impairment losses and reversals on financial assets under PSAK 109 (para. 82(ba)); share of profit or loss of associates and joint ventures under the equity method; tax expense; a single amount for discontinued operations; and profit or loss (paras. 81A–82; insurers add the PSAK 117 lines). The OCI section and the allocation of profit and comprehensive income between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests follow (paras. 81B–82A). Further line items, headings and subtotals are added when they help a reader understand performance (para. 85). An added subtotal must be made of recognised amounts, labelled clearly, presented consistently, and not given more prominence than the required totals (para. 85A).

The OCI section is taught in the Other Comprehensive Income essay, and the split of profit (3,001,475 to owners and 119,560 to non-controlling interests in 2024, Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15) in the Non-controlling Interest essay. Earnings per share under PSAK 233 (formerly PSAK 56, IAS 33) is required only of entities whose ordinary shares are traded publicly or are being listed, so PHE, a non-listed subsidiary of PT Pertamina (Persero), shows none. The notes give the formula as net income less preference dividends "dibagi total outstanding share"; the denominator is the
number of ordinary shares outstanding in the period, not the year-end count.
3. Classifying expenses by nature or by function
Every expense can be described two ways. By
it is what was consumed: employee benefits, materials, outside services, depreciation. By

it is what the cost was for: cost of sales, distribution, administration. PSAK 201 requires an analysis by one or the other, whichever gives information that is reliable and more relevant (para. 99), and the choice depends on history, industry and the nature of the entity (para. 105).

The nature method needs no allocation, so it is simpler and harder to manipulate. The function method shows the business model, gross margin above all, but rests on judgmental allocations, which is why PSAK 201 makes an entity that classifies by function disclose additional information on the nature of expenses, including depreciation and amortisation and employee benefits expense (para. 104).

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary records 6,000 of costs in a year by nature: employee benefits 1,000, contractor and outside services 2,400, materials used 600, depreciation and depletion 1,800, office rent and utilities 200. Production staff take 600 of the employee cost and administration 400; field contractors take 2,000 of the services and consultants 400; 550 of materials go to the field and 50 to offices.

Profit is the same under both. The function column needs a note disclosing employee benefits of 1,000 and depreciation and depletion of 1,800, and it is mixed, because depreciation keeps its nature label. PSAK 201 does not expressly provide for that mixture; PSAK 118 does (section 7). Charging the costs out to functions is one entry.
Dr Production expenses 3,150, Dr General and administration expenses 1,050 / Cr Employee benefits expense 1,000, Cr Outside services 2,400, Cr Materials used 600, Cr Rent and utilities 200
What production expense holds at an upstream company.

For an oil and gas producer the function "production" means the cost of lifting hydrocarbons from wells that already exist: operating and maintaining wells and facilities, field support, the field workforce, and the materials issued to routine work (see the Inventories essay). Finding costs are a separate function, exploration, and the cost of the wells themselves reaches profit through depreciation, depletion and amortisation (DD&A); both are taught in the Oil and Gas Properties essay. Analysts divide production expense by volume to get
per barrel of oil equivalent (boe). For example (illustration), if PHE's group had produced 380 million boe in 2024:
Lifting cost = USD 4,647,647 thousand / 380,000 thousand boe = USD 12.23 per boe
PHE's financial statements give no volumes, so the real figure cannot be computed from them.
The same expenses can be laid out in three formats, which the lecture notes describe. A
statement adds all revenues and income, adds all expenses, and subtracts once. A
statement separates the main business from the rest and shows subtotals along the way. A
statement itemises revenue but shows expenses in a few totals, with the detail in schedules.
For example, take PHE's 2024 figures. In single-step form other income enters as one net figure, because PHE gives no gross amount.
Revenues and income = 14,330,340 + 251,561 finance income + 315,440 other income, net = 14,897,341
Expenses = 9,330,714 costs of revenue + 215,666 impairment + 453,906 finance cost + 4,479 foreign exchange loss = 10,004,765

The multiple-step form in the lecture notes runs: sales revenue, less cost of goods sold, equals gross profit; less selling and administrative expenses, plus or minus other income and expense, equals income from operations; less financing costs equals income before tax; less tax equals income from continuing operations. PHE uses a multiple-step form but draws the first line differently. Its "costs of revenue" (this page keeps that term for PHE's line and "cost of sales" for the generic concept) include exploration and general and administration. DD&A of producing wells belongs there under any function layout, as factory depreciation does in a manufacturer's cost of sales (see the Inventories essay). Recast with administration below gross profit, as in the notes, gross profit changes.
General and administration below gross profit

The bottom line is the same, but the gross margin moves 6.3 points, so gross margins compare only between companies that draw the line in the same place. PHE does not say why it draws it there. One reading (see Least-confident) is that under a production sharing contract (PSC) administration and exploration are operating costs recovered from production (section 10), so the entity treats them as part of the cost of earning its entitlement revenue.
5. Gross profit, operating profit and other income and expense
is net revenue less cost of sales, and the notes call it useful for evaluating performance and predicting future profit.

is not defined by PSAK 201. An entity may present it, but leaving out clearly operating items such as inventory write-downs or restructuring costs because they are irregular would mislead (IAS 1.BC56).

The lecture notes put other income and expense inside income from operations and say the IASB requires it ("IASB menyaratkan"). PSAK 201 contains no such requirement, since it defines no operating subtotal, and under PSAK 118 not all of it stays there. The notes' example of other income is "interest revenue akibat dia nabung di bank" for a trading company; under PSAK 118 that interest goes to the investing category, below operating profit.
What other income and expense holds.
It collects income and expenses outside the main revenue-producing activity: gains and losses on disposals, penalties received from vendors, donations, contributions. The Conceptual Framework's
includes both revenue, from ordinary activities, and
, which may or may not be ordinary; the theory notes on expenses make the same point, that the framework "tidak memisahkan biaya dengan rugi".

Income and expenses are not offset unless a standard requires or permits it (para. 32), but gains and losses on disposals of non-current assets are presented net of the carrying amount and selling costs (para. 34(a)). For example (illustration), a subsidiary sells a compressor that cost 500, with accumulated depreciation of 420, for 110.
Dr Cash 110, Dr Accumulated depreciation 420 / Cr Fixed assets 500, Cr Gain on disposal of fixed assets 30
Only the 30 reaches other income, instead of 110 of income against 80 of expense.
6. Unusual items, discontinued operations and intraperiod tax allocation

PSAK 201 forbids presenting any item as extraordinary, on the face of the statement or in the notes (para. 87). Material items are instead disclosed by nature and amount (para. 97). Typical cases are write-downs of inventories or fixed assets and their reversals, restructuring costs, disposals of fixed assets and investments, discontinued operations, litigation settlements and other reversals of provisions (para. 98). The lecture notes place restructuring severance in other expense; under the function method it can equally go to the staff's function, with its amount disclosed.

under PSAK 105 (formerly PSAK 58, IFRS 5) is a component that has been disposed of or is held for sale and is a separate major line of business or geographical area, part of a single plan to dispose of one, or a subsidiary acquired only to resell, the three cases the lecture notes list. Its result is presented as a single amount after tax, so that the lines above show the business that continues. For example (illustration), take the services segment's 2024 profit before tax of 89,566 (Note 46, Daftar 5/220, PDF p. 237) and suppose the group had decided to sell the whole segment and that it qualified. Assume a tax rate of 22 percent, the general rate under UU HPP (Elnusa, a listed company, may qualify for 19 percent under PP 30/2020 if it meets the float and shareholder conditions; that is ignored here), and a loss of 10,000 on remeasuring the segment to fair value less costs to sell.

Each section of the statement carries its own tax, so the 62,061 is presented net, and tax expense on continuing operations excludes the tax on the discontinued segment. The notes call this "interperiod tax allocation"; the term for allocation within one period is
. Interperiod allocation is deferred tax, taught in the Deferred Tax essay.
7. PSAK 118: categories, subtotals and management-defined performance measures
PSAK 118 exists because PSAK 201 left the middle of the statement to each entity, so two companies' "operating profit" could hold different things. The IASB issued IFRS 18
Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements

in April 2024, effective 1 January 2027. DSAK IAI ratified PSAK 118 on 28 May 2025 with the same effective date, and it replaces PSAK 201. PHE's 2024 statements were authorised on 28 March 2025 (Note 1c, Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25), before the ratification, so their list of standards not yet effective does not include it. Early application is permitted, and sharia entities stay under PSAK 401.
Every item of income and expense goes into one of five categories: operating, investing, financing, income taxes and discontinued operations.

holds the returns on assets that earn largely independently of the entity's other resources: income from associates and joint ventures accounted for by the equity method (always here), and income from cash and cash equivalents and other investments.

holds income and expenses on liabilities that only raise finance, such as bank loans and sukuk, plus interest and the unwinding of discounts on other liabilities: leases, decommissioning provisions, defined benefit liabilities.
is the residual, everything not in another category.
Foreign exchange differences follow the category of the item that produced them. An entity whose main business is lending, such as a bank, classifies its interest income and expense in operating.
Operating profit, profit before financing and income taxes, and profit. Gross profit is optional.

For example (illustration), recast PHE's 2024 statement. Assume that the foreign exchange loss arises on operating balances such as tax receivables and payables, that the gain on sale of subsidiaries stays in operating, and that the net interest on the defined benefit liability, which PHE now charges to costs of revenue and administration (Note 25b, Daftar 5/123, PDF p. 140), moves to financing.
Net interest on the defined benefit liability = interest cost 46,048 − interest income 20,760 = 25,288
Other income in operating = 315,440 − 162,620 share of associates = 152,820
Gross profit (4,999,626 + 25,288 net interest moved out)
Other income, net, excluding associates (includes 57,813 of receivable impairment and correction, a line of its own under PSAK 109)
Interest income on bank placements and time deposits
Share of profit of associates and joint venture
Profit before financing and income taxes
Net interest on the defined benefit liability

Profit before tax does not move. Within it, 414,181 of investment returns leave operating profit and 25,288 of interest leaves production and administration. Every part of Note 41 is financing for a company whose main business is not lending (see the Finance Cost essay).

PSAK 118 allows a mixed presentation, the column from section 3, if it gives the most useful structured summary. A cost-of-sales line must include all inventory expense. An entity presenting any line by function must disclose in one note, for each function, the amounts of depreciation, amortisation, employee benefits, impairment losses and reversals, and inventory write-downs and reversals (para. 83). For the section 3 subsidiary it would show employee benefits of 600 in production and 400 in administration.

An MPM is a subtotal of income and expenses that an entity uses in public communications outside the financial statements to express management's view of an aspect of overall performance, other than the subtotals PSAK 118 lists or another standard requires. Each MPM is disclosed in one note with an explanation, a reconciliation to the most comparable listed subtotal, and the tax and non-controlling-interest effect of each reconciling item. The listed subtotals include gross profit and "operating profit before depreciation, amortisation and impairments" within the scope of PSAK 236 (para. 118), so an EBITDA computed that way is not an MPM. For example (illustration), from the recast above:
Operating profit before DD&A and impairment = 4,957,589 + 2,443,000 + 215,666 = 7,616,255

If PHE published an "adjusted EBITDA" that also added back the BUMD contribution of 52,791, that figure, 7,669,046, would be an MPM. Its note would reconcile it to 7,616,255 and show the tax effect of the add-back, at an illustrative 40 percent rate 52,791 × 40% = 21,116.
8. The statement of profit or loss across industries
have no cost of sales. Their main income is the margin between interest earned and interest paid, so the statement opens with
, and under PSAK 118 that interest is operating. Islamic banks report murabahah margins and
(profit-sharing) under the PSAK 4xx series instead. For example (illustration), interest income 1,000, interest expense 450, fee income 120, operating expenses 300, expected credit losses 80.
Net interest income = 1,000 − 450 = 550; operating income = 550 + 120 = 670; profit before tax = 670 − 300 − 80 = 290
(formerly PSAK 74, IFRS 17), effective from 1 January 2025 (PHE Note 3b, Daftar 5/32, PDF p. 49). Premiums received are no longer revenue. The statement shows
, the net result of reinsurance, and a separate
beside investment income. For example (illustration), insurance revenue 1,000, insurance service expenses 820, net reinsurance expense 30, investment income 90, insurance finance expense 60.
Insurance service result = 1,000 − 820 − 30 = 150; net financial result = 90 − 60 = 30; total = 180

classify by function. Cost of sales is mostly inventory expense under PSAK 202, so gross margin measures pricing and shrinkage (see the Inventories essay), and store and head-office costs fall below it.
usually classify by nature (fuel, staff, maintenance, airport charges, depreciation), since a flight's cost has no useful split into cost of sales and administration.
9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 37, 38, 39 and 42
PHE classifies by function above gross profit and by nature in the notes (Notes 37–39, Daftar 5/149, PDF p. 166).
Production expense growth = 4,647,647 / 4,233,242 − 1 = 9.8%, against revenue growth of 14,330,340 / 14,568,384 − 1 = −1.6%
Personnel share of production expense = 688,343 / 4,647,647 = 14.8% (2023: 12.3%), up 31.8% in a year

Note 38 splits administration into salaries and benefits of 510,007, office and rental of 202,308, consultants of 143,632 and others of 50,382, for a total of 906,779. Expense from other operations is "the direct costs associated with goods and services provided by Elnusa and PDSI", the service subsidiaries, led by outside services of 340,911 (up 54.7 percent on 2023), so it is the services segment's cost of sales after intra-group eliminations (Note 39).

Note 46 gives a second view (Daftar 5/220, PDF p. 237). It splits the same 9,330,714 into cost of revenues 5,980,936 (exploration, production and other operations, 5,980,935 by the face lines), DD&A 2,443,000, and salaries 473,026 and others 433,752, which together are the G&A line (906,778 against 906,779; in 2023 they tie exactly). It also shows an "operating profit" of 5,099,400, which is gross profit less impairment plus other income, net, a subtotal that does not appear on the face of the statement.

PHE discloses depreciation by function only for fixed assets (74,311, Note 12, Daftar 5/101, PDF p. 118) and oil and gas properties (2,187,085, Note 17, Daftar 5/109, PDF p. 126). Personnel cost appears in three notes (together 1,453,337), but exploration administration of 123,932 (Note 36) is not split, so the total employee benefits expense PSAK 201.104 asks for cannot be read.

Note 42 (Daftar 5/150–5/151, PDF pp. 167–168) shows what other income collects: a contribution to regional government-owned enterprises (BUMD) of 52,791, vendor penalties of 72,502, a gain on the sale of subsidiaries of 34,242, a net credit of 57,813 for impairment and correction of receivables, and the share of associates and a joint venture of 162,620 (51.6 percent of the line). PSAK 201.82(c) and (ba) list the last two as face line items. Of the 428,193 swing, 254,946 came from the smaller BUMD contribution and 90,552 from 2023 items that did not recur (a profit-sharing correction and incident costs). The share of associates fell 87,658, and PHE states that its 2024 figure includes 234,223 of PRDL income for 2019–2023 recorded in the year.
10. Upstream note: cost recovery and lifting imbalances

Under a cost recovery PSC the contractor recovers current-year non-capital costs, current-year amortisation of capital costs and earlier unrecovered costs from production (Note 2a(iii), Daftar 5/10, PDF p. 27). Production, administration and exploration costs all feed that recovery, which fits PHE placing them together above gross profit. PHE also books adjustments for overlifting and underlifting, lifting more or less than its final entitlement, "as part of direct sales costs" because they are "not transactions with customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). Gross split contracts have no cost recovery; the balances are taught in the Due from the Government essay.
: the other function lines, sections 3, 4 and 9.
: the rest of costs of revenue, taught in the Oil and Gas Properties essay.
: the top line and entitlement revenue.
: the investing and financing categories under PSAK 118.
That PHE puts administration and exploration in costs of revenue because PSC cost recovery treats them as operating costs is this page's reading. PHE does not explain its layout.

The PSAK 118 recast rests on stated assumptions: the foreign exchange loss is treated as operating, the gain on sale of subsidiaries stays in operating, the residual, because the investing category covers associates, joint ventures and unconsolidated subsidiaries (secondary sources; none addresses a consolidated subsidiary directly), and the defined benefit net interest is taken as 46,048 − 20,760 from Note 25b, leaving aside a 241 "return on plan assets" that Note 25b also shows in profit or loss.

Note 38's 2024 rows (510,007 + 202,308 + 143,632 + 50,382) add to 906,329, not the 906,779 printed and carried to the face of the statement, a gap of 450, checked on the PDF page; it equals a transposition of 50,832 to 50,382 in "others". Note 37 prints "2..631.022". Note 46 calls a 2024 loss of 4,479 "foreign exchange gain, net" and prints 2023 DD&A as 2,856,854 against 2,856,853 on the face.

Note 46 splits G&A into salaries of 473,026 and others of 433,752; Note 38 puts 510,007 in salaries and benefits. The 36,981 difference in the salary row is not explained. The segment "operating profit" of 5,099,400 includes the share of associates, which PSAK 118 would place in investing.

PHE presents its 162,620 share of associates and its 57,813 receivable credit inside other income, net, though PSAK 201.82(c) and (ba) list both as face line items; PHE may judge them immaterial (para. 31), at 3.3 and 1.2 percent of profit before tax.

PHE booked 234,223 of PRDL associate income for 2019–2023 in 2024 profit (Daftar 5/151, PDF p. 168), more than the 124,942 "income of associates" row it sits in. If it corrects an error, PSAK 208 would require restating comparatives; PHE does not say why it did not.
The PSAK 201 paragraph numbers other than 99, 104 and 105 are from knowledge of IAS 1, not checked against the Indonesian text.

presentation.deck: How the statement of profit or loss is built, from what it must show to the new PSAK 118 categories, worked through PHE's production, administration and other operating costs and set beside banks, insurers, retailers and airlines
key_takeaways: An expense line is a classification choice. Under PSAK 201 an entity analyses its expenses either by nature (what was consumed: staff, materials, depreciation) or by function (what the cost was for: production, administration), whichever is more reliable and relevant. An entity that uses function must also disclose depreciation, amortisation and employee benefits by nature.

PSAK 201 fixes a list of line items, including impairment of financial assets and the share of associates, but no operating subtotal, so "gross profit" and "operating profit" mean what each entity decides. Other income and expense is a residual for items outside the main business, and no item may be called extraordinary.

PSAK 118 (IFRS 18), effective in Indonesia from 1 January 2027, sorts every income and expense into operating, investing and financing categories, requires operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes as subtotals, and brings management-defined performance measures into an audited note.

title: Restricted Cash at an Upstream Contractor: When money in a bank account stops being cash, where the twelve-month line falls, and why the abandonment fund never nets against the obligation it exists to pay
snippet: When money in a bank account stops being cash, where the twelve-month line falls, and why the abandonment fund never nets against the obligation it exists to pay
content:
In brief

  • A bank balance leaves cash and cash equivalents when the entity cannot draw it on demand. An Indonesian contractor's abandonment fund sits in a joint account with SKK Migas, and a debt service reserve sits in an account the lenders control, so both are restricted cash.

  • The current/non-current split follows when the restriction lifts or the money is spent. The same deposit can change sides without moving, and no such reclassification is a cash flow.

  • The abandonment fund and the abandonment provision are presented gross. No standard lets one cancel the other, and under a cost-recovery contract any surplus left in the fund at the end belongs to the state, which caps what the fund is worth to the contractor.

Restricted cash grew 11 percent while cash and cash equivalents nearly halved, and the face of the balance sheet cannot say what it secures

The balance sheet on this page reports restricted cash, non-current, of 1,890,493 at 31 December 2024 against 1,700,675 a year earlier, in thousands, a rise of 189,818 or 11.2 percent. The current line rose 15.5 percent to 154,217, while cash and cash equivalents fell 47.9 percent to 2,614,318. The non-current line is now 6.24 percent of total assets (1,890,493 / 30,303,898) and 72.3 percent of cash and cash equivalents, against 33.9 percent a year earlier.

This essay uses PT Hulu Energi Nusantara ("HEN"), an upstream contractor operating production sharing contracts (PSCs) with SKK Migas, the regulator of Indonesian upstream contracts. HEN reports in USD under Indonesian SAK with a 31 December year end. HEN and every figure attached to it are constructed for this essay alone, and HEN amounts are in USD thousand.

HEN holds two restricted balances. Its Kenari field is operated under a cost-recovery PSC, one in which the contractor recovers its approved costs from production before the remainder is split with the state, and HEN holds 100 percent. Kenari has an abandonment and site restoration (ASR) fund, money set aside to plug wells and remove facilities when production ends, and an ASR provision, the liability for that future work. HEN's reserve-based lending (RBL) facility, a bank loan sized on the value of its reserves, requires a debt service reserve account (DSRA) holding 4,500. The CFO's draft 2025 statements make three choices. Cash and cash equivalents include the DSRA's 4,500, because the account is in HEN's name and earns interest. The ASR provision is shown net of the fund at 17,305, since "the fund exists only to pay it". The cash flow statement shows the 3,000 paid from the fund for plugging four wells as an operating outflow, with a matching investing inflow. The auditor objects to all three.

The governing claim of this essay is that restricted cash is defined by who can withdraw it and when, so its classification, cash flow presentation and link to the ASR provision follow from the terms of the account.

This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that HEN's cash and cash equivalents fall by 4,500, that its restricted cash is 30,500, that the ASR provision of 43,305 stands gross beside the 26,000 fund, and that the 3,000 plugging payment never touched cash and cash equivalents. The standards are PSAK 207 Statement of Cash Flows (formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7), PSAK 201 Presentation of Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) and PSAK 237 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37).

A balance stops being cash when the entity cannot draw it on demand, and a restriction on its use is not enough

Cash is money the entity can withdraw today. PSAK 207 defines it as cash on hand and demand deposits, and cash equivalents as short-term, highly liquid investments held to meet short-term cash commitments and readily convertible to known amounts of cash. "Restricted cash" has no definition in the standards; preparers use the label for balances kept apart because of limits on their use.

The test is narrower than "earmarked". In 2022 the IFRS Interpretations Committee considered a demand deposit that a seller had agreed with a buyer to use only for warranty claims but could still withdraw at any time, and concluded it remained cash. A contractual restriction on use changes the classification only if the deposit is no longer withdrawable on demand. The restriction is still disclosed, since PSAK 207 requires disclosure of significant balances not available for use by the group.

HEN's two balances fail the test for different reasons.

  • The ASR fund fails because of who must sign. Under Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Regulation 15 of 2018 on post-operation activities, contractors reserve ASR funds in stages under the approved work program and budget (Art. 11(2)), starting in the year production is declared commercial, in a joint account between SKK Migas and the contractor at a state-owned commercial bank (Art. 11(3)). HEN cannot withdraw them alone, so they are not demand deposits for HEN.

  • The DSRA fails because the bank will not pay out. The RBL's account control agreement, an agreement among HEN, the lenders and the account bank that tells the bank whose instructions to follow, requires the bank to refuse HEN's withdrawals while the loan is outstanding unless the lenders consent.

Removing the DSRA lowers cash and cash equivalents by 4,500. Restricted cash at 31 December 2025 is 26,000 + 4,500 = 30,500.

The twelve-month line follows when the restriction lifts or the money is spent, so a deposit can change sides without moving

A restricted balance is current when, within twelve months, the restriction lifts or the money is applied to the obligation it secures. That follows from PSAK 201, which classifies cash as current unless it is restricted from being exchanged or used to settle a liability for at least twelve months after the reporting date.

Both events occur at HEN.

  • In November 2024 SKK Migas approved plugging four idle Kenari wells in 2025 at 3,000, paid from the fund, so at 31 December 2024 that 3,000 is current.

  • In November 2025 SKK Migas approved 2,500 of plugging for three more wells in 2026. At 31 December 2025, 2,500 of the fund is current.

  • The DSRA is released when the RBL is repaid on 30 June 2026, eighteen months after 31 December 2024 (non-current) and six months after 31 December 2025 (current).

Total restricted cash is 30,500 at the 2024 and 2025 year ends, while 4,000 moves from non-current to current. The DSRA's 4,500 crossed the line with no transaction at all. The rest of the fund stays non-current until the field stops producing, which HEN expects in 2034.

A movement in restricted cash is a cash flow only when it crosses the cash boundary, and its activity class is a judgment

The cash flow statement explains the change in cash and cash equivalents, so a deposit from HEN's operating account into the fund is an outflow, while interest credited inside the fund, a payment from the fund to a vendor and a reclassification are not.

Interest at a constructed 3 percent of the opening balance is credited in early December, before the deposit and any drawing.

The classification of the 2,220 is a policy choice. PSAK 207 allows a payment in investing activities only if it results in a recognised asset, and the deposit creates one, so HEN classifies deposits as investing. Operating can be argued, because the PSC treats the deposit as an operating cost. HEN's earlier statements used investing, and PSAK 208 requires a policy to be applied consistently. HEN presented the DSRA's funding (4,500 in 2023) as financing, because the account exists only because of the loan, and will present its release on repayment in June 2026 the same way; investing would also be defensible.

HEN uses the indirect method, which starts from profit and removes non-cash items, so the 780 of interest is deducted and the 2,205 of unwinding on the provision (next section) added back. The 3,000 plugging payment settled the provision from a restricted asset, so it stays out of the statement and is disclosed as a non-cash transaction. The draft's pair of 3,000 flows would be right only if the fund had reimbursed HEN's operating account, which then paid the vendor.

The fund and the provision stay gross, because no route in the standards lets one cancel the other

The Kenari provision grows each year by unwinding even when no new obligation arises. Under PSAK 237, as in the owner's study notes, the present value of the expected removal and restoration cost is added to the asset and recognised as a liability, and the discount unwinds each year as a finance cost. The Kenari provision stood at 40,000 on 1 January 2023, discounted at a constructed 5 percent.

2023: 40,000 + 40,000 × 5% = 42,000

2024: 42,000 + 42,000 × 5% = 44,100

2025: 44,100 + 44,100 × 5% − 3,000 used for plugging = 43,305

Dr Finance cost, unwinding of discount 2,205 / Cr ASR provision 2,205

Like the fund, the provision at 31 December 2025 splits into 2,500 current and 40,805 non-current. The draft nets the two to 17,305. Three routes could permit that, and each fails.

  1. PSAK 201 prohibits offsetting assets and liabilities unless a standard requires or permits it.

  2. PSAK 232 (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) permits offsetting a financial asset and a financial liability only with a legally enforceable right of set-off and an intention to settle net or simultaneously. The provision is an obligation to perform work, not a financial liability, and HEN has no right of set-off.

  3. When another party will reimburse expenditure on a provision, PSAK 237 recognises the reimbursement, once virtually certain, as a separate asset no larger than the provision; only the expense may be shown net. The fund holds HEN's own deposits, so the rule may not apply, and if it does, it keeps the fund on the asset side.

IFRIC 5 covers decommissioning funds whose assets are administered separately and to which contributors' access is restricted. A contributor without control, joint control or significant influence over the fund (the power to direct it, alone or with others, or to take part in its policy decisions) keeps its obligation and its interest separate, measuring the interest at the lower of the obligation and its share of the fair value of the fund's net assets. The Indonesian Institute of Accountants (IAI) has not adopted IFRIC 5, listing it in a June 2022 public hearing as not relevant to Indonesian fact patterns. A contractor could consult it only through the hierarchy of PSAK 208 (formerly 25, IAS 8), which allows IFRS pronouncements to be considered where no SAK addresses an issue. Every route leaves the two items gross.

The IFRIC 5 cap matters more than its scope. Under Art. 15 of Regulation 15/2018, any difference between actual post-operation cost and the fund reserved reduces or increases operating cost, with SKK Migas approval. Under Art. 16, whatever remains when a cost-recovery contract ends belongs to the state; under a gross split contract, a PSC with no cost recovery in which gross production is split and the contractor bears its own costs, it returns to the contractor. A cost-recovery contractor therefore benefits from the fund only up to the cost it must incur. Kenari's fund of 26,000 is below the provision of 43,305, so the cap does not bind in 2025. If a revision cut the provision below the fund, the essay's reading is that the excess should not be carried as HEN's asset, since HEN can never use it.

Interest belongs to the fund, and under cost recovery the state shares its value

Regulation 15/2018 counts interest earned on the fund toward the amount the contractor must reserve (Art. 11(4)). HEN's approved work program requires the Kenari fund to receive 3,000 a year from deposits and interest combined, so the deposit is the remainder.

2023 deposit = 3,000 − 600 = 2,400

2024 deposit = 3,000 − 690 = 2,310

2025 deposit = 3,000 − 780 = 2,220

HEN records the 780 as finance income, because the fund is its asset. Under a cost-recovery PSC the deposit is a recoverable operating cost (Art. 12(1)), so each dollar of interest cuts HEN's cost recovery by a dollar and leaves more production to split, of which the state takes its contractual share; this essay does not model the split. Under a gross split contract the deposit is a deductible cost the contractor bears (Art. 12(2)) and the surplus returns to it, so the interest benefits the contractor directly.

Deposits are deducted when made and expensed with the provision, and the difference is deferred tax

PSAK 212 (formerly 46, IAS 12) measures deferred tax on temporary differences, the gaps between an item's carrying amount and its tax base (the amount the tax computation will recognise for it), which reverse in later years. This section assumes, as the essay's reading of the PSC terms, that each deposit is recovered and deducted in the year it is made, that fund interest is neither taxed nor deducted, and that plugging paid from the fund gives no second deduction. Those assumptions fix each item's tax base.

  • the fund settles costs that are neither taxable nor deductible when paid, so its tax base equals its carrying amount;

  • the ASR cost in oil and gas properties is never deducted itself, so its tax base is nil (carrying amount 24,000 on 1 January 2023, less units-of-production depreciation of a constructed 2,000 a year);

  • the provision's future deductions are the deposits still to come, which in today's money equal the provision less the fund, so its tax base is the fund.

The net difference fell by 4,000 − 695 = 3,305, so 2023–2025 carry a deferred tax credit of 3,305 × 40% = 1,322, at HEN's combined PSC rate of 25% + 20% × (1 − 25%) = 40%. The income statement gives the same 3,305: net book charges of 10,235 (unwinding 6,305 + depreciation 6,000 − fund interest 2,070) less deductions of 6,930 (2,400 + 2,310 + 2,220). The differences reverse because Art. 15 adds or deducts any shortfall or surplus as operating cost, so total deductions come to the ASR cost less interest, the same as total net book charges. Allocating the differences among the three items is a judgment preparers resolve differently. Since a 2021 amendment, adopted in PSAK 46 from 2023, the initial recognition exemption no longer lets entities skip deferred tax on decommissioning assets and liabilities recognised together.

Corrected, HEN moves 4,500 out of cash, shows 30,500 of restricted cash and keeps the 43,305 provision gross

HEN's corrected 31 December 2025 statements reverse all three draft choices.

Cash and cash equivalents = draft figure − 4,500 DSRA

Restricted cash, current = 2,500 ASR + 4,500 DSRA = 7,000

Restricted cash, non-current = 26,000 − 2,500 = 23,500

ASR provision = 43,305 (current 2,500; non-current 40,805), gross of the fund

Cash flow statement, 2025: deposit of 2,220 in investing; plugging of 3,000 disclosed as non-cash; interest of 780 deducted and unwinding of 2,205 added back in the operating reconciliation

The draft's 17,305 is the unfunded gap measured in today's money. Because the provision accretes at 5 percent and the fund earns 3 percent, the deposits still to come are larger in nominal terms. The ASR provision is 2.5 times the netted figure (43,305 / 17,305).

The reported line on this page may hold abandonment funds, debt reserves, cash collateral for bank guarantees, or all three. To read it, the notes must say what the money secures, when each part comes free, which activity class the transfers use, and how the ASR fund compares with the ASR provision.

Least-confident assertions

  • The PSC mechanics were confirmed against the full text of Regulation 15/2018 (Arts. 11, 12, 15, 16). Art. 20 lets SKK Migas set the amount and method for older contracts without an ASR clause. Whether the regulation has since been amended was not confirmed.

  • Art. 17 passes the obligation and the fund to a successor contractor if the PSC ends and a new contractor takes over. The essay assumes HEN operates Kenari to the end of production; a handover would limit how much of the fund HEN ever uses.

  • The timing of recovery and deduction, and the tax treatment of fund interest, are assumed, and the tax base of the provision rests on them. If deposits were deductible only when spent from the fund, the deferred tax figures would change.

  • Treating the DSRA as outside cash depends on the account control agreement. A DSRA HEN could draw freely, subject only to a covenant, would stay in cash under the 2022 agenda decision.

  • Capping the fund at the provision under cost recovery is the essay's reading, by analogy with IFRIC 5. Indonesian contractors appear to present the fund at its full balance, and the investing and financing classes are HEN's policy choices, not a survey of practice.

The fund and the provision stay gross, because no route in the standards lets one cancel the other

The Kenari provision grows each year by unwinding even when no new obligation arises. Under PSAK 237, as in the owner's study notes, the present value of the expected removal and restoration cost is added to the asset and recognised as a liability, and the discount unwinds each year as a finance cost. The Kenari provision stood at 40,000 on 1 January 2023, discounted at a constructed 5 percent.
Dr Finance cost, unwinding of discount 2,205 / Cr ASR provision 2,205
Like the fund, the provision at 31 December 2025 splits into 2,500 current and 40,805 non-current. The draft nets the two to 17,305. Three routes could permit that, and each fails.
PSAK 201 prohibits offsetting assets and liabilities unless a standard requires or permits it.

PSAK 232 (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) permits offsetting a financial asset and a financial liability only with a legally enforceable right of set-off and an intention to settle net or simultaneously. The provision is an obligation to perform work, not a financial liability, and HEN has no right of set-off.

When another party will reimburse expenditure on a provision, PSAK 237 recognises the reimbursement, once virtually certain, as a separate asset no larger than the provision; only the expense may be shown net. The fund holds HEN's own deposits, so the rule may not apply, and if it does, it keeps the fund on the asset side.

IFRIC 5 covers decommissioning funds whose assets are administered separately and to which contributors' access is restricted. A contributor without control, joint control or significant influence over the fund (the power to direct it, alone or with others, or to take part in its policy decisions) keeps its obligation and its interest separate, measuring the interest at the lower of the obligation and its share of the fair value of the fund's net assets. The Indonesian Institute of Accountants (IAI) has not adopted IFRIC 5, listing it in a June 2022 public hearing as not relevant to Indonesian fact patterns. A contractor could consult it only through the hierarchy of PSAK 208 (formerly 25, IAS 8), which allows IFRS pronouncements to be considered where no SAK addresses an issue. Every route leaves the two items gross.

The IFRIC 5 cap matters more than its scope. Under Art. 15 of Regulation 15/2018, any difference between actual post-operation cost and the fund reserved reduces or increases operating cost, with SKK Migas approval. Under Art. 16, whatever remains when a cost-recovery contract ends belongs to the state; under a gross split contract, a PSC with no cost recovery in which gross production is split and the contractor bears its own costs, it returns to the contractor. A cost-recovery contractor therefore benefits from the fund only up to the cost it must incur. Kenari's fund of 26,000 is below the provision of 43,305, so the cap does not bind in 2025. If a revision cut the provision below the fund, the essay's reading is that the excess should not be carried as HEN's asset, since HEN can never use it.
Interest belongs to the fund, and under cost recovery the state shares its value

Regulation 15/2018 counts interest earned on the fund toward the amount the contractor must reserve (Art. 11(4)). HEN's approved work program requires the Kenari fund to receive 3,000 a year from deposits and interest combined, so the deposit is the remainder.

HEN records the 780 as finance income, because the fund is its asset. Under a cost-recovery PSC the deposit is a recoverable operating cost (Art. 12(1)), so each dollar of interest cuts HEN's cost recovery by a dollar and leaves more production to split, of which the state takes its contractual share; this essay does not model the split. Under a gross split contract the deposit is a deductible cost the contractor bears (Art. 12(2)) and the surplus returns to it, so the interest benefits the contractor directly.
Deposits are deducted when made and expensed with the provision, and the difference is deferred tax

PSAK 212 (formerly 46, IAS 12) measures deferred tax on temporary differences, the gaps between an item's carrying amount and its tax base (the amount the tax computation will recognise for it), which reverse in later years. This section assumes, as the essay's reading of the PSC terms, that each deposit is recovered and deducted in the year it is made, that fund interest is neither taxed nor deducted, and that plugging paid from the fund gives no second deduction. Those assumptions fix each item's tax base.
the fund settles costs that are neither taxable nor deductible when paid, so its tax base equals its carrying amount;

the ASR cost in oil and gas properties is never deducted itself, so its tax base is nil (carrying amount 24,000 on 1 January 2023, less units-of-production depreciation of a constructed 2,000 a year);
the provision's future deductions are the deposits still to come, which in today's money equal the provision less the fund, so its tax base is the fund.
ASR asset, taxable difference (carrying amount; tax base nil)

The net difference fell by 4,000 − 695 = 3,305, so 2023–2025 carry a deferred tax credit of 3,305 × 40% = 1,322, at HEN's combined PSC rate of 25% + 20% × (1 − 25%) = 40%. The income statement gives the same 3,305: net book charges of 10,235 (unwinding 6,305 + depreciation 6,000 − fund interest 2,070) less deductions of 6,930 (2,400 + 2,310 + 2,220). The differences reverse because Art. 15 adds or deducts any shortfall or surplus as operating cost, so total deductions come to the ASR cost less interest, the same as total net book charges. Allocating the differences among the three items is a judgment preparers resolve differently. Since a 2021 amendment, adopted in PSAK 46 from 2023, the initial recognition exemption no longer lets entities skip deferred tax on decommissioning assets and liabilities recognised together.
Corrected, HEN moves 4,500 out of cash, shows 30,500 of restricted cash and keeps the 43,305 provision gross
HEN's corrected 31 December 2025 statements reverse all three draft choices.
Cash and cash equivalents = draft figure − 4,500 DSRA
ASR provision = 43,305 (current 2,500; non-current 40,805), gross of the fund
Cash flow statement, 2025: deposit of 2,220 in investing; plugging of 3,000 disclosed as non-cash; interest of 780 deducted and unwinding of 2,205 added back in the operating reconciliation

The draft's 17,305 is the unfunded gap measured in today's money. Because the provision accretes at 5 percent and the fund earns 3 percent, the deposits still to come are larger in nominal terms. The ASR provision is 2.5 times the netted figure (43,305 / 17,305).

The reported line on this page may hold abandonment funds, debt reserves, cash collateral for bank guarantees, or all three. To read it, the notes must say what the money secures, when each part comes free, which activity class the transfers use, and how the ASR fund compares with the ASR provision.

The PSC mechanics were confirmed against the full text of Regulation 15/2018 (Arts. 11, 12, 15, 16). Art. 20 lets SKK Migas set the amount and method for older contracts without an ASR clause. Whether the regulation has since been amended was not confirmed.

Art. 17 passes the obligation and the fund to a successor contractor if the PSC ends and a new contractor takes over. The essay assumes HEN operates Kenari to the end of production; a handover would limit how much of the fund HEN ever uses.

The timing of recovery and deduction, and the tax treatment of fund interest, are assumed, and the tax base of the provision rests on them. If deposits were deductible only when spent from the fund, the deferred tax figures would change.
Treating the DSRA as outside cash depends on the account control agreement. A DSRA HEN could draw freely, subject only to a covenant, would stay in cash under the 2022 agenda decision.

Capping the fund at the provision under cost recovery is the essay's reading, by analogy with IFRIC 5. Indonesian contractors appear to present the fund at its full balance, and the investing and financing classes are HEN's policy choices, not a survey of practice.

Owner's study notes, "Inter 2 - Chapter 13 - Current Liabilities.pdf" (Rumpun Akuntansi Keuangan), section on environmental provisions (capitalisation into the asset, unwinding as interest, settlement entry). NOTES. The notes measure the liability at a market-based fair value; PSAK 237 uses the best estimate, discounted, which this essay follows.
