presentation.deck: When money in a bank account stops being cash, where the twelve-month line falls, and why the abandonment fund never nets against the obligation it exists to pay
key_takeaways: A bank balance leaves cash and cash equivalents when the entity cannot draw it on demand. An Indonesian contractor's abandonment fund sits in a joint account with SKK Migas, and a debt service reserve sits in an account the lenders control, so both are restricted cash.
The current/non-current split follows when the restriction lifts or the money is spent. The same deposit can change sides without moving, and no such reclassification is a cash flow.

The abandonment fund and the abandonment provision are presented gross. No standard lets one cancel the other, and under a cost-recovery contract any surplus left in the fund at the end belongs to the state, which caps what the fund is worth to the contractor.

title: Restricted Cash: When Money in the Bank Stops Being Cash
snippet: The theory of restricted balances from the access test to disclosure, worked through PHE's abandonment funds and set beside the industries that hold money they cannot spend
content:
In brief

  • A bank balance leaves cash and cash equivalents only when the entity cannot withdraw it on demand. A contract that limits what the money may be spent on is not enough; a bank that blocks it, or a third party whose consent each withdrawal needs, is.

  • Restricted cash is current or non-current according to when the restriction lifts or the money is applied to what it secures. Paying into a restricted account is a cash flow; interest credited inside it, a reclassification, or a payment straight from it to a supplier is not.

  • A fund set aside for an obligation stays on the asset side, gross of the obligation. No standard lets the two be netted, and in Indonesian upstream contracts the fund sits in a joint account with SKK Migas that the contractor cannot draw alone.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report restricted cash of 154,217 (current) and 1,890,493 (non-current) at 31 December 2024, against 133,537 and 1,700,675 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). Together the two lines are 2,044,710, or 6.7 percent of total assets, up from 1,834,212 and 5.9 percent. The non-current line alone is 92.5 percent of the total. This page uses those balances as the starting point for its examples, and it covers both lines.

After reading it a student should be able to decide whether a balance is restricted, place it on the right side of the twelve-month line, record its movements, and show them correctly in the cash flow statement.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The order follows the chapter on cash in Kieso's Intermediate Accounting (IFRS edition), on restricted cash and compensating balances, and the structure of PSAK 207 and PSAK 201.

1. What makes cash restricted

"Restricted cash" is not defined in any standard; it is the label preparers use for balances that fail the definition of cash. PSAK 207 Statement of Cash Flows (formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7) defines cash as "cash on hand and demand deposits" (para. 6), and a demand deposit is one the holder can withdraw at any time. So the question for any balance is whether the entity can get the money out today.

The IFRS Interpretations Committee answered the harder version of that question in April 2022. An entity held a deposit it could withdraw at any time, but had agreed with a third party to keep a set amount in it and use it only for specified purposes. The Committee concluded that such restrictions "do not result in the deposit no longer being cash, unless those restrictions change the nature of the deposit in a way that it would no longer meet the definition of cash". Breaking the contract would be a breach, but the bank would still pay. The deposit stays in cash, with disclosure and, if relevant, its own line within cash.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary holds three deposits at 31 December 2024.

Deposit

Terms

Can the entity withdraw on demand?

Line

(a) 2,000 earmarked for capital spending

A loan covenant says the money may be used only for a compressor upgrade; the bank pays on any instruction

Yes

Cash and cash equivalents, with disclosure

(b) 4,500 debt service reserve

An account control agreement, among the borrower, the lenders and the account bank, tells the bank to refuse the borrower's withdrawals without lender consent

No

Restricted cash

(c) 11,000 abandonment fund

A joint account with SKK Migas, the upstream regulator, released only with its approval

No

Restricted cash

Cash and cash equivalents include 2,000; restricted cash = 4,500 + 11,000 = 15,500

The earmark in (a) changes what management may do with the money. It does not change what the bank will do, and only the second matters for the definition.

2. Kinds of restriction

Kieso lists the common reasons cash is set aside, and each fits the access test differently.

  • Compensating balances: a minimum deposit a lender requires as part of a loan. If the agreement legally blocks it, it is restricted; otherwise it stays in cash and is disclosed.

  • Funds for a specific purpose: a plant expansion fund or a bond sinking fund, money accumulated to repay a bond. Under Kieso these are investments or other assets, usually non-current.

  • Collateral: cash pledged to a bank as security for a bank guarantee or letter of credit. The bank holds it until the guarantee expires.

  • Escrow and regulatory funds: money held by a third party or in a joint account until a condition is met, such as abandonment funds in upstream oil and gas or reclamation guarantees in mining (section 8).

A compensating balance also raises the true cost of the loan, because the borrower pays interest on money it cannot use. For example (illustration), a subsidiary borrows 50,000 at 6 percent a year and must keep 5,000 blocked at the lending bank, earning nothing.

Interest paid = 50,000 × 6% = 3,000

Money the borrower can use = 50,000 − 5,000 = 45,000

Effective cost = 3,000 / 45,000 = 6.67% a year

The 5,000 is shown as restricted cash, and the arrangement is disclosed so a reader can see the 6.67 percent behind the 6 percent.

3. Current or non-current

Restricted cash is current when, within twelve months of the reporting date, the restriction lifts or the money is applied to the obligation it secures. That follows from PSAK 201 Presentation of Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1), which classifies cash as current "unless the asset is restricted from being exchanged or used to settle a liability for at least twelve months after the reporting period" (para. 66(d)). Because of the words "used to settle a liability", money that will pay an obligation due next year is current even though the entity cannot spend it on anything else.

PHE's policy applies the same idea through the obligation. Restricted cash "for repayment of currently maturing obligations" is current, and restricted cash for obligations "maturing after one year" is non-current (Note 3f, Daftar 5/38, PDF p. 55).

For example (illustration), an abandonment fund holds 11,000 at 31 December 2024. In November 2024 SKK Migas approved 1,500 of plugging work for 2025, to be paid from the fund. Separately, the debt service reserve of 4,500 from section 1 is released when the loan is repaid on 30 June 2026.

31 Dec 2024

31 Dec 2025

Abandonment fund, current (approved for use in the next twelve months)

1,500

Depends on approvals given in 2025

Abandonment fund, non-current

11,000 − 1,500 = 9,500

The remainder

Debt service reserve

Non-current: release is 18 months away

Current: release is 6 months away

The debt service reserve crosses the line at 31 December 2025 without any transaction at all. Classification follows the calendar, so a reclassification is never a cash flow.

4. Recording restricted cash

Restricted cash is measured like any bank balance, at amortised cost, with interest accrued and, for foreign-currency balances, retranslation at the closing rate under PSAK 221 (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21). The page cash-and-cash-equivalents works both through. What is particular to restricted cash is its life cycle. Money goes in, earns interest inside, and leaves either to settle the obligation or back to the entity.

Take PHE's own deposits as the starting point. The subsidiary PHE OSES paid USD 180,027.96 into its abandonment and site restoration (ASR) fund on 21 May 2024 and USD 172,672.89 on 23 December 2024, each on a letter from SKK Migas setting the semester's placement (Note 45i, Daftar 5/208, PDF p. 225). ASR is the work of plugging wells and removing facilities when a field ends.

Total 2024 placements = 180.0 + 172.7 = 352.7 (USD thousand)

21 May: Dr Restricted cash, non-current (ASR fund) 180.0 / Cr Cash in banks 180.0

23 December: Dr Restricted cash, non-current (ASR fund) 172.7 / Cr Cash in banks 172.7

The rest of the life cycle, for example (illustration), on the fund of section 3. Interest at a constructed 3 percent of the opening balance is credited inside the fund. The approved work programme requires the fund to grow by 1,000 a year from deposits and interest combined, so the deposit is the remainder.

ASR fund

Opening balance

1,000 − 300 = 700

1,000 − 330 = 670

Paid to plugging contractor

Journal

The last entry never touches cash in banks. The fund settles the provision directly, which is the reason the money was set aside.

5. Restricted cash in the cash flow statement

The cash flow statement explains the change in cash and cash equivalents, so a movement in restricted cash is a cash flow only when it crosses that boundary. Applying this to the fund in section 4:

Event

Crosses the cash boundary?

Cash flow statement

Deposit of 670

Yes, out of cash in banks

Outflow, 670

Interest of 330 credited inside the fund

No

None; deducted as non-cash income in an indirect-method reconciliation

Payment of 1,500 from the fund to the contractor

No

None; no cash or cash equivalent moves

Reclassification between current and non-current

No

None

Release of a fund back to the operating account

Yes, into cash in banks

Inflow

Which activity the deposit belongs to is a policy choice, applied consistently under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8). Investing is supported because the deposit creates a recognised asset, the condition PSAK 207 sets for investing classification (para. 16). Operating can be argued because the fund pays for a cost of operations, and for a debt service reserve financing can be argued because the account exists only because of the loan. When the fund pays the contractor, no cash or cash equivalent moves, so the payment is not in the statement. PSAK 207 requires investing and financing transactions that do not use cash to be disclosed elsewhere (para. 43); that applies here if the entity classifies decommissioning spending as investing, and disclosure is still useful to the reader if it classifies it as operating.

PHE's direct-method statement has no separate line for placements into or releases from restricted cash (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17), so the 210,498 rise in the two lines in 2024 is not visible on its face.

6. The fund and the obligation stay gross

An ASR fund exists to pay the ASR provision, which invites netting the two. Every route in the standards refuses it.

  1. PSAK 201 prohibits offsetting assets and liabilities unless a standard requires or permits it (para. 32).

  2. PSAK 232 Financial Instruments: Presentation (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) permits offsetting a financial asset and a financial liability only with a legally enforceable right of set-off and an intention to settle net or simultaneously (para. 42). The provision is an obligation to perform work, which falls outside the definition of a financial liability.

  3. PSAK 237 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) treats a reimbursement from another party as a separate asset, recognised only when virtually certain and capped at the provision (para. 53). A fund built from the entity's own deposits is hard to read as a reimbursement from another party, and even if it were one, it would stay on the asset side.

IFRIC 5, which deals with interests in decommissioning funds administered separately, has not been adopted in Indonesia. DSAK IAI listed it in June 2022 as not relevant to Indonesian fact patterns.

For example (illustration), the field behind the fund in section 4 carries an ASR provision of 24,000 at the end of 2024 against a fund of 11,000.

Gross presentation: restricted cash 11,000 (assets); provision 24,000 (liabilities)

Netted (not permitted): net liability = 24,000 − 11,000 = 13,000

Netting would show 13,000 where the field owes 24,000 of work and holds 11,000 of money it cannot spend without SKK Migas approval.

The fund's value to a cost recovery contractor also has a ceiling. Under the Indonesian rule in section 10, a surplus left in the fund when a cost recovery contract ends goes to the state, so the contractor benefits from the fund only up to the cost it must incur. The ceiling bites only if the fund, with its interest, ends above the cost actually incurred. Art. 15 first adjusts operating cost for any difference, and Art. 16 deals with what is left at contract end.

7. Disclosure

Restricted cash is disclosed because its reader is usually a lender or analyst asking how much cash is free to use. PSAK 207 requires the amount of significant cash balances "not available for use by the group", with a commentary by management (para. 48), and the components of cash and cash equivalents with a reconciliation to the balance sheet (para. 45). The 2022 agenda decision adds that an entity should consider liquidity risk disclosures under PSAK 107 Financial Instruments: Disclosures (formerly PSAK 60, IFRS 7), and further information where these are not enough for users to understand the effect of the restrictions (PSAK 201.31).

A useful note says, for each restricted balance, what it secures, who must consent to its release, when it comes free, and which activity its movements use.

8. Restricted cash across industries

The access test is the same everywhere. What differs is the obligation behind the money and the forms the regulator allows.

Mining. Holders of Indonesian mining licences must provide a reclamation guarantee (jaminan reklamasi) for land disturbed by mining. Under Government Regulation 78 of 2010, the production-stage guarantee could take the form of a joint account or a time deposit at a state bank, a bank guarantee, or an accounting reserve (cadangan akuntansi), and each form produced a different balance sheet. Since Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Decision 344/2025 (Kepmen ESDM 344/2025) the form is a time deposit, no longer a bank guarantee (ESDM, as reported in October 2025). For example (illustration), a coal miner's reclamation plan requires a guarantee of 2,000 for the year.

Form under PP 78/2010

Entry

Restricted cash

Joint-account time deposit

Dr Restricted cash, reclamation guarantee 2,000 / Cr Cash in banks 2,000

2,000

Bank guarantee, with a 20% cash margin required by the bank

Dr Restricted cash, guarantee margin 400 / Cr Cash in banks 400; the guarantee itself is disclosed

2,000 × 20% = 400

Accounting reserve

No entry; the company keeps the cash

0

The reclamation provision under PSAK 237 is the same in all three. Only the cash set aside against it differs. Under Kepmen 344/2025 the first row becomes the rule, so the miner shows restricted cash of 2,000 whatever its balance sheet strength.

Project finance. Power, toll-road and renewable-energy projects financed on their own cash flows usually keep a debt service reserve account (DSRA) holding several months of loan payments, controlled by the lenders. For example (illustration), a geothermal project pays 24,000 a year in principal and interest, and its loan requires six months in reserve.

DSRA = 24,000 × 6 / 12 = 12,000

At financial close: Dr Restricted cash, DSRA 12,000 / Cr Cash in banks 12,000

Final six months, paid from the DSRA: Dr Bank loans (principal) and Dr Interest payable, together 12,000 / Cr Restricted cash, DSRA 12,000

The final entry is a financing transaction that uses no cash and cash equivalents, so it is disclosed rather than shown as a flow (para. 43), and the repayment appears as a non-cash change in the reconciliation of liabilities from financing activities (paras. 44A–44E).

Property developers. When an Indonesian developer sells a house through a bank mortgage (kredit pemilikan rumah, KPR) before the title certificate or the building is ready, the bank commonly holds back part of the loan until the developer delivers. Where the held amount sits in a blocked account in the developer's name, it is restricted cash, current or non-current according to when delivery is expected. For example (illustration), on a house sold for IDR 1,000 million with a 10 percent holdback, IDR 100 million is restricted until the certificate is handed over.

Groups with subsidiaries under exchange controls. Cash that local law keeps inside a country is a contrast case. The subsidiary can withdraw it, so it remains cash; it is the group that cannot use it, and PSAK 207 requires that to be disclosed (para. 48) while the balance stays in cash.

Guarantee collateral in service contracts. Cash pledged as collateral for guarantees is the most common restricted balance outside regulated funds. PHE's subsidiaries PDSI and PT Badak NGL hold current restricted cash "as collateral for bank guarantees in relation to the Group's drilling rig contracts and project with customer" (Note 7, Daftar 5/95, PDF p. 112).

9. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 7

PHE gives restricted cash by currency, by bank and by purpose (Note 7, Daftar 5/93–5/95, PDF pp. 110–112).

The note names four purposes. Restricted cash is ASR funds at ten subsidiaries, including PHR, PHE ONWJ and PHE OSES; the current portion at PHE WMO is gas revenue not yet distributed to SKK Migas and partners; the current portion at PDSI and PT Badak NGL is guarantee collateral; and the current portion elsewhere is deposits required for work programmes and joint studies. Of the total, 1,917,572 (93.8 percent) is held at government-related banks (Note 44b, Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199). The rupiah share of the non-current line fell from 50,625 to 4,461, leaving it 99.8 percent in dollars.

The note's wording implies that the non-current line is ASR money, which invites a rough comparison with the ASR provision of 3,826,222 (Note 29, Daftar 5/145, PDF p. 162). PHE also holds 66,719 of "restricted funds for site restoration in joint operation" within other non-current assets, cash deposited by operators of blocks in which PHE is a partner (Note 14b, Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122).

Non-current restricted cash / ASR provision = 1,890,493 / 3,826,222 = 49.4% (2024); 1,700,675 / 3,784,917 = 44.9% (2023)

Including joint-operation funds = (1,890,493 + 66,719) / 3,826,222 = 51.2% (2024); (1,700,675 + 296,555) / 3,784,917 = 52.8% (2023)

On the restricted cash line alone, coverage rose. Including joint-operation funds, it fell slightly. The two move apart because the joint-operation funds dropped by 229,836 while non-current restricted cash rose by 189,818. PHE explains that site restoration funds not yet transferred were moved by SKK Migas and the former operators into the SKK Migas–PHR joint account (Note 14b, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123), which may mean part of the rise came from a transfer between lines; the FS do not quantify it. The ratio is rough in any case, because the provision is a present value and the fund a nominal balance, and both are spread across many contracts.

10. Upstream note: the Indonesian ASR fund

PHE describes the mechanism in its policy. The group must place ASR funds in restricted bank accounts, "maintained in joint bank accounts between SKK Migas and the Group", usable only for ASR "with approval from SKK Migas", or "transferred to SKK Migas if the activities are not conducted by the Group" (Note 3o, Daftar 5/61, PDF p. 78). That joint signature is why the fund fails the access test.

Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Regulation 15 of 2018 on post-operation activities sets the rules behind the policy. Funds are reserved in stages under the approved work programme and budget, from the year production is declared commercial, in a joint account at a state-owned bank (Art. 11(2)–(3)); interest counts toward the amount to be reserved (Art. 11(4)). Under a cost recovery contract, in which the contractor recovers approved costs from production before the rest is split with the state, the reserve is a recoverable operating cost (Art. 12(1)); under a gross split contract, with no cost recovery, it is a cost the contractor bears and deducts for tax (Art. 12(2)). A difference between actual cost and the fund adjusts operating cost (Art. 15), and what remains at the end of a cost recovery contract goes to the state, while under gross split it returns to the contractor (Art. 16).

11. Related lines

  • cash-and-cash-equivalents: the line restricted balances are taken out of.

  • decommissioning-site-restoration-provision: the obligation the ASR fund exists to pay, presented gross.

  • other-non-current-assets: holds PHE's share of joint-operation restoration funds.

  • long-term-bank-loans-non-current: the loans that debt service reserves and compensating balances secure.

  • finance-income: interest earned inside the funds.

Least-confident assertions

  • The provisions of Regulation 15/2018 were checked against the full JDIH text in October 2026 and not reopened for this version; whether the regulation has since been amended was not confirmed.

  • Reading the non-current line as wholly ASR money, and the 2024 movement as partly a transfer from other non-current assets, rests on the wording of Notes 7 and 14b. PHE does not give a reconciliation.

  • The reclamation-guarantee forms follow Government Regulation 78 of 2010 as summarised by a BPK paper. The change to time deposits under Kepmen ESDM 344/2025 rests on an ESDM official quoted by Dunia Energi (27 October 2025); the decision itself was not opened, so its transitional rules and any remaining forms are not confirmed.

  • The KPR holdback treatment describes a common arrangement; contracts differ, and some developers present the held amount as a receivable from the bank.

  • The classification of fund deposits, and of decommissioning spending paid from the fund, as investing, operating or financing is presented as a policy choice, and with it whether para. 43 disclosure applies; no survey of Indonesian practice was made.

content.text: A bank balance leaves cash and cash equivalents only when the entity cannot withdraw it on demand. A contract that limits what the money may be spent on is not enough; a bank that blocks it, or a third party whose consent each withdrawal needs, is.

Restricted cash is current or non-current according to when the restriction lifts or the money is applied to what it secures. Paying into a restricted account is a cash flow; interest credited inside it, a reclassification, or a payment straight from it to a supplier is not.

A fund set aside for an obligation stays on the asset side, gross of the obligation. No standard lets the two be netted, and in Indonesian upstream contracts the fund sits in a joint account with SKK Migas that the contractor cannot draw alone.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report restricted cash of 154,217 (current) and 1,890,493 (non-current) at 31 December 2024, against 133,537 and 1,700,675 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). Together the two lines are 2,044,710, or 6.7 percent of total assets, up from 1,834,212 and 5.9 percent. The non-current line alone is 92.5 percent of the total. This page uses those balances as the starting point for its examples, and it covers both lines.

After reading it a student should be able to decide whether a balance is restricted, place it on the right side of the twelve-month line, record its movements, and show them correctly in the cash flow statement.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The order follows the chapter on cash in Kieso's
(IFRS edition), on restricted cash and compensating balances, and the structure of PSAK 207 and PSAK 201.
"Restricted cash" is not defined in any standard; it is the label preparers use for balances that fail the definition of cash. PSAK 207

(formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7) defines cash as "cash on hand and demand deposits" (para. 6), and a demand deposit is one the holder can withdraw at any time. So the question for any balance is whether the entity can get the money out today.

The IFRS Interpretations Committee answered the harder version of that question in April 2022. An entity held a deposit it could withdraw at any time, but had agreed with a third party to keep a set amount in it and use it only for specified purposes. The Committee concluded that such restrictions "do not result in the deposit no longer being cash, unless those restrictions change the nature of the deposit in a way that it would no longer meet the definition of cash". Breaking the contract would be a breach, but the bank would still pay. The deposit stays in cash, with disclosure and, if relevant, its own line within cash.
For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary holds three deposits at 31 December 2024.
Can the entity withdraw on demand?
A loan covenant says the money may be used only for a compressor upgrade; the bank pays on any instruction
Cash and cash equivalents, with disclosure
, among the borrower, the lenders and the account bank, tells the bank to refuse the borrower's withdrawals without lender consent
A joint account with SKK Migas, the upstream regulator, released only with its approval
Cash and cash equivalents include 2,000; restricted cash = 4,500 + 11,000 = 15,500
The earmark in (a) changes what management may do with the money. It does not change what the bank will do, and only the second matters for the definition.
Kieso lists the common reasons cash is set aside, and each fits the access test differently.
: a minimum deposit a lender requires as part of a loan. If the agreement legally blocks it, it is restricted; otherwise it stays in cash and is disclosed.
: a plant expansion fund or a bond
, money accumulated to repay a bond. Under Kieso these are investments or other assets, usually non-current.
: cash pledged to a bank as security for a bank guarantee or letter of credit. The bank holds it until the guarantee expires.
: money held by a third party or in a joint account until a condition is met, such as abandonment funds in upstream oil and gas or reclamation guarantees in mining (section 8).

A compensating balance also raises the true cost of the loan, because the borrower pays interest on money it cannot use. For example (illustration), a subsidiary borrows 50,000 at 6 percent a year and must keep 5,000 blocked at the lending bank, earning nothing.
The 5,000 is shown as restricted cash, and the arrangement is disclosed so a reader can see the 6.67 percent behind the 6 percent.
Restricted cash is current when, within twelve months of the reporting date, the restriction lifts or the money is applied to the obligation it secures. That follows from PSAK 201

(formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1), which classifies cash as current "unless the asset is restricted from being exchanged or used to settle a liability for at least twelve months after the reporting period" (para. 66(d)). Because of the words "used to settle a liability", money that will pay an obligation due next year is current even though the entity cannot spend it on anything else.

PHE's policy applies the same idea through the obligation. Restricted cash "for repayment of currently maturing obligations" is current, and restricted cash for obligations "maturing after one year" is non-current (Note 3f, Daftar 5/38, PDF p. 55).

For example (illustration), an abandonment fund holds 11,000 at 31 December 2024. In November 2024 SKK Migas approved 1,500 of plugging work for 2025, to be paid from the fund. Separately, the debt service reserve of 4,500 from section 1 is released when the loan is repaid on 30 June 2026.
Abandonment fund, current (approved for use in the next twelve months)
The debt service reserve crosses the line at 31 December 2025 without any transaction at all. Classification follows the calendar, so a reclassification is never a cash flow.

Restricted cash is measured like any bank balance, at amortised cost, with interest accrued and, for foreign-currency balances, retranslation at the closing rate under PSAK 221 (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21). The page
works both through. What is particular to restricted cash is its life cycle. Money goes in, earns interest inside, and leaves either to settle the obligation or back to the entity.

Take PHE's own deposits as the starting point. The subsidiary PHE OSES paid USD 180,027.96 into its abandonment and site restoration (ASR) fund on 21 May 2024 and USD 172,672.89 on 23 December 2024, each on a letter from SKK Migas setting the semester's placement (Note 45i, Daftar 5/208, PDF p. 225). ASR is the work of plugging wells and removing facilities when a field ends.
21 May: Dr Restricted cash, non-current (ASR fund) 180.0 / Cr Cash in banks 180.0
23 December: Dr Restricted cash, non-current (ASR fund) 172.7 / Cr Cash in banks 172.7

The rest of the life cycle, for example (illustration), on the fund of section 3. Interest at a constructed 3 percent of the opening balance is credited inside the fund. The approved work programme requires the fund to grow by 1,000 a year from deposits and interest combined, so the deposit is the remainder.
Dr Restricted cash, ASR fund 330 / Cr Finance income 330
Dr Restricted cash, ASR fund 670 / Cr Cash in banks 670
Dr Provision for decommissioning and site restoration 1,500 / Cr Restricted cash, ASR fund 1,500
The last entry never touches cash in banks. The fund settles the provision directly, which is the reason the money was set aside.
5. Restricted cash in the cash flow statement
The cash flow statement explains the change in cash and cash equivalents, so a movement in restricted cash is a cash flow only when it crosses that boundary. Applying this to the fund in section 4:
Yes, out of cash in banks
Interest of 330 credited inside the fund
None; deducted as non-cash income in an indirect-method reconciliation
Payment of 1,500 from the fund to the contractor
None; no cash or cash equivalent moves
Release of a fund back to the operating account

Which activity the deposit belongs to is a policy choice, applied consistently under PSAK 208 (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8). Investing is supported because the deposit creates a recognised asset, the condition PSAK 207 sets for investing classification (para. 16). Operating can be argued because the fund pays for a cost of operations, and for a debt service reserve financing can be argued because the account exists only because of the loan. When the fund pays the contractor, no cash or cash equivalent moves, so the payment is not in the statement. PSAK 207 requires investing and financing transactions that do not use cash to be disclosed elsewhere (para. 43); that applies here if the entity classifies decommissioning spending as investing, and disclosure is still useful to the reader if it classifies it as operating.
PHE's direct-method statement has no separate line for placements into or releases from restricted cash (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17), so the 210,498 rise in the two lines in 2024 is not visible on its face.
6. The fund and the obligation stay gross
An ASR fund exists to pay the ASR provision, which invites netting the two. Every route in the standards refuses it.
PSAK 201 prohibits offsetting assets and liabilities unless a standard requires or permits it (para. 32).

(formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) permits offsetting a financial asset and a financial liability only with a legally enforceable right of set-off and an intention to settle net or simultaneously (para. 42). The provision is an obligation to perform work, which falls outside the definition of a financial liability.
Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets

(formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) treats a reimbursement from another party as a separate asset, recognised only when virtually certain and capped at the provision (para. 53). A fund built from the entity's own deposits is hard to read as a reimbursement from another party, and even if it were one, it would stay on the asset side.
IFRIC 5, which deals with interests in decommissioning funds administered separately, has not been adopted in Indonesia. DSAK IAI listed it in June 2022 as not relevant to Indonesian fact patterns.
For example (illustration), the field behind the fund in section 4 carries an ASR provision of 24,000 at the end of 2024 against a fund of 11,000.
Netting would show 13,000 where the field owes 24,000 of work and holds 11,000 of money it cannot spend without SKK Migas approval.

The fund's value to a cost recovery contractor also has a ceiling. Under the Indonesian rule in section 10, a surplus left in the fund when a cost recovery contract ends goes to the state, so the contractor benefits from the fund only up to the cost it must incur. The ceiling bites only if the fund, with its interest, ends above the cost actually incurred. Art. 15 first adjusts operating cost for any difference, and Art. 16 deals with what is left at contract end.

Restricted cash is disclosed because its reader is usually a lender or analyst asking how much cash is free to use. PSAK 207 requires the amount of significant cash balances "not available for use by the group", with a commentary by management (para. 48), and the components of cash and cash equivalents with a reconciliation to the balance sheet (para. 45). The 2022 agenda decision adds that an entity should consider liquidity risk disclosures under PSAK 107
(formerly PSAK 60, IFRS 7), and further information where these are not enough for users to understand the effect of the restrictions (PSAK 201.31).
A useful note says, for each restricted balance, what it secures, who must consent to its release, when it comes free, and which activity its movements use.
The access test is the same everywhere. What differs is the obligation behind the money and the forms the regulator allows.
Holders of Indonesian mining licences must provide a

) for land disturbed by mining. Under Government Regulation 78 of 2010, the production-stage guarantee could take the form of a joint account or a time deposit at a state bank, a bank guarantee, or an accounting reserve (

), and each form produced a different balance sheet. Since Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Decision 344/2025 (Kepmen ESDM 344/2025) the form is a time deposit, no longer a bank guarantee (ESDM, as reported in October 2025). For example (illustration), a coal miner's reclamation plan requires a guarantee of 2,000 for the year.
Dr Restricted cash, reclamation guarantee 2,000 / Cr Cash in banks 2,000
Bank guarantee, with a 20% cash margin required by the bank
Dr Restricted cash, guarantee margin 400 / Cr Cash in banks 400; the guarantee itself is disclosed
No entry; the company keeps the cash

The reclamation provision under PSAK 237 is the same in all three. Only the cash set aside against it differs. Under Kepmen 344/2025 the first row becomes the rule, so the miner shows restricted cash of 2,000 whatever its balance sheet strength.
Power, toll-road and renewable-energy projects financed on their own cash flows usually keep a

(DSRA) holding several months of loan payments, controlled by the lenders. For example (illustration), a geothermal project pays 24,000 a year in principal and interest, and its loan requires six months in reserve.
At financial close: Dr Restricted cash, DSRA 12,000 / Cr Cash in banks 12,000
Final six months, paid from the DSRA: Dr Bank loans (principal) and Dr Interest payable, together 12,000 / Cr Restricted cash, DSRA 12,000

The final entry is a financing transaction that uses no cash and cash equivalents, so it is disclosed rather than shown as a flow (para. 43), and the repayment appears as a non-cash change in the reconciliation of liabilities from financing activities (paras. 44A–44E).
When an Indonesian developer sells a house through a bank mortgage (

, KPR) before the title certificate or the building is ready, the bank commonly holds back part of the loan until the developer delivers. Where the held amount sits in a blocked account in the developer's name, it is restricted cash, current or non-current according to when delivery is expected. For example (illustration), on a house sold for IDR 1,000 million with a 10 percent holdback, IDR 100 million is restricted until the certificate is handed over.
Groups with subsidiaries under exchange controls.

Cash that local law keeps inside a country is a contrast case. The subsidiary can withdraw it, so it remains cash; it is the group that cannot use it, and PSAK 207 requires that to be disclosed (para. 48) while the balance stays in cash.

Cash pledged as collateral for guarantees is the most common restricted balance outside regulated funds. PHE's subsidiaries PDSI and PT Badak NGL hold current restricted cash "as collateral for bank guarantees in relation to the Group's drilling rig contracts and project with customer" (Note 7, Daftar 5/95, PDF p. 112).
PHE gives restricted cash by currency, by bank and by purpose (Note 7, Daftar 5/93–5/95, PDF pp. 110–112).

The note names four purposes. Restricted cash is ASR funds at ten subsidiaries, including PHR, PHE ONWJ and PHE OSES; the current portion at PHE WMO is gas revenue not yet distributed to SKK Migas and partners; the current portion at PDSI and PT Badak NGL is guarantee collateral; and the current portion elsewhere is deposits required for work programmes and joint studies. Of the total, 1,917,572 (93.8 percent) is held at government-related banks (Note 44b, Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199). The rupiah share of the non-current line fell from 50,625 to 4,461, leaving it 99.8 percent in dollars.

The note's wording implies that the non-current line is ASR money, which invites a rough comparison with the ASR provision of 3,826,222 (Note 29, Daftar 5/145, PDF p. 162). PHE also holds 66,719 of "restricted funds for site restoration in joint operation" within other non-current assets, cash deposited by operators of blocks in which PHE is a partner (Note 14b, Daftar 5/105, PDF p. 122).

On the restricted cash line alone, coverage rose. Including joint-operation funds, it fell slightly. The two move apart because the joint-operation funds dropped by 229,836 while non-current restricted cash rose by 189,818. PHE explains that site restoration funds not yet transferred were moved by SKK Migas and the former operators into the SKK Migas–PHR joint account (Note 14b, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123), which may mean part of the rise came from a transfer between lines; the FS do not quantify it. The ratio is rough in any case, because the provision is a present value and the fund a nominal balance, and both are spread across many contracts.
10. Upstream note: the Indonesian ASR fund

PHE describes the mechanism in its policy. The group must place ASR funds in restricted bank accounts, "maintained in joint bank accounts between SKK Migas and the Group", usable only for ASR "with approval from SKK Migas", or "transferred to SKK Migas if the activities are not conducted by the Group" (Note 3o, Daftar 5/61, PDF p. 78). That joint signature is why the fund fails the access test.

Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Regulation 15 of 2018 on post-operation activities sets the rules behind the policy. Funds are reserved in stages under the approved work programme and budget, from the year production is declared commercial, in a joint account at a state-owned bank (Art. 11(2)–(3)); interest counts toward the amount to be reserved (Art. 11(4)). contract, in which the contractor recovers approved costs from production before the rest is split with the state, the reserve is a recoverable operating cost (Art. 12(1)); under a

contract, with no cost recovery, it is a cost the contractor bears and deducts for tax (Art. 12(2)). A difference between actual cost and the fund adjusts operating cost (Art. 15), and what remains at the end of a cost recovery contract goes to the state, while under gross split it returns to the contractor (Art. 16).

title: Retained Earnings: Profit Allocation, Dividends and the Statutory Reserve
snippet: The theory of earned capital from the closing entry to the statement of changes in equity, worked through PHE's 2024 allocation to Pertamina and set beside the industries whose distributions are regulated
content:
In brief

  • Retained earnings is the part of equity the entity earned rather than received from its owners: cumulative profit attributable to the owners, less what has been distributed, adjusted for corrections of past errors and changes in accounting policy. It is a claim on net assets and can be far larger than the cash on hand.

  • In an Indonesian limited company the shareholders' meeting (RUPS) allocates last year's profit. A statutory reserve must be set aside until it reaches 20 percent of issued and paid-up capital, and dividends may be paid only while retained earnings are positive (UU PT arts. 70–71). A cash dividend becomes a liability when it is declared, not when the year ends.

  • Dividends in kind are measured at the fair value of what is given (ISAK 117), share dividends move amounts within equity without changing the total, and a "dividend" that exceeds retained earnings returns capital. Banks and cooperatives add their own rules on what may be distributed, and in sharia banks the profit share of mudharabah fund holders comes off before profit reaches the owners.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report retained earnings of 4,352,620 at 31 December 2024 against 3,430,896 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is split into appropriated retained earnings of 1,167,892 and unappropriated retained earnings of 3,184,728. It is 14.3 percent of total assets and 30.2 percent of the equity attributable to owners of the parent (11.1 and 25.3 percent a year earlier).

After reading this page a student should be able to roll retained earnings forward, record each kind of dividend and its dates, apply the Indonesian rules on reserves and distributions, and correct a prior-period error through opening retained earnings.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Share capital and additional paid-in capital are taught in the Share capital essay, accumulated OCI in the Other comprehensive income essay, and non-controlling interest in its own essay.

1. What retained earnings is

Equity has two sources. Contributed capital (paid-in capital) is what owners put in: share capital and share premium. Earned capital is what the business generated and kept. The lecture notes call it "earning capital" and identify it with retained earnings. PHE's contributed capital is 13,631,466 of share capital less 3,649,862 of negative additional paid-in capital, or 9,981,604 (Daftar 1/3).

Closing retained earnings = opening retained earnings + profit attributable to owners of the parent − dividends declared ± corrections of prior-period errors and changes in accounting policy ± transfers from other components of equity

A negative balance is an accumulated deficit (saldo laba negatif or defisit). Profit or loss attributable to non-controlling interests never enters the parent's retained earnings; it goes to the NCI column.

Retained earnings is not cash. Profit is measured on the accrual basis and the cash it brings in is spent on wells, debt service and working capital. For example (illustration), a new PHE subsidiary earns profit of 1,000 in its first year, collects all of it in cash, and spends 900 on drilling.

Retained earnings = 0 + 1,000 = 1,000

Cash = 0 + 1,000 − 900 = 100

The balance sheet says the owners have left 1,000 in the business. Only 100 of it can be paid out without borrowing or selling assets. At PHE, retained earnings of 4,352,620 sat beside cash of 2,614,318 at the end of 2024 (Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11).

Closing the books. At year end each legal entity closes revenue and expenses to an income summary and the profit to retained earnings (Dr Income summary / Cr Retained earnings). The consolidated 3,001,475 comes from combining the closed ledgers.

2. Allocating profit: what the law and the shareholders decide

An entity rarely pays out all it legally may. The lecture notes give four reasons: agreements with creditors to keep part of earnings as protection, laws that block distribution of earnings equal to the cost of treasury shares (an entity's own shares bought back), the wish to smooth dividends across years, and a buffer against losses or errors in measuring profit. Before declaring, management must also look at cash. The notes put it as a test of financial condition: current liabilities will need cash, so a dividend should be paid only if the present and expected financial position supports it.

Indonesian company law, UU No. 40/2007 on Limited Liability Companies (UU PT), sets the order.

  1. The company must set aside part of each year's net profit as a reserve, but only while it has positive retained earnings, until the reserve reaches at least 20 percent of issued and paid-up capital (art. 70(1)–(3)).

  2. The RUPS decides how net profit is used, including the amount set aside (art. 71(1)).

  3. Net profit after the reserve is distributed as dividends unless the RUPS decides otherwise (art. 71(2)).

  4. Dividends may be paid only if the company has positive retained earnings (art. 71(3)).

UU PT does not say whether the test uses the company's own or its consolidated figures. Prudence points to the company's own retained earnings, because consolidated retained earnings include subsidiaries' profit that the parent can reach only when the subsidiaries pay it up. In practice Indonesian groups, PHE among them (Note 34), allocate consolidated profit attributable to owners.

For example, take PHE's 2023 profit attributable to owners of the parent, 2,599,686 (Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15), as what the RUPS in May 2024 had to allocate. Suppose it sets aside 20 percent and distributes the rest.

Reserve = 2,599,686 × 20% = 519,937 (rounded)

Dividend = 2,599,686 − 519,937 = 2,079,749

Dr Retained earnings, unappropriated 2,599,686 / Cr Retained earnings, appropriated 519,937 / Cr Dividends payable 2,079,749

These are PHE's actual 2024 movements, declared by the RUPS recorded in a notarial deed of 31 May 2024 (Note 34, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165). The reserve entry moves an amount between two columns of retained earnings; only the dividend leaves equity.

3. Cash dividends and their dates

A cash dividend has three dates, and only two of them carry an entry.

  • Declaration date: the competent body approves the dividend. From then on the entity has an obligation it cannot withdraw, so it recognises a liability. In an Indonesian company the body is the RUPS for a final dividend, and the board of directors with the board of commissioners' approval for an interim one (UU PT art. 72).

  • Date of record: the register is closed to decide who receives the dividend. No entry.

  • Payment date: cash goes out and the liability is settled.

For example, the lecture notes' company declares USD 0.50 a share on 1,800,000 shares on 10 June, with a record date of 24 June and payment on 16 July.

10 June: Dr Dividend 900,000 / Cr Dividend payable 900,000

24 June: no entry

16 July: Dr Dividend payable 900,000 / Cr Cash 900,000

The notes debit an account called "Dividend"; closed to retained earnings at year end, it gives the same result as debiting retained earnings directly. A dividends payable account is a current liability because payment follows within weeks.

Dividends declared after the reporting date are not a liability at that date, because no obligation existed then (PSAK 210 Peristiwa setelah Periode Pelaporan, formerly PSAK 8, IAS 10, paras. 12–13). They are disclosed. PHE's statements were authorised on 28 March 2025 (Note 1c, Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25), and Note 52 reports no dividend declared before that date, so a dividend on 2024 profit belongs to the 2025 statements. PHE's policy says the same thing: dividends are recognised as a liability in the period in which they are declared (Note 3x, Daftar 5/73, PDF p. 90).

Interim dividends. UU PT art. 72 allows a dividend before the year ends if the articles of association permit it and the company's net assets do not fall below issued and paid-up capital plus the statutory reserve. If the year then ends in a loss, shareholders must return the interim dividend. For example (illustration), a subsidiary has issued capital of 1,000, a statutory reserve of 120 and net assets of 1,400 in September.

Maximum interim dividend = 1,400 − (1,000 + 120) = 280

That is a ceiling. The dividend must also not leave the company unable to pay its creditors or disrupt its business (art. 72(3)), and if shareholders do not return an interim dividend after a loss year, the directors and commissioners are jointly liable (art. 72(6)).

4. Property dividends

A property dividend (dividend in kind) distributes a non-cash asset such as inventory, land or shares in another company. The question is at what amount the distribution reduces retained earnings, and where the difference between the asset's book value and its worth goes.

The lecture notes follow Kieso. At declaration the asset is remeasured to fair value with the gain in profit, then the dividend is recorded at fair value. The notes' example has securities with a book value of 1,250,000 and a fair value of 2,000,000, so a gain of 750,000 at declaration and a dividend of 2,000,000.

PSAK follows ISAK 117 Distribusi Aset Nonkas kepada Pemilik (formerly ISAK 11, IFRIC 17), which works from the liability side.

  • The dividends payable is recognised when the dividend is authorised and no longer at the entity's discretion, and is measured at the fair value of the assets to be distributed.

  • It is remeasured at each reporting date and at settlement, with the changes in equity.

  • At settlement, the difference between the carrying amount of the assets and the carrying amount of the liability goes to profit or loss as a separate line.

For example (illustration), a listed company whose shares are widely held declares a dividend of land carried at 800 when its fair value is 1,000. At the year end the fair value is 1,050, and at distribution 1,060.

Under ISAK 117 the gain waits until the asset leaves, because the land is still the entity's until then. The interpretation excludes distributions where the same party controls the asset before and after. If PHE handed a subsidiary to Pertamina, Pertamina would control that subsidiary before and after the distribution, so ISAK 117 would not apply, and the same exclusion covers a PHE subsidiary distributing to PHE. Practice then usually uses carrying amounts, the logic of PSAK 338 for common-control transactions (see the Share capital essay).

5. Liquidating dividends

A liquidating dividend is a distribution not covered by retained earnings, so in substance it returns the owners' capital. The lecture notes' example is a company that pays a "dividend" of 1,200,000 when only 900,000 is covered by retained earnings, and records:

Dr Retained earnings 900,000 / Dr Share capital – ordinary 300,000 / Cr Dividends payable 1,200,000

Kieso debits share premium for the 300,000. Under Indonesian law, article 71(3) allows dividends only out of positive retained earnings, so the excess is not a dividend at all. Returning share capital needs a formal capital reduction approved by the RUPS with notice to creditors (UU PT arts. 44–47). Kieso's debit to share premium has no clean Indonesian counterpart either, because share premium is not retained earnings and cannot be paid out as a dividend under art. 71(3). Single-field and single-mine companies meet this at the end of a project's life. Depletion and decommissioning have consumed the asset, and the cash left over exceeds accumulated profit. The receiving investor treats the excess as a return of its investment (see the Long-term investments essay).

6. Share dividends and share splits

A share dividend (stock dividend, dividen saham) gives existing owners new shares pro rata instead of cash. Nothing leaves the entity, and each owner's percentage is unchanged. Part of retained earnings is capitalised, moved into share capital, so that it can no longer be distributed. A share split divides each share into more shares of lower par value and moves nothing.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary has 10,000,000 shares of USD 1 par (share capital 10,000) and retained earnings of 6,000. It declares a 10 percent share dividend when the shares are worth USD 3 each, or alternatively splits each share in two.

The lecture notes use the par method, as Kieso's IFRS edition does; IFRS has no rule on the amount. US GAAP uses fair value for small share dividends, below about 20–25 percent of shares outstanding, on the view that holders see them as income. A share dividend distributable sits in equity, not liabilities, because it will be settled in shares, not assets. Indonesian saham bonus are a different transaction, capitalising share premium rather than retained earnings (Dr Share premium / Cr Share capital). PHE's 2022 split is covered in the Share capital essay.

7. Appropriations, the statutory reserve and restrictions

An appropriation earmarks part of retained earnings, in Indonesian saldo laba yang telah ditentukan penggunaannya, so that it is not seen as available for dividends. It is a transfer within retained earnings. No cash is set aside, and the total does not change. The lecture notes add that many companies show restrictions by note disclosure instead of a separate account.

The statutory reserve is the one appropriation the law requires. For example, take PHE's issued and paid-up capital, 13,631,466 in its USD records, and its appropriated balance of 1,167,892 (Note 33, Daftar 5/147, PDF p. 164).

20% threshold = 13,631,466 × 20% = 2,726,293

Reached so far = 1,167,892 / 2,726,293 = 42.8%

Remaining = 2,726,293 − 1,167,892 = 1,558,401, or about 3.0 years at 2024's 519,937

The law states capital in rupiah. PHE's issued capital is Rp198,112,621,170,000 (Note 32), so the legal threshold is about Rp39.6 trillion, and whether the USD comparison above matches the rupiah test depends on the exchange rates used. Until the reserve reaches 20 percent, it may be used only to cover losses that other reserves cannot cover (art. 70(4)). For example (illustration), a subsidiary has an appropriated reserve of 300 and, after a loss year, unappropriated retained earnings of −500. Its RUPS uses the reserve.

Dr Retained earnings, appropriated 300 / Cr Retained earnings, unappropriated 300

Remaining deficit = −500 + 300 = −200, so no dividend until later profits clear it

Contractual restrictions. Loan agreements often limit distributions directly (a cap on dividends as a share of profit) or indirectly (a minimum net worth or a maximum leverage ratio). For example (illustration), a covenant capping dividends at 50 percent of prior-year profit of 2,000 allows 1,000, although the law would allow 1,600 after a 20 percent reserve. The restriction is disclosed. PHE states that some of its debt instruments impose maximum leverage ratios and that it complied with all externally imposed capital requirements (Note 49f, Daftar 5/235, PDF p. 252).

8. Corrections of errors and changes in accounting policy

Retained earnings is where past mistakes are fixed. PSAK 208 Kebijakan Akuntansi, Perubahan Estimasi Akuntansi, dan Kesalahan (formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8) sorts accounting changes into three kinds and treats each differently (the lecture notes for Inter 2 Chapter 22 give the same three).

Change in accounting policy

Change in accounting estimate

Correction of a prior-period error

Example

Average cost to FIFO

Useful life 20 to 25 years

Depreciation omitted in a prior year

Method

Retrospective, unless a new standard's transition rules say otherwise

Prospective

Retrospective restatement

Comparatives restated

Yes

No

Yes

Opening retained earnings of the earliest period shown

Adjusted for the cumulative effect

Not adjusted

Adjusted

If retrospective application is impracticable, the entity applies the change from the earliest date it can. When a policy change or restatement has a material effect on the opening statement of financial position, a third balance sheet at the start of the comparative period is required (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1, para. 40A).

For example (illustration), in 2025 a non-PSC PHE subsidiary taxed at 22 percent finds that it omitted 5,000 of depreciation from its 2023 accounts, although its tax return deducted it, so only deferred tax was misstated. Its 2025 statements show 2024 as the comparative.

Effect on retained earnings = 5,000 × (1 − 22%) = 3,900

Tax effect = 5,000 × 22% = 1,100, a lower deferred tax liability

Dr Retained earnings, opening 3,900, Dr Deferred tax liability 1,100 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 5,000

The 2024 column is restated, and the statement of changes in equity shows opening retained earnings at 1 January 2024 as previously reported, the 3,900 correction, and the restated balance. The error belongs to 2023, so 2025 profit is untouched.

The lecture notes' version of this case is a Pertamina refinery whose 2019 depreciation of 250,000 was left out, with tax at 40 percent. They list "Accumulated depreciation $250.000 decrease", "Deffered tax liability $100.000 Increase" and "Retained Earnings $150.000 Increase" under the statement of financial position, and tax expense and net income as "Increase" under the income statement. Restating for the omitted depreciation does the opposite. Accumulated depreciation rises by 250,000, the deferred tax liability and tax expense fall by 100,000, and net income and retained earnings fall by 150,000. Only "Retained earnings ending balance $150.000 Decrease" has the right sign.

Policy changes work the same way. In the notes' long-term contract example, moving from cost recovery to percentage of completion at the start of 2019 adds 500,000 of pre-tax profit for earlier years, booked as Dr Construction in process 500,000 / Cr Deferred tax liability 200,000 / Cr Retained earnings 300,000. Under PSAK 115 progress measurement follows the contract facts, so this would now be a change in estimate or a correction rather than a free policy choice; the example teaches the mechanics of the cumulative adjustment.

Transfers from OCI. Non-recycled OCI items, such as a revaluation surplus, may be transferred directly to retained earnings when the asset is sold or used up (see the Other comprehensive income essay).

9. Retained earnings across industries

Banks. Prudential regulation limits what a bank may distribute. Under POJK No. 17/2023 on bank governance, a bank must have a dividend policy (art. 108), and OJK may order a bank to postpone, limit or prohibit dividends, or to hold a RUPS to cancel one, when the bank needs to strengthen its capital or resolve problems. Retained earnings is the core of a bank's common equity tier 1 capital, so every rupiah paid out lowers its capital ratio.

Insurers. Distributions are constrained by OJK's solvency (risk-based capital) requirements, because an insurer's retained earnings back its obligations to policyholders.

Cooperatives. A cooperative's profit is sisa hasil usaha (SHU): revenue for the year less costs, depreciation and other obligations including tax. After the reserve, SHU is distributed to members in proportion to the business each did with the cooperative, and part may fund cooperative education and other purposes; the size of the reserve is set by the members' meeting (UU No. 25/1992, art. 45). For example (illustration), SHU of 1,000, a reserve of 25 percent set by the members' meeting, and 40 percent of SHU shared by member transactions.

Reserve = 1,000 × 25% = 250

Member share pool = 1,000 × 40% = 400; a member with 2% of transactions receives 400 × 2% = 8

The law ties the member's share to use rather than to capital, which is the difference from a company; in practice the articles often also reward members' savings.

Sharia entities. In a sharia bank, funds placed under a mudharabah (profit-sharing) contract are temporary syirkah funds, presented between liabilities and equity (PSAK 401, formerly PSAK 101). The share of profit paid to those fund holders comes off before profit for the owners, so it never passes through retained earnings, while dividends to shareholders follow UU PT as for any company.

State-owned groups. PHE's dividends go to Pertamina (Persero), its shareholder, and the 2025 reform does not change that step. It changes the level above. In 2024 Pertamina's RUPS decided what Pertamina paid to the state as non-tax state revenue (PNBP). UU No. 1/2025, the third amendment to the SOE Law, gives the new investment agency BPI Danantara the authority to manage the dividends of SOEs and of its investment and operational holdings (art. 3F(2)(a)), so from 2025 SOE dividends flow to Danantara rather than to the state budget.

11. Upstream note: the "dividend tax" in a PSC

PSC contractors are taxed on their taxable income from PSC operations "at a combined rate comprising corporate income tax and dividend tax" (Note 2, Daftar 5/9, PDF p. 26). The dividend part, which for a foreign contractor's Indonesian branch is branch profit tax, is charged on after-tax profit whether or not any dividend is declared, so it sits in income tax expense and reduces profit before it reaches retained earnings. A dividend PHE declares to Pertamina is a separate event (see the Corporate and dividend taxes essay).

12. Related lines

  • share-capital and additional-paid-in-capital: contributed capital, the 20 percent reserve base, and common-control differences.

  • other-comprehensive-income: accumulated OCI and non-recycled items transferred to retained earnings.

  • non-controlling-interest: the NCI share of profit and the dividends declared to NCI.

  • cash-and-cash-equivalents: the resource dividends are paid from.

  • long-term-bank-loans-non-current: the covenants that restrict distributions.

  • corporate-dividend-taxes-payable-current: the PSC dividend (branch profit) tax.

Least-confident assertions

  • The 2024 appropriation equals exactly 20 percent of 2023 profit attributable to owners, and the dividend the other 80 percent, which suggests the RUPS allocated the whole of 2023's profit. The 2023 allocation (3,664,303 + 327,955 = 3,992,258) cannot be checked because 2022 is not in these statements, and press reports put PHE's 2022 net profit at about USD 4.6–4.67 billion on an unstated basis. The 183,255 left after each allocation in both years follows arithmetically from the 2024 allocation equalling 2023 profit. If the 2023 allocation was likewise the whole of 2022 profit, that profit was 3,992,258, with 8.2 percent reserved and 91.8 percent paid out.

  • The appropriated balance of 1,167,892 is labelled "Statutory reserve and general and investment reserve" in the statement of changes in equity, while Note 33's Indonesian title is the statutory reserve balance. How much of it is statutory and how much general or investment reserve is not disclosed, so the 42.8 percent progress toward the 20 percent threshold is an upper bound for the statutory part, and it is computed in USD while the law's capital is in rupiah.

  • Note 33 gives the 2023 transfer as USD 327,995, but the statement of changes in equity shows 327,955, and 320,000 + 327,955 = 647,955 agrees with the balance sheet. Note 33 is read as a typing slip.

  • Over 2023–2024 dividends declared to owners and NCI exceed dividends paid by 25,924 (paid exceeded declared by 10,281 in 2024 and fell short by 36,205 in 2023). The 2023 shortfall exceeds that year's NCI declaration of 18,881, so part relates to owners or to a payable brought forward from 2022. No dividend payable appears in Notes 21, 44f or 51, and withholding tax cannot explain the owners' part, because dividends between Indonesian companies are exempt.

  • UU PT arts. 70–72 were checked only through secondary sources, and art. 70(4) and arts. 44–47 are from knowledge. UU PT does not say whether arts. 70–71 use separate or consolidated figures; the prudence argument in section 2 is this page's. Who holds Pertamina's shares after UU No. 1/2025 and UU No. 16/2025 (the fourth amendment) was not checked. That a common-control distribution is usually made at carrying amount is practice, not a stated PSAK rule.
