content.text: Retained earnings is the part of equity the entity earned rather than received from its owners: cumulative profit attributable to the owners, less what has been distributed, adjusted for corrections of past errors and changes in accounting policy. It is a claim on net assets and can be far larger than the cash on hand.

In an Indonesian limited company the shareholders' meeting (RUPS) allocates last year's profit. A statutory reserve must be set aside until it reaches 20 percent of issued and paid-up capital, and dividends may be paid only while retained earnings are positive (UU PT arts. 70–71). A cash dividend becomes a liability when it is declared, not when the year ends.

Dividends in kind are measured at the fair value of what is given (ISAK 117), share dividends move amounts within equity without changing the total, and a "dividend" that exceeds retained earnings returns capital. Banks and cooperatives add their own rules on what may be distributed, and in sharia banks the profit share of mudharabah fund holders comes off before profit reaches the owners.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report retained earnings of 4,352,620 at 31 December 2024 against 3,430,896 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is split into appropriated retained earnings of 1,167,892 and unappropriated retained earnings of 3,184,728. It is 14.3 percent of total assets and 30.2 percent of the equity attributable to owners of the parent (11.1 and 25.3 percent a year earlier).

After reading this page a student should be able to roll retained earnings forward, record each kind of dividend and its dates, apply the Indonesian rules on reserves and distributions, and correct a prior-period error through opening retained earnings.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Share capital and additional paid-in capital are taught in the Share capital essay, accumulated OCI in the Other comprehensive income essay, and non-controlling interest in its own essay.
(paid-in capital) is what owners put in: share capital and share premium.

is what the business generated and kept. The lecture notes call it "earning capital" and identify it with retained earnings. PHE's contributed capital is 13,631,466 of share capital less 3,649,862 of negative additional paid-in capital, or 9,981,604 (Daftar 1/3).

Closing retained earnings = opening retained earnings + profit attributable to owners of the parent − dividends declared ± corrections of prior-period errors and changes in accounting policy ± transfers from other components of equity
(saldo laba negatif or defisit). Profit or loss attributable to non-controlling interests never enters the parent's retained earnings; it goes to the NCI column.

Profit is measured on the accrual basis and the cash it brings in is spent on wells, debt service and working capital. For example (illustration), a new PHE subsidiary earns profit of 1,000 in its first year, collects all of it in cash, and spends 900 on drilling.

The balance sheet says the owners have left 1,000 in the business. Only 100 of it can be paid out without borrowing or selling assets. At PHE, retained earnings of 4,352,620 sat beside cash of 2,614,318 at the end of 2024 (Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11).

At year end each legal entity closes revenue and expenses to an income summary and the profit to retained earnings (Dr Income summary / Cr Retained earnings). The consolidated 3,001,475 comes from combining the closed ledgers.
2. Allocating profit: what the law and the shareholders decide

An entity rarely pays out all it legally may. The lecture notes give four reasons: agreements with creditors to keep part of earnings as protection, laws that block distribution of earnings equal to the cost of treasury shares (an entity's own shares bought back), the wish to smooth dividends across years, and a buffer against losses or errors in measuring profit. Before declaring, management must also look at cash. The notes put it as a test of financial condition: current liabilities will need cash, so a dividend should be paid only if the present and expected financial position supports it.
Indonesian company law, UU No. 40/2007 on Limited Liability Companies (UU PT), sets the order.

The company must set aside part of each year's net profit as a reserve, but only while it has positive retained earnings, until the reserve reaches at least 20 percent of issued and paid-up capital (art. 70(1)–(3)).
The RUPS decides how net profit is used, including the amount set aside (art. 71(1)).
Net profit after the reserve is distributed as dividends unless the RUPS decides otherwise (art. 71(2)).
Dividends may be paid only if the company has positive retained earnings (art. 71(3)).

UU PT does not say whether the test uses the company's own or its consolidated figures. Prudence points to the company's own retained earnings, because consolidated retained earnings include subsidiaries' profit that the parent can reach only when the subsidiaries pay it up. In practice Indonesian groups, PHE among them (Note 34), allocate consolidated profit attributable to owners.

For example, take PHE's 2023 profit attributable to owners of the parent, 2,599,686 (Daftar 2/2, PDF p. 15), as what the RUPS in May 2024 had to allocate. Suppose it sets aside 20 percent and distributes the rest.
Dr Retained earnings, unappropriated 2,599,686 / Cr Retained earnings, appropriated 519,937 / Cr Dividends payable 2,079,749

These are PHE's actual 2024 movements, declared by the RUPS recorded in a notarial deed of 31 May 2024 (Note 34, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165). The reserve entry moves an amount between two columns of retained earnings; only the dividend leaves equity.
A cash dividend has three dates, and only two of them carry an entry.

: the competent body approves the dividend. From then on the entity has an obligation it cannot withdraw, so it recognises a liability. In an Indonesian company the body is the RUPS for a final dividend, and the board of directors with the board of commissioners' approval for an interim one (UU PT art. 72).
: the register is closed to decide who receives the dividend. No entry.
: cash goes out and the liability is settled.
For example, the lecture notes' company declares USD 0.50 a share on 1,800,000 shares on 10 June, with a record date of 24 June and payment on 16 July.
10 June: Dr Dividend 900,000 / Cr Dividend payable 900,000
16 July: Dr Dividend payable 900,000 / Cr Cash 900,000

The notes debit an account called "Dividend"; closed to retained earnings at year end, it gives the same result as debiting retained earnings directly. A dividends payable account is a current liability because payment follows within weeks.
Dividends declared after the reporting date
are not a liability at that date, because no obligation existed then (PSAK 210

, formerly PSAK 8, IAS 10, paras. 12–13). They are disclosed. PHE's statements were authorised on 28 March 2025 (Note 1c, Daftar 5/8, PDF p. 25), and Note 52 reports no dividend declared before that date, so a dividend on 2024 profit belongs to the 2025 statements. PHE's policy says the same thing: dividends are recognised as a liability in the period in which they are declared (Note 3x, Daftar 5/73, PDF p. 90).

UU PT art. 72 allows a dividend before the year ends if the articles of association permit it and the company's net assets do not fall below issued and paid-up capital plus the statutory reserve. If the year then ends in a loss, shareholders must return the interim dividend. For example (illustration), a subsidiary has issued capital of 1,000, a statutory reserve of 120 and net assets of 1,400 in September.

That is a ceiling. The dividend must also not leave the company unable to pay its creditors or disrupt its business (art. 72(3)), and if shareholders do not return an interim dividend after a loss year, the directors and commissioners are jointly liable (art. 72(6)).

(dividend in kind) distributes a non-cash asset such as inventory, land or shares in another company. The question is at what amount the distribution reduces retained earnings, and where the difference between the asset's book value and its worth goes.

The lecture notes follow Kieso. At declaration the asset is remeasured to fair value with the gain in profit, then the dividend is recorded at fair value. The notes' example has securities with a book value of 1,250,000 and a fair value of 2,000,000, so a gain of 750,000 at declaration and a dividend of 2,000,000.
(formerly ISAK 11, IFRIC 17), which works from the liability side.
The dividends payable is recognised when the dividend is authorised and no longer at the entity's discretion, and is measured at the fair value of the assets to be distributed.
It is remeasured at each reporting date and at settlement, with the changes in equity.
At settlement, the difference between the carrying amount of the assets and the carrying amount of the liability goes to profit or loss as a separate line.

For example (illustration), a listed company whose shares are widely held declares a dividend of land carried at 800 when its fair value is 1,000. At the year end the fair value is 1,050, and at distribution 1,060.
Dr Land 200 / Cr Gain 200; Dr Retained earnings 1,000 / Cr Property dividend payable 1,000
Dr Retained earnings 1,000 / Cr Dividends payable 1,000
Dr Retained earnings 50 / Cr Dividends payable 50
Dr Property dividend payable 1,000 / Cr Land 1,000
Dr Retained earnings 10 / Cr Dividends payable 10; Dr Dividends payable 1,060 / Cr Land 800 / Cr Gain on distribution 260

Under ISAK 117 the gain waits until the asset leaves, because the land is still the entity's until then. The interpretation excludes distributions where the same party controls the asset before and after. If PHE handed a subsidiary to Pertamina, Pertamina would control that subsidiary before and after the distribution, so ISAK 117 would not apply, and the same exclusion covers a PHE subsidiary distributing to PHE. Practice then usually uses carrying amounts, the logic of PSAK 338 for common-control transactions (see the Share capital essay).

is a distribution not covered by retained earnings, so in substance it returns the owners' capital. The lecture notes' example is a company that pays a "dividend" of 1,200,000 when only 900,000 is covered by retained earnings, and records:
Dr Retained earnings 900,000 / Dr Share capital – ordinary 300,000 / Cr Dividends payable 1,200,000

Kieso debits share premium for the 300,000. Under Indonesian law, article 71(3) allows dividends only out of positive retained earnings, so the excess is not a dividend at all. Returning share capital needs a formal capital reduction approved by the RUPS with notice to creditors (UU PT arts. 44–47). Kieso's debit to share premium has no clean Indonesian counterpart either, because share premium is not retained earnings and cannot be paid out as a dividend under art. 71(3). Single-field and single-mine companies meet this at the end of a project's life. Depletion and decommissioning have consumed the asset, and the cash left over exceeds accumulated profit. The receiving investor treats the excess as a return of its investment (see the Long-term investments essay).
) gives existing owners new shares pro rata instead of cash. Nothing leaves the entity, and each owner's percentage is unchanged. Part of retained earnings is
, moved into share capital, so that it can no longer be distributed. A
divides each share into more shares of lower par value and moves nothing.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary has 10,000,000 shares of USD 1 par (share capital 10,000) and retained earnings of 6,000. It declares a 10 percent share dividend when the shares are worth USD 3 each, or alternatively splits each share in two.
Dr Retained earnings 1,000 / Cr Share dividend distributable 1,000; on issue Dr Share dividend distributable 1,000 / Cr Share capital 1,000
Dr Retained earnings 3,000 / Cr Share capital 1,000 / Cr Share premium 2,000

The lecture notes use the par method, as Kieso's IFRS edition does; IFRS has no rule on the amount. US GAAP uses fair value for small share dividends, below about 20–25 percent of shares outstanding, on the view that holders see them as income. A share dividend distributable sits in equity, not liabilities, because it will be settled in shares, not assets. Indonesian
are a different transaction, capitalising share premium rather than retained earnings (Dr Share premium / Cr Share capital). PHE's 2022 split is covered in the Share capital essay.
7. Appropriations, the statutory reserve and restrictions
earmarks part of retained earnings, in Indonesian
saldo laba yang telah ditentukan penggunaannya

, so that it is not seen as available for dividends. It is a transfer within retained earnings. No cash is set aside, and the total does not change. The lecture notes add that many companies show restrictions by note disclosure instead of a separate account.

is the one appropriation the law requires. For example, take PHE's issued and paid-up capital, 13,631,466 in its USD records, and its appropriated balance of 1,167,892 (Note 33, Daftar 5/147, PDF p. 164).

The law states capital in rupiah. PHE's issued capital is Rp198,112,621,170,000 (Note 32), so the legal threshold is about Rp39.6 trillion, and whether the USD comparison above matches the rupiah test depends on the exchange rates used. Until the reserve reaches 20 percent, it may be used only to cover losses that other reserves cannot cover (art. 70(4)). For example (illustration), a subsidiary has an appropriated reserve of 300 and, after a loss year, unappropriated retained earnings of −500. Its RUPS uses the reserve.
Dr Retained earnings, appropriated 300 / Cr Retained earnings, unappropriated 300
Remaining deficit = −500 + 300 = −200, so no dividend until later profits clear it

Loan agreements often limit distributions directly (a cap on dividends as a share of profit) or indirectly (a minimum net worth or a maximum leverage ratio). For example (illustration), a covenant capping dividends at 50 percent of prior-year profit of 2,000 allows 1,000, although the law would allow 1,600 after a 20 percent reserve. The restriction is disclosed. PHE states that some of its debt instruments impose maximum leverage ratios and that it complied with all externally imposed capital requirements (Note 49f, Daftar 5/235, PDF p. 252).
8. Corrections of errors and changes in accounting policy
Retained earnings is where past mistakes are fixed. PSAK 208
Kebijakan Akuntansi, Perubahan Estimasi Akuntansi, dan Kesalahan
(formerly PSAK 25, IAS 8) sorts accounting changes into three kinds and treats each differently (the lecture notes for Inter 2 Chapter 22 give the same three).
Depreciation omitted in a prior year
Retrospective, unless a new standard's transition rules say otherwise
Opening retained earnings of the earliest period shown

If retrospective application is impracticable, the entity applies the change from the earliest date it can. When a policy change or restatement has a material effect on the opening statement of financial position, a third balance sheet at the start of the comparative period is required (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1, para. 40A).

For example (illustration), in 2025 a non-PSC PHE subsidiary taxed at 22 percent finds that it omitted 5,000 of depreciation from its 2023 accounts, although its tax return deducted it, so only deferred tax was misstated. Its 2025 statements show 2024 as the comparative.
Tax effect = 5,000 × 22% = 1,100, a lower deferred tax liability
Dr Retained earnings, opening 3,900, Dr Deferred tax liability 1,100 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 5,000

The 2024 column is restated, and the statement of changes in equity shows opening retained earnings at 1 January 2024 as previously reported, the 3,900 correction, and the restated balance. The error belongs to 2023, so 2025 profit is untouched.

The lecture notes' version of this case is a Pertamina refinery whose 2019 depreciation of 250,000 was left out, with tax at 40 percent. They list "Accumulated depreciation $250.000 decrease", "Deffered tax liability $100.000 Increase" and "Retained Earnings $150.000 Increase" under the statement of financial position, and tax expense and net income as "Increase" under the income statement. Restating for the omitted depreciation does the opposite. Accumulated depreciation rises by 250,000, the deferred tax liability and tax expense fall by 100,000, and net income and retained earnings fall by 150,000. Only "Retained earnings ending balance $150.000 Decrease" has the right sign.

Policy changes work the same way. In the notes' long-term contract example, moving from cost recovery to percentage of completion at the start of 2019 adds 500,000 of pre-tax profit for earlier years, booked as Dr Construction in process 500,000 / Cr Deferred tax liability 200,000 / Cr Retained earnings 300,000. Under PSAK 115 progress measurement follows the contract facts, so this would now be a change in estimate or a correction rather than a free policy choice; the example teaches the mechanics of the cumulative adjustment.
Non-recycled OCI items, such as a revaluation surplus, may be transferred directly to retained earnings when the asset is sold or used up (see the Other comprehensive income essay).

Prudential regulation limits what a bank may distribute. Under POJK No. 17/2023 on bank governance, a bank must have a dividend policy (art. 108), and OJK may order a bank to postpone, limit or prohibit dividends, or to hold a RUPS to cancel one, when the bank needs to strengthen its capital or resolve problems. Retained earnings is the core of a bank's common equity tier 1 capital, so every rupiah paid out lowers its capital ratio.
Distributions are constrained by OJK's solvency (risk-based capital) requirements, because an insurer's retained earnings back its obligations to policyholders.

(SHU): revenue for the year less costs, depreciation and other obligations including tax. After the reserve, SHU is distributed to members in proportion to the business each did with the cooperative, and part may fund cooperative education and other purposes; the size of the reserve is set by the members' meeting (UU No. 25/1992, art. 45). For example (illustration), SHU of 1,000, a reserve of 25 percent set by the members' meeting, and 40 percent of SHU shared by member transactions.
Member share pool = 1,000 × 40% = 400; a member with 2% of transactions receives 400 × 2% = 8
The law ties the member's share to use rather than to capital, which is the difference from a company; in practice the articles often also reward members' savings.
In a sharia bank, funds placed under a

(profit-sharing) contract are temporary syirkah funds, presented between liabilities and equity (PSAK 401, formerly PSAK 101). The share of profit paid to those fund holders comes off before profit for the owners, so it never passes through retained earnings, while dividends to shareholders follow UU PT as for any company.

PHE's dividends go to Pertamina (Persero), its shareholder, and the 2025 reform does not change that step. It changes the level above. In 2024 Pertamina's RUPS decided what Pertamina paid to the state as non-tax state revenue (PNBP). UU No. 1/2025, the third amendment to the SOE Law, gives the new investment agency BPI Danantara the authority to manage the dividends of SOEs and of its investment and operational holdings (art. 3F(2)(a)), so from 2025 SOE dividends flow to Danantara rather than to the state budget.
10. Presentation and analysis: PHE's statement of changes in equity and Notes 33–34
The statement of changes in equity reconciles each component of equity, including retrospective adjustments and dividends (PSAK 201, para. 106). PHE's retained earnings columns (Daftar 3, PDF p. 16):
Statutory reserve and general and investment reserve (Note 33)
Statutory reserve and general and investment reserve (Note 33)
Note 34 dates the dividends by notarial deed, 3,664,303 on 15 May 2023 from 2022 profit and 2,079,749 on 31 May 2024 from 2023 profit. PHE shows no separate dividend payable on either balance sheet.
Payout ratio = dividends / profit attributable to owners of the year allocated = 2,079,749 / 2,599,686 = 80.0%

The 2024 allocations add up to 2023's profit attributable to owners, 20 percent to reserves and 80 percent to the shareholders, Pertamina and Pertamina Pedeve (Note 32). Measured against 2024's own profit the same dividend is 69.3 percent, a figure that mixes two years. Dividends paid in the cash flow statement (2,117,827 and 3,646,979, Daftar 4, PDF p. 17) differ from dividends declared to owners and NCI (2,107,546 and 3,683,184); see Least-confident. Dividends paid of 2,117,827 went out in a year when cash fell by 2,384,682 before exchange effects, the section 1 point at group scale.
11. Upstream note: the "dividend tax" in a PSC

PSC contractors are taxed on their taxable income from PSC operations "at a combined rate comprising corporate income tax and dividend tax" (Note 2, Daftar 5/9, PDF p. 26). The dividend part, which for a foreign contractor's Indonesian branch is branch profit tax, is charged on after-tax profit whether or not any dividend is declared, so it sits in income tax expense and reduces profit before it reaches retained earnings. A dividend PHE declares to Pertamina is a separate event (see the Corporate and dividend taxes essay).
: contributed capital, the 20 percent reserve base, and common-control differences.
: accumulated OCI and non-recycled items transferred to retained earnings.
: the NCI share of profit and the dividends declared to NCI.
: the resource dividends are paid from.

The 2024 appropriation equals exactly 20 percent of 2023 profit attributable to owners, and the dividend the other 80 percent, which suggests the RUPS allocated the whole of 2023's profit. The 2023 allocation (3,664,303 + 327,955 = 3,992,258) cannot be checked because 2022 is not in these statements, and press reports put PHE's 2022 net profit at about USD 4.6–4.67 billion on an unstated basis. The 183,255 left after each allocation in both years follows arithmetically from the 2024 allocation equalling 2023 profit. If the 2023 allocation was likewise the whole of 2022 profit, that profit was 3,992,258, with 8.2 percent reserved and 91.8 percent paid out.

The appropriated balance of 1,167,892 is labelled "Statutory reserve and general and investment reserve" in the statement of changes in equity, while Note 33's Indonesian title is the statutory reserve balance. How much of it is statutory and how much general or investment reserve is not disclosed, so the 42.8 percent progress toward the 20 percent threshold is an upper bound for the statutory part, and it is computed in USD while the law's capital is in rupiah.
Note 33 gives the 2023 transfer as USD 327,995, but the statement of changes in equity shows 327,955, and 320,000 + 327,955 = 647,955 agrees with the balance sheet. Note 33 is read as a typing slip.

Over 2023–2024 dividends declared to owners and NCI exceed dividends paid by 25,924 (paid exceeded declared by 10,281 in 2024 and fell short by 36,205 in 2023). The 2023 shortfall exceeds that year's NCI declaration of 18,881, so part relates to owners or to a payable brought forward from 2022. No dividend payable appears in Notes 21, 44f or 51, and withholding tax cannot explain the owners' part, because dividends between Indonesian companies are exempt.

UU PT arts. 70–72 were checked only through secondary sources, and art. 70(4) and arts. 44–47 are from knowledge. UU PT does not say whether arts. 70–71 use separate or consolidated figures; the prudence argument in section 2 is this page's. Who holds Pertamina's shares after UU No. 1/2025 and UU No. 16/2025 (the fourth amendment) was not checked. That a common-control distribution is usually made at carrying amount is practice, not a stated PSAK rule.

presentation.deck: The theory of earned capital from the closing entry to the statement of changes in equity, worked through PHE's 2024 allocation to Pertamina and set beside the industries whose distributions are regulated
key_takeaways: Retained earnings is the part of equity the entity earned rather than received from its owners: cumulative profit attributable to the owners, less what has been distributed, adjusted for corrections of past errors and changes in accounting policy. It is a claim on net assets and can be far larger than the cash on hand.

In an Indonesian limited company the shareholders' meeting (RUPS) allocates last year's profit. A statutory reserve must be set aside until it reaches 20 percent of issued and paid-up capital, and dividends may be paid only while retained earnings are positive (UU PT arts. 70–71). A cash dividend becomes a liability when it is declared, not when the year ends.

Dividends in kind are measured at the fair value of what is given (ISAK 117), share dividends move amounts within equity without changing the total, and a "dividend" that exceeds retained earnings returns capital. Banks and cooperatives add their own rules on what may be distributed, and in sharia banks the profit share of mudharabah fund holders comes off before profit reaches the owners.

title: Revenues: The Five Steps of PSAK 115 and the Upstream Contractor's Entitlement
snippet: The theory of revenue recognition from the contract to disclosure, worked through PHE's crude, gas and service revenue and set beside the industries where the five steps bite hardest
content:
In brief

  • Revenue is income from an entity's ordinary activities. PSAK 115 measures revenue from contracts with customers through five steps: identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognise revenue when or as control of each promised good or service passes to the customer.

  • Most of the judgment sits in steps 3 and 5. Variable consideration enters the price only to the extent a significant reversal is highly probable not to occur, and an obligation is satisfied over time only if one of three tests is met; otherwise revenue waits for a point in time.

  • An upstream contractor's revenue is the oil and gas it lifts and sells to its customers. When lifting differs from entitlement the gap is settled with the state outside revenue, and barrels sold only on the state's behalf are not revenue at all. Under a cost recovery contract the entitlement itself rises with recoverable cost.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report revenues of 14,330,340 for 2024 against 14,568,384 for 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). Revenue fell 1.6 percent. It is 0.47 times average total assets of 30,661,936.

After reading, a student should be able to run a contract through the five steps with journals, separate revenue from gains and from amounts collected for others, and explain what an upstream contractor's revenue measures.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Examples taken from the lecture notes keep the notes' figures in full dollars, and the industry illustrations in section 9 are in plain currency units. The standard is PSAK 115 Pendapatan dari Kontrak dengan Pelanggan (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15), effective in Indonesia since 1 January 2020, when it replaced PSAK 23 (revenue), PSAK 34 (construction contracts), PSAK 44 (real estate) and ISAK 10, 21 and 27.

1. What revenue is

PSAK 115 defines revenue as income arising in the course of an entity's ordinary activities (Appendix A). The older PSAK 23 definition in the lecture notes for Teori Akuntansi Ch 9, a gross inflow of economic benefits that increases equity other than from owners, gives the two characteristics that matter: an inflow or increase of assets (or a settlement of liabilities), and an origin in the entity's central, continuing operations. The IASB, unlike the FASB, puts revenue and gains under one element, income.

The separation still changes the numbers. For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary sells a used rig carried at 800 for 1,000.

Revenue view (wrong): revenue 1,000, cost 800

Gain view: Dr Cash 1,000 / Cr Fixed assets 800 / Cr Gain on disposal 200

Selling rigs is not the subsidiary's business, so 200 appears as a net gain outside revenue.

PSAK 115 adds a second filter. It covers only contracts with a customer, a party that has contracted to obtain goods or services that are an output of the entity's ordinary activities in exchange for consideration (Appendix A). The TA Ch 9 notes set out the older test, that revenue be realised or realisable and earned. The Inter 2 Ch 18 notes describe the asset-liability approach that replaced it, recognising revenue as contract rights and obligations change. The Deferred revenue essay covers the resulting balances.

2. Step 1: identify the contract

A contract is an agreement that creates enforceable rights and obligations, in writing, orally or by customary practice. PSAK 115 accounts for it only when all five criteria hold (para. 9): the parties have approved it and are committed; each party's rights can be identified; the payment terms can be identified; it has commercial substance; and collection of the consideration is probable, judged on the customer's ability and intention to pay.

The collectability test stops revenue that will never turn into cash. For example (illustration), if a PHE subsidiary agrees to deliver 1,000 of gas to a buyer already in arrears with no financing, the contract does not yet exist for PSAK 115. Cash received is held as a liability until collection becomes probable, or until the contract ends and the cash is non-refundable.

3. Step 2: identify the performance obligations

A performance obligation is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service, or a series of distinct goods or services that are substantially the same and transfer with the same pattern (para. 22). A good or service is distinct if the customer can benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and if the promise is separately identifiable from the other promises in the contract (para. 27). The lecture notes use Airbus selling an aircraft to Garuda for USD 100 million: one obligation, unless the contract adds maintenance, which must then be separated. Their second case, a turbine sold "ready to use", has two, the turbine and its installation.

Activities the entity must perform to set up a contract are not obligations unless they transfer something to the customer (para. 25). For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary signs a 90-day drilling contract at a day rate of 30, with a mobilisation fee of 450 paid on signing to bring the rig to site.

Transaction price = 90 × 30 + 450 = 3,150

Revenue per drilling day = 3,150 / 90 = 35

At 31 December, after 40 days: revenue = 40 × 35 = 1,400

Cash and billings = 450 + 40 × 30 = 1,650; contract liability = 1,650 − 1,400 = 250

Moving the rig gives the customer nothing it can use on its own, so the 450 is not revenue on arrival at site. It is spread over the drilling days, and the 250 still unearned is 450 × 50/90.

On signing: Dr Cash 450 / Cr Contract liability 450

Each drilling day: Dr Trade receivables 30, Dr Contract liability 5 / Cr Revenue, drilling services 35

Daily gas deliveries under a long-term sale, each distinct but identical, form one series obligation.

4. Step 3: determine the transaction price

The transaction price is the consideration the entity expects to be entitled to for the promised goods or services, excluding amounts collected for third parties such as sales taxes. The lecture notes list four complications, and PSAK 115 adds a constraint to the first.

Variable consideration. Discounts, rebates, bonuses, penalties and price concessions make the price depend on future events. The entity estimates it by the expected value, the probability-weighted sum, which suits many similar contracts, or the most likely amount, which suits a contract with two outcomes (para. 53). The notes' example, a builder with a contract of 100,000 and a completion bonus of 50,000 that falls 10 percent for each week of delay, uses the expected value:

On time: 60% × 150,000 = 90,000

One week late: 30% × 145,000 = 43,500

Two weeks late: 10% × 140,000 = 14,000

Transaction price = 147,500

The constraint. An estimate enters the price only to the extent that it is highly probable a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur once the uncertainty is resolved (para. 56). For example (illustration), the drilling contract in section 3 pays a bonus of 300 if the well is finished within 80 days, and the subsidiary puts the probability at 70 percent.

Expected value

Most likely amount

After the constraint

Price

3,150 + 70% × 300 = 3,360

3,150 + 300 = 3,450

3,150

With two outcomes the most likely amount fits, but a 70 percent chance in untested ground may not be "highly probable", so the bonus waits. PHE's policy measures variable consideration at the amount it expects to be entitled to "less the estimated amount of service performance guarantees to be paid during the contract period" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/61, PDF p. 78), which treats expected penalties as a reduction of price.

Significant financing component. When payment and transfer are far apart, part of the price is interest (paras. 60–65). The notes' example has Pertamina selling a tanker of crude to Shell for a four-year zero-interest note when the market rate is 12 percent:

Face value of the note = 1,000,000 × 1.12⁴ = 1,573,519, which the notes round to 1,573,520

Sale: Dr Notes receivable 1,000,000 / Cr Sales revenue 1,000,000

Interest to 31 December 2019: 1,000,000 × 12% × 6/12 = 60,000; 2020: 1,060,000 × 12% = 127,200

Revenue is the cash-equivalent price, and the rest is interest income, presented apart from revenue (para. 65). The prepayment case is in the Deferred revenue essay.

Non-cash consideration, such as the notes' shares received for consulting, is measured at fair value (para. 66).

Consideration payable to a customer, such as a rebate, coupon or a payment the seller makes to the buyer, reduces the price unless it buys a distinct good or service from the customer (para. 70). For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays a buyer 100 to build the spur that connects the buyer to its pipeline under a 5,000 gas contract. The spur is the buyer's asset and gives the seller nothing distinct, so revenue over the contract is 4,900.

For provisionally priced sales, the price movement after delivery sits in the receivable (see the Trade receivables essay).

5. Step 4: allocate the transaction price

A contract with several obligations needs one price split among them, in proportion to standalone selling prices (SSP), the prices at which each would sell separately. The notes' example sells a turbine, installation and training for 5,000,000, with SSPs of 5,000,000, 100,000 and 50,000:

Total SSP = 5,150,000

Turbine = 5,000,000 × 5,000,000 / 5,150,000 = 4,854,369

Installation = 5,000,000 × 100,000 / 5,150,000 = 97,087

Training = 5,000,000 × 50,000 / 5,150,000 = 48,544

On installation, 1 November 2019: Dr Cash 5,000,000 / Cr Sales revenue 4,854,369 / Cr Service revenue 97,087 / Cr Unearned service revenue (a contract liability) 48,544

When an SSP cannot be observed it is estimated by one of three methods (para. 79). The adjusted market assessment starts from what customers in the market, or competitors, charge. Expected cost plus a margin builds the price up from cost. The residual approach takes the total price less the observable SSPs of the other items, and is allowed only when the item's price is highly variable or not yet established. The notes place the turbine example under the residual heading, but it is the relative SSP method, since all three prices are observable.

For example (illustration), a PHE services subsidiary sells seismic acquisition (SSP 1,800), data processing (SSP 600) and an interpretation licence it has never priced separately, all for 2,700.

Residual: interpretation = 2,700 − 1,800 − 600 = 300

Cost plus margin: expected cost 230 × 1.25 = 287.5; allocated = 2,700 × 287.5 / 2,687.5 = 288.84

PHE's policy uses the second, estimating an SSP that "cannot be observed directly" from "expected cost plus a margin" (Note 3p).

6. Step 5: recognise revenue at a point in time or over time

Revenue is recognised when, or as, the customer obtains control of the good or service, meaning the ability to direct its use and obtain substantially all of its remaining benefits. An obligation is satisfied over time if any one of three tests holds (para. 35):

  • the customer receives and consumes the benefit as the entity performs, as with a drilling day or a month of monitoring;

  • the entity's performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls as it is built, such as a platform on the customer's site;

  • the asset has no alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date.

Otherwise the obligation is satisfied at a point in time, judged by indicators such as a present right to payment, legal title, physical possession, the risks and rewards of ownership, and the customer's acceptance (para. 38). The notes' list of indicators ends with "the company has received the asset"; the standard means that the customer has accepted it. For crude, control typically passes at the terminal's loading flange. PHE treats goods as generally satisfied at a point in time and services over time (Note 3p).

Measuring progress. For over-time obligations the entity picks one method per obligation: output methods, such as metres drilled or units delivered, or input methods, such as cost incurred against total expected cost (paras. 39–41, B14–B19). The notes work Kieso's bridge contract of 4,500,000 with the cost-to-cost method.

When progress cannot yet be measured reasonably but costs are expected to be recovered, revenue equals cost incurred until it can (para. 45). That is the notes' "cost-recovery (zero-profit) method", which defers the bridge's whole 450,000 profit to 2021.

Loss contracts. The notes' second loss case raises the 2020 estimate of cost to complete to 1,640,250, so the whole contract now loses money.

Total estimated cost = 2,916,000 + 1,640,250 = 4,556,250; percent complete = 2,916,000 / 4,556,250 = 64%

Revenue in 2020 = 4,500,000 × 64% − 1,125,000 = 1,755,000; cost in 2020 = 1,916,000; loss on work done = 161,000

Loss on work still to do = 1,640,250 − 4,500,000 × 36% = 20,250

Loss recognised in 2020 = 161,000 + 20,250 = 181,250 = 125,000 profit already booked + 56,250 total contract loss

The notes stop at 161,000 and print 66½ percent in the label while computing with 64 percent. Kieso recognises the whole expected loss at once, and under PSAK the 20,250 for the remaining work is an onerous contract provision under PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37), since PSAK 115 itself has no loss rule.

7. Other recognition issues

Sales with a right of return. Revenue excludes products expected to be returned; the seller records a refund liability and an asset for the right to recover the goods (paras. B20–B21). Using the notes' camera example (100 cameras at 100, cost 60, three returns expected):

Dr Accounts receivable 10,000 / Cr Sales revenue 9,700 / Cr Refund liability 300

Dr Cost of goods sold 5,820, Dr Right to recover returned goods 180 / Cr Inventory 6,000

The notes reach the same net sales and cost by booking returns afterwards, against receivables.

Repurchase agreements. If the seller must or may buy the asset back at or above the selling price, the customer never gets control, so the deal is a financing (paras. B66–B68). The notes' Morgan sells an asset for 100,000 and must buy it back for 121,000 two years later, so it books a liability of 100,000 and interest of 10,000 and 11,000 at 10 percent, and no revenue.

Bill-and-hold. The notes recognise revenue once the goods cannot be sold elsewhere; PSAK 115 requires four conditions: a substantive reason (the customer asked), goods identified as the customer's, goods ready for transfer, and no ability for the seller to use them or send them elsewhere (para. B81).

Principal or agent. When another party is involved, the entity asks whether it controls the good before it passes to the customer (paras. B34–B35). A principal reports gross consideration; an agent reports only its fee or commission (para. B36). Since the 2016 clarifications the indicators point to a principal: primary responsibility for fulfilment, inventory risk, and discretion over price. Credit risk and the form of payment no longer count. The notes' consignment example is the classic agent: Best Valve sells 40,000 of the consignor's goods and records only its 4,000 commission.

The same question decides what an upstream contractor reports. For example (illustration), a cargo of 500 kbbl at USD 75 per barrel (37,500) includes 300 kbbl of the contractor's entitlement and 200 kbbl that belong to the state, sold by the contractor with the proceeds passed on.

Contractor as principal for its own barrels only: revenue = 300 × 75 = 22,500

Proceeds of the state's barrels: 200 × 75 = 15,000, a payable to the Government, not revenue

Here the contractor sells the state's barrels as its agent and never controls them. An overlift is different. The contractor takes the state's barrels as its own and owes the state their value, so the sale is revenue and the debt is booked in cost (section 8).

Warranties and options. Assurance warranties are provisions; service warranties and material rights are obligations deferred through a contract liability (see the Deferred revenue essay).

8. How an upstream contractor's revenue is measured

Under a production sharing contract (PSC) the state owns the hydrocarbons up to the point of delivery (UU 22/2001 art. 6(2)(a)), and the contractor's entitlement is its share of each year's production, set by the contract (Note 2a, Daftar 5/9–5/11, PDF pp. 26–28). The contractor's revenue is what it lifts and sells to customers, priced for crude at the Indonesian Crude Price (ICP) and for gas at each sales contract's price (Note 2a(iv)).

  • Lifting, not entitlement. For sales from blocks held with partners, PHE recognises crude and gas revenue on "the actual lifting amount and sold to customers". Underlifting and overlifting against final entitlements are valued at the annual weighted average crude price or the gas contract price and booked in direct cost of sales, because they "are not transactions with customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62–5/63, PDF pp. 79–80). The Due from the Government essay works the imbalance.

  • The DMO fee is revenue from the state. The domestic market obligation (DMO) makes the contractor supply part of its crude to the domestic market at the weighted average price or another price set in the PSC (Note 2a(v)). PHE shows DMO fees of 429,402 (Note 35).

  • Cost recovery makes entitlement depend on cost. Under a cost recovery PSC the contractor's entitlement includes barrels that repay its recoverable costs. The Due from the Government essay computes an illustrative entitlement of 2,200 kbbl, worth 165,000, from 4,000 kbbl of production at USD 75, first tranche petroleum (FTP) of 20 percent, a contractor share of 25 percent, and recoverable costs of 120,000. Raise recoverable costs by 12,000 (illustration):

Cost recovery = 1,600 + 12,000 / 75 = 1,760 kbbl

Equity to be split = 4,000 − 800 FTP − 1,760 = 1,440 kbbl; contractor's share = 1,440 × 25% = 360 kbbl

Entitlement = 1,760 + 200 FTP share + 360 = 2,320 kbbl, up 120 kbbl; revenue up 120 × 75 = 9,000

  • Gross split removes that link. Under a gross split PSC the contractor takes a percentage of gross production, which under the 2017 regulation cited in PHE's Note 2b is made of a base split adjusted by variable and progressive components and ministerial discretion, with no cost recovery (Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). The 2024 regulation dropped the base split. With an illustrative contractor split of 60 percent, revenue is 4,000 × 60% × 75 = 180,000 whatever the costs, and the extra 12,000 of cost falls entirely on the contractor's profit.

PHE holds both kinds, and its Corridor PSC moves from gross split to cost recovery from 1 January 2025 (Note 2b). It also has operation cooperation contracts (KSO) in which partners recover costs and split the rest with PHE (Note 2g), and a technical service contract for West Qurna-1 in Iraq, where the contractor earns a remuneration fee on production above a baseline plus recovered petroleum costs, a service fee from the Iraqi state (Note 2f, Daftar 5/23–5/24, PDF pp. 40–41).

9. Revenue across industries

Telecom bundles. A "free" handset with a 24-month plan is two obligations. For example (illustration), a customer pays 30 a month for 24 months (720). Standalone, the handset sells for 600 and the plan for 25 a month (600).

Handset = 720 × 600 / 1,200 = 360, recognised on day one; Dr Contract asset 360 / Cr Revenue, equipment 360

Service = 360 over 24 months = 15 a month, though 30 is billed; the contract asset unwinds by 15 a month

Real estate and construction. Under PSAK 44 Indonesian developers used percentage of completion for apartments meeting its conditions. Construction contracts usually meet the second over-time test. Under PSAK 115 a pre-sold apartment is recognised over time only if the developer has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date (para. 35(c)); otherwise revenue waits for handover.

Software and licences. A licence that gives a right to use the software as it exists when granted is recognised at a point in time. One that gives a right to access intellectual property the licensor keeps changing, typical of software as a service, is recognised over the licence period (paras. B56–B58). A three-year subscription of 1,000 earns 27.78 a month.

Marketplaces and agents. An e-commerce platform that never controls the goods reports its commission. On gross merchandise value of 10,000 at an 8 percent commission its revenue is 800.

Banks and Islamic finance. Interest income is outside PSAK 115 and follows PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9); a bank's fees for services are within PSAK 115. In a murabahah under PSAK 402 (formerly PSAK 102), the seller's margin is profit on a sale, recognised as the Trade receivables essay describes.

10. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Note 35

PSAK 115 asks for revenue from contracts with customers apart from other income (para. 113), disaggregation into categories that show how economic factors affect the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue (para. 114), contract balances and the revenue released from opening contract liabilities (para. 116), and the price allocated to remaining obligations (para. 120), unless the contract lasts a year or less or the entity bills amounts matching performance to date (para. 121).

PHE disaggregates by counterparty and product (Note 35, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165).

11. Related lines

  • deferred-revenue-current and deferred-revenue-non-current: contract liabilities, take-or-pay, financing on prepayments.

  • trade-receivables-net: unconditional rights to consideration, contract assets, provisional pricing.

  • due-from-government and due-to-government-current: underlifting, overlifting, DMO fees.

  • production-expenses: the costs PHE recognises "on the basis of the costs incurred for the actual amount sold".

  • decommissioning-site-restoration-provision: onerous contract provisions.

  • other-income-expense-net: gains outside revenue.

Least-confident assertions

  • Reading PHE's "after deduction by PNBP" as net reporting of the state's share is an inference. The FS do not say whether PHE ever sells the state's barrels, and the illustration of 200 kbbl of state crude is constructed.

  • What "Adjustment split PSC" (703,811 in 2024, 859,924 in 2023) compensates is not disclosed; its counterparty is SKK Migas (Notes 35, 44g), as the Due from the Government essay also reports. One unverified reading is compensation from the state's share for gas sold at regulated prices to designated industries (harga gas bumi tertentu, HGBT), since Permen ESDM 15/2022 funds that price cut from the state's share and keeps the contractor's share whole. On that reading it is consideration for gas delivered, consistent with Note 3p. A split true-up is the other possibility.

  • PHE's Note 2b still cites ESDM Regulations 8/2017 and 52/2017 for gross split. Regulation 13/2024 revoked them in August 2024, before the year end, dropped the base split and, per ESDM, puts contractor shares at 75–95 percent (secondary sources); existing contracts may keep their signed terms. The 60 percent split is an illustration.

  • Note 3p's list of five steps is garbled in both languages: "identify contracts" is unnumbered, then steps 1 and 2 both read "identification of performance obligations". Note 35's PT Kilang Pertamina Internasional figure (7,372,296) differs by 1 from Note 44g (7,372,295). The about 7.39 million of related-party crude is approximate, because the Note 44g rows also carry services.

  • Treating TSC cost recovery as part of service revenue, and the control point for crude at the loading flange, are general industry readings. PHE does not state either.

content.text: Revenue is income from an entity's ordinary activities. PSAK 115 measures revenue from contracts with customers through five steps: identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognise revenue when or as control of each promised good or service passes to the customer.

Most of the judgment sits in steps 3 and 5. Variable consideration enters the price only to the extent a significant reversal is highly probable not to occur, and an obligation is satisfied over time only if one of three tests is met; otherwise revenue waits for a point in time.

An upstream contractor's revenue is the oil and gas it lifts and sells to its customers. When lifting differs from entitlement the gap is settled with the state outside revenue, and barrels sold only on the state's behalf are not revenue at all. Under a cost recovery contract the entitlement itself rises with recoverable cost.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report revenues of 14,330,340 for 2024 against 14,568,384 for 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of profit or loss, Daftar 2/1, PDF p. 14; "Daftar" is the printed page). Revenue fell 1.6 percent. It is 0.47 times average total assets of 30,661,936.

After reading, a student should be able to run a contract through the five steps with journals, separate revenue from gains and from amounts collected for others, and explain what an upstream contractor's revenue measures.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Examples taken from the lecture notes keep the notes' figures in full dollars, and the industry illustrations in section 9 are in plain currency units. The standard is PSAK 115
(formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15), effective in Indonesia since 1 January 2020, when it replaced PSAK 23 (revenue), PSAK 34 (construction contracts), PSAK 44 (real estate) and ISAK 10, 21 and 27.

PSAK 115 defines revenue as income arising in the course of an entity's ordinary activities (Appendix A). The older PSAK 23 definition in the lecture notes for Teori Akuntansi Ch 9, a gross inflow of economic benefits that increases equity other than from owners, gives the two characteristics that matter: an inflow or increase of assets (or a settlement of liabilities), and an origin in the entity's central, continuing operations. The IASB, unlike the FASB, puts revenue and gains under one element,
The separation still changes the numbers. For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary sells a used rig carried at 800 for 1,000.
Gain view: Dr Cash 1,000 / Cr Fixed assets 800 / Cr Gain on disposal 200
Selling rigs is not the subsidiary's business, so 200 appears as a net gain outside revenue.
PSAK 115 adds a second filter. It covers only contracts with a

, a party that has contracted to obtain goods or services that are an output of the entity's ordinary activities in exchange for consideration (Appendix A). The TA Ch 9 notes set out the older test, that revenue be realised or realisable and earned. The Inter 2 Ch 18 notes describe the
that replaced it, recognising revenue as contract rights and obligations change. The Deferred revenue essay covers the resulting balances.

A contract is an agreement that creates enforceable rights and obligations, in writing, orally or by customary practice. PSAK 115 accounts for it only when all five criteria hold (para. 9): the parties have approved it and are committed; each party's rights can be identified; the payment terms can be identified; it has commercial substance; and collection of the consideration is probable, judged on the customer's ability and intention to pay.

The collectability test stops revenue that will never turn into cash. For example (illustration), if a PHE subsidiary agrees to deliver 1,000 of gas to a buyer already in arrears with no financing, the contract does not yet exist for PSAK 115. Cash received is held as a liability until collection becomes probable, or until the contract ends and the cash is non-refundable.
is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service, or a series of distinct goods or services that are substantially the same and transfer with the same pattern (para. 22). A good or service is

if the customer can benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and if the promise is separately identifiable from the other promises in the contract (para. 27). The lecture notes use Airbus selling an aircraft to Garuda for USD 100 million: one obligation, unless the contract adds maintenance, which must then be separated. Their second case, a turbine sold "ready to use", has two, the turbine and its installation.

Activities the entity must perform to set up a contract are not obligations unless they transfer something to the customer (para. 25). For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary signs a 90-day drilling contract at a day rate of 30, with a mobilisation fee of 450 paid on signing to bring the rig to site.
Moving the rig gives the customer nothing it can use on its own, so the 450 is not revenue on arrival at site. It is spread over the drilling days, and the 250 still unearned is 450 × 50/90.
On signing: Dr Cash 450 / Cr Contract liability 450
Each drilling day: Dr Trade receivables 30, Dr Contract liability 5 / Cr Revenue, drilling services 35
Daily gas deliveries under a long-term sale, each distinct but identical, form one series obligation.

is the consideration the entity expects to be entitled to for the promised goods or services, excluding amounts collected for third parties such as sales taxes. The lecture notes list four complications, and PSAK 115 adds a constraint to the first.
Discounts, rebates, bonuses, penalties and price concessions make the price depend on future events. The entity estimates it by the
, the probability-weighted sum, which suits many similar contracts, or the

, which suits a contract with two outcomes (para. 53). The notes' example, a builder with a contract of 100,000 and a completion bonus of 50,000 that falls 10 percent for each week of delay, uses the expected value:

An estimate enters the price only to the extent that it is highly probable a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur once the uncertainty is resolved (para. 56). For example (illustration), the drilling contract in section 3 pays a bonus of 300 if the well is finished within 80 days, and the subsidiary puts the probability at 70 percent.

With two outcomes the most likely amount fits, but a 70 percent chance in untested ground may not be "highly probable", so the bonus waits. PHE's policy measures variable consideration at the amount it expects to be entitled to "less the estimated amount of service performance guarantees to be paid during the contract period" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/61, PDF p. 78), which treats expected penalties as a reduction of price.

When payment and transfer are far apart, part of the price is interest (paras. 60–65). The notes' example has Pertamina selling a tanker of crude to Shell for a four-year zero-interest note when the market rate is 12 percent:
Face value of the note = 1,000,000 × 1.12⁴ = 1,573,519, which the notes round to 1,573,520
Sale: Dr Notes receivable 1,000,000 / Cr Sales revenue 1,000,000
Revenue is the cash-equivalent price, and the rest is interest income, presented apart from revenue (para. 65). The prepayment case is in the Deferred revenue essay.
, such as the notes' shares received for consulting, is measured at fair value (para. 66).

, such as a rebate, coupon or a payment the seller makes to the buyer, reduces the price unless it buys a distinct good or service from the customer (para. 70). For example (illustration), a subsidiary pays a buyer 100 to build the spur that connects the buyer to its pipeline under a 5,000 gas contract. The spur is the buyer's asset and gives the seller nothing distinct, so revenue over the contract is 4,900.
For provisionally priced sales, the price movement after delivery sits in the receivable (see the Trade receivables essay).
A contract with several obligations needs one price split among them, in proportion to
(SSP), the prices at which each would sell separately. The notes' example sells a turbine, installation and training for 5,000,000, with SSPs of 5,000,000, 100,000 and 50,000:
On installation, 1 November 2019: Dr Cash 5,000,000 / Cr Sales revenue 4,854,369 / Cr Service revenue 97,087 / Cr Unearned service revenue (a contract liability) 48,544
When an SSP cannot be observed it is estimated by one of three methods (para. 79). The
starts from what customers in the market, or competitors, charge.
builds the price up from cost. The

takes the total price less the observable SSPs of the other items, and is allowed only when the item's price is highly variable or not yet established. The notes place the turbine example under the residual heading, but it is the relative SSP method, since all three prices are observable.
For example (illustration), a PHE services subsidiary sells seismic acquisition (SSP 1,800), data processing (SSP 600) and an interpretation licence it has never priced separately, all for 2,700.
Cost plus margin: expected cost 230 × 1.25 = 287.5; allocated = 2,700 × 287.5 / 2,687.5 = 288.84
PHE's policy uses the second, estimating an SSP that "cannot be observed directly" from "expected cost plus a margin" (Note 3p).
6. Step 5: recognise revenue at a point in time or over time

Revenue is recognised when, or as, the customer obtains control of the good or service, meaning the ability to direct its use and obtain substantially all of its remaining benefits. An obligation is satisfied
if any one of three tests holds (para. 35):
the customer receives and consumes the benefit as the entity performs, as with a drilling day or a month of monitoring;
the entity's performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls as it is built, such as a platform on the customer's site;
the asset has no alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date.
Otherwise the obligation is satisfied at a

, judged by indicators such as a present right to payment, legal title, physical possession, the risks and rewards of ownership, and the customer's acceptance (para. 38). The notes' list of indicators ends with "the company has received the asset"; the standard means that the
has accepted it. For crude, control typically passes at the terminal's loading flange. PHE treats goods as generally satisfied at a point in time and services over time (Note 3p).
For over-time obligations the entity picks one method per obligation:
, such as metres drilled or units delivered, or
, such as cost incurred against total expected cost (paras. 39–41, B14–B19). The notes work Kieso's bridge contract of 4,500,000 with the cost-to-cost method.

When progress cannot yet be measured reasonably but costs are expected to be recovered, revenue equals cost incurred until it can (para. 45). That is the notes' "cost-recovery (zero-profit) method", which defers the bridge's whole 450,000 profit to 2021.
The notes' second loss case raises the 2020 estimate of cost to complete to 1,640,250, so the whole contract now loses money.
Loss recognised in 2020 = 161,000 + 20,250 = 181,250 = 125,000 profit already booked + 56,250 total contract loss

The notes stop at 161,000 and print 66½ percent in the label while computing with 64 percent. Kieso recognises the whole expected loss at once, and under PSAK the 20,250 for the remaining work is an onerous contract provision under PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37), since PSAK 115 itself has no loss rule.
Sales with a right of return.

Revenue excludes products expected to be returned; the seller records a refund liability and an asset for the right to recover the goods (paras. B20–B21). Using the notes' camera example (100 cameras at 100, cost 60, three returns expected):
Dr Accounts receivable 10,000 / Cr Sales revenue 9,700 / Cr Refund liability 300
Dr Cost of goods sold 5,820, Dr Right to recover returned goods 180 / Cr Inventory 6,000
The notes reach the same net sales and cost by booking returns afterwards, against receivables.

If the seller must or may buy the asset back at or above the selling price, the customer never gets control, so the deal is a financing (paras. B66–B68). The notes' Morgan sells an asset for 100,000 and must buy it back for 121,000 two years later, so it books a liability of 100,000 and interest of 10,000 and 11,000 at 10 percent, and no revenue.

The notes recognise revenue once the goods cannot be sold elsewhere; PSAK 115 requires four conditions: a substantive reason (the customer asked), goods identified as the customer's, goods ready for transfer, and no ability for the seller to use them or send them elsewhere (para. B81).
When another party is involved, the entity asks whether it controls the good before it passes to the customer (paras. B34–B35). A

reports only its fee or commission (para. B36). Since the 2016 clarifications the indicators point to a principal: primary responsibility for fulfilment, inventory risk, and discretion over price. Credit risk and the form of payment no longer count. The notes' consignment example is the classic agent: Best Valve sells 40,000 of the consignor's goods and records only its 4,000 commission.

The same question decides what an upstream contractor reports. For example (illustration), a cargo of 500 kbbl at USD 75 per barrel (37,500) includes 300 kbbl of the contractor's entitlement and 200 kbbl that belong to the state, sold by the contractor with the proceeds passed on.
Contractor as principal for its own barrels only: revenue = 300 × 75 = 22,500
Proceeds of the state's barrels: 200 × 75 = 15,000, a payable to the Government, not revenue

Here the contractor sells the state's barrels as its agent and never controls them. An overlift is different. The contractor takes the state's barrels as its own and owes the state their value, so the sale is revenue and the debt is booked in cost (section 8).
Assurance warranties are provisions; service warranties and material rights are obligations deferred through a contract liability (see the Deferred revenue essay).
8. How an upstream contractor's revenue is measured
Under a production sharing contract (PSC) the state owns the hydrocarbons up to the point of delivery (UU 22/2001 art. 6(2)(a)), and the contractor's

is its share of each year's production, set by the contract (Note 2a, Daftar 5/9–5/11, PDF pp. 26–28). The contractor's revenue is what it lifts and sells to customers, priced for crude at the Indonesian Crude Price (ICP) and for gas at each sales contract's price (Note 2a(iv)).

For sales from blocks held with partners, PHE recognises crude and gas revenue on "the actual lifting amount and sold to customers". Underlifting and overlifting against final entitlements are valued at the annual weighted average crude price or the gas contract price and booked in direct cost of sales, because they "are not transactions with customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62–5/63, PDF pp. 79–80). The Due from the Government essay works the imbalance.
The DMO fee is revenue from the state.

The domestic market obligation (DMO) makes the contractor supply part of its crude to the domestic market at the weighted average price or another price set in the PSC (Note 2a(v)). PHE shows DMO fees of 429,402 (Note 35).
Cost recovery makes entitlement depend on cost.

Under a cost recovery PSC the contractor's entitlement includes barrels that repay its recoverable costs. The Due from the Government essay computes an illustrative entitlement of 2,200 kbbl, worth 165,000, from 4,000 kbbl of production at USD 75, first tranche petroleum (FTP) of 20 percent, a contractor share of 25 percent, and recoverable costs of 120,000. Raise recoverable costs by 12,000 (illustration):
Equity to be split = 4,000 − 800 FTP − 1,760 = 1,440 kbbl; contractor's share = 1,440 × 25% = 360 kbbl
Entitlement = 1,760 + 200 FTP share + 360 = 2,320 kbbl, up 120 kbbl; revenue up 120 × 75 = 9,000

Under a gross split PSC the contractor takes a percentage of gross production, which under the 2017 regulation cited in PHE's Note 2b is made of a base split adjusted by variable and progressive components and ministerial discretion, with no cost recovery (Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). The 2024 regulation dropped the base split. With an illustrative contractor split of 60 percent, revenue is 4,000 × 60% × 75 = 180,000 whatever the costs, and the extra 12,000 of cost falls entirely on the contractor's profit.

PHE holds both kinds, and its Corridor PSC moves from gross split to cost recovery from 1 January 2025 (Note 2b). It also has operation cooperation contracts (KSO) in which partners recover costs and split the rest with PHE (Note 2g), and a technical service contract for West Qurna-1 in Iraq, where the contractor earns a remuneration fee on production above a baseline plus recovered petroleum costs, a service fee from the Iraqi state (Note 2f, Daftar 5/23–5/24, PDF pp. 40–41).

A "free" handset with a 24-month plan is two obligations. For example (illustration), a customer pays 30 a month for 24 months (720). Standalone, the handset sells for 600 and the plan for 25 a month (600).
Handset = 720 × 600 / 1,200 = 360, recognised on day one; Dr Contract asset 360 / Cr Revenue, equipment 360
Service = 360 over 24 months = 15 a month, though 30 is billed; the contract asset unwinds by 15 a month

Under PSAK 44 Indonesian developers used percentage of completion for apartments meeting its conditions. Construction contracts usually meet the second over-time test. Under PSAK 115 a pre-sold apartment is recognised over time only if the developer has an enforceable right to payment for work done to date (para. 35(c)); otherwise revenue waits for handover.
the software as it exists when granted is recognised at a point in time. One that gives a
intellectual property the licensor keeps changing, typical of software as a service, is recognised over the licence period (paras. B56–B58). A three-year subscription of 1,000 earns 27.78 a month.
An e-commerce platform that never controls the goods reports its commission. On gross merchandise value of 10,000 at an 8 percent commission its revenue is 800.

Interest income is outside PSAK 115 and follows PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9); a bank's fees for services are within PSAK 115. In a murabahah under PSAK 402 (formerly PSAK 102), the seller's margin is profit on a sale, recognised as the Trade receivables essay describes.
PSAK 115 asks for revenue from contracts with customers apart from other income (para. 113),

into categories that show how economic factors affect the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty of revenue (para. 114), contract balances and the revenue released from opening contract liabilities (para. 116), and the price allocated to remaining obligations (para. 120), unless the contract lasts a year or less or the entity bills amounts matching performance to date (para. 121).
PHE disaggregates by counterparty and product (Note 35, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165).
Related parties and Government: crude oil and gas
Energy distribution, logistics, drilling and support services
Note 44g lists the related buyers, including feed gas to the DSLNG plant (523,722), and states that sales are "after deduction by PNBP" (

, non-tax state revenue) (Daftar 5/186, PDF p. 203), which fits net reporting of the state's share. The segment note gives the second cut: exploration and production 13,902,984 and services 1,296,023 before eliminating 868,667 of intra-group sales, and by geography 13,642,166 in Indonesia and 1,556,841 overseas (Note 46, Daftar 5/220 and 5/222, PDF pp. 237 and 239), 10.2 percent of the 15,199,007 total before elimination.

Collection slowed in 2024. Receipts from customers of 12,661,461 (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17) are 95.9 percent of revenue excluding the 1,133,213 billed to SKK Migas, which is collected through the separate line for receipts from the Government.

Note 35 leaves three gaps. The related-party crude and gas line is split only indirectly: Note 44g says sales to Pertamina and KPI are crude (about 7.39 million) and the rest gas. "Adjustment split PSC", 703,811, is billed to SKK Migas, whose revenue in Note 44g (1,133,213; 2023: 1,308,765) equals the DMO fees plus this line in both years, but PHE does not say what it compensates. And there is no revenue released from the opening deferred revenue of 11,143 (para. 116(b)), an omission immaterial at 0.08 percent of revenue.
: contract liabilities, take-or-pay, financing on prepayments.
: unconditional rights to consideration, contract assets, provisional pricing.
: the costs PHE recognises "on the basis of the costs incurred for the actual amount sold".

Reading PHE's "after deduction by PNBP" as net reporting of the state's share is an inference. The FS do not say whether PHE ever sells the state's barrels, and the illustration of 200 kbbl of state crude is constructed.

What "Adjustment split PSC" (703,811 in 2024, 859,924 in 2023) compensates is not disclosed; its counterparty is SKK Migas (Notes 35, 44g), as the Due from the Government essay also reports. One unverified reading is compensation from the state's share for gas sold at regulated prices to designated industries (

, HGBT), since Permen ESDM 15/2022 funds that price cut from the state's share and keeps the contractor's share whole. On that reading it is consideration for gas delivered, consistent with Note 3p. A split true-up is the other possibility.

PHE's Note 2b still cites ESDM Regulations 8/2017 and 52/2017 for gross split. Regulation 13/2024 revoked them in August 2024, before the year end, dropped the base split and, per ESDM, puts contractor shares at 75–95 percent (secondary sources); existing contracts may keep their signed terms. The 60 percent split is an illustration.

Note 3p's list of five steps is garbled in both languages: "identify contracts" is unnumbered, then steps 1 and 2 both read "identification of performance obligations". Note 35's PT Kilang Pertamina Internasional figure (7,372,296) differs by 1 from Note 44g (7,372,295). The about 7.39 million of related-party crude is approximate, because the Note 44g rows also carry services.
Treating TSC cost recovery as part of service revenue, and the control point for crude at the loading flange, are general industry readings. PHE does not state either.
