presentation.deck: The theory of revenue recognition from the contract to disclosure, worked through PHE's crude, gas and service revenue and set beside the industries where the five steps bite hardest
key_takeaways: Revenue is income from an entity's ordinary activities. PSAK 115 measures revenue from contracts with customers through five steps: identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognise revenue when or as control of each promised good or service passes to the customer.

Most of the judgment sits in steps 3 and 5. Variable consideration enters the price only to the extent a significant reversal is highly probable not to occur, and an obligation is satisfied over time only if one of three tests is met; otherwise revenue waits for a point in time.

An upstream contractor's revenue is the oil and gas it lifts and sells to its customers. When lifting differs from entitlement the gap is settled with the state outside revenue, and barrels sold only on the state's behalf are not revenue at all. Under a cost recovery contract the entitlement itself rises with recoverable cost.

title: Right-of-Use Assets, Net: The Lessee's Side of PSAK 116
snippet: The theory of lease accounting for the lessee from identification to disclosure, worked through PHE's leased vessels, tanks and buildings and set beside the industries where leases dominate
content:
In brief

  • Since PSAK 116 a lessee puts almost every lease on its balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. The liability is the present value of the lease payments over the lease term, and the asset is the liability plus prepayments, initial direct costs and restoration costs, less incentives received.

  • Two judgments drive the numbers. One is whether the contract is a lease at all, which turns on who controls an identified asset. The other is the lease term, which includes option periods the lessee is reasonably certain to use.

  • Afterwards the asset is depreciated, usually straight-line, while interest on the liability falls as it is repaid, so a lease costs more in its early years than the even rent of the old standard. Changes in term, index-linked rent or scope remeasure the liability and move the asset with it.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report right-of-use assets, net, of 123,977 at 31 December 2024 against 203,379 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11). The line fell 39.0 percent and is 0.4 percent of total assets (0.7 percent a year earlier). Against it stand lease liabilities of 112,926, of which 50,575 is current and 62,351 non-current, against 173,189 a year earlier (87,223 and 85,966) (Note 30, Daftar 5/146, PDF p. 163). This page covers both liability lines.

A student should come away able to decide whether a contract holds a lease, measure the asset and liability, run them through their life with journals, and read a lessee's lease notes.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 116 Sewa (formerly PSAK 73, IFRS 16), which PHE adopted on 1 January 2020 (Note 18, Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129).

1. Why leases are on the lessee's balance sheet

Under the old standard, PSAK 30 (IAS 17), a lessee split leases in two. A finance lease, one that transferred substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership, went on the balance sheet. An operating lease did not. The lessee expensed the rent and disclosed its commitments in a note. Kieso calls the result off-balance-sheet financing. Two airlines flying identical fleets could show very different debt depending on how their leases were drafted.

PSAK 116 removes the split for lessees. A lease gives the lessee a right to use an asset, which is an asset, and an obligation to pay for it, which is a liability, whatever the contract is called. For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary adds to its ships and aircraft class (45,240 net at the end of 2024, Note 18) by chartering a supply vessel for three years at 1,000 a year, paid at each year end, and could borrow for three years at 6 percent.

PSAK 30, operating lease

PSAK 116

Balance sheet at the start

nothing

asset and liability of 1,000 × 2.673012 = 2,673.01

Profit or loss each year

rent expense 1,000

depreciation plus interest

2.673012 is the annuity factor at 6 percent for three years, (1 − 1.06^−3) / 0.06, the present value of 1 a year.

2. Is the contract a lease?

A contract is or contains a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration (para. 9). PHE's policy uses the same words (Note 3n, Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74). Control has two parts, tested over the period of use.

  • Identified asset. The asset is named or implied in the contract, and the supplier has no substantive right to substitute another. A substitution right is substantive only if the supplier can practically swap the asset and would benefit from doing so. A right to substitute only when the asset breaks down does not count.

  • Right to control. The customer obtains substantially all the economic benefits from use, and directs how and for what purpose the asset is used.

For example (illustration), the charter names one vessel. The subsidiary decides which platforms it serves, in what order and when it sails, while the owner's crew operates it. The customer directs the use, so the charter contains a lease. If instead a marine contractor agreed to move a set tonnage of cargo each month with whichever boats it chose, the contractor would be directing its own fleet and the subsidiary would be buying a transport service, with nothing on this line.

Separating components. A charter usually pays for the vessel and for services such as crew, fuel management and catering. The consideration is split on relative stand-alone prices, and only the lease component goes into the liability (paras. 12–13). Suppose the day rate is 30, a bareboat charter (the vessel alone, with the charterer finding the crew) would cost 21 a day, and comparable crew services would cost 14.

Lease component = 30 × 21 / (21 + 14) = 18 a day; annual lease payment = 18 × 365 = 6,570

Non-lease component = 30 × 14 / 35 = 12 a day; 12 × 365 = 4,380 a year, expensed as the services are received

A lessee may elect, by class of asset, to treat the whole payment as lease (para. 15), which would put 30 × 365 = 10,950 a year into the liability instead of 6,570.

3. The lease term

The lease term is the non-cancellable period plus periods under an extension option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise, and periods under a termination option it is reasonably certain not to exercise (para. 18). Reasonably certain is a high threshold, above "more likely than not". The entity weighs every economic incentive, such as rent in the option period against market rent, significant improvements it has made to the asset, the cost of relocating, and how important the asset is to its operations (para. 19).

For example (illustration), the vessel charter runs three years with an option to extend for two more at the same rate. At commencement the subsidiary's field work is contracted for only three years, so the extension is not reasonably certain and the term is three years. The term is reassessed only when a significant event within the lessee's control changes that view (para. 20), which section 8 picks up.

4. Initial measurement

The lease liability is the present value of the lease payments not yet paid at commencement (para. 26). Lease payments are (para. 27):

  • fixed payments, including payments that are fixed in substance, less incentives receivable;

  • variable payments that depend on an index or a rate, measured at the index or rate at commencement;

  • amounts the lessee expects to pay under a residual value guarantee, a promise that the asset will be worth at least a set amount at the end;

  • the exercise price of a purchase option the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise;

  • penalties for terminating the lease, if the term assumes termination.

The discount rate is the rate implicit in the lease if it can be readily determined, otherwise the lessee's incremental borrowing rate, what it would pay to borrow over a similar term with similar security for an asset of similar value. PHE uses the incremental borrowing rate, because the implicit rate is not readily determinable (Note 3n, Daftar 5/59, PDF p. 76).

The right-of-use asset is the liability plus lease payments made at or before commencement, initial direct costs, and the estimated cost of dismantling or restoring the asset that the lease obliges the lessee to bear, less lease incentives received (para. 24). PHE's policy lists the same components except restoration costs (Note 3n, Daftar 5/58, PDF p. 75).

For example (illustration), the vessel charter pays 6,570 a year in arrears for three years at an incremental borrowing rate of 6 percent. The subsidiary pays a broker 120 to arrange it, and the owner pays the subsidiary 150 toward fitting the vessel with its equipment.

Lease liability = 6,570 × 2.673012 = 17,561.69

Right-of-use asset = 17,561.69 + 120 initial direct costs − 150 incentive = 17,531.69

5. Subsequent measurement

The two sides now follow different rules. The liability is carried at amortised cost, with interest added at the discount rate on the opening balance and payments deducted (the effective interest method). The asset is depreciated under PSAK 216's rules, usually straight-line (PHE's policy), from commencement over the shorter of the lease term and its useful life, or over its useful life if ownership passes or a purchase option is reasonably certain (paras. 31–32). It is also tested for impairment under PSAK 236 (para. 33).

The total over three years is the same as under PSAK 30, where the cost would have been (19,710 + 120 − 150) / 3 = 6,560 a year. The timing differs. PSAK 116 charges 337.60 more in year 1 and 344.22 less in year 3, because interest is largest when the liability is largest. A portfolio of leases of different ages smooths this out, but a single new lease is front-loaded.

The statements also look different. Depreciation sits in operating expenses and interest in finance costs, so EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) rises when a company moves from PSAK 30 to PSAK 116. In the cash flow statement the principal part of each payment is a financing outflow, and payments for short-term and low-value leases and variable payments outside the liability are operating (para. 50). PHE shows "payments of lease liabilities" of 146,158 in financing activities (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17).

6. Variable payments, guarantees and purchase options

The standard sorts variable payments by what they depend on.

Index- or rate-linked payments go into the liability at the current index, and when the index moves the liability is remeasured at the original discount rate (here 6 percent), with the asset adjusted by the same amount (paras. 39, 42–43). For example (illustration), an office lease pays 500 a year for five years, linked to the consumer price index. After the second payment the index rises 4 percent, so the three remaining payments become 520.

Increase in lease liability = 20 × 2.673012 = 53.46

Dr Right-of-use assets 53.46 / Cr Lease liabilities 53.46

Usage- or performance-based payments, such as a stand-by rate per day a rig waits on weather, or rent as a share of a shop's sales, stay out of the liability and are expensed when they arise (para. 38). PHE's policy says the same (Note 3n, PDF p. 75).

Residual value guarantees enter the liability only at the amount the lessee expects to pay under them.

Purchase options reasonably certain to be exercised enter the liability at their exercise price, and the asset is then depreciated over its useful life because the lessee expects to keep it. For example (illustration), a subsidiary leases a vehicle for three years at 30 a year with an option to buy it for 10 at the end, which it is reasonably certain to take. The vehicle will last six years and the incremental borrowing rate is 7 percent.

Lease liability = 30 × 2.624316 + 10 / 1.07^3 = 78.73 + 8.16 = 86.89

Depreciation = 86.89 / 6 = 14.48 a year, over the useful life

7. Short-term and low-value leases

Two exemptions let a lessee skip the balance sheet and expense payments straight-line (paras. 5–8). A short-term lease has a term of 12 months or less at commencement and no purchase option, and the election is made by class of asset. A low-value lease is judged lease by lease on the value of the asset when new; the IASB had in mind items such as laptops and phones, around USD 5,000 or less in whole dollars. PHE applies both (Note 3n, Daftar 5/59, PDF p. 76). For example (illustration), a four-month crane hire at 25 a month.

Dr Lease expense, short-term 25 / Cr Cash 25, each month; 100 in total

A short-term lease that is extended or modified becomes a new lease and is tested again (para. 7).

8. Reassessments and modifications

Reassessment happens when something already in the contract is seen differently, for example when the lessee becomes reasonably certain to use an extension option, or stops being certain. The liability is remeasured with the revised payments at a revised discount rate, the current incremental borrowing rate, and the asset moves by the same amount (paras. 39–41). For example (illustration), at the end of year 1 the subsidiary signs a five-year field contract that needs the vessel, an event within its control that makes the two-year extension reasonably certain. Four payments now remain, and its incremental borrowing rate has risen to 7 percent.

Revised liability = 6,570 × 3.387211 = 22,253.98, where 3.387211 = (1 − 1.07^−4) / 0.07

Increase = 22,253.98 − 12,045.39 = 10,208.59

Right-of-use asset = (17,531.69 − 5,843.90) + 10,208.59 = 21,896.38, depreciated over four years at 5,474.10 a year

Dr Right-of-use assets 10,208.59 / Cr Lease liabilities 10,208.59

A modification is a change in scope or price outside the original terms (para. 44). If it adds the right to use another asset at a price matching its stand-alone price, it is a separate new lease. If it reduces scope, for example by returning a physically distinct asset, the lessee first removes the proportion of asset and liability given up, with the difference in profit or loss, and then remeasures what remains at a revised rate (para. 46(a)). Half of one vessel's capacity would not do, because a capacity portion that is not physically distinct is not an identified asset (para. B20). For example (illustration), suppose the charter had covered two identical vessels, each carrying half the payments, and at the end of year 1 the owner agreed to take one back for the remaining two years. Half of the asset (11,687.79 × 50% = 5,843.90) and half of the liability (12,045.39 × 50% = 6,022.70) are derecognised.

Dr Lease liabilities 6,022.70 / Cr Right-of-use assets 5,843.90 / Cr Gain on lease modification 178.80

The remaining liability would then be remeasured on the new payments, with the asset adjusted. PHE's policy lists modifications, changes in term or payments and changes in purchase-option assessments as triggers for remeasurement (Note 3n, PDF p. 76).

9. Impairment, other models and presentation

A right-of-use asset is tested for impairment like any fixed asset, usually within a cash-generating unit (para. 33). If the lessee revalues the class of fixed assets the leased asset belongs to, it may revalue the right-of-use assets in that class too (para. 35). A right-of-use asset that meets the definition of investment property, a building leased and sublet for rent, follows PSAK 240 (para. 34).

Right-of-use assets and lease liabilities are presented separately or disclosed by line, and interest on the liability is presented as a finance cost (paras. 47, 49). Disclosure covers depreciation by class, interest, short-term and low-value expense, variable payments, total cash outflow, additions, and carrying amounts by class (para. 53), plus a maturity analysis of the liability.

The liability is split between current and non-current under PSAK 201 like any borrowing. The current portion is the principal to be repaid within twelve months, not the payments due. For example (illustration), the vessel liability of 12,045.39 at the end of year 1 splits as follows.

Current = 6,570.00 − 722.72 interest of year 2 = 5,847.28

Non-current = 12,045.39 − 5,847.28 = 6,198.11, the closing liability of year 2

The maturity analysis shows undiscounted payments (para. 58), so its first bucket, 6,570, exceeds the current portion by the interest still to accrue.

10. Sale and leaseback

In a sale and leaseback the owner sells an asset and leases it straight back. If the transfer is a sale under PSAK 115, the seller keeps on its books only the part of the old carrying amount that relates to the right of use it retains, and recognises a gain only on the rights actually passed to the buyer (paras. 99–100). If the transfer is not a sale, the asset stays and the cash is a financial liability (para. 103). A 2022 amendment, which PHE notes had no significant effect on it, stops the seller-lessee from measuring the lease liability in a way that recognises gain on the retained right (Note 2, Daftar 5/30, PDF p. 47).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary sells an office building with a carrying amount of 600 to an investor for 1,000, its fair value, and leases it back for five years at 80 a year in arrears. The incremental borrowing rate is 6 percent.

Lease liability = 80 × 4.212364 = 336.99

Right-of-use asset = 600 × 336.99 / 1,000 = 202.19, the share of the old carrying amount retained

Total gain = 1,000 − 600 = 400; gain recognised = 400 × (1,000 − 336.99) / 1,000 = 265.20

The remaining 134.80 of the gain is never booked as such. It is embedded in the lower right-of-use asset and reaches profit through lower depreciation over the five years.

11. The lessor's side, briefly

Lessors keep the two-model split that lessees lost. A lease that transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership is a finance lease, and the lessor replaces the asset with a receivable. Any other lease is an operating lease, and the lessor keeps the asset and recognises rent straight-line (paras. 61–66). Kieso's indicators are transfer of ownership, a purchase option priced to be exercised, a term covering the major part of the asset's life, and payments with a present value close to its fair value. PHE's lessor policy describes operating leases, with rent recognised straight-line in other operating income (Note 3n, Daftar 5/59, PDF p. 76).

12. Right-of-use assets across industries

PSAK 116 matters most where the business runs on assets it does not own.

Airlines. Aircraft are the classic leased asset, and many Indonesian carriers lease most of their fleets. Leases often carry return conditions, obligations to hand the aircraft back with a set amount of engine and airframe life, which add restoration-type costs to the asset as the obligation arises, with a provision under PSAK 237, and maintenance reserves paid to the lessor during the term.

Telecommunications and towers. Mobile operators lease space on towers, rooftops and land for their sites, often for long terms with renewal options, so the lease term judgment in section 3 drives the liability. The tower companies on the other side are lessors with operating leases.

Retail and banking. Shops and bank branches are leased buildings. Rent that varies with sales stays out of the liability under section 6, so a retailer on turnover rent carries a smaller liability than one on fixed rent for the same store.

Shipping and offshore services. A bareboat charter (vessel only) is usually a lease. A time charter (vessel with crew, the charterer directing where it goes) usually contains one, with the crew as a non-lease component, as in section 2. A voyage charter, where the owner directs the vessel to deliver a cargo, is usually a service.

Land rights. Indonesian land rights such as hak guna bangunan are tested under ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36). A right that is in substance a land purchase is a fixed asset, and a right to use is a lease. PHE applies that test (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69) and carries land rights of 127, net, in this line.

Islamic finance. An ijarah, the sharia lease, is accounted for under PSAK 407 Akuntansi Ijarah (formerly PSAK 107) where the entity applies the sharia standards (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).

Upstream oil and gas. Leases to explore for or use oil and gas are outside PSAK 116 (para. 3(a)), which covers the right to the resource itself. Rigs, vessels, tanks and buildings used in those operations are inside it. When an operator signs a lease for a joint operation, it recognises the full liability if it is the party the lessor can pursue for payment, and recovers the partners' shares through joint billings (IFRS Interpretations Committee, agenda decision, March 2019).

PHE's Note 18 shows cost and accumulated depreciation by class (Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129). Net book values, computed from that table:

The correction columns change cost by −131,884 and accumulated depreciation by +136,834, raising net book value by 4,950. They do not offset class by class, and PHE does not explain them. Two ratios are consistent with a portfolio running off.

Accumulated depreciation / cost = 901,080 / 1,025,057 = 87.9% (2023: 931,493 / 1,134,872 = 82.1%)

Undiscounted payments due within one year = 61,542 / 119,135 = 51.7%; due after five years = 393

The liability side reconciles in Note 30 (Daftar 5/146, PDF p. 163).

173,189 + additions 82,334 + interest 7,354 − payments 146,158 − exchange differences 3,793 = 112,926

Implied interest rate = 7,354 / ((173,189 + 112,926) / 2) = 5.1%

The split does not fit section 9 on the printed figures. Payments due within one year are 61,542, so even if all 6,209 of future interest fell in that year, principal due within it would be at least 61,542 − 6,209 = 55,333, above the current portion of 50,575. The 2023 figures fit (93,649 − 11,096 = 82,553, below 87,223). PHE does not explain the gap.

Additions to the liability (82,334) are more than three and a half times additions to the asset (22,519), although under section 4 they normally move together, and PHE does not reconcile the two. The finance cost note reports lease interest of 17,225 (Note 41, Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167), against 7,354 here. Its narrative names finance leases of state-owned assets and leases of LPG plants and gas pipelines among the sources of interest, without saying which sit in that line. The state-owned asset leases are carried in "due to the Government", 63,825 at PEP (Note 20, Daftar 5/114, PDF p. 131). Lease debt across the two notes is therefore at least 112,926 + 63,825 = 176,751.

14. Upstream note: state-owned assets under lease

Some of what PHE uses belongs to the state. Assets of the former Pertamina entity that were left out of its opening balance sheet are state property (Barang Milik Negara), and PEP leases them from the Ministry of Finance (Note 20, PDF pp. 131–132; Note 45b, Daftar 5/189, PDF p. 206). Under gross split contracts, assets of earlier PSCs that the state now owns are used through a lease scheme, with rent set on their appraised fair value (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). Equipment bought under a cost recovery PSC is also state property that the contractor has the right to use (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). Whether each of these arrangements is a lease under PSAK 116, and where it is presented, is a judgment the FS shows only in part.

15. Related lines

  • lease-liabilities-current and lease-liabilities-non-current: the other side of every right-of-use asset, covered on this page.

  • fixed-assets-net: the depreciation and impairment rules the asset follows, and land rights that are purchases.

  • due-to-government-current and due-to-government-non-current: where the state-owned asset leases sit.

  • depreciation-depletion-amortization: where right-of-use depreciation is charged.

Least-confident assertions

  • Note 18's correction columns (net +4,950) and the positive 59,120 in the tanks depreciation column are unexplained in the FS. This page does not guess at them; the ratios drawn from the table assume its totals are right.

  • The total lease debt of at least 176,751 adds two notes on the assumption that the state-owned asset leases in Note 20 are leases in the same sense as Note 30. PHE calls them finance leases and does not say whether they are measured under PSAK 116. Note 41's 17,225 of lease interest may include them and third-party LPG plant and pipeline leases; the FS does not split it.

  • The current portion of 50,575 in Note 30 is below the minimum principal due within a year implied by the maturity table (55,333). The page reads the split as principal within twelve months, the usual practice; PHE may define it differently or one figure may be misprinted.

  • The industry descriptions (airline return conditions, tower leases, charter types) are general practice from knowledge of IFRS 16 application, not researched for named Indonesian companies. The treatment of ijarah under PSAK 407 and its interaction with PSAK 116 was not checked.

content.text: Since PSAK 116 a lessee puts almost every lease on its balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. The liability is the present value of the lease payments over the lease term, and the asset is the liability plus prepayments, initial direct costs and restoration costs, less incentives received.

Two judgments drive the numbers. One is whether the contract is a lease at all, which turns on who controls an identified asset. The other is the lease term, which includes option periods the lessee is reasonably certain to use.

Afterwards the asset is depreciated, usually straight-line, while interest on the liability falls as it is repaid, so a lease costs more in its early years than the even rent of the old standard. Changes in term, index-linked rent or scope remeasure the liability and move the asset with it.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report right-of-use assets, net, of 123,977 at 31 December 2024 against 203,379 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11). The line fell 39.0 percent and is 0.4 percent of total assets (0.7 percent a year earlier). Against it stand lease liabilities of 112,926, of which 50,575 is current and 62,351 non-current, against 173,189 a year earlier (87,223 and 85,966) (Note 30, Daftar 5/146, PDF p. 163). This page covers both liability lines.
A student should come away able to decide whether a contract holds a lease, measure the asset and liability, run them through their life with journals, and read a lessee's lease notes.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. The governing standard is PSAK 116
(formerly PSAK 73, IFRS 16), which PHE adopted on 1 January 2020 (Note 18, Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129).
1. Why leases are on the lessee's balance sheet
Under the old standard, PSAK 30 (IAS 17), a lessee split leases in two. A
, one that transferred substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership, went on the balance sheet. An

did not. The lessee expensed the rent and disclosed its commitments in a note. Kieso calls the result off-balance-sheet financing. Two airlines flying identical fleets could show very different debt depending on how their leases were drafted.

PSAK 116 removes the split for lessees. A lease gives the lessee a right to use an asset, which is an asset, and an obligation to pay for it, which is a liability, whatever the contract is called. For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary adds to its ships and aircraft class (45,240 net at the end of 2024, Note 18) by chartering a supply vessel for three years at 1,000 a year, paid at each year end, and could borrow for three years at 6 percent.

A contract is or contains a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an
for a period in exchange for consideration (para. 9). PHE's policy uses the same words (Note 3n, Daftar 5/57, PDF p. 74). Control has two parts, tested over the period of use.
. The asset is named or implied in the contract, and the supplier has no

right to substitute another. A substitution right is substantive only if the supplier can practically swap the asset and would benefit from doing so. A right to substitute only when the asset breaks down does not count.
. The customer obtains substantially all the economic benefits from use, and directs how and for what purpose the asset is used.

For example (illustration), the charter names one vessel. The subsidiary decides which platforms it serves, in what order and when it sails, while the owner's crew operates it. The customer directs the use, so the charter contains a lease. If instead a marine contractor agreed to move a set tonnage of cargo each month with whichever boats it chose, the contractor would be directing its own fleet and the subsidiary would be buying a transport service, with nothing on this line.

A charter usually pays for the vessel and for services such as crew, fuel management and catering. The consideration is split on relative stand-alone prices, and only the lease component goes into the liability (paras. 12–13). Suppose the day rate is 30, a bareboat charter (the vessel alone, with the charterer finding the crew) would cost 21 a day, and comparable crew services would cost 14.
Lease component = 30 × 21 / (21 + 14) = 18 a day; annual lease payment = 18 × 365 = 6,570
Non-lease component = 30 × 14 / 35 = 12 a day; 12 × 365 = 4,380 a year, expensed as the services are received
A lessee may elect, by class of asset, to treat the whole payment as lease (para. 15), which would put 30 × 365 = 10,950 a year into the liability instead of 6,570.

to exercise, and periods under a termination option it is reasonably certain not to exercise (para. 18). Reasonably certain is a high threshold, above "more likely than not". The entity weighs every economic incentive, such as rent in the option period against market rent, significant improvements it has made to the asset, the cost of relocating, and how important the asset is to its operations (para. 19).

For example (illustration), the vessel charter runs three years with an option to extend for two more at the same rate. At commencement the subsidiary's field work is contracted for only three years, so the extension is not reasonably certain and the term is three years. The term is reassessed only when a significant event within the lessee's control changes that view (para. 20), which section 8 picks up.

fixed payments, including payments that are fixed in substance, less incentives receivable;
variable payments that depend on an index or a rate, measured at the index or rate at commencement;

, a promise that the asset will be worth at least a set amount at the end;

penalties for terminating the lease, if the term assumes termination.

, what it would pay to borrow over a similar term with similar security for an asset of similar value. PHE uses the incremental borrowing rate, because the implicit rate is not readily determinable (Note 3n, Daftar 5/59, PDF p. 76).

is the liability plus lease payments made at or before commencement, initial direct costs, and the estimated cost of dismantling or restoring the asset that the lease obliges the lessee to bear, less lease incentives received (para. 24). PHE's policy lists the same components except restoration costs (Note 3n, Daftar 5/58, PDF p. 75).

For example (illustration), the vessel charter pays 6,570 a year in arrears for three years at an incremental borrowing rate of 6 percent. The subsidiary pays a broker 120 to arrange it, and the owner pays the subsidiary 150 toward fitting the vessel with its equipment.
Right-of-use asset = 17,561.69 + 120 initial direct costs − 150 incentive = 17,531.69

It is also tested for impairment under PSAK 236 (para. 33).

is a change in scope or price outside the original terms (para. 44). If it adds the right to use another asset at a price matching its stand-alone price, it is a separate new lease. If it reduces scope, for example by returning a physically distinct asset, the lessee first removes the proportion of asset and liability given up, with the difference in profit or loss, and then remeasures what remains at a revised rate (para. 46(a)). Half of one vessel's capacity would not do, because a capacity portion that is not physically distinct is not an identified asset (para. B20). For example (illustration), suppose the charter had covered two identical vessels, each carrying half the payments, and at the end of year 1 the owner agreed to take one back for the remaining two years. Half of the asset (11,687.79 × 50% = 5,843.90) and half of the liability (12,045.39 × 50% = 6,022.70) are derecognised.
Dr Lease liabilities 6,022.70 / Cr Right-of-use assets 5,843.90 / Cr Gain on lease modification 178.80

The remaining liability would then be remeasured on the new payments, with the asset adjusted. PHE's policy lists modifications, changes in term or payments and changes in purchase-option assessments as triggers for remeasurement (Note 3n, PDF p. 76).

A right-of-use asset is tested for impairment like any fixed asset, usually within a cash-generating unit (para. 33). If the lessee revalues the class of fixed assets the leased asset belongs to, it may revalue the right-of-use assets in that class too (para. 35). A right-of-use asset that meets the definition of investment property, a building leased and sublet for rent, follows PSAK 240 (para. 34).

Right-of-use assets and lease liabilities are presented separately or disclosed by line, and interest on the liability is presented as a finance cost (paras. 47, 49). Disclosure covers depreciation by class, interest, short-term and low-value expense, variable payments, total cash outflow, additions, and carrying amounts by class (para. 53), plus a maturity analysis of the liability.

The liability is split between current and non-current under PSAK 201 like any borrowing. The current portion is the principal to be repaid within twelve months, not the payments due. For example (illustration), the vessel liability of 12,045.39 at the end of year 1 splits as follows.
Non-current = 12,045.39 − 5,847.28 = 6,198.11, the closing liability of year 2
The maturity analysis shows undiscounted payments (para. 58), so its first bucket, 6,570, exceeds the current portion by the interest still to accrue.

the owner sells an asset and leases it straight back. If the transfer is a sale under PSAK 115, the seller keeps on its books only the part of the old carrying amount that relates to the right of use it retains, and recognises a gain only on the rights actually passed to the buyer (paras. 99–100). If the transfer is not a sale, the asset stays and the cash is a financial liability (para. 103). A 2022 amendment, which PHE notes had no significant effect on it, stops the seller-lessee from measuring the lease liability in a way that recognises gain on the retained right (Note 2, Daftar 5/30, PDF p. 47).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary sells an office building with a carrying amount of 600 to an investor for 1,000, its fair value, and leases it back for five years at 80 a year in arrears. The incremental borrowing rate is 6 percent.
Right-of-use asset = 600 × 336.99 / 1,000 = 202.19, the share of the old carrying amount retained
The remaining 134.80 of the gain is never booked as such. It is embedded in the lower right-of-use asset and reaches profit through lower depreciation over the five years.

Lessors keep the two-model split that lessees lost. A lease that transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership is a finance lease, and the lessor replaces the asset with a receivable. Any other lease is an operating lease, and the lessor keeps the asset and recognises rent straight-line (paras. 61–66). Kieso's indicators are transfer of ownership, a purchase option priced to be exercised, a term covering the major part of the asset's life, and payments with a present value close to its fair value. PHE's lessor policy describes operating leases, with rent recognised straight-line in other operating income (Note 3n, Daftar 5/59, PDF p. 76).
PSAK 116 matters most where the business runs on assets it does not own.
Aircraft are the classic leased asset, and many Indonesian carriers lease most of their fleets. Leases often carry

, obligations to hand the aircraft back with a set amount of engine and airframe life, which add restoration-type costs to the asset as the obligation arises, with a provision under PSAK 237, and maintenance reserves paid to the lessor during the term.

Mobile operators lease space on towers, rooftops and land for their sites, often for long terms with renewal options, so the lease term judgment in section 3 drives the liability. The tower companies on the other side are lessors with operating leases.

Shops and bank branches are leased buildings. Rent that varies with sales stays out of the liability under section 6, so a retailer on turnover rent carries a smaller liability than one on fixed rent for the same store.
(vessel only) is usually a lease. A
(vessel with crew, the charterer directing where it goes) usually contains one, with the crew as a non-lease component, as in section 2. A
, where the owner directs the vessel to deliver a cargo, is usually a service.

are tested under ISAK 336 (formerly ISAK 36). A right that is in substance a land purchase is a fixed asset, and a right to use is a lease. PHE applies that test (Note 3i, Daftar 5/52, PDF p. 69) and carries land rights of 127, net, in this line.
, the sharia lease, is accounted for under PSAK 407
(formerly PSAK 107) where the entity applies the sharia standards (STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED).

Leases to explore for or use oil and gas are outside PSAK 116 (para. 3(a)), which covers the right to the resource itself. Rigs, vessels, tanks and buildings used in those operations are inside it. When an operator signs a lease for a joint operation, it recognises the full liability if it is the party the lessor can pursue for payment, and recovers the partners' shares through joint billings (IFRS Interpretations Committee, agenda decision, March 2019).
13. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 18 and 30
PHE's Note 18 shows cost and accumulated depreciation by class (Daftar 5/112, PDF p. 129). Net book values, computed from that table:
Tanks, pipeline installations and other equipment
203,379 + additions 22,519 − cost "correction" 131,884 − reclassification 450 − depreciation 107,172 + accumulated depreciation "correction" 136,834 + reclassification 751 = 123,977

The correction columns change cost by −131,884 and accumulated depreciation by +136,834, raising net book value by 4,950. They do not offset class by class, and PHE does not explain them. Two ratios are consistent with a portfolio running off.
Undiscounted payments due within one year = 61,542 / 119,135 = 51.7%; due after five years = 393
The liability side reconciles in Note 30 (Daftar 5/146, PDF p. 163).
Undiscounted payments 119,135 − future interest 6,209 = 112,926 = current 50,575 + non-current 62,351

The split does not fit section 9 on the printed figures. Payments due within one year are 61,542, so even if all 6,209 of future interest fell in that year, principal due within it would be at least 61,542 − 6,209 = 55,333, above the current portion of 50,575. The 2023 figures fit (93,649 − 11,096 = 82,553, below 87,223). PHE does not explain the gap.

Additions to the liability (82,334) are more than three and a half times additions to the asset (22,519), although under section 4 they normally move together, and PHE does not reconcile the two. The finance cost note reports lease interest of 17,225 (Note 41, Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167), against 7,354 here. Its narrative names finance leases of state-owned assets and leases of LPG plants and gas pipelines among the sources of interest, without saying which sit in that line. The state-owned asset leases are carried in "due to the Government", 63,825 at PEP (Note 20, Daftar 5/114, PDF p. 131). Lease debt across the two notes is therefore at least 112,926 + 63,825 = 176,751.
14. Upstream note: state-owned assets under lease
Some of what PHE uses belongs to the state. Assets of the former Pertamina entity that were left out of its opening balance sheet are state property (

), and PEP leases them from the Ministry of Finance (Note 20, PDF pp. 131–132; Note 45b, Daftar 5/189, PDF p. 206). Under gross split contracts, assets of earlier PSCs that the state now owns are used through a lease scheme, with rent set on their appraised fair value (Note 2b, Daftar 5/17, PDF p. 34). Equipment bought under a cost recovery PSC is also state property that the contractor has the right to use (Note 2a(vii), Daftar 5/11, PDF p. 28). Whether each of these arrangements is a lease under PSAK 116, and where it is presented, is a judgment the FS shows only in part.
: the other side of every right-of-use asset, covered on this page.
: the depreciation and impairment rules the asset follows, and land rights that are purchases.
: where the state-owned asset leases sit.

Note 18's correction columns (net +4,950) and the positive 59,120 in the tanks depreciation column are unexplained in the FS. This page does not guess at them; the ratios drawn from the table assume its totals are right.

The total lease debt of at least 176,751 adds two notes on the assumption that the state-owned asset leases in Note 20 are leases in the same sense as Note 30. PHE calls them finance leases and does not say whether they are measured under PSAK 116. Note 41's 17,225 of lease interest may include them and third-party LPG plant and pipeline leases; the FS does not split it.

The current portion of 50,575 in Note 30 is below the minimum principal due within a year implied by the maturity table (55,333). The page reads the split as principal within twelve months, the usual practice; PHE may define it differently or one figure may be misprinted.

The industry descriptions (airline return conditions, tower leases, charter types) are general practice from knowledge of IFRS 16 application, not researched for named Indonesian companies. The treatment of ijarah under PSAK 407 and its interaction with PSAK 116 was not checked.

presentation.deck: The theory of lease accounting for the lessee from identification to disclosure, worked through PHE's leased vessels, tanks and buildings and set beside the industries where leases dominate
key_takeaways: Since PSAK 116 a lessee puts almost every lease on its balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. The liability is the present value of the lease payments over the lease term, and the asset is the liability plus prepayments, initial direct costs and restoration costs, less incentives received.

Two judgments drive the numbers. One is whether the contract is a lease at all, which turns on who controls an identified asset. The other is the lease term, which includes option periods the lessee is reasonably certain to use.

Afterwards the asset is depreciated, usually straight-line, while interest on the liability falls as it is repaid, so a lease costs more in its early years than the even rent of the old standard. Changes in term, index-linked rent or scope remeasure the liability and move the asset with it.

title: Right-of-Use Assets, Net, and What a 39 Percent Fall Can Hide: Lease or service, measurement, term judgments and the operator's gross-up at a PSC contractor, and how the lease liability and maturity table separate runoff from termination
snippet: Lease or service, measurement, term judgments and the operator's gross-up at a PSC contractor, and how the lease liability and maturity table separate runoff from termination
content:
In brief

  • A right-of-use asset is a lessee's right to use a leased asset, measured from the present value of the lease payments and depreciated straight-line. Whether a rig contract creates one depends on who directs the rig.

  • The line falls every year through depreciation. In the case below, a three-year and a five-year lease lose 45.7 percent of their carrying amount in their second year with no event at all.

  • A fall has to be split into depreciation, terminations and extensions using the asset rollforward, the lease liability and the maturity table. In the case, the three combine into a 39.0 percent fall.

The reported line fell 39 percent, and a fall that size can come from depreciation alone

The balance sheet on this page reports right-of-use assets, net, of 123,977 at 31 December 2024 against 203,379 a year earlier, in thousands. That is a fall of 79,402, or 39.0 percent, taking the line from 0.65 to 0.41 percent of total assets.

This essay uses PT Hulu Energi Nusantara ("HEN"), an upstream oil and gas contractor operating under production sharing contracts (PSCs) with SKK Migas, reporting in USD under Indonesian SAK with a 31 December year end. HEN and every figure attached to it are constructed for illustration. HEN amounts are in USD thousand; day rates are in USD thousand per day.

HEN operates its block with a 60 percent participating interest, its share of the block's costs and production; partners hold the other 40 percent, and the PSC runs to 2040 (constructed). On 1 January 2023 HEN leased a jack-up rig (an offshore drilling rig that stands on legs lowered to the seabed) for three years and an onshore warehouse for five. In February 2025 the audit committee chair, reading the draft 2024 notes, sees right-of-use assets down from 37,801.0 to 23,051.7, a fall of 39.0 percent, and asks whether the rig was released early or the leases are running down.

The governing claim of this essay is that a change in right-of-use assets nets depreciation, which runs every year, against term events, which only the lease liability and the maturity table (the note listing undiscounted lease payments by due date) reveal, so the percentage alone cannot say which happened.

This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that HEN's 39.0 percent fall nets a 45.7 percent fall from depreciation, a rig release and a warehouse extension, a split any reader can rebuild from the notes.

The governing standard is PSAK 116 Leases (formerly PSAK 73, IFRS 16), effective in Indonesia since 2020 under its old number. It replaced PSAK 30 (IAS 17), which kept operating leases off the lessee's balance sheet.

A rig contract creates a right-of-use asset only if HEN directs the rig

A contract contains a lease when it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration (PSAK 116 paragraph 9), which means the right to substantially all of its economic benefits and the right to direct how and for what purpose it is used. Otherwise it is a service, and nothing reaches this line.

HEN's contract names one jack-up, and the owner may substitute another only if that rig is damaged. A right that applies only when the asset is not working does not stop it being identified (paragraph B18). A general right would also fail, because a substitution right counts only if the supplier could practically substitute and would gain from doing so (paragraph B14), and moving a jack-up costs its owner several million USD (in whole dollars). The asset is identified.

HEN decides which wells the rig drills, in what order, to what depth and when it moves. Those are the decisions about how and for what purpose the rig is used (paragraph B24). The owner's crew operates the rig on HEN's instructions, which gives the owner no such right. HEN has a lease. Had a drilling company undertaken to drill five wells with any rig from its fleet, choosing which rig and when, HEN would be buying a service.

The exclusion of leases to explore for or use oil and gas (paragraph 3(a)) covers the PSC's right to the resource, not the rig or the warehouse.

The day rate also pays for services. HEN pays USD 80 thousand a day for the rig, crew, maintenance and catering. Rigs of this class charter bareboat, the rig alone with the charterer supplying the crew, for about USD 48 thousand a day, and the services are priced at USD 32 thousand. PSAK 116 allocates the price on relative stand-alone prices (paragraph 13).

Lease component = 80 × 48 / (48 + 32) = USD 48 thousand per day

Annual lease payment = 48 × 365 = 17,520; annual service cost = 32 × 365 = 11,680, recognised as the services are received

A lessee may elect, by class of asset, not to separate the components (paragraph 15). The liability would then capitalise 29,200 a year, 76,630.0 instead of the 45,978.0 computed below, 67 percent more.

The liability is the present value of the payments, and the asset adds what HEN spent to get the assets into use

The lease liability at commencement is the present value of the unpaid lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease or, if that cannot be readily determined, at the lessee's incremental borrowing rate, what it would pay to borrow over a similar term against similar security (paragraph 26). HEN uses 7 percent. Both leases pay annually in arrears, simplifying monthly invoicing, and the annuity factor (the present value of 1 a year for n years) is (1 − 1.07^−n) / 0.07.

Rig liability = 17,520 × (1 − 1.07^−3) / 0.07 = 17,520 × 2.624316 = 45,978.0

Warehouse liability = 1,925 × (1 − 1.07^−5) / 0.07 = 1,925 × 4.100197 = 7,892.9

The right-of-use asset is the liability plus lease payments made at or before commencement, initial direct costs and the estimated cost of restoring the site that the lease obliges the lessee to bear (paragraph 24). HEN paid the rig owner a mobilisation fee of 1,000 in December 2022 to tow the rig to location. HEN treats it as a payment for making the leased rig available and puts it all in the lease component; a 48/32 allocation would put 600 there. HEN paid an agent's commission of 60 on the warehouse, and must restore the floor slab at exit at an estimated 210.4 in 2027, 150.0 discounted at 7 percent.

Rig asset = 45,978.0 + 1,000 = 46,978.0

Warehouse asset = 7,892.9 + 60 + 150.0 = 8,102.9

Dr Right-of-use assets 55,080.9
Cr Lease liabilities 53,870.9
Cr Prepaid mobilisation 1,000.0
Cr Cash (agent's commission) 60.0
Cr Restoration provision 150.0

Straight-line depreciation plus effective interest front-loads the cost of a lease

The rig costs HEN 18,877.8 in its first year against a payment of 17,520, because interest is charged on the opening liability at the discount rate (the effective interest method) and is largest when the liability is largest, while depreciation is straight-line over the shorter of the lease term and the asset's life.

Depreciation = 46,978.0 / 3 = 15,659.3 a year, with 0.1 of rounding in 2025

Total charge = 46,978.0 + 3,218.5 + 2,217.4 + 1,146.2 = 53,560.1, the 52,560 of payments plus the 1,000 fee, with 0.1 of rounding

Under PSAK 30 the rig would have cost 17,520 + 1,000 / 3 = 17,853.3 a year; PSAK 116 charges 1,024.5 more in 2023 and 1,047.7 less in 2025. Where the rig drills development wells, the depreciation and the services are capitalised into oil and gas properties and reach profit through depletion.

The warehouse depreciates at 8,102.9 / 5 = 1,620.6 a year. At 31 December 2023 the line holds 31,318.7 for the rig and 6,482.3 for the warehouse, 37,801.0 in total.

The asset is non-current in full. The current/non-current boundary runs through the liability, whose current part is the principal due within twelve months. At 31 December 2023 that is 15,302.7 for the rig (31,676.5 − 16,373.8) and 1,468.6 for the warehouse (6,520.4 − 5,051.8), 16,771.3 in total, leaving 38,196.9 − 16,771.3 = 21,425.6 non-current.

Short-term and low-value leases never reach the line

A lessee may expense two kinds of lease straight-line instead (paragraph 5). A short-term lease runs 12 months or less from commencement with no purchase option, elected by class of asset. A low-value lease, judged lease by lease, is one whose asset is worth about USD 5,000 (in whole dollars) or less when new, such as a laptop. In 2024 HEN expensed a 75-day liftboat (a self-elevating service vessel) hire at USD 12 thousand a day, 900 in total.

The lease term is a judgment, and it moves the line in both directions

Two board decisions on 31 December 2024 moved HEN's leases in opposite directions. The lease term is the non-cancellable period plus option periods the lessee is reasonably certain, a threshold well above "more likely than not", to extend into or not to terminate. The warehouse carried a ten-year extension option at the same rent. At commencement HEN had not decided where to hold production spares after drilling, and a shared base with a neighbouring operator was an option, so the extension was not reasonably certain.

The term is reassessed when a significant event within the lessee's control changes that certainty (paragraph 20), such as a business decision or significant leasehold improvements (paragraph B41). In 2024 an appraisal well, drilled to measure a discovery, came up dry. That ended drilling, but it was outside HEN's control and says nothing about storage. On 31 December 2024 the board approved a production plan that makes the warehouse the field's spares hub until 2037, within the PSC's term. By that date HEN had bolted 1,800 of heavy racking to the slab; leaving early would forfeit most of it and cost about 250 to remove. The decision and the racking are within HEN's control, as paragraph 20 requires, and make the extension reasonably certain. The liability is remeasured over thirteen remaining payments at the incremental borrowing rate at that date, 8 percent for the tenor, and the asset moves by the same amount (paragraphs 39–40).

Revised warehouse liability = 1,925 × (1 − 1.08^−13) / 0.08 = 1,925 × 7.903776 = 15,214.8

Increase = 15,214.8 − 5,051.8 = 10,163.0

Dr Right-of-use assets 10,163.0 / Cr Lease liabilities 10,163.0

After two years of unwinding at 7 percent, charged as finance cost, the restoration provision stood at 210.4 / 1.07^3 = 171.7; due in 2037 it is 210.4 / 1.07^13 = 87.3, and under ISAK 101 (IFRIC 1) the 84.4 change reduces the asset.

Dr Restoration provision 84.4 / Cr Right-of-use assets 84.4

The board's other decision cut the drilling programme after the dry well. The rig contract had no early-termination option, but on 31 December 2024 the owner agreed to an early release (a partial termination) on 30 June 2025, six months early and without a fee, because another client was waiting. A change agreed after commencement and outside the original terms is a lease modification, and one that decreases scope is accounted for in two steps (paragraph 46(a)). First, asset and liability are cut in proportion to the scope removed, the difference going to profit or loss. Second, the liability is remeasured at a revised rate (HEN's six-month rate, 7 percent), and the asset moves by that amount. HEN measures scope by remaining term, a judgment, so it removes half.

Rig asset before the modification = 31,318.7 − 15,659.3 = 15,659.4; rig liability = 16,373.8

Step 1: asset reduced by 15,659.4 × 50% = 7,829.7; liability reduced by 16,373.8 × 50% = 8,186.9

Gain on modification = 8,186.9 − 7,829.7 = 357.2

Step 2: revised liability = 8,760 due 30 June 2025 / 1.07^0.5 = 8,468.6; adjustment = 8,468.6 − (16,373.8 − 8,186.9) = 281.7

Dr Lease liabilities 8,186.9 / Cr Right-of-use assets 7,829.7 / Cr Gain on lease modification 357.2

Dr Right-of-use assets 281.7 / Cr Lease liabilities 281.7

The rig's carrying amount at 31 December 2024 is 15,659.4 − 7,829.7 + 281.7 = 8,111.4. Had a termination right been in the original contract, becoming reasonably certain to use it would have been a reassessment, with the whole change taken to the asset and no gain.

The rollforward, the liability and the maturity table separate depreciation from term events

HEN's line fell 14,749.3 in 2024, less than its depreciation of 17,279.9, because the term events added a net 2,530.6.

Depreciation alone = 37,801.0 − 17,279.9 = 20,521.1, a fall of 45.7 percent

Adding the rig modification = 20,521.1 − 7,829.7 + 281.7 = 12,973.1, a fall of 65.7 percent

Adding the warehouse events = 12,973.1 + 10,163.0 − 84.4 = 23,051.7, a fall of 39.0 percent

The liability gives a second test, because with no term events it falls by the principal repaid. HEN paid 19,445 in 2024 against interest of 2,217.4 + 456.4 = 2,673.8, repaying 16,771.2. The liability fell from 38,196.9 to 23,683.4 (8,468.6 for the rig and 15,214.8 for the warehouse), only 14,513.5. The gap is the rig modification, 8,186.9 − 281.7 = 7,905.2 down, and the extension, 10,163.0 up (0.1 of rounding). A liability that falls more than principal repaid signals terminations; less signals new leases or extensions.

The maturity table, which PSAK 116 paragraph 58 requires through PSAK 107 (formerly 60, IFRS 7) paragraphs 39 and B11, places the event in time.

Last year's "1 to 2 years" amount of 19,445 should reappear as this year's "within 1 year". It shows 10,685, so 8,760, six months of rig payments, has gone, a termination. The "over 5 years" amount appears from nothing, an extension or a new long lease. The total is 33,785 against 42,740 − 19,445 = 23,295 with no events, the difference being 10 × 1,925 = 19,250 added less 8,760 removed. The same tests would say whether the reported 39 percent is runoff without renewal or leases ended early.

At a PSC operator the line carries the partners' share, and cost recovery runs on a different clock

HEN carries 100 percent of both leases on its balance sheet although it bears only 60 percent of their cost, because it signed them in its own name as operator. In March 2019 the IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded that under IFRS 11, now PSAK 111 (formerly 66), a joint operator recognises the liabilities for which it has primary responsibility, including a lease on which it is the primary obligor, the party the lessor can pursue for payment. The partners repay 40 percent of each payment as partner reimbursements billed under the joint operating agreement (JOA), so 40% × 23,051.7 = 9,220.7 of the line is theirs in substance.

The asset side is less settled, and the Committee left it unaddressed. If the JOA gives the partners a right to use the rig, HEN has a sublease, a lease of the asset onward to them, and moves their share of the asset into a receivable. If HEN alone directs the rig, it keeps the full asset, which is HEN's policy. It then books partner reimbursements as they are billed, in 2024 Dr Receivable from partners 7,778 (40% × 19,445) / Cr Lease costs 7,778. Reimbursements follow the payments while the expense follows depreciation and interest, so HEN's net charge is front-loaded. Non-operating partners book their share through the billings.

Cost recovery is the PSC mechanism by which the contractor recoups approved operating costs from production before the remainder is split with the government. This essay assumes rentals are recovered as the lease payments fall due, not as depreciation and interest, and that the rig, unlike equipment HEN buys, stays the owner's property. If PSC tax deductions follow the same payments, the asset, the lease liability and (if restoration is deductible when spent) the provision all have a tax base, the amount the tax rules attribute to them, of nil. Since the PSAK 212 (formerly 46, IAS 12) single-transaction amendment, effective 1 January 2023, these differences are recognised gross. On HEN's 60 percent share at the combined PSC rate of 40 percent, that is a deferred tax liability of 5,532.4 on the asset against deferred tax assets of 5,684.0 on the lease liability and 21.0 on the provision, a net asset of 172.6 at 31 December 2024.

HEN's line fell 39.0 percent because a warehouse extension offset most of a rig release in a year when depreciation alone would have cut 45.7 percent

The chair's answer is that the rig was released early, the leases ran down, and a third event pulled the other way. Depreciation alone would have left 20,521.1; the rig release removed a net 7,548.0 (7,829.7 less 281.7) with a gain of 357.2; the warehouse extension added a net 10,078.6 (10,163.0 less 84.4). Without the rollforward, the modification gain and the maturity table in the notes, HEN's 39.0 percent reads exactly like the reported company's.

Least-confident assertions

  • Cost recovery and PSC tax following lease payments and restoration spend, and the rig remaining the lessor's property, were not checked against a PSC, PP 79/2010 as amended or SKK Migas rules. If deductions followed the accounting charge, the deferred tax would be nil.

  • The asset-side treatment in the joint operation (no sublease, partner reimbursements credited to lease costs) is a constructed policy. Deferred tax on the partners' 40 percent carried gross is left out.

  • Putting the whole mobilisation fee in the lease component is a judgment; an auditor could require the 48/32 allocation, which would make the rig asset 46,578.0.

  • Measuring a term reduction by remaining term in step 1 is one reading; the standard's illustrative example reduces floor space, not term.

  • The PSAK 116 paragraph numbers follow IFRS 16 and were not checked against the Indonesian text; real rig contracts add standby and moving rates that complicate the 48/32 allocation.

The decision addressed the operator's liability and expressly left the asset side unaddressed. VERIFIED (web, ifrs.org agenda decision and iasplus.com summary).

content.text: A right-of-use asset is a lessee's right to use a leased asset, measured from the present value of the lease payments and depreciated straight-line. Whether a rig contract creates one depends on who directs the rig.
The line falls every year through depreciation. In the case below, a three-year and a five-year lease lose 45.7 percent of their carrying amount in their second year with no event at all.
A fall has to be split into depreciation, terminations and extensions using the asset rollforward, the lease liability and the maturity table. In the case, the three combine into a 39.0 percent fall.
The reported line fell 39 percent, and a fall that size can come from depreciation alone

The balance sheet on this page reports right-of-use assets, net, of 123,977 at 31 December 2024 against 203,379 a year earlier, in thousands. That is a fall of 79,402, or 39.0 percent, taking the line from 0.65 to 0.41 percent of total assets.

This essay uses PT Hulu Energi Nusantara ("HEN"), an upstream oil and gas contractor operating under production sharing contracts (PSCs) with SKK Migas, reporting in USD under Indonesian SAK with a 31 December year end. HEN and every figure attached to it are constructed for illustration. HEN amounts are in USD thousand; day rates are in USD thousand per day.

HEN operates its block with a 60 percent participating interest, its share of the block's costs and production; partners hold the other 40 percent, and the PSC runs to 2040 (constructed). On 1 January 2023 HEN leased a jack-up rig (an offshore drilling rig that stands on legs lowered to the seabed) for three years and an onshore warehouse for five. In February 2025 the audit committee chair, reading the draft 2024 notes, sees right-of-use assets down from 37,801.0 to 23,051.7, a fall of 39.0 percent, and asks whether the rig was released early or the leases are running down.

The governing claim of this essay is that a change in right-of-use assets nets depreciation, which runs every year, against term events, which only the lease liability and the maturity table (the note listing undiscounted lease payments by due date) reveal, so the percentage alone cannot say which happened.

This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that HEN's 39.0 percent fall nets a 45.7 percent fall from depreciation, a rig release and a warehouse extension, a split any reader can rebuild from the notes.
(formerly PSAK 73, IFRS 16), effective in Indonesia since 2020 under its old number. It replaced PSAK 30 (IAS 17), which kept operating leases off the lessee's balance sheet.
A rig contract creates a right-of-use asset only if HEN directs the rig

A contract contains a lease when it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration (PSAK 116 paragraph 9), which means the right to substantially all of its economic benefits and the right to direct how and for what purpose it is used. Otherwise it is a service, and nothing reaches this line.

HEN's contract names one jack-up, and the owner may substitute another only if that rig is damaged. A right that applies only when the asset is not working does not stop it being identified (paragraph B18). A general right would also fail, because a substitution right counts only if the supplier could practically substitute and would gain from doing so (paragraph B14), and moving a jack-up costs its owner several million USD (in whole dollars). The asset is identified.

HEN decides which wells the rig drills, in what order, to what depth and when it moves. Those are the decisions about how and for what purpose the rig is used (paragraph B24). The owner's crew operates the rig on HEN's instructions, which gives the owner no such right. HEN has a lease. Had a drilling company undertaken to drill five wells with any rig from its fleet, choosing which rig and when, HEN would be buying a service.
The exclusion of leases to explore for or use oil and gas (paragraph 3(a)) covers the PSC's right to the resource, not the rig or the warehouse.

The day rate also pays for services. HEN pays USD 80 thousand a day for the rig, crew, maintenance and catering. Rigs of this class charter bareboat, the rig alone with the charterer supplying the crew, for about USD 48 thousand a day, and the services are priced at USD 32 thousand. PSAK 116 allocates the price on relative stand-alone prices (paragraph 13).
Lease component = 80 × 48 / (48 + 32) = USD 48 thousand per day
Annual lease payment = 48 × 365 = 17,520; annual service cost = 32 × 365 = 11,680, recognised as the services are received

A lessee may elect, by class of asset, not to separate the components (paragraph 15). The liability would then capitalise 29,200 a year, 76,630.0 instead of the 45,978.0 computed below, 67 percent more.
The liability is the present value of the payments, and the asset adds what HEN spent to get the assets into use

The lease liability at commencement is the present value of the unpaid lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease or, if that cannot be readily determined, at the lessee's incremental borrowing rate, what it would pay to borrow over a similar term against similar security (paragraph 26). HEN uses 7 percent. Both leases pay annually in arrears, simplifying monthly invoicing, and the annuity factor (the present value of 1 a year for n years) is (1 − 1.07^−n) / 0.07.

The right-of-use asset is the liability plus lease payments made at or before commencement, initial direct costs and the estimated cost of restoring the site that the lease obliges the lessee to bear (paragraph 24). HEN paid the rig owner a mobilisation fee of 1,000 in December 2022 to tow the rig to location. HEN treats it as a payment for making the leased rig available and puts it all in the lease component; a 48/32 allocation would put 600 there. HEN paid an agent's commission of 60 on the warehouse, and must restore the floor slab at exit at an estimated 210.4 in 2027, 150.0 discounted at 7 percent.
Straight-line depreciation plus effective interest front-loads the cost of a lease

The rig costs HEN 18,877.8 in its first year against a payment of 17,520, because interest is charged on the opening liability at the discount rate (the effective interest method) and is largest when the liability is largest, while depreciation is straight-line over the shorter of the lease term and the asset's life.
Depreciation = 46,978.0 / 3 = 15,659.3 a year, with 0.1 of rounding in 2025
Total charge = 46,978.0 + 3,218.5 + 2,217.4 + 1,146.2 = 53,560.1, the 52,560 of payments plus the 1,000 fee, with 0.1 of rounding

Under PSAK 30 the rig would have cost 17,520 + 1,000 / 3 = 17,853.3 a year; PSAK 116 charges 1,024.5 more in 2023 and 1,047.7 less in 2025. Where the rig drills development wells, the depreciation and the services are capitalised into oil and gas properties and reach profit through depletion.
The warehouse depreciates at 8,102.9 / 5 = 1,620.6 a year. At 31 December 2023 the line holds 31,318.7 for the rig and 6,482.3 for the warehouse, 37,801.0 in total.

The asset is non-current in full. The current/non-current boundary runs through the liability, whose current part is the principal due within twelve months. At 31 December 2023 that is 15,302.7 for the rig (31,676.5 − 16,373.8) and 1,468.6 for the warehouse (6,520.4 − 5,051.8), 16,771.3 in total, leaving 38,196.9 − 16,771.3 = 21,425.6 non-current.
Short-term and low-value leases never reach the line

A lessee may expense two kinds of lease straight-line instead (paragraph 5). A short-term lease runs 12 months or less from commencement with no purchase option, elected by class of asset. A low-value lease, judged lease by lease, is one whose asset is worth about USD 5,000 (in whole dollars) or less when new, such as a laptop. In 2024 HEN expensed a 75-day liftboat (a self-elevating service vessel) hire at USD 12 thousand a day, 900 in total.
The lease term is a judgment, and it moves the line in both directions

Two board decisions on 31 December 2024 moved HEN's leases in opposite directions. The lease term is the non-cancellable period plus option periods the lessee is reasonably certain, a threshold well above "more likely than not", to extend into or not to terminate. The warehouse carried a ten-year extension option at the same rent. At commencement HEN had not decided where to hold production spares after drilling, and a shared base with a neighbouring operator was an option, so the extension was not reasonably certain.

The term is reassessed when a significant event within the lessee's control changes that certainty (paragraph 20), such as a business decision or significant leasehold improvements (paragraph B41). In 2024 an appraisal well, drilled to measure a discovery, came up dry. That ended drilling, but it was outside HEN's control and says nothing about storage. On 31 December 2024 the board approved a production plan that makes the warehouse the field's spares hub until 2037, within the PSC's term. By that date HEN had bolted 1,800 of heavy racking to the slab; leaving early would forfeit most of it and cost about 250 to remove. The decision and the racking are within HEN's control, as paragraph 20 requires, and make the extension reasonably certain. The liability is remeasured over thirteen remaining payments at the incremental borrowing rate at that date, 8 percent for the tenor, and the asset moves by the same amount (paragraphs 39–40).
Dr Right-of-use assets 10,163.0 / Cr Lease liabilities 10,163.0

After two years of unwinding at 7 percent, charged as finance cost, the restoration provision stood at 210.4 / 1.07^3 = 171.7; due in 2037 it is 210.4 / 1.07^13 = 87.3, and under ISAK 101 (IFRIC 1) the 84.4 change reduces the asset.
Dr Restoration provision 84.4 / Cr Right-of-use assets 84.4

The board's other decision cut the drilling programme after the dry well. The rig contract had no early-termination option, but on 31 December 2024 the owner agreed to an early release (a partial termination) on 30 June 2025, six months early and without a fee, because another client was waiting. A change agreed after commencement and outside the original terms is a lease modification, and one that decreases scope is accounted for in two steps (paragraph 46(a)). First, asset and liability are cut in proportion to the scope removed, the difference going to profit or loss. Second, the liability is remeasured at a revised rate (HEN's six-month rate, 7 percent), and the asset moves by that amount. HEN measures scope by remaining term, a judgment, so it removes half.
Rig asset before the modification = 31,318.7 − 15,659.3 = 15,659.4; rig liability = 16,373.8
Step 1: asset reduced by 15,659.4 × 50% = 7,829.7; liability reduced by 16,373.8 × 50% = 8,186.9
Dr Lease liabilities 8,186.9 / Cr Right-of-use assets 7,829.7 / Cr Gain on lease modification 357.2
Dr Right-of-use assets 281.7 / Cr Lease liabilities 281.7

The rig's carrying amount at 31 December 2024 is 15,659.4 − 7,829.7 + 281.7 = 8,111.4. Had a termination right been in the original contract, becoming reasonably certain to use it would have been a reassessment, with the whole change taken to the asset and no gain.
The rollforward, the liability and the maturity table separate depreciation from term events
HEN's line fell 14,749.3 in 2024, less than its depreciation of 17,279.9, because the term events added a net 2,530.6.
Depreciation alone = 37,801.0 − 17,279.9 = 20,521.1, a fall of 45.7 percent
Adding the rig modification = 20,521.1 − 7,829.7 + 281.7 = 12,973.1, a fall of 65.7 percent
Adding the warehouse events = 12,973.1 + 10,163.0 − 84.4 = 23,051.7, a fall of 39.0 percent

The liability gives a second test, because with no term events it falls by the principal repaid. HEN paid 19,445 in 2024 against interest of 2,217.4 + 456.4 = 2,673.8, repaying 16,771.2. The liability fell from 38,196.9 to 23,683.4 (8,468.6 for the rig and 15,214.8 for the warehouse), only 14,513.5. The gap is the rig modification, 8,186.9 − 281.7 = 7,905.2 down, and the extension, 10,163.0 up (0.1 of rounding). A liability that falls more than principal repaid signals terminations; less signals new leases or extensions.
The maturity table, which PSAK 116 paragraph 58 requires through PSAK 107 (formerly 60, IFRS 7) paragraphs 39 and B11, places the event in time.

Last year's "1 to 2 years" amount of 19,445 should reappear as this year's "within 1 year". It shows 10,685, so 8,760, six months of rig payments, has gone, a termination. The "over 5 years" amount appears from nothing, an extension or a new long lease. The total is 33,785 against 42,740 − 19,445 = 23,295 with no events, the difference being 10 × 1,925 = 19,250 added less 8,760 removed. The same tests would say whether the reported 39 percent is runoff without renewal or leases ended early.
At a PSC operator the line carries the partners' share, and cost recovery runs on a different clock

HEN carries 100 percent of both leases on its balance sheet although it bears only 60 percent of their cost, because it signed them in its own name as operator. In March 2019 the IFRS Interpretations Committee concluded that under IFRS 11, now PSAK 111 (formerly 66), a joint operator recognises the liabilities for which it has primary responsibility, including a lease on which it is the primary obligor, the party the lessor can pursue for payment. The partners repay 40 percent of each payment as partner reimbursements billed under the joint operating agreement (JOA), so 40% × 23,051.7 = 9,220.7 of the line is theirs in substance.

The asset side is less settled, and the Committee left it unaddressed. If the JOA gives the partners a right to use the rig, HEN has a sublease, a lease of the asset onward to them, and moves their share of the asset into a receivable. If HEN alone directs the rig, it keeps the full asset, which is HEN's policy.
