key_takeaways: A right-of-use asset is a lessee's right to use a leased asset, measured from the present value of the lease payments and depreciated straight-line. Whether a rig contract creates one depends on who directs the rig.
The line falls every year through depreciation. In the case below, a three-year and a five-year lease lose 45.7 percent of their carrying amount in their second year with no event at all.
A fall has to be split into depreciation, terminations and extensions using the asset rollforward, the lease liability and the maturity table. In the case, the three combine into a 39.0 percent fall.

title: Share Capital: Contributed Capital, Share Issues and Common-Control Restructurings
snippet: The theory of contributed capital from authorised shares to pooling of interests, worked through PHE's Rp198 trillion of issued capital and its negative additional paid-in capital, and set beside the industries with capital rules of their own
content:
In brief

  • Equity is a residual, but company law carves out a fixed slice, legal capital, equal to the nominal value of issued shares, which in Indonesia must be paid in full and, for at least 25 percent of authorised capital, at incorporation. Anything paid above nominal is share premium (agio), shown with other contributions as additional paid-in capital.

  • Shares issued for cash are recorded at what is received less issue costs; shares issued for non-cash assets at the fair value of what is received, or of the shares if that is more reliable. Treasury shares and preference shares sit at the border with liabilities. A buyback is deducted from equity and never produces a gain or loss in profit, while a preference share the issuer must redeem is a liability whose dividends are interest.

  • When businesses move between companies under one controlling party, PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and books the difference from the consideration in additional paid-in capital. That difference is negative whenever the consideration exceeds the carrying amount taken over.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report share capital of 13,631,466 at both 31 December 2024 and 31 December 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; "Daftar" is the printed page). Beside it sit additional paid-in capital (APIC) of −3,649,862 and an "other equity component" of −4,958 (−11,098 a year earlier). Share capital is 44.8 percent of total assets (44.1 percent in 2023) and 90.2 percent of total equity (96.1 percent).

After reading this page a student should be able to explain what share capital legally is, record share issues, issue costs, preference shares and treasury shares, and apply pooling of interests to a group restructuring.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Rupiah amounts are full rupiah. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Retained earnings, other comprehensive income (OCI) and non-controlling interest (NCI) have their own essays.

1. What share capital is

Equity is the residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). The lecture notes split it by source: share capital, share premium, retained earnings, accumulated OCI, treasury shares (a deduction) and NCI.

The first two are contributed capital, what owners paid in. Retained earnings are earned capital, what the entity generated and kept; this page also counts accumulated OCI there, which the notes do not. On PHE's 2024 figures:

Contributed = 13,631,466 − 3,649,862 = 9,981,604 (69.2% of equity attributable to owners of 14,433,117)

Earned = 1,167,892 + 3,184,728 + 103,851 = 4,456,471 (30.9%); the other equity component of −4,958 closes the total

Company law locks part of contributed capital in, through three amounts in UU 40/2007 on Limited Liability Companies (UU PT).

  • Authorised capital (modal dasar) is the nominal value of all shares the articles of association allow (art. 31(1)). Authorisation creates no asset and no claim, so it needs no journal entry, only a memorandum.

  • Issued capital (modal ditempatkan) is the nominal value of shares actually taken up.

  • Paid-up capital (modal disetor) is what has been paid for them. At least 25 percent of authorised capital must be issued and fully paid (art. 33(1)), and every later issue must be paid in full (art. 33(3)); the elucidation adds that instalments are not possible. Issued and paid-up are therefore the same number, and Kieso's subscriptions receivable hardly arises.

Cipta Kerja replaced art. 32's minimum authorised capital of Rp50,000,000 with an amount the founders decide (art. 109 point 3 of Perppu 2/2022, enacted as UU 6/2023; PP 8/2021), leaving art. 33 unchanged.

PHE's figures fit the rule (Note 32, Daftar 5/147, PDF p. 164). Authorised capital is Rp790,000,000,000,000, divided into 1,580,000,000,000 shares of Rp500.

Issued = 396,225,242,340 shares × Rp500 = Rp198,112,621,170,000

Issued / authorised = 198,112,621,170,000 / 790,000,000,000,000 = 25.08%

PT Pertamina (Persero) holds 99.9968 percent and PT Pertamina Pedeve Indonesia 0.0032 percent.

Each share gives the right to vote at the general meeting of shareholders (RUPS) and to receive dividends and remaining assets in liquidation (art. 52(1)); the notes add the pre-emptive right to new shares.

2. Par value, no-par shares and the stock split

Par value (nominal value) is a legal amount unrelated to fair value. It marks out legal capital, which the company may return to shareholders only through procedures the law sets, such as a capital reduction or a limited buyback (section 6). No-par shares have no such amount; some jurisdictions then require a stated value.

Indonesia requires par. Share values must be stated in rupiah and no-par shares cannot be issued (UU PT art. 49(1)–(2)), unless capital-market legislation provides otherwise (arts. 31(2) and 49(3)). When shares are sold for more than nominal, the excess is agio (share premium), recorded in the statements as such (elucidation to art. 8(2)(c)). Indonesian statements present it within additional paid-in capital (tambahan modal disetor).

The lecture notes also record an issue below par: "Assets/service $40,000 / PIC – COMMON STOCK $10,000 / Common stock $50,000". There is no Indonesian counterpart. Issued capital is the nominal value and must be paid in full, so a share cannot be paid for with less than its nominal value. The standard-setter, DSAK IAI, reads the law as prohibiting disagio on the initial payment of capital (PSAK 338 Basis for Conclusions, DK10).

A rupiah par in a dollar entity. PHE's functional currency is the US dollar (Note 3r, Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83), but its shares carry a rupiah par. Contributed equity is not a monetary item, so it is translated once, at the rate on the contribution date. For example (illustration), a subsidiary with a USD functional currency issues 1,000,000,000 shares of Rp500 nominal for Rp600 each when the rate is Rp15,000 per USD.

Cash = 1,000,000,000 × Rp600 / 15,000 / 1,000 = 40,000

Share capital = 1,000,000,000 × Rp500 / 15,000 / 1,000 = 33,333.33; share premium = 6,666.67

Dr Cash 40,000 / Cr Share capital 33,333.33 / Cr Share premium 6,666.67

A later move in the rate is not booked. PHE's share capital carries at least two historical rates, each an average of the issues behind it.

Pertamina: Rp198,106,221,170,000 / 13,630,780 thousand = Rp14,533.7 per USD

Pedeve: 12,800,000 × Rp500 = Rp6,400,000,000 / 686 thousand = Rp9,329.4 per USD

Stock splits. A split cuts the par in proportion to the new number of shares. Nothing moves between equity accounts, so it needs only a memorandum entry. PHE split its shares from Rp2,500 to Rp500 by resolution of an extraordinary RUPS on 2 November 2022 (Note 32).

Shares before = 396,225,242,340 / 5 = 79,245,048,468 at Rp2,500; after = 396,225,242,340 at Rp500

Issued capital = Rp198,112,621,170,000 before and after

3. Issuing shares for cash

A cash issue is recorded at what is received: nominal to share capital, the rest to share premium.

Issue costs. Underwriting, legal, accounting and printing fees for new shares are costs of raising equity. PSAK 232 Financial Instruments: Presentation (formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) deducts them from equity, net of any related income tax (paras. 35A, 37), and the notes deduct them from paid-in capital. For example (illustration), a USD-functional subsidiary raising rupiah lists 2,000,000,000 new shares of Rp500 nominal at Rp1,000 when the rate is Rp16,000 per USD, and pays 2,500 of issue costs.

Gross proceeds = 2,000,000,000 × Rp1,000 / 16,000 / 1,000 = 125,000; share capital = 62,500; share premium = 62,500

Dr Cash 125,000 / Cr Share capital 62,500 / Cr Share premium 62,500

Dr Share premium 2,500 / Cr Cash 2,500; net premium = 60,000

Shares sold in a package. A price for ordinary and preference shares sold together is split by relative fair value (proportional method) or, if only one fair value is known, by giving that class its fair value and the other the rest (incremental method). For example (illustration), a package sells for 11,000; the ordinary shares are worth 7,200 and the preference shares 4,800.

Proportional: ordinary = 11,000 × 7,200 / 12,000 = 6,600; preference = 4,400. Incremental (preference value unknown): preference = 11,000 − 7,200 = 3,800

4. Issuing shares for non-cash assets (inbreng)

Shares paid for with land, patents, services or shares in another company are an inbreng. A contribution in another form is valued at fair value, set by market price or by an expert unaffiliated with the company, and a contribution of immovable property must be announced in a newspaper within 14 days (UU PT art. 34(1)–(3)).

The lecture notes and Kieso record the asset at the fair value of what is received, or at the fair value of the shares if that is clearer, and never at book value or nominal. For example (illustration), a regional government company contributes land appraised at 12,000 for new shares with a nominal value equivalent to 9,000.

Dr Land 12,000 / Cr Share capital 9,000 / Cr Share premium 3,000

The notes' patent example needs one correction. In its third case, with an independent valuation of USD 125,000 for 10,000 shares of USD 10 par, the notes credit "Share capital – ordinary $25.000" and "Share premium – ordinary $100.000". Share capital is always the nominal, 10,000 × 10 = 100,000, so the premium is 25,000.

A business contributed by the receiving company's own controlling party is the exception, because PSAK 338 (section 7) replaces fair value with carrying amount.

5. Preference shares

A preference share ranks ahead of ordinary shares for dividends, for assets in liquidation, or both. UU PT lets the articles create classes with or without votes, redeemable or convertible after a period, and with cumulative or non-cumulative dividend priority or liquidation priority, one of them designated ordinary (art. 53(3)–(4)). The notes' "no votes" is a common feature, not a legal rule.

The lecture notes record preference shares exactly like ordinary shares and only remark that redeemable ones resemble bonds. PSAK 232 decides by substance, not name. An instrument is a financial liability if the issuer has a contractual obligation to deliver cash, such as a mandatory redemption on a fixed date or at the holder's option (para. 18(a)). It is equity if dividends and redemption are at the issuer's discretion. For example (illustration), a subsidiary issues two classes of 10,000 each with a 6 percent dividend.

Class A: cumulative, never redeemable, dividend declared at RUPS discretion

Class B: mandatorily redeemable at par after five years, dividend mandatory

Classification

Equity

Financial liability

Issue

Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Share capital, preference 10,000

Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Redeemable preference shares 10,000

Annual dividend of 600

Dr Retained earnings 600 / Cr Dividends payable 600, only when declared

Dr Interest expense 600 / Cr Cash 600

Cumulative means unpaid dividends carry forward and must be paid before ordinary dividends. The notes say arrears "akan dianggap sebagai utang dividend" (will be treated as dividends payable). No liability exists until the RUPS declares a dividend, so arrears on Class A are disclosed, not accrued. A share redeemable only at the issuer's option, with discretionary dividends, stays equity. A participating share also shares in profits beyond its fixed rate; a convertible one can be exchanged for ordinary shares.

6. Treasury shares

Shares a company buys back are treasury shares. The purchase returns capital to the sellers, so PSAK 232 deducts their cost from equity and records no gain or loss in profit or loss on their purchase, sale, issue or cancellation (para. 33).

Indonesian law adds its own limits. A buyback must not reduce net assets below issued capital plus the mandatory reserve already set aside, and the nominal value of shares bought back must not exceed 10 percent of issued capital unless capital-market rules say otherwise (art. 37(1)). Treasury shares may be held for at most three years (art. 37(4)), need RUPS approval (art. 38), and carry no votes and no dividends (art. 40).

The cost method, which both sets of lecture notes and most companies use, debits Treasury shares at cost and puts the result of a resale in equity. For example (illustration), a listed subsidiary buys back shares for 900, then resells half for 520 and the other half for 400.

Purchase: Dr Treasury shares 900 / Cr Cash 900

First resale: Dr Cash 520 / Cr Treasury shares 450 / Cr Share premium, treasury shares 70

Second resale: Dr Cash 400, Dr Share premium, treasury shares 50 / Cr Treasury shares 450; balance left = 70 − 50 = 20

Had the second resale come first, with no treasury-share premium to absorb it, the 50 would be debited to retained earnings (Inter 1 Ch 13). Profit is unaffected either way.

The net-asset test compares net assets in the company's latest statements approved by the RUPS with issued capital plus the mandatory reserve, and the law states issued capital in rupiah. For example (illustration), a company with issued capital of Rp100 billion and a mandatory reserve of Rp20 billion has net assets of Rp150 billion, of which Rp30 billion is the negative balance of a common-control difference.

Headroom = 150 − (100 + 20) = Rp30 billion; without the negative APIC it would be Rp60 billion

For PHE the test cannot be run from the published statements. It applies to the company's own net assets, PHE publishes only consolidated figures, and its year-end rate is disclosed only as USD 0.06 per Rp1,000 (Note 3r). The consolidated figures show only the direction. In USD at historical rates, the negative APIC of 3,649,862 offsets most of the retained earnings of 4,352,620.

7. Common-control restructurings: PSAK 338

The problem. If each transfer of a subsidiary within a group were an acquisition under PSAK 103 Business Combinations (formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3), the receiving company would remeasure everything at fair value and recognise goodwill, though nothing left the group and no outsider set a price. PSAK 103 excludes combinations of entities under common control from its scope, and IFRS has no standard for them, so Indonesia keeps its own standard, PSAK 338 (2012) Business Combinations of Entities under Common Control (formerly PSAK 38, renumbered from 1 January 2024). PHE's 2024 statements apply this version; a 2025 revision, effective 2026, is described below.

The principle. A transfer of a business within a group to reorganise it is not a change of ownership in economic substance, so it can create no profit or loss for the group or for any entity in it (para. 07). One example is a parent transferring a subsidiary to another subsidiary it owns (para. 08(b)). Buying out non-controlling shareholders is excluded, because ownership does change (para. 09). The receiving entity uses the pooling-of-interests method at carrying amounts (para. 10), and:

  • recognises the difference between the consideration and the carrying amount of the business in equity, presented in APIC (para. 11);

  • presents the current and comparative periods as if the combination had happened from the start of common control (para. 12);

  • expenses the combination's costs, except costs of issuing debt or equity, which follow PSAK 109 and PSAK 232 (para. 14).

The transferring entity books its own difference, between the consideration received and the carrying amount it gives up, in APIC too (para. 15). These APIC balances are never recycled to profit or reclassified to retained earnings, even if the business later leaves the group (Basis for Conclusions DK12–DK14). PSAK 38 (2004) had kept the difference in a separate account (SNTRES) and released it to profit when common control ended; its balances moved to APIC on 1 January 2013 (para. 20).

An example. For example (illustration, sized to sit close to PHE's APIC of −3,649,862; PHE does not disclose its own combinations' figures), a parent transfers 100 percent of an upstream company to its subholding. The company's net assets have a carrying amount of 6,000,000; the fair value of its identifiable net assets is 8,500,000; an unaffiliated appraiser values the business at 9,650,000. The subholding pays by issuing new shares with a nominal value of 9,650,000, which art. 34 allows because the contribution is valued at 9,650,000.

Acquisition method (PSAK 103, if the parties were unrelated)

Pooling of interests (PSAK 338)

6,000,000 at carrying amount

Dr Net assets 8,500,000, Dr Goodwill 1,150,000 / Cr Share capital 9,650,000

Dr Net assets 6,000,000, Dr APIC 3,650,000 / Cr Share capital 9,650,000

Company law values the contribution at fair value and lets the nominal value of shares issued for it go up to that amount, never above it, with any excess of value over nominal recorded as agio. PSAK 338 puts the asset side at book value. When the parties set the nominal near fair value, or pay cash above book value, the gap is a debit, a negative APIC. DSAK IAI answered the objection that this looks like disagio. The legal ban concerns only the initial payment of capital, and APIC holds more than agio, so a negative common-control difference may sit there (DK10).

The parent books the mirror image (Dr Investment in subholding 9,650,000 / Cr Investment in subsidiary 6,000,000 / Cr APIC 3,650,000), and on consolidation at the ultimate parent the two APIC entries cancel.

Whose carrying amounts. The 2012 text, which rejected push-down accounting (DK19–DK22), points to the carrying amounts in the transferred entity's own statements, so goodwill or fair-value uplifts the parent recognised when it first bought the business stay behind. PHE's policy says "the book value of the net assets of the acquiree" (Note 3d), though IAI found practice divided (DK23A of the 2025 exposure draft). The 2025 revision (approved 29 October 2025, effective 1 January 2026, prospective) switches to the transferring entity's carrying amounts unless impracticable and allows impracticable restatement to be skipped (exposure draft paras. 10A–10C, 12A–12B).

Restating comparatives. Indonesian practice shows the equity of a business not yet legally owned in a separate column of the statement of changes in equity, closed against share capital and APIC when the transfer is completed (practice, not the standard's text). PHE's statement of changes in equity has such a column, "Penggabungan Entitas/Merging Entities", which is nil at every date shown (Daftar 3, PDF p. 16), consistent with no common-control combination in progress in 2023 or 2024. It matters for an upstream group because Note 1b lists PHE's subsidiaries largely as one company per working area (Daftar 5/4, PDF p. 21), so blocks change hands inside the Pertamina group by moving shares.

8. Other components of contributed capital

APIC can also hold contributions with no shares issued, such as the benefit of a below-market shareholder loan (see the Long-term bank loans essay). Other equity lines hold items that are neither profit nor OCI: changes in a parent's stake in a subsidiary without loss of control (PSAK 110, formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10), share-based payment reserves (PSAK 102), and the equity component of convertible bonds. PSAK 201 asks for the nature and purpose of each reserve and a reconciliation of every component.

9. Share capital across industries

Banks and insurers. PP 8/2021, which implements the amended art. 32, keeps the higher minimums that sector rules set for certain businesses (art. 5); before Cipta Kerja the elucidation to art. 32(2) named banking, insurance and freight forwarding. Commercial banks had to hold core capital (paid-up capital plus reserves and retained earnings) of at least Rp3 trillion by the end of 2022 under POJK 12/POJK.03/2020. Insurers face a minimum equity under POJK 23/2023. For both, the regulator's capital measure is wider than legal capital, and a new licence also needs a minimum paid-up capital.

State-owned enterprises. The state funds a Persero by penyertaan modal negara (state equity participation), in cash or in kind, and builds holdings by inbreng of state shares. Government Regulation 6/2018 added to the state's equity in Pertamina by contributing the state's 13,809,038,755 Series B shares in Perusahaan Gas Negara, with the value set by the Minister of Finance; the state kept control through the Series A Dwiwarna share, a single share with special rights.

Listed companies. Capital-market law can override UU PT on buyback limits (art. 37(1)(b)) and on no-par shares (art. 49(3)). Listed companies raise equity through rights issues (hak memesan efek terlebih dahulu, the pre-emptive right in tradeable form), whose costs follow section 3.

What Note 31 says. 11. Related lines

  • additional-paid-in-capital: share premium and common-control differences, covered on this page.

  • other-equity-component: equity adjustments in subsidiaries, covered on this page.

  • retained-earnings: dividends, the statutory reserve and the reserve transfer in the table above.

  • other-comprehensive-income: the accumulated OCI of 103,851.

  • non-controlling-interest: the 674,235 and the 53,470 adjustment.

  • long-term-investments and intangible-assets-net: investments in associates and goodwill from acquisitions that are not under common control.

Least-confident assertions

  • That PHE's APIC arose mainly from the 2021 subholding restructuring is inferred. Note 31 gives only the definition, the FS cover 2023–2024, and the transfer of eleven subsidiaries and Elnusa comes from PHE publications and press reports, not the audited statements. UU PT does not force a negative difference: nominal value may be set anywhere up to the contribution's fair value, so the negative balance reflects a consideration (shares or cash) the parties set above the transferred carrying amounts.

  • The reading that UU PT bars issuing shares below nominal rests on art. 33 (full payment of issued capital) and DSAK IAI's Basis for Conclusions DK10, not on an article that says so in terms.

  • The buyback net-asset test is not run for PHE. The law states capital in rupiah and tests the company's own net assets; PHE publishes neither separate statements nor a precise year-end rate. Translated at a year-end rate the rupiah value of USD net assets has risen since 2021 while rupiah capital is fixed, so a USD comparison at historical rates would mislead. Note 33's Indonesian title ("SALDO CADANGAN WAJIB") treats the whole appropriation as the mandatory reserve, while the statement of changes in equity adds "general and investment reserve".

  • The reading of the other equity component as equity transactions in subsidiaries rests on its label and Note 3c. PHE does not describe it, which falls short of PSAK 201's request to describe each reserve. The 2024 investing receipt of 64,578 and Note 42's gain of 34,242 on sale of subsidiaries more likely relate to TPDC's January 2024 exercise of its call option over the Mnazi Bay interest (Note 5g) than to this row; PHE does not connect them, and a sale to an outsider would not reduce NCI.

  • PHE inconsistencies not used in the body: APIC, which Note 31 defines as common-control differences only, moved by 7 in 2023 in the "equity adjustment in subsidiaries" row; Note 32 describes issued capital as 25 percent of authorised capital where it is 25.08 percent.

content.text: Equity is a residual, but company law carves out a fixed slice,

, equal to the nominal value of issued shares, which in Indonesia must be paid in full and, for at least 25 percent of authorised capital, at incorporation. Anything paid above nominal is share premium (agio), shown with other contributions as additional paid-in capital.

Shares issued for cash are recorded at what is received less issue costs; shares issued for non-cash assets at the fair value of what is received, or of the shares if that is more reliable. Treasury shares and preference shares sit at the border with liabilities. A buyback is deducted from equity and never produces a gain or loss in profit, while a preference share the issuer must redeem is a liability whose dividends are interest.

When businesses move between companies under one controlling party, PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and books the difference from the consideration in additional paid-in capital. That difference is negative whenever the consideration exceeds the carrying amount taken over.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report share capital of 13,631,466 at both 31 December 2024 and 31 December 2023, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; "Daftar" is the printed page). Beside it sit additional paid-in capital (APIC) of −3,649,862 and an "other equity component" of −4,958 (−11,098 a year earlier). Share capital is 44.8 percent of total assets (44.1 percent in 2023) and 90.2 percent of total equity (96.1 percent).

After reading this page a student should be able to explain what share capital legally is, record share issues, issue costs, preference shares and treasury shares, and apply pooling of interests to a group restructuring.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Rupiah amounts are full rupiah. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration. Retained earnings, other comprehensive income (OCI) and non-controlling interest (NCI) have their own essays.

Equity is the residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1). The lecture notes split it by source: share capital, share premium, retained earnings, accumulated OCI, treasury shares (a deduction) and NCI.

shares have no such amount; some jurisdictions then require a

Indonesia requires par. Share values must be stated in rupiah and no-par shares cannot be issued (UU PT art. 49(1)–(2)), unless capital-market legislation provides otherwise (arts. 31(2) and 49(3)). When shares are sold for more than nominal, the excess is
(share premium), recorded in the statements as such (elucidation to art. 8(2)(c)). Indonesian statements present it within additional paid-in capital (tambahan modal disetor).
The lecture notes also record an issue

par: "Assets/service $40,000 / PIC – COMMON STOCK $10,000 / Common stock $50,000". There is no Indonesian counterpart. Issued capital is the nominal value and must be paid in full, so a share cannot be paid for with less than its nominal value. The standard-setter, DSAK IAI, reads the law as prohibiting
on the initial payment of capital (PSAK 338 Basis for Conclusions, DK10).
A rupiah par in a dollar entity.

PHE's functional currency is the US dollar (Note 3r, Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83), but its shares carry a rupiah par. Contributed equity is not a monetary item, so it is translated once, at the rate on the contribution date. For example (illustration), a subsidiary with a USD functional currency issues 1,000,000,000 shares of Rp500 nominal for Rp600 each when the rate is Rp15,000 per USD.
Dr Cash 40,000 / Cr Share capital 33,333.33 / Cr Share premium 6,666.67
A later move in the rate is not booked. PHE's share capital carries at least two historical rates, each an average of the issues behind it.
Pertamina: Rp198,106,221,170,000 / 13,630,780 thousand = Rp14,533.7 per USD

A split cuts the par in proportion to the new number of shares. Nothing moves between equity accounts, so it needs only a memorandum entry. PHE split its shares from Rp2,500 to Rp500 by resolution of an extraordinary RUPS on 2 November 2022 (Note 32).
Issued capital = Rp198,112,621,170,000 before and after
A cash issue is recorded at what is received: nominal to share capital, the rest to share premium.
Underwriting, legal, accounting and printing fees for new shares are costs of raising equity. PSAK 232

(formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32) deducts them from equity, net of any related income tax (paras. 35A, 37), and the notes deduct them from paid-in capital. For example (illustration), a USD-functional subsidiary raising rupiah lists 2,000,000,000 new shares of Rp500 nominal at Rp1,000 when the rate is Rp16,000 per USD, and pays 2,500 of issue costs.
Gross proceeds = 2,000,000,000 × Rp1,000 / 16,000 / 1,000 = 125,000; share capital = 62,500; share premium = 62,500
Dr Cash 125,000 / Cr Share capital 62,500 / Cr Share premium 62,500
Dr Share premium 2,500 / Cr Cash 2,500; net premium = 60,000
A price for ordinary and preference shares sold together is split by relative fair value (
) or, if only one fair value is known, by giving that class its fair value and the other the rest (
). For example (illustration), a package sells for 11,000; the ordinary shares are worth 7,200 and the preference shares 4,800.
Proportional: ordinary = 11,000 × 7,200 / 12,000 = 6,600; preference = 4,400. Incremental (preference value unknown): preference = 11,000 − 7,200 = 3,800
Shares paid for with land, patents, services or shares in another company are an

. A contribution in another form is valued at fair value, set by market price or by an expert unaffiliated with the company, and a contribution of immovable property must be announced in a newspaper within 14 days (UU PT art. 34(1)–(3)).

The lecture notes and Kieso record the asset at the fair value of what is received, or at the fair value of the shares if that is clearer, and never at book value or nominal. For example (illustration), a regional government company contributes land appraised at 12,000 for new shares with a nominal value equivalent to 9,000.
Dr Land 12,000 / Cr Share capital 9,000 / Cr Share premium 3,000

The notes' patent example needs one correction. In its third case, with an independent valuation of USD 125,000 for 10,000 shares of USD 10 par, the notes credit "Share capital – ordinary $25.000" and "Share premium – ordinary $100.000". Share capital is always the nominal, 10,000 × 10 = 100,000, so the premium is 25,000.
A business contributed by the receiving company's own controlling party is the exception, because PSAK 338 (section 7) replaces fair value with carrying amount.

ranks ahead of ordinary shares for dividends, for assets in liquidation, or both. UU PT lets the articles create classes with or without votes, redeemable or convertible after a period, and with cumulative or non-cumulative dividend priority or liquidation priority, one of them designated ordinary (art. 53(3)–(4)). The notes' "no votes" is a common feature, not a legal rule.

The lecture notes record preference shares exactly like ordinary shares and only remark that redeemable ones resemble bonds. PSAK 232 decides by substance, not name. An instrument is a financial liability if the issuer has a contractual obligation to deliver cash, such as a mandatory redemption on a fixed date or at the holder's option (para. 18(a)). It is equity if dividends and redemption are at the issuer's discretion. For example (illustration), a subsidiary issues two classes of 10,000 each with a 6 percent dividend.
Class A: cumulative, never redeemable, dividend declared at RUPS discretion
Class B: mandatorily redeemable at par after five years, dividend mandatory
Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Share capital, preference 10,000
Dr Cash 10,000 / Cr Redeemable preference shares 10,000
Dr Retained earnings 600 / Cr Dividends payable 600, only when declared

means unpaid dividends carry forward and must be paid before ordinary dividends. The notes say arrears "akan dianggap sebagai utang dividend" (will be treated as dividends payable). No liability exists until the RUPS declares a dividend, so arrears on Class A are disclosed, not accrued. A share redeemable only at the issuer's option, with discretionary dividends, stays equity. A
share also shares in profits beyond its fixed rate; a
one can be exchanged for ordinary shares.
Shares a company buys back are
. The purchase returns capital to the sellers, so PSAK 232 deducts their cost from equity and records no gain or loss in profit or loss on their purchase, sale, issue or cancellation (para. 33).

Indonesian law adds its own limits. A buyback must not reduce net assets below issued capital plus the mandatory reserve already set aside, and the nominal value of shares bought back must not exceed 10 percent of issued capital unless capital-market rules say otherwise (art. 37(1)). Treasury shares may be held for at most three years (art. 37(4)), need RUPS approval (art. 38), and carry no votes and no dividends (art. 40).

, which both sets of lecture notes and most companies use, debits Treasury shares at cost and puts the result of a resale in equity. For example (illustration), a listed subsidiary buys back shares for 900, then resells half for 520 and the other half for 400.
Purchase: Dr Treasury shares 900 / Cr Cash 900
First resale: Dr Cash 520 / Cr Treasury shares 450 / Cr Share premium, treasury shares 70
Second resale: Dr Cash 400, Dr Share premium, treasury shares 50 / Cr Treasury shares 450; balance left = 70 − 50 = 20
Had the second resale come first, with no treasury-share premium to absorb it, the 50 would be debited to retained earnings (Inter 1 Ch 13). Profit is unaffected either way.

The net-asset test compares net assets in the company's latest statements approved by the RUPS with issued capital plus the mandatory reserve, and the law states issued capital in rupiah. For example (illustration), a company with issued capital of Rp100 billion and a mandatory reserve of Rp20 billion has net assets of Rp150 billion, of which Rp30 billion is the negative balance of a common-control difference.
Headroom = 150 − (100 + 20) = Rp30 billion; without the negative APIC it would be Rp60 billion

For PHE the test cannot be run from the published statements. It applies to the company's own net assets, PHE publishes only consolidated figures, and its year-end rate is disclosed only as USD 0.06 per Rp1,000 (Note 3r). The consolidated figures show only the direction. In USD at historical rates, the negative APIC of 3,649,862 offsets most of the retained earnings of 4,352,620.
If each transfer of a subsidiary within a group were an acquisition under PSAK 103

(formerly PSAK 22, IFRS 3), the receiving company would remeasure everything at fair value and recognise goodwill, though nothing left the group and no outsider set a price. PSAK 103 excludes combinations of entities under common control from its scope, and IFRS has no standard for them, so Indonesia keeps its own standard, PSAK 338 (2012)
Business Combinations of Entities under Common Control
(formerly PSAK 38, renumbered from 1 January 2024). PHE's 2024 statements apply this version; a 2025 revision, effective 2026, is described below.

A transfer of a business within a group to reorganise it is not a change of ownership in economic substance, so it can create no profit or loss for the group or for any entity in it (para. 07). One example is a parent transferring a subsidiary to another subsidiary it owns (para. 08(b)). Buying out non-controlling shareholders is excluded, because ownership does change (para. 09). The receiving entity uses the
recognises the difference between the consideration and the carrying amount of the business in equity, presented in APIC (para. 11);
presents the current and comparative periods as if the combination had happened from the start of common control (para. 12);
expenses the combination's costs, except costs of issuing debt or equity, which follow PSAK 109 and PSAK 232 (para. 14).

The transferring entity books its own difference, between the consideration received and the carrying amount it gives up, in APIC too (para. 15). These APIC balances are never recycled to profit or reclassified to retained earnings, even if the business later leaves the group (Basis for Conclusions DK12–DK14). PSAK 38 (2004) had kept the difference in a separate account (SNTRES) and released it to profit when common control ended; its balances moved to APIC on 1 January 2013 (para. 20).

For example (illustration, sized to sit close to PHE's APIC of −3,649,862; PHE does not disclose its own combinations' figures), a parent transfers 100 percent of an upstream company to its subholding. The company's net assets have a carrying amount of 6,000,000; the fair value of its identifiable net assets is 8,500,000; an unaffiliated appraiser values the business at 9,650,000. The subholding pays by issuing new shares with a nominal value of 9,650,000, which art. 34 allows because the contribution is valued at 9,650,000.
Acquisition method (PSAK 103, if the parties were unrelated)
Not restated; results from acquisition date
Restated as if combined since common control began
Dr Net assets 8,500,000, Dr Goodwill 1,150,000 / Cr Share capital 9,650,000
Dr Net assets 6,000,000, Dr APIC 3,650,000 / Cr Share capital 9,650,000

Company law values the contribution at fair value and lets the nominal value of shares issued for it go up to that amount, never above it, with any excess of value over nominal recorded as agio. PSAK 338 puts the asset side at book value. When the parties set the nominal near fair value, or pay cash above book value, the gap is a debit, a negative APIC. DSAK IAI answered the objection that this looks like disagio. The legal ban concerns only the initial payment of capital, and APIC holds more than agio, so a negative common-control difference may sit there (DK10).

The parent books the mirror image (Dr Investment in subholding 9,650,000 / Cr Investment in subsidiary 6,000,000 / Cr APIC 3,650,000), and on consolidation at the ultimate parent the two APIC entries cancel.
The 2012 text, which rejected push-down accounting (DK19–DK22), points to the carrying amounts in the

own statements, so goodwill or fair-value uplifts the parent recognised when it first bought the business stay behind. PHE's policy says "the book value of the net assets of the acquiree" (Note 3d), though IAI found practice divided (DK23A of the 2025 exposure draft). The 2025 revision (approved 29 October 2025, effective 1 January 2026, prospective) switches to the
carrying amounts unless impracticable and allows impracticable restatement to be skipped (exposure draft paras. 10A–10C, 12A–12B).

Indonesian practice shows the equity of a business not yet legally owned in a separate column of the statement of changes in equity, closed against share capital and APIC when the transfer is completed (practice, not the standard's text). PHE's statement of changes in equity has such a column, "Penggabungan Entitas/Merging Entities", which is nil at every date shown (Daftar 3, PDF p. 16), consistent with no common-control combination in progress in 2023 or 2024. It matters for an upstream group because Note 1b lists PHE's subsidiaries largely as one company per working area (Daftar 5/4, PDF p. 21), so blocks change hands inside the Pertamina group by moving shares.

APIC can also hold contributions with no shares issued, such as the benefit of a below-market shareholder loan (see the Long-term bank loans essay). Other equity lines hold items that are neither profit nor OCI: changes in a parent's stake in a subsidiary without loss of control (PSAK 110, formerly PSAK 65, IFRS 10), share-based payment reserves (PSAK 102), and the equity component of convertible bonds. PSAK 201 asks for the nature and purpose of each reserve and a reconciliation of every component.

PP 8/2021, which implements the amended art. 32, keeps the higher minimums that sector rules set for certain businesses (art. 5); before Cipta Kerja the elucidation to art. 32(2) named banking, insurance and freight forwarding. Commercial banks had to hold core capital (paid-up capital plus reserves and retained earnings) of at least Rp3 trillion by the end of 2022 under POJK 12/POJK.03/2020. Insurers face a minimum equity under POJK 23/2023. For both, the regulator's capital measure is wider than legal capital, and a new licence also needs a minimum paid-up capital.
The state funds a Persero by

(state equity participation), in cash or in kind, and builds holdings by inbreng of state shares. Government Regulation 6/2018 added to the state's equity in Pertamina by contributing the state's 13,809,038,755 Series B shares in Perusahaan Gas Negara, with the value set by the Minister of Finance; the state kept control through the Series A Dwiwarna share, a single share with special rights.
Capital-market law can override UU PT on buyback limits (art. 37(1)(b)) and on no-par shares (art. 49(3)). Listed companies raise equity through rights issues (
, the pre-emptive right in tradeable form), whose costs follow section 3.
10. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 31 and 32 and the statement of changes in equity
PHE's equity components and their 2024 movements (statement of financial position, Daftar 1/3, PDF p. 13; statement of changes in equity, Daftar 3, PDF p. 16):
Every row and column reconciles. Share capital has not moved since at least the end of 2022; APIC moved only by 7 in 2023.

APIC "represent[s] the difference between the purchase consideration and the carrying value from business combination transaction of entities under common control" (Note 31, Daftar 5/146, PDF p. 163), and the policy applies pooling of interests with the difference in APIC (Note 3d, Daftar 5/37, PDF p. 54). It gives no transactions, dates or amounts. The likely source is the subholding restructuring. Pertamina designated PHE as parent of the Upstream Subholding in June 2020 (Note 1a, Daftar 5/2, PDF p. 19), and by a circular shareholders' resolution of 1 September 2021 PHE took over the shares Pertamina held in its upstream subsidiaries, eleven according to PHE's own publications, including, by one press list, Elnusa, whose 41.1 percent moved that day; PHE bought a further 9.99 percent from Dana Pensiun Pertamina in December 2021, reaching the 51.10 percent in Note 1b. PHE does not disclose the consideration. Shares issued at a nominal value above the transferred carrying amounts, or cash above them, would both produce the negative balance; the §7 mechanism is an inference from Notes 31 and 3d, not a disclosed fact.
Book value per share and legal headroom.
Book value per share = 14,433,117 thousand / 396,225,242,340 = USD 0.0364
Share capital per share at historical rates = 13,631,466 thousand / 396,225,242,340 = USD 0.0344
Equity per share is only 6 percent above what the shares were paid in at, the same squeeze section 6 described.

PHE gives no note. The statement of changes in equity labels every movement "Equity adjustment in subsidiaries": −23,459 in 2023, with no effect on NCI, and +6,140 in 2024, in the same row as −53,470 against NCI. The consolidation policy treats changes in ownership of a subsidiary without loss of control as equity transactions (Note 3c, Daftar 5/34, PDF p. 51), which fits the label, but no transaction behind the 2024 row is disclosed. The Non-controlling interest essay analyses that movement.
: share premium and common-control differences, covered on this page.
: equity adjustments in subsidiaries, covered on this page.
: dividends, the statutory reserve and the reserve transfer in the table above.
: investments in associates and goodwill from acquisitions that are not under common control.

That PHE's APIC arose mainly from the 2021 subholding restructuring is inferred. Note 31 gives only the definition, the FS cover 2023–2024, and the transfer of eleven subsidiaries and Elnusa comes from PHE publications and press reports, not the audited statements. UU PT does not force a negative difference: nominal value may be set anywhere up to the contribution's fair value, so the negative balance reflects a consideration (shares or cash) the parties set above the transferred carrying amounts.
The reading that UU PT bars issuing shares below nominal rests on art. 33 (full payment of issued capital) and DSAK IAI's Basis for Conclusions DK10, not on an article that says so in terms.

The buyback net-asset test is not run for PHE. The law states capital in rupiah and tests the company's own net assets; PHE publishes neither separate statements nor a precise year-end rate. Translated at a year-end rate the rupiah value of USD net assets has risen since 2021 while rupiah capital is fixed, so a USD comparison at historical rates would mislead. Note 33's Indonesian title ("SALDO CADANGAN WAJIB") treats the whole appropriation as the mandatory reserve, while the statement of changes in equity adds "general and investment reserve".

The reading of the other equity component as equity transactions in subsidiaries rests on its label and Note 3c. PHE does not describe it, which falls short of PSAK 201's request to describe each reserve. The 2024 investing receipt of 64,578 and Note 42's gain of 34,242 on sale of subsidiaries more likely relate to TPDC's January 2024 exercise of its call option over the Mnazi Bay interest (Note 5g) than to this row; PHE does not connect them, and a sale to an outsider would not reduce NCI.

PHE inconsistencies not used in the body: APIC, which Note 31 defines as common-control differences only, moved by 7 in 2023 in the "equity adjustment in subsidiaries" row; Note 32 describes issued capital as 25 percent of authorised capital where it is 25.08 percent.

presentation.deck: The theory of contributed capital from authorised shares to pooling of interests, worked through PHE's Rp198 trillion of issued capital and its negative additional paid-in capital, and set beside the industries with capital rules of their own
key_takeaways: Equity is a residual, but company law carves out a fixed slice, legal capital, equal to the nominal value of issued shares, which in Indonesia must be paid in full and, for at least 25 percent of authorised capital, at incorporation. Anything paid above nominal is share premium (agio), shown with other contributions as additional paid-in capital.

Shares issued for cash are recorded at what is received less issue costs; shares issued for non-cash assets at the fair value of what is received, or of the shares if that is more reliable. Treasury shares and preference shares sit at the border with liabilities. A buyback is deducted from equity and never produces a gain or loss in profit, while a preference share the issuer must redeem is a liability whose dividends are interest.

When businesses move between companies under one controlling party, PSAK 338 replaces fair values with carrying amounts (pooling of interests) and books the difference from the consideration in additional paid-in capital. That difference is negative whenever the consideration exceeds the carrying amount taken over.

title: Trade Payables: Recognition, Measurement and Derecognition of What a Business Owes Its Suppliers
snippet: The theory of accounts payable from the definition of a liability to supplier finance arrangements, worked through PHE's payables to suppliers, partners and the Pertamina group and set beside the industries where payables behave differently
content:
In brief

  • A trade payable is the simplest liability on the balance sheet, for goods or services received and invoiced, with amount and date known. That certainty separates it from an accrual (received, not yet invoiced) and a provision (timing or amount uncertain).

  • Payables are recognised when control of the goods passes or the service is performed, measured at the invoice amount because discounting a short-term balance changes nothing material, and kept in current liabilities because they belong to the operating cycle.

  • A payable leaves the balance sheet only when the obligation is paid, cancelled or expires, or when its terms change substantially. Supplier finance arrangements test that rule. Since 2024 PSAK 207 and PSAK 107 require entities to disclose them so that users can see how much of "trade payables" a bank has already paid.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report trade payables of 1,091,822 at 31 December 2024 against 883,688 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 7.1 percent of total liabilities and 17.7 percent of current liabilities (5.3 and 14.7 percent a year earlier), and 3.6 percent of total assets (2.9 percent). Beside it PHE reports other payables of 613,718 (481,963) and other current liabilities of 224 (324), which this page also covers.

After reading it a student should be able to say when a payable exists, record it through its life in journals, judge whether a supplier finance arrangement has turned it into a borrowing, and read a payables note.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What a liability is, and which liabilities are current

A liability is a present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events (Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting 2018, para. 4.26). For a payable the past event is the delivery of goods or the performance of a service. An undelivered purchase order for drilling chemicals is no liability yet.

The lecture notes define a current liability as one settled within a year with a resulting cash outflow. The 2018 framework drops the probability language from the definition, so uncertainty about the outflow affects recognition and measurement, and PSAK 201 adds the operating cycle to the one-year test.

Current or non-current. PSAK 201 Presentation of Financial Statements (formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) classifies a liability as current if any of four tests holds: the entity expects to settle it in its normal operating cycle, holds it for trading, must settle it within twelve months after the reporting date, or has no right at that date to defer settlement for at least twelve months (para. 69). Trade payables and accruals for operating costs are part of the working capital used in the operating cycle, so they are current even when due more than twelve months later (para. 70). PHE's policy uses the twelve-month and operating cycle tests (Note 3t, Daftar 5/70, PDF p. 87). The 2024 amendments to PSAK 201 on covenants and the right to defer settlement bite mainly on loans; see the long-term bank loans essay.

Payable, accrual or provision. PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) draws the line (para. 11). Trade payables are liabilities for goods or services received or supplied that have been invoiced or formally agreed with the supplier. Accruals are liabilities for goods or services received or supplied that have not been invoiced or formally agreed. Provisions are liabilities of uncertain timing or amount. For example (illustration), three items at a PHE subsidiary on 31 December 2024:

Item

What is known

Line

Workover rig hire for November, invoiced 20 December, 1,800 due on 19 January

amount and date

trade payables

Helicopter flying hours in December, logged at 240 but not yet invoiced

amount nearly certain, no invoice

accrued expenses

A contractor's claim of 3,000 for standby days, disputed

amount and timing uncertain

provision or contingent liability

The accrued expenses essay and the decommissioning provision essay own the second and third rows.

2. Recognising and measuring accounts payable

A payable arises from a time lag between receiving goods or services and paying for them. The lecture notes tie recognition to the transfer of control. For goods that depends on the shipping terms. Under FOB (free on board) shipping point the payable arises when the seller hands the goods to the carrier, under FOB destination when they arrive (see the inventories essay). For a service the trigger is performance.

Initial measurement. A trade payable is a financial liability under PSAK 109 Financial Instruments (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9) and is first measured at fair value. For a short-term payable with no stated interest, fair value is the invoice amount, because discounting 30 or 60 days of credit changes nothing material. PHE states its payables at their "notional amounts, which approximate their fair values" (Note 3, financial liabilities, Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63) and reports that its trade payables are unsecured and non-interest bearing (Note 19, Daftar 5/113, PDF p. 130). Afterwards they are carried at amortised cost, which for a non-interest-bearing payable is the amount still owed.

Cut-off. In practice a payable is booked after a three-way match of purchase order, receiving report and invoice, and a late invoice means a missed payable. For example (illustration), take the 803,062 that PHE owes third parties at the end of 2024 (Note 19) as the population, and suppose two items were missed at year end.

Casing worth 2,000 shipped FOB shipping point on 29 December and invoiced on 30 December, invoice posted on 6 January: inventories and trade payables both understated by 2,000; profit unchanged

Well-servicing work worth 500 performed and invoiced in December, invoice posted in January: production expenses and trade payables understated by 500; profit overstated by 500

Correcting entry, 31 December: Dr Inventories 2,000, Dr Production expenses 500 / Cr Trade payables 2,500

The first error only shrinks the balance sheet. The second flatters profit, which is why auditors search for unrecorded liabilities by reading payments made after year end. Had the invoices not yet arrived at year end, the same entry would credit accrued expenses instead (see the accrued expenses essay).

3. Purchase discounts and the cost of not taking them

A cash discount for prompt payment turns every payable into a small financing decision. The lecture notes record it in two ways. The gross method books the invoice amount and recognises the discount only when taken. The net method books the discounted amount, treating it as the real price, so a discount missed is shown as a finance cost (the inventories essay works both through to the cost of casing). For example (illustration), the lecture notes' purchase of 10,000 on terms of 2/10, net 30: a 2 percent discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount by day 30.

Gross method

Net method

Purchase

Dr Inventories 10,000 / Cr Trade payables 10,000

Dr Inventories 9,800 / Cr Trade payables 9,800

Paid on day 10

Dr Trade payables 10,000 / Cr Inventories 200 / Cr Cash 9,800

Dr Trade payables 9,800 / Cr Cash 9,800

Paid on day 30

Dr Trade payables 10,000 / Cr Cash 10,000

Dr Trade payables 9,800, Dr Purchase discounts lost 200 / Cr Cash 10,000

The net method shows what the gross method hides. Paying on day 30 instead of day 10 borrows 9,800 for 20 days at a cost of 200.

Rate for 20 days = 200 / 9,800 = 2.04%

Annual rate, simple = 2.04% × 365 / 20 = 37.2%; compounded = (1 + 2.04%)^(365/20) − 1 = 44.6%

Any entity that can borrow below 37 percent a year should take the discount.

4. Notes payable

A note payable is a written promise to pay a set sum on a set date, here arising from an overdue account payable. The lecture notes give two kinds.

Interest-bearing notes state an interest rate, and interest accrues with time. For example (illustration), on 31 October a foreign supplier of a PHE subsidiary (PHE owes foreign suppliers 189,687, Note 19) agrees to convert an overdue invoice of 10,000 into a six-month note at 8 percent a year.

31 October: Dr Trade payables 10,000 / Cr Notes payable 10,000

31 December, two months of interest = 10,000 × 8% × 2/12 = 133.33: Dr Interest expense 133.33 / Cr Interest payable 133.33

30 April, maturity, interest for six months = 400.00: Dr Notes payable 10,000, Dr Interest payable 133.33, Dr Interest expense 266.67 / Cr Cash 10,400

Zero-interest-bearing notes state only the amount due at maturity, so the interest sits in the gap between that amount and the present value received. A note of 110,000 due in a year at a market rate of 10 percent is recorded at 100,000, and 10,000 of interest expense accrues over the year; the long-term bank loans essay works such notes through.

5. Payables in a foreign currency

A payable in a currency other than the entity's functional currency is a monetary item, a right or obligation to a fixed number of currency units. PSAK 221 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates (formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21) records it at the spot rate on the transaction date (para. 21), retranslates it at the closing rate at each reporting date (para. 23), and takes the exchange differences to profit or loss (para. 28). PHE's functional currency is the US dollar for every entity except Elnusa, which uses the rupiah (Note 3r, Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83). Rupiah trade payables were 518,011 at the end of 2024 (Note 19b). Those of the dollar entities are retranslated through profit or loss; Elnusa's are translated on consolidation, with the difference in other comprehensive income. Note 48 shows the same payables as Rp8,369,504 million (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242), which implies a closing rate of 8,369,504 / 518.011 = Rp16,157 per US dollar.

For example (illustration), a dollar-functional subsidiary receives a rupiah invoice for Rp32,000 million on 1 December 2024 when the rate is Rp15,800, and pays it on 15 January 2025 at Rp16,300.

1 December: 32,000 / 15,800 × 1,000 = 2,025.32: Dr Production expenses 2,025.32 / Cr Trade payables 2,025.32

31 December at 16,157: 32,000 / 16,157 × 1,000 = 1,980.57; gain = 2,025.32 − 1,980.57 = 44.75: Dr Trade payables 44.75 / Cr Foreign exchange gain 44.75

15 January at 16,300: cash = 1,963.19; gain = 1,980.57 − 1,963.19 = 17.38: Dr Trade payables 1,980.57 / Cr Cash 1,963.19 / Cr Foreign exchange gain 17.38

The expense stays at 2,025.32, the rate on the day of the service. The weaker rupiah cut the dollar cost of settlement by 62.13, split between the two years in which the rate moved.

6. Related-party payables and offsetting

Related parties. A payable to a parent, a fellow subsidiary or another government-related entity is measured like any other payable, but PSAK 224 Related Party Disclosures (formerly PSAK 7, IAS 24) requires the relationship, the transactions and the outstanding balances to be disclosed, because the terms may not be those an independent supplier would set. Entities controlled by the same government may use a reduced disclosure for balances with one another (paras. 25–26). PHE discloses its related-party trade payables by counterparty (Note 44e, Daftar 5/185, PDF p. 202).

Offsetting. A payable and a receivable with the same party are shown net only when the entity has a legally enforceable right of set-off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (PSAK 232, formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32, para. 42); the trade receivables essay works this through PHE's Pertamina balances. PHE settles those balances by offset but presents them gross, a receivable of 18,434 and a payable of 105,797 (Note 44c, Daftar 5/184, PDF p. 201).

7. Supplier finance arrangements

In a supplier finance arrangement, also called supply chain finance, payables finance or reverse factoring, one or more finance providers pay what an entity owes its suppliers, and the entity pays the provider on or after the date the suppliers are paid (PSAK 207, formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7, para. 44G). The supplier gets cash early, priced on the buyer's credit, and the buyer often gets longer to pay.

The IFRS Interpretations Committee's December 2020 agenda decision on reverse factoring answered three questions from existing standards.

  • Presentation. A liability stays in trade payables only if it is a liability to pay for goods or services, is invoiced or formally agreed with the supplier (PSAK 237.11(a)), and is part of the working capital used in the normal operating cycle (PSAK 201.70). Extra security given to the bank, or terms that differ materially from those of other payables, point to a separate line or to borrowings.

  • Derecognition. If the obligation to the supplier is extinguished, the payable is derecognised and a new liability to the bank is recognised (section 8).

  • Cash flows. These follow the classification. A payable that stays in working capital is settled through operating cash flows. If it has become a borrowing, the bank's payment to the supplier is a non-cash transaction (PSAK 207.43), and the later payment to the bank is a financing outflow.

For example (illustration), a subsidiary owes a supplier 10,000 due in 60 days. A bank pays the supplier 9,900 on day 10, with the supplier bearing the 1 percent discount.

Case A: entity pays the bank 10,000 on day 60, no security

Case B: entity pays the bank 10,150 on day 150, guaranteed by the parent

Nature of the liability

the same trade payable, now owed to the bank

a 140-day financing with interest and security

Day 10

no entry, or Dr Trade payables / Cr Trade payables, supplier finance, 10,000

Dr Trade payables 10,000 / Cr Supplier finance borrowings 10,000

Day 150

Dr Supplier finance borrowings 10,000, Dr Interest expense 150 / Cr Cash 10,150

Cash flow statement

operating outflow 10,000 on day 60

no operating outflow; financing outflow 10,000 and interest 150 by policy

In case B operating cash flow is 10,000 higher than if the entity had paid the supplier itself, with nothing in its operations changed, which is why analysts asked for disclosure.

The 2024 disclosures. Amendments to PSAK 207 and PSAK 107 Financial Instruments: Disclosures (formerly PSAK 60, IFRS 7), effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024, require the terms of the arrangements; at the start and end of the period, the liabilities in them, the lines they sit in, and how much the providers have already paid to suppliers; the range of due dates against comparable payables outside the arrangements; and non-cash changes such as exchange differences (PSAK 207.44H). PSAK 107 brings supplier finance into the liquidity risk disclosures. PHE adopted the amendments in 2024 and reports no significant impact on its financial reporting (Note 3b, Daftar 5/31, PDF p. 48). It does not say whether it has any such arrangements. Yet Note 44e lists PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia (8,454) and PT Bank Mandiri (4,897) among related-party trade creditors, and a bank in trade payables is what a supplier finance arrangement or a usance letter of credit would produce. The absence of a PSAK 207.44H disclosure suggests these balances are immaterial or of another kind.

8. Derecognition

A payable leaves the balance sheet in one of two ways under PSAK 109.

Extinguishment (para. 3.3.1). The obligation is discharged by payment, cancelled by the creditor, or expires. Waiting is not enough. For example (illustration), a subsidiary carries 300 owed to a supplier that has not chased it for three years. Unless the debt has been legally released or has expired under the law of the contract, the 300 stays. A write-back on the strength of silence overstates profit and understates liabilities.

Substantial modification (paras. 3.3.2–3.3.3). A substantial change of terms is accounted for as extinguishing the old liability and recognising a new one at fair value, with the difference in profit or loss. The quantitative test is whether the new cash flows, discounted at the original effective interest rate, differ by at least 10 percent (para. B3.3.6; the long-term bank loans essay teaches it on a loan).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary owes a struggling contractor 10,000, overdue. They agree that the contractor will accept 8,500 payable in one year, without interest. The original payable carried no interest, so its effective rate is 0 percent, and the market rate for this subsidiary's one-year debt is 8 percent.

Present value of new cash flows at the original rate = 8,500 / 1.00 = 8,500

Difference = (10,000 − 8,500) / 10,000 = 15% ≥ 10%: extinguishment

Fair value of the new liability = 8,500 / 1.08 = 7,870.37

Gain = 10,000 − 7,870.37 = 2,129.63

Dr Trade payables 10,000 / Cr Notes payable 7,870.37 / Cr Gain on extinguishment of payables 2,129.63

Over the year: Dr Interest expense 629.63 / Cr Notes payable 629.63, bringing it to 8,500

Had the contractor accepted 9,500 instead, the difference would be 5 percent. The payable would stay, adjusted to 9,500 with a modification gain of 500.

9. Trade payables across industries

Retail. Supermarkets often sell goods before paying for them, so days payable exceed the days goods sit on shelves plus the days customers take to pay, and working capital is negative. For example (illustration), days in inventory 40, days sales outstanding 2, days payable outstanding 60.

Cash conversion cycle = 40 + 2 − 60 = −18 days

Suppliers finance the business. Goods taken on consignment create no payable until the retailer sells them, because the supplier keeps control, and supplier rebates reduce the cost of inventory (PSAK 202.11).

Construction. Contractors keep a retention, commonly 5 to 10 percent of each subcontractor's certified progress, until the work passes inspection. The retention is owed, with timing tied to completion. For example (illustration), a subcontractor certificate of 2,000 with 5 percent retention.

Dr Contract costs 2,000 / Cr Trade payables 1,900 / Cr Retentions payable 100

Banks and insurers. A bank's main liabilities are customer deposits, at amortised cost under PSAK 109, and an insurer's claims payable sits inside insurance contract liabilities under PSAK 117 (IFRS 17). Neither has a large trade payables line.

Islamic finance. A buyer that purchases an asset under murabahah, a sale at cost plus a disclosed margin with deferred payment, records a murabahah payable for the full agreed price, with the margin as deferred murabahah expense, shown as a deduction from the payable and amortised as the payable is settled (PSAK 402, formerly PSAK 102; STANDARD — NOT VERIFIED). For example (illustration), equipment costing 1,000 bought with a margin of 100 payable in one year.

Dr Equipment 1,000, Dr Deferred murabahah expense 100 / Cr Murabahah payable 1,100

The economics are those of the zero-interest note in section 4, with the cost of credit called a margin.

Upstream oil and gas. Joint operations create their own payables between operator and partners (section 11).

Trade payables rose 23.6 percent from the end of 2023. Third parties account for more than all of it (up 40.6 percent, mostly local suppliers), while related-party payables fell 7.7 percent. Rupiah payables were 47.4 percent of the line.

Days payable outstanding. DPO measures how long an entity takes to pay its suppliers.

DPO = average trade payables / purchases on credit × 365

PHE does not disclose purchases, but its direct-method cash flow statement shows cash paid to suppliers of 5,117,737 in 2024 (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17), which can stand in for them.

Average trade payables = (1,091,822 + 883,688) / 2 = 987,755

DPO ≈ 987,755 / 5,117,737 × 365 = 70 days

At year end: 1,091,822 / 5,117,737 × 365 = 78 days (2023: 883,688 / 4,640,992 × 365 = 69 days)

The proxy is rough. Trade payables include suppliers of drilling and other capital work, whose payments sit in investing cash flows (purchase of oil and gas properties, 3,933,616 in 2024 and 3,948,075 in 2023). Adding them to the denominator gives about 44 days at year end (2023: 38). Both measures rise, so the slower payment at the end of 2024 does not depend on the proxy.

Related parties. Related-party trade payables were 1.88 percent of total liabilities, led by PT Pertamina (Persero) 105,797, PT Pertamina Patra Niaga 73,164 and PT Perusahaan Gas Negara 30,891; the list also includes PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia 8,454, PT Bank Mandiri 4,897 and the Ministry of Finance 3,665 (Note 44e). Note 44e says these payables arise from drilling, gas processing and other oil and gas services, but Note 44c labels the whole 105,797 owed to Pertamina as "payables in relation to payment of cash calls", Pertamina's funding of the group's operations, offset against what it owes for sales. A liability for cash advanced is not a liability for goods or services invoiced by a supplier (PSAK 237.11(a)). The balance barely moved over the year (103,376 a year earlier), Note 49d describes "funding arrangements with Pertamina", and the cash flow statement reports Pertamina funding within operating activities, nil in 2024 and an outflow of 4,633 in 2023 (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17). This page reads the 105,797 as closer to a borrowing; PHE does not explain the classification. The two banks are related to PHE through banking services (Note 44a, Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199), a point section 7 takes up.

Maturity. PHE's liquidity table puts all trade and other payables in the "less than one year" band (Note 49d, Daftar 5/233, PDF p. 250).

Other current liabilities of 224 (324) carry no note reference.

11. Upstream note: cash calls and joint interest billings

PHE's subsidiaries operate some working areas and are non-operators in others, and both roles create payables. A partner in a joint operation recognises its share of jointly incurred liabilities (PSAK 111, formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11). PHE's policy for unitised fields says that as operator it recognises a payable to non-operators when the cash calls, requests for funds in advance, it has received exceed their share of revenues, costs, capital spending and liabilities, and a receivable when they fall short (Note 3y, Daftar 5/75, PDF p. 92). As non-operator, PHE classifies its proportional share of the operator's joint interest billing (JIB) reports, statements of actual spending, as other payables, 429,695 at the end of 2024, and owes operators 28,933 of cash calls not yet paid (Note 21). The same relationship runs the other way in advances: cash calls paid to operators ahead of spending are 76,196 (Note 15, Daftar 5/106, PDF p. 123). For example (illustration), a non-operating subsidiary with a 30 percent interest receives a JIB showing 5,000 of operating costs for December.

Share = 5,000 × 30% = 1,500

Dr Production expenses 1,500 / Cr Other payables, JIB 1,500

Note 21 gives the basis for putting them in other payables, that they come from "a proportional share of the Joint Interest Billing (JIB) report" sent by the operator.

12. Related lines

  • accrued-expenses: services received but not yet invoiced, before they become payables.

  • decommissioning-site-restoration-provision: where uncertain obligations and contingencies are taught.

  • trade-receivables-net: offsetting, worked through PHE's Pertamina balances.

  • inventories-net: the asset side of purchases on credit, and purchase discounts.

  • advances-prepayments-current: cash calls paid to operators in advance.

  • other-taxes-payable: VAT and withholding taxes on supplier invoices.

  • long-term-bank-loans-non-current: where a supplier finance liability that has become a borrowing would sit; zero-interest notes, the 10 percent test and the PSAK 201 covenant amendments.

Least-confident assertions

  • That the 105,797 owed to Pertamina for cash calls is closer to a borrowing than to a trade payable is this page's reading of Notes 44c, 44e and 49d and the cash flow statement against PSAK 237.11(a). PHE does not explain the classification, the two notes describe the same balances differently, and Pertamina funding is reported in operating cash flows.

  • Note 19's English text says PHE's trade payables "were denominated in US Dollars", while the Indonesian text, the governing version, says "berdominasi" (mostly) US dollars, and the currency table shows 47.4 percent in rupiah. This page follows the Indonesian text and the table.

  • DPO rests on proxies, because PHE does not disclose credit purchases. Cash paid to suppliers alone gives about 70 days on average (year end 69 to 78); adding payments for oil and gas properties gives 38 to 44 at year end. The level depends on the denominator; the rise does not.

  • Why PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia and PT Bank Mandiri (13,351 together, 1.2 percent of trade payables) appear among trade creditors is not disclosed; supplier finance or usance letters of credit are this page's hypotheses. The Ministry of Finance's 3,665 may be rent for state-owned assets (Note 44a lists asset lease services), but that is inference.

  • The murabahah buyer entries under PSAK 402 and the PSAK 117 placement of insurers' claims payable are from knowledge and were not checked against the PSAK text.
