content.text: A trade payable is the simplest liability on the balance sheet, for goods or services received and invoiced, with amount and date known. That certainty separates it from an accrual (received, not yet invoiced) and a provision (timing or amount uncertain).

Payables are recognised when control of the goods passes or the service is performed, measured at the invoice amount because discounting a short-term balance changes nothing material, and kept in current liabilities because they belong to the operating cycle.

A payable leaves the balance sheet only when the obligation is paid, cancelled or expires, or when its terms change substantially. Supplier finance arrangements test that rule. Since 2024 PSAK 207 and PSAK 107 require entities to disclose them so that users can see how much of "trade payables" a bank has already paid.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report trade payables of 1,091,822 at 31 December 2024 against 883,688 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/2, PDF p. 12; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 7.1 percent of total liabilities and 17.7 percent of current liabilities (5.3 and 14.7 percent a year earlier), and 3.6 percent of total assets (2.9 percent). Beside it PHE reports other payables of 613,718 (481,963) and other current liabilities of 224 (324), which this page also covers.

After reading it a student should be able to say when a payable exists, record it through its life in journals, judge whether a supplier finance arrangement has turned it into a borrowing, and read a payables note.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
1. What a liability is, and which liabilities are current
A liability is a present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events (
2018, para. 4.26). For a payable the past event is the delivery of goods or the performance of a service. An undelivered purchase order for drilling chemicals is no liability yet.

The lecture notes define a current liability as one settled within a year with a resulting cash outflow. The 2018 framework drops the probability language from the definition, so uncertainty about the outflow affects recognition and measurement, and PSAK 201 adds the operating cycle to the one-year test.

(formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1) classifies a liability as current if any of four tests holds: the entity expects to settle it in its normal operating cycle, holds it for trading, must settle it within twelve months after the reporting date, or has no right at that date to defer settlement for at least twelve months (para. 69). Trade payables and accruals for operating costs are part of the working capital used in the operating cycle, so they are current even when due more than twelve months later (para. 70). PHE's policy uses the twelve-month and operating cycle tests (Note 3t, Daftar 5/70, PDF p. 87). The 2024 amendments to PSAK 201 on covenants and the right to defer settlement bite mainly on loans; see the long-term bank loans essay.
PSAK 237 (formerly PSAK 57, IAS 37) draws the line (para. 11).
are liabilities for goods or services received or supplied that have been invoiced or formally agreed with the supplier.
are liabilities for goods or services received or supplied that have not been invoiced or formally agreed.
are liabilities of uncertain timing or amount. For example (illustration), three items at a PHE subsidiary on 31 December 2024:
Workover rig hire for November, invoiced 20 December, 1,800 due on 19 January
Helicopter flying hours in December, logged at 240 but not yet invoiced
A contractor's claim of 3,000 for standby days, disputed
The accrued expenses essay and the decommissioning provision essay own the second and third rows.

A payable arises from a time lag between receiving goods or services and paying for them. The lecture notes tie recognition to the transfer of control. For goods that depends on the shipping terms. Under FOB (free on board) shipping point the payable arises when the seller hands the goods to the carrier, under FOB destination when they arrive (see the inventories essay). For a service the trigger is performance.
A trade payable is a financial liability under PSAK 109

(formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9) and is first measured at fair value. For a short-term payable with no stated interest, fair value is the invoice amount, because discounting 30 or 60 days of credit changes nothing material. PHE states its payables at their "notional amounts, which approximate their fair values" (Note 3, financial liabilities, Daftar 5/46, PDF p. 63) and reports that its trade payables are unsecured and non-interest bearing (Note 19, Daftar 5/113, PDF p. 130). Afterwards they are carried at amortised cost, which for a non-interest-bearing payable is the amount still owed.
In practice a payable is booked after a

of purchase order, receiving report and invoice, and a late invoice means a missed payable. For example (illustration), take the 803,062 that PHE owes third parties at the end of 2024 (Note 19) as the population, and suppose two items were missed at year end.
Casing worth 2,000 shipped FOB shipping point on 29 December and invoiced on 30 December, invoice posted on 6 January: inventories and trade payables both understated by 2,000; profit unchanged
Well-servicing work worth 500 performed and invoiced in December, invoice posted in January: production expenses and trade payables understated by 500; profit overstated by 500
Correcting entry, 31 December: Dr Inventories 2,000, Dr Production expenses 500 / Cr Trade payables 2,500

The first error only shrinks the balance sheet. The second flatters profit, which is why auditors search for unrecorded liabilities by reading payments made after year end. Had the invoices not yet arrived at year end, the same entry would credit accrued expenses instead (see the accrued expenses essay).
3. Purchase discounts and the cost of not taking them
A cash discount for prompt payment turns every payable into a small financing decision. The lecture notes record it in two ways. The
books the invoice amount and recognises the discount only when taken. The

books the discounted amount, treating it as the real price, so a discount missed is shown as a finance cost (the inventories essay works both through to the cost of casing). For example (illustration), the lecture notes' purchase of 10,000 on terms of 2/10, net 30: a 2 percent discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount by day 30.
Dr Trade payables 10,000 / Cr Inventories 200 / Cr Cash 9,800
Dr Trade payables 9,800, Dr Purchase discounts lost 200 / Cr Cash 10,000
The net method shows what the gross method hides. Paying on day 30 instead of day 10 borrows 9,800 for 20 days at a cost of 200.
Any entity that can borrow below 37 percent a year should take the discount.
A note payable is a written promise to pay a set sum on a set date, here arising from an overdue account payable. The lecture notes give two kinds.

state an interest rate, and interest accrues with time. For example (illustration), on 31 October a foreign supplier of a PHE subsidiary (PHE owes foreign suppliers 189,687, Note 19) agrees to convert an overdue invoice of 10,000 into a six-month note at 8 percent a year.
31 October: Dr Trade payables 10,000 / Cr Notes payable 10,000
31 December, two months of interest = 10,000 × 8% × 2/12 = 133.33: Dr Interest expense 133.33 / Cr Interest payable 133.33
30 April, maturity, interest for six months = 400.00: Dr Notes payable 10,000, Dr Interest payable 133.33, Dr Interest expense 266.67 / Cr Cash 10,400

state only the amount due at maturity, so the interest sits in the gap between that amount and the present value received. A note of 110,000 due in a year at a market rate of 10 percent is recorded at 100,000, and 10,000 of interest expense accrues over the year; the long-term bank loans essay works such notes through.
A payable in a currency other than the entity's functional currency is a
, a right or obligation to a fixed number of currency units. PSAK 221
The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates

(formerly PSAK 10, IAS 21) records it at the spot rate on the transaction date (para. 21), retranslates it at the closing rate at each reporting date (para. 23), and takes the exchange differences to profit or loss (para. 28). PHE's functional currency is the US dollar for every entity except Elnusa, which uses the rupiah (Note 3r, Daftar 5/66, PDF p. 83). Rupiah trade payables were 518,011 at the end of 2024 (Note 19b). Those of the dollar entities are retranslated through profit or loss; Elnusa's are translated on consolidation, with the difference in other comprehensive income. Note 48 shows the same payables as Rp8,369,504 million (Daftar 5/225, PDF p. 242), which implies a closing rate of 8,369,504 / 518.011 = Rp16,157 per US dollar.
For example (illustration), a dollar-functional subsidiary receives a rupiah invoice for Rp32,000 million on 1 December 2024 when the rate is Rp15,800, and pays it on 15 January 2025 at Rp16,300.
1 December: 32,000 / 15,800 × 1,000 = 2,025.32: Dr Production expenses 2,025.32 / Cr Trade payables 2,025.32

A payable to a parent, a fellow subsidiary or another government-related entity is measured like any other payable, but PSAK 224

(formerly PSAK 7, IAS 24) requires the relationship, the transactions and the outstanding balances to be disclosed, because the terms may not be those an independent supplier would set. Entities controlled by the same government may use a reduced disclosure for balances with one another (paras. 25–26). PHE discloses its related-party trade payables by counterparty (Note 44e, Daftar 5/185, PDF p. 202).

A payable and a receivable with the same party are shown net only when the entity has a legally enforceable right of set-off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (PSAK 232, formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32, para. 42); the trade receivables essay works this through PHE's Pertamina balances. PHE settles those balances by offset but presents them gross, a receivable of 18,434 and a payable of 105,797 (Note 44c, Daftar 5/184, PDF p. 201).

, also called supply chain finance, payables finance or reverse factoring, one or more finance providers pay what an entity owes its suppliers, and the entity pays the provider on or after the date the suppliers are paid (PSAK 207, formerly PSAK 2, IAS 7, para. 44G). The supplier gets cash early, priced on the buyer's credit, and the buyer often gets longer to pay.
The IFRS Interpretations Committee's December 2020 agenda decision on reverse factoring answered three questions from existing standards.

A liability stays in trade payables only if it is a liability to pay for goods or services, is invoiced or formally agreed with the supplier (PSAK 237.11(a)), and is part of the working capital used in the normal operating cycle (PSAK 201.70). Extra security given to the bank, or terms that differ materially from those of other payables, point to a separate line or to borrowings.
If the obligation to the supplier is extinguished, the payable is derecognised and a new liability to the bank is recognised (section 8).

These follow the classification. A payable that stays in working capital is settled through operating cash flows. If it has become a borrowing, the bank's payment to the supplier is a non-cash transaction (PSAK 207.43), and the later payment to the bank is a financing outflow.
For example (illustration), a subsidiary owes a supplier 10,000 due in 60 days. A bank pays the supplier 9,900 on day 10, with the supplier bearing the 1 percent discount.

In case B operating cash flow is 10,000 higher than if the entity had paid the supplier itself, with nothing in its operations changed, which is why analysts asked for disclosure.

(formerly PSAK 60, IFRS 7), effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024, require the terms of the arrangements; at the start and end of the period, the liabilities in them, the lines they sit in, and how much the providers have already paid to suppliers; the range of due dates against comparable payables outside the arrangements; and non-cash changes such as exchange differences (PSAK 207.44H). PSAK 107 brings supplier finance into the liquidity risk disclosures. PHE adopted the amendments in 2024 and reports no significant impact on its financial reporting (Note 3b, Daftar 5/31, PDF p. 48). It does not say whether it has any such arrangements. Yet Note 44e lists PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia (8,454) and PT Bank Mandiri (4,897) among related-party trade creditors, and a bank in trade payables is what a supplier finance arrangement or a usance letter of credit would produce. The absence of a PSAK 207.44H disclosure suggests these balances are immaterial or of another kind.
A payable leaves the balance sheet in one of two ways under PSAK 109.

(para. 3.3.1). The obligation is discharged by payment, cancelled by the creditor, or expires. Waiting is not enough. For example (illustration), a subsidiary carries 300 owed to a supplier that has not chased it for three years. Unless the debt has been legally released or has expired under the law of the contract, the 300 stays. A write-back on the strength of silence overstates profit and understates liabilities.

(paras. 3.3.2–3.3.3). A substantial change of terms is accounted for as extinguishing the old liability and recognising a new one at fair value, with the difference in profit or loss. The quantitative test is whether the new cash flows, discounted at the original effective interest rate, differ by at least 10 percent (para. B3.3.6; the long-term bank loans essay teaches it on a loan).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary owes a struggling contractor 10,000, overdue. They agree that the contractor will accept 8,500 payable in one year, without interest. The original payable carried no interest, so its effective rate is 0 percent, and the market rate for this subsidiary's one-year debt is 8 percent.

10. Presentation and analysis: PHE's Notes 19, 21 and 44
PHE splits its payables by supplier and by currency (Note 19, Daftar 5/113, PDF p. 130; Note 21, Daftar 5/115–5/116, PDF pp. 132–133).
Other payables from subsidiaries' oil and gas operations

Trade payables rose 23.6 percent from the end of 2023. Third parties account for more than all of it (up 40.6 percent, mostly local suppliers), while related-party payables fell 7.7 percent. Rupiah payables were 47.4 percent of the line.
DPO measures how long an entity takes to pay its suppliers.
DPO = average trade payables / purchases on credit × 365
PHE does not disclose purchases, but its direct-method cash flow statement shows cash paid to suppliers of 5,117,737 in 2024 (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17), which can stand in for them.

The proxy is rough. Trade payables include suppliers of drilling and other capital work, whose payments sit in investing cash flows (purchase of oil and gas properties, 3,933,616 in 2024 and 3,948,075 in 2023). Adding them to the denominator gives about 44 days at year end (2023: 38). Both measures rise, so the slower payment at the end of 2024 does not depend on the proxy.

Related-party trade payables were 1.88 percent of total liabilities, led by PT Pertamina (Persero) 105,797, PT Pertamina Patra Niaga 73,164 and PT Perusahaan Gas Negara 30,891; the list also includes PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia 8,454, PT Bank Mandiri 4,897 and the Ministry of Finance 3,665 (Note 44e). Note 44e says these payables arise from drilling, gas processing and other oil and gas services, but Note 44c labels the whole 105,797 owed to Pertamina as "payables in relation to payment of cash calls", Pertamina's funding of the group's operations, offset against what it owes for sales. A liability for cash advanced is not a liability for goods or services invoiced by a supplier (PSAK 237.11(a)). The balance barely moved over the year (103,376 a year earlier), Note 49d describes "funding arrangements with Pertamina", and the cash flow statement reports Pertamina funding within operating activities, nil in 2024 and an outflow of 4,633 in 2023 (Daftar 4, PDF p. 17). This page reads the 105,797 as closer to a borrowing; PHE does not explain the classification. The two banks are related to PHE through banking services (Note 44a, Daftar 5/182, PDF p. 199), a point section 7 takes up.
PHE's liquidity table puts all trade and other payables in the "less than one year" band (Note 49d, Daftar 5/233, PDF p. 250).
11. Upstream note: cash calls and joint interest billings

PHE's subsidiaries operate some working areas and are non-operators in others, and both roles create payables. A partner in a joint operation recognises its share of jointly incurred liabilities (PSAK 111, formerly PSAK 66, IFRS 11). PHE's policy for unitised fields says that as operator it recognises a payable to non-operators when the

, requests for funds in advance, it has received exceed their share of revenues, costs, capital spending and liabilities, and a receivable when they fall short (Note 3y, Daftar 5/75, PDF p. 92). As non-operator, PHE classifies its proportional share of the operator's

(JIB) reports, statements of actual spending, as other payables, 429,695 at the end of 2024, and owes operators 28,933 of cash calls not yet paid (Note 21). For example (illustration), a non-operating subsidiary with a 30 percent interest receives a JIB showing 5,000 of operating costs for December.
Dr Production expenses 1,500 / Cr Other payables, JIB 1,500
Note 21 gives the basis for putting them in other payables, that they come from "a proportional share of the Joint Interest Billing (JIB) report" sent by the operator.

That the 105,797 owed to Pertamina for cash calls is closer to a borrowing than to a trade payable is this page's reading of Notes 44c, 44e and 49d and the cash flow statement against PSAK 237.11(a). PHE does not explain the classification, the two notes describe the same balances differently, and Pertamina funding is reported in operating cash flows.

DPO rests on proxies, because PHE does not disclose credit purchases. Cash paid to suppliers alone gives about 70 days on average (year end 69 to 78); adding payments for oil and gas properties gives 38 to 44 at year end. The level depends on the denominator; the rise does not.

Why PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia and PT Bank Mandiri (13,351 together, 1.2 percent of trade payables) appear among trade creditors is not disclosed; supplier finance or usance letters of credit are this page's hypotheses. The murabahah buyer entries under PSAK 402 and the PSAK 117 placement of insurers' claims payable are from knowledge and were not checked against the PSAK text.

presentation.deck: The theory of accounts payable from the definition of a liability to supplier finance arrangements, worked through PHE's payables to suppliers, partners and the Pertamina group and set beside the industries where payables behave differently
key_takeaways: A trade payable is the simplest liability on the balance sheet, for goods or services received and invoiced, with amount and date known. That certainty separates it from an accrual (received, not yet invoiced) and a provision (timing or amount uncertain).

Payables are recognised when control of the goods passes or the service is performed, measured at the invoice amount because discounting a short-term balance changes nothing material, and kept in current liabilities because they belong to the operating cycle.

A payable leaves the balance sheet only when the obligation is paid, cancelled or expires, or when its terms change substantially. Supplier finance arrangements test that rule. Since 2024 PSAK 207 and PSAK 107 require entities to disclose them so that users can see how much of "trade payables" a bank has already paid.

title: Trade Receivables, Net: Recognition, Expected Credit Losses and Derecognition
snippet: The theory of trade receivables from the sale that creates them to the factor that buys them, worked through PHE's crude and gas customers and set beside the industries with their own rules
content:
In brief

  • A trade receivable is born with revenue, at the moment control of goods or services passes to a customer and the seller's right to payment depends only on time. Revenue is measured at the PSAK 115 transaction price, net of trade discounts and of the discounts, returns and financing the seller expects, and the receivable records the unconditional right to payment.

  • The "net" in the line is an allowance for expected credit losses (ECL) under PSAK 109. Trade receivables without a significant financing component must use the simplified approach, lifetime losses from day one, usually through a provision matrix of loss rates by days past due adjusted for forecasts. The old incurred-loss model, which waited for a loss event, is gone.

  • A receivable leaves the balance sheet when it is collected, written off because recovery is no longer reasonably expected, or transferred with substantially all its risks and rewards. Factoring without recourse is a sale; factoring with recourse usually stays on the balance sheet as a secured borrowing.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report trade receivables, net, of 3,146,868 at 31 December 2024 against 2,768,397 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 10.3 percent of total assets and 39.2 percent of current assets (9.0 and 28.0 percent a year earlier), the largest current asset PHE has. This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to say when a receivable arises, measure it at recognition and at the reporting date, record write-offs, recoveries and transfers, and see where banks, Islamic financiers, builders and miners depart from the plain model.

All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.

1. What a trade receivable is

A receivable is a claim on someone else for cash. Kieso sorts claims three ways. Trade receivables arise from selling goods or services in the ordinary course of business; nontrade receivables arise from anything else, such as insurance claims, advances to employees or deposits. Accounts receivable are open-account promises with no formal instrument; notes receivable are written promises to pay a sum at a date, usually with interest. And receivables are current if collection is expected within the operating cycle or twelve months, non-current otherwise (PSAK 201, formerly PSAK 1, IAS 1).

PHE's policy uses the first split. Trade receivables are amounts due from customers for crude oil, natural gas, drilling services, oil and gas support services, and energy distribution and logistics services; other receivables are amounts from third or related parties "beyond the ordinary course of business" (Note 3h, Daftar 5/51, PDF p. 68). Collection within one period puts a receivable in current assets, otherwise non-current (same note). PHE's separate "long term receivables" of 2,087 (2023: 2,997) carry no note reference on the face.

PSAK 115 (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15) adds a distinction that matters most for builders. A receivable is a right to consideration that is unconditional, meaning only the passage of time is required before payment falls due (para. 108). A contract asset is a right that still depends on something other than time, typically further performance.

2. Recognition: the receivable follows revenue

A receivable appears in the same journal entry as revenue, so "when do we record it?" is the revenue question. Kieso's Intermediate Accounting sets out the five steps of PSAK 115. Identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognise revenue when each obligation is satisfied, that is, when the customer obtains control.

For a crude seller, control typically passes at lifting, on FOB terms when the cargo crosses the custody point into the buyer's tanker. PHE recognises crude and gas revenue "based on the actual lifting amount and sold to customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79). For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary lifts 600 thousand barrels for a domestic refinery at USD 75 per barrel, payable in 30 days.

Invoice = 600 × 75 = 45,000

Dr Trade receivables 45,000 / Cr Revenue from crude oil 45,000

There is no matching "Dr Cost of goods sold / Cr Inventory" of the kind a merchandiser records. Note 11 lists only materials, and Note 3p charges the related costs on the amount actually sold, so the cost of producing the barrels has already gone to expense.

Signing a contract creates no receivable. Until delivery each side holds only an unperformed promise, and the two cancel out.

3. Measurement at recognition

The receivable starts at the transaction price, the consideration the seller expects to be entitled to (PSAK 115.47). Four things can make that differ from the list price.

Trade discounts are price reductions given to a class of customer. They never reach the books, so a list price of 80 per barrel less a 6.25 percent volume discount is recorded at 75.

Cash discounts reward prompt payment. Kieso gives two methods, mirror images of the purchase methods in the inventories essay. The gross method records the full invoice and the discount only when taken; the net method records the discounted amount and shows a discount the customer forfeits as income. For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary bills 2,000 on terms of 2/10, net 30, so prompt payment saves the customer 2,000 × 2% = 40.

Gross method

Net method

Invoice

Dr Trade receivables 2,000 / Cr Service revenue 2,000

Dr Trade receivables 1,960 / Cr Service revenue 1,960

Paid within 10 days

Dr Cash 1,960, Dr Sales discounts 40 / Cr Trade receivables 2,000

Dr Cash 1,960 / Cr Trade receivables 1,960

Paid late

Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Trade receivables 2,000

Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Trade receivables 1,960, Cr Sales discounts forfeited 40

PSAK 115 replaces this choice with an estimate. A prompt-payment discount is variable consideration, so the seller includes in revenue the amount it expects, using the expected value or the most likely amount. If 70 percent of such customers take the discount:

Expected transaction price = 2,000 − 70% × 40 = 1,972

A common treatment keeps the receivable at the invoice amount of 2,000, which is what the customer owes if it pays late, and holds the expected discount of 28 as a refund liability.

Sales returns and allowances follow the same logic. A crude cargo rarely comes back, but price allowances for off-specification quality do happen. If a buyer is expected to claim 1 percent on the 45,000 cargo in section 2, revenue is 44,550 and the 450 sits as a refund liability (or as a credit to the receivable once agreed).

Dr Revenue from crude oil (allowance) 450 / Cr Refund liability 450

Time value. When payment comes long after delivery, part of what the customer pays is interest, and PSAK 115 takes it out of revenue (paras. 60–65). An entity may ignore it when it expects at contract inception that the gap will be one year or less (para. 63), which is why a 30-day crude invoice is never discounted. The lecture notes this series follows adapt Kieso's long case to a crude cargo sold on 1 July 2019 for a four-year zero-interest note when the market rate is 12 percent. Revenue is the cash price of 1,000,000, the note's face value is 1,000,000 × 1.57352 (the four-year factor at 12 percent) = 1,573,520, and interest is 1,000,000 × 12% × 6/12 = 60,000 for 2019 (accrued at 31 December) and 1,060,000 × 12% = 127,200 for 2020.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary bills 10,500 for a drilling campaign and agrees that the customer pays three annual instalments of 3,500 starting a year after completion on 31 December 2024, with no interest. The customer would pay 8 percent a year to borrow.

The current/non-current boundary runs through this receivable. One method puts the present value of the 2025 instalment, 3,240.74, in current assets and 5,779.10 in non-current. The other puts in current assets only the fall in carrying amount during 2025, 9,019.84 − 6,241.43 = 2,778.41, leaving 6,241.43 non-current. PSAK 201 prescribes neither; the choice must be applied consistently.

4. Subsequent measurement: amortised cost

PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9) classifies a financial asset by two tests: the business model (is it held to collect contractual cash flows?) and the cash flows (are they solely payments of principal and interest, SPPI?). A trade receivable passes both, so it is measured at amortised cost: the initial amount, plus interest at the effective interest rate (EIR), less cash collected, less the loss allowance. For a 30-day invoice the EIR is effectively nil, so amortised cost is the invoice less cash and allowance. For the instalment receivable above it is the schedule.

PHE's policy says trade and other receivables are "recognized initially at fair value and subsequently measured at amortized cost using the effective interest method, less provision for impairment" (Note 3h). PSAK 109 actually starts trade receivables without a significant financing component at the transaction price, which for short invoices is the same number.

5. Expected credit losses

Why the model changed. Under IAS 39 an asset was written down only when there was objective evidence that it was impaired. That was the incurred-loss model. It waited for a loss event, a missed payment or a bankruptcy, so allowances arrived late, typically after the recession that caused them. PSAK 109 replaced it with expected credit losses, the probability-weighted present value of cash shortfalls, recognised before any default. Kieso's ageing schedule survives as the provision matrix.

Two approaches. The general approach has three stages. A new asset carries 12-month ECL (stage 1). After a significant increase in credit risk, presumed when payments are more than 30 days past due, it carries lifetime ECL (stage 2). When it is credit-impaired it carries lifetime ECL and earns interest only on the net amount (stage 3); default is presumed no later than 90 days past due. Both presumptions are rebuttable with reasonable and supportable evidence. The simplified approach skips the tracking and recognises lifetime ECL from day one. It is required for trade receivables and contract assets without a significant financing component and is a policy choice for those with one, and for lease receivables (PSAK 109.5.5.15).

PHE applies the simplified approach because its receivables "do not contain significant financing component" (Note 3g, Daftar 5/43, PDF p. 60).

The provision matrix. A matrix groups receivables that share credit risk, ages each group by days past due, and applies a loss rate to each bucket, drawn from history and adjusted for forecasts (PHE Note 4b(vi), Daftar 5/84, PDF p. 101). For example (illustration), PHE's third-party gross receivables of 536,508 at the end of 2024 (Note 8a) are split into five buckets. The split is assumed; PHE ages only the total.

6. Write-offs and recoveries

A write-off removes the part of a receivable the entity has no reasonable expectation of recovering (PSAK 109.5.4.4; PHE Note 3g, Daftar 5/44, PDF p. 61). Under the allowance method it does not touch profit, because the loss was expensed when the allowance was built. For example (illustration), a third-party gas customer owing 1,200 is declared bankrupt with nothing for unsecured creditors.

Kieso keeps the direct method for illustration only. It puts the expense in the year a customer fails instead of the year of the sale, and it carries the receivable at more than will be collected. PSAK 109 does not permit it.

The year's expense is whatever brings the allowance to its required balance after write-offs and recoveries.

Impairment expense = closing allowance − opening allowance + write-offs − recoveries

PHE's 2024 movement has no write-offs. It runs from 92,346 at the start of the year, less a reversal of 57,813 and a foreign exchange deduction of 17,124, to 17,409 (Note 8d, Daftar 5/96, PDF p. 113). The reversal appears as "Impairment and correction of receivables" of 57,813 in other income (Note 42, Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167), so 2024 profit gained that amount from releasing allowances.

7. Derecognition, factoring and offsetting

A receivable can be turned into cash before it is due. Kieso describes two routes. Assignment or pledging uses receivables as security for a loan; the receivables stay on the books and the loan is a liability. Factoring sells them to a finance company, the factor, which then collects from the customers.

Whether a factoring is a sale turns on PSAK 109's derecognition tests. An asset is derecognised when the rights to its cash flows expire, or when they are transferred together with substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership. If the seller keeps substantially all the risks, typically by guaranteeing the factor against bad debts (recourse), the asset stays on the balance sheet and the cash is a borrowing. If risks are neither substantially transferred nor kept, the asset goes if the buyer controls it and stays to the extent of continuing involvement if not (PHE Note 3g, Daftar 5/42, PDF p. 59, summarises the same tests).

For example (illustration), a subsidiary factors 20,000 of gas receivables. The factor charges 2 percent and holds back 5 percent, 1,000, against disputes, so it pays 18,600 now.

Without recourse (sale)

With recourse (secured borrowing)

Dr Cash 18,600 / Cr Liability to factor 18,600

(holdback included above)

Total cost is 400 either way. The borrowing route keeps 20,000 of receivables and 18,600 of debt in view until the customers pay.

Offsetting is the other way a receivable can shrink without cash. A receivable and a payable with the same party are shown net only when the entity has a legally enforceable right to set them off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (PSAK 232, formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32, para. 42). PHE's arrangement with PT Pertamina (Persero) shows the difference between settling by offset and presenting net. Pertamina funds operations through cash calls that are offset against what it owes for PHE's sales, and Note 44c computes a net payable of 157,404 at the end of 2024 (Daftar 5/184, PDF p. 201). The balance sheet still carries the 18,434 receivable from Pertamina inside related-party trade receivables and the payables separately (Daftar 5/183, PDF p. 200), so PHE has not applied presentation offset.

8. Trade receivables across industries

The plain model above fits a seller of goods and services on short credit. Four industries change it.

Banks. A bank's loans are its trade receivables, but they carry interest and long terms, so the general three-stage approach applies (PSAK 109). For example (illustration), a loan of 10,000 with a 12-month PD of 1 percent and LGD of 40 percent carries 10,000 × 1% × 40% = 40 in stage 1. If a downgrade lifts the lifetime PD to 5 percent, it moves to stage 2 and carries 10,000 × 5% × 40% = 200. The jump from 40 to 200 without any missed payment is the cliff effect of the stage model, and PSAK 107 (formerly PSAK 60, IFRS 7) requires banks to reconcile the allowance by stage.

Islamic finance. A murabahah is a sale at cost plus a disclosed margin, paid in instalments. Under PSAK 402 Akuntansi Murabahah (formerly PSAK 102) the seller records the receivable at the amount the customer owes, cost plus margin, with the unearned margin as a contra account. When the seller is a financier that bears no significant inventory risk, as a sharia bank usually is, ISAK 401 (formerly ISAK 101) has it recognise the margin over the term by the effective method. A trader that does carry the inventory risk recognises profit when the goods pass on a short deferred sale. For example (illustration), a financier sells goods costing 100 for 120 over 12 months:

Dr Murabahah receivable 120 / Cr Inventory 100, Cr Deferred murabahah margin 20

Each month: Dr Cash 10 / Cr Murabahah receivable 10; Dr Deferred margin / Cr Murabahah income for the month's share of the 20 under the effective method

Impairment is where murabahah leaves the plain model. ISAK 402 Penurunan Nilai Piutang Murabahah (formerly ISAK 102) is a bridging interpretation that lets the entity keep its existing impairment policy, incurred loss or regulatory provisioning, until a sharia standard on impairment is issued, so these receivables need not follow PSAK 109's expected credit losses.

Construction. Kieso's cost-to-cost bridge example shows why PSAK 115 separates contract assets from receivables. In its first year the builder is 25 percent complete and recognises revenue of 4,500,000 × 25% = 1,125,000, but has billed 900,000 and collected 750,000.

Receivable = billed − collected = 900,000 − 750,000 = 150,000

Contract asset = revenue − billed = 1,125,000 − 900,000 = 225,000

The receivable is unconditional; the contract asset becomes one only when the next milestone is billed. Kieso's "Billings on construction in process" account does the same job in the older vocabulary.

Mining and commodity sellers with provisional prices. Concentrate is often invoiced at a provisional price and settled on a later market average. The receivable then carries price risk on top of credit risk, so its cash flows are not solely principal and interest, and it is measured at fair value through profit or loss under PSAK 109, with price changes kept out of PSAK 115 revenue from customers.

Lessors hold lease receivables under PSAK 116 (IFRS 16), where the simplified approach is optional.

10. Upstream note: what the receivable does not contain

PHE's trade receivables cover only barrels it has lifted and sold. Where a subsidiary lifted less than its entitlement, the shortfall is owed by SKK Migas and sits in due from the Government; PHE's policy says such imbalances "are not transactions with customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). The domestic market obligation fee sits there too. Crude sales to Pertamina moved to PT Kilang Pertamina Internasional from 1 September 2021 (Note 44c).

11. Related lines

  • revenues: the other side of every trade receivable.

  • due-from-government: underlifting and DMO fees owed by the state.

  • other-receivables-net: nontrade claims under the same policy and allowance method (Note 10).

  • long-term-receivables: the non-current claims reported separately.

  • other-income-expense-net: where PHE's 57,813 reversal lands (Note 42).

  • finance-income: interest unwound on receivables with a financing component.

Least-confident assertions

  • PSAK 109 paragraph numbers (5.4.4, 5.5.15) and the 30- and 90-day presumptions were confirmed through secondary summaries, not the standard's text. The derecognition tests are stated at the level of principle.

  • The claim that a provisionally priced receivable fails the SPPI test and goes to fair value through profit or loss is from knowledge of IFRS 9 practice in mining and was not checked here.

  • Murabahah points (receivable at cost plus margin, ISAK 401's effective method for financiers, ISAK 402 keeping existing impairment policies) rest on secondary sources; the adopted texts were not opened. Keeping the receivable at the invoice with a refund liability for an expected prompt-payment discount is one treatment; measuring it at the transaction price under PSAK 109.5.1.3 is another.

  • Placing the 2024 release in the related-party group is inferred from the change in the allowance by customer group; PHE does not split the movement. Reading the ageing labels as a carried-over IAS 39 format is this page's interpretation.

  • That PHE's 360-day default definition departs from the 90-day presumption is this page's reading; PHE may hold evidence that rebuts it, which it does not disclose.

content.text: A trade receivable is born with revenue, at the moment control of goods or services passes to a customer and the seller's right to payment depends only on time. Revenue is measured at the PSAK 115 transaction price, net of trade discounts and of the discounts, returns and financing the seller expects, and the receivable records the unconditional right to payment.

The "net" in the line is an allowance for expected credit losses (ECL) under PSAK 109. Trade receivables without a significant financing component must use the simplified approach, lifetime losses from day one, usually through a provision matrix of loss rates by days past due adjusted for forecasts. The old incurred-loss model, which waited for a loss event, is gone.

A receivable leaves the balance sheet when it is collected, written off because recovery is no longer reasonably expected, or transferred with substantially all its risks and rewards. Factoring without recourse is a sale; factoring with recourse usually stays on the balance sheet as a secured borrowing.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi and subsidiaries (PHE) report trade receivables, net, of 3,146,868 at 31 December 2024 against 2,768,397 a year earlier, in USD thousand (PHE FS 2024, statement of financial position, Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11; "Daftar" is the printed page). The line is 10.3 percent of total assets and 39.2 percent of current assets (9.0 and 28.0 percent a year earlier), the largest current asset PHE has. This page uses those numbers as the starting point for its examples.

After reading it a student should be able to say when a receivable arises, measure it at recognition and at the reporting date, record write-offs, recoveries and transfers, and see where banks, Islamic financiers, builders and miners depart from the plain model.
All amounts are in USD thousand unless stated. Figures from PHE's statements are cited to their note. Every other number is labelled an illustration.
A receivable is a claim on someone else for cash. Kieso sorts claims three ways.
arise from selling goods or services in the ordinary course of business;
arise from anything else, such as insurance claims, advances to employees or deposits.
are open-account promises with no formal instrument;
are written promises to pay a sum at a date, usually with interest. And receivables are
if collection is expected within the operating cycle or twelve months,

PHE's policy uses the first split. Trade receivables are amounts due from customers for crude oil, natural gas, drilling services, oil and gas support services, and energy distribution and logistics services; other receivables are amounts from third or related parties "beyond the ordinary course of business" (Note 3h, Daftar 5/51, PDF p. 68). Collection within one period puts a receivable in current assets, otherwise non-current (same note). PHE's separate "long term receivables" of 2,087 (2023: 2,997) carry no note reference on the face.
PSAK 115 (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15) adds a distinction that matters most for builders. A
is a right to consideration that is unconditional, meaning only the passage of time is required before payment falls due (para. 108). A
is a right that still depends on something other than time, typically further performance.
A receivable appears in the same journal entry as revenue, so "when do we record it?" is the revenue question. Kieso's

sets out the five steps of PSAK 115. Identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognise revenue when each obligation is satisfied, that is, when the customer obtains control.

For a crude seller, control typically passes at lifting, on FOB terms when the cargo crosses the custody point into the buyer's tanker. PHE recognises crude and gas revenue "based on the actual lifting amount and sold to customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/62, PDF p. 79). For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary lifts 600 thousand barrels for a domestic refinery at USD 75 per barrel, payable in 30 days.
Dr Trade receivables 45,000 / Cr Revenue from crude oil 45,000

There is no matching "Dr Cost of goods sold / Cr Inventory" of the kind a merchandiser records. Note 11 lists only materials, and Note 3p charges the related costs on the amount actually sold, so the cost of producing the barrels has already gone to expense.
Signing a contract creates no receivable. Until delivery each side holds only an unperformed promise, and the two cancel out.
The receivable starts at the transaction price, the consideration the seller expects to be entitled to (PSAK 115.47). Four things can make that differ from the list price.
are price reductions given to a class of customer. They never reach the books, so a list price of 80 per barrel less a 6.25 percent volume discount is recorded at 75.
reward prompt payment. Kieso gives two methods, mirror images of the purchase methods in the inventories essay. The
records the full invoice and the discount only when taken; the

records the discounted amount and shows a discount the customer forfeits as income. For example (illustration), a PHE drilling subsidiary bills 2,000 on terms of 2/10, net 30, so prompt payment saves the customer 2,000 × 2% = 40.
Dr Trade receivables 2,000 / Cr Service revenue 2,000
Dr Trade receivables 1,960 / Cr Service revenue 1,960
Dr Cash 1,960, Dr Sales discounts 40 / Cr Trade receivables 2,000
Dr Cash 2,000 / Cr Trade receivables 1,960, Cr Sales discounts forfeited 40
PSAK 115 replaces this choice with an estimate. A prompt-payment discount is
, so the seller includes in revenue the amount it expects, using the expected value or the most likely amount. If 70 percent of such customers take the discount:
A common treatment keeps the receivable at the invoice amount of 2,000, which is what the customer owes if it pays late, and holds the expected discount of 28 as a refund liability.

follow the same logic. A crude cargo rarely comes back, but price allowances for off-specification quality do happen. If a buyer is expected to claim 1 percent on the 45,000 cargo in section 2, revenue is 44,550 and the 450 sits as a refund liability (or as a credit to the receivable once agreed).
Dr Revenue from crude oil (allowance) 450 / Cr Refund liability 450

When payment comes long after delivery, part of what the customer pays is interest, and PSAK 115 takes it out of revenue (paras. 60–65). An entity may ignore it when it expects at contract inception that the gap will be one year or less (para. 63), which is why a 30-day crude invoice is never discounted. The lecture notes this series follows adapt Kieso's long case to a crude cargo sold on 1 July 2019 for a four-year zero-interest note when the market rate is 12 percent. Revenue is the cash price of 1,000,000, the note's face value is 1,000,000 × 1.57352 (the four-year factor at 12 percent) = 1,573,520, and interest is 1,000,000 × 12% × 6/12 = 60,000 for 2019 (accrued at 31 December) and 1,060,000 × 12% = 127,200 for 2020.

For example (illustration), a PHE subsidiary bills 10,500 for a drilling campaign and agrees that the customer pays three annual instalments of 3,500 starting a year after completion on 31 December 2024, with no interest. The customer would pay 8 percent a year to borrow.
Revenue and receivable at 31 Dec 2024 = 9,019.84; interest to be earned = 10,500 − 9,019.84 = 1,480.16
31 Dec 2024: Dr Trade receivables 9,019.84 / Cr Service revenue 9,019.84
31 Dec 2025: Dr Trade receivables 721.59 / Cr Interest income 721.59; Dr Cash 3,500 / Cr Trade receivables 3,500

The current/non-current boundary runs through this receivable. One method puts the present value of the 2025 instalment, 3,240.74, in current assets and 5,779.10 in non-current. The other puts in current assets only the fall in carrying amount during 2025, 9,019.84 − 6,241.43 = 2,778.41, leaving 6,241.43 non-current. PSAK 201 prescribes neither; the choice must be applied consistently.

PSAK 109 (formerly PSAK 71, IFRS 9) classifies a financial asset by two tests: the business model (is it held to collect contractual cash flows?) and the cash flows (are they solely payments of principal and interest, SPPI?). A trade receivable passes both, so it is measured at

: the initial amount, plus interest at the effective interest rate (EIR), less cash collected, less the loss allowance. For a 30-day invoice the EIR is effectively nil, so amortised cost is the invoice less cash and allowance. For the instalment receivable above it is the schedule.

PHE's policy says trade and other receivables are "recognized initially at fair value and subsequently measured at amortized cost using the effective interest method, less provision for impairment" (Note 3h). PSAK 109 actually starts trade receivables without a significant financing component at the transaction price, which for short invoices is the same number.
Under IAS 39 an asset was written down only when there was objective evidence that it was impaired. That was the
model. It waited for a loss event, a missed payment or a bankruptcy, so allowances arrived late, typically after the recession that caused them. PSAK 109 replaced it with
, the probability-weighted present value of cash shortfalls, recognised before any default. Kieso's ageing schedule survives as the provision matrix.

has three stages. A new asset carries 12-month ECL (stage 1). After a significant increase in credit risk, presumed when payments are more than 30 days past due, it carries lifetime ECL (stage 2). When it is credit-impaired it carries lifetime ECL and earns interest only on the net amount (stage 3); default is presumed no later than 90 days past due. Both presumptions are rebuttable with reasonable and supportable evidence. The

skips the tracking and recognises lifetime ECL from day one. It is required for trade receivables and contract assets without a significant financing component and is a policy choice for those with one, and for lease receivables (PSAK 109.5.5.15).
PHE applies the simplified approach because its receivables "do not contain significant financing component" (Note 3g, Daftar 5/43, PDF p. 60).

A matrix groups receivables that share credit risk, ages each group by days past due, and applies a loss rate to each bucket, drawn from history and adjusted for forecasts (PHE Note 4b(vi), Daftar 5/84, PDF p. 101). For example (illustration), PHE's third-party gross receivables of 536,508 at the end of 2024 (Note 8a) are split into five buckets. The split is assumed; PHE ages only the total.

The adjustment needs a reason that links a forecast to customers' ability to pay. PHE names gross domestic product as the most relevant factor and adjusts historical loss rates for its expected change (Note 49c, Daftar 5/229, PDF p. 246). Here the illustration assumes that a forecast one-point fall in GDP growth has, in past cycles, raised loss rates by a tenth. Current receivables carry an allowance too, which the incurred-loss model rarely gave them.

A matrix is valid only for receivables that share credit characteristics. PHE's related-party receivables of 2,627,769 are owed mostly by state-owned companies. Applying the third-party average rate (17,099.28 / 536,508 = 3.19 percent) to them would give an allowance of about 83,751. A rate built from the debtor's own probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD), which PHE says its models use (Note 49c), gives a much smaller number. Assume a one-year PD of 0.3 percent, LGD of 40 percent and an average time to collection of 60 days:
The allowance is a contra account, so the ledger keeps each customer at the gross amount. Starting from PHE's opening third-party allowance of 15,815 (Note 8a, 2023):
Dr Impairment loss on trade receivables 1,284.28 / Cr Allowance for expected credit losses 1,284.28

A write-off removes the part of a receivable the entity has no reasonable expectation of recovering (PSAK 109.5.4.4; PHE Note 3g, Daftar 5/44, PDF p. 61). Under the allowance method it does not touch profit, because the loss was expensed when the allowance was built. For example (illustration), a third-party gas customer owing 1,200 is declared bankrupt with nothing for unsecured creditors.
Dr Bad debt expense 1,200 / Cr Trade receivables 1,200
Dr Trade receivables 300 / Cr Allowance 300; Dr Cash 300 / Cr Trade receivables 300
Dr Cash 300 / Cr Bad debt recovery 300

Kieso keeps the direct method for illustration only. It puts the expense in the year a customer fails instead of the year of the sale, and it carries the receivable at more than will be collected. PSAK 109 does not permit it.
The year's expense is whatever brings the allowance to its required balance after write-offs and recoveries.
Impairment expense = closing allowance − opening allowance + write-offs − recoveries

PHE's 2024 movement has no write-offs. It runs from 92,346 at the start of the year, less a reversal of 57,813 and a foreign exchange deduction of 17,124, to 17,409 (Note 8d, Daftar 5/96, PDF p. 113). The reversal appears as "Impairment and correction of receivables" of 57,813 in other income (Note 42, Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167), so 2024 profit gained that amount from releasing allowances.
A receivable can be turned into cash before it is due. Kieso describes two routes.
uses receivables as security for a loan; the receivables stay on the books and the loan is a liability.
sells them to a finance company, the factor, which then collects from the customers.

Whether a factoring is a sale turns on PSAK 109's derecognition tests. An asset is derecognised when the rights to its cash flows expire, or when they are transferred together with substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership. If the seller keeps substantially all the risks, typically by guaranteeing the factor against bad debts (

), the asset stays on the balance sheet and the cash is a borrowing. If risks are neither substantially transferred nor kept, the asset goes if the buyer controls it and stays to the extent of continuing involvement if not (PHE Note 3g, Daftar 5/42, PDF p. 59, summarises the same tests).
For example (illustration), a subsidiary factors 20,000 of gas receivables. The factor charges 2 percent and holds back 5 percent, 1,000, against disputes, so it pays 18,600 now.
Dr Cash 18,600, Dr Due from factor 1,000, Dr Loss on sale of receivables 400 / Cr Trade receivables 20,000
Dr Cash 18,600 / Cr Liability to factor 18,600
Customers pay the factor: no entry
Customers pay the factor 20,000: Dr Liability to factor 18,600, Dr Interest expense 400, Dr Cash 1,000 / Cr Trade receivables 20,000
Holdback returned: Dr Cash 1,000 / Cr Due from factor 1,000
Total cost is 400 either way. The borrowing route keeps 20,000 of receivables and 18,600 of debt in view until the customers pay.

is the other way a receivable can shrink without cash. A receivable and a payable with the same party are shown net only when the entity has a legally enforceable right to set them off and intends to settle net or simultaneously (PSAK 232, formerly PSAK 50, IAS 32, para. 42). PHE's arrangement with PT Pertamina (Persero) shows the difference between settling by offset and presenting net. Pertamina funds operations through cash calls that are offset against what it owes for PHE's sales, and Note 44c computes a net payable of 157,404 at the end of 2024 (Daftar 5/184, PDF p. 201). The balance sheet still carries the 18,434 receivable from Pertamina inside related-party trade receivables and the payables separately (Daftar 5/183, PDF p. 200), so PHE has not applied presentation offset.
The plain model above fits a seller of goods and services on short credit. Four industries change it.

A bank's loans are its trade receivables, but they carry interest and long terms, so the general three-stage approach applies (PSAK 109). For example (illustration), a loan of 10,000 with a 12-month PD of 1 percent and LGD of 40 percent carries 10,000 × 1% × 40% = 40 in stage 1. If a downgrade lifts the lifetime PD to 5 percent, it moves to stage 2 and carries 10,000 × 5% × 40% = 200. The jump from 40 to 200 without any missed payment is the
of the stage model, and PSAK 107 (formerly PSAK 60, IFRS 7) requires banks to reconcile the allowance by stage.
A murabahah is a sale at cost plus a disclosed margin, paid in instalments. Under PSAK 402

(formerly PSAK 102) the seller records the receivable at the amount the customer owes, cost plus margin, with the unearned margin as a contra account. When the seller is a financier that bears no significant inventory risk, as a sharia bank usually is, ISAK 401 (formerly ISAK 101) has it recognise the margin over the term by the effective method. A trader that does carry the inventory risk recognises profit when the goods pass on a short deferred sale. For example (illustration), a financier sells goods costing 100 for 120 over 12 months:
Dr Murabahah receivable 120 / Cr Inventory 100, Cr Deferred murabahah margin 20
Each month: Dr Cash 10 / Cr Murabahah receivable 10; Dr Deferred margin / Cr Murabahah income for the month's share of the 20 under the effective method
Impairment is where murabahah leaves the plain model. ISAK 402

(formerly ISAK 102) is a bridging interpretation that lets the entity keep its existing impairment policy, incurred loss or regulatory provisioning, until a sharia standard on impairment is issued, so these receivables need not follow PSAK 109's expected credit losses.

Kieso's cost-to-cost bridge example shows why PSAK 115 separates contract assets from receivables. In its first year the builder is 25 percent complete and recognises revenue of 4,500,000 × 25% = 1,125,000, but has billed 900,000 and collected 750,000.

The receivable is unconditional; the contract asset becomes one only when the next milestone is billed. Kieso's "Billings on construction in process" account does the same job in the older vocabulary.
Mining and commodity sellers with provisional prices.

Concentrate is often invoiced at a provisional price and settled on a later market average. The receivable then carries price risk on top of credit risk, so its cash flows are not solely principal and interest, and it is measured at fair value through profit or loss under PSAK 109, with price changes kept out of PSAK 115 revenue from customers.
hold lease receivables under PSAK 116 (IFRS 16), where the simplified approach is optional.

PSAK 107 asks for credit-risk information, including a reconciliation of the allowance and the exposure by credit-risk grade, for which a provision matrix by days past due may serve, plus concentrations and collateral. PHE gives receivables by customer, currency and age, and the allowance movement (Note 8, Daftar 5/95–5/96, PDF pp. 112–113).

Three things stand out. First, the related-party allowance fell by 74,945, from 76,531 to 1,586, which is close to the whole fall in the allowance (74,937), so the 2024 release sits almost entirely in that group, although PHE does not split the movement. Note 44c adds that related-party receivables are fully collectible (Daftar 5/184, PDF p. 201). Second, PT Kilang Pertamina Internasional alone owes 2,237,285, 85.1 percent of related-party and 70.7 percent of all gross trade receivables (Note 44c, Daftar 5/183, PDF p. 200), while Note 8 says there is no significant concentration of credit risk. Third, parts of the note keep the pre-PSAK 109 format. The ageing uses the old labels, including "past due and impaired, more than 365 days" for 560,851 against a total allowance of 17,409 (3.1 percent). The risk note says allowances cover "only … losses that have been incurred" (Note 49c(iii), Daftar 5/230, PDF p. 247), and the English text of Note 3g reverses the 12-month ECL condition that the Indonesian states correctly (PDF p. 60). The policy itself treats a receivable as in default at 360 days past due (Note 3g, PDF p. 61), longer than the 90-day presumption of section 5, which the standard allows only with supporting evidence.
The usual analysis compares revenue with the average balance.
Receivables turnover = 14,330,340 / ((3,146,868 + 2,768,397) / 2) = 4.85 times; days sales outstanding = 365 / 4.85 = 75.3 days

Revenue includes 1,133,213 billed to SKK Migas (Note 35, Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165), and Note 44c shows no trade receivable from SKK Migas at the end of 2024. Excluding it gives 13,197,127 / 2,957,632.5 = 4.46 times, or 81.8 days. For PHE's largest customer, year-end balance over its 2024 revenue of 7,372,296 (Note 35) gives 2,237,285 / 7,372,296 × 365 = 110.8 days.
10. Upstream note: what the receivable does not contain

PHE's trade receivables cover only barrels it has lifted and sold. Where a subsidiary lifted less than its entitlement, the shortfall is owed by SKK Migas and sits in due from the Government; PHE's policy says such imbalances "are not transactions with customers" (Note 3p, Daftar 5/63, PDF p. 80). The domestic market obligation fee sits there too. Crude sales to Pertamina moved to PT Kilang Pertamina Internasional from 1 September 2021 (Note 44c).
: the other side of every trade receivable.
: underlifting and DMO fees owed by the state.
: nontrade claims under the same policy and allowance method (Note 10).
: interest unwound on receivables with a financing component.

PSAK 109 paragraph numbers (5.4.4, 5.5.15) and the 30- and 90-day presumptions were confirmed through secondary summaries, not the standard's text. The derecognition tests are stated at the level of principle.
The claim that a provisionally priced receivable fails the SPPI test and goes to fair value through profit or loss is from knowledge of IFRS 9 practice in mining and was not checked here.

Murabahah points (receivable at cost plus margin, ISAK 401's effective method for financiers, ISAK 402 keeping existing impairment policies) rest on secondary sources; the adopted texts were not opened. Keeping the receivable at the invoice with a refund liability for an expected prompt-payment discount is one treatment; measuring it at the transaction price under PSAK 109.5.1.3 is another.

Placing the 2024 release in the related-party group is inferred from the change in the allowance by customer group; PHE does not split the movement. Reading the ageing labels as a carried-over IAS 39 format is this page's interpretation.
That PHE's 360-day default definition departs from the 90-day presumption is this page's reading; PHE may hold evidence that rebuts it, which it does not disclose.

PT Pertamina Hulu Energi dan Entitas Anak, consolidated financial statements 31 December 2024 (audited, USD thousand): statement of financial position (Daftar 1/1, PDF p. 11); Note 3g (Daftar 5/42–5/44, PDF pp. 59–61); Note 3h (Daftar 5/51, PDF p. 68); Note 3p (Daftar 5/62–5/63, PDF pp. 79–80); Note 4b(vi) (Daftar 5/84, PDF p. 101); Note 8 (Daftar 5/95–5/96, PDF pp. 112–113); Note 35 (Daftar 5/148, PDF p. 165); Note 42 (Daftar 5/150, PDF p. 167); Note 44c (Daftar 5/183–5/184, PDF pp. 200–201); Note 49c (Daftar 5/229–5/230, PDF pp. 246–247). presentation.deck: The theory of trade receivables from the sale that creates them to the factor that buys them, worked through PHE's crude and gas customers and set beside the industries with their own rules
key_takeaways: A trade receivable is born with revenue, at the moment control of goods or services passes to a customer and the seller's right to payment depends only on time. Revenue is measured at the PSAK 115 transaction price, net of trade discounts and of the discounts, returns and financing the seller expects, and the receivable records the unconditional right to payment.

The "net" in the line is an allowance for expected credit losses (ECL) under PSAK 109. Trade receivables without a significant financing component must use the simplified approach, lifetime losses from day one, usually through a provision matrix of loss rates by days past due adjusted for forecasts. The old incurred-loss model, which waited for a loss event, is gone.

A receivable leaves the balance sheet when it is collected, written off because recovery is no longer reasonably expected, or transferred with substantially all its risks and rewards. Factoring without recourse is a sale; factoring with recourse usually stays on the balance sheet as a secured borrowing.

title: Trade Receivables at an Upstream Contractor: Transaction price, amortised cost, expected credit losses by counterparty, and the discount on cash that arrives late
snippet: Transaction price, amortised cost, expected credit losses by counterparty, and the discount on cash that arrives late
content:
In brief

  • A trade receivable is a right to cash for crude or gas already delivered. It starts at the transaction price, sits at amortised cost, and is reduced by an allowance for lifetime expected credit losses from the day it is recognised.

  • The allowance depends on how customers are grouped. In the case below, applying the industrial buyers' loss rates to a state-linked affiliate would give an allowance of 420; a rate built from the affiliate's own default risk gives 9.21. The related-party label is a disclosure requirement and changes neither figure.

  • Cash due beyond normal terms carries a financing component. A disputed gas invoice of 12,000 settled by three annual instalments of 3,500 is worth 9,019.84 discounted at 8 percent a year, and 5,779.10 of that is non-current.

The reported line rose 6.8 percent while total assets fell, and the page cannot show how much of it is collectable

The balance sheet on this page reports trade receivables, net, of 2,203,018 at 31 December 2024 against 2,063,070 a year earlier, in thousands. That is a rise of 139,948, or 6.8 percent, in a year when total assets fell 2.9 percent. The line is 7.3 percent of total assets at 31 December 2024 (2,203,018 / 30,303,898), against 6.6 percent a year earlier. A separate line, trade receivables, net, non-current, holds 544,278 (2023: 522,121), so 19.8 percent of all trade receivables (544,278 / 2,747,296) are not expected in cash within twelve months.

Two further lines, "Third parties" at 520,885 (2023: 715,327) and "Related parties" at 823,348 (2023: 801,429), sit beside trade receivables. They total 1,344,233, not 2,203,018, so they are not its breakdown. Their labels were garbled by OCR, and they may be other receivables split by counterparty. The page cannot tell which. Either way, related-party balances are 1.58 times the third-party ones (2023: 1.12 times), and they grew 2.7 percent while third-party balances fell 27.2 percent. An upstream group often sells crude and gas to a state-owned or affiliated offtaker (the buyer that takes the production), such as a refining affiliate or the state gas company, so a related-party balance of this size is common.

This essay uses PT Hulu Energi Nusantara ("HEN"), an upstream oil and gas contractor operating under production sharing contracts (PSCs) with SKK Migas, reporting in USD under Indonesian SAK with a 31 December year end. HEN and every figure attached to it are constructed for illustration. HEN amounts are in USD thousand, except per-barrel prices in USD. HEN's parent is a state-owned energy holding. HEN sells its crude to PT Kilang Nusantara, a refining affiliate owned by the same parent, and its gas to industrial buyers and a distributor outside the group (all constructed).

At 31 December 2024 HEN's draft applies one provision matrix to all customers, and the external auditor has sent the CFO three questions. Why does the allowance treat 45,000 owed by the affiliate, of which 5,000 is 31 to 90 days past due, like a balance owed by an industrial gas buyer? Has the matrix been adjusted for conditions expected in 2025? And how should a disputed gas invoice of 12,000, settled on 31 December 2024 for three annual instalments, be measured and split between current and non-current?

The governing claim of this essay is that a trade receivable is measured as the cash HEN expects to collect, so its net figure depends on two judgments, the loss rate assigned to each group of customers and the discount applied to cash that arrives beyond normal terms. The related-party label decides what is disclosed and leaves the measurement unchanged.

This is a mechanism essay. Its verdict is that the reported line can be read only with three figures from the notes to the financial statements, the allowance as a share of gross by counterparty group, days sales outstanding by group, and the movement in the allowance, because in HEN's case the grouping alone moves the allowance by 410.79 and the discount moves 1,480.16 of revenue into interest income.

The governing standards are PSAK 115 (formerly PSAK 72, IFRS 15) for revenue, PSAK 109 (formerly 71, IFRS 9) for measurement and credit losses, PSAK 107 (formerly 60, IFRS 7) for credit-risk disclosures, PSAK 224 (formerly 7, IAS 24) for related parties, and PSAK 201 (formerly 1, IAS 1) for the current/non-current split.

A receivable starts at the transaction price, because a sale on 30-day terms has nothing to discount

A trade receivable arises when HEN has delivered and its right to payment depends only on time passing. PSAK 115 sets revenue at the transaction price, the consideration HEN expects to be entitled to. PSAK 109 then measures a trade receivable without a significant financing component (a gap between delivery and payment long enough to give one party a significant benefit of financing, whether or not interest is stated) at that same transaction price. PSAK 115 lets a seller ignore financing when the gap is expected at contract inception to be one year or less.

In December 2024 HEN lifted 480,000 barrels of its entitlement crude from PSC East and sold them to Kilang Nusantara at USD 76 per barrel, payable in 30 days. The invoice is part of the 40,000 not yet due from Kilang Nusantara at the year end.

Invoice = 480,000 × USD 76 / 1,000 = 36,480

Dr Trade receivables, related parties 36,480
Cr Revenue from crude sales 36,480

The receivable is then held at amortised cost, because HEN's business model is to collect it and its cash flows are solely principal (and, for longer receivables, interest). For a 30-day invoice, amortised cost is the invoice less cash received and less the allowance for credit losses. That allowance is the "net" in the line's name.

Under PSAK 109 the allowance covers lifetime losses from day one, estimated through a provision matrix

PSAK 109 replaced the old incurred-loss model, under which a receivable was impaired only after a loss event such as a missed payment, with expected credit losses (ECL), the probability-weighted shortfall in cash over the receivable's life. For trade receivables without a significant financing component the standard requires the simplified approach, which means lifetime ECL from initial recognition, with no tracking of whether credit risk has increased. For trade receivables with a financing component, the simplified approach is a policy choice.

A provision matrix is the usual way to apply it. Receivables are grouped by shared credit risk, each group's balances are aged by days past due, and each bucket gets a loss rate drawn from history and adjusted for forward-looking information, conditions expected over the receivables' life that history does not reflect.

HEN's third-party receivables on normal terms are owed by industrial gas buyers in ceramics, glass and fertiliser, and five years of loss history give the historical rates below. At 31 December 2024 HEN's credit committee had a sector forecast, published in November 2024, that output in those industries would contract in 2025. Lower output cuts the buyers' sales and margins and so their capacity to pay. In the last contraction, in 2020, HEN's loss rates ran about a fifth above their five-year average, so the committee raised every rate by a fifth.

The related-party offtaker still needs an allowance, but at a rate built from its own default risk

A related party's receivable is a financial asset like any other, so PSAK 109 requires an allowance for it. The matrix groups receivables by shared credit risk characteristics, and Kilang Nusantara shares none of the industrial buyers' history. Applied anyway, HEN's matrix would give it an allowance of 420.00.

Matrix applied to the affiliate = 40,000 × 0.30% + 5,000 × 6.00% = 120.00 + 300.00 = 420.00

The alternative builds the rate from the affiliate's probability of default (PD) and the loss given default (LGD), the share of the balance lost if it defaults, over the time the balance is expected to stay outstanding. Kilang Nusantara's parent is state-owned and rated investment grade (BBB− or better), and the refinery is strategic to domestic fuel supply, so HEN estimates a one-year PD of 0.4 percent and an LGD of 40 percent (both constructed). The 5,000 past due is held up because the affiliate is itself waiting for compensation payments from the government, and HEN expects it within six months. HEN keeps the PD at 0.4 percent because the delay traces to the government's payment chain, not to the affiliate's own finances. If the balance reached 90 days past due, PSAK 109's rebuttable presumption of default would force a review.

Not past due = 40,000 × 0.4% × 30/365 × 40% = 5.26

Past due, six months expected = 5,000 × 0.4% × 180/365 × 40% = 3.95

Allowance, related parties = 5.26 + 3.95 = 9.21

The gap between 420.00 and 9.21 is the answer to the auditor's first question, and it rests on the parent's credit, not on the relationship. If the state's support for the refinery weakened, the PD would rise and so would the allowance. Past-due status still matters, because it lengthens the period over which default can occur, which is why the 5,000 carries 3.95 against 0.66 had it been current (5,000 × 0.4% × 30/365 × 40%).

PSAK 224 adds disclosure and nothing else. The full package covers the relationship, transactions, balances, terms, allowances and bad-debt expense. PSAK 224 (paragraphs 25–26) lets entities controlled by the same government give reduced disclosure, and that covers Kilang Nusantara as a sister company. Individually significant transactions, such as HEN's crude sales to the affiliate, must still be disclosed by nature and amount. In such a group "related parties" may reach every state-owned company, so the page's two counterparty lines say nothing about risk.

Cash due beyond twelve months carries a financing component, so the receivable is discounted and its interest unwinds

When payment falls due much later than delivery, part of the consideration is interest, and PSAK 115 removes it from revenue. The discount rate is the rate the parties would use in a separate financing transaction, which reflects the customer's credit risk. The owner's notes teach this with a crude cargo sold for a four-year non-interest-bearing note, recognised at present value with the difference earned as interest each year.

HEN's case is a gas dispute. In November and December 2023 HEN invoiced 12,000 of price escalation under a gas sales contract with PT Gas Distribusi Barat, a third-party distributor. The buyer had not objected by 29 February 2024, when HEN's 2023 statements were issued, so HEN recognised the revenue in 2023. In March 2024 the buyer disputed the escalation index and withheld payment. On 31 December 2024 the parties settled at 10,500, payable in three instalments of 3,500 on 31 December 2025, 2026 and 2027, with no interest. Gas Distribusi Barat would pay 8 percent a year on a three-year unsecured loan (constructed).

PV of 2025 instalment = 3,500 / 1.08 = 3,240.74

PV of 2026 instalment = 3,500 / 1.08² = 3,000.69

PV of 2027 instalment = 3,500 / 1.08³ = 2,778.41

Settlement receivable at 31 Dec 2024 = 9,019.84

Price concession = 12,000 − 10,500 = 1,500

Financing component = 10,500 − 9,019.84 = 1,480.16

Because the dispute concerned the price HEN was entitled to, not the buyer's ability to pay, this essay treats both amounts as a change in the transaction price of the 2023 sales, recognised as a reduction of 2024 revenue. Practice is divided. The IASB's April 2024 post-implementation review of IFRS 15 recorded that some entities treat a price reduction as a price concession under IFRS 15 and others as an expected credit loss under IFRS 9.

Dr Trade receivables, settlement (at present value) 9,019.84
Dr Revenue from gas sales 2,980.16
Cr Trade receivables, third parties (disputed invoices) 12,000.00

The current/non-current boundary runs through this receivable. HEN splits it by the present value of each instalment, so the current portion is the present value of the 2025 instalment. Some preparers instead classify as current the 2,778.41 by which the carrying amount falls in 2025 (3,500 less 721.59 of interest), leaving 6,241.43 non-current. PSAK 201 prescribes neither, and HEN's policy uses the first.

Current portion = 3,240.74

Non-current portion = 9,019.84 − 3,240.74 = 5,779.10

At 31 December 2025 the 6,241.43 splits again, 3,240.74 current and 3,000.69 non-current. HEN's policy applies the simplified approach to this receivable too, at a lifetime rate of 2 percent (constructed) for a buyer that has just agreed to pay.

Allowance, settlement receivable = 9,019.84 × 2% = 180.40

Current portion = 3,240.74 × 2% = 64.81

Non-current portion = 180.40 − 64.81 = 115.59

Writing off a bankrupt buyer leaves profit unchanged, because the expense arose when the allowance was built

Writing off the 400 owed by an industrial gas buyer that went bankrupt in 2024, with nothing for unsecured creditors, had no effect on 2024 profit. A write-off derecognises (removes from the balance sheet) the part of a receivable HEN has no reasonable expectation of recovering, and it is booked against the allowance.

Dr Allowance for expected credit losses 400
Cr Trade receivables, third parties 400

The year's impairment loss is whatever brings the allowance to its required closing balance after write-offs. HEN's allowance opened 2024 at 900.

Required closing allowance = 637.20 + 9.21 + 180.40 = 826.81

Impairment loss for 2024 = 826.81 − 900.00 + 400.00 = 326.81

Dr Impairment loss on trade receivables 326.81
Cr Allowance for expected credit losses 326.81

At a PSC contractor the receivable covers only HEN's own liftings, and take-or-pay clauses blur the line with revenue

Under an Indonesian PSC the government's share of crude is not HEN's revenue, so it never enters HEN's trade receivables. HEN's receivable covers only the barrels it lifts as its entitlement (under a cost-recovery PSC, its cost recovery and profit share) and sells. Differences between what HEN lifted and what it was entitled to are settled with the government under the PSC. The page's separate "Due from the Government" line is the likelier home for such underlifting balances and for the fee the government pays on domestic market obligation crude. This essay has not confirmed how every contractor presents them.

Gas is often sold under take-or-pay contracts, under which a buyer that takes less than a contracted minimum pays for the shortfall.
